f.d:
lha las phul byung gi bstod pa'i 'grel pa bshad ma thag pas mdzad pa las/
de yang 'di ltar thos te/ tshangs pas bsgo bas phyogs gcig tu ni lha gnas phyogs gcig na ni lha ma yin rnams 'dug nas/ ri bo man+d+ha ra'i steng nas ni khyab 'jug gis bzung / klu'i rgyal po nor rgyas kyis bsrub thag byas/ 'og nas ni rus sbal gyi rgyab kyis [39]brten te 'o ma can gyi rgya mtsho bsrubs par gyur to/ / de nas shin tu 'jigs su rung ba'i dug gi skyes bu nag po brtsegs pa zhes bya ba zhig byung bar gyur ba dang / de khyab 'jug gis mid par gyur ba dang dran pa stor [40]te sa la 'gyel bar gyur nas cang mi smra bar gnas pa dang / lha chen pos de las drangs te mgrin par bzhag par gyur to/ / des de'i mgrin pa sngon por gyur to/ / de nas zla ba tshes pa byung bar gyur ba dang / de lha chen pos blangs te mgo la bzhag go/ de nas dpal mo zhes bya ba byung ste/ rang nyid kyis khyab 'jug gi chung mar khas blangs te 'dus so/ / de'i 'og tu rta mgrin rings dang / shing yongs 'du la sogs pa byung ste/ de dag ni brgya byin la sogs pa lha rnams kyis ci rigs par khyer ro/ / de nas bud med shin tu yid du 'ong ba zhig byung ba dang / de la khyod su yin zhes dris pa na/ nga ni chang zhes bya ste/ nga 'thungs na myos pa dang brgyal ba dang dregs pa la sogs pa'i rnam par 'gyur ba 'byung bar 'gyur ro zhes smras pa dang / lha ma yin rnams 'jigs nas ma 'thungs pa dang lha ma yin zhes bya bar gyur la/ lha rnams kyis 'thungs pas ni [41]lha zhes bya bar gyur to/ /

Also, in Commentary on Praises from the Gods by the same author:
This I have also heard. Under the orders of Brahmā the gods were gathered in one direction, the demigods in another. Viṣṇu took hold of Mount Mandara from above, the nāga king Vāsuki used himself as the churning rope, and the mountain was supported from below by the back of the great turtle. In this way they churned the ocean of milk. Suddenly a terrifying personification of the kālakūṭa poison appeared. Viṣṇu took it and swallowed it, whereupon he lost consciousness, fell to the ground, and lay speechless. Mahādeva took the poison from Viṣṇu and placed it in his throat, which then turned blue. Then a crescent moon appeared, which Mahādeva took and placed upon his own head. Then Śrī appeared, who proclaimed herself to be the bride of Viṣṇu. After her appeared Hayagrīva and the pārijāta wish-fulfilling tree. These were taken by Indra and the other gods. Then a very beautiful woman appeared from the ocean. “Who are you?” they asked. “I am surā. If you drink me, you will become intoxicated, lose your senses, and become arrogant.” The demigods were afraid to drink and so were known as asura. The gods, however, readily partook of the drink and so were known as sura.[92]

d.div: [39] rgyab la/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[40] 'thor/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[41] pas na/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[92] Making the final a in sura (“god”) long turns it into surā, or alcohol. The prefix a is a negating particle.

de nas bdud rtsi byung ba na snod chen po brgyad gang ba lha ma yin rnams kyis khyer bar gyur pa dang / lha rnams shin tu yi mug par gyur pa na/ khyab 'jug shin tu yid du 'ong zhing gzugs bzang ba'i bud med kyi gzugs su bsgyur te der song ba la/ brgya byin yang mi snang ba'i gzugs kyis nam mkha' la 'dug go/ de'i tshe lha ma yin rnams kyis 'di ni kho bo cag gi bud med yin no snyam nas bdud rtsi'i bsrung [42]mar bzhag nas rang nyid khrus la song ste/ chos kyi bstan bcos las/
ma bkrus dri ma sbyong gyur pas/ / khrus ma byas par zan mi za/ / zhes smos pa'i phyir de dag khrus la song ngo / /

Then ambrosia arose from the ocean, and the demigods carried it off in eight great containers. The gods became greatly distressed. So Viṣṇu manifested as a very beautiful woman and went to the demigods, while Indra became invisible and waited in the skies. The demigods thought that the woman was one of them and gave her the ambrosia to guard, saying “We are going to bathe. As it says in the Dharma Śāstra:
Without washing one is not clean, so one does not eat before washing.” They went off to bathe.
[42] srung / mtsho sngon deb dpar/

f.d: skabs der khyab 'jug dang brgya byin gyis bdud rtsi brkus te brgya byin gyi khang par khyer ro/ / de rnams khrus byas nas slar log pa dang bdud rtsi ma mthong nas de tshol ba la brtson pa na/ lha rnams kyis khyer ro zhes thos nas/ lha rnams ni steng du 'gro ba yin pa ni bden no snyam mo/ / de'i tshe lha rnams bdud rtsi la longs spyod pa'i phyir 'dus pa dang / sgra gcan lha'i cha lugs su bsgyur te/ der zhugs nas bdud rtsi'i skal ba thob pa dang / de nyi mas mthong ste/ khyab 'jug la 'di ni sgra gcan no zhes smras pa dang / de'i 'khor los mgo bo bcad par gyur la/ 'on kyang bdud rtsi la longs spyad cing bldags pa'i mgo bo ni/ deng sang na yang gnas la/ lus lhag ma rnams ni shi bar gyur to/ / de nas sgra gcan 'dzin dang nyi ma zhe 'gras par gyur bas/ gang gis nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor 'gebs shing sgrib par byed pa yin no zhes gtam du grags so/[43] / zhes dang /

d.div: Viṣṇu and Indra took the nectar and carried it to Indra’s palace. When the demigods returned after bathing, they could not find the ambrosia and set off in search of it. When they heard that the gods had taken it, they thought, “Now, surely the gods will rise above us.” Meanwhile, the gods gathered to partake of the ambrosia. However, Rāhu had taken on the form of a god, and in their company he was able to drink a portion of nectar. Sūrya, the sun god, recognized him and said to Viṣṇu, “That is Rāhu!” Viṣṇu immediately threw his mighty wheel and cut off Rāhu’s head. However, the head had tasted the ambrosia and is still alive today. The rest of the body died. From then on Rāhu became the enemy of Sūrya, and from time to time he covers and obscures the disc of the sun. This is the story.[93]
[43] sde dge_1113_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_shes rab go cha/ lha las phul byung bstod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa/ shog_57_na5
[93] Devātiśayastotraṭīkā, Toh 1113 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 57a5.

f.d:
yang de nyid las/
de ni 'di skad thos te bdud rtsi 'phrogs pa las lha dang lha ma yin 'gras par gyur bas brdeg par 'dod pa na/ lha de dag la mtshon cha med pas brdeg par ma nus pa dang / phur bus lha rnams la smras pa/ ba tsa su tsa ra zhes bya ba'i drang srong chen po'i bu zho 'thung zhes bya ba lo bye ba phrag bdun gyi bar bka' thub la gnas par gyur bas de'i rus pa rdo rjer gyur ba yod de/ de'i rus pa bslangs [44]te mtshon char byas na sa gsum las rgyal par nus par 'gyur bas/ de blangs la mtshon cha des lha ma yin gzhom par rigs so zhes smras pa dang / lha rnams kyis drang srong de la de bzhin du gsol ba btab bo/ / des kyang de rnams la phan gdags pa'i phyir lus la bldag du bcug ste rus pa 'ba' zhig lus par byas nas de dag la byin na/ de nas las thams cad pas rtsibs logs kyi rus pa las rdo rjer byas pa ni brgya byin gyis khyer ro/ / byin pa'i rus pa las dbyig par byas pa ni khyab 'jug gis khyer ro/ /

Also, in the same text it says:
This I have also heard. After the theft of the ambrosia, the gods and the demigods became enemies and were spoiling for battle. However, the gods could not attack because they had no weapons. Bṛhaspati said to the gods, “There is a great rishi called Vacasucara.[94] His son Dadhici has dwelled in ascetic conduct for seventy million years, and his bones have become as strong as vajras. With these bones as weapons you will be victorious in the three worlds. Take them and you will defeat the demigods.” The gods approached the rishi and requested him accordingly. In response the rishi assisted them by encouraging them to lick his flesh until only his bones remained, which he then donated to the gods. From his ribs Viśvakarman fashioned a vajra and gave it to Indra. From the bones of the lower leg he made a club, which was taken by Viṣṇu.

d.div: [44] blangs/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[94] This is the name as transliterated in the text. Degé has Praca. Elsewhere the father of Dadhici is Atharvan.

las thams cad pa'i bu mo ne ru ka zhes bya ba nyi mas bslangs pa las/ de gzi byin pa'i gzugs can du gyur pas/ de yi gzi brjid ma bzod pa dang / khyod dang lhan cig rol zhing rtse bar ma 'dod pa dang / grul bum gyi bu mo dang lha'i bu mo gzhan dag gis kyang nyi ma'i gzi brjid bsten par mi nus pas/ de dag bros te pha'i khyim du zhugs ste 'dug pa dang phas spyos pas skyo ba skyes te/ rgod ma'i gzugs su byas nas ri bo ti se'i ri sul na dka' thub spyod cing 'dug go/ nyi ma yang chung ma tshol zhing song ba na/ gtam de thos nas der song ste rta'i gzugs su mnan par gyur ba dang / skyes bu gzhan gyi mngal chags par mi bya'o zhes byas pa dang / nyi mas bgad de rang nyid kyi gzugs su bstan nas nga las bu chags pa yin no/ / zhes smras pa dang / chung ma'i sna las tha skar gyi bu gnyis su gyur to/ /

Sūrya, the sun god, took Reṇukā,[95] the daughter of Viśvakarman, for his wife, but because his form was so dazzling, she was unable to bear the brightness and did not enjoy his company. Kuṣmāṇḍa and other celestial maidens also could not bear the brightness of Sūrya. They all fled, and she returned to her father’s house. The father became upset. This distressed Reṇukā, who then assumed the form of a mare and went to Mount Kailash to perform ascetic practices. Sūrya meanwhile had set out to search for his wife, and when he learned of her actions, he went to her in the form of a horse and forced himself upon her. She protested, saying, “I will not become pregnant by another man!” Sūrya laughed and revealed his true form, saying, “It is from me your child will be born.” From her nostrils the two sons of Aśvinī were born.
[95] In most versions of this popular legend, the sun god’s wife is referred to as Saṃjñā or Saṃjañā.

f.d: gtam de las thams cad pas thos pas nyi ma la smras pa/ gal te khyod kyis tshor ba brnag nus na/ ngas khyod gzugs yid du 'ong bar byas la/ gang gi tshe lhag par mi bzod pa de'i tshe ni btang bar bya'o/ / zhes smras pa dang / de bzhin du bya'o/ / zhes pa dang / des de sa la bsgyel te 'khor los cha bcu gnyis su byas te long mo'i bar du brdar te de sa la bor ro/ / de phan chad ni nyi ma rkang pa ma brdar ba zhes bya bar grags so/ / de nas gzi brjid kyi dum bu de dag bsdus nas 'khor lor byas la/ de shin tu 'bar bas lta na sdug pa zhes bya bar btags so/ / de brgya byin gyis khyab 'jug la byin la/ des kyang gang gi tshe sgra gcan 'dzin gyis bdud rtsi brkus te 'thungs pa de'i tshe 'khor lo des de'i mgo bcad par gyur to/[45] / zhes dang /

d.div: On hearing this Viśvakarman said to Sūrya, “If you can tolerate it, I can make you more attractive. When something has become unbearable, it has to be discarded.” Sūrya agreed. Viśvakarman tied him down. A wheel was fashioned into twelve blades and his radiance was sheared off as far as his ankles. The shorn off part was thrown to earth. From then on Sūrya was known as He of Unshorn Feet. The pieces of brightness cast away were gathered and made into a wheel. This wheel was of an intense brightness and so was called sudarśana, “beautiful to behold.” Indra gave it to Viṣṇu, and this was the wheel Viṣṇu used to cut off the head of Rāhu after he had stolen and drunk the nectar.[96]
[45] sde dge_1113_bstan/ bstod tshogs/ ka_shes rab go cha/ lha las phul byung bstod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa/ shog_46_na6
[96] Devātiśayastotraṭīkā, Toh 1113 Tengyur, bstod tshogs, ka, 46a6.

f.d:
rta'i tshe'i rig byed drang srong sha li ho tras bsdus pa'i le'u bzhi par/
'o ma'i rgya mtsho bsrubs pa'i tshe/ / rta dang bdud rtsi lhan cig byung / / de ming a tsa sra ba ste/ / sgra ni sprin chen lta bu yin/ / rgya mtsho de las nam mkha' la/ / shugs kyi rnam par grol ba na/ / lha min stobs dang lha 'khrugs pas/ / phyi rkang gnyis ni bzung bar gyur/ /
stobs chen stobs ldan gyis drangs pas/ / dpyi ni cung zad nyams par gyur/ / de bas rta rnams da dung ni/ / dpyi ni myur bar mi 'degs shing / / ngal gso ba na rkang pa ni/ / phyi ma res kyis dal bar 'degs/[46] / zhes mdor bstan nas/

In the fourth chapter of Horse Āyurveda Compiled by Rishi Śālihotra it says:
During the churning of the ocean, the horse arose with the ambrosia; its name was Uccaiḥ Śravas. Its sound was like that of thunder, and as it rose powerfully into the skies, the demigod Bala and the god Akula seized its hind legs.
Gripped by these two powerful forces, its hind quarters were a little weakened. Because of this, even now, hind quarters of horses do not move quickly, and when standing still, they slowly lift each hind leg.[97] This is a synopsis.

d.div: [46] sde dge_4345_bstan/ lugs kyi bstan bcos/ ngo drang srong sha li ho tra/ rta'i tshe'i rig byed/ le'u/ 4_shog_161_ba4
[97] Śālihotra, Śālihotrīyāśvāyurvedasaṃhitā, Toh 4345 Tengyur, lugs kyi bstan bcos, ngo, 161b4.

f.d:
rgyas pa ni/
skye dgu dang po byung ba'i tshe/ / 'tsho ba'i 'jig rten bde gnas gyur/ / de rjes lha dang lha min gyi/ / 'jig rten kun la tshangs pa yis/ / 'jig rten thams cad khyab byed pa'i/ / skom gyis gdung ba nyid du byas/ /

The more extensive account is as follows:
When living beings first arose, the world they lived in was a peaceful place. Then in the realms of gods and demigods, Brahmā caused a pervasive drought.

d.div: 'jig rten pa yi srog chags rnams/ / slar yang rgyug cing 'gro bar byed/ / lha dang lha min sha za dang / / lto 'phye srin po de rnams kyang / / stobs dang ldan pa'i skom gyis ni/ / gdung bas nye bar zin par gyur/ / lha dang lha min kha zas dang / / mal stan la ni dga' med gyur/ / de rnams de ltar sems pa na/ / de yi tshe na blo skyes pa/ / gang 'di chu yi snying por ni/ / gnas des bdag cag skom sel nus/ /

Again the creatures of the world fled. The gods, demigods, the gandharva spirits, the mahoraga serpents, and the rākṣa demons were also gripped and tormented by terrible thirst, unable to enjoy their food and sleep. Reflecting on this, the thought arose, “By that which abides in the heart of water, will we quench our thirst.”

de nas ri bo man+d+ha ra/ / grags ldan srubs shing nyid du byas/ / klu yi rgyal chen mtha' yas ni/ / srubs thag tu ni yang dag sbyar/ / der ni phyogs gcig lha rnams te/ / phyogs gcig tu ni lha min gnas/ / srub thag 'dren cing mtsho chen ni/ / 'jigs pa'i sgra rnams bsrubs pa las/ /

Therefore, the celebrated Mandara was the churning rod, and the nāga king Ananta tied on to it as churning rope. With the gods gathered in one place and the demigods in another, the rope was pulled and the ocean churned, provoking a fearsome sound.
mtsho chen der ni lha dang mi'i/ / sman ni rtsa ba lo ma dang / / 'o mar bcas pa bsdus nas ni/ / thams cad bcug pa nyid du gyur/ /
Roots and leaves, the medicines of gods and men, together with milk were cast into the ocean;

gzi brjid che zhing gzi brjid can/ / ro la sogs pa 'byung zhing dge/ / me tog ser dang go sring gi/ / de bzhin ser me la spyod dang / / mdangs ldan dzA ti sa ra dang / / 'tsho byed 'chi ba gso byed dang / / de bzhin rma gso byed la sogs/ / gzhan yang tshangs pas gang sprul ba'i/ / bcud dang mthu stobs bsam mi khyab/ / sman rnams mtsho chen der bcug ste/ / rgya mtsho bsrubs par gyur ba na/ /

medicine bright and radiant, full of taste, full of virtue, yellow flower, white sister, aṅgulacarya[98] bright jātisāra, medicine that denies death and cures wounds, elixirs manifested by Brahmā, medicines strong and of unimaginable power, all were cast into the ocean, and the waters churned.
[98] Sor mo la spyod, but other editions have ser me la spyod. Either way, it remains unidentified.

de tshe dang po kho nar ni/ / dpal mo la sogs byung bar gyur/ / gang gis nang par brjod na ni/ / rmi ngan la sogs 'jigs byed pa'i/ / dge ba zhes bya'i rin po che/ / brgyad ni chu las byung bar gyur/ /

nyi ma bzhon pa'i shing rta ni/ / 'dren pa'i rta dang lha yi chang / / de bzhin nor bzang ko thu ba/ / nor bu'i rna cha bzang po dang / / bdud rtsi zhes bya'i sman dang ni/ / bdud rtsi nyid kyang byung bar gyur/ /

bstan bcos thams cad 'dzin pa'i mchog / sman pa thang la 'bar dang ni/ / sgra mtho zhes ni bya ba'i rta/ / snying stobs che zhing stobs che la/ / 'brug dang rnga yi sgra dang ni/ / dung dang rnga chen sgra 'dra ba/ / gang zhig skad gsang mthon po yis/ sgra des ming du btags pa ni/ / de tshe lha dang lha min gyis/ / sgra mtho zhes ni bya bar btags/ /

the physician Dhavantari, supreme holder of all scriptures; and the horse Uccaiḥ Śravas, brave and strong, with a sound (śravas) like thunder, like a drum, or like a conch, like the great celestial drum, a high-pitched (uccaiḥ) roar giving birth to his name, so that the gods and demigods christened him Uccaiḥ Śravas.

f.d: sprin dkar gyi ni mdog 'dra zhing / / mgyogs shing bdud rtsi las byung ba/ / mdangs ldan rgya mtsho tshen po las/ / byung ste mkha' la 'gro bar byed/ / stobs ldan zhes bya'i snang byed bus/ / de yis rkang pa gnyis las bzung / / de tshe lha min thams cad kyis/ / man+d+ha ra dang de bzhin du/ / klu yi rgyal po bor nas ni/ / rta yi rin chen la 'jus te/ / 'o ma'i rgya mtsho spangs nas ni/ / sa gzhi 'dir ni phyin par gyur/[47] / zhes dang /

d.div: His body the color of the white clouds, this swift horse rose from the ambrosia, from the bright ocean and into the skies, and Bala, son of Bhānu, seized its legs. Then all the demigods left Mandara and the nāga king, and holding on to the precious horse, left Milk Ocean and came to this world.[99]

[99] Śālihotra, Śālihotrīyāśvāyurvedasaṃhitā, Toh 4345 Tengyur, lugs kyi bstan bcos, ngo, 162b4.

f.d:
'chi med mdzod gyi 'grel pa rab 'byor zla bas mdzad pa 'dod 'jor/
bcud ldan zhes pa ni lha dang lha ma yin rnams kyis rgya mtsho bsrubs te lak+Sh+mI byung ba khyab 'jug gis 'khyer/ zla ba phyed pa byung ba dbang phyug gis spyi bo'i rgyan du byas/ dug bum pa gang byung ba dbang phyug gis mgrin par bzhag pas mgrin pa sngon por song / chang bum pa gang byung ba de lha rnams kyis 'khyer bas su ra su ra zhes chang ngam mtsho'i bcud dam bdud rtsir yang rung ngo /[48] / zhes dang /

In The Wish-Fulfilling Cow: A Commentary to the Treasury of Immortality by Subhūticandra it says:
Elixir (bcud len, rasa): When the gods and demigods were churning the ocean, Lakṣmī arose and was carried off by Viṣṇu. A crescent moon arose and was worn by Īśvara on his crown. A vase full of poison arose. Īśvara placed it in his throat and his neck turned blue. A vase of alcohol arose and was taken by the gods. They are therefore known as sura sura, which means alcohol, essence of the ocean, or ambrosia.[100]

d.div: [48] sde dge_4300_bstan/ sgra mdo/ se_rab 'byor zla ba/ 'chi med mdzod kyi rgya cher 'grel/ mtho ris sde tshan/ shog_252_na6
[100] Amarakoṣaṭīkākamadhenu, Toh 4300 Tengyur, sgra mdo, se, 242a6.

f.d:
rtogs brjod rin po che dpag bsam 'khri shing las/ rgyu med par 'bras bu ston pa'i srid pa can gyi dper brjod du/
bdud rtsi'i chu gter ma bsrubs shing / / nor rgyas thang yang ma bcad la/ / ri bo bsgril ba med par ni/ / glang po 'di ni su yis bskrun/[49] / zhes dang /

In Wish-Fulfilling Tree of the Bodhisattva’s Lives, using the vibhāvana poetic device[101] to illustrate an effect seemingly without a cause, it says:
Without the churning of the ambrosia ocean and the untiring effort of Vāsuki in binding the mountain, who created this elephant?[102]

d.div: [49] sde dge_4155_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ke_dge ba'i dbang po/ dpag bsam gyi 'khri shing / yal 'dab/ 1_shog_4_na1

[101] Vibhāvanālaṃkāra (srid pa can gyi rgyan), literally, “causing to appear.” According to Monier-Williams this device of Sanskrit poetics is “the description of effects, the causes of which are left to be conjectured.” According to the Great Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary it is a device used to show effects from obscure causes and is one of the thirty-five embellishments of meaning (arthālaṃkāra, don gyi rgyan).
[102] Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā, chap. 1, Toh 4155 Tengyur, skye rabs, ke, 4a1.

f.d:
dpal ldan rgyud bzhi'i man rgyud le'u brgyad cu rtsa dgu pa las/
sngon gyi dus su lha dang lha min gyis/ / bdud rtsi 'dod nas rgya mtsho bsrubs pa las/ / skyes bu skra ser mig nas me 'bar ba/ / 'jigs pa'i gzugs can don te tshangs pa yis/ / hUM brjod pra yas rgyu mi rgyu la thim/[50] /

In chapter 89 of the Instruction Tantra of Four Tantras it says:
In ancient times the gods and demigods sought out the ambrosia, and from their churning of the ocean arose a man of fair hair, fire blazing from his eyes and of terrifying form. Brahmā chanted hūṃ, the illusion vanished, and it absorbed into animate and inanimate forms.[103]

d.div: [50] g.yu thog yon tan mgon pos rtsam sgrig mdzad pa/ man ngag gi rgyud/ le'u/ 89_shog_544_yig phreng 6
[103] Four Tantras, Instruction Tantra, 89.544.6.

f.d:
zhes dang / brgyad par/
sngon ni lha dang lha ma yin/ / bdud rtsi 'dod nas srubs pa yis/ / bdud rtsi 'byung ba'i snga rol tu/ / skyes bu shin tu 'jigs pa'i gzugs/ / skra ser mig ni me 'bar ba/ / mche ba bzhi pa gzi brjid 'bar/ / de mthong 'gro ba sdug bsngal 'gyur/ / tshangs pa'i hUM zhes brjod pa dang / / bslu ba'i bdag nyid can spangs te/ / dug ni rgyu dang mi rgyu ba'i/ / rang bzhin gnyis la thim par gyur/[51] /

And in the Essence of Eight Branches:
In earlier times in their search for ambrosia the gods and demigods churned the ocean, but before the ambrosia appeared, there arose a man of terrifying form, with fair hair, fire-spitting eyes, and four glistening fangs. Seeing him all were filled with fear. With Brahmā’s hūṃ the illusion vanished, and the poison took on animate and inanimate forms.[104]

f.d:
zhes sogs la/ ye shes le'u'i tshigs bcad brgyad cu rtsa gnyis par/
dpal mo thor thos lha'i ljon pa glang po'i bdag dang lha mo kau stu b+ha dang zla ba dang / / bdud rtsi stobs ldan rgyal srid dus su chu gter bsrubs las lha yul mkha' la gal te byung gyur na/ / an d+ha ka nyid rgyal srid la ni zla ba med pas gza' tshes dus kyi tshogs kyang med par gyur/[52] /

Concerning all the above citations, the Kālacakra Tantra, in verse 82 of the Gnosis chapter:
The goddess Śrī, the horse Uccaiḥ Śravas, the celestial tree, the lord of elephants, the apsaras goddess,[105] the kaustubha jewel, the moon, and the ambrosia— if these all arose in the celestial realms during the churning of the ocean in the reign of Bala, there would have been no moon in the reign of Andhaka and therefore no lunar or planetary division of time.[106]

d.div: [52] sde dge_845_bka'/ rgyud/ shrI_dus 'khor rtsa rgyud/('grel chen dri med 'od/) ye shes le'u/ shog_430_na7

[105] In the verse the horse is identified merely as thor thos (untraced as a Tibetan word) and the apsaras goddess as “goddess” (lha mo). The identifications as translated come from Puṇḍarīka’s Vimalaprabhā commentary on the Kālacakra Tantra in the Peking Tengyur. According to Monier-Williams, the apsaras goddess who appeared at the churning was was Rambhā.
[106] Cited in Puṇḍarīka, Stainless Light (Vimalaprabhā), Toh 845 Kangyur, rgyud, śrī, 430a7.

f.d:
zhes dang / chos kyi grags pa'i tshad ma rnam 'grel le'u dang por/
rig byed tshad ma dang ni 'gal byed smra/ / khrus las chos 'dod pa dang rigs smras dregs/ / sdig pa gzhom phyir gdung ba rtsom byed pa/ / blun po shes rab 'chal ba'i rtags lnga yin/[53] / zhes dus 'khor dang tshad ma sogs las dgag bya gnang yang / rig byed rang lugs su/ gong gi lung rnams dang / bla ma brgyud pa'i gsung rgyun sogs las byung ba thams cad kyi dgongs pa phyogs gcig tu blangs na 'di ltar thob par snang ste/

Also in the first chapter of Treatise of Valid Cognition by Dharmakīrti:
They assert the Vedas to be valid, they speak in contradictions, they claim bathing to be Dharma, they are arrogant in spouting their knowledge, they torture themselves to be free of sin: these are five reasons why they are fools.[107] Clearly, the Vedas are presented as objects of refutation in the Kālacakra, the literature on valid cognition, and elsewhere. However, if the previous citations that comment on the Vedas’ own position and the essential meaning of the traditional explanations found in the guru lineages are brought together, we arrive at the following understanding.

d.div: [53] sde dge_4210_bstan/ tshad ma/ ce_chos grags/ tshad ma rnam 'grel/ rang don le'u/ sh+loka343_shog_107_ba2
[107] Pramāṇavārttika, 1:343, Toh 4210 Tengyur, tshad ma, ce, 107b2.

f.d:
'jam dpal rtsa rgyud kyi le'u rab 'byams bco brgyad par/
rang nyid 'od ldan sems can ni/ / de yi dus su rdzogs ldan yin/ / thams cad nam mkha' la 'gro zhing / / rga dang 'chi ba rnam par spangs/ / de yi dus su rgyu skar dang / / nyi ma zla ba skar ma med/ / lha dang lha min 'jig rten med/[54] / ces dang /
de nas dus ni 'bri ba na/ / 'jig rten snod min rab tu 'jug / sngon gyi las kyis drangs nas ni/ / de nas sa yi steng du 'gro/[55] / zhes dang /
de nas nyin zhag zla ba dang / / gza' yi 'od ni byung bar gyur/[56] / zhes pa ltar

In the eighteenth chapter of the Mañjuśrī Root Tantra it says:
During the era of perfection[108] living beings had their own light, they flew through the skies, and old age and death were unknown. At that time there were no planets, no sun, moon, or stars, and no realms of gods and demigods.[109] Also:
Then the times degenerated, and their world became unsuitable. Impelled by previous karma, they fell to the earth.[110] Also:
Then came the solar day and the light from the moon and the planets.[111]

d.div: [54] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na 'jam dpal rtsa rgyud/ le'u/ 18_shog_194_ba1
[55] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na 'jam dpal rtsa rgyud/ le'u/ 18_shog_194_ba3
[56] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na 'jam dpal rtsa rgyud/ le'u/ 18_shog_194_ba5

[108] This refers to the four ages of the Buddha’s doctrine: the age of perfection (rdzogs ldan, caturyuga), the age of three (gsum ldan, treatyuga), the age of two (gnyis ldan, dvāparayuga), and the age of troubles (rtsod ldan, kaliyuga).
[109] Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Toh 543 Kangyur, rgyud, na, 194b1.

f.d: sngon du rdzogs ldan gyi mjug tu bdud rtsi sa zhag la sogs pa'i zas zos pas rdzu 'phrul dang lus kyi 'od nyams nas mi'i 'jig rten du mun pa byung ba'i tshe/ 'o ma'i rgya mtsho chen po'i dbus na 'chi med kyi bcud dam bdud rtsis gang ba'i rin chen chu shel gyi bum pa zhig lhang nge lhan ner 'dug pa/ sgra gcan gling bzhir rgyu bas mthong ba dang / des lha dang lha ma yin rnams la/ kye grogs po dag / rgya mtsho chen po rnam par mi g.yo ba'i klong na bdud rtsis gang ba'i rin po che'i bum pa gcig bdag gis mthong ngo zhes smras pa na/ der lha dang lha ma yin rnams kyis bdud rtsi de 'dod nas len par brtsams pa'am lha dang lha ma yin thams cad skom pa'i nad kyi gdung ba lhag par 'phel ba ci yin brtags na chu yi snying por gnas pas gdung ba zhi bar mthong nas sman dang bcud thams cad mtshor bcug ste snying po 'dod pa'i phyir khyab 'jug gis ri bo man+d+ha ra'am ri rab kyis bsrub shing byas klu'i rgyal po nor rgyas sam tshul 'dir klu'i drang srong mu khyud 'dzin lus sbrul du song nas bsrub thag dang mes po tshangs pas spyi bo mnan/ 'og nas rus sbal gyi rgyab rten byas rgya mtsho bsrubs pa las/

At the end of the age of perfection, living beings began to partake of natural-earth[112] ambrosia and the like, diminishing their miraculous powers and natural luminosity, and the human world was plunged into darkness. At that time, in the midst of the great Milk Ocean, a shining crystal vase sat filled with ambrosia, the elixir of immortality. It was seen by Rāhu as he traveled around the four continents. He addressed the gods and demigods, “Friends! In the still depths of the great ocean I have seen a precious vase filled with ambrosia.” The gods and demigods wanted this ambrosia and set out to retrieve it. In an alternative version of this story, they were tormented by a great and increasing thirst, which they realized on investigation could be alleviated by “that which abides in the essence of water.” Therefore, they cast medicine and various essences into the ocean, and because they wanted its essence, they needed to churn the ocean. Viṣṇu used Mount Mandara or Mount Meru as a churning stick, the nāga king Vāsuki—or the nāgarṣi Nemindhara manifesting in the form of Vāsuki—transformed his body into the churning rope, while Brahmā held down Vāsuki’s head. Below, the back of the giant turtle Kūrma acted as a base. Together they churned the great ocean.

d.div: [112] Sa zhag. Glistening film or skin left after rainwater has dried up.

f.d: thog mar rin po che me shel las grub cing rta bdun dang ldan pa 'jig rten 'od kyi snang bar byed pa zhig thon pas [57]sems can kun gyis nyi dga' la ma ru 'dug ces smras pas ming nyi mar btags/ yang bsrubs pas rin po che chu shel las grub cing rta lnga dang ldan pa'i dkyil 'khor thon pas sngon ma de'i zla bor 'dug zer ming zla bar grags pa lha dbang phyug chen po'i cod pan du byas/ de nas glang po che sa srungs thon pa lha'i dbang po brgya byin gyis bzhon par bzung / dpag bsam gyi shing ngam yongs 'du sa brtol thon pa lhas khyer/ lha mo dpal mo byung ba rang nyid nas khyab 'jug gi chung mar khas blangs te 'dus/ de nas bud med shin tu yid du 'ong ba zhig byung ba khyod su yin dris pas nga chang zhes bya ba 'thungs na myos pa dang brgyal ba dang dregs pas smyo ba'i rnam pa 'gyur ro zhes zer bas lha min rnams kyis 'thung bar ma nus lhas btungs pas lha'i skad dod su ra de'i sngon du dgag tshig a bzhag pas lha min te lha dang lha min gyi ming yang grags/

First an object made of precious fire-crystal appeared. Accompanied by seven horses, it gave light to the world. Living beings were overjoyed (nyi) and exclaimed, “It is the mother (ma).” Therefore, it was named “sun” (nyi ma). Again the mighty ocean churned, and from it appeared a disk made of water-crystal and accompanied by five horses. People exclaimed, “It is the companion (zla bo) of the sun. Therefore, it became known as the moon (zla ba), and the god Īśvara took it for his crown ornament. Then came the great elephant Airāvata, which the god Indra took for his mount. The wish-fulfilling, or pārijāta, tree appeared, which the gods claimed for themselves. The goddess Śrī, or Lakṣmī, appeared and proclaimed herself the wife of Viṣṇu. Then a very beautiful girl appeared. “Who are you?” they asked. “I am Surā,” she replied. If you drink me, you will become intoxicated, lose your senses, become crazy with arrogance.” The demigods could not drink it but the gods partook of it. In Sanskrit “god” is sura and the prefix a is a negating particle, and so these two classes of beings are known as sura and asura.

d.div: [57] ma dper don pas/ bton pas/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/ 'dir thon pas zhes bcos/

f.d: de nas nad dang gdon dang bkra mi shis pa thams cad sel bar byed pa'i nor bu rin po che dge ba zhes bya ba brgyad dang / ki thu ba dang / nor bu'i rna cha bzang po dang / bdud rtsi dang cha 'dra ba'i sman la sogs pa don pa spyi nor byas/ de rjes mgrin rings/ thor thos/ sgra mtho zhes ming gi rnam grangs du ma dang ldan pa'i rta nam mkha' la 'phur shes shing sprin gyi kha dog ltar dkar ba don pa lha dang lha min hab sha byas pa'i mthar lha ma yin stobs ldan gyi rkang pa gnyis nas bzung ste de 'khyer nas rang gi gnas su bros/

Next to appear were substances such the eight śubha jewels, which eliminate disease, demons, and all misfortune; the kausthubha jewel; the beautiful jeweled earrings; and ambrosia and ambrosia-like medicine. These became wealth to be utilized by all. Then appeared the horse, known by various names such as Uccaiḥ Śravas and Hayagrīva. It was able to move through the skies and was the color of the white clouds. The gods and the demigods all scrambled to gain this horse, and finally the demigod Bala grasped its two hind legs and fled to his abode.

de nas yang bsrub pas shin tu 'jigs su rung ba'i dug gi skyes bu nag po brtsegs pa zhes bya ba gdong dgu pa skra ser mig nas me 'bar ba zhig byung ba/ khyab 'jug gis mid pas zhu bar ma gyur nas dran pa stor te sa la 'gyel cing mi smra bar gnas pa dang / lha chen pos de las drangs te mgrin par bzhag pas des de'i mgrin pa sngon por song ba sogs kun gyis ma thul ba lha tshangs par gsol ba btab pas/ tshangs pa la sngon sangs rgyas shAkya thub pa chen pos skyes bu de 'dra ba byung ba'i tshe hUM zhes pa'i rig sngags kyis thul zhig pa'i lung bstan yod pa dran te/ hUM zhes brjod cing sdigs mdzub gdengs pas de'i lus zhig nas dug sbrul dang khyi dang srin bu la sogs pa rgyu ba dang / bong nga thang phrom la sogs pa mi rgyu ba'i dug gnyis la thim/

Again the ocean was churned. From it arose a fearsome creature, the personification of the poison kālakūta, with nine heads, fair hair, and fire shooting from his eyes. Viṣṇu swallowed his poison but was unable to digest it, and he fell to the ground and lay there speechless. Then Mahādava took the poison from Viṣṇu and placed it in his own mouth, which turned his throat blue. No one could overcome this creature, and so they turned and prayed to the god Brahmā. He in turn recalled a teaching of the past in which Buddha Mahāśākyamuni had conquered a similar creature with the mantra hūṃ. Brahmā uttered the syllable hūṃ and raised the threatening gesture. The body of the creature broke up and dissolved into the bodies of poisonous creatures, such as snakes, rabid dogs, and rākṣa demons, and into inanimate poisons such as aconite and datura.

de'i 'og tu bdud rtsi byung ba na snod chen po brgyad gang ba sgra pa shes rin pa sogs tshangs pas sgos su 'khyer bas sgra gcan gyi 'khor lo 'phangs pa dpral bar phog par smra yang / slob dpon shes rab go cha sogs yig cha phal cher mthun par lha ma yin rnams kyis khyer bas lha rnams shin tu yi mug pa'i tshe khyab 'jug gis ches yid du 'ong zhing gzugs bzang ba'i bud med kyi lus su bsgyur te lha ma yin rnams ga la ba der song zhing brgya byin gyis kyang mi snang ba'i gzugs kyi nam mkha' la 'dug go/

Then the ambrosia appeared, contained in eight great containers. According to Drapa Sherap Rinchen[113] and others, the ambrosia was taken by Brahmā for his personal use, because of which Rāhu threw his wheel at Brahmā and injured his forehead. However, Ācārya Prajñāvarman,[114] in agreement with most other commentators, say that the ambrosia was taken by the demigods. This upset the gods enormously. Viṣṇu transformed himself to a beautiful and alluring woman and went to the abode of the demigods, while Indra remained unseen in the skies above.

d.div: [113] Better known as Taktsang Lotsāwa (b. 1405).
[114] Author of Commentary on Praise of the Exalted, quoted previously.

f.d: de'i tshe lha ma yin rnams kyis 'di ni kho bo cag gi bud med yin no snyam nas khyab 'jug bud med du bsgyur ba de bdud rtsi'i srung mar bzhag nas khrus la song ba dang / skabs der khyab 'jug dang brgya byin gnyis kyis bdud rtsi bum pa brgyad po de brkus nas brgya byin gyi khang pa rnam par rgyal byed du khyer ro/ / de rnams khrus byas nas slar log pa dang / bdud rtsi ma mthong nas de 'tshol ba la brtson pa na lha rnams kyis khyer ro/ / zhes thos nas lha rnams steng du 'gro ba ni bden no snyam mo/ / de'i tshe lha rnams bdud rtsi la longs spyod pa'i phyir 'dus pa na sgra gcan lha'i cha lugs su bsgyur te der zhugs pas/ bdud rtsi'i skal pa thob pa dang de zla bas mthong ste 'di ni lha ma yin gyi dbang po sgra gcan no zhes lha rnams la sbran pa dang / de ma thag sgra gcan bros pa na brgya byin gyis rdo rje/ skem byed kyis mdung / stobs bzang gis gshol la sogs pa mtshon cha ji snyed cig thogs te lha rnams kyis ded/

The demigods thought that this woman was one of theirs and so entrusted her to look after the ambrosia while they went to bathe. Indra and Viṣṇu then stole the vases of ambrosia and took them to Indra’s palace, Vaijayanta. When the demigods returned from bathing, they could not find the vases and so set out in search of them. When they heard that the gods had taken them, they thought, “Now surely the gods will rise above us.” When the gods had gathered to enjoy the ambrosia, Rāhu took on the form of a god and joined them. Only after he had received his share of ambrosia was he recognized by Candra, the moon god, who called out to the other gods, “It’s Rāhu, king of the demigods!” Rāhu fled. Indra took his vajra, Skanda took his spear, Balabhadra took his plow-like halāyudha, and with whatever other weapons were at hand, the gods set out in pursuit.

zin la khad par khyab 'jug gi lag par drang srong zho 'thung gi rus pa bden pa sra ba/ brtan pa/ thams cad du thogs pa med pa/ thams cad du ma pham pa ste mdor na phar la dngos por 'dzin pa thams cad 'joms shing tshur la gang gi'ang [58]gzhig par mi nus pa'i rdo rjer gyur pa nyi ma'i dum bu bsdus pa la las sna tshogs pas bzos pa'i 'khor lo gang la brgyab pa der mi 'phog mi srid/ 'phog pas mi bsnad mi srid/ bsnad pas mi 'chi mi srid/ 'chi bas ngan song du mi ltung mi srid pa ste dam bca' bzhi ldan yod pa 'phangs pas sgra gcan gyi ske bcad de lus byings shi bar gyur kyang /

The vajra that Viṣṇu carried in his hands had been fashioned from the bones of the rishi Dadhici. It was hard, reliable, unstoppable, and unconquerable. In short, it destroyed everything in its path but could not be destroyed in return. Viṣṇu also carried a wheel fashioned by Viśvakarman from the shards of the sun. It carried four guarantees. Whoever it was thrown at, it could not fail to hit. Whoever it hit, it could not fail to injure. Whoever it injured would not fail to die. Whoever died when struck by this wheel would not fail to fall to the lower realms. As they closed in upon Rāhu, Viṣṇu threw the wheel and cut off his head.

d.div: [58] gang gis kyang gzhom mi nus pa'i/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

f.d:
brgyad pa'i phyi mar/
sgra gcan bdud rtsi rku ba na/ / khyab 'jug gis ni ske bcad pas/[59] / zhes pa ltar bdud rtsi mthus mgo bo ma shi bar slar 'khor lo phyir g.yugs su 'phangs pas tshangs pa'i dpral ba'am mkhur tshos la 'phog

As it says in the Essence of Eight Branches,
“When Rāhu stole the ambrosia, Viṣṇu cut off his head.”[115] However, although his body was generally dead, by the power of the ambrosia he had drunk, his head did not die, and he was able to throw the wheel back and wound Brahmā’s forehead or cheek.

d.div: [59] sde dge_4310_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ he_pha khol/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa/ le'u/ 39_shog_328_ba6
[115] Pitṛceṭa, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhita, chap. 39, Toh 4310 Tengyur, gso rig, he, 328b6.

f.d: dus der lha min dbang po'i khrag dang bdud rtsi 'dres pa thigs pa gcig sa la lhungs par a ru ra dang sgog skya byung de'i phyir sgra gcan zin dang zla ba zhe 'gras par 'gyur zhing gang gis tshe zla ba'i dkyil 'khor rgyas pa'i dus 'gebs shing sgrib par byed pa'ang de nas byung zhes grags/

During the fight a drop of ambrosia mixed with the blood of this demigod king fell to the ground, and from this sprang myrobalan[116] and garlic. From that time on, Rāhu became the enemy of the moon, and it is said that his habit of eclipsing and veiling the face of the full moon dates from this time also.

d.div: [116] Arura: Terminalia chebula Retz; renowned as the king of medicinal plants. See glossary, chebulic myrobalan.

f.d:
tshangs pa rang gi rma'i zug rngu dang sgra gcan gyi ske chad pa'i snying rjes zhi ba'i ting nge 'dzin la snyoms par zhugs pas/ sngon sangs rgyas shAkya thub chen por sman gyi rgyud thos pas rkyen byas/ rma nang nas tshe'i rig byed kyi thog ma oM A tha zhes bya ba thon pa la brten nas tshe'i rig byed sogs rig byed bzhi yan lag dang bcas pa byung ba/ zla zer las/
yi ge oM dang A tha'i sgra/ / gnyis po 'di dag sngon tshangs pa'i/ / mkhur tshos brtol nas byung ba ste/ / des na 'di dag bkra shis yin/[60] / zhes bshad cing bklag pa'i tshe yang nges brjod kyi rig byed ni oM/ snyan ngag gi u/ srid srung gi e/ mchod sbyin gyi a ste de bzhi po'i tshad du 'don dgos par bzhed/

From the pain of his wound and from compassion for the decapitated Rāhu, Brahmā entered the samādhi of peace, and by the force of having listened to a medical tantra from Buddha Mahāśākyamuni in the past, the sound oṃ ātha[117] emerged from the wound. This was the start of Āyurveda teachings, and all four Vedas and their branches followed. In Moonlight: A Commentary on the Essence of Eight Branches, it says:
The two syllables oṃ and ātha arose from the cheeks of Brahmā; these, therefore, are for auspiciousness.[118] It is said that in the practice of recitation, the syllable oṃ should be recited as if it possessed the measure of the Ṛg Veda, the letter u as having the measure of the Sāma Veda, the letter e as the measure of Atharva Veda, and the letter a as having the measure of the Yajur Veda.

d.div: [60] sde dge_4312_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ ko_slob dpon zla ba la dga' ba/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po'i rnam par 'grel ba'i tshig gi don gyi zla zer/ shog_3_na4
[117] Possibly atha, meaning “then.” In the Degé edition of the quote below it says, “The syllable oṃ and the word ‘then’ (de nas).”
[118] Candranandana, Candrikāprabhāsa, Toh 4312 Tengyur, gso rig, ko, 3a4.

f.d: de yang brda sprod dbyangs can ma'i dgongs pa ltar bsgrubs par/ a bsrung ba la ste skyong ba la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag / byings mtha'i a dbyi'o/ /pa'o srog gi a phyis/ uN la sogs pa ni rtag tu'o zhes/ rkyen mu ku byin/ ka 'gro ba la 'os pa de/ saM pra sA ra Nas ur bsgyur/ ka de'i don yin pas phyis/ u brjod don a u la o/ ma nga ror byas pas oM 'grub pas bsrung ba'i don la 'jug[61]

The formulation of the syllable oṃ according to the Sarasvatī Grammar Sutra is as follows. The Dhātusūtra says, “Ava means to protect, to guard.” This is the root. “The a at the end of the root is elided.” Therefore, the life-letter a of va is dropped. Then “uṇ and so forth always” [The uṇ category of affixes, and so on, can always be added to roots, regardless of tense and case]. Therefore, the affix muku is added. “The ya, va, ra of yaj, and so on, added to ka anubandha take samprasāraṇa into i, u, ṛt” [When roots such as yaj meet anubandha affixes such as ka, then the ya, va, and ra of those roots perform a vowel interchange, or samprasāraṇa, with i, u, and ṛ]. Therefore, by the process of saṃprasāraṇa, v becomes u. Ku follows the same rule and is elided. U is for purposes of pronunciation and is elided. A and u merge to become o. Then an anusvāra is added to m to form oṃ. Therefore, oṃ has the meaning of “protect.”[119]

d.div: [61] sde dge_4297_bstan/ sgra mdo/ se_a nu b+hu ti/ brda sprod pa dbyangs can gyi mdo/ shog_1_nas 9_bar bzhugs/
[119] Anubhūti, Sarasvatīvyākaraṇsūtra, 1:1–9, Toh 4297 Tengyur, sgra mdo, se.

f.d:
rdo rje rtse mo las/
oM ni ci zhig yin par bshad/ / mchog dang nor ster dpal dang g.yang / / skal bzang rnam pa dang ldan zhing / / dam bca' ba dang bkra shis don/ / nor bu 'dzin pa'i snying po yin/[62] / zhes dang /

In the Vajraśekhara Tantra it says:
The meaning of oṃ is this: it has the qualities of being supreme, of being the granter of wealth, of glory, auspiciousness, and merit; it is a sacred pledge and it is good fortune, the essence of maṇidhārin, holder of the jewel.[120]

d.div: [62] sde dge_480_bka'/ rgyud/ nya gsang ba rnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud rdo rje rtse mo/ le'u/ 2_shog_156_na2
[120] Vajraśekharatantra, chap. 2, Toh 480 Kangyur, rgyud, nya, 156a2.

f.d:
'dul ba rgya cher 'grel las/
yi ge oM ldan phyed dang bzhi/ / tshad du byas pa snyan par brjod/[63] / ces bstod bkur bsngags gsum du bshad pa dang /

In the Extensive Commentary on Basic Vinaya it says:
That with the letter oṃ is three and a half measures and is spoken pleasingly.[121] Therefore, oṃ is spoken of in terms of esteem, respect, and praise.

d.div: [63] sde dge_4113_bstan/ 'dul ba/ tsu_dge legs bshes gnyen/ 'dul ba gzhi rgya cher 'grel pa/ shog_189_na7

[121] Citation untraced. Probably to be found in Vinayavastuṭīkā. Toh 4113 Tengyur, dul ba, tsu. “Measure” (tshad, mātrā) probably refers to the intonation length of the syllable. This is one meaning of mātrā, a term cognate with “meter.”

f.d:
rtog ge 'bar bar rig byed kyi lung drangs pa las/
tshangs pa dang ni nor lha yi/ / glur blangs gsang ba oM zhes bya/ / tshangs pa'i yi ge de nyid ni/ / yod de kun la khyab pa yin/ / de ni tshad gsum gsal ba yin/ / de bzhin shin tu phra bar bstan/ /
dang po'i rgyu ni yi ge a/ / ngag dang snying stobs sa me bsdus/ / las dang nam mkha' nyid dag kyang / / yid rdul snying stobs u dang ldan/ /
byed po'i yi ge mi'i ming can/ / grog dang mun pa gsum pa yin/ / 'gro ba thams cad sdud par byed/ / gnyid chen shin tu log pa'i rgyu'o/[64] /

A passage from the Vedas quoted in Blaze of Reasoning states:
The syllable oṃ is the mystical song of Brahmā and Vasudeva. This syllable of Brahmā pervades all things. It possesses the clarity of three measures and is taught to be very subtle.
The first cause is the letter a, comprising speech, sattva, fire, and earth and also body[122] and space. Mind, rajas, and sattva possess the letter u.
The letter m, the creating letter, is the third— life and tamas—which gathers all beings and causes the great sleep.[123]

Also:
With senses and their objects withdrawn like a turtle’s limbs, the self will be freed by worship while recalling and reciting the letter oṃ.[124] The syllable oṃ, of the nature of the three letters—a Viṣṇu, u Īśvara, and m Brahmā—is a formulation from the euphonic amalgamation of these three letters. This is its provisional meaning.

Also in the Commentary to the Saṃpuṭa Tantra by Kāyastha it says:
The letter a is Nairātmyā, the letter u is Vajrayoginī, the letter m is Akśobhyavajra, therefore, oṃ is the three vajras. The Kālacakra Root Tantra states
“Glorious holder of the body vajra!”[128] thereby assigning a to the body vajra, u to the speech vajra, and m to the mind vajra to form the syllable oṃ as the representation of the three vajras as the entity of the Buddha. This concept can be further elaborated on using the reasoning that establishes the meaning of the syllables evaṃ and is seen in countless phenomena, such as the drops, moon-bodhicitta, fluid, and the bases of correspondence for the outer, inner, and other Kālacakra.

In the Sutra of the Great Mantra Protection from the five great dhāraṇīs[132] it says:
“By the moon going for refuge to the sugatas, who are destroyers of the enemies of the world, save the moon, enlightened ones, out of compassion for the world! Rāhu, release the moon, dispeller of darkness, let its light shine in the pure skies again, bright and shining, aglow with pure light, unfettered in the pure skies, set free this light of living beings.”
Accordingly, Rāhu begins to sweat; he becomes afraid and, like a sick man, suddenly leaves and releases the moon.[133]

f.d: g.yung drung bon gyi klu 'bum khra bor grags pa la yang 'di dang mthun par snang /[73] gsung rab la lar nyi zla spyang kis zin pa zhes dang / dran nyer lha min dbang po'i lag pas sgribs pa sogs kun rdzob drang ba'i don du bshad tshul ji snyed dang /[74] gnam stong du nyi ma sgrib pa'ang gtso bor zla bar yin rung lhan cig tu gnas pa'i dbang las yin pa lo rgyus la lar byung ba thun mong ba'i gdul bya'i snang ngor tsam ste don nyi zla khams kyi dngos ma'i rnam par sgra gcan bar srid kyi tshul du sbyor zhing / go la'i rgyu lam du chu shel dang me shel gyi dkyil 'khor shin tu dngas pa'i steng du gdong mjug nor bu baiDUR+ya'i mdangs can steng nas phog pa'i grib ma las gnod pa byas pa'i tha snyad med cing d+hU ti sgra gcan dang ro rkyang nyi zlar byas nas phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi sbyor tshul dang po'i sangs rgyas su gsungs pa'i don baiDUR+ya dkar po ma bur rgyas par bshad pa ltar ro/[75] /

The Yungdrung Bön work known as the Mottled Nāga Collection[134] says the same. In some scriptures it says that the sun and moon are eclipsed by a wolf. The Sutra of Remembering the Sacred Dharma states that it is the hand of the king of the demigods that causes the eclipses. There are many such provisional and conventional explanations of this phenomenon. Also, concerning the eclipsing of the sun on the day of the empty sky,[135] some accounts describe it being primarily the moon, but brought about by sun and moon being in conjunction. These are merely observations made by the minds of ordinary disciples. The real significance is that Rāhu, in the aspect of the intermediate existence, acts upon the sun and moon in the forms of essences of bodily elements. Moreover, there is no textual evidence that counteracts the description of Rāhu’s head and tail casting beryl-colored shadows upon the moon and sun’s brightly vivid water-crystal and fire-crystal discs as they make their way through the gola[136] firmament. The mother and son White Beryl texts extensively explain the way that the central channel as Rāhu and the left and right channels as the sun and moon are used in the correspondences of the inner, outer, and other Kālacakra.[137]

The grandfather Brahmā taught the science to Prajāpati, the second Brahmā. He in turn taught it to the Aśvinī sons, who are said to be last two of King Pāṇḍu’s five sons: Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Sahadeva, and Nakula. They in turn passed the science of healing to Indra, king of the gods, and from then on it became widespread.
gso rig mi yul du dar tshul/
Part 1.The Science of Healing in India
'gro ba mi la dar rgyas su gyur pa ni/
4. Early Indian Medical Traditions

sngon 'dzam bu'i gling 'dir mi rnams chags nas yun ring zhig gi bar du zas su bsam gtan gyi dga' ba za bas kham zas rags pa'i ming med cing / rang 'od kyis rang gsal bas nyi zla gza' skar dang nyin mtshan la sogs pa med pa/ rdzu 'phrul gyis nam mkha' la 'gro ba/ gzugs dang longs spyod thams cad 'od gsal gyi lha dang mnyam par spyod pa'i mjug tu mi yul du thog mar skyes pa'i shed bu zhes bya bas sred pa'i bag chags kyis sa zhag zos pa la brten ma zhu ba'i nad kyi zug rngu drag pos btab ste smre sngags phyungs pa mes po tshangs pas thos nas rang gis byas par 'dod pa'i 'gro ba la brtse bas blos sam la lar sngon sangs rgyas shAkya thub chen gyis gsungs pa'i gso dpyad 'bum sde las ma zhu ba'i nad la chu skol gtong ba'i tshul yod pa dran par 'dod pa ste/ gang ltar tshangs pas chu skol gyi sbyor ba bslab pas shed bu'i nad zhi/

When human beings were first created ages ago in this world of Jampudvīpa, they subsisted for a long time on the joys of meditative concentration, and even the name of coarse and ordinary food did not exist. Because they radiated their own light, there was no sun, moon, stars, or planets, no day and no night. They had the power to fly, and they enjoyed their bodies and pleasures on a par with the gods of light. After some time, instincts of craving awoke in those of the race known as Manu,[138] who were the first to be born in the human realm, and they began to partake of natural-earth ambrosia, which gave them indigestion. Brahmā heard their cries of pain, and moved by pity for the beings that he is said to have created, he conceived the idea of giving them boiled water as medicine for the indigestion. Alternatively, some say that he remembered a teaching from the Hundred Thousand Versed Science of Healing Collection taught by Mahāśākyamuni Buddha at an earlier time, which prescribed boiled water as a cure for indigestion. Whatever the origin, Brahmā taught them the preparation of boiled water, and the indigestion was cured.

d.div: [138] Shed bu; mānava or manu, from which the English word “man” comes.

f.d: rgyu mtshan de la dpags nas nad la snga ba ma zhu ba/ nad pa la snga ba shed bu/ sman la snga ba chu skol/ sman pa la snga ba lha tshangs pa yin par 'jig rten du grags/
From this it is well known in the world that the first illness was indigestion, the first patients were the Manu, the first medicine was boiled water, and the first doctor was Brahmā.

de nas rim gyis tshangs pa las skyes par 'dod cing brA h+ma Na tshangs pa'i skad dod de bu brgyud kyi rkyen an byin bra ring por byas pas tshangs pa'i bu ste bram zer grags pa de'i rjes su zhugs pa rnams kyis mtho ris kyi sman pa rnams las brgyud pa'i tshe'i rig byed kyi lung rnams dar zhing rgyas par byas te rgya cher 'phel ba bskal bzang lha'i lugs dang rig 'dzin drang srong gi lugs gnyis gsham du 'chad rgyu ltar dang /

When the affix an is added to denote a descendent and the vowel a of bra is lengthened, one arrives at the term Brāhmaṇa, meaning the “children of Brahmā” commonly known as brahmans, who are asserted to be his descendents. Through their high-birth physicians, the brahmans developed and spread the transmission of Āyurveda. This can be seen in the widespread Fortunate Eon Deva tradition and the Vidyādhara Rishi tradition. These will be explained later.
ston pa sangs rgyas pa'i lugs/
ston pa sangs rgyas pa'i lugs su bzhed pa ni/ bskal ba bzang po 'di la mtshon na sangs rgyas 'od srungs kyi bstan pa yan la sangs rgyas kyis bka' stsal ba dang gzhan dag gis bshad pa

The tradition known as the Buddhist scriptural tradition is explained as follows. In this particular eon, the fortunate eon, we cannot say with certainty that teachings given by the buddhas and the commentaries on them by others up to the era of Buddha Kāśyapa have entirely disappeared,

sogs med pa'i mtha' ma bkag kyang deng sang 'di'o zhes gsal bar brjod pa'i skabs ma 'tshal zhing / ston pa shAkya'i dbang pos 'khor lo dang po wa ra NA sir bden bzhi'i chos 'khor gyi skabs gso dpyad bi ma la mu tra le'u bdun khri nyis stong yod pa dang yan lag brgyad pa bam po nyi khri ba zhig gsungs par grags la/ 'dul ba sman gyi gzhi las/ dge slong nad pas ni sman pa la dris te bya'o/[76] / zhes pa lta bu'i 'phros la brten nas 'dul ba lung gi dum bu gsum par sman dang mas btang ba'i dpyad la sogs pa nyung ngu tsam zhig bshad cing gtso bor smos pa ni/

but these days we cannot identify them with any certainty. As for Buddha Śākyamuni, concurrent with teaching the four truths during the first turning of the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, it is believed that he also taught the Vimalagutra Medical Collection in 72,000 Chapters [139] and the Eight Branches in 20,000 Fascicles. The Basic Vinaya on the topic of medicine says, “A sick monk should approach a doctor and follow his advice.”[140] Expanding on this somewhat, the third section of this Vinaya work talks a little on medicines, suppositories, and so on, whereas the bulk of the teaching can be illustrated by the following summarizing verse:

f.d: sman ni rjes su gnang ba dang / / tshil dang g.yam pa mig sman dang / / smyon pa dang ni pi lin da/ / nam gru dang ni skyur khu'o/[77] / zhes pa'i sdoms bzhin bcom ldan 'das rgyal bu rgyal byed kyi tshal mgon med zas sbyin gyi kun dga' ra ba na bzhugs pa'i tshe dge slong rnams ston ka'i bro nad kyis skya bo seng seng por gyur pa'i tshe sman so sor bstan par gsungs kyang dus su ma gtogs de las yol bar mi bstan pas skya bor gyur pa la/

On medicine: that which is permitted, medicinal fats, medicine for scabrous skin, eye medicines, medicine for the insane, for the monk Pilinda, for the monk Revati, and acidic juice.[141] Therefore, when the Buddha was dwelling in the Anāthapiṇḍada retreat in Jeta Grove and the monks became pale through autumnal illnesses, he allowed them to rely on specific remedies, but he did not allow medicines to be taken beyond specific times. The monks remained pale:

d.div: [77] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka_sman gzhi/ bam po/ 22_shog_277_ba6

[141] Ibid., 277b6. This is a summarizing verse that comes at the beginning of a section and as such is little more than a listing of topics. The first topic is general medicines permitted for the monastic community. Other topics are medicines or foods that have come to be permitted due to a specific incident. Permitted fats allowed are of five types: fish, frog, crocodile, bear, and pig. This came about when a monk was told to eat fat because no other medicine would cure him. Another was prescribed astringents for scabrous skin. Another monk went insane and had to be force fed raw meat. Pilinda, or the son of Pilinda, was constantly ill, and as a result monks were allowed to carry medicine pouches. Revati was a monk who doubted everything and was called Doubting Revati; his doubts led to certain food being allowed. Acidic juice refers to Indian gooseberry (amla) juice with salt.

/ shi ri sha'i bska ba dang / ko sham pa'i bska ba'o/[81] /

Ānanda, therefore, the following is permitted. Monks should rely on four types of medicine: taken at the right times, taken at specific times, seven-day medicines, and life-long medicines.[142] Foods to be eaten at the right times include pastes, boiled rice, gruel, meat, and fried or baked breads. Drinks that are to be taken at specific times include the juices from the fruit of the chocha tree, plantains, Indian juniper, aśvattha figs, udumbara figs, parūṣaka berries, grapes, and dates. Seven-day medicines include ghee, sesame oil, molasses, honey, and white sugar. Life-long medicines are of nine kinds: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, the five resin decoctions, the five powders, the five salts, and the five astringents. Root medicines include nutgrass, sweet flag, turmeric, wild ginger, white aconite, and any other medicinal roots that are not normally used for food. Stem or trunk medicines include sandalwood, clematis, juniper, deodar, heart-leaved moonseed, Indian barberry, and any other stems not used for food. Leaf medicines include the leaves of paṭola, vāśaka, the neem tree, kośātaka, and the seven-leaved saptaparṇa, and any other leaves not normally used for food. Flower medicines include vāśaka flowers, the neem tree, coriander, śata, and lotus filament, and any other flowers not normally used for food. Fruit medicines include chebulic myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, beleric myrobalan, black pepper, long pepper, and any other fruits not normally used for food. The five resin decoctions are asafetida, sal tree resin, lac, beeswax, and black pepper. The five powders are those made from barley, barley husk, corn smut, sesame, and aloe wood. The five salts are rock salt, brown salt, sanchal salt, white salt, and sea salt. The five astringents come from the mango, neem, jambū, śiriṣa, and kośam trees.[143]
[78] rgun 'brum gyi / mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[79] sge gsher dang / mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[80] dbyi mong dang / mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[81] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka_sman gzhi/ bam po/ 22_shog_277_ba6
[142] Seven-day medicines must be consumed within seven days. Life-long medicine can be taken for the duration of life.
[143] Vinayavastu, Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 278b1.

f.d: zhes sogs sman bsten tshul la sogs pa byin gyis brlab tshul dang bcas te bka' stsal/[82] 'khor lo bar ba mtshan nyid med pa'i chos bya rgod phung rir gsungs pa'i dus su lha chen po tshangs pa la gso dpyad 'bum pa gsungs shing / dus der lho phyogs be ta'i tshal grong khyer bde skyid bya bar rgyal po pad+ma_'i dpal gyi sangs rgyas dbyar gnas la spyan drangs pa'i tshe/ spyan ras gzigs dang tshangs pa/ shA ri'i bu sogs theg pa chen po'i rigs can la gcer mthong rig pa'i brgyud le'u sum stong lnga brgya pa sh+loka 'bum pa gsungs pa 'di dang gso dpyad 'bum pa gcig par bzhed pa'ang snang / gnas bya rgod phung po'i ri yin kyang 'khor lo tha ma'i dus su gser 'od dam pa rgya nag 'gyur mchog tu rnam par rgyal ba mdo sde rgyal po'i nad rab tu zhi bar byas pa'i le'u nyi shu rtsa bzhi pa las/

This and further passages teach the use of medicine and the consecration of the medicine. At the time of the middle turning of the wheel of Dharma, the “phenomena devoid of signs” turning on Vulture’s Peak, the Buddha taught the Hundred Thousand Versed Science of Healing Collection to the supreme god Brahmā. During the same period, when King Padmaśrī had invited the Buddha for the rainy-season retreat in Matkuṇa Grove in the southern town of Sukhakara, the Buddha taught the Clearly Seeing Knowledge Tantra of a hundred thousand verses in 3,500 chapters to Avalokiteśvara, Brahmā, Śāriputra, and others of the Mahayana family. It is also asserted that this work is the same as the Hundred Thousand Versed Science of Healing Collection. In the Sutra of Golden Light: King of the Supremely Victorious Sutras, which was also taught on Vulture’s Peak but during the period of the third turning, it says in chapter 24 on the elimination of illness in the version translated from the Chinese:

d.div: [82] bka' bstsal/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

rigs kyi lha mo sngon byung ba 'das pa'i dus kyi bskal pa grangs med bsam gyis mi khyab pa de'i tshe de'i dus na/ de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas rig pa dang zhabs su ldan pa bde bar gshegs pa/ 'jig rten mkhyen pa/ bla na med pa'i skyes bu kha lo bsgyur ba/ lha dang mi rnams kyi ston pa/ sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rin chen gtsug phud can zhes bya ba 'jig rten du byung la/ de'i chos kyi gzugs brnyan la spyod pa'i tshe/ rgyal po lha'i dbang phyug 'od kyi yul na tshong dpon chu 'dzin zhes bya ba sman gyi rigs la shin tu mkhas pa shes pa'i yan lag brgyad legs par khong du chud pa/ sems can gyi nad kyi sdug bsngal 'byung ba chen po bzhi mi mthun pa las gyur pa thams cad skyob cing gso bar byed pa zhig la bu khyi'u chu 'bebs zhes bya ba byad bzhin sdug cing mdzes pa mang po kun gyis mos par blta ba/ rang bzhin gyis sems myur ba/ gtsug lag rnams legs par rtogs pa/ yi ge dang / ri mo dang / rtsis dang / grangs rnams mngon par mi rtogs pa med pa zhig yod par gyur to/ /

Goddess of the family, at a time in the past countless eons ago, Buddha Ratnacūḍa, the tathāgata, the destroyer, the perfect buddha, perfectly enlightened, with an enlightenment built on the foundation of the three trainings, the sugata, knower of the world, the greatest of all beings, the charioteer, teacher of gods and men, the bhagavān buddha, came to this world. When his doctrine had become a mere reflection, there lived in the land of King Sureśvaraprabhā the merchant Jalada, who was very learned in medicine, who had fully comprehended the eight branches of knowledge, and who tended to living beings and protected them from the sufferings of illness caused by an imbalance in the four great elements. This merchant had a son called Jalavāhana, who was fair of face and of handsome build, so that all gazed upon him with great delight. By nature he was of a quick mind. He soon mastered the scriptures, and there was nothing he did not understand in matters of language, the arts, astronomy, and arithmetic.

de'i tshe rgyal po de'i yul khams na sems can brgya stong tshad med snyed nad kyi sdug bsngal sna tshogs kyis gzir bar gyur pas tha na dga' ba'i sems cung zad kyang med par gyur pa la tshong dpon gyi bu chu 'bebs snying rje skyes te/ pha sman pa'i rgyal po chen po ni rgas 'khogs gtugs pas sems can mang po'i don bya bar rngo mi thog gi/ bdag gis rang gi pha las nad gso ba'i sman dpyad gsang ba dris te/ sems can rnams kyi nad rnam pa sna tshogs gsos la yun ring por bde ba myong bar bya'o snyam nas/ pha'i thad du song ste phyag byas tshigs su bcad pas 'di skad ces dris so/ /
bdag ni sems can skyob pa'i slad/ / sman dpyad rnams ni zhu lags na/ / byams pa'i yab kyis brtser dgongs te/ / bdag la bkas ni bshad du gsol/ / zhes gsol ba btab pa thos pa dang /

At that time thousands upon thousands of the citizens of that kingdom were being tormented by sufferings brought on by all manner of diseases, so much so that a joyful mind was not to be found anywhere. Jalavāhana, the son of the merchant, felt great pity for them and thought to himself, “My father, the great doctor, is now very old and is unable to tend to so great a number of sick people. I will ask him if I may study the secret science of healing from him and by so doing cure all these beings of their illnesses and bring them the joys of a long life.” With these thoughts he approached his father, prostrated, and made his request in verse:
To protect living beings, I ask for teachings on medicine; loving father, with your great compassion, teach me with your words. His father heard his request and

tshigs su bcad de smras pa/
ngas de drang srong snying po yi/ / nad gso dpyad la brten nas ni/ / rim bzhin khyod la rab bstan gyis/ / legs par nyon la sems can skyob/ /
zla ba gsum ni dpyid kyi dus/ / zla ba gsum ni dbyar zhes grags/ / zla ba gsum ni ston gyi phyogs/ / zla ba gsum ni dgun zhes bya/ / 'di ni lo gcig las brtsams pas/ / gsum gsum so sor bshad par bya/ /

answered with the following verses:
Relying upon the science of medicine from the essence of the Rishi tradition, these things I will gradually teach you; listen well and protect all beings.
Three months is the time of spring, three months lasts the summer, three months is the autumn, three months the months of winter. This is the time of a single year explained in sets of three.

div.div: gnyis gnyis dus tshigs gcig byas nas/ / lo gcig dus ni drug tu 'gyur/ / dang po gnyis ni me tog dus/ / gsum dang bzhi ni tsha ba'i dus/ / lnga dang drug pa char pa'i dus/ / bdun dang brgyad pa ston gyi dus/ / dgu dang bcu pa grang bar gyur/ / phyi ma gnyis ni kha ba'i dus/ /

de ltar bye brag shes gyur na/ / 'gal ba med par sman btang bya/ / dus ni 'di dag rjes mthun par/ / zas skom legs par sbyor byed na/ / ltor [83]ni myur du 'ju 'gyur bas/ / nad mang dag ni skye mi 'gyur/ / dus tshigs gal te log gyur zhing / / 'byung tshan bzhi ni 'phos gyur la/ / de tshe gsos sman med gyur na/ / nges par nad kyi sdug bsngal skye/ / sman pas dus bzhi shes bya zhing / / dus tshigs dag kyang shes par bya/ /

Taking two months as a single set, the seasons number six. The first two comprise the season of flowers, the third and the fourth the hot season, the fifth and sixth the rains, the seventh and eighth are autumn, the ninth and tenth the cold months, and the last two are the time of snow.

If you know these specifics, you will administer medicine without fault. Food and drink taken in accord with the seasons produces ease of digestion in the stomach, and many an illness will not occur. Going against the dictates of the seasons produces shifts in the four elements that if not remedied by medicine, will surely bring the pains of illness. A doctor knows the four seasons and must also know the six.

d.div: [83] lto ni/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

div.div: lus kyi khams bdun rig byas nas/ / 'gal ba med par zas sman btang / / ro yi khams dang khrag dang sha/ / rus dang rkang dang klad rgyas su/[84] / nad ni 'di dag zhugs pa'i tshe/ / gsor [85]rung mi rung shes par bya/ /

nad ni tha dad rnam bzhi yod/ / rlung dang mkhris pa bad kan dang / / kun 'dus pa yi nad yin te/ / g.yo ba'i dus ni shes par bya/ / dpyid ka'i dus ni bad kan g.yo/ / dbyar ni rlung nad skye bar 'gyur/ / ston gyi dus su mkhris pa rgyas/ / dgun ni gsum po cig car ldang / /

Knowing the seven bodily constituents, you will administer food and medicine correctly. When illness enters the essence, the element, blood, flesh, bones, marrow, and fatty tissue,[144] you must know if it is curable or not.

Disease is of four types: wind, bile, phlegm, and their combinations; you should know the times of their movements. In spring phlegm is on the move, in summer wind illnesses arise, in autumn bile increases, and in winter all three arise together.

d.div: [84] rgyungs su/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[85] gso rung / mtsho sngon deb dpar/

[144] Some of the seven bodily constituents are not listed here as they usually are elsewhere (see glossary). Maybe this is because the text was translated from the Chinese. “Fatty tissue” (klad rgyas) would normally read “fat” (tshil). Prof. Losang Tenzin said this could be rendered as “brain.” “Essence” (ro) is normally “plasma” (dangs ma), and “element” (khams) is usually “semen” (khu ba).

div.div: dpyid ni tsha rtsub dro ba bza'/ / dbyar ni snum dro lan tshwa skyur/ / ston ni grang dang mngar dang snum/ / dgun ni rtsub skyur snum dang mngar/ / dus ni bzhi po 'di dag tu/ / sman dang zas skom gang bza' ba/ / gal te de bzhin bza' byed na/ / nad mang dag ni skye mi 'gyur/ /
zos 'og na ba bad kan dang / / zhu che na ba mkhris par gyur/ / zhu 'og ldang ba rlung gi dbang / / dus dang sbyar la nad shes bya/ /
After eating, phlegm disorders have power, during digestion bile disorders arise, after digestion the power of wind is strong; know illness in conjunction with its time.
nad kyi rtsa ba shes gyur nas/ / nad ni ji bzhin sman btang bya/ / nad dbyibs bye brag tha dad kyang / / sngar ni rtsa ba shes par bya/ /

rlung nad dag la snum bag btang / / mkhris pa'i nad ni 'khru na bzang / / bad kan nad ni skyug par bya/ / kun 'dus la ni sman gsum dgos/ / rlung mkhris bad kan gsum ldang ba/ / de ni kun 'dus par shes bya/ /
Knowing the root of the illness, administer medicine accordingly. Illnesses may have different forms, but first know the root.

nad ldang dus ni shes gyur kyang / / rang bzhin dag ni shes par bya/ / de ltar brtags te shes gyur nas/ / dus bzhin du ni sman dpyad bya/ / zas skom sman ni 'gal med pa/ / de ni sman pa mkhas shes bya/ /
shes pa'i yan lag brgyad rig nas/ / sman dpyad rnams ni kun sdud pas/ / 'di dag la ni gsal byas nas/ / sems can nad ni gso bar bya/ /
gtur ba dang ni rmas bsnad dang / / lus kyi nad dang 'dre gdon dang / / ma rungs dug dang byis pa dang / / tshe bsreng dang ni mthu bskyed yin/ /

Though you know the times that illnesses arise, you should also know their natures. Therefore examine in this way, and when you know, administer the medicine appropriate to the time. Food, drink, and medicine all appropriate— this is the sign of a wise doctor.
Knowing the eight branches, you will cover the entire practice of medicine. Comprehending these well, you will cure living beings of their illnesses.
Bloodletting, wounds, internal illnesses, demonic influence, poisons, infant illnesses, longevity, and potency are the eight.[145]

d.div: [145] This list differs from the eight branches detailed in Four Tantras, which are: internal illnesses, children’s illnesses, women’s illnesses, demonic influence, wounds and surgery, poisons, illnesses affecting the elderly, and aphrodisiacs.

div.div: sngar ni de yi kha dog dang / / smra tshig rang bzhin rab brtags nas/ / de 'og rmi lam dris gyur na/ / rlung mkhris bad kan bye brag shes/ /
skem rid mgo yi skra ngan zhing / / sems kyi rang bzhin mi brtan pa/ / tshig mang rmi lam 'phur mthong na/ / de ni rlung gi rang bzhin can/ /
gzhon nu skra dkar skye ba dang / / rngul che gsher ba mang ba dang / / yid gzhungs rmi lam me mthong ba/ / de ni mkhris pa'i rang bzhin can/ /
sems brtan lus ni mnyam la drang / / zhib rtog mgo dang snum zhing rlan/ / rmi lam chu dang rdzas dkar mthong / / bad kan rang bzhin shes par bya/ /
First examine their complexion and their speech, then question them on their dreams, and you will learn about their wind, bile, and phlegm.
Thin, with bad hair, a mind not firm or stable, excessive talk, and dreams of flying: these possess the nature of wind.
Prematurely gray hair, excessive perspiration, much moisture, a strong spirit, and dreams of fire: these are of the nature of bile.
Stable minds, bodies well balanced and erect, precision in thought, head oily and moist, water and white in their dreams: these possess the nature of phlegm.
kun 'dus rang bzhin gcig ldan pas/ / kha cig gnyis dang gsum ldan pas/ / phyogs gcig lhag par gang mang ba/ / de yi rang bzhin shes par byos/ /
rang bzhin rig par gyur nas ni/ / nad bzhin sman ni btang bar bya/ / 'chi ba'i mtshan ma med gyur na/ / mi de gsor rung ba zhes bya/ /
dbang pos log pa la 'dzin zhing / / bla ma sman pa dag la brnyas/ / nye du dag la khong khro na/ / 'chi ba'i mtshan mar shes par bya/ /
Having comprehended their natures, administer medicine accordingly. If the signs of death are absent, that person will recover.
Distorted sensory perceptions, abuse of one’s guru or doctor, hostility toward friends and relatives: know these as signs of death.

f.d:
mig g.yon kha dog dkar 'gyur zhing / / lce gnag [86]sna zur yo ba dang / / rna ba'i 'khor lo sngo las gyur/ / mchu thur 'phyang ba 'chi ba'i mtshan/ /
a ru ra ni rnam gcig la/ / ro ni rnam pa drug ldan te/ / nad ni thams cad sel byed pas/ / nyes med sman rnams kun gyi rgyal/ /
'bras bu gsum dang tsha ba gsum/ / sman rnams nang na rnyed par sla/ / bu ram sbrang rtsi 'o ma mar/ / 'di dag nad mang gso bar nus/ / de las gzhan pa'i sman rnams ni/ / nad dang sbyar te bskyed par bya/ /
sngar ni brtse ba'i sems bskyed nas/ / nor dang khe la blta mi bya/ / ngas ni khyod la nad gso ba'i/ / gces pa'i don ni bstan pa yin/[87] / zhes dang /

div.div: The eyes become crossed, the whites showing, the tongue turns black, nostrils flaring, the ears change their position, the lips hang down: these are signs of death.
Myrobalan, a single form of all six tastes, eliminating all disease without fault, the king of medicines.[146]

The three fruits and the three spices[147] are among medicines easy to obtain. Molasses, honey, milk, and ghee have the power to cure many an ailment. Other medicines should be compounded according to the illness.
From the outset have a compassionate mind, do not look to wealth or gain. I have explained to you the precious principles of the science of healing.[148]

d.div: [86] lce nag_mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[87] sde dge_555_bka'/ rgyud/ pa_'phags pa gser 'od dam pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 24_shog_130_na2

[146] Of the six types of chebulic myrobalan, King or Conqueror (vijaya, rnam rgyal) is supreme and is usually found only in the celestial realms. The verse plays with its name: “form” (rnam), “king” (rgyal).
[147] Chebulic, emblic, and baleric myrobalan, black pepper, long pepper, and ginger.
[148] Sutra of Golden Light: King of the Supremely Victorious Sutras, chap. 24, Toh 555 Kangyur, rgyud, pa, 130a2.

f.d:
mdo sde'i dbang po'i rgyal po le'u nyer dgu pa ye shes sde'i 'gyur dang / gser 'od dam pa le'u nyer gcig pa gnyis ha lam mtshungs par de bzhin gshegs pa gtsug phud can gyi mtshan la rin chen gtsug tor can/ khye'u chu 'bebs kyi yab la ral pa 'dzin/ tshigs su bcad pa'ang /
zla gsum dbyar te zla gsum ston du shes/ / gsum ni dgun te gsum ni dpyid yin no/[88] / zhes rgyas bsdus dang 'gyur gyi khyad par che tsam yod la/

The Sutra of Golden Light: Mighty King of Sutras in twenty-nine chapters translated by Yeshé Dé and the Sutra of Golden Light in twenty-one chapters give similar accounts.[149] In these two versions the name of Tathāgata Ratnacūḍa is given as Ratnaśikhin, and the father of Jalavāhana is rendered as Jaṭiṃdhara. As for content, these latter two versions say, for example:
Three months are summer, three are autumn, three are winter, and three are spring. There are quite big differences in length and translation between these versions.

d.div: [88] sde dge_555_bka'/ rgyud/ pa_'phags pa gser 'od dam po'i mdo/ le'u/ 24_shog_131_na2

[149] There are three versions of Sutra of Golden Light in the Degé Kangyur: Sutra of Golden Light: King of the Supremely Victorious Sutras (Toh 555); and two versions under the name Sutra of Golden Light: Mighty King of Sutras (Toh 556 and 557). The sutra quoted at length above is Toh 555, the version translated by Chödrup from a Chinese text. The version of the sutra translated from the Sanskrit into English by R. E. Emmerick is Toh 557 (Oxford: Pali Text Society, 1979).

f.d: gang ltar ston pa rang nyid sngon khye'u chu 'bebs su gyur dus yab tshong dpon ral pa 'dzin las sman dpyad gsan pa'i tshul bskyar te gsungs shing skabs 'di nyid du gso ba rig pa kun gyi snying por gyur pa bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsung ba'i gnas grong khyer lta na sdug ces pa snga rabs rdza pa sogs nub phyogs a+yon gyi yul dang / bi byi sogs ri rab kyi rtse sum cu rtsa gsum gyi dbus lta na sdug dang gcig pa/ stong mi nyag 'ug pa gdong nag pa sogs thub pa gangs can mtsho'i zhing khams gzhi dang snying po me tog gis brgyan pa'i gnas kyi dum bu gcig yin zhes dang /[89] gdong nag pa sogs/ gangs can 'bigs byed ri sogs dbus su ni/ /zhes gzhal yas khang ri bzhi rgya dpangs dang bcas zhib par bshad pa/

Nevertheless, in all versions our Teacher recalls a time when, born as Jalavāhana, he learned the science of medicine from his father Jaṭiṃdhara. At this time too the Buddha taught the Essence of Ambrosia: The Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches, the very heart of all aspects of the science of healing, in a place called Sudarśana. Concerning the location of Sudarśana, Dza[150] and other early Tibetans place it in the western land of Oḍḍiyāna.[151] Biji[152] and others maintain that it refers to the Sudarśana situated in the center of Trāyastriṃśa heaven on the summit of Mount Meru. Ukpa Dong Nakpa from Tongmi Nyak and others say that it is in the realm of the Buddha Himasaras and is one part of the place known as Foundation and Essence Adorned with Flowers. Dong Nakpa and others say, “Amid the mountain ranges Himavat, Vindhya, etc.…”[153] and go on to describe in detail the palace, the four mountains, and the respective dimensions.

d.div: [89] bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsungs pa'i gnas gang yin ngos 'dzin srol mi 'dra ba 'di gsum zur khar blo gros rgyal po'i mes po'i zhal lung/ shog_19_na6_nang yang byung /
[150] Dza Yeshé Sung, twelfth-century medical scholar.

[151] Orgyen, or Urgyen, in Tibetan. The Indian spelling has several variants as well, e.g., Uḍḍiyāna, Oḍiyān. Oḍḍiyāna was the seat of the early development of Buddhist tantra. Its exact location is a subject of some debate.
[152] A.k.a. Tsenpashilaha. See the account of his life later in the text.
[153] Cited in Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors by Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, 19a6.

f.d: bdag chen pa sogs mngon pa mdzod nas gsungs pa'i ri bzhi dang sbyar ba/ brang ti dpal ldan 'tsho byed 'bigs byed sogs ri bzhi po'i dbus na yod pas so so skye bos blta bar mi nus pa/ chos rgyal byang pa rdo rje gdan kho nar bzhed pa/[90] rje zur mkhar ba d+harma swa mi gso dpyad kun gyi rgyal po dpal ldan rgyud bzhi zhes bka' sor bzhag de don ltar bzhed pa las gnas dang bka' bstan sogs kyi bgros mi mdzad pa/

Dakchenpa and others identify the four mountains[154] with the four mountains taught in the Treasury of Abhidharma. Drangti Palden Tsojé says that because Sudarśana is in the middle of the four mountains, Vindhya, and so on, it cannot be seen by ordinary beings. The Dharma lord Jangpa asserts it to be exclusively in Bodhgāya.[155] The master Surkhar Dharmaswāmi says, “The glorious four tantras, supreme among all medical literature…” thereby staking his position by simply leaving the text as it is without entering into discussions on the location of Sudarśana or on whether Four Tantras is the word of the Buddha.[156]

d.div: [90] bod kyi 'tsho byed mkhas pa snga ma'i bzhed pa mi 'dra ba 'dir bkod pa rnams zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i mes po'i zhal lung / shog_21_ba4_nang du'ang byung /

[154] These are the four mountains, mentioned in Four Tantras, that surround Sudarśana. The Dakchenpa referred to here is presumably an early master from the Sakya tradition, but I am unable to identify him.

[155] These assertions are all cited in Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, 21b4. The identities have been inserted as annotations in between the text, but here the author has included them as main text.
[156] In Tibetan medical literature there is much discussion on whether Four Tantras is the word of the Buddha or composed at a later date. The author investigates this matter later.

f.d: mtsho smad mkhan chen dang byar paN gnyi ga rdza pa dang mthun par nub phyogs a+yon gyi yul/ byar pos lugs gcig tu phyi nang gsang gsum du phye bar phyi lha'i grong khyer lta na sdug / nang rdo rje gdan byang pa dang mthun/ gsang ba rang sems su ngos bzung ba dang / bla rta tshe dbang gis phyi nang gsang gsum g.yu thog tu sman rgyal gyis gsungs pa rjes mthun kho na dang / 'brug pa pad+ma dkar po 'o skol gyi ston pas 'tsho byed gzhon nu ri bo spos kyi ngad ldan du 'khrid nas de'i khengs pa bcag rjes zlos bur [91]gsungs pa yang mkhas pa la la dag gnas de gdos bcas su grub pa med de/ ston pa sman pa'i rgyal po'i thugs rnam par mi rtog pa'i ye shes kyi spyod yul rnam pa de dang de dag tu snang ba dang / gsung pa po'i bdag rkyen du gyur pa'i sman rgyal de ston pa thub pa'i dbang pos gang la gang 'dul gyi tshul bstan par bzhed pa/

Tsomé Khenchen and Jarpo Panchen agree with Dza that Sudarśana is located in Oḍḍiyāna. Jarpo talks of one tradition with outer, inner, and secret aspects: the outer celestial city of Sudarśana, the inner Sudarśana of Bodhgāya, as asserted by Jangpa, and the secret Sudarśana identified with one’s own mind. Lata Tsewang follows the outer, inner, and secret division as taught by Medicine Buddha to Yuthok Gönpo.
