Drukpa Pema Karpo says that our Teacher took the physician Jivaka Kumāra[157] to Gandhamārdana Mountain[158] to humble his pride and taught him Four Tantras through repetition.[159] However, some scholars say that this place has no physical materiality, because it was the sphere of perception enjoyed by the nonconceptual gnosis that is the mind of our Teacher as Medicine Buddha appearing in that form. Also, Medicine Buddha, who was the dominant cause for the creation of the speaker of the tantras, was Śākyamuni Buddha appearing in a form suitable for taming disciples.

d.div: [91] 'brug pa pad+ma dkar po'i gsung 'bum/ ka_rgyud bzhi'i 'grel pa gzhan la phan gter/ shog_3_ba2
[157] Famous Indian doctor at the time of the Buddha to whom a whole chapter is dedicated below.
[158] One of the four mountains surrounding Sudarśana.
[159] Treasure for the Benefit of Others: A Presentation of Four Tantras, Collected Works, ka, 3b2.

f.d: sog bzlog pa 'og phyogs su 'jig rten gyi khams baiDUR+ya ltar snang ba yod pa'i sman bla dang zhing 'dir g.yu thog mgon po zhes grags pas sprul pa'i gnas yin pa/ de nyid byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa spyad pa'i tshe sgrubs pa'i dge ba'i rtsa ba las byung ba'i gnas su 'dod pa sogs lung rigs gang gis kyang mi 'grub pa/ kha cig shar phyogs baiDUR+ya snang gi zhing du 'dod pa sogs mtha' klas shing /

Sokdok Lodrö Gyaltsen says, “In the lower region the world called Shining Like Beryl with Medicine Buddha, and in this world Yönten Gönpo…” thereby asserting that it is known to be a manifested place and claiming that it was created from virtues accumulated during the pursuit of bodhisattva practices. These claims do not stand up to scripture or reasoning. Some assert it to be in the eastern realm of Beryl Light. There are so many assertions.

zur mkhar blo gros rgyal pos mes po'i zhal lung du lugs de dag thams cad bkag nas/[92] bye brag tu bshad pa zhes kha cig dbyig gnyen gyis mdzad par grags kyang / don dgra bcom pa bdun gyi mngon pa sde bdun gyi lung khol bur 'gyur ba bu ston chos 'byung sogs su drangs par/

Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo in his Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors rejects all these assertions[160] and then quotes a passage—which can be found in Buton’s History of the Dharma and other works—from the Great Ocean of Specific Explanation (Mahāvibhāṣa), which some people say was written by Vasubandhu but which actually has been extracted from the seven categories of knowledge composed by the seven arhats:

d.div: [92] zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i gsung / mes po'i zhal lung / ka shog /22_na2
[160] Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, 22a2.

chos 'khor gnas dang yangs pa can/ / sa dkar can dang lha yi gnas/ / byis pa gsod dang kau shA m+bI/ / 'brog dang mchod rten ri dang ni/ / 'od ma'i grong dang sgrar bcas dang / / ser skya'i gnas kyi grong khyer du/ / 'di rnams su ni thub pa yi/ / skyes mchog lo re lo re bzhugs/ / nyi shu rtsa gsum mnyan yod du/ / sman gyi nags su lo bzhi ste/ / 'bar ba'i phug gi gnas su gnyis/ / rgyal po'i khab kyi grong du lnga/ / dka' ba spyad pa lo drug ste/ / nyi shu rtsa dgu khab gnas su/ / rgyal ba de ltar brgyad cu la/ / thub mchog dam pa mya ngan 'das/[93] /

In the places of turning the wheel of Dharma, in Vaiśālī, Paṇḍubhūmi, the celestial realms, Bālaghna, Kauśāmbī, the wilderness, in Uśīragiri and the Bamboo Grove, in Saśabda and Kapilavastu, the greatest of all beings spent a single year in each. In Śrāvastī twenty-three years, four in the medicine forest, two in Indraśaila, five in Rajgir, six in ascetic practice, and twenty-nine years in the palace. In this way the Conqueror spent his eighty years and then passed into supreme nirvana.[161]
[93] bu ston rin chen grub kyi gsung 'bum/ ya_bde bar gshegs pa'i bstan pa'i gsal byed chos kyi 'byung gnas gsung rab rin po che'i mdzod/ shog_78_na6
[161] Collected Works, ya, 78a6. The author is saying that Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo rests his assertion on the line in bold.

f.d: zhes pa'i lung tsam la yid bzung ste smra na'ang / de ltar du sgrubs na/ bka' 'gyur rin po che rgyal rtse them spang ma'i rgyud tha par bzhugs pa/ zhang ye shes sde'i 'gyur la slad mar jo bo rje dang dge slong tshul khrims rgyal bas skad gsar bcad kyis bcos pa/ de bzhin gshegs pa'i stobs bskyed pa baiDUR+ya'i 'od ces bya ba'i gzungs kyi gleng gzhir/

Thus, he asserts the whereabouts of Sudarśana by relying on this scripture alone. If this establishes the whereabouts of Sudarśana, however, then consider this passage from the introduction to the Beryl Light Dhāraṇī Developing the Power of the Tathāgata Meditative Concentration. This text is found in the precious Gyantsé Thempangma Kangyur[162] in the tha volume on tantra, and was translated by Shang Yeshé Dé and edited and revised by Jowo Jé and the monk Tsültrim Gyalwa:

d.div: [162] An edition of the Kangyur, or collected words of the Buddha, deposited in the fifteenth century in Palkhor Chöde Monastery in Gyantsé. See Paul Harrison in Cabezón and Jackson, eds., Tibetan Literature: A Study in Genre, p. 80.

bcom ldan 'das sman gyi gnas na/ dge slong gi dge 'dun chen po dang / byang chub sems dpa'i dge 'dun chen po dang thabs gcig tu bzhugs te/ de'i tshe bcom ldan 'das kyis sangs rgyas kyi zhing bskul ba zhes bya ba'i ting nge 'dzin la snyoms par zhugs so/ / de ma thag tu stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams thams cad rab tu g.yos so/ / lha'i tsan dan gyi phye ma dang me tog gi char dpag tu med pa bab bo/ / de bzhin gshegs pa bdun 'khor dang bcas pa yang 'jig rten gyi khams 'dir gshegs te/ de bzhin gshegs pa'i sngon gyi dge ba'i rtsa ba las byung ba'i seng ge'i khri la bzhugs shing / byang chub sems dpa' thams cad kyas ni bskor/ lha dang / klu dang / gnod sbyin dang / dri za dang / lha ma yin dang / nam mkha' lding dang / mi'am ci dang / lto 'phye chen po dang / rgyal po dang / blon po dang / bram ze dang / khyim bdag rnams kyis yongs su bskor bar gyur to/ / de nas sangs rgyas kyi mthus 'jam dpal gzhon nur gyur pa stan las langs te/ thal mo sbyar nas 'di skad ces gsol to/ / da bzhi+en gshegs pa thams cad dgongs su gsol/ sems can thams cad kyi sdig pa thams cad sbyang ba dang / nad thams cad bsal ba dang / re ba thams cad bskang du gsol/[94]

The Bhagavān was staying in the place of medicine together with a great gathering of monks and a great gathering of bodhisattvas. At that time the Bhagavān was dwelling in the meditative concentration known as invoking buddhafields. Suddenly every world in the great trichiliocosmic universe shook, and celestial sandalwood dust and countless flowers rained down from above. The seven tathāgatas with their vast entourages appeared in this world and sat upon lion thrones created from their previous merits and surrounded by the bodhisattvas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, demigods, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas, kings, ministers, brahmans, and lay people. Then, by the power of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, put his palms together, and said, “Tathāgatas, hear this request. Purify all beings from their wrong deeds, cure them of their illnesses, fulfill their hopes.”[163]
[94] sde dge_505_bka'/ rgyud/ da_'phags pa de bzhin gshegs pa'i ting nge 'dzin gyi stobs bskyed pa'i baiDUR+ya'i 'od ces bya ba'i gzungs/ shog_284_na2
[163] Toh 505 Kangyur, rgyud, da, 284a2.

f.d: zhes gsol bar bdag cag gi ston pas de bzhin gshegs pa brgyad/ yum chen mo/ /'jam dpal la sogs pa byang chub sems dpa' bcu drug /mchog zung / tshangs pa/ brgya byin/ rgyal chen bzhi/ klu'i dge bsnyen/ gnod sbyin gyi sde dpon bcu gnyis rnams la phyag 'tshal ba gsungs pa'i rjes thogs su/ sman bla mched bdun bdag cag gi ston pa bcas gsung dbyangs gcig gis gzungs kyi tshig bka' bstsal pa/[95] de'i dus su rgyud gsungs byas na lung gong gsal las btsan pa tsam mchis te/

To this request our Teacher pays homage to the eight tathāgatas, the great mother,[164] the sixteen bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī and so forth—Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Brahmā, Indra, the four great kings,[165] the great nāga upāsakas, and the twelve yakṣa chieftains. Then the seven medicine buddhas and our Teacher teach the dhāraṇī in unison. If you assert that the medical tantras were taught at this time, then apart from the previous citation, such an assertion can be nothing but stubborn insistence,

d.div: [95] sde dge_505_bka'/ rgyud/ da_'phags pa de bzhin gshegs pa'i ting nge 'dzin gyi stobs bskyed pa'i baiDUR+ya'i 'od ces bya ba'i gzungs/ shog_285_na5
[164] Yum chen mo, but “Prajñāpāramitā” in the actual tantra.
[165] The guardians of the four directions in the Cāturmahārājika heaven: Vaiśravaṇa (= Kubera), Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa.

f.d: rgyud rang gi dngos bstan ltar na/ drang srong gi gnas sman gyi grong khyer lta na sdug /ces byung ba gzhon nu don thams cad grub pa bltams nas yun mi ring ba na/ rgya che rol par ri'i rgyal po gangs ri'i ngos nas drang srong nag pos mtshan brtags pa dang /[96] phran tshegs ltar na ri ki skin da na nas drang srong mi dkar bas mtshan brtags pa/[97]

because the actual tantra begins, “The abode of rishis, the city known as Sudarśana.” [There are many “abodes of rishis”:] Soon after he was born, Kumāra Siddhartha—“he who accomplishes all aims”—was named. According to the Sutra of Great Play he was named by Rishi Asita from the slopes of the Himalaya, the king of mountain ranges.[166] According to the Short Vinaya he was named by Rishi Asita from Kiskindana Mountain.[167]

d.div: [96] sde dge_95_bka'/ mdo sde/ kha_rgya cher rol pa'i mdo/ shog_54_na7
[97] sde dge_6_bka'/ 'dul ba/ tha dang da_'dul ba phran tshegs kyi gzhi/ shog_310na nas 333na bar bzhugs/
[166] Lalitavistara Sutra, Toh 95 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 54a7.
[167] The whole story is found in Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu, Toh 6 Kangyur, ’dul ba, over volumes tha and da, 310–33.

f.d: 'dul ba gzhi dang mngon 'byung mthun pa ltar na ri bo kun 'dzin zhes bya bar gnas pa'i drang srong nyon mongs med 'khor dang bcas pa ser skyar 'ongs te/ rgyal bu'i mtshan bltas nas/ sa bdag rtog pa po rnams blo 'khrul te/ /rtsod pa'i dus na 'khor lo bsgyur mi 'byung / /zhes sogs mngon par rdzogs par 'tshang rgya bar lung bstan pa dang /[98]

According to the Basic Vinaya and the Sutra of Going Forth a Rishi Araṇa who lived on Ādhara Mountain came with his retinue to Kapilavastu. He examined the signs on the prince and announced, “Mighty ruler, those who examined are wrong! Universal sovereigns do not appear in the kaliyuga,” thereby prophesizing the young prince’s enlightenment.[168]

d.div: [98] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_mngon par byung ba'i mdo/ shog_15_na4
[168] Abhiniṣkramaṇa Sutra, Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 15a4.

f.d: grong khyer ser skya dang dpag tshad bcu gnyis kyis bar chod pa na drang srong ngan spong gi gnas me tog dang 'bras bu la sogs pa phun sum tshogs pa zhig yod pa der shing ta la rnams lo bcu gnyis kyi bar gser gyi me tog dang 'bras bur ldan par gyur pa/ gzhon nu don grub rab tu byung ba'i nyin mo nas shing phal bar gyur pa/

Twelve leagues[169] from the city of Kapilavastu was the abode of Rishi Bhṛgu, blessed with the most beautiful fruits and flowers. There the palmyra tree held its golden flowers and its fruits for twelve years uninterrupted. From the day Kumāra Siddhartha went forth into homelessness, this tree became an ordinary tree.

d.div: [169] Yojana, a distance reckoned to be around either four or nine miles.

f.d: dka' ba spyod pa'i tshe bya rgod phung po'i ri dang ha cang mi ring ba drang srong rnams kyi bsti gnas su gshegs te/ rkang pa ya gcig 'greng ba dang / me lngas gdung ba sogs dka' ba nyis 'gyur du mdzad pa/

During his years of asceticism, he went to stay in a community of rishis who lived very close to Vulture’s Peak. There he underwent ascetic practices, such as standing on one leg and enduring the torment of the five fires, to twice the amount required.
cho 'phrul chen po bstan pa'i tshe nags tshal zhig na drang srong lnga brgya yod pa mu stegs ston pa drug gis grogs su sbran pa bden pa mthong ba/
During the display of miracles, five hundred forest-dwelling rishis who were summoned as companions by the six non-Buddhist teachers developed great insights.
mnyan yod dang nye ba'i nags khrod gcig na drang srong lnga brgya gnas pa sbyin sreg byed pa'i tshe/ ston pas de dag gi thab nang du zhabs rjes re sprul zhing me spar mi nus par byin gyis brlabs pa/

Once while five hundred rishis[170] were performing fire offerings in the middle of a dense forest near Śrāvastī, our Teacher manifested his footprint in the hearth and by its power prevented the fire from blazing.

d.div: [170] Here “five hundred” is a term of quantity meaning “a considerable number.”

f.d: khyim bdag gdangs can gyi lo rgyus skabs lho phyogs nas drang srong lnga brgya yul dbus su mgon med zas sbyin gyi sar 'ongs pa bcom ldan 'das la tshur shog gi bsnyen par rdzogs pa/
In the story of the householder Ghoṣila, five hundred rishis came from the south to the Anāthapiṇḍada retreat in Magadha and became monks under the ordination injunction, “Come here.”

ston pa'i sku tshe'i smad bstan pa 'od srung la gtod par nye ba'i dus u dum pa'i nags su bzhugs te nyin par rdzing bu dal 'bab kyi 'gram na phebs pa dang / drang srong ke na'i bu 'khor dang bcas pa der gnas pas chos nyan nas phyir mi 'ong ba thob pa dang / drang srong ri bo 'khor lnga brgya dang bcas pa mchog tu dad de bsnyen par rdzogs pa sogs

In the latter part of his life, when he was preparing to entrust the doctrine to Kāśyapa, the Buddha was staying in an udumbara forest. In the daytime he went to a pool by the Mandākinī River, and there lived Rishi Kenavaputra with his retinue, who on hearing the teaching attained the level of nonreturner. Rishi Parvata and his retinue of five hundred disciples developed great faith in the Buddha and became ordained.

bdag cag gi ston pa'i sku ring la 'phags yul du drang srong gi gnas mang du yod cing 'khor yang ji snyed cig 'dus par gsungs par ma zad/ sangs rgyas kyi bka' rgya mtsho lta bu nas chu thigs tsam gangs can du 'gyur bar yang drang srong rgyas pas zhus pa'i mdo yod pa sogs nas drang srong lhung ba ri dwags kyi nags sam u dum pa'i nags sogs drang srong gi gnas su ston pa shAkya thub pa sman blar bzhengs te ri dang grong khyer gzhal med khang sogs der 'dus kyi 'khor gyi snang ngor gsar du sprul nas gsungs so zhes smras kyang klan ka 'jug pa'i yul min pa dang /

Therefore, in the accounts of our Teacher’s life are mentioned many “abodes of rishis” in India and as many retinues. Moreover, from the vast ocean of Buddha’s teaching, the tiny drop of teachings translated into Tibetan contains sutras such as the Sutra Requested by the Rishi Vyāsa, which talk about the deer forest or udumbara forest where the rishis fell to earth. However, the argument that in one of these “abodes of rishis” our Teacher Śākyamuni arose in the form of Medicine Buddha, manifested the mountains, city, and the palace for the eyes of the audience gathered there, and then taught the medical tantras is unfounded.

blon po'i bka' thang gi le'u nyer bzhi par/
nad kyis zin pa sman gyi gso ba la: sangs rgyas sman bla 'tsho byed gzhon nu yis: rgya gar pad+ma can gyi yul khams nas: bdud rtsi snying po'i rgyud dang man ngag rgyud:[99] ces 'phags yul pad+ma can du bshad pa'ang yod mod/

In the twenty-fourth chapter of the Chronicles of Ministers from the Five Chronicles it says:
For the curing of those in the clutches of illness, the Essence of Ambrosia Tantra and Instruction Tantra came from Medicine Buddha and Jivaka Kumāra in the lotus land of India.[171] This describes the place of the teaching as being in the lotus land of India.

d.div: [99] slob dpon pad+ma 'byung gnas kyi bka' thang sde lnga/ blon po bka'i thang yig /le'u/ 24_sman gtan la phab pa'i skabs/ shog_499_yig phreng 1
[171] Orgyen Lingpa, Five Chronicles, 24.499.1.

f.d: 'on te bdag gi bla ma nges pa don gyi thams cad mkhyen pa ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsan yig gang+gA'i chu rgyun dang / bca' bsko/ dkar chag rnams su o rgyan yul kho nar bzhed cing /[100]

However, in his Stream of Ganges: An Account of Teachings Received, as well as in his compositions on constitutional documents and cataloging of scripture, my lama, Ngawang Losang Gyatso, in reality an omniscient buddha, asserts it to be in the land of Oḍḍiyāna.

d.div: [100] bdag gi bla ma nges pa don gyi thams cad mkhyen pa ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsan yig gang+gA'i chu rgyun dang / bca' bsko/ dkar chag rnams su o rgyan yul kho nar bzhed cing /

f.d: zur mkhar blo gros rgyal pos/ o rgyan gyi yul du 'dod pa ni gzhung 'di gsang sngags kyi rgyud du bzung bas nongs pa yin te rgyud phal cher gsungs pa'i gnas o rgyan yin par bsams pa'i phyir ro/[101] /

According to Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, “Asserting Oḍḍiyāna to be the place where this tantra was taught is a mistake that arises from holding that this scripture is a tantra of secret mantra because most tantras were taught in Oḍḍiyāna.”[172]

d.div: [101] zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i gsung / mes po'i zhal lung / ka shog /19_na4
[172] Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, 19a4.

f.d: zhes pa ni sgrub byed ma dgongs par dgag pa mdzad pa ste/ rgyud gsungs sar nges pa ci yod/ rnam snang mngon byang lta bu ri rab kyi rtse dang dus 'khor du rgyud thams cad dpal ldan 'bras spungs kyi mchod rten du gsungs par bshad pas mtha' ma bkag cing / gso ba rig pa'i rgyud 'di nyid sde snod du bsdu dus mdo sde'i sde snod du bsdu bar bzhed pa dang / sman mdo brgyad brgya pa bya rgyud yin pas bya rgyud du bzhed pa de dag la bdag bskyed kyi skor dgag gzhag du ma zhig yod mod de/ rje bla mas bca' bskor/

This statement is a refutation without considering a proper proof, for what certainty is there on the locale where the tantras were taught? Some tantras, such as the Vairocana Enlightenment Tantra were taught on the summit of Mount Meru, and according to the Kālacakra Tantra, all tantras were taught in the great stupa of Dhānyakaṭaka. Therefore, we cannot be so conclusive. Also, when this science of medicine tantra is classified in a particular scriptural basket, it belongs to the basket of sutra. The Medicine Sutras in Eight Hundred Verses are action tantras, and there is much assertion and refutation around the topic of self-generation when classifying them this way. However, my lama says in his Monastic Regulations:

zab mo snying tig dang 'grel ba sogs bya rgyud du 'grel ba'i ngal ba mi dgos par bskyed pa ma hA yo ga'i sgrub sde brgyad kyi nang nas che mchog bdud rtsi'i rgyud kyi sde tshan du bzhugszhes bka' stsal pa ltar dang gong du brjod pa bzhin o rgyan gyi yul kho na yin la/[102]

Without the hardship of trying to categorize the Profound Heartdrop and related texts as action tantras, they can be placed into the category of the Supreme Ambrosia Tantras from among the eight classifications of generation-stage Mahāyoga practice.[173] Also, as explained above, he asserts the the tantra was taught exclusively in Oḍḍiyāna.

d.div: [102] rje bla mas bca' bskor/ zab mo snying tig dang 'grel ba sogs bya rgyud du 'grel ba'i ngal ba mi dgos par bskyed pa ma hA yo ga'i sgrub sde brgyad kyi nang nas che mchog bdud rtsi'i rgyud kyi sde tshan du bzhugs zhes bka' stsal pa ltar dang gong du brjod pa bzhin o rgyan gyi yul kho na yin la/
[173] Untraced.

f.d: dus kyang gser 'od dam pa'i le'u nyer bzhi par sngon sangs rgyas rin chen gtsug tor can gyi bstan pa la/ shAkya la ga na be con rgyal po lha'i dbang phyug 'od dang / yab sras gtsang ma tshong dpon ral pa 'dzin zhes bya ba sman pa gso bar byed pa khams la mchog tu mkhas pa/ tshe'i rig byed yan lag brgyad kyi rgyud dang ldan pa dang / bdag cag gi ston pa tshong dpon de'i sras khye'u chu 'bebs rnams su gyur pa'i tshe/ yul de'i sems can rnams la rims nad drag po byung bas khye'u chu 'bebs kyis yab tshong dpon ral pa 'dzin la sman dpyad rnams gsan pa'i sngon byung bya rgod phung po'i rir rigs kyi lha mo byang chub yang dag par bsdus pa la gsungs pa'i snga phyi tsam du yin la/

Concerning the time in Buddha’s life when the tantra was taught, the twenty-fourth chapter of the Sutra of Golden Light talks of a previous age during the existence of the doctrine of Buddha Ratnaśikhin when the Śākya king Daṇḍapāṇi was born as king Sureśvaraprabhā, and when the Buddha’s father Śuddhodana was born as the merchant Jaṭiṃdhara, a physician and healer skilled in the workings of the bodily constituents[174] and possessed of the eight branches of Āyurveda. At that time our Teacher was born as his son Jalavāhana, and during the life of this pure father and pure son there occurred a great epidemic that brought much suffering to the beings of the land. Therefore, the son Jalavāhana decided to learn the science of medicine from his father. The tantra was taught around the time this story of past events was taught on Vulture’s Peak to the goddess Bodhisamuccayā.[175]

d.div: [174] Khams, dhātu. This term can be used for the four elements of earth, water, fire, and air that make up the body or it can refer to the seven bodily constituents or tissues (see glossary).

[175] In the Great Garuḍa History of Medicine (p. 10) from Eighteen Auxiliary Texts, one of the reference history books used by the author, it states that Four Tantras was taught at the time of this sutra.

f.d: de yang gleng gzhir byang chub sems dpa' mdzes pa'i tog bcom ldan 'das shAkya thub pa dgung lo brgyad cu zhig thub ste 'di ltar sku tshe thung snyam pa'i rtog pa skyes pa dang / slob dpon lung ston pa bram ze ko'u dan+ya zhes bya bas de bzhin gshegs pa yongs su mya ngan las 'da' ba'i sgra thos nas yungs 'bru tsam gyi ring bsrel stsol bar gsol ba sogs snang gshis mchog zung mya ngan las ma 'das pa'i gong tsam ston pa'i sku tshe'i smad char/ dpal au Di ya na'i yul drang srong gi gnas sman gyi nags de'i dbus ri bo ngos bzhi pa rgyar dpag tshad brgyad dang dpangs su gsum dang ldan pa'i ri de dag gi rtse mor ston pas gsar du sprul pa'i gnas lag mthil ltar mnyam pa gseg ma la sogs pa ma dag pa'i rdzas med pa khyon yangs shing tha gru mnyam pa rnam pa kun tu 'od dang 'od zer 'phro ba nyin mtshan gyi snang ba med pa sa gzhi de nyid mnan na nem nem zhing btegs na 'phar ba/ bdug spos kyi dri mngar ba/

In the introduction to this sutra, the bodhisattva Ruciraketu sees that the Bhagavān Śākyamuni will live to be eighty and thinks this is too short a lifespan. Also the ācārya and soothsayer brahman Kauṇḍinya hears that the Tathāgata will soon pass away and requests a relic the size of a mustard seed. Based on this we can say that in the latter part of our Teacher’s life, a little before the passing of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, in the land of Śrī Oḍḍiyāṇa, in the midst of the medicine forest known as the abode of rishis, on the summit of a four-sided mountain[176] eight leagues long and three leagues high, our Teacher manifested a place as smooth as one’s palm, free of all obstructions such as stones and gravel, a wide open area glowing with light and light rays blurring the distinction between day and night, soft and springy to the touch, and pervaded by the sweet smell of incense.

d.div: [176] Although the tantra clearly talks of four distinct mountains, according to Prof. Losang Tenzin, Desi Sangyé Gyatso asserts these mountains should be seen as possessing one side each. Otherwise, each mountain would have sides facing all four directions, which would contradict the descriptions in the tantra detailing the different types of medical plants growing on these mountains depending on the particular direction they faced. Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo in his Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors also says that this is one mountain with four sides and that the names of actual mountains given to these sides—Gandhamārdana, Himavat, Vindhya, and Malaya or Malabar—are not to be taken literally.

f.d: de'i dbus na sman gyi grong khyer lta na sdug ces bya ba mi'i rin po che gser dang dngul dang mu tig dkar dmar baiDUR+ya sogs yid bzhin gyi nor bu rin po che sna lnga las yongs su grub pa'i gzhal yas khang gru bzhi sgo bzhi pa rgyan rtsig pa rim pa lnga dang ldan pa sgo re na rgyal chen re yod de gzhal yas khang de'i rgyan ni sman gyi nor bu rin po che rnam pa sna tshogs pas brgyan pa ste mda' yab pu shu lha'i rin po che sna lngas dra ba dra phyed mig mangs ris su byas pa/ byang chub sems dpa'i rin po che sna lngas thog gi rgyal mtshan dang g+ha Ta rnams kyi tog la sogs pa byas pa 'od dang 'od zer dus kun tu 'phro ba phyi ltas nang gsal ba dang nang ltas phyi gsal ba ste/

In its midst was the city of Sudarśana, boasting a palace built entirely from the precious stones of the human realm—gold, silver, white and red pearls, and beryl—and from the five precious wish-fulfilling jewels. The palace has four sides and four doors, and its ornamented walls are five layers thick. At each door stands one of the great king guardians. The palace’s decorations include various medicinal jewels adorning parts of the palace. Five types of celestial jewels adorn the parapets, forming a crisscross pattern of garlands and half garlands. Five types of bodhisattva jewels adorn the tops of the victory standards on the roof and the ghaṭa.[177] At all times these jewels glow and radiate light, and they have the power to explain the inner meaning of external signs and the outer meaning of inner signs.

d.div: [177] Possibly the large vases that stand on the roofs of palaces.

f.d:
dpal mgon 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis/
mi'i nor bu rin po che ni yongs su dag pa'i kha dog dang ldan pas dug dang gdon dang mun pa dang skrangs pa dang tsha ba la sogs pa'i sdug bsngal sel bar byed pas na yon tan gyi khyad par bdun dang ldan la/ lha'i nor bu rin po che la yon tan snga ma rnams kyi steng du rtag par lha'i lus kyi rjes su 'brang ba dang / yang dag pa dang / smra bar rung ba dang / yang zhing mi lci ba ste yon tan bcu gcig dang ldan zhing / byang chub sems dpa'i nor bu rin po che de la ni/ snga ma'i yon tan bcu gcig gi steng du/ sems can rnams kyi 'chi 'pho ba rtogs pa dang / skye ba'i mtha' shes pa dang chos kyi sgra skad sna tshogs pa 'byung ba ste yon tan gyi khyad par bcu bzhi dang ldan pa'o/[103] / zhes gsungs pa ltar nor bu'am rin po che de rnams kyi mthu dang nus pa des ni rlung gi nad dang mkhris pa'i nad dang bad kan gyi nad dang ldan pa'i nad dang 'dus pa'i nad las gyur pa'i nad bzhi brgya rtsa bzhi thams cad sel bar byed pa ste/

The master Ārya Nāgārjuna said:
Precious jewels and stones of the human realm have a purity of color and possess seven qualities, including eliminating the sufferings of poison, demons, darkness, swellings, and fever. Celestial jewels possess these qualities, too, as well as continuously accompanying the body of the celestial being being perfectly pure, having the ability to talk, and being light in weight. Therefore they possess eleven qualities. Bodhisattva jewels have these eleven qualities and are furthermore able to tell when living beings will pass away and when their births will be at an end, and are able to communicate the Dharma in various languages. Thus they possess these fourteen qualities.[178] Therefore, these jewels or precious stones possessing these powers and abilities can eliminate the 404 types of illness that arise from the disorders of wind, bile, phlegm, dual combinations, and triple combinations.

d.div: [103] dpal mgon 'phags pa klu sgrub kyi gsung 'di paN+Di ta ma hA o Sha d+his mdzad pa'i rin po che'i brtag thabs su drangs par zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i mes po'i zhal lung / shog_23_ba6_par gsal/
[178] Cited in Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, 23b6.

f.d: de yang tsha ba'i nad rnams la de'i nus pa bsil du gyur pa nas tsha ba sel ba/ grang ba'i nad rnams la de'i nus pa drod du gyur pa nas grang ba sel ba/ lus dang bsam pa la bar du gcod pa'i bgegs rigs stong phrag brgyad cu zhi bar byed pa sogs mi mthun pa mtha' dag las srung zhing skyob pa dang / mthun pa'i rkyen rang rang gi yid la ji ltar bsams pa'i dgos 'dod thams cad yid bzhin du 'grub par byed pa'i rin po che'i gzhal yas khang mchog tu gyur pa dag yod do//

For hot disorders they become cool and dispel the fever. For cold disorders they develop the power of heat and banish the cold. In this way this precious jeweled palace guards and protects from all harmful forces by pacifying the eighty thousand hindrances that plague the body and mind and so forth, while at the same time granting and fulfilling one’s needs and wishes as soon as these appear to the mind.

grong khyer kyi lho na nyi ma'i stobs ldan ri la grang nad sel ba'i drod sman gyi rigs dang / byang phyogs na tshad nad sel ba'i bsil sman gyi rigs/ shar du a ru rnam pa lnga'am bdun/ nub tu bzang po drug cong zhi dang brag zhun sogs chu tshan dang sman chu rigs lnga/ sman gyi ljon shing gi rtse na skad snyan par sgrog pa'i bya dang / rtsa ba na glang po che dang dom gla ba sogs sman bzang po lus la yod pa'i srog chags dang ldan pa'i nags tshal gyis skor ba'i dbus gzhal yas khang mtshan nyid dang ldan pa

To the south of the city lies a mountain range “endowed with the power of the sun”[179] on which can be found medicines of hot power that eliminate cold disorders. To the north grow medicinal plants of cold power that eliminate hot disorders. In the east grow the five or seven types of chebulic myrobalan. To the west are found the six excellent plants—calcite, bitumen, and so on—as well as hot springs and medicinal water, all of five varieties. On the tops of the medicinal trees, birds sing sweet songs, while elephants, bears, musk deer, and other creatures whose bodies contain good medicine roam on the floor of the forest surrounding this perfect palace.

d.div: [179] Here in his description of the setting for the teaching of Four Tantras the author is interspersing his text with actual text from the introduction to Four Tantras.

f.d: de'i nang na nor bu sna tshogs dang / baiDUR+ya dkar ser sngo'i khri seng ge dang glang po che rta mchog khyung dang rma byas bteg pa'i steng du lha'i gos rin thang med pa'i gdan la chos gsung ba'i ston pa ni/ spyir sman bla zhes pa la sman mdo brgyad brgya pa che chung gnyis su/ 'jam dpal sangs rgyas kyi zhing 'di nas shar phyogs su sangs rgyas kyi zhing gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed 'das pa na/ zhes pa nas/ lha dang mi rnams kyi ston pa sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das baiDUR+ya 'od kyi rgyal po zhes bya ba bzhugs/[104] zhes pa'i bde gshegs bdun gyi gtso bo'i sman bla dang / bskal bzang gi sangs rgyas stong gi nang tshan gyi sman bla dang 'jam dpal sgyu 'phrul dra ba las bshad pa'i sman bla/ bdag cag gi ston pa zas gtsang gi sras po sman blar bzhed tshe/ de dag sprul longs kyi khyad par/ sku mdog baiDUR+ya ste sngon por bzung ba mtshan dpe tshang mi tshang sogs dgos gzhi dang bshad khungs mang tsam snang ste 'dir tshogs che bas gzhan du smras la/

Within the palace on a throne made of various precious stones and white, yellow, and blue beryl, supported by lions, elephants, thoroughbred horses, garudas, and peacocks, sat the Teacher of this Dharma on a cushion of priceless celestial cloth. Generally, it is said that the term medicine buddha (sman bla) can be applied to Medicine Buddha as lord of the seven sugatas, as described in the passage from the greater and lesser versions of the Medicine Sutras in Eight Hundred Verses beginning, “Mañjuśrī, east of this buddha realm, beyond buddha realms as many as grains of sand in the Ganges…” up to “dwelled the teacher of gods and men, the bhagavān, the buddha, the lord of blue beryl light.”[180] It can also be applied to the medicine buddhas found among the thousand buddhas of this fortunate eon, to the description of Medicine Buddha as found in the Illusory Net Tantra, and to our Teacher, the son of Śuddhodana, as Medicine Buddha. There are quite a few questions and many scriptural references on whether these forms described above are emanation bodies or enjoyment bodies and, because of having a form the color of beryl—blue—whether the major and minor marks of enlightenment are complete or not. However, because this would take up a lot of space, it has been dealt with elsewhere.

d.div: [104] sde dge_504_bka'/ rgyud/ da_'phags pa bcom ldan 'das sman gyi bla baiDUR+ya'i 'od kyi sngon gyi smon lam gyi khyad par rgyas pa/ shog_274_ba2
[180] Found in Medicine Buddha Sutra (Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaidūryaprabhāsyapūrva-praṇidhānaviśeṣavistāra-sūtra), Toh 504 Kangyur, rgyud, da, 174b2.

f.d:
nges pa'i don du mdo dkon cog 'byung gnas kyi bam po bdun pa las/
'jam dpal de lta bu'i rnam grangs su gang sangs rgyas kyi zhing tha dad pa rnams su sangs rgyas kyi bya ba byed pa'i tshe/ nga la sems can rnams kyis tha dad par shes pa ni bskal par smras kyang shar gyi phyogs cha'i sangs rgyas kyi zhing gi mtha' rtogs par mi nus so/ / de bzhin du phyogs cha gzhan thams cad kyi sangs rgyas kyi zhing du nga la sems can rnams kyis ming tha dad pa'i de bzhin gshegs par shes pa yang brjod du med pa'i bskal par smras kyang sangs rgyas kyi zhing tha dad pa'i mtha' bde bar mi rig go[105] /

The definitive position is found in the seventh fascicle of the Mine of Jewels Sutra:
Mañjuśrī, in these different forms, while I am working in these different buddha realms, at those times sentient beings know me by different names. However, even if they were to quote them for an eon they would never be able to perceive the end of the buddha realms of the east. Similarly, in the buddha realms of the other directions sentient beings know me as tathāgatas of different names. However, if they were to quote them for an inconceivable number of eons, they would not easily perceive the end of all the different buddha realms.[181]

d.div: [105] sde dge_124_bka'/ mdo sde/ tha_'phags pa dkon mchog 'byung gnas zhes bya ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 7_shog_289_ba4
[181] Ratnākarasūtra, vol. 7, Toh 124 Kangyur, mdo sde, tha, 289b4.

f.d:
zhes dang / dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo'i bam po bzhi pa las/ sangs rgyas kyi zhing 'di nas sangs rgyas kyi zhing gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed drug cu 'das pa'i steng gi phyogs su 'jig rten gyi khams sgron ma gcig pa na de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas rnam par 'phrul pa'i rgyal po bzhugs pa'i rgyu mtshan 'jam dbyangs kyis bdag cag gi ston par zhus pas/
sangs rgyas bcom ldan rnams kyi sangs rgyas kyi gnas la yang bsam gyis mi khyab ste/ sangs rgyas de ni nga nyid yin no/ / 'jam dpal de ltar na sangs rgyas kyi zhing bye ba khrag khrig brgya stong du nga'i yul 'jug go/ / der ni nyan thos dang rang sangs rgyas thams cad kyis mi chud do/[106] /

Also, in the fourth chapter of the Samādhi of Śūraṅgama Sutra when Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha about “the tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly enlightened buddha, Vikurvānarāja dwelling beyond this buddha realm, beyond as many buddha realms as there are in sixty times the number of grains of sand in the Ganges, in the upper direction, in the world of Ekadipa,” the Buddha replied:
The buddha realms of the bhagavān buddhas are inconceivable. That buddha is me. Mañjuśrī, in this way the billions of buddha realms are worlds that I engage in. There the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not enter.[182]

d.div: [106] sde dge_132_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting nge 'dzin gya mi_do/ bam po/ 4_shog_296_na3
[182] Śūraṅgamasamādhi Sutra, Toh 132 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 296a3.

f.d:
zhes dang / bam po lnga par/
shar phyogs su sangs rgyas kyi zhing 'di nas sangs rgyas kyi zhing sum khri nyis stong 'das pa na/ 'jig rten gyi khams rnam par spud ba zhes bya bar de bzhin gshegs pa rnam par snang mdzad 'od zer gyis brgyan pa zhes bya ba bzhugs pa de yang nga nyid yin no/[107] / zhes sogs theg chen gyi mdo sde phal cher las phyogs mtshungs su gsungs pa dang /

And in the fifth chapter:
In the east, thirty-two thousand buddha realms beyond this buddha realm, in the world known as Vijaya, dwells Tathāgata Vairocana Prabhāmaya. This buddha too is me.[183] There are other similar passages, and most Mahayana sutras talk along similar lines.

d.div: [107] sde dge_132_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_309_na1

f.d: pha rgyud 'dus pa'i 'grel pa zla ba grags pas mdzad pa'i sgron gsal du gsang ba rnal 'byor chen po'i lung drangs pa las/ 'di lta ste/ 'jam dpal ni rgyal po zas gtsang ma/ zhes sogs nas/ rnam par snang mdzad chen po ni yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas shAkya thub par gyur to/[108] / zhes gzhi dang snying po me tog gis brgyan pa'i zhing khams rgya mtsho zhes bya ba de'i nang du ma 'thus pa'i sangs rgyas kyi zhing gi rnam gzhag med cing / de dag thams cad du bzhugs pa'i sku'i bkod pa mtha' yas pa rnams ni longs spyod rdzogs sku gcig pu de las 'phros pa'i phyir ston pa nyid kyi rnam par 'phrul pa 'ba' zhig nas/ mched bdun po sman bla yin min dang / sman bla zhes gcig la dmigs kyis bsal nas bshad khungs gzhan rnams kyi sman bla dang gcig mi gcig sogs kyi dogs pa ma dgos shing /

In Bright Lamp by Candrakīrti, a commentary on the father tantra Guhyasamāja, a passage is cited from the Mahāguhya Yogatantra,[184] running from, “It is like this: Mañjuśrī was King Śuddhodana…” up to “Mahā-vairocana was the perfectly enlightened buddha Śākyamuni.”[185] No buddha realm is excluded from the “foundation and essence adorned with flowers” ocean of realms,[186] and the limitless and varied enlightened forms that dwell there emanate from the same enjoyment body. Therefore wondering—from the standpoint of Medicine Buddha being solely a manifestation of our Teacher—whether the seven brothers are also medicine buddhas, and wondering—from the standpoint of Medicine Buddha referring to a separate being—whether specific instances of medicine buddhas mentioned in other scriptural references are the same, become unnecessary doubts.

d.div: [108] sde dge_1785_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ ha_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ sgron gsal/ shog_9_ba1
[184] This may be the Vajraśekhara Explanatory Tantra, Toh 480 Kangyur, rgyud ’bum, nya.
[185] Candrakīrti, Bright Lamp (Pradīpoddyotana), Toh 1785 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, ha, 9b1.
[186] The largest area of world realms in Buddhist cosmology.

f.d:
snang tshul gyi dbang yang / stong chen rab 'joms kyi mdo las/
rdzogs sangs rnam par sangs rgyas tshe/ / 'jig rten skyong bas phyogs bzhi nas/ / snod bzhi dag ni blangs nas su/ / bde bar gshegs la phul ba dang / / mthu yis gcig tu sprul mdzad pa/ /
lha yi snod mchog de dang ni/ / bdud rtsi 'dra ba'i sman gyi mchog / ston pa'i phyag na bsnams gyur pa/ / bden pa'i tshig ni de dag gis/ / sman rnams bdud rtsir 'gyur bar shog /
de bzhin lha mo 'phrog ma yis/ / lha rdzas dge ba a ru ra/ / blangs nas ston la rab phul ba/ /
bdud rtsi 'dra ba'i sman mchog bsnams/ / bden ba'i tshig ni de dag gis/ / nad pa rnams kyi nad gsos shing / / nyes pa thams cad 'phrog byed pa/ / sman rnams bdud rtsir 'gyur bar shog[109] / ces sman blar dngos su bstan pa dang /

This point can also be understood by the forms of his appearance. In the Destruction of the Great Thousand Sutra it says:
At the time of the perfect enlightenment, the guardians of the world held aloft four bowls from the four directions and offered them to the Sugata, by whose power they became a single bowl.
These supreme celestial bowls, holding supreme ambrosia-like medicine, sit in the hands of the Teacher. By the power of these words of truth, may all medicine become ambrosia.
Likewise the goddess Harī held aloft the celestial and wonderful myrobalan and offered it to the Teacher.
The supreme ambrosia-like medicine now sits in the hands of the Teacher. By the power of these words of truth, may the sick be cured of their illness, may all faults be driven out, may all medicine become ambrosia.[187] Here the Buddha reveals himself as Medicine Buddha.

d.div: [109] sde dge_558_bka'/ rgyud/ pha_stong chen mo rab tu 'joms pa zhes bya ba'i mdo/ shog_80_ba5
[187] Mahāsahasrapramardana, Toh 558 Kangyur, rgyud ’bum, pha, 80b5.

f.d:
sgyu ma lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo las/ 'dul ba'i don du gzugs kyi rnam pa mtha' yas ston/[110] / zhes dang / zung gi mdo las/ kun tu dpa' ba ngas sems can rnams ci lta bu'i gzugs kyi 'dul ba de dang de lta bu'i chos bstan te/[111] zhes dang / 'jam dpal gyis dris pa'i mdo las/
de bzhin gshegs pa ni skus 'jig rten thams cad khyab pa yin te/ kha dog dang / dbyibs dang / spyod pa'i bye brag gang dang gang gis 'dul sems can rnams 'dul bar 'gyur ba'i kha dog dang dbyibs dang spyod pa'i bye brag de dang de lta bur de bzhin gshegs pa sems can rnams kyis mthong ngo /[112] / zhes dang /

In the Illusion-Like Samādhi Sutra it says, “In order to tame others he shows countless forms.”[188] In the Saṃghāṭa Sutra it says, “Sarvaśūra, I teach the Dharma in whatever form is necessary for the taming of others.”[189] In Questions of Mañjuśrī it says:
With his forms the Tathāgata pervades all worlds. By whatever color, shape, or aspect of behavior living beings will be tamed, the Tathāgata in that color, shape, or aspect of behavior will be seen by living beings.[190]

d.div: [110] sde dge_130_bka'/ mdo sde/ da_'phags pa sgyu ma lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo/ bam po/ 1_shog_219_na2
[111] sde dge_102_bka'/ mdo sde/ nga 'phags pa zung gi mdo'i chos kyi rnam grangs/ bam po/ 2_shog_247_na6
[112] sde dge_172_bka'/ mdo sde/ ma_'phags pa 'jam dpal gyis dris pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ shog_4_ba7
[188] Māyopamāsamādhisūtra, Toh 130 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 219a2.
[189] Saṃghāṭasūtradharmaparyāya, Toh 102 Kangyur, mdo sde, nga, 247a6.
[190] Mañjuśrīparipṛrcchā, Toh 172 Kangyur, mdo sde, ma, 4a7.

f.d:
rje btsun byams pas theg pa chen po'i bstan bcos mngon rtogs rgyan gyi skabs brgyad pa las/
rgyu ni yongs su smin gyur nas/ / gang dang gang la gang dang ni/ / gang tshe bya ba phan gyur pa/ / de dang de la der snang ngo /[113] / zhes dang /

In the eighth chapter of the Ornament of Realization, the Mahayana treatise by the noble Maitreya, it says:
When the causes come to fruition, then to whomever, as whatever, and whenever it will be of help, to that being, in that form, he appears.[191]

d.div: [113] sde dge_3786_bstan/ sher phyin/ ka_byams pa mgon po/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs brgyad pa/ sh+loka9_shog_11_ba5
[191] Abhisamayālaṃkāra, 8:9, Toh 3786 Kangyur, shes phyin, ka, 11b5.

f.d:
mnyam sbyor le'u lnga pa las/
sems can rnams ni 'dul ba dang / / bde ba thams cad 'grub pa'i phyir/ / bcom ldan rnal 'byor de nyid ni/ / sangs rgyas thams cad rnam 'phrul ba/[114] / zhes dang /

In the fifth chapter of the Yoga Equal to All Buddhas Later Tantra it says:
To tame sentient beings, to create every happiness, that yoga of the Bhagavān is manifest as every buddha.[192]

d.div: [114] sde dge_366_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_sangs rgyas mnyam sbyor/ rtog pa lnga pa/ shog_155_ba3
[192] Sarvabuddhasamayogatantra, Toh 366 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 155b4.

f.d: yang dag sgrub pa gcig pu nyid/ / ji ltar 'dod pa bzhin du snang /[115] / zhes dang /

From the same tantra:
The one perfect state[193] appears as desired.[194]

d.div: [115] sde dge_366_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_sangs rgyas mnyam sbyor/ rtog pa lnga pa/ shog_155_ba4
[193] Yang dag sgrub pa, saṃsiddhi.
[194] Sarvabuddhasamayogatantra, chap. 5, Toh 366 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 155b3.

f.d:
mngon brjod bla ma'i le'u sum cu rtsa lnga par/
thams cad mkhyen cing thams cad pa/ / ji ltar 'dod pa'i sku las 'chang /[116] / zhes dang /

In the thirty-fifth chapter of the Abhidhana Later Tantra it says:
All knowing and all things, holding forms as desired….[195]

d.div: [116] sde dge_369_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_mngon par brjod pa'i rgyud bla ma/ le'u/ 35_shog_323_ba7
[195] Abhidhana-uttaratantra, chap. 35, Toh 369 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 323b5.

f.d:
khro bo gtum po'i rgyud kyi rim par phye ba bcu gcig pa las/
gang dang gang gi gzugs kyis ni/ / sems can gdul byar nga nyid 'jug[117] / zhes gang la gang 'dul der ston par mdzad pa ni de bzhin gshegs pa'i thabs la mkhas pa'i ye shes kyi khyad par nyid yin par gsungs so//

In the eleventh chapter of the Tantra of the Fierce and Wrathful it says:
I take on different forms to tame living beings.[196] Therefore, these citations are saying that to appear as a teacher in forms appropriate to those to be tamed is the skillful means of the tathāgata gnosis.

d.div: [117] sde dge_431_bka'/ rgyud/ nga gtum po khro bo'i rgyud kyi rgyal po dpa' bo gcig pa/ rim par phye ba/ 11_shog_320_na3
[196] Ekavīrākhyāśrīcaṇḍamahāroṣaṇa-tantrarāja, Toh 431 Kangyur, rgyud, nga, 320a3.

f.d: de ltar ma yin na bstan pa gcig la ston pa gnyis mi 'byung ba dang / gzhan gyi 'khor du kun dga' bo dang 'tsho byed gzhon nus gsos sogs 'khor bzhi 'gal med du sgrub pa la tshegs che ba sogs nas bdag cag gi ston pa zas gtsang sras po bcom ldan 'das 'tsho mdzad sman gyi bla baidUR+ya 'od kyi rgyal po zhes bya ba'i skur bzhengs te skye rgu'i bdag po sogs lha'i 'khor dang / rgyun shes kyi bu sogs drang srong gi 'khor/ tshangs pa sogs phyi pa'i 'khor/ spyan ras gzigs sogs nang pa'i 'khor mang po dang bcas bzhugs pa'i dus su sku gsung thugs yon tan 'phrin las lnga nas ye shes lnga'i rang gdangs kyi sprul pa'i drang srong mched lnga 'phros te gsung sprul gyi zhu ba po dang / gzhan bzhis 'chad po'i tshul du gsungs pa rang rang gi lugs su lha rnams kyis gso dpyad 'bum par go/ drang srong rnams kyis tsa ra ka sde brgyad du/ phyi pa rnams kyis dbang phyug nag po'i rgyud du go/ nang pa rnams kyis rigs gsum mgon po'i skor du go ba/

Were that not the case, it would be difficult to reconcile the fact of there being one doctrine but not two teachers with the fact of Ānanda, Kumāra Jivaka Bhṛtya, and others who made up the four circles of medical disciples being the disciples of another. Therefore, our Teacher, the son of Śuddhodana, arose in the form of the Bhagavān, the physician, the buddha of medicine, the lord of beryl light. The vast audience included the circle of gods such as Prajāpati, the circle of rishis such as Ātreya, the circle of outsiders such as Brahmā, and the circle of insiders such as Avalokita. At that time, the five rishi brothers emerged from the five aspects of enlightened body, speech, mind, qualities, and activities as the innate tones of the five kinds of gnosis. One became the manifestation of enlightened speech and was the requestor of the teaching, while the other four manifested as the teacher of the tantra. Each circle of disciples understood the teaching as their own tradition. The gods understood it as the Science of Healing Collection. The rishis heard it as the Caraka Aṣṭavarga. The outsiders heard it as the Black Īśvara Tantra. The insiders heard it as the Guardian of the Three Lineages Collection.

mjug don yongs gtad las/
bde gshegs rnams kyi sprul pas 'gro don du/ / rgya gar yul du sman gyi sbyor ba gsungs/ / rgya nag yul du me btsa' rtsa sbyongs gsungs/ / dol po'i yul du gtar kha gtso bor bstan/ / bod kyi yul du rtsa chu'i brtag pa bstan/ / lha yi 'khor la gso dpyad 'bum pa gsungs/ / drang srong 'khor la tsa ra ka sde brgyad/ / mu stegs 'khor la dbang phyug nag po'i rgyud/ / nang pa'i 'khor la rigs gsum mgon po'i skor/ /
gso dpyad rgyud 'dir thams cad 'dus par bstan/ / 'dir ma 'dus pa'i gso dpyad gzhan med de/ / 'phags pa'i thugs rje phyogs ris med mod kyang / / gang zag mos pa'i mthong snang so sor shar/ / dper na mkha' la zla ba gcig shar na/ / chu yi skyogs rer zla ba re re bzhin/ / gcig tu gsungs kyang so sos du mar go[118] / zhes pa ltar dang /

As it says in the Entrustment chapter from Four Tantras:
For the sake of living beings, the emanations of the Sugata taught the preparation of medicine in India, cauterization and channel cleansing in China, mainly bloodletting in the land of Dölpo,[197] pulse and urine diagnosis in Tibet, the Science of Healing Collection to the gods, the Caraka Aṣṭavarga to the rishis, the Black Īśvara Tantra to the tīrthika outsiders, and the Guardian of the Three Lineages to the insiders.
All these are included in this medical tantra; there is no medical practice not within it. The great compassion has no partiality, but things appear according to individual disposition. Just as a single moon in the sky appears as individual moons in every water urn, one teaching was delivered, but many were understood.[198]

d.div: [118] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ phyi ma rgyud/ le'u nyer drug pa/ shog_660_yag phri_nge 6
[197] These days a region of western Nepal.
[198] Four Tantras, Final Tantra, 26.660.6.

f.d: snang mtha'i rang gzugs gsung sprul drang srong yid las skyes nyid kyi go bar bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag rgyud ces pa'i bshad rgyud phal cher dang rtsa rgyud tho long phyi ma man rgyud kyi cha tsam dang bcas pa'i rgyud bzhi/ yan lag brgyad/ gnas bcu gcig skabs bco lnga/ mdo bzhi/ le'u brgya dang lnga bcu rtsa drug dang / sh+loka lnga stong dgu brgya lhag bcas rnams yod par grags pa'i tshig don 'di lta bur go ba gser ljang brdungs kyi spang leb la baiDUR+yas bris pa'i glegs bam dngos o rgyan mkha' 'gro'i gling na bzhugs skad/

In the understanding of Manasija,[199] the speech-emanation rishi, whose own form is that of Amitāyus, the teaching received was the Essence of Ambrosia: The Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches. This teaching was Four Tantras, comprising most of the Explanatory Tantra, large parts of the Root Tantra, and parts of the Instruction and Final Tantras, and which was said to cover the eight branches, the eleven topics, the fifteen fields of practice, and the four compilations, with the whole work consisting of 156 chapters and more than 5,900 verses. The original text, written down on sheets of pure gold in beryl ink, is supposedly kept in Oḍḍiyāna ḍākinī land.

d.div: [199] Yid las skyes, Manasija. As there is no extant Sanskrit original, the rendering of Tibetan names in Sanskrit presents some problems, mainly those of choice. Here and elsewhere I have mainly followed Lokesh Chandra and Vaidya Bhagwan Dash.

f.d: snga 'gyur gu ru chos kyi dbang phyug gi gter byon la/ ston pa bde bar gshegs pa'i thugs tshad med bzhi'i dgongs pa gab pa'i gter mngon du phyungs pa sman gyi bla baiDUR+ya 'od kyi rgyal por byon/ gso byed sman gyi rgyud thugs la gab gter bka' ru byon te/ rgyud chen po tsa ra ka sde brgyad/ yan lag brgyad pa'i rgyud/ bdud rtsi thigs pa'i rgyud bco brgyad la sogs pa bka' stsal ba las/ drang srong chen po dung gi thor tshugs can la sogs pa nyi shu rtsa gcig / khye'u chung kun spong yid las skyes la sogs pas bka' bsdus/ bstan pa dar zhing rgyas nas mtha' btsan par bya ba'i phyir rgya gar rdo rje gdan gyi nags gling dang / o rgyan baiDUR+ya'i mchod rten/ a su ra gsang ba'i brag phug /bal yul 'phags pa shing kun/ rgya nag gaude shan phug la sogs par bse sgrom du gter la sbas pa/ slob dpon pad+ma/ klu sgrub snying po/ mu stegs thub rgyal la sogs pas gter phyungs te chig brgyud du 'gro don mdzad par yang grags/

Guru Chökyi Wangchuk of the old translation school, in his revealed treasures, says that a hidden enlightened-mind treasure from the mind of the four immeasurables of the Teacher and Sugata was revealed as Medicine Buddha Lord of Beryl Light. The medical tantras were mind treasures that became part of the Transmission tradition[200] because the Caraka Aṣṭavarga great tantra, Tantra of Eight Branches, the eighteen Ambrosia Drop Tantras, and others were taught by the Buddha and were then compiled by the great rishi Śañkacūḍa and others from the twenty-one rishis, as well as by the youth Avadhūta, Manasija, and so on, and were widely disseminated. Then, to keep them safe and secure, they were put in containers and hidden as treasure in the Bodhgāya forests in India, in the beryl stupa in Oḍḍiyāna, in the secret Asura cave, in Swayambhu in Nepal, and in the Gaudeshan cave in China. Ācārya Padmasambhava, Nāgārjuna Hṛdaya, Tīrthika Munirāj, and others unearthed these treasures and, for the sake of living beings, transmitted them in a one-to-one lineage.

d.div: [200] “Treasure” (gter ma) refers to the unearthing of texts previously hidden; “transmission” (dka’ ma) refers to the unbroken transmission of a text from early Indian times without any intervening hidden period.

f.d: brang ti'i khog 'bugs shes bya rab gsal ltar na/ 'khor lo tha ma'i tshe/ gnod sbyin lag na rdo rje'i gnas su de bzhin gshegs pa'i 'khor la chos ston pa'i tshe/ gzhan 'phrul dbang byed la sogs pa bdud kyi tshogs lhags te sgyogs nag po mgo dgu pa 'phangs pa na/ bcom ldan 'das la ba ku la dang dzam+b+ha las gab pas/ ba ku la tshe'i dus byas/ dzam+b+ha la'i lus zug rngur gyur pa'i dus bcom ldan 'das kyi mdzod spu nas 'od zer bdud rtsi lnga ldan zhes bya ba byung ste dzam+b+ha la'i zug rngu zhi bar mdzad/ tshangs pa la sogs pa'i lha dang / 'tsho byed gzhon nu la sogs pa mi'i drang srong gi tshogs la sman gyi rgyud shel gyi me long le'u lnga bcu pa gsungs zhes bshad/[119]

According to Drangti Palden Tsojé’s Illumination of Knowledge, during the third turning of the wheel, while the Tathāgata was teaching the Dharma to his retinue in the place of the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, a horde of māras, such as the paranirmita-vaśavartins,[201] arrived and fired a black, nine-headed yantra, causing Bakula and Jambala to flee to the Buddha. Bakula died and Jambala was in great pain. Light of the five nectars radiated from the coil of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows, easing Jambala’s pain. The Buddha then taught the Crystal Mirror Medicine Tantra in fifty chapters to gods such as Brahmā and to human rishis such as Kumāra Jivaka.[202]

d.div: [119] 'dir brang ti'i khogs 'bugs shes bya rab gsal gsungs pa dus rabs bcu gsum pa'i nang phebs pa'i brang ti dpal ldan 'tsho byed kyi gsung gso ba rig pa'i khog phub shes bya rab gsal la dgongs mdo/ de'i dpe lag son ma gyur pas 'dir khungs bkod ma thub/

[201] Gzhan ’phrul dbang byed; usually described in Buddhist texts as a class of gods “able to enjoy the pleasures of others,” but also described as being the abode of Māra. So here presumably it is the name of the kind of māras that live there.
[202] According to the Eighteen Accessory Texts, the Crystal Mirror Medicine Tantra was taught to Ānanda during the second turning of the wheel of Dharma.

f.d:
rtswa mchog tu gsungs pa'i myang 'das chen po rgya nag 'gyur bam po gnyis pa las/ grong khyer rtswa mchog gi shing mkhan gyi bu dge bsnyen tsun da zhes bya ba ris mthun pa'i 'khor lnga bcu rtsa gcig dang bcas pas bshos phul ba'i tshe dge slong rnams kyis
bcom ldan 'das kyi sngar chos thams cad bdag med kyis khyed de lta bu'i tshul nan tan gyis shig nas/ nga rgyal dang bral na mya ngan las 'da'o/[120] / zhes gsungs pa'i don ji lta bu lags zhus pas/

In the second chapter of the Great Nirvana Sutra taught in the town of Kuśanagar, in the version translated from Chinese,[203] while Upāsaka Cunda, the son of a woodworker from Kuśanagar, together with fifty-one like-minded companions was performing an offering of food, the monks asked:
“The Bhagavān has said that we should persist through the power of all dharmas being without self and in so doing, we will be freed from pride and pass beyond sorrow. What is the meaning of that?”

d.div: [120] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_'phags pa yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_18_ba3

[203] Some of the following three citations from this sutra I have translated according to the edition translated from the Sanskrit (Toh 120, mdo sde, tha); it seems to make the greater sense. The two editions broadly agree but there are differences in detail.

'di lta ste dper na/ rgyal po mi mkhas pa shes pa chung ba la sman pa yang mi mkhas pa glen pa zhig yod na/ rgyal pos ma rtogs pas sman pa de la bya dga' cher stsal to/ / sman pa glen pa des ni nad thams cad la sman du 'o ma gtong ste/ nad thog ma ci las gyur ba yang mi shes la/ sman du 'o ma gtong ba la yang mi mkhas pas/ rlung nad dang / bad kan dang / mkhris pa'i nad thams cad la yang sman du 'o ma gtong ste/ rgyal pos ni sman pa nyid kyang ma rtogs la/ 'o ma bzang ngam ngan pa'i bye brag kyang mi phyed do/ /

The Bhagavān replied, “It is like this. Say there is an unwise king—a man of little knowledge—and an equally unwise and foolish doctor. The king in his ignorance bestows gifts upon this doctor. The foolish doctor, for his part, treats all illnesses with milk, having no idea of the origins of the illness. He does not even use milk as medicine properly, treating with milk all disorders, whether wind, bile, or phlegm in nature. The king, not knowing what makes a good doctor, cannot even distinguish between good and bad milk.

de la sman pa mkhas pa rig pa brgyad dang ldan pa/ nad thams cad gso ba la shin tu mkhas pa/ dpyad thams cad khong du chud pa zhig yul gzhan nas 'ongs na/ de'i tshe sman pa mi mkhas pa des mkhas pa de la 'dri ba'am/ slob par mi byed kyis/ phyir nga rgyal gyi sems bskyed do/ / de'i tshe sman pa mkhas pa des mi mkhas pa de la brten nas slob dpon du bzung ste/ sman dpyad gsang ba dag bslab pa'i phyir sman pa glen pa de la bdag ni khyod la slob dpon du gsol gyis dpyad rnams bstan cing bshad du gsol/ zhes gsol ba btab na/ sman pa de mkhas pa de la 'di skad ces dam 'cha'o/ / khyod ci ste lo bzhi bcu rtsa brgyad kyi bar du kho bo'i g.yog bya na/ dpyad rnams kyang bstan no zhes bsgo'o/ / de nas sman pa mkhas pa des mi mkhas pa'i lung bzhin du bdag gis de bzhin du bgyi'o/ / bdag gis kyang rngo ci thogs kyis khyod kyi g.yog bgyi'o zhes smras so/ /

From another land comes another doctor, one possessing the eight sciences, skilled in the art of curing all diseases, and master of all medical practices. The stupid doctor does not question or learn from this wise doctor but instead develops thoughts of superiority and arrogance. The wise doctor, on the other hand, devotes himself to the stupid doctor and regards him as his teacher. So that he may learn any secret medical knowledge he makes a request: “I beseech you to be my master. Show me and teach me the medical practices.” In reply the other doctor commands, “If you serve me for forty-eight years, I will teach you the practices.” The wise doctor accedes to the demands of the foolish doctor saying, “I will do as you command and do all I can to serve you.”

de nas sman pa glen pa des sman pa gsar pa khrid nas rgyal po'i pho brang du chas so/ / rgyal po dang phrad nas de'i tshe sman pa gsar pa des rgyal po de la dpyad rnam pa sna tshogs dang / gzhan yang rgyu rtsal mang po'i gtam dang / yul gyi srid bzung ba dang / nad pa gso ba'i thabs 'di'o/ / rgyal po chen po thugs su chud par gyis shig ces gtam byas so/ /

Then the stupid doctor takes the new doctor to the palace to meet the king. There the wise doctor talks about various medical techniques, about many kinds of skills and arts, about how to protect the country, and about remedies for different illnesses, saying, “Great king, you should learn and understand these.”

de'i tshe rgyal po de skad ces smras pa thos pa dang / sman pa rnying pa de mi mkhas par shes nas/ yul de nas bskrad do/ / de nas kyang sman pa gsar pa de la lhag par rim gro dang bkur sti bskyed do/ / de'i tshe sman pa gsar pa de 'di snyam du/ rgyal po 'di la bstan pa'i dus la bab snyam du bsam nas/ rgyal po la 'di skad ces gsol to/ / rgyal po chen po bdag la dgongs med na/ bdag gi gsol ba gcig gnang bar mdzod cig /rgyal pos smras pa/ kho bo'i lag pa g.yas pa nas/ lus kyi yan lag thams cad kyi bar du yid bzhin du slongs shig dang / thams cad sbyin par bya'o/ /

The king listens and realizes that the old doctor is not at all a wise doctor and expels him from the land. From then on he pays great honor and respect to this new doctor. The doctor thinks to himself, “The time has come to teach the king,” and says, “Great king, if you think highly of me, please grant me a request.” The king replies, “From my right arm to every other part of my body, take all that you desire. I willingly offer it all to you.”

sman pa des gsol ba/ 'di ltar rgyal pos lus kyi yan lag thams cad kyang bdag 'tshal bar gnang mod kyi/ bdag thugs mi thub la mang po yang mi gsol na/ deng slan chad yul mi thams cad kyis sman pa rnying pa'i dpyad sman du 'o ma gtong ba shos bcad par bkar gdags su gsol/ de ci'i slad du zhe na/ sman de ni gdug pa dang bcas pas mang du 'chi ba'i phyir ro/ / gal te sman de gtong ba yod na yan lag gi dam pa mgo bcad do zhes bkar btags na/ sman 'o ma las gtong ba chod pas/ dus ma ran par 'chi ba med de/ thams cad bde zhing skyid par 'gyur gyis/ bdag gi gsol ba 'di gnang bar mdzod cig /

The doctor replies, “Although your majesty willingly grants every part of his body to me, I cannot accept his offer. I do not seek much. All I ask is that from now on, you issue a decree saying that all the people of this country should cease the practice of taking milk as medicine, as was prescribed by the old doctor. Why? Because that medicine is harmful and will cause the death of many. If you issue a proclamation saying that anyone caught administering this medicine will be beheaded, the practice of using milk as medicine will be halted, there will be no untimely death, and everybody will be happy. Please grant me this request.”

de nas rgyal pos smras pa/ khyod gsol ba 'di shin tu phan par 'gyur ba yin te/ deng phyin chad yul mi las na ba zhig yod na sman 'o ma gtong du mi gnang ngo / / gal te 'o ma gtong ba zhig yod na/ yan lag gi dam pa mgo bcad do zhes bkar btags so/ / de'i tshe na sman pa mkhas pa de tsha ba dang / kha ba dang / skyur ba dang / dngar ba dang / mngar ba la sogs te/ ro rnam pa sna tshogs kyis sman sbyar te nad gsos na gang yang ma sos pa med do/ / de nas phyis ring por ma lon par rgyal po de nad kyis btab nas sman pa de bkug ste/ 'di ltar nga ni nad kyis shin tu sdug bsngal bar gyur na/ ji ltar gso zhes smras pa dang / sman pa des rgyal po'i nad bltas na/ sman du 'o ma dgos pa 'dra nas rgyal po la gsol ba/ rgyal po nad thabs dang sbyar na/ sman du 'o ma btang 'tshal te/ bdag gi sngar sman du 'o ma gtang du mi rung zhes gsol ba rdzun du gyur te/ sman du 'o ma las bzang ba ma mchis la/ rgyal po'i nad kyang tsha ba las gyur pas/ sman du 'o ma btang na bzang ngo / /

The king replies, “This request of yours will be of great benefit. From now on if there is sickness in the land, no one will be allowed to take milk as medicine. If there is anyone who does, they will be beheaded.” After the proclamation the wise doctor prepares medicines of various tastes—hot, bitter, sour, sweet, salty, and so on. When they are administered to the sick, there are none who do not recover. Not long after, the king himself becomes sick and summons the doctor. “I am in great pain,” he said, “How can I be helped?” The doctor examines the king, and it is clear the king needs milk as medicine. He says, “Your majesty, if this illness is to be treated, you should take milk as your medicine. Previously when I said it was not right to take milk as medicine, it was not true. There is no better medicine than milk. Because your illness arises from a hot disorder, you should take milk as medicine.”

rgyal pos smras pa/ sman pa khyod 'on te smyos sam/ tsha ba'i nad kyi btab na/ nad 'di la 'o ma phan no zhes smra/ khyod kyis sngar 'o ma la dug yod do zhes smras na/ da ji ltar btung / khyod kyis nga la bgam mam/ sman pa snga mas bsngags pa la dug yod do zhes byas pas/ sman pa gcig bskrad pa'i 'og tu/ da yang na ba la sman du 'o ma bzang ngo zhes khyod smra ba dang sbyar na/ nga'i sman pa rnying pa ni khyod pas mkhas nges so//

“Doctor, have you gone mad?” asks the king. “You are saying that when one is suffering from a heat disorder, milk will help? Previously you said milk was poisonous. How can I possibly drink it now! Are you deceiving me?[204] You said that which was praised by a previous doctor was actually poisonous, because of which he was expelled. Now you are saying that milk makes for good medicine. I can see that the old doctor was certainly much wiser than you!”
[204] This is according to the translation from the Sanskrit. The other, from the Chinese, has “testing” (bgam).

de nas sman pas yang rgyal po la 'di skad ces gsol to/ / rgyal po de skad ma gsungs shig / dper na srin bu shing zan gyi rjes las yi ger rung ba yang yod do/ / srin bus ni yi ge yin nam ma yin pa mi shes kyi/ de la mkhas pa shes rab can gyis mthong na/ srin bu'i yi ge shes so zhes ngo mtshar du mi 'dzin te/ rgyal po chen po sman pa snga ma yang de dang 'dra ste/ nad rnams mi rtogs pas thams cad la sman 'o ma gtong ba ni ji ltar srin bu'i rjes las yi ger 'gyur ba bzhin te/ sman pa snga mas ni 'o ma bzang ngan dang rung mi rung mi shes so/ / rgyal pos smras pa/ sman pa snga mas ji ltar ji lta bur mi shes/

Then the doctor says to the king, “Your majesty, please don’t say such things. Let me explain with an example. A wood-eating insect can leave a trail carved in the wood that resembles a letter. It does not know that it is a letter, and any intelligent person who saw it would not utter in amazement, ‘Oh look, this insect knows how to write!’ Great king, the former doctor was like this; he did not understand illness. His giving of milk as medicine to everyone is like the insect forming a letter in the wood, because he does not know the difference between good and bad milk, or when it is suitable and when it is unsuitable.” The king asks, “Exactly what did he not understand?”

sman pas smras pa/ sman 'o ma zhes bya ba ni gdug pa yang lags la/ bdud rtsi yang lags so/ / de la ji ltar na 'o ma de gdug pa yang yin la/ bdud rtsi yang yin zhe na/ gal te ba nyid sbang ma dang / rtswa sbyin pa dang / phug ma ma zos la/[121] be'u yang shin tu dul zhing 'tsho ba'i sa yang ri mthon po'i steng ma yin/ nags khrod ma yin pa na 'tsho zhing / chu yang 'bab chu dwangs ma las blud de/ drag tu mi bda'/ khyu mchog dang khyu gcig tu mi 'tsho bar bag yangs su za zhing 'thung la 'gro ba dang sdod pa yang bag yangs su gyur pa'i ba'i 'o ma ni nad rnams la phan pas bdud rtsi zhes bya'o/ / 'o ma de ma yin pa ni thams cad kyang gdug pa dang bcas pa zhes bya'o/ /

The doctor replies, “Milk as medicine is both poison and ambrosia. How can it be both harmful and ambrosia? I will explain. If a cow does not eat leftover grain, cut grass, and husks or chaff; if its calf is well behaved; if it lives neither high in the mountains nor low in the forests; if its drinking water comes from a clear-flowing stream and is not too sweet; if, while not living[205] close to the bull, it grazes contentedly and is generally content whether moving or sitting; then the milk of that cow is good for all kinds of illness and is ambrosia. Any other kind of milk is harmful.”
[121] phur ma ma zos la/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[205] The text has btsa’, “to be born.” I have gone with Degé, ’tsho, “to live.”

de'i tshe rgyal po chen pos de skad ces smras pa thos nas/ sman pa lags so/ / shin tu legs par smras so/ / da slan chad 'o ma bzang ngan dang rung mi rung yang shes so/ / de nas sman du 'o ma btang nas nad kyang byang bar gyur te/ yul mi thams cad la da phyin chad sman du 'o ma thong shig ces bkar btags so/ / yul mi rnams kyis de skad ces thos nas/ thams cad gshe rgya ste/ rgyal po chen po 'di ni yi dwags kyis brlams sam/ smyos sam ci nyes na/ bdag cag bslus te sman du 'o ma thong zhig ces gsungs/ yul mi thams cad khros bzhin du rgyal po'i spyan sngar lhags so/ /

The king listens and says, “Excellent, doctor, very well said! Now I know the difference between good and bad milk, and when it is suitable and unsuitable.” The doctor gives him the milk medicine and he recovers. The king issues an order to his people saying that from then on, milk should be given as medicine. When the people hear this they complain, “What is wrong with the king. Has he been possessed by ghosts? Has he gone mad? He is deceiving us by telling us to use milk as medicine.” They became angry and came before the king.

f.d: de la rgyal pos bka' stsal pa/ khyed nga la ma gshe shig / sman du 'o ma btang du rung ngam mi rung ba ni sman pa 'di'i dpyad yin gyi ngas ni ma nyes so/ / de'i tshe rgyal po chen po dang yul mi thams cad kyang shin tu dga' zhing mgu bar gyur nas/ sman pa de la lhag par rim gro dang bkur sti bskyed de/ nad pa thams cad la sman 'o ma btang bas nad kyang byang bar gyur to/[122] / zhes dang /

d.div: “Do not blame me,” said the king. “The suitability or unsuitability to take milk as medicine has been decided by this doctor. I have done nothing wrong.” The king and his people were pleased and redoubled their reverence and service to the doctor. All who were given milk as medicine were cured.[206]
[122] sde dge_119_bka'/ mdo sde/ nya_'phags pa yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po'i mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_35_ba7
[206] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, Toh 119 Kangyur, mdo sde, nya, 35b7.

f.d:
bam po nyer lnga pa las/
sman pa mkhas pa rig pa brgyad la mkhas pas sngar nad kyi mtshan nyid rtog go/ / mtshan nyid la rnam pa gsum yod de/ rlung dang / mkhris pa dang / bad kan no/ / rlung nad yod pa la ni mar sbyin no/ / mkhris pa'i nad yod pa la ni sha ka ra sbyin no/ / bad kan gyi nad yod pa la ni lga'i [123]khu ba blud do/ / de ltar nad kyi mtshan nyid shes nas sman byin te bsos par gyur pas sman pa mkhas pa zhes bya'o/[124] /

In the twenty-fifth chapter of the same sutra it says:
A wise doctor, well versed in the eight branches of knowledge, first investigates the illness for its type. Illness is of three types: wind, bile, and phlegm. For a wind illness he gives ghee, for a bile illness he gives white sugar, and for a phlegm illness he gives a ginger extract. Therefore, treating illness on the basis of understanding the illness is a mark of a good doctor.[207]

d.div: [123] sga'i khu ba/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[124] sde dge_120_bka'/ mdo sde/ tha_yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po/ bam po/ 3_shog_34_na1
[207] Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra, Toh 120 Kangyur, mdo sde, tha, 34a1.

f.d:
zhes dang / bam po zhe gcig pa las/
'jig rten gyi nad ni gsum ste/ mkhris pa dang / rlung dang / bad kan no/ / nad rnam pa gsum la yang sman rnam pa gsum gyis 'tsho ste/ mkhris pa'i nad la ni mar gyis 'tsho'o/ / rlung la ni 'bru mar phan no/ / bad kan la ni sbrang rtsi phan no/[125] / zhes pa la sogs te gsog ldang zhi gsum dpe'i sgo nas mang du bstan no/ /

And in the forty-first chapter:
There are three types of illness in the world: bile, wind, and phlegm. These three types of illness are to be treated with three types of medicine. Bile disorder is treated with ghee, wind disorder is helped with oil, phlegm disorder is helped with honey.[208] Here and elsewhere many passages teach the science of healing through the gathering, arising, and pacifying of illness, and by way of examples.

d.div: [125] sde dge_120_bka'/ mdo sde/ tha_yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa chen po/ bam po/ 9_shog_110_na1_tshig sna mi mthun/

f.d:
gzhan yang yan lag brgyad pa bam po stong rtsa gnyis yod pa zhig gsungs par yang grags/ ma rgyud rdo rje mkha' 'gro'i rim par phye ba zhe dgu pa las/
'das pa'i dus su sngon byung ba/ / bskal pa dang po bde ba che/ / der ni rdo rje sems dpa' che/ / lhag pa yi ni lha gcig bzhugs/ / lha min grub pa sogs mthong ste/ / lha yi tshogs ni skrag gyur nas/ / sangs rgyas thams cad 'dus nas ni/ / myur du nga la bskul bar byed/ / thig ler zhu las lha mo che/ / bdud kyi kun tu gtor ba ni/ / thams cad rmongs par byed pa yi/ / dngul chu zhes ni bya bar grags/ / chu gting las byung dman pa ste/ / de bzhin ri las skyes pa mchog[126] /

It is also reputed that the Buddha taught the eight branches of medicine in 1002 fascicles. In the forty-ninth chapter of the mother tantra, the Vajraḍāka, it says:
In the distant past, during the mahāsukha first eon, dwelled the great Vajrasattva, great god of gods. When seen by the demigods, siddhas, and others, as well as by the host of gods, they were afraid. The buddhas assembled and beseeched me. Great goddess, they had melted into drops, to be scattered everywhere by the māras, the great stupefier of all, hailed as quicksilver; its inferior kind is found in the ocean depths, the superior kind on mountains.[209]

d.div: [126] sde dge_370_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma/ rim par phye ba/ 49_shog_111_ba3

[209] Vajraḍākatantra, chap. 49, Toh 370 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 111b3. This cryptic verse is best explained by the commentary to this tantra (Toh 1415 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, tsha), which says that Vajrasattva manifested as Mahādeva and consort, producing great light and fire, thereby terrifying the gods, demigods, siddhas, etc. This fire was the fire of a passion that melted the two into drops, and the buddhas saw that these drops were to be scattered around the world by the māras. Through the medium of song they beseeched Vajrasattva to awake from his passion and prevent this from happening. This is the origin of mercury, or quicksilver.

f.d:
ces dang /
a ru ra ni 'bigs byed kyi/ / nags dang ri bo dbang chen skyes/ / nar ma dA yi chu skyes mchog / gzhan dag dman dang 'bring po yin/ /

Also:
Myrobalan is found in the Vindhya forests and on the Mahendra mountains. The best is by the waters of Narmadā, others are middling or inferior.

d.div: smyung [127]po dang ni 'jigs med dang / / 'tsho dang de bzhin bdud rtsi ste/ / gtsang ma dang ni 'phel ba dang / / rnam par rgyal ba bdun du brjod/ /
Oval, Fearless, Life-giving, Ambrosia, Purity, Increase, and Victorious are its seven types.[210]
[127] snyung po/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

[210] In Tibetan medicine myrobalan is usually described as being of five types. These seven types broadly correspond with the seven types mentioned in Indian Āyurveda. (Dash, Encyclopedia of Tibetan Medicine, p. 8.)

ri mo gsum pa smyung po ste/ / 'jigs med ri mo lnga pa yin/ / 'tsho ba gser mdog shes par bya/ / bdud rtsi sha chen zhes bya ste/ / de bzhin gtsang ma sha med yin/ ser skya 'phel ba zhes bya ste/ / ku ba lta bu rnam par rgyal/ /
dri la smyung po sbyar bya ste/ / bcud kyis len pa bdud rtsi bsngags/ / 'jigs med rnam par rgyal ba 'bring / / lhag ma rnams ni don med do/ /
skyu ru ra ni sha che zhing / / rus pa chung la ro dang ldan/ / rdo ba can gyi ri las skyes/ / shin tu smin pa mchog tu bshad/ /
ba ru ra ni tha mal pa'i/ / ri las skyes pa'am gzhan yang rung /[128] /
Baleric myrobalan is found on ordinary hills and elsewhere.[211]
[128] sde dge_370_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma/ rim par phye ba/ 49_shog_112_na5
[211] Vajraḍākatantra, chap. 49, Toh 370 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 112a5.

f.d: zhes sman rags rim gyi skye gnas dang rigs bzang ngan sogs dang /
These passages describe general locations of medicines, superior and inferior types, and so on. In the same work it says:

gser gyi mdog ni bzang por 'gyur/ / dngul gyis so ni bzang por 'gyur/ / mu tig mig ni dag par 'gyur/ / mu men skra dang spu la phan/ / rdo rjes thog ni bzlog 'gyur te/ / lcags kyis chu dang mtshon rnams bzlog[129] / ces bcangs pa'i yon tan dang /

Gold is good for complexion, silver is good for teeth, pearl is a purifier, lapis is good for hair, diamond turns away thunderbolts, iron resists water and weapons.[212] This passage describes the benefits of wearing various substances. Also:

d.div: [129] sde dge_370_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma/ rim par phye ba/ 49_shog_115_na5
pi pi ling dang gur gum ni/ / cha ni mnyam por byas nas su/ / so ka'i dus su bza' bar bya/ / de rjes gci ba dro 'thungs na/ / kha zas yi gar 'ong zhing 'ju/ /
Long pepper and saffron taken in spring in equal measures, followed by a drink of warm urine, will aid appetite and digestion.
nir guN+Di yi khu ba dang / / gci bar bcas pa sna sman sbyin/ / bad kan las gyur nad rnams 'phrog / de nyid pad ma'i dri ma dang / / bcas par byugs na glang shu sel/ /
Nirguṇdi juice with urine taken as nose drops eliminates disorders arising from phlegm; when mixed with lotus aroma and applied as a lotion, it cures bull sores.[213]
[213] Glang shu. See glossary.
ma raka da yi rtsa ba dang / / so dang sen mo'i rdul du bsre/ / rma ni dang po mar gyis bkru/ / de rjes sman des byugs na ni/ / rma ni 'drub par byed pa'i mchog /
The root of markata mixed with ground nails and teeth: to first wash the wound with ghee and then apply this medicine is the best cure for a wound.

f.d: so phag rdul dang sug smel phye/ / gi ri kar+Na'i khu ba ru/ / mnyes te mig la byugs na ni/ / rab rib dag ni 'joms pa'i mchog[130] / ces dngul chu sogs bcud len gyi sbyor ba dang / gzhan yang gsog ldang zhi gsum rags tsam gsungs/

Brick dust and greater cardamom mixed into the juice of girikarṇā and rubbed onto the eyes is best for curing poor vision.[214] The passages from the above tantra speak of the elixir preparation of mercury, and so on, and in general terms of the gathering, arising, and pacifying of disorders.

d.div: [130] sde dge_370_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_rgyud kyi rgyal po chen po dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma/ rim par phye ba/ 49_shog_116_ba5
[214] Vajraḍākatantra, chap. 49, Toh 370 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 116b5.

f.d:
dpal mkha' 'gro rgya mtsho'i rgyud kyi le'u sum cu rtsa brgyad par/
rdul can ma dang yung ba gnyis/ / yongs bzung ba yi dar ba dang / / bre do bsdu bar bya ba ste/ / bre gang ma gyur bar du'o/ / de ltar 'thungs bas nyin bdun na/ / bcud len rdzogs par byed pa yin/[131] / zhes sogs bcud len gyi rnam pa du ma dang /

In the thirty-eighth chapter of the Ḍāka Ocean Tantra it says:
Black zedorary and turmeric combined in whey, two measures boiled until they become one; drink this, and in seven days it will become the complete elixir.[215] This and other verses describe different types of elixirs.

d.div: [131] sde dge_372_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_mkha' 'gro rgya mtsho rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud/ le'u/ 38_shog_215_na1
[215] Ḍākārṇavatantra, Toh 372 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 215a1.

f.d:
sdom 'byung rgyud kyi+i rim par dbye ba gnyis par/
dang po'i rnam pa nur nur po/ / mer mer po ni gnyis pa yin/ / ltar ltar por skyes gsum pa ste/ / de bzhin bzhi pa gor gor po/[132] / zhes lus gnas chags tshul dang /

In the second chapter of the Saṃvarodaya Tantra it says:
The initial form is coagulation, the second is a mass, the third becomes elongated, the fourth is solid.[216] This is the forming of the embryo.

[216] Cakrasaṃvara/Saṃvarodaya Tantra, Toh 373 Kangyur, rgyud, kha, 266a7.

f.d:
rim par dbye ba bcu dgu par/
bshad dang gci ba'i dus dag tu/ / dus mtshungs sbrid pa byung gyur na/ / lo gcig na dus de nyid kyi/ / dus tshod la ni 'chi zhing brlag[133] / ces 'chi ltas kyi rim pa du ma dang /

In the nineteenth chapter:
One who sneezes while defecating and urinating will die within a year.[217] This and other verses talks of the various stages of the signs of death. Also:

d.div: [133] sde dge_373_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_bde mchog gi 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud/ rim par phye ba/ 19_shog_288_na4

With the proper instructions, death will be bought off.[218] This talks of the ritual for cheating death.[219]

d.div: [134] slu bar/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[135] sde dge_373_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_bde mchog gi 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud/ rim par phye ba/ 19_shog_289_na2
[219] ’Chi ba blu ba.

f.d:
rim par dbye ba nyer lnga bar/
so phag tshos 'gyur 'dag gu dang / / nir gun+Di dang bal gul dza/ / smyo byed 'dab dang ni rayA sa/ / gla rtsi tsan dan ldan pa dang / / bA li ka dang tso rar ldan/ / rang gis lus ni dril byas na/ / nad rnams kun las rnam grol zhing / / dug med mdangs dang ldan par 'gyur/ /
'bras bu gsum dang tsan dan gyi/ / phye mar bcas dang gla rtsi ni/ / bsil dang lhan cig lo gcig 'thungs/ / nad med rgas pa'ang med par 'gyur/[136] / zhes nad 'joms rgas gso la sogs pa'i rnam grangs mang ba dang /

In the twenty-fifth chapter:
Colored brick dust, mud, nirguṇdi, avalguja, unmatta decoction, musk with sandalwood, bālaka, and angelica, when rubbed into the body, will eliminate all illness, leaving one free of poisons with a healthy glow.
The three fruits, powdered sandal, and musk, taken for a year with cool medicine, will eliminate illness and aging as well.[220] These verses talk of the curing of various illnesses and rejuvenation therapy.

d.div: [136] sde dge_373_bka'/ rgyud/ kha_bde mchog gi 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i rgyud/ rim par phya be / 25_shog_298_na1
[220] Cakrasaṃvara/Saṃvarodaya Tantra, Toh 373 Kangyur rgyud, kha, 298a1.

f.d:
dam pa dang po'i sangs rgyas kyis bsdus pa'i rgyud kyi nang ler/
