nad kun nas slong ba la mkhas pa ci lta bu zhe na/ de la sman pa zug rngu 'byin pas nad shes shing 'di ni rlung gis kun nas bslang ba'am/ mkhris pas kun nas bslang ba'am/ bad kan gyis kun nas bslang ba'am/ bdag las gyur pa'am/ gzhan las gyur pa'am/ 'dus pa las gyur pa'o/ /zhes de nyid nad kun nas slong ba la mkhas pa yin no/ /

What does it mean to know what causes illness? It means that the pain-relieving doctor knows the illness and is able to say that this illness is caused by wind, this by bile, this by phlegm, this by oneself, this by others, and this by a combination of these factors. That is what it means to know what causes illness.

nad byung ba spong ba la mkhas pa ci lta bu zhe na/ de la sman pa zug rngu 'byin pa nad shes shing nad 'di ni mig sman nam/ bsku mnye 'am/ skyugs sman nam/ bkru sman nam/ snar blug pa'am/ du bas bdug pa'am/ nan rtsi'i las kyis spong bar 'gyur ro/ /zhes de ltar nad byung ba spong ba la mkhas pa yin no//

What does it mean to know how to eradicate illness? It means that the pain-relieving doctor knows the illness and knows that it will be eradicated by eye medicine, by massage, emetics, purgatives, nasal medication, fumigation, or enema. That is what it means to know how to eradicate illness.

nad spangs pa phyis mi 'byung ba la mkhas pa ci lta bu zhe na/ de la sman pa zug rngu 'byin pa nad shes shing nad 'di ni 'phrod pa'i cho ga 'di lta bu dang 'di lta bu dag byas te spangs na phyis mi 'byung ngo / /zhes de ltar nad spangs pas phyis mi 'byung ba la mkhas pa yin te/

What does it mean to know how to ensure the illness does not return? It means that the doctor knows the illness and knows that following a particular regimen will ensure the illness does not return. That is what it means to know how to ensure the illness does not return.

de ltar sman pa zug rngu 'byin pa yan lag bzhi dang ldan pa rgyal po la 'os pa yin/ rgyal po la mkho ba yin/ rgyal po'i yan lag gi grangs su 'gro ba yin no/ / de bzhin du de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas yan lag bzhi dang ldan pa'ang sman pa zug rngu 'byin pa bla na med pa zhes bya'o/ /

In this way a pain-relieving doctor who possesses these four qualities is fit to be in the company of a king, is essential to a king, is included in the retinue of the king. “Likewise, the tathāgata, the arhat, the perfected buddha, possesses four qualities and is the supreme pain-relieving doctor.

'tsho byed bzhi gang zhe na/ de la de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas ni/ 'di ni sdug bsngal 'phags pa'i bden pa'o/ / 'di ni sdug bsngal kun 'byung ba'o/ / 'di ni sdug bsngal 'gog pa'o/ / 'di ni sdug bsngal 'gog par 'gro ba'i lam 'phags pa'i bden pa'o/ / zhes yang dag par ji lta ba shin tu rab tu mkhyen to/ /

What are these four Jivaka? The tathāgata, the arhat, the perfected buddha, he knows that this is the truth of suffering, that this is the origin of suffering, that this is the cessation of suffering, and that this is the path of the noble ones that leads to the cessation of suffering. In this way he knows the truth exactly as it is.

'tsho byed sman pa zug rngu 'byin pas ni skye ba'i rtsa ba can gyi sdug bsngal rnams spangs ba'i sman mi shes so/ / rga ba dang na ba dang 'chi ba dang mya ngan dang smre sngags 'don pa dang sdug bsngal ba dang / yid mi bde ba dang 'khrugs pa'i rtsa ba can gyi sdug bsngal rnams spong ba'i sman mi shes so/ / 'tsho byed de de bzhin gshegs pa ni skye ba'i rtsa ba can gyi sdug bsngal rnams spong ba'i sman mkhyen no/ / rga ba nas 'khrugs pa'i rtsa ba can gyi bar gyi sdug bsngal rnams spong pa'i sman mkhyen no/ / de bas na de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas ni sman pa zug rngu 'byin pa bla na med pa zhes bya'o//

“Jivaka, the doctor who relieves pain does not know the medicine that eradicates the sufferings of birth. He does not know the medicine that eradicates the pains of old age, sickness, death, grief, anguish, distress, unhappiness, and disturbance. Jivaka, the tathāgata knows the medicine that puts an end to the sufferings of birth. He knows the medicine that ends all sufferings from aging to disturbance. Therefore, the tathāgata, the arhat, the perfected buddha, is the supreme pain-relieving doctor.”

zhes pa'i chos kyi rnam grangs bstan cing / ston pa'i zhal sgo nas 'od zer 'phros pas a+yon gyi yul sman gyi grong khyer lta na sdug khyab/ drang srong chen po yid las skyes dngos su byon te 'tsho byed gzhon nu rgyud gsung ba'i dus 'khor du yod pas lung sogs ma dgos kyang glegs bam gtad/ ston pas rgyal po gzugs can snying po rnam thos sras kyi bur skyes pa rgyal ba khyu mchog gam zhang blon rdo rje bdud 'dul bkug ste rgyud bzhi'i srung mar bskos/ 'di la chos 'khor rim pa gsum dus la sbyar ba dang rtogs dpyod mkhan pos brtags na snga phyi mi mtshungs pa'i dogs pa skye srid de/ don dam par chos 'khor rim gsum cig car du gsungs pa dang / sangs rgyas kyi gsang ba bsam gyi mi khyab pa'i spyod yul du so skyes 'khrul rtog gi klan kha mi 'tshol la/ dus der 'tsho byed gzhon nus bskyed chos rnams la chos kyi mig rdul med cing dri ma dang bral ba skyes so/ /

In this way Jivaka was taught different aspects of the Dharma, and then from the mouth of our Teacher came light that pervaded the medicine city of Sudarśana in the land of Oḍḍiyāna. The great Rishi Manasija appeared, and during the teaching of the tantra, Kumāra Jivaka was part of the audience. Therefore, although he did not need the transmission of the teachings, he was entrusted with the scripture. Our Teacher summoned King Bimbisāra, who had been reborn as the son of Vaiśravaṇa, and Jinarṣabha or Rājānaka Vajra Mārajit, and appointed them guardians of the tantra. If you examine the above, thinking the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma were sequential events, discerning minds may raise some concerns regarding the discrepancies the narrative displays. However, from the highest perspective the three turnings were taught simultaneously, and in the inconceivable realm of perception that is the mystery of the Buddha the disorted perceptions of ordinary beings are no basis for argument. At this time Kumāra Jivaka Bhṛtya developed the eye of Dharma, free of all obstruction, free of all taints, for all phenomena.

de nas 'tsho byed gzhon nus bskyed kyis chos mthong ba dang thos pa dang / chos kyi gting sleb pa dang / som nyi dang the tshom las brgal ba dang / gzhan gyi dring mi 'jog pa dang / gzhan gyi mi bkri ba dang / ston pas bstan pa'i chos rnams la mi 'jigs pa thob nas bstan las langs te blo gos phrag pa gcig tu gzar nas bcom ldan 'das ga la ba der thal mo sbyar ba btud de 'di skad ces gsol to/ / btsun pa bdag ni 'phags so/ / mngon par 'phags so/ / bcom ldan 'das dang chos dang dge slong gi dge 'dun la skyabs su mchi'o/ / bdag dge bsnyen du bzung du gsol/ deng slan chad ji srid 'tsho ba'i bar du srog dang bsdos te skyabs su mchi lags so zhes gsol ba sogs bden pa mthong /

Then Kumāra Jivaka saw the Dharma and heard the Dharma. He penetrated to the very depths of the Dharma and passed over all doubts and hesitancy. He no longer needed to rely on others, no longer needed to be guided by others. He gained the state of fearlessness toward the teachings given to him by the Buddha. He rose from his seat, draped his shawl over his shoulder, placed his hands together, bowed to the Buddha, and said, “I the monk have been elevated, truly elevated. I go for refuge to the Bhagavān, to the Dharma, and to the Sangha of monks. Please accept me as an upāsaka. From today for as long as I live, I go for refuge even if it should cost me my life.” In this way he saw the truth.

de'i tshe ri'i rgyal po gangs can rtag tu kha bas g.yogs shing lhags pa che bas bcom ldan 'das grang nad kyi bsnyun gyis thebs pa dang / 'tsho byed kyis bsams pa/ dper na 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po la byed pa bzhin bcom ldan 'das kyi rim gro bdag nyid kho nas bya'o snyam mo/ / de nas me tog ut+pal sum cu rtsa gnyis dang bkru sman gyi rdzas sbyar nas phul te 'di rnams shangs kyi bsnams su gsol/ bcom ldan 'das kyis bsnams pa las thengs sum cu rtsa gnyis 'khrus par gyur to/ / de nas bcom ldan 'das la ci dgar legs par 'khrus lags sam/ bka' stsal pa/ 'tsho byed/ skyon gang dag g.yos la ma 'khrus pa dag kyang yod/ 'khrus la ma g.yos pa'ang yod/ 'khrus la g.yos pa'ang yod/ ma 'khrus ma g.yos pa dag kyang yod do/ / gsol ba de lta na/ bu ram dang a ru ra gsol la 'khru ba'i rim pa yang mdzod cig /des de bzhin mdzad pas snyun dwangs par gyur to/ / 'tsho byed kyi kun tu spyod pa ni rgyal po'am blon po'am gang su'i dpyad byas kyang rung ste/ des de la grong ngam mchog sbyin par byed pa yin no//

At that time the Himalayas were permanently covered in snow and very windy, and the Buddha became ill with a cold disorder. Jivaka thought to himself, “Like a universal emperor, I alone am here to perform service the Bhagavān.” He mixed purgative medicine with thirty-two utpala flowers and offered them to the Buddha to ingest as a nasal purgative. The Bhagavān accepted the medicine, and the purging was performed thirty-two times. Then Jivaka asked, “Has the purgative worked?” The Buddha replied, “Jivaka, part of the disorder has been stirred without being purged, part has been purged without being stirred, part has been both purged and stirred, and part has been neither purged nor stirred. In that case, offer molasses and myrobalan and perform the purging once again.” Jivaka did as he was asked and the illness subsided. Jivaka’s practice was that whoever he treated, be it kings, ministers, or anyone in need, he did it as work for the community or as an act of offering.

de nas 'dul ba phran tshegs kyi bam po nyi shu rtsa gsum pa [160]dang nyer bzhi pa las 'byung pa'i lo rgyus su/[161] yul 'phags rgyal gyi rgyal po mu khyud mtha' yas kyi bu bcom ldan 'das dang dus mnyam du skyes shing de'i tshe sangs rgyas kyi mthus 'jig rten 'od kyis snang bar byas pa rang gi bu'i ltas su go ste rab snang zhes btags pa dbang po lnga dang nye dbang lnga dang nyin zhag gcig la dpag tshad brgya'i sa chod pa glang po che 'dam bu'i ri dpag tshad brgyad cu chod pa glang mo bzang ldan/ bdun cu chod pa rnga mo rgya mtsho'i rkang / lnga bcu chod pa rta gos mgrin/ nyi shu chod pa 'phar ma ba khwa ste yan lag mchog lnga la sogs pa phun sum tshogs kyang nad du gnyid med cing mar la sdang ba chang la dga' ba zhig pas/ de la sman pa rnams kyis rdzas kyi khyad par sna tshogs pa mar dang sbyar te blud par brtsams pa'i tshe mi 'thung zhing / mar gyi ming tsam 'byin pa de dang / nam gyi thun dang po btsun mo rnams dang rtse/ gnyis pa rta dang glang po rnams la blta/ thun gsum par mel tshe ba rnams la 'bod cing lan ma lon pa de'i mgo bo gcod par byed pas gtum po rab snang zhes bya bar grags so/ /

In chapters 23 and 24 of the Short Vinaya are the following accounts.[269] The son of Anantanemi, king of Avanti, was born at the same moment as the Bhagavān, and at that time the whole world shone with light owing to the Buddha’s power. The king thought this was a sign brought on by his son’s birth and so named him Pradyota, meaning “shining.” Pradyota possessed the five forces, the five secondary forces, the elephant Nalagiri, which could cover a distance of a hundred leagues in one day, the she-elephant Bhadravat, which could cover eighty leagues in one day, the camel Samudrapada, which could cover seventy leagues in one day, the horse Ambarakaṇṭha, which could cover fifty leagues in one day, and the messenger Kāka, who could cover twenty leagues in one day. These were known as the five limbs. He had everything, but he suffered from insomnia, and he had an aversion to ghee and a liking for alcohol. His doctors had prepared special medicine and mixed it with ghee, but when they tried to administer it, he refused to drink it, and even the word ghee was banished from his presence. In the first part of the night he enjoyed himself with his queens, and in the second part he went to look at his horses and elephants. In the third part of the night he called to his night watchmen, and those who did not answer had their heads cut off. Therefore, he became known as Caṇḍapradyota, meaning Pradyota the Fearsome.

d.div: [160] sde dge_6_bka'/ 'dul ba/ tha_phran tshegs kyi gzhi/ bam po/ 23_shog_265_na6
[161] sde dge_6_bka'/ 'dul ba/ tha_phran tshegs kyi gzhi/ bam po/ 24_shog_273_na3
[269] Vinayavastu, Toh 6 Kangyur, ’dul ba, tha, 265a6 and 273a3.

f.d:
de gnyid med pas thams cad kyi re mos su mel tshe bgyid dgos pa la/ spos tshong gi khye'u zhig la bab pas gnyid du song ste lan ma lon na bsad dogs nas sa 'dzin pa zhig karaSha pa Na lnga brgyas brngan nas tshab la btang / de mkhas pa zhig pas/
'ug pa khrung khrung mun+dza dang / / nag mo sreg pa bum pa dang / / lan tsha phye dang shi ba dang / / dong thags rnga ma sdig pa'o/ / zhes pa'i bsdoms dang mthun par srog chags 'ug pa'i sgro dang bcas pa dang sgro ma mchis par srang la gzhal na mnyam pa/ khrung khrung gis chu dang 'o ma bsres pa las 'o ma 'thung zhing chu 'dor ba/ rtsa mun+dza tho bas brdungs pa dang ma brdungs pa srang la bcal na lcid mnyam pa/ spra mgo nag mo la lus ji tsam pa de tsam gyi 'jug ma yod pa/ sreg pa'i gshog pa la sgro bkra ba dang mi bkra ba cha mnyam du yod pa/ bye ma bum pa gang gi nang du chab bum gang blugs kyang shong ba/ lan tsha phul gang gi nang du chu phul gang blug kyang mang du mi 'gro ba/ phye gzhib phul gang gi nang du chab phul gang stsal kyang sla ba dang gar bar mi 'gyur ba/ shi ba dang ma shi ba lcid mi mnyam pa/ dong brus pa'i sa de nyid du mi shong ba/ tha ga pas nyin mtshan du gos btags pa dang rdza mkhan gyis nyin mtshan du snod bgyis pa gar mchis mi 'tshal ba sogs kyis rgyu mtshan khungs dang bcas pa'i sgrung gis rgyal po dga' bar byed do/ /

Because of his insomnia, everybody had to take it in turns to act as night watchmen. One night it was the turn of a son of an incense seller. He was concerned that he might fall asleep, not hear the summons, and so lose his life. He therefore bribed a storyteller with five hundred kārṣāpaṇa to take his place. This storyteller was a clever man and kept the king amused with various stories, which are listed in the summary verse:
The owl, crane, and munjā reed, the black-faced monkey and the partridge, a pot, salt, flour, and a corpse, a pit, a weaver, a potter, and a scorpion. These stories concerned how an owl with feathers weighs the same as an owl without feathers; how a crane drinking water mixed with milk is able to drink the milk and discard the water; how munjā reed whether beaten or not beaten with a hammer weighs the same; how the tail of a black-faced monkey is the same length as its body; how the wings of the partridge have equal areas of color and non-color; how a pot full of water can be poured into a pot full of sand without overflowing; how a handful of water can be poured into a handful of salt and not increase; how a handful of water mixed with a handful of fine flour becomes neither thick nor thin; how a living body and its corpse do not weigh the same; how earth dug out of a pit does not fit back in again; how a weaver spent all day and night weaving cloth and a potter spent all day and night making pots, yet nobody knew where their products went. With these stories, backed up with reasons and evidence, he kept the king amused.

mjug tu de ltar khyod kyis thams cad shes na nga gnyid med pa'i rgyu mtshan ci yin/ mi 'jigs pa stsol na'o/ / sbyin no/ / sdig pa las skyes pa'i rgyu mtshan gyis so/ / gang las shes mngon sum du bya'o zhes smras nas/ sa dong du ba lang gi lci ba skam pos bkang ba'i steng du rgyal po'i mal bcas nas nyal ma thag gnyid la song ngo / / sad nas de ltar yin pa shes kyang yum la dris pas mi 'jigs pa stsol na'o/ / de ltar bgyi'o gsungs shig / / khyod kyi yab btsun mo'i 'khor rgya chen po dang ldan pas/ de ljongs gzhan du song ba na/ bdag zla mtshan dang ldan pa'i dus su khrus byed pa'i tshe sdig pa zhig mthong ba la 'di pho zhig yin mchis na 'dod pa spyod pa'i blo skyes pa la de las dbang gis skyes pa 'dra bar gyur nas 'dod pa spyad pas khyod skyes so/ / rgyal pos bsams pa/ sa 'dzin pa de mkhas pa zhig pas des gzhan la smra 'ong / mi 'jigs pa byin pas bsad du mi rung yang gzhan du dbyung ngo snyam kar Sha pa Na lnga brgya byin te bskrad do//

When the stories were over, the king said, “You seem to know everything; what is the cause of my insomnia?” “Will you guarantee my safety if I tell you?” “I will,” replied the king. “It is because you were born from a scorpion,” said the storyteller. “How do you know this? Prove it to me,” demanded the king. A pit was dug and filled with dry cow dung. On top of this was placed the king’s mattress. As soon as he lay down he fell asleep. On waking he realized that what the storyteller had said was true.[270] Nevertheless, the king asked his mother about this. “Will you guarantee my safety?” she asked. “I will. Now tell me.” “Your father had a large harem of queens, and when he went away to other places, to them, during my menstruation periods, I would go to bathe. Once, while bathing, I saw a scorpion and thought, ‘If only this were a man.’ By the power of these lustful thoughts, the scorpion took the form of a man and we made love. This is how you were born.” The king thought to himself, “That storyteller is very clever. Even if he tells this to others, I can’t kill him because I have promised him protection. However, I could send him elsewhere.” Therefore, he gave the storyteller five hundred kārṣāpaṇa and sent him away.

d.div: [270] Probably because dried cow dung is known to stupefy scorpions.

f.d: des nas nad de gzhi cher gyur pa la sman pa rnams bsags nas dpyad gyis shig par bsgos kyang / de rnams na re/ nged cag rnams kyis rngo mi thogs kyi/ rgyal po'i khab na gzugs can snying po'i bu sman pa'i rgyal po 'tsho byed gzhon nus gsos zhes bya ba yod kyi des rngo thogs so/ / des yi ge springs te 'tsho byed 'gro bar brtsams pa na/ 'phar ma ba'am bang chen pa la ni lugs dris te chang gi dri ro kha dog yod pa'i mar sbyar te khur nas phyin no/ / lam gyi yul ka nya ku pa jar sman pa'i khye'u zhig yod pa de dang phrad/ 'tsho byed la a ru ra gcig phul/ rgyal po gtum po rab snang nad ci zhig gis thebs/ sman pa des smras pa/ gnyid med pa'i nad kyis thebs te de la mar phan na/ rgyal po ni chang la dga' zhing mar la sdang bas mdun du mar gyi ming 'bod pa de yang mgo gcod pas bdag cag gis de'i dpyad rngo ma thogs zhes smras pa dang / 'tsho byed na re/ de'i phyir ngas chang gi kha dog dang / chang gi dri dang / chang gi ro bro ba'i mar skol te khyer 'ong ba 'di yin pas/ ngas khyod la brda byas pa de'i tshe mar 'di tsam zhig byin la cung zad khyod kyis rim gro byos shig sogs bslabs te mnyam por 'phags rgyal du song ngo / / sleb pa na gtum po rab snang gis bkur sti yang dag pas nang du bos nas dpyad gyis shig zer to/ / de la 'bros pa goms su 'jug pa'i ched du sman dkon pa 'tshol ba ltar byas nas/ nyin zhag gcig la dpag tshad brgyad cur bgrod pa'i glang mo bzang ldan la zhon te snga phyi ci rigs pa'i tshul gyi sleb par byas nas mthar sman pa'i khye'u la brda byas nas khrus mdzad cing / gdugs tshod gsol zhig /bdag gis 'khur ba'i skyems shig ces byas nas bros so/ /

The insomnia became worse and he brought together his doctors and ordered them to cure it. They replied, “We are unable to treat this problem. However, in Rājagṛha, lives Kumāra Jivaka Bhṛtya, a master of medicine and the son of King Bimbisāra. He will be able to treat this illness.” A letter was sent to him, and just before he set out on his journey, Jivaka asked the messenger or servant about the nature of the illness. He then made up some ghee that had the smell, taste, and color of alcohol, and set off. On the way, in the district of Kanyakubja, he met a young doctor, who offered Jivaka myrobalan. “What is this illness of King Caṇḍapradyota?” asked Jivaka. “He suffers from insomnia,” replied the doctor. “Ghee would help him but he detests ghee and loves alcohol. Anyone who even mentions the word ghee in his presence is executed. Therefore, we dare not treat him.” “It is for that reason,” said Jivaka, “that I boiled some ghee and mixed in it the color of alcohol, the smell of alcohol, and the taste of alcohol. When I give you the signal, give him this much of this ghee and then wait on him for a while.” Together they set off for Avanti. When they arrived Caṇḍapradyota received them with due ceremony, invited them inside, and then requested treatment from them. In order to familiarize himself with his plan of escape, Jivaka said that he needed to go out and search for some rare medicine. He mounted the she-elephant Bhadravat, which was able to travel eighty leagues in one day, and after an appropriate time returned to the king. He told the king first to bathe and then take his midday meal. Then giving the signal to the young doctor, he said, “Majesty, please drink what I have brought for you.” With these words he left and fled the palace.

de 'thung ma thag gnyid du song nas nam phyed na sad pa'i tshe mar gyi sgreg pa byung nas mi dga' bas gsod par brtsams pa na bros par shes nas 'phar ma pa kha zhes pa nyin zhag gcig la dpag tshad nyi shu chod pa de nyin zhag gcig la dpag tshad brgya chod pa'i glang po che la bskyon nas 'tsho byed ded la sgyu ma mkhan des khyod la ci byin yang ma len par ske nas thogs la khrid shog bsgos so/ /

As soon as the king had drunk the medicine he fell asleep. He awoke in the middle of the night and belched up some ghee. He became angry and wanted to kill Jivaka. When he realized he had fled, this deceitful king sent the messenger Kāka, who could travel twenty leagues in a day, on the elephant Nalagiri, which could cover a hundred leagues in one day, in pursuit of Jivaka, saying, “Don’t accept anything that trickster gives you, but bind him by the neck and bring him here.”
zin la khad pa na glang mo'i chu btang ba'i dris cung zad thogs so/ / de nas skyu ru ra'i tshal zhig tu zin nas khrid par brtsams pa na/ da ci rings re zhig skyu ru ra zo zhig /

As Kāka became closer, his elephant was somewhat held up by the smell of a she-elephant’s urine. Finally, he caught up with Jivaka in a grove of emblic myrobalan. As he was about to lead him away, Jivaka said, “Kāka, what’s the hurry? Have some myrobalan.”

lha'i gsung gis ci byin kyang ma za zer bas so/ / de ltar na phyed phyed za'o byas nas sen mo 'khru sman gyis bkang bas bcad nas byin pas shin tu 'khrus nas ri bor zhig tu bzhag ste/ 'di rnams rgyal po'i mchog gsum yin pas rim gro 'di dang 'di lta bu gyis la phul zhig / gzhan du khyod rnams 'phung bar 'gyur ro byas nas rgyal po'i khab tu song ngo / / gtum po rab snang 'tsho byed kyis sbyar ba'i mar gyi khu ba des gnyid med pa'i nad gsos so/ /

“My master told me not to accept anything from you.” “Well, let’s each eat half,” suggested Jivaka. Jivaka cut the fruit in half with his fingernail, which was harboring a purgative, and gave that half to Kāka, who took it and was thoroughly purged. He left him on a hillside and told the people living there, “These three are cherished by the king.[271] Do such and such practice and return them to him. Otherwise, you will seriously suffer.” With these words he returned to Rājagṛha. Meanwhile the ghee potion prepared by Jivaka had cured the king of insomnia.

d.div: [271] This passage suffers from considerable cropping of the original story. In the Degé Tengyur Kāka suffers from leprosy, and the medicine Jivaka surreptitiously administers cures him. He is left on the side of the mountain with the two elephants. These are the “three cherished by the king.” His words are to the local people.

f.d: khwa de [162]mdze can zhig yin pa gsos nas log pa'i tshe rgyal po'ang nad de las grol nas dris pas/ bros so/ / ma legs/ lha zin na ci bgyi/ gsod do/ / ce nged rang gnyis ka gsos par byas pa ma yin nam/ 'o na ci bya/ bya dga' ster mod/ legs te de bzhin bgyi'o zhes byas nas nor mang po springs pa na/ 'tsho byed kyis kho bo la nor yod kyi/ sman pa'i khye'u la gnang ba'i rigs so// des sman pa'i khye'u la bya dga' chen po byin zhing 'tsho byed la'ang karaSha pa Na brgya stong ri ba'i ras yug po che byin no/ / de'ang bcom ldan 'das la phul nas na bza' chos gos gsum dang / kun dga' bo'i bla gos mthang gos/ sgra gcan zin gyi ral chung dpung chad gcig rnams byas/ yang de'i tshe dge slong gzhon nu zhig kha zas dang spyod lam nyes pas 'bras zhes bya ba'i nad kyis btab ste sdug bsngal ba 'tsho byed kyis brtol bas zhi bar gyur/

Kāka too had been cured of his leprosy. When he returned to the palace, the king questioned him about Jivaka. “He escaped,” said Kāka. “That is not good,” said the king. “What was I supposed to do when I caught him?” “Kill him, of course.” “But your majesty,” protested Kāka, “hasn’t he cured us both of our ailments?” “So, what should we do?” asked the king. “Surely, we should reward him,” replied Kāka. “That is good. I will do that,” said the king. The king therefore sent a large amount of money to Jivaka, who returned it, saying, “I have money. It would be better to give the money to the young doctor.” This the king did, and he sent Jivaka also a beautiful cloth worth one hundred thousand kārṣāpaṇa. Jivaka offered this cloth to the Bhagavān, and from it was made a set of the three robes for the Buddha, an upper and lower robe for Ānanda, and a small supplementary robe for Rāhula. At that time there was a young monk suffering from a growth resulting from faulty diet and behavior. Jivaka pierced the growth, and the monk’s suffering was relieved.

d.div: [162] khwa ta mdze can/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

f.d: bcom ldan 'das 'od ma'i tshal bya ka lan ta ka gnas pa la bzhugs dus kun dga' bo'i spyi bor phol mig byung ba/ 'tsho byed la dpyad byos shig par bka' stsal pa ltar/ kun dga' bo bcom ldan 'das la chos nyan pa'i tshe phol mig smin par gyur pa'i rdzas dag bskus nas gral de nyid du nad pa la tshor ba'i zug rngu til 'bru tsam med par gsos/

Once when the Bhagavān was residing in the Kalandaka Nivās bamboo grove, Ānanda developed an abscess on his head, and the Buddha asked Jivaka to treat him. While Ānanda was listening to the teachings of the Bhagavān, Jivaka applied ripening medicine to the abscess, and there, not having moved from his seat, he was cured without the slightest sensation of pain.

skabs shig bcom ldan 'das snyun gyis thebs nas 'tsho byed la bka' stsal pa dang / des bsam pa bcom ldan 'das ni rdo rje'i sku mnga' la sku che ba yin pas skye bo phal pa lta bu'i nyung ngus ni gdang mi nus so snyam ste mar srang sum cu rtsa gnyis la sbyar ba'i sman mar lcags mda' phul ba bzhes te snyun las grol ba dang / lhas byin gyi bsam pa bdag gis kyang de bzhin du btang ngo snyam nas 'tsho byed la dris pa/ 'tsho byed dge sbyong go'u ta mas mar ji tsam gyi tshad gsol/ mar srang sum cu rtsa gnyis so/ /

Once the Bhagavān himself was ill and told this to Jivaka, who thought to himself, “The Bhagavān’s vajra body is large. The small amount of medicine needed to treat an ordinary being will not be sufficient.” Therefore, he prepared the medicine known as iron-arrow medicinal ghee using thirty-two measures of ghee and offered it to the Bhagavān, who accepted it and was cured. Devadatta thought to himself, “I, too, will take the same amount of medicine.” He approached Jivaka: “Jivaka, how much ghee did you give to the monk Gautama?” “I gave him thirty-two measures,” replied Jivaka.

'o na kho bos kyang de ltar 'thung ngo / / 'tsho byed kyis smras pa/ bcom ldan 'das ni rdo rje'i sku mnga' la sku che ba yin pas ji tsam yang 'ju bar spyod kyi/ khyod kyis ni 'ju bar mi nus so/ / des smras pa/ kho bo yang rdo rje'i lus can yin na ci'i phyir mi 'ju zhes mar srang sum cu rtsa gnyis 'thungs so/ / de'i phyi nyin par 'tsho byed kyis bcom ldan 'das la 'jam gsol lo/ / lhas byin gyis kyang mar ma zhu bzhin du thug pa btungs pas sbos gzer nas gnad du phog pa'i tshor ba nyam nga la rtsub pa yid du mi 'ong bas thebs pa/ kun dga' bos bcom ldan 'das la zhus pa dang / bkra shis kyis 'khor los mtshan pa'i phyag g.yas pa glang po'i sna lta bu brkyang ste lhas byin gyi mgo la bzhag nas/ ji ltar nga bu gcig pa sgra gcan 'dzin bzang po la dgongs pa de bzhin lhas byin la yang lhag chad med pa yin zhe na/ bden pa des lhas byin gyi nad zhi bar gyur cig ces gsungs ma thag nad las grol kyang / bcom ldan 'das kyi phyag yin pa ngo shes te des smras pa/ don grub khyod kyis sman la'ang mkhas par slobs pa lta ste mi 'dod do zer ro//

“Well then, I will take the same,” retorted Devadatta. “The Bhagavān’s vajra body is large,” replied Jivaka. “Such a powerful body can digest that much. You would not be able to digest it.” Devadatta replied, “I also have a vajra body, so why can’t I digest it?” With these words he drank thirty-two measures of the same medicine. The next day Jivaka offered the Bhagavān some broth. Devadatta also took some broth on top of his undigested ghee, and as a result his stomach distended, reaching a precarious point and leaving him feeling wretched and in a sorry state. Ānanda spoke of this to the Bhagavān, who, like an elephant with his trunk, stretched out his right hand adorned with an auspicious wheel and laid it on Devadatta’s head, saying, “I declare that the way I regard Rāhula, my beautiful and only son, is no more and no less than the way I regard Devadatta. By the truth of these words may this illness of Devadatta be cured.” No sooner had he spoken these words than Devadatta was cured. Devadatta, however, recognized Buddha’s hand upon him and said, “Siddhartha, you have obviously become proficient in medicine, too, but I am not interested.”

bcom ldan 'das la lhas byin gyis sgyogs 'phangs pa'i rdo ba'i dum bus zhabs kyi mthe bong la rma byung nas khrag chad du ma btub pa'i tshe sman pa'i rgyal po 'tsho byed bcom ldan 'das kyi snyun brtag pa'i phyir dus gsum du spyan sngar 'gro'o/ / rgyal po'i khab na gnas pa'i skye bo tshogs thams cad 'dus te sman 'di ni de la bzang ngo / / gzhan dag na re 'di ni de bas kyang bzang ngo / / 'tsho byed kyis smras pa/ mod la snyun dwangs par 'gyur pa'i sman yod mod kyi rnyed par dka' 'o/ / kun dga' bos smras pa de ci yin/ tsan dan sa mchog yin no/ / ji tsam na tshong dpon zhig gis tsan dan sa mchog phul ba bzhes nas dge ba'i rtsa ba des rang sangs rgyas tsan dan byin zhes bya bar 'gyur bar lung bstan/ 'on kyang khrag chad du ma btub ste 'jog go/ / 'tsho byed kyis smras pa/ da ni bud med gzhon nu bu thog ma btsas pa'i 'o mas gdab 'tshal lo/ / rgyal po'i khab na bud med gzhon nu 'o ma nyung ste rang gi bu yang mi ngoms pa zhig yod pa des bdag ni bu dang bral yang bla'i snyam 'o ma phul ba bzhes nas rang sangs rgyas 'o ma byin du lung bstan no//

Once, a piece of stone fired by Devadatta in a catapult injured the large toe of the Bhagavān’s foot. When the bleeding would not stop, Jivaka, the master physician, remained constantly by the Buddha’s side in order to treat him. The people of Rājagṛha gathered. “This medicine is good,” said some; “But this medicine is better,” said others. Jivaka said, “There is medicine that will help at once, but it is hard to find.” “What is it?” asked Ānanda. “It is called gośīrṣa sandalwood,” replied Jivaka. After some time a merchant offered some gośīrṣa sandalwood to the Buddha. Accepting it the Buddha prophesized that as a result of his virtuous deed, he would become the pratyekabuddha Candandatta, “Giver of Sandalwood.” However, the bleeding did not stop. Jivaka said, “Now we must apply the milk of a young mother who has given birth to her first son.” In Rājagṛha was a young mother who had little milk and a thirsty child. However, she thought, “For me to be without my son is not important.” She offered her milk to the Buddha, who prophesized that she would become the pratyekabuddha Kṣīradatta, “Giver of Milk.”

bcom ldan 'das rgyal po'i khab na bzhugs pa'i tshe dge slong zhig pho mtshan nad kyis gzir ba 'tsho byed la bstan pas/ bud med kyi khar chug ces smras pa bzhin byas pas 'phral du zhi/ rgyal po ma skyes dgras yab chos kyi rgyal po bden pa mthong ba bsad/ lhas byin dang bsdongs nas sangs rgyas kyi sku la ngan sems kyi khrag phyungs/ dge 'dun mthun pa'ang dbye/ dge slong ma ut+pa la'i mdog can kyang bsad pa sogs mtshams med pa bzhi byas pas lus la 'brum bu me dpal nad kyis thebs/ ma ga ng+ha'i sa skor thams cad rnag dris khyab/ nam mkha' nas rgyal po chen po khyod zla ba phyi ma'i tshes brgyad la sa'i mthongs bye nas sems can dmyal ba chen por 'gro zhes pa'i sgra byung ba dang / mu stegs ston pa drug la sdig pa bshags pa'i thabs dris kyang ma byung bas shin tu 'gyod cing sdug bsngal mi bzad pas thebs pa na/ sman pa'i rgyal po 'tsho byed gzhon nu na re/ yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas da lta gyad kyi yul na bzhugs pa'i drung du song la zhus shig dang / khyod sdug bsngal 'di las thar bar 'gyur zhes smras pa dang /

In Rājagṛha at that time lived a monk whose penis was very painful. He showed it to Jivaka. “Put it in the mouth of a woman,” said Jivaka. This he did and was immediately cured.[272] King Ajātaśatru had killed his father, a Dharma king who had insight into the nature of phenomena. Together with Devadatta he had spilled the blood of the Buddha with ill intent. He had caused a schism in the community of monks and had killed the nun Utpalavarṇī. In this way he had committed four heinous crimes, and as a result his body was plagued with burning sores, and moreover, the whole of Magadha was pervaded by a putrid smell. One day a voice came from the skies: “Great king, on the eighth day of the next month, the earth will open up, and you will be sucked down into the great hell.” Ajātaśatru went to the six non-Buddhist teachers and asked them how he could purify himself of his crimes, but they were unable to help. He was now overcome with remorse and regret, and he suffered relentlessly. Jivaka the master physician came to him and said, “The perfectly enlightened Buddha is residing in Mallavāstu. Go to him. Ask him what to do, and your sufferings will be ended.”

d.div: [272] This may be a mischievous insertion.

f.d: rgyal po na re/ 'tsho byed sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das de ni dgra bcom pa'i 'khor gyis bskor te yang dag pa'i snying po la gnas pa yin na/ bdag lta bu sems can dmyal ba'i khongs su gtogs pa 'dis ji ltar 'gro bar bya zhes zer ba dang /
The king replied, “Jivaka, Bhagavān Buddha is surrounded by arhats, immersed in the very heart of the Dharma. How can someone like me who belongs in the hell realms possibly go there?”

'tsho byed kyis smras pa/ rgyal po chen po khyod thugs las chung ngur gyis shig /sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das de ni dbang po rnon po shA ri'i bu la chos ston par ma zad/ shin tu brtul ba lam chung ba lta bu la yang chos ston par mdzad/ phyug po rgyal po gsal rgyal lta bu'i bsod snyoms bzhes par yang ma zad/ dbul po ba ba si lta bu'i bsod snyoms kyang bzhes/ sras gcig po sdug pa yid du 'ong ba sgra gcan zin bzang po dang lhas byin gnod pa du ma bskyed pa gnyis la'ang thugs snyoms pa yin pas khyod kyi 'gyod pa sel nges so/ /

“Great king,” said Jivaka, “Do not be so concerned. The Bhagavān Buddha does not only teach intelligent disciples like Śāriputra but also unintelligent disciples such as Kāpatha. He does not only accept alms from the rich, such as King Prasenajit, but also from the poor, such as Vasi. He has the same feelings for Devadatta, who has tried to hurt him many times, as he does for his only son, the good and beautiful Rāhula. He will definitely relieve your remorse.”

'tsho byed de ltar na khyed dang nga gnyis glang po che gcig gi steng du bsdad nas de bzhin gshegs pa'i drung du 'gro bar bya'i de'i bar du sa'i mthongs bye nas bdag dmyal bar song na khyod kyis gzung zhig zer nas/ glang po chen po gcig gi steng du zhon te skye bo'i tshogs 'bum phrag du ma dang thabs cig gyad kyi yul du phyin to//

“Jivaka, in that case, you and I shall mount an elephant and go before the Tathāgata. If on the way the earth opens up to take me to hell, hold me and prevent me falling,” replied the king. They mounted the elephant, and with a crowd of many thousands they traveled to Mallavāstu.

de nas sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das lha dang mi la sogs pa 'dus pa rgya mtsho lta bu'i dbus na bzhugs pas/ rgyal po chen po zhes lan gnyis su gsungs pa na/ 'khor rnams dang ma skyes dgra nyid kyi bsam pa la 'dus pa chen po 'di'i nang na rgyal po chen po gsung bar mdzad pa de tshangs pa'am/ brgya byin nam/ gling gzhan las byung ba'i 'khor lo bsgyur ba lta bu su yin snyam pa dang / lan gsum pa la rgyal po chen po ma skyes dgra zhes bka' stsal pa dang / yid rab tu dga' bas de nyid du brgyal lo/ /

There the Bhagavān was sitting amid an ocean-like gathering of gods and men. Suddenly he called out twice, “Great king, great king!” Those in the gathering and even Ajātaśatru himself wondered whom among the assembly the Buddha was referring to. Was it Brahmā, or Indra, or a great emperor from another country?The third time, the Buddha said, “Great king, Ajātaśatru!” When he heard this Ajātaśatru fainted with joy.

gdong la chu grang mo gtor bas sad pa dang / rgyal po ma skyes dgras/ bcom ldan 'das bdag nam mkha' dang mnyam pa'i sems can thams cad kyi sdig pa thams cad so sor bshags pas so sor bshags so/ / zhes lan gsum gsol ba dang /

Water was sprinkled on his face to bring him round, and he said, “Bhagavān, I confess; I confess the wrong deeds of myself and of all living beings as vast in number as the realms of space.” Three times he repeated this.

bcom ldan 'das kyis bka' stsal ba/ rgyal rigs dri ma chen po legs so legs so/ / khyod rang nyid kyi sdig pa bshags pa'i steng du sems can thams cad kyi sdig pa bshags pa ni shin tu legs so zhes gsungs shing / sdig pa dag nas mthun pa'i chos la bzod pa thob pa sogs rgyal po mi dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyis [163]zin pa thabs mkhas pas ldog cing / lan gsum tu sman pa'i rgyal po chen por dbang bskur ba/ tshe'i rig pa 'dzin pa rdo 'jog gi sman pa rgyun shes kyi bu bstan tshul tsam las/ thog ma nas nad kyi ngos 'dzin sman ngo thod pa dbye ste srin bu len pa'i dpyad sogs gang yang rang nyid slob dpon las mkhas par grub cing da lta'ang sku tshe'i rig 'dzin brnyes nas bzhugs pa'i 'tsho byed gzhon nus gsos de'i slob mar gso rig rang skad du 'dzin pa/

The Bhagavān said, “Noble one of the royal caste! Excellent! Excellent! As well as confessing your own wrong deeds, you confess those of all living beings. This is wonderful!” Having purified himself of his wrong actions, he went on to gain forbearance in appropriate practice.[273] Jivaka had skillfully turned Ajātaśatru away from wrong teachers. He himself had been honored three times as a master physician. He studied the basic principles of Āyurveda under the Takṣaśila doctor Ātreya, and yet the accounts of his knowledge from the very outset of his practice—his ability to recognize illness, his knowledge of medicine preparation, his skill in removing an insect safely from the brain—all indicate that he had become more learned than his master. Moreover, he is still alive today because he attained the vidyādhara of longevity.

d.div: [163] mthong / mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[273] Bzod pa; usually referring to a level of attainment where realizations are not immediately overcome by fear, doubt, and so on, but gain a foothold in the mind.

f.d: 6. Nāgārjuna, Pitṛceṭa, and Candranandana
dpal mgon klu sgrub kyis sman spel tshul/

d.i: The contribution of the glorious Nāgārjuna to the science of medicine

f.d:
lang kar gshegs pa nas/
blo gros chen po khyod shes kyi/ / lho phyogs bai ng+ha'i yul du ni/ / dge slong dpal ldan cher grags pa/ / de ming klu zhes 'bod pa de/ / yod dang med pa'i phyogs 'jig pa/ / nga yi theg pa 'jig rten du/ / bla med theg chen rab bshad nas/ / rab tu dga' ba'i sa sgrubs te/ / bde ba can du de 'gro'o/[164] / zhes dang /

In the tradition of the science of medicine, Jivaka’s disciple was Nāgārjuna. Entering Laṅka Sutra says:
Mahāmati, you should know this: in the south, in the region of Vedalī,[274] will arise a monk of great renown. He will be known as Nāga, and he will destroy the extremes of existence and nonexistence. To the world he will teach my doctrine in the form of the sublime Mahayana, attaining the level known as Joyous, and be reborn in the land of Sukhāvatī.[275]

d.div: [164] sde dge_107_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca lang kar gshegs pa'i mdo/ shog_165_na4
[274] Vedalī was in the south of India, in what is now Andhra Pradesh. The Tibetan vai dha (be ṭa or be ta) also sometimes refers to Vidarbha, in what is now Maharashtra.
[275] Laṅkāvatārasūtra, Toh 107 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 165b4. The Joyous level is the first of the ten bodhisattva bhūmis.

f.d:
'jam dpal rtsa rgyud le'u rab 'byams so drug pa las/
de bzhin gshegs pa nga 'das nas/ / lo ni bzhi brgya lon pa na/ / dge slong klu zhes de 'bod 'byung / / bstan pa la ni dad cing phan/ / rab tu dga' pa'i sa thob pa/ / lo ni drug brgya dag tu 'tsho/ / rig pa rma bya chen mo ni/ / bdag nyid chen po des gang 'grub/ / bstan bcos sna tshogs don dang ni/ / dngos po med pa'i don de rig / gang tshe lus de bor ba na/ / bed ba can du skye bar 'gyur/ / de ni mthar gyi sangs rgyas nyid/ / nges pa kho na yang dag thob/[165] / ces dang /

And in the thirty-sixth chapter of the Mañjuśrī Root Tantra:
Four hundred years after the Tathāgata passes away, the monk known as Nāga will appear, of great faith and benefit to the doctrine; he will attain the level known as Joyous and live for six hundred years. This great being will gain Mahāmayūrī knowledge[276] and will master the meanings of various teachings and the meaning of nonreality. When he leaves his mortal form, he will be reborn in Sukhāvatī. Finally, he will without doubt become a buddha.[277]

d.div: [165] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na_'phags pa 'jam dpal gyi rtsa ba'i rgyud/ le'u/ 36_shog_308_ba6
[276] Rma bya chen mo; Great Peacock; one of the five great dhāraṇī or spells.
[277] Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Toh 543 Kangyur, rgyud, na, 308b6.

f.d: gzhan yang sprin chen/[166] dus 'khor gyi rgyud phyi ma sogs du ma nas lung gis zin cing /[167] rgyal ba'i bstan pa rin po che la ston pa gnyis par grags pa shing rta chen po dpal mgon klu sgrub ni lho phyogs bai dar+b+ha'i yul du bram ze phun sum tshogs pa zhig la bu med pa na rmi lam du bram ze brgya la chos ston drangs na bu 'byung bar lhas lung bstan pa ltar byas pas khyi'u byad gzugs mtshar ba zhig btsas te mtshan mkhan la bstan pas mtshan bzang mod kyi 'on kyang zhag bdun gyi tshe las med par bstan/ thabs dris pa na/ bram ze brgya la chos ston drangs pas zla bdun/ dge slong brgya la chos ston drangs pas lo bdun thub zer ba ltar byas lo rdzogs par nye bas bu'i ro pha mas mthong ma bzod de g.yog dang bcas 'khyam du btang ba/ na len+da'i sgo drung la byis pas snyan ngag gi rig byed bsgrags pa bram ze sa ra has gsan de nang du khrid tshul ji bzhin du bshad pas/ rab tu byung na thabs yod gsungs pa bzhin rab tu byung / tshe dpag med kyi dkyil 'khor du bcug nas dbang bskur gzungs 'don bcug pas 'chi bdag las thar pa'i mtshan rtags thob/ gsang sngags snga 'gyur du gsung gi rig 'dzin sogs gsang sngags gsar snying gi rgyud sde rab 'byams rgya mtsho dang sde snod gsum sogs shes bya rig pa'i gnas mtha' dag la mkhas par sbyangs slar pha ma dngam jal te thog mar pha ma yid ma ches kyang rjes su lo rgyus bshad pas yid ches par gyur/ na len+da'i mkhan po sgra gcan 'dzin bzang po la bsnyen par rdzogs/ mtshan dge slong dpal ldan du grags/

Furthermore, the Great Cloud Sutra,[278] the Later Kālacakra Tantra,[279] and many other texts prophesized the glorious guide and pioneer Nāgārjuna, famed as the second teacher of the Conqueror’s precious doctrine. His life is as follows. In the southern district of Vedalī lived a wealthy brahman who had no son. In a dream it was foretold that if he invited one hundred brahmans and made offerings to them, he would have a son. He did as the deity suggested and was rewarded with a beautiful son. The son was shown to a seer, who said that the child indeed had auspicious marks but that he would not live beyond seven days. His father asked what could be done. He was told that if he invited and made offerings to one hundred brahmans, the child would live for seven months, but if he did the same for one hundred monks, the child would live for seven years. The parents followed this advice. As the seven years drew to a close the parents were unable to bear the thought of seeing their child as a corpse, and so, accompanied by an attendant, they sent the boy away. At the gates of Nālandā Monastery the child recited some verses from the Sāmaveda. Overhearing this, Brahman Saraha invited them inside, where they explained the reason for their journey. Saraha said that if the boy were to become ordained, he could avoid his fate. He therefore became a monk. He was initiated into the mandala of Amitāyus and told to recite mantras. As a result he received signs indicating that he had been released from the hold of the lord of death. He studied and became learned in all fields of knowledge, especially the three baskets of scriptures, and the vast ocean-like collection of new and old tantras, including the vidyādhara tantras of the old translations. Later on he again met his parents, who at first refused to believe it was their son, but he explained what had happened and dispelled their doubts. He took the full ordination of a monk from Rāhula Śrībhadra, the abbot of Nālandā, and received the ordination name of Bhikṣu Śrīmata.

d.div: [166] sde dge_232_bka'/ mdo sde/ wa_sprin chen po/ shog_187_ba7
[167] sde dge_363_bka'/ rgyud/ ka_dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgyud phyi ma rgyud kyi snying po/ shog_137_ba3
[278] Mahāmeghasūtra, Toh 232 Kangyur, mdo sde, wa, 187b7.
[279] Kālacakratantrottaratantra, Toh 363 Kangyur, rgyud, ka, 132b3.

f.d: de nas rma bya chen mo dang / ku ru ku l+le dang / gnod sbyin mo dgu dang / nag po chen po rnams bsgrubs pas/ ri lu/ mig sman/ ral gri/ rkang mgyogs/ bcud len/ gter la sogs pa dngos grub mang po dang / tshar gcod pa dang / slar gso ba la sogs pa'i nus pa thams cad grub/ klu dang gnod sbyin la sogs pa mi ma yin thams cad bran du 'khol/ khyad par bcud len grub pas rdo rje'i skur gyur/ rdzu 'phrul dang mngon shes la mnga' brnyes/

He propitiated deities such as Mahāmayūrī, Kurukullā, the nine yakṣī, and Mahākāla and gained many attainments, including the power of the pill, eye ointment, sword, speed, essence medicine, and earth treasures, among others, as well as the power to kill and bring back to life. He brought under his control all kinds of nonhuman beings, such as nāgas and yakṣas. In particular he mastered the art of elixirs and gained the vajra body. He also developed clairvoyance and the power of miraculous display.

mgon po'i rig sngags 'grub nas ng+ha nya ka Ta ka'i gling na nag po chen po'i rgyud bzhugs pa spyan 'dren par dgongs/ gling der mi g.yo ba la brten te sgyu ma sgrubs/ sgyu mas mkha' 'gro ma rnams mgo 'khor ba'i bar la lha mo nag mo dang nag po chen po'i rgyud brgyad dang / ku ru kul+le'i rtogs pa la sogs pa spyan drangs/ ye shes kyi mkha' 'gro ma rnams kyi gdams pa thob/ sgrub thabs mi gcig pa brgya drug cu yang gdan drangs/

He thought that if he mastered the Mahākāla vidyā mantra, he could bring back the Mahākāla Tantra from Dhānyakaṭaka, where it resided. When he arrived there he invoked Acala and created an illusory display. While the ḍākinīs were distracted by his illusion, he carried off the tantra of goddess Kālī and the eight tantras of Mahākāla, the Kurukulle kalpa,[280] and others. He received teachings from the gnosis ḍākinīs and brought to this world 160 different sādhanas.

d.div: [280] Tārākurulullekalpa, Toh 437 Kangyur, rgyud, ca.

f.d: ma ga ng+har lo bcu gnyis su mu ge byung ste grong khyer stongs pa tsam du song ba na gser 'gyur gyi sbyor bas dge 'dun shin tu mang ba la 'tsho ba sbyar ba slar lo bcu gnyis lon nas slob dpon sgra gcan 'dzin gyis gsan pas/ ma legs zas gyi char 'bebs pa'i nus pa nga la yod bzhin du dge 'dun log 'tsho la sbyor ba khyod snying rje chung / byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa dang 'gal/ da ni de'i sdig sbyong la gtsug lag khang brgya rtsa brgyad/ lha khang stong / mchod rten khri phrag bzheng dgos gsung pa/ dge slong mi gcig gis de ltar mi 'grub par gzigs nas/ gnod sbyin dzam+b+ha lar nor gang dgos bslangs/ las grogs klu rnams la 'tshol dgongs te/ ku ru ku l+le'i rig sngags kyis klu rgyal 'jog po'i bu mo 'khor dang bcas pa bkug pas chos gsung ba'i tshogs su mi'i bu mo'i rnam pa gnyis 'khor mang po dang bcas byung bas/ dpag tshad tsam tsan dan sa mchog gi dris khyab/ bu mo gnyis la sgrol ma'i sku bzheng bar tsan dan ster ba dang / gtsug lag khang bzhengs pa'i grogs byed dgos stsal bas/ pha la dris nas lan 'bul zer/

Once there was a twelve-year famine in the land of Magadha, and when the towns and cities had almost emptied, Nāgārjuna introduced a large number of monks to the alchemical production of gold. After the famine had ended, Rāhula Śrībhadra came to hear of it and remarked, “This was not good. When I have the power to bring about rains of food, you involve the monks in wrong livelihood. You are a man of little compassion. What you did goes against bodhisattva conduct. To purify this wrong you must construct 108 temples, one thousand shrines, and ten thousand stupas.” Nāgārjuna realized that one monk could not possibly accomplish these tasks alone. He begged the necessary money from the yakṣa Jambala and decided to entrust the actual work to the nāgas. With the vidyā mantra of Kurukullā, he summoned the two daughters of the nāga king Takṣaka with their attendants. When these two nāgas and their large retinues sat in human form amid the congregation at the teachings, the air around for a few leagues was permeated with the aroma of gośīrṣa sandalwood. Nāgārjuna asked the two nāgas for some sandalwood to construct a statue of Tārā and for some workers to help in the construction of the temples. “We will ask our father and give you our answer,” they replied.

de'i nang par bu mo gnyis sngar bzhin byung / klu'i rgyal po'i mchid nas/ slob dpon nyid klu yul du phebs na bka' bzhin byed/ gzhan sgrub par mi nus zer ba'i lon phul/ sher phyin 'bum spyan 'dren pa sogs dgos pa khyad par can gzigs te klu'i yul du phebs/

The next morning the young girls appeared again with a message from their father, who said that only if the Ācārya himself came to the land of the nāgas would he do as the Ācārya asks. Seeing the added advantage of bringing back the One Hundred Thousand Perfection of Wisdom Sutra and other texts, he traveled to the land of the nāgas.

'od srung dang gser thub la sogs pa'i dus kyi dge slong lus gzhan las che ba mang po dang / bdag cag gi ston pa'i dgra bcom pa du ma klu'i mchod gnas su 'dug pa rnams na re/ nged rnams ni dgra bcom pa yin la/ khyod dug gsum dang bcas pa'i mi zhig 'dir 'ong ba la dug gis mi gnod pa ci yin 'dri bar/ ngas rma bya chen mo'i rig sngags 'grub pas yin gsungs/ klu rnams dam pa'i chos kyis tshim par mdzad/ sher phyin stong phrag brgya pa dang gzungs dang rtog pa'i rigs du ma spyan drangs/ sa'i steng du phebs/ dge slong bed byed la sogs pa theg chen la sdang ba rnams rtsod pas sun dbyungs/ nyan thos sen ng+ha pa rnams kyis brtsams pa'i rtog ge theg chen la rtsod pa'i gzhung mang po dar ba thams cad sa 'og tu sbas/ lho phyogs dzaT so g+ha ra'am ral ba 'joms par grags pa'i gnas su mu stegs kyi rgol ba 'dus pa lnga brgya tsam tshar bcad de nang pa'i bstan par bcug / dril bu'i brag dang byang phyogs ng+hing ko Ta sogs ri mang du gser du bsgyur bar bzhed pa la/ rje btsun sgrol mas ma 'ongs pa na rtsod pa'i gzhir 'gyur pas ma byed gsungs te bzlog / byang sgra mi snyan du phebs pa'i lam khar byis pa mang po rtse ba las gcig rgyal por lung bstan/ mi dang mi ma yin gyi don du lo bcu gnyis tsam lon pa na tshur phebs/ sngar gyi byis pa rgyal por gyur ba bde spyod kyis bsnyen bkur/ gzhi med kyi skur ba cung zad byung ba 'phags pa lha'i thabs mkhas kyi 'phrul la brten nas sangs/ sgrol ma mngon sum du zhal gzigs lung bstan/ klu'i skad dod nA ga ni chos dbyings su skyes pa la rtags dpyad gnyis kyi mtha' mi gnas pa dang gsung rab rin po che'i bang mdzod la mnga' brnyes pa sreg cing gsal ba'i lta ba dang ldan pas klu'o/ / ar dzu na ni srid sgrub ste chos kyis rgyal srid skyong ba dang nyes pa'i dgra phyogs 'dul bar srid sgrub ste de gnyis mtshams sbyar bas nA gArdzun ste klu sgrub ces grags/

When he arrived there, he found many monks from the time of Buddha Kāśyapa, Buddha Kanakamuni, and others, whose bodies were larger than the others, as well as many arhats from our Teacher residing in the land of the nāgas as objects of reverence. They asked him, “We are arhats, whereas you are a human being possessed by the three poisons. How is it you were not harmed by the nāga poison in coming here?” “By my attainment of the vidyā mantra of Mahāmayūrī,” replied Nāgārjuna. He satisfied the nāgas with Dharma and brought the One Hundred Thousand Perfection of Wisdom Sutra and many dhāraṇī and kalpa rituals back to this world. He defeated in debate the monk Śaṅkara and others who had an aversion to the Mahayana. He buried in the ground many polemic texts written by the Saindhava[281] śrāvakas that argued against the Mahayana, which had become widespread. In the south, in a place known as Jaṭāsaṃghāta, he defeated a gathering of about five hundred non-Buddhists and converted them to Buddhism. On mountains such as Ghaṇṭa Rock and Dhīkoṭa in the north, he wanted to produce gold through alchemy. However, Tārā told him that this would lead to controversy in the future, and so he refrained. On the way to the northern land of Uttarakuru, he came across a group of children playing. He picked out one of them and predicted that he would one day become a king. He stayed in Uttarakuru for twelve years working for the sake of humans and non-humans and then returned. The child had by then become King Udayibhadra and served and devoted himself to Nāgārjuna. One time some baseless slander was leveled against the ācārya, but with the help of miraculous feats performed by Āryadeva, he was able to dispel them. He had a vision of Tārā, who gave him a prophecy. He is Nāga because, born into the dharmadhātu, he does not dwell in the extreme of existence or nonexistence, because he has control over the treasury of the jewels of the Buddha’s teachings, and because he possesses a view that burns and illuminates.[282] Arjuna means “ruler,” and he is called Arjuna because he governs the kingdom of Dharma and rules by subduing the foes of delusion. These two terms through the process of euphonic amalgamation (sandhi) become Nāgārjuna.

d.div: [281] Written as Senda; Buddhist sect opposed to the Mahayana.

[282] Nāgas are (1) born in the ocean, which here is likened to the dharmadhātu, or realm of ultimate truth; (2) live between the animal and spirit realm but not in either; (3) famed for their jealous guardianship of treasures; and (4) have fiery eyes and breathe fire from their mouths.

f.d:
mtha' bral dbu ma rig tshogs drug /rgyud kun las btus la sogs pas mtshon mdo sngags rig gnas kun la bka' drin che zhing / khyad par gso rig tu/
ring du grags pa'i gso dpyad nas/ / mtha' yas rgyud kyi gces pa blangs/ / sman pa mkhas par rab mchod pa'i/ / sbyor ba brgya yis bcings bar bya/[168] / zhes bstan bcos sbyor ba brgya pa/

In his compositions on sutra and tantra, as illustrated by his six philosophical texts on the Madhyamaka free of extremes[283] and his Compendium of Tantra,[284] his contribution to the sciences has been enormous. Specifically, in the field of medicine:
Taking the very essence of the countless tantras from the renowned science of medicine, here is compiled a hundred preparations praised by the masters of medicine.[285] This is from his Hundred Medical Preparations.

d.div: [168] sde dge_4306_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ he_slob dpon klu sgrub/ sbyor ba brgya pa/ shog_1_na2

[283] Fundamental Stanzas on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), Sixty Verses of Reasoning (Yuktiṣaṣṭhikā), Seventy Verses on Emptiness (Śūnyatāsaptati), Finely Woven Scripture (Vaidalyasūtra), Refutation of Arguments (Vigrahavyāvartanī), and Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī).
[284] Rgyud kun la btus pa. Butön also mentions this work, but it is not listed in either the Degé or Peking Tengyur.
[285] Yogaśataka, Toh 4306 Tengyur, gso ba rig pa, he, 1a2.

f.d: sman pa'i mchog ste nyon mongs nad sel de la phyag btsal nas/ / 'phags pa'i brtul zhugs drang srong ma gtogs skyes bu blo ldan pas/ / rlung mkhris bad kan gsum dang 'phrod spyad bag bya spyod lam gyis/ / mi lus 'di thob don yod 'tsho ba'i mdo tsam bstan par bya/[169] / zhes sogs 'tsho ba'i mdo tshigs su bcad pa/

Also:
Having paid homage to the physician supreme, dispeller of the sicknesses of delusion, I will write this Sutra of Life not for those rishis of elevated conduct but for those of intelligent minds, who by living a healthy life of conscientious conduct in accord with the humors of wind, bile, and phlegm will give meaning to this human life.[286] This is from his Sutra of Life.

d.div: [169] sde dge_4307_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ he_slob dpon klu sgrub/ sman 'tsho ba'i mdo/ shog_8_ba5
[286] Jīvasūtra, Toh 4307 Tengyur, gso ba rig pa, he, 8b5.

f.d: rtsa a ba'i cho ga / sngo sbyor bdud rtsi gsang ba/ sman rin po che'i rim pa/ dngul chu'i sbyor ba rin chen 'phreng ba rnams dang / gzhan yang lhog pa spun bzhi gnyan bcas kyi bcos sogs 'dis mdzad zer ba shin tu mang / mchod rten dang lha khang mang po btab/ rdo rje gdan la dra mig gi ra bas bskor/ lho phyogs dpal ldan 'bras spungs kyi bkod pa bzhengs/

The following texts among others are also said to have been composed by Nāgārjuna: Ritual of Ava Medicine, Secret Ambrosia: Preparation of Medicinal Plants, Precious Medicine, Jewel Garland Preparation of Mercury, and Treatment for the Four Kinds of Lhok and Infectious Fevers.[287] He founded many shrines and temples. He surrounded the vajra seat of Bodhgāya with stone mesh fencing and was instrumental in constructing edifices at Dhānyakaṭaka in the south.

d.div: [287] Only the first of these is listed in the Tengyur (Toh 4308, gso rig, he). In Tibetan Medicine (p. 66) Dash lists nine other Sanskrit medical works attributed to Nāgārjuna. One of these nine—the Rasaratnākara—appears to be the fourth in this list.

f.d:
spyi lugs la lo drug brgya dang snga 'gyur ltar na lo stong gi ring 'gro don mdzad/ rgyal po bde spyod kyi bu gzhon nu nus ldan zhes pa rgyal srid la rings pa'i gtam ma la smras pa dang / de na re khyod kyi yab dang slob dpon klu sgrub sku tshe'i bcud len stabs gcig tu 'grub pas 'grongs rgyu med/ rgyal sras snga ma rnams kyang rgyal srid ma thob par 'das pa mang zer bas/ shin tu yi mug pa'i tshe/ ma na re/ khyod de ltar mi dga' ches na slob dpon la dbu slongs/ byang chub sems dpa' yin pas ster/ klu sgrub gshegs pa dang yab kyang 'grongs te rgyal srid thob nges zhes bslabs pa ltar gzhon nu nus ldan gyis dbu bslangs pa ral gris bcad pa ma chod par ngas sngon rtswa sngon pos srog chags kyi ske bcad pa'i rnam smin yod pas ku shas chod gsung ba ltar bregs pa'i tshe/ mgul nas byang chub kyi sems 'dzags te/
nga ni bde ba can gyi 'jig rten du/ /phyin nas lus 'di la yang 'jug par 'gyur/[170] /zhes gsungs te sku tshe 'phos/

It is generally accepted that Nāgārjuna lived and worked for the welfare of others for six hundred years, although the early translations talk of a thousand years. Kumāra Śaktimān, the son of king Udayibhadra, told his mother that he was in a hurry to ascend the throne. His mother replied, “The lifespan of your father is linked to that of Ācārya Nāgārjuna’s by the elixir power of longevity. He will not die. Previous heirs to the throne have also died without becoming king.” This made the son very upset. His mother said, “If you are so unhappy, go to the ācārya and ask for his head. He is a bodhisattva and will give it to you. If the ācārya dies, your father will also die, and you will surely become king.” Kumāra Śaktimān did as his mother suggested. The ācārya offered his head, but no sword could cut it off. “In the past I cut the head off an insect with a blade of grass. I have yet to experience the ripening of that act. Therefore, take some kuśa grass and cut off my head,” suggested the ācārya. As the blow was struck, bodhicitta[288] flowed from the wound, and the ācārya said,
“I am going to the world of Sukhāvatī. Later I shall again return to this body.” With these words he died.

d.div: [170] kun mkhyen pad+ma dkar po'i gsung 'bum pod/ kha_chos 'byung bstan pa'i pad+ma rgyas pa'i nyin byed/ shog_34_ba2
[288] In tantra bodhicitta can mean blood or semen, but this use would be unusual here. Other sources say the blood turned to milk as it flowed.

f.d: slob dpon bcud len 'grub pas 'grig gi dogs nas dbu dpag tshad du ma'i sar 'khyer ba gnod sbyin mos 'phrog nas bshad khungs du ma yod kyang pha bong gcig gi khar bzhag pas pha bong gas pa'i sa der 'phags pa spyan ras gzigs lha lnga'i rdo sku rang byon byung / dbu dang sku lus gnyi ga la yon bdag gnod sbyin mo des so sor lha khang brtsigs/ de gnyis kyi bar du sngon dpag tshad bzhi tsam yod pa/ da lta rgyang grags gcig kyang cung mi longs pa'i khad nye zhing / lha khang de'i rdo brtsigs rnams 'brel bas brag lta bur song ba'i cho 'phrul dang gnyan cha che ba/

Since the ācārya had developed the elixir siddhi, the prince feared that the head and body would rejoin, and so he carried the severed head many leagues away, where some sources maintain it was taken by a yakṣī. However, the head was placed in the crevice of a boulder, which split apart, and a five-deity stone statue of Ārya Avalokiteśvara sprung forth naturally. The yakṣī funded the building of two temples, one for the head and one for the body. Previously these temples were about four leagues apart. Now they are separated by less than a kilometer.[289] The walls of the temples have joined to look like a large rock, and it is a strange and frightening place.

d.div: [289] Literally, a krośa, which is an eighth of a league (yojana, about four miles). In other words, the temples went from more than fifteen miles apart to being a half mile apart.

f.d: sgo med pa'i skar khung nas bltas na/ dbu dang sku rdo sku'i dum bu 'dra ba re yod par grags la/ rim gyis sku lus dang je nyer song ste ma 'ongs pa na 'gro ba'i don mdzad par 'dod do//

It is said that looking through an opening, one sees the head and body as separate parts of a stone statue. Gradually the head is moving toward the body, and it is said that sometime in the future the ācārya will return to work for the welfare of living beings.
dpal ldan pha khol gyis sman spel tshul/

d.div: [290] Pha khol. Pitṛceṭa is the literal translation. As author of Essence of Eight Branches (Aśṭāṅgahṛdaya), he is often referred to as Vāgbhaṭa by Sanskrit scholars. However, he is known by many names, as the author points out below. Even the following citation refers to him as Mātṛceṭa.

f.d:
de'i slob mar gso dpyad rang lugs su bzhed pa dpal ldan pha khol ni/ 'jam dpal rtsa rgyud rab 'byams so drug pa las/
nyams dga' grong khyer rgyal po'i khab/ / 'od ma'i tshal gyi sa steng du/ / slob ma'i tshogs dang lhan cig tu/ / ji ltar bde bar nga bzhugs tshe/ / bya rog gcig gi thal btang yang / / nga la sems ni dad byas nas/ / lus zhig nas ni mtho ris song / /
lha rnams las ni shi 'phos nas/ / mi yi nang du skyes nas kyang / / nga yi bstan la rab tu byung / / yon tan ldan zhing tshul khrims ldan/ / mang du thos shing chos kyang smra/ / ma khol zhes bya'i brtul zhugs can/ /
de ni de tshe 'byung bar 'gyur/ / nga la ji bzhin bstod pas mchod/ / rnams pa sna tshogs de dag gis/ / legs par dpyad la rab byed pa'o/ / blo ldan de ni mthar gyis kyang / / thams cad mkhyen pa byang chub thob/[171] / ces lung bstan pa ltar

According to the science of medicine’s own system, the medical disciple of Nāgārjuna was Śrī Pitṛceṭa. In the thirty-sixth chapter of the Mañjuśrī Root Tantra:
While I was happily residing with a group of disciples in the bamboo grove of the delightful city of Rājagṛha, a crow let his droppings fall upon me yet nevertheless developed faith in me, and as a result will be reborn into a higher realm.
Moving on from the celestial realms, he will be reborn a human and become ordained into my doctrine. Possessed of great qualities and great ethics, he will be very learned and a preacher of Dharma, one of strict conduct known as Mātṛceṭa.
At that time he will appear and will honor me by way of praise. By various means and to benefit all living beings, he will perform his practices well; and finally this intelligent being will come to the omniscience of enlightenment.[291]

d.div: [171] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na_'phags pa 'jam dpal gyi rtsa ba'i rgyud/ le'u/ 36_shog_308_ba1
[291] Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Toh 543 Kangyur, rgyud, na, 308b1.

f.d: 'khrungs yul 'brug pa pad dkar lho phyogs su bzhed par tha snyad cher ma mthong rung /[172] bu ston dang jo nang pa [173] sogs mkhas pa phal cher shar phyogs su bzhed pa bzhin rang gi snga rtsom g.ya' sel du'ang yod rung /[174] snga rabs zhang ston zhig po'i rgyal mtshan rtser 'bar du slob dpon 'di'i skye ba snga ma shar phyogs su 'khrungs te nags la gnas pa'i dge slong zhig la yan lag brgyad pa'i khrims blangs te bsrung ba'i tshe/ nub phyogs pa'i phyi rol pa 'gas dbang phyug chen po la bstod cing bsngags pas de'i rjes su song ste dbang phyug gis rjes su 'dzin pa'i smon lam btab/ yan lag brgyad pa'i khrims nyams/ tshe 'phos pa ngan song du skyes/ sdig pa rags pa byang nas nub phyogs kha che'i grong khyer du 'khrungs par bshad 'dug pa dang /[175]

His birthplace, according to Drukpa Pema Karpo,[292] was in the south, but I have not seen any authority for this. Most scholars, including Butön and the Jonang tradition,[293] maintain it was in the east, and in a previous composition, Cleaning the Beryl,[294] I say the same. However, according to the early scholar Shangtön Shikpo in his Compendium of Knowledge: Blazing from the Top of a Victory Banner, this ācārya in his previous life was born in the east, where he took the eight-branched precepts from a forest monk. However, some outsiders from the west came and praised Mahādeva.[295] He became his follower and prayed to be cared for by Mahādeva. As a result his precepts waned, and he was reborn in the lower realms. When the coarse karma of his wrong deeds had expired, he was reborn in a Kashmiri city in the west.

d.div: [172] kun mkhyen pad+ma dkar po'i gsung 'bum/ kha_chos 'byung bstan pa'i pad+ma rgyas pa'i nyin byed/ shog_36_ba2
[173] rje btsun tA ra nA tha'i gsung 'bum/ mdam pa'i chos rin po che 'phags pa'i yul du ji ltar dar ba'i tshul gsal bar ston pa dgos 'dod kun 'byung / shog_64_ba5
[174] sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho'i gsung 'bum/ pod bzhi pa/ g.ya' sel/ glegs bam gnyis pa/ shog_176_ba4
[175] gzhung 'di ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[292] Pema Karpo, Chos ’byung bstan pa’i padma rgyas pa’i nyin byed, Collected Works, kha, 36b2.

[293] Referring to Tāranātha’s Dam pa’i chos rin po che ’phag yul du ji ltar dar ba’i tshul gsal bar ston pa dgos ’dod kun ’byung, 64b5. Translated by Lama Chimpa and Alaka Chattopadhyaya as History of Buddhism in India (Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1997).
[294] Cleaning the Dirt from Vaidūrya to Reveal Its True Face [Bai dūrya g.ya’ sel don gyi bzhin ras ston byed], Collected Works of Desi Sangyé Gyatso, vol. 4, section 2, 176b4.
[295] Epithet of the god Śiva.

f.d: gsham du gsal ba bzhin kha che zla mngon gyi mes po yin dgos pa sogs nas nub phyogs kha cher gaSh+Nika'i pho brang dang nye bar bram ze tshe'i rig byed yan lag brgyad la byang chub pa sman pa chen po sing+g+ha gu h+ya ste seng ge sbas pa dang dge 'dun gsang ba 'gyur gyi bzhed pa gnyis las da lta bsgrubs na seng ge gsang bar bde ba dang / yum rat+na sing+ng+hi ste/ bde ldan ma'am da lta bsgrubs na rin chen dngos grub ces bya ba'i sras su bltam/

Moreover, as will be made clear later, he was an ancestor of the Kashmiri Candranandana. From these and other references we can say the following. He was born in the west, in Kashmir, near the palace of King Kaniṣka, where his father was a great physician who had mastered the eight branches of medicine in the brahman Vedic tradition. In Sanskrit he is known as Siṃhaguhya. Some translations render this Sengé Bepa (Siṃhagupta), others as Gendün Sangwa (Saṃghaguhya). These days it might be easier to refer to him as Sengé Sangwa (Siṃhaguhya). His mother was called Ratnasiddhi in Sanskrit, also known as Dedenma (Satyaśālinī) in Tibetan. In Tibetan the Sanskrit translates as Rinchen Ngödrup.

lhums su zhugs pa'i tshe yum nam mkha' la 'phur ba sogs ngo mtshar ba'i ltas du ma byung ba bram ze mtshan mkhan la bstan pas/
mdzes shing sman gyi bum pa thogs/ / dga' ba'i tshul gyis lta byed cing / / dri zhim mdangs dang ldan gyur pas/ / zug rngu sel byed rgyal gyur cig[176] / ces brjod nas ming bdud rtsi bum par btags/

While she was carrying her child, she received many auspicious omens, such as dreams of flying, and so she approached a brahman seer, who said:
Beautiful, holding the medicine vase, looking with eyes of joy, of fragrant and glowing complexion, may he become the conqueror of pain.[296] Because of this prediction the child at birth was named Pīyūṣa Kalaśa, “vase of ambrosia.”

d.div: [176] 'di zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i sman pa rnams kyis mi shes su mi rung ba'i shes bya spyi'i khog dbubs/ shog_210_phreng 9_nang du'ang drangs/ gzhung dngos gzhi gang nas bkod ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[296] Cited in Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo’s General Compendium, 210.9.

f.d:
bskyed bsrings te gzugs mdzes yab yum la gus pas pha khol ma khol dang / ring por ma thogs par bram ze'i chos rig byed bzhi dang / rig byed kyi yan lag bzhi/ nye ba'i yan lag bzhi/ las drug la sogs pa mkhas par byed pa la ma ti tsi tra ste blo gros bkra bar grags/ khyad par yab la gso ba rig pa bslabs pas tshegs med du mkhyen pas yab kyis/
ka ling ka ni dmag gi bdag / ga gon bzang po nor gyi bdag / mdzes ma 'od ldan tshal gyi bdag / dpal ldan dpa' bo sman gyi bdag[177] / ces dpa' bor thogs/

He grew into a beautiful child, and because of his devotion to his parents he was known as Pitṛceṭa Mātṛceṭa, “obedient to father and mother.” Before long he became learned in brahman philosophy, comprised of the four Vedas, the four subsidiary Vedas, the four branch Vedas, the six activities, and so on. He was henceforth known as Maticitra—“a beautiful mind.” In particular, he studied medicine with his father, and because he mastered it with ease, his father said:
Kaliṅga was the master of war, Trapuṣa the master of business, the beautiful Prabhāvatī was mistress of the grove, glorious Śūra is the master of medicine.[297] Henceforth, he was known as Śūra.

d.div: [177] gong mtshungs/ shog_210_phreng 17
[297] Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, General Compendium, 210.17.

f.d: yum sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa la gus pas nan gyis bskul yang ston pa'i dbur bya thal btang ba'i rten 'brel dang shar phyogs su 'khrungs dus kyi smon lam gyi dbang las phyi pa mu stegs kyi grub mtha' la zhugs gsung snyan pas ming rta dbyangs su grags/

His mother had great devotion for the teachings of the Buddha. Yet despite her urging he entered the non-Buddhist outsider doctrine because of the causal factor of the crow droppings falling on the Buddha’s head and the power of his prayers made during his previous birth in the east. At that time he became known for his beautiful voice, and was henceforth also known as Aśvaghoṣa—“the song of the horse.”

mu stegs rtag par smra ba'i lugs la mkhas par sbyangs/ dbang phyug chen po'i rten ling+gi shwa ra rab du grub pa nub phyogs a+yon du yod pa der 'byon par brtsams pa yab yum gyis bshol btab pa ma gsan pas pha khol ma khol du grags/ rten de'i drung khrus kyi rdzing bu la khrus byas te rtswa dang lo ma'i stan la 'dug /

He became learned in the tradition of the outsiders with their philosophy of permanence. He decided to make a pilgrimage to the Maheśvara shrine of Liṅgaśvara Prasiddha in the western land of Oḍḍiyāna. As he was about to set off, his parents asked him to delay his journey, but he did not listen to them, and he became known as Pitṛceṭa Mātṛceṭa—one who is and who is not obedient to his father.[298] Arriving at the shrine he bathed in the nearby bathing pool and sat on a seat of leaves and grass.

d.div: [298] Pha khol ma khol. This seems to be a play on the Tibetan word ma, which means both “mother” and “not.” As indicated previously this term was used to indicate his obedience to his parents—“obedient to father, obedient to mother”—and here to mean almost the opposite—“obedient and disobedient to father.” However, this cannot work with the Sanskrit term pitṛceṭa-mātṛceṭa, which does not carry the sense of disobedient.

f.d: 'bras chan gsol/ dbang phyug ma 'grub kyi bar gnas 'di nas mi ldang zhing / 'bras nyag re tsam mi za/ chu thigs gcig tsam yang mi 'thung bar dam bcas te brtson pa chen pos bsgrubs pas zhag bdun gyi tha mar zhal dngos su bstan te/ dngos grub ci 'dod gsungs par/ phyogs las rnam par

He ate some rice and vowed that he would not rise from that place and not eat a single grain of rice nor drink a drop of water until he had invoked Maheśvara. Thus he practiced with great devotion, and after seven days he received a vision of Maheśvara. “What power do you seek?” asked Maheśvara. “I want to be victorious everywhere,” he replied.

rgyal ba 'dod zhus pas/ tshangs pa khyab 'jug dbyangs can ma gsum gyis grogs gyis/ des kyang ma thub na nga rang snying la bab nas rtsod kyi/ cis kyang rgyal bar ma nus na kha nas zhe sdang gi me phyungs te bsreg go/ / zhes mngal skyes gang gis kyang mi thub pa'i dngos grub tu dbyangs can mas sring mo paN+Di ta sgra tshad la mkhas pa dang / tshangs pas ne tso paN+Di ta sgra mkhas pa/ khyab 'jug gis thod le kor paN+Di ta sgra tshad kyi yi ge rang bris 'ong ba ste rnam pa gsum byin te nang pa sangs rgyas pa'i bstan pa ming gi lhag mar gyis shig gsungs pa ltar nub phyogs kyi paN+Di ta rnams dang rtsod pas rgyal te nang pa'i bstan pa bsnubs phyi pa'i ring lugs su bsgyur bas nag po thub rgyal du grags/

Maheśvara stated, “Be accompanied at all times by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Sarasvatī. Whenever they are unable to defeat others, I will enter your heart and debate. If your opponents cannot be conquered by any means, then the fire of anger will pour from your mouth and burn them up.” Granted, therefore, the siddhi of invincibility in debate with any womb-born human, he was accompanied by Sarasvatī in the form of his pandit sister, learned in language and logic, by Brahmā in the form of his pandit parrot, learned in language, and by Viṣṇu in the form of his “chalk” pandit, which could make the words of logic and language appear miraculously. He was told to destroy the doctrine of the Buddha until only its name remained. Consequently, he debated and defeated pandits in the west, causing the Buddha’s doctrine to decline and forcing many to convert to the outsider doctrine. He thus became known as the black Durdharṣa—“difficult to conquer.”

ma'i gam du phyin pa na/ sgrol ma'i ras bris shig la mchod pa byed pa mthong ste/ 'di gang yin dris pas nang pa'i lha'o smras pas/ da rung nang pa yod dam zer/ bu nang pa sangs rgyas pa'i bstan pa ni rta'i lus dang 'dra ste/ khyod kyis pham par byas pa ni nub phyogs mtha' 'khob pa ste rta'i rna ba tsam/ phyogs dbus gzhan mtha' dag nang pas gang ngo smras pas/ lho phyogs su yang 'gro bar brtsams pa na/ ma'i bsam pa la lho phyogs pas kyang mi thub dogs te/ rtsod pa'i grags pa thob par 'dod na yul dbus 'gyur tshal nyid du song la mkhas pa'i mthu thob pa nam mkha'i skar tshogs lta bu yod kyi/ de dag dang rtsod pa'i rgyal rnga sgrogs shig par bskul ba ltar 'khor dang bcas te bgrod pa las/

Once he was with his mother and saw her performing her devotions before a painting of Tārā. “Who is this?” he enquired. “This is a Buddhist deity,” she replied. “Are there still Buddhists?” he asked. “Son,” replied his mother, “The doctrine of the Buddha is like the body of a horse. Those you have defeated in this uncivilized western land are only the ears of that horse. The rest of this country is filled with Buddhists.” On hearing this he prepared to travel to the south. However, his mother realized that there were none in the south who could defeat him and therefore urged him, “If you really desire fame in debate you should travel to the central Buddhist country itself. There, those with the power of wisdom shine like the multitude of stars in the nighttime sky. Go and beat the drum of victory in debate over them!” He took his mother’s advice and set out with his retinue.

nA len+d+ra dang nye ba'i char bu mo chu'i bum pa spyi bor bkod nas lag pa gnyis rked par bzhag ste 'gro ba dang phrad/ gtsug lag khang nA ga len+d+ra gang na yod dris pas/ de na re/ blun po mtha' 'khob pa tshig gi brjod pas phongs pa khyod ci zer/ mkhas pa bye ba'i bsti gnas dpal na len+d+ra'i gtsug lag khang zer mod ces tshig brdungs btang bas yid la khu 'phrig cher skyes/ 'on kyang nA len+d+ra'i gnas gan+d+ho la chen po bdun/ lha khang bcu bzhis brgyan pa/ paN+Di ta stong dang lnga brgya 'du ba der sleb ste dge 'dun rnams la nga mu stegs thub dka' nag po yin te/ sngar nub phyogs kyi nang pa rnams rtsod pas pham par byas/ dge sbyong go'u ta ma'i rtags phyungs nas phyi pa'i rtags ral ba dang ri dwags pags pa dbyig pa dang ril ba spyi blugs thal pa'i tshon ris dag gis spras par bsgyur ba ni nga'i 'khor na yod pa 'di dag yin la/ da khyed cag dang rtsod la nged pham na 'khor bcas gang+gA'i chur mchong zhing / khyod rnams pham na mu stegs kyi chos lugs su bsgyur ro zhes smra zhing

When he arrived in the vicinity of Nālandā Monastery, he met a girl carrying a pot of water on her head and her hands on her hips. “Where is the Nāgalandā Monastery?” he asked. “Fool from some uncivilized land, you are ridiculed by your own words! What are you saying?” she retorted. “You should say, ‘the glorious Nālandā Monastery, home of many a great scholar.’” Chastened by these words he was suddenly plagued by doubt. Nevertheless, he traveled on to Nālandā, with its seven great gaṇḍola halls, its fourteen temples, and its fifteen hundred pandits. There he introduced himself to the monks, “I am the tīrthika, Durdharṣa the black. I have debated and defeated the Buddhists in the west. I have ousted all the identifying signs of the śramaṇa Gautama and replaced them with the outsider signs of longhair, deerskins, staffs, and drinking bottles colored with ash. Such converts are in my retinue now. I will debate with you. If you win, I will jump and drown with my retinue in the Ganges. If I beat you, you will convert to the tīrthika doctrine.”

don de'i yi ge sdeb legs tshig gi srad bur brgyus pa na len+d+ra'i sgo bzhir sbyar te rtsod par brtsams pa na/ der 'khod kun gyis thub par mi nus par shes te gaN+Di'i sgras bsdus nas gsang gros btab pas/ gang bcom ldan 'das kyis mdo sde dri ma med pa nas lung bstan pa'i mu stegs rta dbyangs su grags pa ni 'di yin pas/ rdzus skyes 'phags pa lha ma gtogs gang gis kyang 'dul bar mi nus pas spyan 'dren du gtong dgos zhes bsgros pa dang / kha cig rmi lam du rmis par bshad pa gang ltar lho phyogs dpal gyi ri la 'phags pa klu sgrub dang / de'i slob ma pad+ma las brdzus te 'khrungs pa 'phags pa lha gnyis dbus kyi paN+Di ta rnams kyis sbran par brtsams pa rta dbyangs kyis shes te re zhig phyi pa nang du ma 'gro nang pa phyir ma 'gro zhes sgo la nyal nas 'grul bcad/

He strung the letters of this proclamation onto a well-composed thread of words and pinned them to the four doors of the monastery and prepared to debate. The whole monastery knew they could not defeat him, and so they beat the gaṇḍi drum and convened a secret meeting. There they concluded, “This person is the outsider Aśvaghoṣa prophesized by the Bhagavān in his peerless sutras. Only the miraculously born Āryadeva can tame him. Therefore we must invite him here.” Some writers say that this was revealed to the monks in a dream. However it happened, the pandits of the central country planned to call Nāgārjuna and his disciple the lotus-born Āryadeva from Śrīparvata in the south.
