However, Aśvaghoṣa came to hear of this plan, and so he lay down in front of the main gate to cut off the path saying, “Now, no one can enter and no one can leave.”

dge 'dun rnams gdugs tshod gsol par sgo brdeg cing der dge 'dun rnams kyis slob dpon yab sras spyan 'dren la rkang pas phyin na rtsod pa'i dus tshod la mi sleb/ bstan pa'i gag la thug pa'i gal po cher bsams te/ paN+Di ta stong dang lnga brgya'i gtsug gi nor bu b+hik+Shu mahA s+tha bIr nA gen+d+ra gup+ta zhes bya bas/ rgyal ba'i bstan pa la rjes su sems pa'i dbang las spyan chab g.yo ba'i ngang nas/
kye ma bstan pa'i shing rta ni/ / mu stegs rgol ba'i 'dam du byings/ / 'di na nus bral stobs zad 'gyur/ / khyed cag khur yin phrag par long / / zhes sogs kyi 'phrin yig myur bar bris nas gtor ma'i snod nang du bzhag pa dang /

The monks went to their midday meal and locked the door. Inside they realized that were they to send an invitation by foot, the ācārya and his disciple would arrive too late for the debate, and that this was a critical time for the doctrine of the Buddha. The crown jewel of the fifteen hundred pandits was Bhikṣu Mahāsthavirā Nagendra Gupta. Tears flowed from his eyes through his love for the doctrine of the Buddha as he hurriedly wrote:
Alas, the chariot of the teachings sinks in the mud of tīrthika debate. Here we are powerless, our strength weakens. This burden lies with you, now is the time to shoulder it. The letter was placed in a offering dish.

nag po chen po'i sku brnyan gyi thugs ka nas bya rog cig thon te 'phrin yig mchus khyer nas skad cig la dpal gyi rir sleb pa na/ slob dpon klu sgrub kyis rta dbyangs kyis bstan pa nyams par byas yod 'dug /de bzlog par nga 'gro gsungs pas 'phags pa lhas slob dpon gshegs mi 'tshal bdag gis 'dul gsungs/ khyod kyis thub min blta'o zhes slob dpon gyis rta dbyangs kyi grub mtha' bzung 'phags pa lha dang rtsod pas slob dpon rgyal zhes dang / la lar don la 'phags pa lha rgyal kyang / slob dpon nyid phyi pa'i grub mtha' la shin tu mkhas par dad pa log ces pa ji ltar rung / gang ltar mchil lham rgyab pa slob dpon gyi spyan la 'phog /de ma thag 'gyod de chad pa bcad du gsol ba na/ de'i tshe khyod kyis bdag phyi rol par mthong ba yin pas nyes pa cher med mod/ 'on te lam du slong ba po byung na gang la yang ma chags par byin cig ces bka' stsal/

From the heart of a statue of Mahākāla emerged a crow, which took the letter in its beak and in an instant was in Śrīparvata. Ācārya Nāgārjuna said, “Aśvaghoṣa is damaging the teachings. I will go and stop him.” Āryadeva replied, “The ācārya should not go. I will go instead.” “We will see if you can defeat him or not,” said Nāgārjuna. The ācārya took the philosophical position of Aśvaghoṣa, debated with Āryadeva, and beat him. Some writers say that Āryadeva actually won the debate, but because of the ācārya’s supreme skill in outsider philosophy, Āryadeva lost faith. How could that be correct? Whatever happened, he threw his boots and accidentally struck the ācārya on the eye. He was at once filled with remorse and asked the ācārya to punish him. “At the time you saw me as an outsider,” said Nāgārjuna, “so this is not a serious fault. However, if on the road a mendicant approaches you, do not be attached to whatever they ask for.”

mu stegs de bdag gis 'dul bar mi nus sam dgongs pa'i tshe/ slob dpon gyis khyod de 'dra ba'i yid gnyis mi dgos sngon bdag cag gi ston pa 'od ma'i tshal na 'khor 'dus pa'i dbus su chos gsung pa'i dus bar snang nas pho rog cig gis dbur bya thal dor kyang dad pa'i sems skyes te song bas/ der 'khor rnams yid gnyis su gyur nas 'di ci'i ltas lags zhus pas/ bya rog 'di ma 'ongs pa na mu stegs thub dka' nag po zhes bya bar gyur nas nga'i bstan pa la gnod pa chen po byed cing mngal skyes gang gis kyang 'dul ba'i gnas med pa 'byung ngo gsungs/ der 'khor 'dus pa'i nang nas li tsa byi lag na me tog can bya ba'i khyi'u na re/ bdag de'i tshe brdzus te skyes nas mu stegs de yang dag par btul/ nang pa'i bstan pa la 'dzud par shog ces smon lam btab/ ston pas kyang mthun 'gyur gnang ba'i gang zag de khyod yin pas/ khyod rang gi smon lam gyi dbang gis dang / bya rog mthar dad pa'i sems skyes pas thul te nang pa'i bstan pa la 'jug thub par 'dug song zhig gsungs pa ltar/ rdzu 'phrul gyis byon pa'i lam du sa'i lha mos bram zer brdzus nas spyan ya gcig bslangs pa ltar byin/ nA len+d+ra'i chu len la nga 'ongs so gyis byas pas/ des 'phrin bskyal bas yid ma ches chu lug rmig gang me long gi nang du blug nas bskur btang bas des khrus byas chu sngar bzhin ma god par btang bas ngo shes te des na chu len gyi cha lugs su byos la byon cig zhus pa bzhin nang du byon/ chu len du bskos pa rnams phyi nang du 'gro ba na mu stegs sgo srung bar phyag bya dgos pa la/ slob dpon gyis mu stegs de'i mgo bo rdog pas brdzis kyang nang gi ting nge 'dzin gyi nus pas rgol bar ma spobs te dge 'dun gyi gral smad der bzhugs pa dang / gdugs tshod gsol dus rta dbyangs kyis bgrangs pas grangs lhag nas sngon med kyi mgo zlum po ga las yong zer ba'ang byung ste yongs zer ba dang /

Before he set out, Āryadeva began to wonder, “What if I cannot defeat this tīrthika?” “You need not have such doubts,” said the ācārya. “Once, our Teacher was in the bamboo grove teaching the Dharma amid his disciples when a crow above let its droppings fall onto his head. The crow developed great faith in our Teacher in that moment. The disciples wondered at this occurrence and asked the Buddha what it foretold. Our Teacher replied, ‘This crow will at some later time become the tīrthika Durdharṣa the black and will cause great harm to my doctrine. No womb-born human will have any chance of defeating him.’ “In the gathering of disciples was the young son of the Licchavi, Puṣpapaṇīkāra. He prayed, ‘At that time, may I be born miraculously, defeat that tīrthika, and lead him to the Buddhist teachings.’ Our Teacher concurred with this prayer. That young boy was you. Therefore, because of your prayer and because that crow subsequently developed faith, you will be able to defeat him and lead him to the Buddhist doctrine. Now go.” Āryadeva set off and traveled with the aid of miraculous power. On the road an earth goddess manifesting as a brahman appeared and asked him for an eye, which he promptly gave. Outside the monastery he said to a Nālandā water bearer, “Tell them I have arrived.” The message was relayed but not believed. Therefore, Āryadeva poured an amount of water sufficient only to fill a sheep’s hoofprint onto a mirror and sent it inside the monastery. When the monks used it for bathing they found that the amount of water would not diminish but stayed the same. From this they recognized him and sent a message asking him to enter disguised as a water bearer, which he did. When those appointed water bearers came and went from the monastery, they had to bow to the tīrthika guards at the door. However, Ācārya Āryadeva trampled on the head of the tīrthika, and by the power of the ācārya’s inner samādhi, the tīrthika was unable to raise any protest. The ācārya took his place in the lower ranks of the monastic order. At the midday meal, Aśvaghoṣa counted the monks and found one extra. “Where is[299] this new bald head?” He asked. Alternatively, the verb is “arise,” meaning “Where does this new bald head come from?”

d.div: [299] Yod; although other versions have yong (come).

f.d: yang bshad khungs gcig la dkar thug 'thung ngam dmar thug 'thung dris te dkar thug 'thung ba rnams la mgor dbyug pa brdeg pa/ 'phags pa lhar brdeg pas mgo zlum du ma brdeg gsungs pas mgo zlum ga nas 'ongs zer bas/ gnyi ga'i lan du mgo zlum po ske'i stengs nas yongs gsungs pas lan med pa dang rta dbyangs kyi mtshun gtor byed pa'i sar byon te ci byed bris pas/ sngar shi ba'i pha mes rnams la ster zer/ 'o na nga yang lho phyogs dpal gyi rir me tog gi ldum rar chu gtor dgos byas gtor bas/ dpal gyi ri la 'di nas gtor bas ci la phan zer bar/ 'o na pha mes sngar shi ba la chu da lta gtor bas ci zhig bya zhes pas lan med/ yang bum pa gcig mi gtsang bas bkang nas phyi bkrus pas kho na re/ mi gtsang ba nang du yod pa la phyi bkrus pas ci la phan zer/ de ltar na sdig pa sems la chags pa lus bkrus pas ci la phan gsungs pas rtsod par 'os pa de yin par shes nas/ rta dbyangs kyis bye'u gcig chang bar bzung 'di shi 'am ma shi zer/ de khyod la rag las so zhes brjod pas/ them pa'i steng na 'dug ste nga phyi na 'dug nang na 'dug gam zer/ khyod kyi spyod lam la rag las gsungs pas spobs pa lan med du gyur/ dge 'dun rnams kyis dbang phyug gis dngos grub la stsal ba'i grogs gsum po 'di dang 'di 'dug ces zhus/ sring mo paN+Di ta'i gnyen por 'ga' zhig bong bu'i pho mtshan du bzhed na'ang dge bsnyen ngo tsha med pa/ ne tso la byi la/ thod le kor la mar nag gsum bsngags pa sta gon mdzad/ sang rtsod pa ngo bo byed pa'i nub dbus su tshar gcod rjes 'dzin gyi dpang po rgyal po snying po thig le/ g.yas su slob dpon 'phags pa lha/ g.yon du mu stegs rta dbyangs gsum gyi khri bshams/ rta dbyangs kyi khri'i 'og tu dbang phyug chen po 'khor mi thub pa'i phyir krad rnying la sogs pa mi gtsang ba'i rdzas bzhag / bden rdzun shan 'byed dang rjes brjod kyi dpang po sogs dang bcas sang nyin tshogs nas

Another account of this event says that Aśvaghoṣa asked, “Who drinks vegetable soup and who drinks the meat soup?” Those who drank vegetable soup were hit on the head with a stick. Āryadeva was hit and remarked, “Do not strike a bald head.” To which Aśvaghoṣa replied, “Where does this bald head come from?” The answer from Āryadeva to either question was, “This bald head has come from its neck,” to which Aśvaghoṣa had no response. On another occasion Āryadeva went to where Aśvaghoṣa was making ancestor offerings. “What are you doing?” he asked. “I am offering these to my ancestors,” he replied. “Oh, I too must water the flowers in my garden in Śrīparvata,” said Āryadeva and began throwing water in the air. “What use is it throwing water here for a garden far away in Śrīparvata?” asked Aśvaghoṣa. “Well,” replied Āryadeva, “What is the use making offerings now to ancestors who died long ago?” The tīrthika had no answer. Another time Āryadeva filled a pot with excrement and began cleaning it from the outside. “When the filth is inside, what can you possibly achieve by cleaning the outside?” asked Aśvaghoṣa. “If that is so, when the contamination is in the mind, what can possibly be achieved by cleaning the body?” he replied. Aśvaghoṣa now realized that this was the man the monks had summoned to debate him. He took a bird in his hand and asked Āryadeva, “Is this bird going to die or not?” “That depends on you,” he replied. Standing in a doorway, Aśvaghoṣa asked, “Am I outside or inside?” “That depends on what you are doing,” came the reply. Aśvaghoṣa could give no assured reply. The monks told Āryadeva about the three helpers Maheśvara had granted as a siddhi to Aśvaghoṣa. To counteract these, Āryadeva brought in an immodest layman—although some assert it was a donkey’s penis—to ward off the pandit sister, a cat for the parrot, and black oil for the chalk. On the evening before the debate, three thrones were erected: one in the center of the debating area for King Hṛdayatilaka, who was responsible for banishing the loser and rewarding the victor; one on the right for Ācarya Āryadeva; and one on the left for the tīrthika Aśvaghoṣa. In order to prevent Īśvara coming near, the soles of old shoes and other dirty rags were placed under Aśvaghoṣa’s throne. Analyzers along with summarizers were summoned, and on the following day all participants gathered for the contest.

rta dbyangs kyis ral pa bteg ste mig gcig bstan pa dang / slob dpon gyis zhabs mthil nas mig bstan te/
mig gsum drag pos mthong min zhing / / mig stong ldan pas mthong dka' ba'i/ / AR+ya de ba'i mig gcig gis/ / srid pa gsum gyi de nyid mthong / / zhes smra ba'i sgo snyan zhing 'jebs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa'i che ba rgya cher brjod de bsrung ba'i bslab pa mang du thos pa'i nor sogs las brtsams nas sgo phye ba dang /

Aśvaghoṣa lifted up his long hair and revealed an eye. Āryadeva lifted up his foot, revealing an eye on his sole, saying:
Not seen by the three-eyed demon, hard to perceive by the thousand-eyed one, yet Āryadeva with his single eye sees the nature of the three worlds. This was the prologue to the debate. He then began the debate by presenting the greatness of the beautiful doctrine of the Buddha, its precepts, the great jewel of learning, and so on.

der kho na re khyod kyis nga yi rtsod zla mi yong sring mo paN+Di ta khyod kyis 'di nyid sun phyungs shig bsgo ba na/ yid dbang rab tu 'phrog pa'i mdzes ma des/ /
dri mas dri ma bkru ba lta'i/ / 'dod ldan 'dod pas yid sbyong la/ / yid bsdus khyed cag mi sdug pa'i/ / skoms pas lus dbang nyams par byas/ / zhes sgra tshad spyi dang bye brag sgra rig pa smra bar brtsams pa dang / dge bsnyen des zhum pa dang bag tsha ba med par smad gos bsal te dbang po'i rgyal mtshan sgrengs nas bstan pas dbang phyug gi grub mtha' pa rnams kyi 'dud pa'i gnas yin pa'i phyir mdzes mas tshogs pa'i dbus su phyag byas pas/ der 'khod thams cad gad mos sa g.yo ba bzhin du gyur te spobs pa lan med du song /

Aśvaghoṣa said, “You cannot match my arguments,” and called on the pandit sister to defeat Āryadeva. Beginning by using logic and language generally, and then specifically concentrating on the science of language, this beautiful and alluring woman began:
As stains are washed away with stains, the desirous purify their minds with desire. You of introspective minds, the thirst borne of meditation on ugliness will only shrivel up your bodies. The layman with no inhibitions or shame removed his lower garment and showed her his erect victory banner. Because the penis is an object of worship in the Maheśvara tradition, she immediately prostrated to it. Everybody was amused and the ground shook with laughter. She was unable to continue.

de nas thub dka' nag po bag tsam skyengs na'ang ne tso paN+Di ta la sngar bzhin bsgos pas de na re/
sgra nyams phal ba'i kha sgo can/ / ming tshig yi ge'i 'byung khungs bral/ / tshig brjod dman pas don mtshon phyir/ / sgra'i gnas las bslab gnas ci/ / zhes sring mos sgra nas smra bar brtsams pa la nye ngan pas sgra la sun phyung nas tshad ma las smra bar brtsams pa'i tshe/ shin tu dregs shing rgyags pa'i byi la btang bas mchongs pa gcig gis rno ngar dang ldan pa'i sder mos bzung ste mche ba mi bzad pas ne tso'i ske bcad de bkum/

Durdharṣa, although a little embarrassed, nevertheless turned to the parrot pandit and commanded him likewise. The parrot began:
Language as expressed in the mouths of the mundane lacks the grammatical authority of words, names, and letters. These inferior words uttered to clarify meanings are mere sounds; where is the teaching? Because the sister pandit’s contribution using the art of language had got off to an inauspicious start, the parrot rebutted language and began using logic. Suddenly a ferocious cat was let loose and with one jump seized the parrot in its sharp claws, sunk its fearsome teeth into its neck, and killed it.

thub dka' na re/ khyed cag las 'bras khas 'che bzhin du sdig pa bsags zer ba dang / 'phags lhas 'di'i sdig pa bdag gi bla ma klu sgrub kyis sbyong bar mdzad do gsungs/ khyod kyis bsags pa'i sdig pa klu sgrub kyis sbyong bar ga la nus zhes pas/ 'o na byi las ne tso bsad pa'i sdig pa nged la ji ltar 'byung gsungs pas smra rgyu ma byung / de nas thod le kor paN+Di ta la sngar ltar bsgo ba na de nyid skad cig la 'phar nas sgra tshad kyi yi ge rang bris su byung ba la mar nag gi bum pa byo bas yi ge zubs te mi snang bar gyur/ sngon dbang phyug gis byin gyis brlab par khas blangs pa'i don yid la bsams te bsam gtan la gnas kyang krad rnying la sogs pa'i rdzas kyis 'khor ma nus/

Durdharṣa said, “You believe in cause and effect, and so you have committed a heinous act here.” Āryadeva replied, “My guru Nāgārjuna said he would purify me of this sin.” “How is it possible for Nāgārjuna to purify an action you have committed?” asked Durdharṣa. “Well,” replied Āryadeva, “How can the action of a cat killing a parrot rebound on me?” Durdharṣa had no answer, but commanded the chalk pandit as he had the other two. The chalk jumped up and began to write using logic and language. But Āryadeva poured a pot of oil on the writing and erased it. Durdharṣa recalled Īśvara’s pledge to bless his mind and entered meditation to invoke him, but the dirty cloth under the throne meant that Īśvara could not come near.

sgra tshad la lan gsum rtsod pas pham kyang dregs pa'i dbang gis pham par khas ma blangs par rjes brjod kyi dpang pos rjes brjod ma zin/ bden rdzun shan 'byed kyi dpang pos shan ma phyed/ de'i stobs kyis rgyal pos kyang tshar gcod ma shes pas rta dbyangs kyis blen spyad la 'dri'o zer ba lang rdzi'u la dris par slob dpon thams la mkhas pas gling bu 'bud gin byon pa/ ba lang rdzi rnams byis pa'i rang bzhin gyi gling bur dga' ste slob dpon rgyal zer/ de nas rdzu 'phrul 'gran pas khyed rang nam mkhar dkyil 'khor bris ngas bsubs/ yang na ngas 'dri khyed rang bsubs zhes pa rta dbyangs 'dri bcug pa 'phags pa lhas bsubs/ yang na ngas nam mkha' la 'phur yang na khyed 'phur zer ba/ khyod rang 'phur gsungs pas rta dbyangs rgyang ring la 'phur bas/ 'phags pa lhas yum chen mo'i sku shin tu che bar sprul nas pus mo'i lha nga'i steng phyag bkab ste 'phur ma bcug /

Three times Aśvaghoṣa was beaten in debates on language and logic, but his arrogance would not allow him to admit defeat. The summarizers could not summarize, the analyzers could not analyze, and so the king could not adjudicate. “Ask a simpleton to decide,” said Aśvaghoṣa, and so they went to ask some cowherds. The ācārya very cleverly came along playing a flute. The cowherds with their childlike nature loved the flute and declared the ācārya the winner. They held a competition of miraculous powers. Aśvaghoṣa suggested, “Either you draw a circle in space and I will erase it, or I draw a circle and you erase it.” Aśvaghoṣa was encouraged to draw the circle and Āryadeva was able to erase it. “Either I fly into space or you fly into space,” said Aśvaghoṣa. “You do it,” replied Āryadeva. Since Aśvaghoṣa had the ability to fly far into space, Āryadeva manifested as a very large Mahāmātṛ goddess, placed his hands on Aśvaghoṣa’s knees, and prevented him from flying.

de ltar rtsod pa dang rdzu 'phrul gang yang 'gran ma nus shing dbang phyug snying la zhugs nas byin gyis brlab par khas blang ba yang mi gtsang ba'i rdzas kyis 'khor ma nus pas/
lha dbang rdzun gyi smra bas ni/ / bdag cag mang po'i dbus 'dir bkum/ / rtsod las pham pa bas kyang gzhan/ / lha yis bslus pa sdug bsngal lo/ / zhes smre sngags bton pa dang /

Therefore, unable to prevail in debate and in miraculous powers, and unable to rely upon Īśvara entering his mind as pledged because of the dirty cloth under the throne, Aśvaghoṣa lamented:
Great god, you have spoken false; in the midst of many we have been destroyed. As well as defeat in debate, we are betrayed by the gods. What suffering this is!

bshad khungs gzhan zhig la dbang phyug mi 'khor ba'i rdzas yod pa rta dbyangs kyis shes te bkrol nas/ dbang phyug chen po snying la zhugs nas rtsod pa dang po paN+Di ta rnams kyi go bar byung / gnyis pa sing sing tsam las go ba'i tshig ma thon te spobs pa dang bral/ dbang phyug chen po mig gsum par byas te dbang du bsdu bar 'dod pa na/ slob dpon gyi pra dz+nya pa ra mi ta spyan stong par sprul/ mthar kha nas zhe sdang gi me spar te bsreg par 'dod pa na/ slob dpon gyi spyan ras gzigs chu rgyun gyi ting nge 'dzin la bzhugs te zhabs yug mdzad pas mi snang bar gyur/

In another version, Aśvaghoṣa comes to know of the dirty rags under the throne and clears them away, and Maheśvara is able to enter his heart. In the first debate the assembled pandits are able to understand him. In the second debate all they hear is a tinkling sound but no comprehensible words, and Aśvaghoṣa loses all confidence. He assumes the form of the three-eyed Maheśvara and tries to assume control over the ācārya, but the ācārya in turn manifests as thousand-eyed Prajñāpāramitā. Finally, Aśvaghoṣa issues the fires of anger from his mouth and tries to burn the ācārya, but Āryadeva enters the Stream of Water samādhi of Avalokiteśvara, holds his foot up to the fire, and extinguishes it.

der 'phags pa lhas/
thub dka' bsam gtan gnas thong zhig / nyi dbang nub ri'i rtse las brgal/ / skye bo dag kyang dub pas nyen/ / smra ba nyams las gnas don ci/ / zhes gsungs pa dang /

der 'dus pa'i skye bo rnams mgrin gcig tu/
mu stegs mig mangs blo rno yang / / shes bya'i cha tsam mthong ma nus/ / AR+ya de wa'i spyan gcig gis/ / gnas don phra ba'ang ji bzhin gzigs/[178] / zhes ched du brjod cing a la la dang ga zha'i sgra chen po bsgrags pas rta dbyangs sngar gyi nga rgyal las skyengs nas tshangs pa'i 'jig rten la 'gro'o snyam nam mkhar 'phur te bros/

The audience in unison cried:
The many-eyed tīrthika with his sharp mind cannot see a single thing. Āryadeva with his single eye sees even the subtle just as it is.[300] With such pointed words coupled with the jeering and laughter, Aśvaghoṣa was ashamed of previous arrogance, and he decided to flee to the Brahmā realms. He flew off through the skies, but

d.div: [178] lo rgyus dang tshigs bcad 'di dag bu ston gyi gsung bde bar gshegs pa'i bstan pa'i gsal byed chos kyi 'byung gnas gsung rab rin po che'i mdzod/ bu ston rin chen grub kyi gsung 'bum/ ya shog_101_ba4_nang byung /
[300] For this narrative and the verses see Butön’s Bde bar gshegs pa’i gsal byed chos kyi ’byung gnas gsung rab rin po che’i mdzod, Collected Works, ya, 101b4.

f.d: 'phags pa lhas bdes pas zin par nye ba dang / khyod 'di nas yar la ma 'gro zhig rlung spu gri can gyis lus dum bur gtub pa yod gsungs pas yod pa sus shes zer/ ral pa gcig 'phongs dang gsungs pa bzhin 'phangs pas skra dum bur song bas kho bred de 'gro ma nus par zin/ khrid nas 'ongs ral pa bregs shig byas pas/ kho na re ral pa 'breg pa las nga rang gang+gAr 'chir 'gro zer yang ral pa bregs nas bka' sde snod bzhugs pa'i gtsug lag khang gcig tu bcug ste sgo lcags rgyab bzhag pas/ rta dbyangs skyo ste mdo rgyud bstan bcos khyad par can rnams la bltas pas rang gi lta ba log par spyad pa nor ba dang / rgyu 'bras khyad bsad kyi dmyal bar skye bar go nas rang gi bya ba ma yin par 'gyod/ nyes pa lces byas lce gcod zer spu gri blangs bar ster du ma bcug /

Āryadeva chased after him and closed in on him, saying, “Go no farther. A razor-like wind will cut your body to pieces.” “Who can possibly know such things?” retorted Aśvaghoṣa. “Throw some of your hair and see,” said Āryadeva. He did and saw his hair shredded. Aśvaghoṣa was so scared he did not venture further. Āryadeva captured him and led him back. There he ordered Aśvaghoṣa to cut off his hair. Although he complained that he would rather drown in the Ganges than cut his hair, he nevertheless did as Āryadeva ordered. He was then locked inside a temple containing a collection of the Buddha’s teachings. There he became bored and began reading the sutras, tantras, and commentaries. This made him realize that his views and behavior were wrong and that his disdain for the law of cause and effect would lead him to hell. He felt great remorse for his wrong actions. “This tongue has caused these problems,” he lamented. “I will cut out this tongue.” Because of this he was not allowed to possess anything sharp.

de nub rmi lam la sngar byas la 'gyod pa skyes kyang sdig pa ma byang / da nang pa sangs rgyas par zhugs nas las rgyu 'bras ston pa'i bstan bcos brtsams na sdig pa 'dag go zhes rje btsun sgrol mas lung bstan pa ltar lus kyi sdig gshags su yan lag brgyad pa chen po/ yan lag brgyad pa la 'jug pa/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa/ de'i rang 'grel dang bzhi/ ngag gi sdig gshags la skyes rabs/ yid kyi sgrib pa sbyang phyir rtsa ltung / bsngags 'os bsngags bstod sogs bstod pa brgya rtsas mtshon rig pa'i gnas lnga'i bstan bcos mang du mdzad cing de'i nang nas yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa rtsom pa'i dus su/
sa gsum dge legs 'gyur ba yi/ / dge ba'i ltas ni sna tshogs byung /[179] / zhes gsungs pa ltar

That night he had a dream in which he was told that although he had remorse for his previous actions, he was still not cleansed of them. However, now that he had entered the doctrine of the Buddha, if he were to write treatises that revealed the workings of the law of cause and effect, he would be cleansed of his past misdeeds. Therefore, as prophesized by Tārā, he composed four medical texts in order to purify himself of past physical misdeeds. These are, Extensive Exposition of Eight Branches; Engaging in Eight Branches; Essence of Eight Branches; and his own commentary on Essence of Eight Branches.[301] In order to purify himself of past nonvirtuous speech, he composed the Garland of Past Lives of the Buddha. To purify himself of past nonvirtuous thought, he composed Vajrayana Root Downfalls and Praise of the Praiseworthy and over a hundred praises. In this way he composed many works on the five major sciences, and while he was composing the Essence of Eight Branches,
Various auspicious signs occurred, auspicious for the three worlds.[302]

d.div: [179] 'di zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i sman pa rnams kyis mi shes su mi rung ba'i shes bya spyi'i khog dbubs/ shog__215_phreng 17_nang du'ang drangs/ gzhung dngos gzhi gang nas bkod ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[301] Only the third and fourth of these are found in the Tengyur. See bibliography under Pitṛceṭa.
[302] Cited in Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo’s General Compendium, 215.17.

f.d: sa 'og klu'i yul du 'od sna tshogs kyi khug sna sprin du chags pa/ de las bdud rtsi'i char 'bab pa/ shing rnams las dus min du 'bras bu smin pa gsum/ sa bla lha'i yul du ba dan dang rgyal mtshan g.yo ba/ de las 'od zer 'phros te phyogs kun khyab pa/ me tog gi char 'bab pa gsum/ sa steng mi'i yul du sa g.yo ba/ ut+pala'i char 'bab pa/ dug gi me tog rnyings pa/ gser gdugs rang bzhin gyis 'khor ba/ dung rnams rang skad 'byin pa/ shing gi bcad mtshams nas 'o ma dang sbrang rtsi 'bab pa/ lus 'phags kyi rgyal po nor 'dzin dmus long la mig byung ba/ yul dbus 'gyur 'chang gi yams nad chad pa/ mu stegs kyi mkhan po ra la pa tra nga rgyal chag nas lto ba sa la sbyar ba/ rdza rnga las rig sngags kyi sgra 'byung ba/ dkon mchog gi rten rnams mdangs dang ldan pa/ nang pa'i paN+Di ta rnams kyis shis pa brjod pa la sogs pa sa gsum du rtsom pa'i rnam 'phrul bco brgyad gsal bar byung ba'i

Three signs occurred in the subterranean world of the nāgas. Wisps of multicolored light formed a cloud, from this cloud fell a rain of ambrosia, and on trees fruits ripened out of season. Three signs occurred in the celestial world of the gods above. Banners and victory standards began to flutter, sending out rays of light pervading all directions, and rains of flowers fell. On the earth in the land of humans, the earth shook; a rain of utpala flowers fell; poison plants withered; golden parasols formed miraculously; conch shells emitted sounds naturally; splits in wood issued milk and honey; Vasudhā, the blind king of Videha, regained his eyesight; an epidemic that had gripped the central region of Magadha suddenly subsided; the tīrthika master Ralapatra freed himself from his pride and threw himself to the ground; mantras were heard issuing from clay drums; Buddhist statues and shrines glowed; Buddhist pandits spoke words of auspiciousness. These eighteen miraculous signs accompanying the composition of Essence of Eight Branches and others were clearly observed in these three worlds.

bstan bcos 'di'i le'u la gnas drug gi dang po mdo gnas le'u thog mas brjod bya yan lag brgyad/ nad kyi ngo bo/ sman sman pa/ nad pa nad g.yogs/ spyi'i rnam gzhag /le'u brgya nyi shu'i grangs rnams bstan pas rtsa rgyud lta bu dang / le'u gnyis pas nyin re'i spyod pa/ gsum pas dus spyod/ bzhi bas nad med bya ba/ lnga pas btung ba'i rdzas/ drug pas zas kyi mtshan nyid/ bdun pas zas bsdam tshul/ brgyad pas zas tshod zin pa/ dgu pas sman la sogs pa'i tshad/ bcu pas ro rnams/ bcu gcig pas nad tshul/ bcu gnyis pas nad kyi bye brag / bcu gsum pas nad gso ba/ bcu bzhi pas gso thabs rnam pa gnyis/ bco lnga pas sbyang ba sogs/ bcu drug pas snum bcos/ bcu bdun pas dugs/ bco brgyad pas rlan khrus/ bcu dgu pas mas btang / nyi shu pas sna nas btang ba/ nyer gcig pas dud pa/ nyer gnyis pas mkhur bkang sogs/ nyer gsum pas mig sman blugs pa/ nyer bzhi pas mig gso ba/ nyer lnga pas cha byad/ nyer drug pas gtar dpyad/ nyer bdun pas gtar ga gdab pa/ nyer brgyad pas zug rngu dbyung ba/ nyer dgu pas gtar kha'i las/ sum cu pas thal sman rnon po dang me btsa'i cho ga bcas le'u sum cu/

The work itself is in six sections.[303] The first section or sthāna is the general or sūtrasthāna and has thirty chapters: 1. The eight branches as the main topic of this work, the nature of disease, doctor and medicine, nurse and patient, general principles, and an enumeration of the 120 chapters, much like the Root Tantra of Four Medical Tantras. 2. Daily behavior 3. Seasonal behavior 4. Prevention of disease 5. Drink 6. Characteristics of food 7. Protecting food 8. Food portions 9. Composition of medicine, and so on 10. Tastes 11. Understanding illness 12. Classification of illnesses 13. Treating illness 14. Two aspects of treatment 15. Purification therapies, and so on 16. Oil therapy 17. Compress therapy 18. Purgatives 19. Suppositories 20. Nasal purgative 21. Fumigation 22. Mouth gargles, and so on 23. Eye salves 24. Eye treatments 25. Instruments 26. Blunt surgical instruments 27. Bloodletting 28. Extraction of foreign bodies 29. Surgery 30. Alkali powders and cauterization procedures

d.div: [303] In all Sanskrit sources the authorship of this work is attributed to Vāgbhaṭa. According to Mukhopadhyaya (p. 791) the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha and the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā were composed by two distinct authors, both named Vāgbhaṭa.

f.d: gnas gnyis pa lus gnas la le'u dang pos mngal du 'jug pa sogs/ gnyis pas de'i nad/ gsum pas yan lag gi bye brag / bzhi pas lus kyi gnad/ lnga pas lus kyi 'gyur ba/ drug pas pho nya sogs le'u drug /

The second section of Essence of Eight Branches is on the body and has six chapters: 1. Embryology 2. Prenatal illnesses 3. Parts of the body 4. Vital points on the body 5. Changes in the body 6. Messengers, and so on

gnas gsum pa nad kyi gnas la/ le'u dang pos nad gzhi/ gnyis pas rims/ gsum pas khrag mkhris lud pa/ bzhi pas dbugs mi bde/ lnga pas glo gcong zad byed sogs/ drug pas chang nad/ bdun pas gzhang 'brum/ brgyad pas tshad 'khru/ dgu pas gcin 'gags/ bcu pas gcin snyi/ bcu gcig pas khong 'bras dang skran/ bcu gnyis pas rmu rdzings/ bcu gsum pas skya rbab 'or me dbal/ bcu bzhi pas mdze sha bkra za gu srin bu/ bco lnga pas rlung / bcu drug pas dred nad rnams kyi nad dmigs te le'u bcu drug /

The third section is on pathology. It has sixteen chapters: 1. Fundamentals of illness 2. Infectious fevers 3. Blood and bile disorder[304] 4. Respiratory ailments 5. Tuberculosis 6. Alcohol-related illness 7. Hemorrhoids 8. Dysentery and diarrhea 9. Urine retention 10. Diabetes 11. Growths and tumors 12. Abdominal dropsy 13. First and second-stage edema and erysipelas 14. Leprosy, white leprosy, and worms 15. Wind-humor ailments 16. Arthritis and gout

The fourth section is on treatment. It has twenty-two chapters: 1. Treatment of infectious fever 2. Treatment of blood and bile 3. Treatment of cough with phlegm 4. Treatment of hiccups and breathing ailments 5. Treatment of tuberculosis 6. Treatment of vomiting, heart disease, and thirst 7. Treatment of alcohol-related illnesses 8. Treatment of hemorrhoids 9. Treatment of dysentery and diarrhea 10. Treatment of stomach disorder 11. Treatment of urine retention 12. Treatment of diabetes 13. Treatment of growths 14. Treatment of swellings 15. Treatment of abdominal dropsy 16. Treatment of first-stage edema 17. Treatment of second-stage edema 18. Treatment of erysipelas 19. Treatment of leprosy 20. Treatment of white leprosy and worms 21. Treatment of wind ailments 22. Treatment of gout and arthritis

The fifth section is on medicinal procedures and their administration. It has six chapters: 1. Emetic preparations 2. Purgative preparations 3. Complications in emetic and purgative therapies 4. Suppositories 5. Complications in suppository therapies 6. Pharmaceutical preparations
gnas drug pa phyi ma'i gnas la le'u dang pos byis pa nyer spyod/ gnyis pas byis pa'i nad/ gsum pas byis pa'i gdon te byis par le'u gsum/
The sixth section is the concluding chapter. It has forty chapters. Three chapters are on pediatrics: 1. Pediatrics 2. Illnesses of infants 3. Demonic forces affecting infants
bzhi pas 'byung po'i gdon/ lnga pas de gso ba/ drug pas smyo byed/ bdun pas brjed byed gso ba ste 'byung por le'u bzhi/
These are the four chapters on illnesses caused by spirits: 4. Spirits 5. Treatment of illnesses caused by spirits 6. Mental illness 7. Epilepsy

brgyad pas mig chu'i nad dmigs/ dgu pas de gso ba/ bcu pas mig 'bras dkar nag gi nad dmigs/ bcu gcig pas de gso ba/ bcu gnyis pas mig nad/ bcu gsum pas rab rib/ bcu bzhi bas de gso ba/ bco lnga pas mig nad sna tshogs kyi dmigs/ bcu drug pas de rnams gso ba bcas lus stod mig la le'u nyer dgu /

khyon le'u brgya nyi shu yod pa sman dpyad kyi srog lta bu 'di la sogs pa legs par bshad pa'i bstan bcos don bzang zhing tshig sbyor nyams dang 'gyur ba stong gis sgeg pas na/ dpal chos kyi grags pas rgyal po me tog kun tu rgyas pa'i dris lan du/
tsan dra go mi brjod pa rnam par dag / snyan ngag dpa' bo las byung sdeb sbyor mkhas/[180] / zhes bstan bcos rtsom pa la phul du byung bar bsngags/ thog mar phyi rol pa'i grub mtha' rgya mtsho'i mthar son rjes su nang pa'i ring lugs su zhugs dpal mgon klu sgrub yab sras kyi slob ma mdzad phyi nang gi grub mtha' dang snyan ngag sogs rig byed la mkhas par gyur/

This work with its 120 chapters, which is the lifeblood of the medical tradition, and his other well-composed works are all on meaningful topics and his writing is graced with a host of beautiful thoughts and expressions, so much so that in reply to a question from King Saṃkusuma, the glorious Dharmakīrti praised Aśvaghoṣa’s excellence in composition:
Candragomin is pure in speech; poetry comes from Śūra, the skillful composer.[305] In the beginning he sailed across the ocean of the tīrthika philosophy and later entered the Buddhist system, where he became a student of Nāgārjuna and his disciples. He was therefore a scholar of both Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophies as well as of poetry and the other Vedas.

d.div: [180] rje btsun tA rA nA tha'i gsung 'bum/ matA rA nA tha'i chos 'byung / shog_143_ba3

f.d: mtshan yang bdud rtsi bum pa/ pha khol ma khol/ dpal chen dge ba/ rta dbyangs/ dga' byed/ ma ti tsi tra/ a shwa ka / thub rgyal nag po zhes par grags shing nang par zhugs nas dkon cog 'bangs/ rab 'byor bskyangs/ b+ha wi lha/ mar me mdzad/ ngo bo gnyis med pa/ bkod ma 'dzin/ btsun pa dpa' bo/ dgra las rnam rgyal/ rdo rje'i mtshon cha/ lha gsum pa/ b+ha ba b+ha/ gzhan la phan pa'i dbyangs te gzhan ma AR+ya shur sogs mtshan du ma zhig mchis mod kyi grags che ba nyi shu rtsa gcig tu grags/

He was also known as Pīyūṣa Kalaśa, Pitṛceṭa, Mātṛceṭa, Saubhāgyaśubha, Aśvaghoṣa, Nandana, Maticitra, Aśvaka, and Durdharṣa. After he had embraced Buddhism he was known as Ratnaceṭa, Subhūtipālita, Bhavideva, Dīpaṃkara, Advayabhāva,[306] Gandharvadhara, Bhikṣu Śūra, Jitāri, Vajrāyudha, Trideva, Bhāvabha, and Parahita Āryaśūra. He was known by many names, but these twenty-one are the most common.

d.div: [306] Ngo bo gnyis med pa. But possibly Asvabhāva (ngo bo nyid med pa).

And in the fortieth chapter of his Moonlight: A Commentary on the Essence of Eight Branches:
My grandfather Saubhāgyanandana,[308] forever hailed by the wise as one of untainted renown. His son was Kāmānandana, and I his son, Candranandana.
Of great intelligence and with the wisdom of the tantras,[309] the ācārya known as Paramārtha, the supreme physician, was born in Kashmir.[310] Concerning this “supreme physician,” prior to the above quote the text says:
The glorious Pitṛceṭa, the supreme physician, perfected in the science of Āyurveda.[311]

f.d: snying po bsdus pa'i rdzogs byang la sman pa'i bdag po dge 'dun gsang ba zhes bya ba'i bu pha khol zhes [184] dpal chen dge ba slob dpon dpa' bo dang / de'i sras chags pa mngon dga'/ de'i sras kha che zla mngon des yan lag brgyad pa chen po/ de la 'jug pa/ snying po bsdus pa rnams dang / tsa ra ka 'bum sde sogs gso rig gi gtsug lag mtha' klas par brten cing / rang nyid kyis rnam par dpyod pa'i rig lam nas drangs te snying po bsdus pa rgyas par 'grel ba tshig don zla zer/ de'i sman ming zur du bkol par tshig don sgra sbyor nges pa sogs mdzad de 'phags yul gyi gso rig 'dzin pa rnams kyi gtsug gi nor bu lta bur gyur/

In the colophon of the Essence of Eight Branches it says, “Pitṛceṭa, son the master physician Saṃghaguhya.”[312] This refers to Saubhāgyaśubha, who is Ācārya Śūra, whose son was Kāmānandana, who in turn was the father of Candranandana from Kashmir. Candranandana devoted himself to countless works on Āyurveda, including the Extensive Exposition of Eight Branches, Engaging in Eight Branches, Essence of Eight Branches, the Caraka Collections, and so on. He himself, using sophisticated reasoning and analysis, composed an extensive commentary on Essence of Eight Branches called Moonlight and a separate lexicon of the medical terms found in Moonlight, among others. He became the crown jewel of those working to preserve and develop the science of healing in India at that time.

Others from India who made major contributions to medicine include the Oḍḍiyāna ācārya, Padmasambhava, who composed many medical texts, including Vajra Armor Prevention, Sun and Moon Union, Ambrosia Vase Treatment, Precious Garland, and Ambrosia Essence. Also included would be Sthiramati from east India who composed Stainless Radiance; the Oḍḍiyāna scholar Jinamitra, who composed One Thousand and Ninety-One Treatments; and the Nepalese Anara,[313] who composed Three Translocations.

d.div: [313] Rendered below as Śrī Ānanda. See Martin, p. 11, where his name is also rendered Pra-a-nan-ta.

f.d: bod yul du gso ba rig pa dar tshul/
Part 2. EARLIER DEVELOPMENT OF MEDICAL SCIENCE IN TIBET
7. Earliest Developments

bsil ldan ra ba dkar pos yongs su bskor ba'i ljongs 'dir/ gso ba rig pa byung tshul la/ spyir kla klo la sogs pa khol bu re gnyis las phal che ba mi rigs yin no cog la rang rang gi yi ge re yod par grags shing / mngon sum du'ang snang la/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i rgya 'grel dri med 'od la sogs par yang de bzhin du bshad mod/ 'on kyang bod yul 'dir chos kyi rgyal po srong btsan sgam po'i yab gnam ri srong btsan yan du yi ge med par 'dod par ltar na sman dpyad gyi gzhung lugs la brten pa'i brtag tshul dang gso thabs med cing / zas phan gnod shes pa tsam dang / rma gsar pa la mar khu btang nas rtsa kha sdom pa/ sbang ma'i 'jib byed pa la sogs pa klo dang bod du mi chags pa nas bzung yod par kha cig grags rung spyi skad la lha tho tho ri snyan shal gyi sku ring nas dar/

The way that the science of healing arose in this land situated amid its white mountainous enclosure is as follows. With the exception of a few barbaric and uncivilized tribes, most human races are reputed to have their own system of writing. This is something we can ascertain by observation, and Stainless Light—the Indian commentary on the Kālacakra Tantra—and other works also assert this to be the case. However, if it is true that a system of writing had not yet developed here in this land of Tibet up to and including the reign of Namri Songtsen, the father of Dharma king Songtsen Gampo (615–50 c.e.), then during those times there was no system of diagnosis nor treatment of disease through reliance on medical texts. People understood only what was good and bad to eat. Melted butter was put on wounds to stop the bleeding. Compresses of fermented grain were used as poultices, and so on. Some say these treatments had existed since humans evolved in Tibet and Lo.[314] However, general opinion is that it began in the reign of Lha Thothori Nyenshal.[315]

d.div: [314] Klo. These days the region of the Lhopa (lho pa) people in the south of the country.

[315] Also called Lhathori Nyentsen (Lha mtho ri gnyan brtsan). Tibet’s twenty-fifth king; 348–468 c.e. (Rechung). Twenty-eighth king, 254–74 c.e. (Dungkar). A contemporary of Vasubhandu according to Tāranātha.

f.d:
de nas rabs gsum pa 'gro gnyan lde'u sa gdon gyis zin pa rgyal brgyud phyi ma rnams la de ltar mi 'byung ba'i phyir gson por dur du zhugs khar/ sras dmus long dkon pa bkrar zhal chems su/
bsam pa bzang po gser dang 'dra ba ste/ / bzang po'i gros ni bdud rtsi yin zhes nyon/ / ngan pa rnams kyang ma dang 'dra bas gsos/ / mi chos rtog pa yin gyi rnam rtog skyungs/ / zhes gnyan po gsang ba la mchod pa bya ba dang / 'a zha'i yul nas sman pa bos la mig phye ste rgyal thabs kyi bya ba byed tshul gsungs pa ltar/ rgyal phran 'a zha rje bya ba sman pa mkhas pa zhig spyan drangs/ rgyal bu'i mig gser gyi thur mas phye/ skyid shod stag mo ri la gnyan 'dug pa gzigs pas stag ri gnyan gzigs su grags/

Three generations later King Dronyen Deu contracted a disease caused by an earth spirit, and in order to shield his royal line from the disease, he buried himself alive. As he did so he gave his final testament to his blind son, Könpa Tra:
A good mind is like gold, good speech like ambrosia, so listen: Even the wicked are like your mother, so heal them; worldly dharma is all distracting thought, so throw it away. The king then instructed his son to worship the Secret Signs,[316] to summon a doctor from the region of Asha[317] who could operate on his eyes, and to carry out the duties of a king. Therefore, Könpa Tra invited Ashajé, a wise doctor from the petty kingdom of Asha, who successfully operated on the prince’s eyes with a golden surgical instrument. Looking with his new sight at the mountains of Kyishö Takri, he saw wild sheep and was henceforth known as Takri Nyensik—“he who sees wild sheep on Takri.”

d.div: [316] Gnyan po gsang ba. During the reign of King Lha Thothori, a box fell from the sky containing three texts and a golden shrine. At first no one knew what they were, and the king called them the Secret Signs and placed them in a box in his palace.

[317] A zha. According to the White Annals, quoted in Dungkar, p. 1834, this area is now part of Mongolia. Others say it is in the region of Kansu and the Blue Lake (Tso Ngön) in the north, but Dungkar rejects this, saying that it refers to an area on the far eastern reaches of Tibet. According to Kachuwa Chölothar, p. 8, it is in Domé Tsongka. Trinlé, p. 16, quotes the Fifth Dalai Lama as saying it is near Blue Lake. Others place it in Ngari.

f.d: de sras gnam ri srong btsan gyi dus rgya nag rtsis dang sman gyi cha lag 'ga' zhig blangs par bshad kyang 'di yin gsal bar mi snang / 'phags pa 'jig rten dbang phyug mi rje'i tshul bzung ba srong btsan sgam po rgyal sar phebs nas/ ming tshig thams cad yi ger gdab tu rung ba dang / rgya mo bza' 'un shing kong jos bsnams pa'i sman dpyad chen mor grags pa ha shang ma hA de ba dang d+ha rma ko Sha gnyis kyis bsgyur zhing /

His son was Namri Songtsen, and in his time it is said that a few astrological and medical works were brought from China, but these cannot be identified. His son was Songtsen Gampo, the noble Lokeśvara in the form of a king. During his reign the spoken word was rendered into writing. Therefore, the medical text known as the Great Treatise on Medicine brought by his Chinese wife, the princess Wen Cheng, was translated into Tibetan by Hvashang Mahādeva and Dharmakośa.

'phags yul gyi sman pa b+ha ra ng+ha dza/ rgya nag gi sman pa hen wen hang de/ stag gzigs gam khrom gyi sman pa ga les nos gsum rgyal po'i snyun gso ba'i phyir gdan drangs/ rgya gar gyi sman pas 'bu shag ma bu che chung dang sbyor ba mar gsar/ rgya nag pas rgya dpyad thor bu che chung / stag gzig pas mgo sngon bsdus pa dang de pho/ rma bya/ ne tso gsum gyi dpyad sogs bsgyur/ gsum ga bka' bgros te mi 'jigs pa'i mtshon cha zhes bya ba bam po bdun yod pa'i gso dpyad kyi gzhung gsar du brtsams nas phul/

Once when the king was ill, the Indian doctor Bharadhaja, the Chinese doctor Hsüan Yüan Huang, and the Taksik or Trom[318] doctor Galenos were invited to Tibet to cure him. There the Indian doctor translated a text called Bushak Extensive and Short Exposition and Fresh Ghee Preparation. The Chinese doctor translated a work called Extensive and Short Expositions of Various Chinese Treatments. The Taksik doctor translated a text called Blue Head Collection and one called Dissection of Cockerels, Peacocks, and Parrots. They held many discussions and jointly composed a medical text in seven chapters called Weapons of Fearlessness, which they offered to the king.

d.div: [318] For more on this locale, see in the introduction on p. 2–4.

A verse in this text reads:
Without knowledge of the three great systems, one is not counted among the great physicians and is unable to benefit oneself or others, like the distance between thumb and finger hoping to measure the vast reaches of space. Bharadhaja, the great rishi, Galenos, the ambassador, Hsüan Yüan Huang, crowned lord of the land, these three great manifestations are praised as worthy vessels of ambrosia.[319] Therefore, all medical science was compiled into these three main systems and propagated by them.

The king gave gifts to the Indian and Chinese doctors, and they traveled back to their own lands. Galenos stayed on as royal physician. It is said that he mostly resided in Lhasa, where he composed many texts. He married and had three sons. It is also said that the eldest was sent to upper Tsang province, where the lineages of Biji and others flourished, the middle son to the Yorpo region, where he developed the southern Lhorong medical tradition, while the youngest son stayed with his father, where he was known as Sogdian doctor. Galenos was later known was Dzoro. Would-be students from upper-class families were discouraged from studying with him, whereas those from the four main lower classes, known as the Tuk, Jang, Nik, and Mong, were urged to take up the study of medicine, and Galenos was asked by the king not to differentiate between upper and lower classes as good or bad but to treat all equally. He was conferred with the title Physician Giver of Life[320] and was rewarded with nine great and three small royal commendations. Jangtsa Lhabön,[321] the son of King Mé Aktsom,[322] took for his queen the princess Chin Cheng from China, who brought with her many medical and astrological texts. Many texts, exemplified by the work known as Moon King, or Somarāja, in 115 chapters, were translated by Hvashang Mahākyinda, the Chinese youth Garkhen, Khyungpo Tsetsé, Khyungpo Damtsuk, and Choklo Mönbar.

d.div: [320] ’Tsho byed sman pa. Tsho byed is also another term for a doctor or healer and is the Tibetan rendering of Jivaka, the name given to the renowned doctor who lived during the time of the Buddha. Sman pa means physician.
[321] According to some accounts, this prince died before the marriage took place.
[322] Thirty-seventh king of Tibet usually known as Tridé Tsukten (b. 704!) (Dungkar, p. 396).

Concerning this work, Somarāja, the Chronicles of Ministers says:
Somarāja, Drop of Ambrosia, Vase of Ambrosia, by Nāgārjuna.[323] This is a corruption indicating that this work was either composed or requested by Nāgārjuna, and because of this mistake there are one or two works in which medical scholars have added the prophecy of Nāgārjuna’s coming, beginning “In the south in the region of Vidarbha….” However, the work was requested by Wang Té, or the Nāgarāja Gapa.

During these times there was a doctor from Trom called Biji in his own language but whose actual name was Tsampashilaha.[324] He gathered many scholars together and translated and composed several medical works. Using his own Crystal Mirror Tantra in fifty chapters as a foundation, there followed Red Ink Illuminating Beacon on the Abdomen Early Volume in forty-two chapters, Red Ink Magic Key to the Abdomen Later Volume in twenty-five chapters, and Teachings on Treatment of the Limbs in forty-two chapters; a commentary, further commentary, and secret commentary on the above; the four mother-and-son medical works, namely, the large and small mother text Heart-Like Network and the black and red son commentaries. There are also four works—Small Commentary, Lesser Network, The Beacon, and Lesser Treatise on Pacification—known as the four son texts of the Heartdrop Collection; six works on treatments for arrow wounds, infected sores, burns, holding the drop, channels, and growths, known collectively as the six essential son texts. Together these make up the three mother texts and the seventeen son commentaries. Also included are Essential Beacon for the Elimination of Hindrances, Four Conclusions from Examinations of Pus, Precious Base Emaciation Medicine, and Gentle Ambrosia Emetic for Pus, known collectively as the four secret and exclusive son texts. These make up the extensive collection.

d.div: [324] Trinlé (p. 48) says that the name is in the language of Trom. Elsewhere in the text he is called Tsenpashilaha, but it appears to be of Sanskrit origin, possibly Campaśīla. See Martin (p. 15) and Beckwith (“The Introduction of Greek Medicine into Tibet,” p. 303).

f.d: 'bring du be bum smug po ti ka yang tig gnyis shin tu bsdus pa yi ge dmar chung rtsa 'grel tig gsum dang / byang khog gi man ngag le'u gsum ga dril ba la bdud rtsi me long gi skor le'u che ba brgyad dang chung ba bcu gsum ste nyer gcig /rma skor gsum ston pa thig le gsal ba'i mdo mgo byang khog 'brel mar bcos pa/ don snying / rnam pa lnga'i dpyad thag / rgya nag gi drang srong gis mdzad pa rin chen dbyig le'u bdun cu pa dang / mo dbyig le'u bdun pa dril bas bam po nyi shu rtsa lnga pa/ phyag rdor gyis mdzad pa mgo bo'i rtsod bzlog / sprul pa'i khyi'us mdzad pa bdud rtsi dar ya kan lhung bzed kyi 'phrul 'khor/ de'i 'grel pa ha shang kran das mdzad pa/ mdo byang che chung bya ba dang / nyes dmigs sum cu rtsa lnga pa/ ro bkra 'phrul gyi me long le'u nyer drug pa/ ro bkra tha gu dgu sbyor/ gson thig ro thag gi rnam gzhag drang srong mi'i khog pa le'u bcu pa/ drang srong rgyun shes kyis mdzad par grags pa byang khog khrems kyi mdo zhes bya ba dang /

The intermediate collection consists of the Essential and Quintessential Versions of Brown Compilation. The abridged collection comprises the root, commentary, and essence of the Lesser Red Ink Text. Also included are the three chapters on the abdomen combined to form the work Mirror of Ambrosia in eight long and thirteen short chapters; Clear Drop Treatise on the Threefold Classification of Wounds; a combined treatment of head and abdomen called Suspended Rope of Five Essentials; Precious Gem in seventy chapters, written by a Chinese rishi, and Feminine Gem in seven chapters, which together make up twenty-five volumes; Resolving Disputes Concerning the Head composed by Vajrapāṇi; Magic Almsbowl[325] of Daryakan Ambrosia, composed by Trulpai Khyeu, and its commentaries by Hvashang Kyinda, these two known as Great and Lesser Concise Annotations; Thirty-Five Faults; Magic Mirror of Anatomy in twenty-six chapters; Combining the Nine Anatomical Threads; Measurements of Living and Dead Bodies; Abdomen of Humans and Rishis in ten chapters; Structure of the Abdomen, reputedly written by Ātreya.

d.div: [325] Lhung bzed (begging bowl), but Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo has lhu med (whole, complete).

f.d: yan lag la drang srong gi keng rus che chung bya ba dang / le'u bcu gsum pa bya ba dang / tshigs kyi sdoms kyi le'u zhes bya ba dang / rin po che'i mdzod phan pa sman gyi le'u bcu pa dang / sman pa la rab tu gces pa'i le'u bzhi pa dang / rin po che'i phreng ba zhes bya ba le'u lnga bcu pa/ rin po che'i dbyig le'u bdun cu pa rnams bsgyur nas rgyal po la phul/

Secondary works include the greater and lesser Bones of the Rishis; Thirteen Chapters; Restoring Joints; Treasure Mine: Ten Chapters of Beneficial Medicine; Four Chapters on Essentials for Physicians; Precious Garland in fifty chapters; and Precious Gem in seventy chapters. All these texts were translated into Tibetan and offered to the king.

de rnams phyogs gcig tu za 'og gi sgrom bur bzhugs pa la bla dpyad kyi gzhung 'tsho ba'i mdor grags/ gzhan yang de'i dus na ha shang ma hA de ba dang khyung po tse tse sogs kyis sman dpyad du ma bsgyur bar bshad cing / tsan pa shi la ha des phyis bod du srid bskyangs/ bi ji'i rgyud sngar byung grub rung 'di nas kyang 'phel bar grags/ slob brgyud la zhang dang stong dang brang ti gsum gyis gtsos du mar 'phel/ de gsum pos mdo khams kyi so kha bsrung pa po lo bzhi byas pa'i bya dga' la rgyal pos rgyud shel kyi me long / rma bcos ma bu bcu bdun sogs rgyas 'bring bsdus gsum yi ge dmar chung dang bcas pa gnang nas rgyud nas brgyud kyi bla sman du dbang bskur zhing dmag nas kyang bton par grags/ la lar stong bzher mes po la mgo dpyad/ brang ti rgyal mnyes khar bur byang khog / zhang lha mo gzi la yan lag rnams kyi bcos gnang yang zer/ mes ag tshogs gnam du gshegs nas btsad po khri srong lde btsan nam tshangs pa lha'i me tog gis rgyal srid 'dzin pa'i thog mar rgya gar gyi sman pa ng+ha rma rA dza/ ha shang ma hA kyin da/ tsan pa shi la ha gsum la sprul ba'i sras gsum du grags te/

They were then wrapped together in the best silk and became known collectively as Collection on Health: Higher Texts on Medical Practice.[326] It is taught that Hvashang Mahādeva and Khyungpo Tsetsé also translated many medical works in these times. Tsenpashilaha later became a ruler in Tibet for a while. The line of Biji was already established in Tibet but now was reputed to be even stronger. His lineage of disciples increased and was exemplified by Shang Lhamo Si, Tongsher Mepo, and Drangti Nyekhar. These three were appointed border protectors in Dokham for four years, and as a reward for their services the king presented them with the Crystal Mirror Tantra and the extensive, intermediate, and abridged commentaries, such as the seventeen mother and son texts on treatment of wounds, and the Lesser Red Text. It is said that they and their descendents were appointed as royal physicians and were taken out of the army.[327] Some accounts say that the king gave a text on the treatments of the head to Tongsher Mepo, treatments of the abdomen to Drangti Nyekhar, and a work on treatment of the limbs to Shang Lhamo Si. After the passing of King Mé Aktsom, the noble Trisong Detsen,[328] known as “the celestial flower of Brahmā,” became king. At the beginning of his reign three great scholars known as the three manifested sons appeared. They were the Indian physician Dharmarāja, Hvashang Mahākyinda, and Tsenpashilaha.[329]

d.div: [326] Trinlé (p. 47) points out that these works are rare indeed these days, although a copy of the Works of Biji exists in the Jong Medical Institute in Tibet.
[327] Dmag (army), but Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo has dmangs (ordinary people).
[328] Dates for this figure vary: 742–97 (Dungkar); born 754 (Rechung); 755–94 (Beckwith).
[329] Trinlé states that this is evidently the same Tsenpashilaha or Tsampashilaha described previously.

f.d: de gsum gyis rgyal khams so so'i lugs dang bstun nas gso ba rig pa'i rtsa ba rtsis nyi zla'i 'khor lo zhes bya ba le'u bdun/ lus gnas nas gzhi gsum gso thabs kyi 'grel pa/ chu brtag pa gser gyi me long / gdams pa'i 'phrul 'khor dngul gyi me long / sgo gtan lcags kyi gzer/ rtsa dpyad rgya'i smra mchu/ kha dmar rgyas pa gser gyi gtan phyis/ bsdus pa lcags kyi sta re/ rin po che bdud rtsi gsang ba'i lung / sman nus sgron ma gser gzong / bcud len rin chen shel 'phreng / sman ming 'bu shag zangs kyi bum pa/ 'dra yig dung gi mig / 'khrug sdebs g.yu'i dra ba/ ro skor lcags kyi phreng ba/ zhi byed mu tig phreng ba/ rna bshal dung gi phyags shing / skyugs rin chen lcags kyu/ bshal dngul gyi bum pa/ 'jam rtsi nyi ma'i gzer bu/ ni ru ha lcags kyi par bu/ sngo sman nags su 'jug pa g.yu'i dra ba/ lums nyi zla'i thigs pa/ byug pa me chu'i gzer/ gtar kha lcags kyi pad+ma/ me btsa' bdud rtsi'i thigs pa/ thur dpyad mtshon cha 'khor lo/ / dmu chu rgya mtsho 'dren skems/ sman gnas mdor bsdus rnams la 'grel chung nyer bdun zhes bya ba khong nad kyi skor/

These three compiled many medical texts in accord with their own country’s traditions and offered them to the king. They include: 1. Calculation of the Orbits of the Sun and Moon: An Essential Root of Medicine 2. Commentary on the Healing of the Three Roots of Disease 3. Golden Mirror Analysis of Urine 4. Silver Mirror Charm Circle of Instruction 5. Iron Door Bolt of the Chinese Oral Tradition of Pulse Examination 6. Golden Door Bolt of Prognosis and Abridged Iron Axe of Prognosis 7. Secret Transmission of Precious Ambrosia 8. Golden Chisel: A Beacon on the Powers of Medicinal Substances 9. Precious Crystal Rosary Elixir 10. Bushak Copper Vase Medical Lexicon 11. Eye of the Conch Illustrations 12. Turquoise Network Compendium 13. Iron Garland of Tastes 14. Pearl Garland of Pacification Remedies 15. Conch Pus Cleanser 16. Precious Hook of Emetics 17. Silver Vase of Purgatives 18. Golden Sun Vase of Suppositories 19. Iron Cup of Strong Enemas 20. Turquoise Network: Entering the Forest of Medical Plants 21. Medical Baths: A Drop of the Sun and Moon 22. Fire and Water Needles of Massage 23. Iron Lotus of Bloodletting 24. Ambrosia Drop of Cauterization 25. Weapon Wheel of Minor Surgery 26. From the Ocean of Dropsy to Dry Land 27. Compilation of Medicine Places These are known as the twenty-seven short commentaries and form the collection on internal diseases.

thor dpyad la spyir rma gcong gnyis dang bye brag nyi shu rtsa gsum/ mgo byang khog yan lag dang bcas pa'i bcos te bsdoms pa la rin chen spungs pa'i skor zhes bya ba brtsams pa dang / li'i rgyal po'i ske'i bcos sogs phul/

Works on minor surgery[330] include two general works on chronic wounds, twenty-three specific works, and a collection of treatments for head, abdomen, and limbs. This is the Heap of Jewels collection. Other works offered to the king include King of Khotan Treatment for the Neck.

d.div: [330] For thor read thur (Prof. Losang Tenzin). Thor is often an abbreviation of thor bu “miscellaneous” and thur an abbreviation of thur ma, “surgical instrument.” More than once these two terms have been confused leading to doubt as to whether the correct reading is “miscellaneous treatments” or “surgical treatments.”

f.d: klu sgrub kyis mdzad zer ba phung po lnga'i nad gso ba/ bdud rtsi'i sman rin po che gsang tig sgron ma/ rin po che'i mdo'i rtsa ba lta bu le'u bcu bdun/ mdo rin po che gsang ba'i 'grel chen le'u don drug / 'du ba rnam bzhi'i ti ka le'u nyer lnga/ don snod ti ka le'u bcu drug / phran bu gser gyi ti ka le'u so bdun/ mgo bo'i ti ka le'u nyer gcig /byang khog gi ti ka 'phrul lde nag po le'u zhe bdun/ yan lag rnam bzhi'i ti ka le'u bzhi bcu ste dril bas le'u nyis brgya bdun cu rtsa dgu'i bdag nyid can/

Several works attributed to Nāgārjuna were translated at this time. They include, Curing Illnesses of the Five Aggregates, Secret Essence Beacon of Ambrosia Gem Medicine, a treatise on precious stones, which is like a root treatise and has seventeen chapters. Also included are the seventy-six chapters of Secret Commentary on the Precious Stones Treatise, the twenty-five chapters of Treatise on the Four Humors, the sixteen chapters of Descriptions of the Organs, the thirty-seven chapters of Short Gold Treatise; the twenty-one chapters of Treatise on the Head; the forty-seven chapters of Magic Black Key Treatise on the Abdomen; and the forty chapters of Treatise on the Four Limbs. These works comprise 279 chapters.

mi dra mi dbang tsan+d+ra dang ha shang de ba bo d+hi'i 'gyur drang srong nyi ma'i dngos grub dang dka' thub gzhon nur 'jam dbyangs kyis gsungs par grags pa gso byed 'phrul gyi mdzod rin po che'i sgron ma zhes bya ba a ru ra rigs bdun la dpe blangs nas nad gzhi'i gnas/ de'i rtags/ so sor bcos pa/ dpyad kyis bcos pa/ de'i ja log /thor dpyad/ rten 'brel gyi sgo nas bcos pa bdun/ rnam rgyal ro drug ldan yin pa ltar gsar pa btsan babs/ rgyas pa thog babs/ bcos nyes yongs bzlog / bla gnyan ja log / kha thor gdams pa/ khyug dpyad rdzu 'phrul bcos dang drug / nus pa brgyad yod pa bzhin du yon tan brgyad ldan/ zhu rjes gsum ldan bzhin du rtags bcos thabs/ rjes gcod gsum du ston pa rnams bsdoms pa'i glegs bam gcig /

Mitra Miwang Chandra[331] and Hvashang Devabodhi translated Siddhi of Rishi Śūrya and Precious Beacon: A Magic Treasury of Medicine, reputed to be the speech of Mañjuśrī to Kumāra Tapas. Using the seven types of myrobalan as illustrations, this work begins with seven sections: fundamentals of illness, symptoms, individual treatments, external therapies, reversal treatments, minor surgery, and treatment through charms. Just as vijaya myrobalan possesses all six tastes, the text continues with six sections on sudden onset of illness, sudden spread of the illness, elimination of mistakes in treatment, complications from other ailments, reversal treatments, miscellaneous instructions, and magical treatments. As there are eight powers found in medicines, the work has eight qualities. As there are three post-digestive tastes, so there are three sections on symptoms, treatment, and complete cure. In total these sections make up one complete volume.

d.div: [331] Lodrö Gyalpo reading mi tra preferred. He also has caṇḍa.

f.d: phyag na rdo rjes gsungs par grags pa rtsa ba'i rgyud le'u bzhi bcu rtsa bzhi/ de'i 'grel pa rtsa ba'i drang srong brgyad dang phran bu bcu gsum gyis byas pa'i le'u nyer bzhi pa/ bcos thabs nyer gnyis pa/ tshig rkang brgyad pa zhes bya ba rnams bsgyur/

Other translations include Root Tantra, reputedly by Vajrapāṇi, in forty-four chapters, its commentary by the eight main rishis and the thirteen lesser rishis in twenty-four chapters, Twenty-Two Chapters on Treatments, and the Eight Verses.

de nas tsan pa shi la ha rang yul du 'byon khar sras la gdams pa be bum nag po'i skor 'jal tshad dang bcas pa dang / tsa ra kas mdzad pa drang srong rnying rgyud mgo byang khog yan yag gi pra 'khrid skor gsum dang / mgo byang khog yan lag 'du ba thor bu dang bcas pa'i bcos thabs rtsa ba'i man ngag don brgyad pa rnams la bi ji'i po ti kha ser du grags pa rnams phul ba las/ phyi ma la rgyal po'i bla yig 'od 'bar du grags/

As Tsenpashilaha was about to return to his own country, he composed for his son Black Compilation Collection with Units of Measurements; Three Collections on Clear Descriptions of the Head, Abdomen, and Limbs from Caraka’s Rishi Essence Tantra; and seventy-eight root instructional works on treatments for disorders of the head, abdomen, limbs, and humors together with miscellaneous topics, known collectively as Biji’s Yellow Collection. This last collection was also known as the Radiant Exalted Documents of the King. All these works were offered to the king.

gzhan yang ha shang pe na tse tas/ rgyal blon dmangs gsum gdams pa rtsa ba rin po che'i mdzod skor lnga ste/ mgo/ byang khog / khong nad/ yan lag / thor bu dang lnga/ mgo rin po che'i mdzod la dras dang bzlum bcos kyi skor shog dril bcu bdun/ byang khog rin po che'i mdzod la dkar chos dmar chos dkar shal dmar shal sogs shog dril bzhi bcu rtsa lnga/ khong nad la bshal rin po che'i phyags shing / dug bcos rin po che'i bum pa/ sha dug nyi zer sprin bral/ btsan dug srog skyabs go cha/ tshad pa gsal byed me long / grang ba rin chen sha sbyor sogs dang /

Hvashang Penatseta composed the Fundamental Treasury of the Five Collections as advice to the king, ministers, and the people. The five collections are the head, abdomen, internal illnesses, supplements, and miscellaneous works. The collection on the head deals with surgery and head compresses, comprising seventeen scrolls. The abdomen collection comprises white phenomena, red phenomena, white purgative, and red purgative[332] and makes up forty-five scrolls. The collection on internal illnesses is made up of Precious Cleanser for Dysentery, Precious Vase of Poison Treatments, Cloudless Sunrays for Meat Poisoning, Lifesaving Armor against Strong Poisons, Clear Mirror for Fevers, and Precious Meat Compound for Cold Diseases.

d.div: [332] Gshal; this is Lodrö Gyalpo’s reading.

f.d: yan lag la mdzod che ba le'u so drug / 'bring rin po che 'bar ba rtsa 'grel/ spyi don 'grel pa dang gnas skabs gegs sel gnyis/ spyi don la'ang phyi ltar dmangs yul mi la gdams pa/ nang ltar blon po la gdams pa/ phyi dmangs lugs la rtsa ba 'phrul lde zhe gnyis/ man ngag 'phrul lde che chung / nang blon po lugs la rtsa ba'i 'grel ba gnad yig dpe chung dang bzhi/ rtsa skor la 'grel ba bdun/ gnad yig bcu/ dpe chung nyer bdun no/ /

The supplement collection consists of greater, intermediate, and lesser treasuries. The greater treasury has thirty-six chapters. The intermediate treasury consists of Brilliant Jewel in root text and commentary, an overview, and a section on dispelling immediate hindrances. The overview contains advice for ordinary people in accord with outer perceptions, advice for ministers in accord with the inner world, and advice for the king in accord with the hidden world. The outer version for the people contains the root-text work Forty-Two Magic Keys and Large and Small Magic Keys of Instruction. The inner version for ministers consists of root text, commentaries, aphorisms and short illustrations. The root text collection has seven commentaries, there are ten aphorisms and twenty-seven short illustrations.

gsang ba rgyal po lugs la/ che tshe ltar bcos pa/ chung tshe ltar bcos pa/ dmar 'khrid ltar bcos pa gsum/ che tshe la ga'u snying 'dra dang snying rtse gnyis/ snying 'dra la skor lnga dang snying rtse la bcu ste bco lnga/ chung tshe la lhan thabs nyid khol gzer bu/ log gnon bzhi las/ lhan thabs la brgyad/ nying khog la bzhi/ gzer bu la drug / log gnon la gsum/ dmar khrid la lde mig dang yang tig gnyis/ de'i 'grel pa gnas skabs gegs sel rtsa ba'i dka' 'grel sgron me lta bu bcu gnyis so/ /

The secret version for the king contains large grouped[333] treatments, lesser grouped treatments, and direct instruction treatments. The first of these consists of Heart-Shaped Amulet and Heart-Peak Amulet. Heart-Shaped Amulet is made up of five collections and Heart Peak Amulet has ten. Short lesser grouped treatments consist of supplements, essentials, rivets, and remedial therapy. There are eight supplements, four sections on essentials, six on rivets, and three on remedial therapy. Treatments according to direct instructions are made up of Key Instructions and Quintessential Instructions. There are twelve commentaries, including Dispelling Immediate Hindrances and Beacon-Like Commentary on Difficult Points of the Root Text.

d.div: [333] Che tsho; amended as per Lodrö Gyalpo from che tshe.

f.d: chung ba la gab pa'i bang mdzod ces bya ba dang / thor bu rin po che'i mdzod la mi 'dra ba brgya rtsa brgyad/ kha byang rin po che'i lde mig sogs yig sna ma bu tshang bar bsgyur ro//

The lesser treasury from the supplement collection is known as the Hidden Treasury. Miscellaneous works consists of 108 different works. He also translated Key to Precious Titles and many other mother-and-son documents.

'di dag gi snga phyir bka' gdams glegs bam rin po che las/
sngon tshe rdo rje gdan du 'dzom/ / deng sang a+yon yul du tshogs/ / ma 'ongs gangs ri'i khrod du 'du/[187] /

On these times the precious Book of Kadam says:
In the past they came together at Vajrāsana, these days they are found in the land of Oḍḍiyāna, in the future they will come to the Land of Snow.[334]

d.div: [187] bka' gdams bu chos/ rgyal bu dkon mchog 'bangs su sku skye ba bzhes pa'i le'u/ shog_153_phreng 20
[334] Book of Kadam: Son Teachings, 143.20.

f.d:
zhes dang /
bla ma dri ma med pas/ bdag kyang gnas der lha 'dre 'dul du 'gro[188] / zhes dang /
dge slong nga la bden pa yod med kyang / / mi dbang khyod kyi grogs byed rtag tu dge[189] / zhes pa ltar 'phags pa phyag na pad mo dang 'jam pa'i dbyangs tha mi dad pa chos rgyal khri srong lde'u btsan dang / sangs rgyas snang ba mtha' yas kyi ngo bo a+yon dus gsum mkhyen pa dus gcig tu zhal 'dzom/ bod kyi lha srin gdug pa can rnams btul/ brag dmar dpal gyi bsam yas mi 'gyur lhun grub kyi sa gzhi byin gyis brlabs/ rten brten par bcas pa gegs med du 'byongs/ rab tu gnas pas dam tshig pa la ye shes sems dpa' dngos su thim pa'i rtags 'jim gzugs rnams mi ltar 'byon zhing gtam gsungs pa sogs dpag par dka' ba'i lha khang dang / mchod rten so sor byung /

Also:
The glorious guru said, “To tame the demons I too will go there.”[335] Also:
Although I am a monk without wisdom, to be your companion, lord among men, would be forever joy.[336] As these citations indicate, the Dharma king Trisong Detsen, who was inseparable from the lotus-holding Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī, and the Oḍḍiyāna knower of the three times,[337] who was inseparable from Buddha Amitābha, both appeared at the same time. They tamed the harmful demons of Tibet, blessed the foundations of the unchanging and spontaneous glorious red-rock Samyé Monastery and purified the building and their contents of hindrances. During the consecration, actual wisdom beings were absorbed into the commitment beings, evidenced by clay structures taking human form, speaking, and so forth. In this manner did its extraordinary temples and shrines arise.

d.div: [188] bka' gdams bu chos/ rgyal bu dkon mchog 'bangs su sku skye ba bzhes pa'i le'u/ shog_203_phreng 1
[189] bka' gdams bu chos/ rgyal bu dkon mchog 'bangs su sku skye ba bzhes pa'i le'u/ shog_203_phreng 4
[337] Padmasambhava.

f.d: 8. From Vairocana to Shangtön Siji Bar
bai ro

bod phrug dbang po gsal zhing blo sgrin pa du ma bos nas lo tsA bslabs kyang / saM skri ta'i skad lces ma 'gyur ba'i rgyal po'i thugs pham par gyur pa na/ slob dpon chen pos/
gtsang gi snye mo bye mkhar bya ba yi: gnas gzhi zhig gi grang khang dmig gu na: pha ming spa gor he 'dod bya ba la: ma ming bran ka bza' sgron skyid kyi bu: gan jag thang ta byis pa lo brgyad pa: pha ma gnyis la bslangs na ster bar mchis: sprul ba'i lo tsA rtsod med grags pa 'byung :[190] zhes lung bstan pa ltar/

Many bright and intelligent young Tibetans were brought together and trained as translators, but they were unable to master spoken Sanskrit, and this distressed the king. However, the great ācārya prophesized:
In the Tsang region of Nyemo Jekhar,[338] in a room in a house in a town, comes Genjak Thangta, son of father Pagor Hedö and mother Drönkyi from the Drenka clan. Having been asked, his parents will bring him here at the age of eight, to become without question a renowned incarnate translator.[339]

d.div: [190] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 68_lo tsA ba gsum lung bstan nas rgyal po'i thugs gsos pa/ shog_405_phreng 6
[338] A district on the Tsangpo river to the west of Lhasa; these days called Nyemo Dzongsang Richü (Dungkar, p. 1399).
[339] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 68.405.6.

f.d: gtsang nyang chab dang gtsang chab 'dzom pa'i 'gram du yab spa gor he 'dod dang sgron bza' sgron skyid gnyis kyi sras su 'khrungs/ dgung lo brgyad pa la rgyal po'i spyan sngar bos/ lo bdun gyi bar kha zas dkar gsum mngar gsum kho nas gsos/ shes rab bskyed thabs su blo 'phel gyi gzungs sgrub tu bcug pa dang / 'dra 'bag ltar na lo dgu nas phyi nang gi blon po lo gsum dang / bcu gnyis nas rje'i gsol ka ba lo gsum mdzad par grags/ gang ltar/ de nas lo tsA sgra rnams mkhas par bslabas:[191] zhes byung ba bzhin o rgyan slob dpon pad ma 'byung gnas dang za hor mkhan po zhi ba 'tsho gnyis la dgung lo bco lnga'i bar sgra rig pa gsan pas mkhas pa'i phul tu gyur/ khrus khang gling du mkhan chen byang chub sems dpar rab tu byung /

Therefore, this child was born to Pagor Hedö and Drönkyi in a place where the Nyangchap and Tsangchap rivers meet. At the age of eight he was brought before the king. For the next seven years he ate nothing but the three white foods and the three sweet foods.[340] In order to increase his knowledge, he was encouraged to practice wisdom-increasing mantra meditations. According to the Great Mask,[341] from the age of nine he served outer and inner ministers for three years, and from the age of twelve he served the king for three years. Whatever the truth, as it is said, “Then he became learned in grammar and translation,”[342] meaning that he studied language with the Oḍḍiyāna ācārya Padmasambhava and the Sahor master Śāntarakṣita until the age of fifteen and became a master scholar. In the bathing-house temple of Samyé, he took his monk vows in front of the great abbot Bodhisattva.

d.div: [191] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 70_lo tsA ba gsum lung bstan nas rgyal po'i thugs gsos pa/ shog_410_phreng 4
[340] Milk, butter, and yogurt are the three white foods; sugar, molasses, and honey the three sweet foods.
[341] Dorjé Lingpa (1346–1405), Great Mask: A Biography of the Translator Vairocana.
[342] Orgyen Linpga, Lotus Chronicles, 70.410.4.

f.d: dus der rgyal pos blon 'bangs mkhas btsun thams cad bsags te/ rgyu 'bras kyi chos bod du rdzogs kyang rgyu 'bras las 'das pa'i chos shig rgya gar na yod 'dug pas tshol du gtong dgos zhes bgros par/ gan jag thang ta dang gtsang sngon legs grub gnyis tshogs pa'i gseb nas langs te/ rjes ji skad gsungs pa bzhin byed pa'i khas len zhus pa ltar/ khye'u gnyis la gser gyi pa tra thod pa'i dbyibs su byas pa mgor bkon/ pa tra dang thur ma dang lu gu rgyud 'ga' ni dug po'i gseb tu sbas/ gser phye ba men gyi rwa do dang / gser thums/ lus chas mi 'dra ba dang gcan gzan gyi sder mo sogs dgos cha thams cad rta mtsha' lu bya gdong sogs la bkal te rgya gar 'phags pa'i yul du byon/ do shi do chad kyi dka' ba chen po bcu drug spyad pa'i mthar/ slob dpon shrI sing+ha la sogs pa paN chen nyi shu rtsa lnga la zab rgyas kyi chos du ma zhus/ khyad par du shrI sing la rtsol med rdzogs pa chen po'i chos rgya gar rang du'ang khyab gdal du mi bsgrags par rdo rje gdan du chos rgyal dang paN+Di ta'i rgya nyis sprod btab nas 'jog pa de/ slob dpon gnod sbyin skar mda' gdong dang / bai ros seng ge rab brtan/ legs grub kyi ngang pa rnams su brdzus ta gden drangs/ dbang dang man ngag rdzogs par zhus/ legs grub ngo so 'dod nas sngon du song ba lam la bar chad kyis 'das/

At that time the king brought together ministers, scholars, monks, and representatives of the people for discussions. They agreed that the cause-and-effect teachings were complete in Tibet but that in India there were teachings beyond cause and effect and that these should be sought. In response Genjak Thangta and Tsangön Lekdrup stood up in the assembly and pledged to fulfill the king’s wishes. As preparation for their journey, gold leaf was molded to the shape of skulls, and the two young men wore them on their heads. Gold leaf, implements, and other strings of objects were hidden in their clothes. Gold dust, a pair of wild ox horns, gold nuggets, silver items,[343] claws from various wild animals, and so on, were all loaded onto white-foot, bird-face, and other types of pack horses, and they set off for the noble land of India. On their travels they endured sixteen life-threatening hardships. Finally, however, they were able to study vast and profound Dharmas with twenty-five pandits, such as Ācārya Śrī Siṃha. Even in India at that time, the effortless Great Perfection was not widely promulgated, and so they received it secretly in Bodhgāya[344] from Ācārya Siṃha as a work doubly sealed by the Dharma kings and pandits, with Ācārya Siṃha disguised in the form of the Yakṣa Ulkāmukha, Vairocana[345] as the lion Susthira, and Lekdrup in the form of a swan. There they received the complete initiations and instructions. Lekdrup sought fame and reputation, and he therefore succumbed to an earlier hindrance he had encountered on the journey.

d.div: [343] Dngul chas. I have gone with Trinlé’s reading here rather than lus chas, as written.
[344] Here rendered as rdo rje gdan, vajrāsana: “vajra seat.”
[345] This is the first instance in this account of Ganjak being called by his well-known name of Vairocana.

f.d: slar yang bai ros gzhung man ngag kun gyi zhun thar bcad cing / dga' rab rdo rje dang 'jam dpal bshes gnyen la sogs pa ye shes kyi sku can rnams dang mjal/ chos bka' sna tshogs pa zhus te dgongs pa gnyis su med par gyur/ rkang mgyogs dpon po ku mA ra la gser gyi pa tra byin grogs po byas/ rkang mgyogs kyi gdams pa bstan dgos byas pas/ bya go bo ri rtsibs gcod pa tsam gyi gdams pa byin nas bod du chas pas tshe/ rgya paN rnams kyi rmi ltas log / man ngag gi chos bod du 'khyer bar rig nas rjes bsnyegs pa btang bas ma zin te/ bod kyi ban des chos ni ma rnyed/ mu stegs kyi chos log khyer zer phra ma'i ya ge+i bod du brdzangs pa rgyal pos gzigs pas/ bai ro rgya nas 'khor 'phral mjal du ma gnang bar brten/ rje la zhu 'phrin phul ba ni/

Vairocana then cleared up all questions and doubts he had on the texts and instructions. He met with great beings that had attained the gnosis body, such as Garap Dorjé and Mañjuśrī Mitra. From them he heard various teachings, and their thoughts became as one. He gave the gold leaf to the Ācārya Kumāra, who possessed the fleet-foot siddhi, and became his companion. He said he himself needed the fleet-foot siddhi and having received the teachings on how to walk at the speed of a vulture flying from the mountains, he returned to Tibet. At that time the pandits in India received bad signs in their dreams. They realized that these profound instructions had been taken to Tibet and set out in pursuit of Vairocana but could not catch him. Therefore, they sent a disruptive letter to Tibet saying, “This Tibetan monk has not found the true Dharma; he has taken the perverted dharma of the outsiders.” The king read these letters and as a result did not immediately send a welcoming party out to meet Vairocana on his return. As a response Vairocana sent a letter to the king:

bod kyi mnga' bdag rgyal po chen po lags/ / 'jig rten 'khor ba'i chos la thugs phyungs te/ / ma nor yang dag bden pa'i chos 'dod nas/ / gser phye brdzangs nas bdag cag 'tshol du btang / / dmyal spyod lam bcad mtha' yi kha bskor te/ / las 'phro dag pas mkhas zhal mang po 'khums/ / bzo dang bstan bcos gso dpyad sman la sogs/ / tshe 'dir dgos pa'i phan bya sna tshogs pa/ / dam nyams sgrol ba'i bstan srungs sna tshogs dang / / phyir rgol bzlog pa'i lung rigs mtshon cha dang / / dbang po'i rim 'jug lam stegs rang rang lam/ / rgyu 'bras theg pa ma lus thams cad dang / / bde chen lhun rdzogs sangs rgyas kun gyi thugs/ / rmad byung bstan pa'i snying po theg pa'i mchog / rgyu 'bras gnyis med rtsol med rdzogs pa che/ / ma lus lus pa med par bdag la mchis/ / zhal g.yar mchis nas bka' mchid gsan du gsol/ / yun du ma mjal g.yar khams snyoms lags sam/ / mnga' bdag rgyal po zhal mjal zhes 'bul/ / zhes phul pas/

d.div: Great king, sovereign of Tibet, casting off all concern for worldly dharmas and yearning for the true and unmistaken Dharma, you dispatched gold dust and sent us off in search. We traveled on paths that would purify hell, and with fortunate karma I heard the words of many a scholar. We bring texts on arts and crafts, the science of medicine, and others, all works necessary for the happiness of this life; texts on guardians of the doctrine, liberating those who break commitments; an armory of scripture of logic to defeat the outsiders; and texts on all paths of practice according to faculty, the complete path of the cause-and-effect vehicle. Also the supreme vehicle, very essence of this wonderful doctrine, the naturally perfected great bliss, mind of every buddha, nonduality of cause and effect, the effortless Great Perfection— all these, without omission, I have brought. In your presence I will offer these for you to hear. It is long since we met, I wonder if you are well? To the mighty king I offer this letter in person.[346]
