[346] Dorjé Lingpa (1346–1405), Great Mask: A Biography of the Translator Vairocana, p. 156. Parts of the letter and the description of the horses below have been translated in accordance with this edition.

f.d: 'khor ba'i rdzings chen 'dra ba'i kha dpon bdag /ces sogs kyi lan gnang / ma 'gyangs par mnga' bdag gi dbu skra them par bkram ste de'i steng nas lo tsA ba chen po spyan drangs/ rta mtsha' lu me stag dang ngang pa gser ldongs gnyis gser sgra g.yu yis spras pa dang / gser dngul/ dar zab/ g.yi spyang gi thul ba/ bzang skyems la sogs pa drangs te zhu don tshigs su bcad nas zhus/ nyin par rje blon 'bangs bcas la rgyu 'bras kyi chos dang / nam gung rje la man ngag gi chos bsgyur bas/ rgyal pos man ngag gi rgya mtsho lha'i rje zhes mtshan gsol/

The king replied with a letter beginning, “Great navigator across the sea of samsara.” Without delay this mighty king spread his hair across the threshold of his palace and invited the great translator to walk upon it. A speckled horse and a gold-flecked cream-colored horse with golden saddles studded with turquoise, gold, and silver, fine brocade, cloaks lined with lynx fur, fine drinking vessels, and much more were sent out to Vairocana, where the invitation was conveyed to him in verse. In the daytime he translated the cause-and-effect teachings for the king, ministers, and people. At night he translated the secret-instruction teachings for the king. In return the king gave him the title Celestial Lord of the Ocean of Instructions.

bai ro 'di slob dpon pad ma'i zhal slob rjes 'bangs nyer lnga dang / grub chen dgur grags pa gnyi gar the zhing / bod du dam pa'i chos bsgyur ba mtha' yas pas/ thang yig las/
'das dang ma 'ongs da lta thams cad du: bai ro tsa na 'dra ba'i lo tsA ba: sngar yang ma byon da yang 'byon re skan: ma 'ongs rgya gar phal skad shes tsam la: lo tsAr bzhed srid bai ro'i char mi nye: lo tsAr btags kyang don la paN+Di ta: 'di yi chos drin yod do phyi rabs rnams:[192] zhes gsungs pa dang mthun par/ phyi 'gyur gyi lo tsA ba chen po blo ldan shes rab kyis/
bai ro tsa na nam mkha'i mtha' dang mnyam/ / ska cog gnyis ni nyi zla zung 'brel yin/ / rin chen bzang po tho rangs skar chen 'dra/ / kho bo yang ni srin bu me khyer tsam/[193] / zhes ched du brjod pa'i bsngags pa dang rang nyid kyis khengs pa skyung bar mdzad la/

Vairocana can be included in the twenty-five royal and commoner disciples of ācārya Padma as well as in those renowned as the nine great siddhas. He was responsible for the translation of so many texts into Tibetan that the Lotus Chronicles says:
Never has there been a translator like Vairocana, and there never will be again. In the future those who speak the languages of India may be called translators, but they will come nowhere near Vairocana. He was called a translator, in reality he was a pandit. Generations hence will look on his work with immense gratitude.[347] Similarly, the later great translator Loden Sherap singled Vairocana out for praise while simultaneously humbling himself:
Vairocana was like the vast reaches of space; Ka and Chok[348] are like the sun and moon; Rinchen Sangpo is the great star of the morning; I am a mere firefly.[349]

d.div: [192] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 85_bod du gsung rab dam chos dag ther bton pa/ shog_503_phreng 3
[193] bai ro tsa na nam mkha'i mtha' dang mnyam/ / zhes sogs kyi lo tsA ba blo ldan shes rab kyi gsung 'di'i khungs rnyed son ma thub/
[347] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 85.503.3.

[348] Ka Lotsāwa Paltsek and Chok Lotsāwa Lui Gyaltsen were two famous early translators of the Nyingma school. Rinchen Sangpo (958–1055), mentioned in the next line, has a section devoted to him in the text below.

[349] Untraced. Ngok Lotsāwa Loden Sherap (1059–1109), a nephew and disciple of Ngok Lekpai Sherap (1018–1115), was a lineage holder of the Kadam school, holding the Sangphu lineage of Atiśa’s stages of the path (lam rim) teachings.

f.d:
mkhyen brtse nus gsum 'gran zla dang bral ba ngo bo rnam par snang mdzad kyi ye shes sgyu ma'i rol gar las gsang ba'i bdag po phyag na rdo rje dang dbyer med pa bdag cag gi ston pa'i zhabs rim bka' thams cad kyi sdud pa po 'phags pa kun dga' bo slar yang skye 'gro'i dpal du phebs pa sprul ba'i lo chen bai ro tsa nas kha che'i zla mngon la sman dpyad kyi cha lag mang du zhus shing / khyad par du thang yig shel brag ma'i le'u gya bzhi par/
bai ro tsa nas bon chos 'dres mar bsgyur: bai ro tsa nas rtsis sman 'dres mar bsgyur: bai ro tsa nas mdo sngags 'dres mar bsgyur: mdo bsgyur nang du ye shes sde zhes bris: sngags bsgyur nang du bai ro tsa na bris: bon bsgyur nang du gan jag thang ta bris: rtsis bsgyur nang du in+d+ra bai ro bris: sman bsgyur nang du chos 'bar bya ba bcug: mdo chos dgongs 'gre+el dang bcas phal cher bsgyur:[194] zhes pa ltar sman dpyad sna tshogs sngo'i man ngag ces pa 'jam dbyangs sngo 'bum du grags pa dang / dug bcos sha mo las dkyus slob dpon nyi ma seng ges mdzad pa sogs bsgyur cing /

d.div: [194] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 84_sgra bsgyur gling du sgra bsgyur ba/ shog_491_phreng 4

f.d:
bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/
khyad par khri srong rje yi gangs can 'dir/ / a+yon sangs rgyas gnyis pa spyan drangs pa'i/ / drin las snying rje'i yul gyur 'gro ba'i srog / 'tsho ba'i gso rig gtsug lag 'byams su klas/ / de 'dra'i rig byed rgyu skar 'phreng ba'i dbus/ / tshig nyung don rgyas rgyud bzhi'i chu shel dbang / / don gyi paN chen 'jig rten mig gcig pu/ / bai ro'i mkhyen dpyod rlung gi shing rtas drangs/[195] / zhes bka' stsal ba bzhin gzhung lugs man ngag thams cad kyi mchog dang rab dang phul du gyur ba bdud rtsi'i snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud legs par bsgyur/ Tik+ka mun sel sgron me dang ming don brda sprod rnam lnga gnyis mdzad par grags/

More particularly, my lama the Great Fifth said:
In particular, the kindness of the great Trisong in inviting the second Buddha from Oḍḍiyāna, brought countless medical works to this snowy land, nourishing the lives of living beings, objects of compassion. Amid this galaxy of knowledge shines the crystal moon of Four Tantras, of few words but vast in meaning, drawn by the wisdom wind chariot of Vairocana, in reality a great pandit, sole eye of the world.[350] Therefore, as stated in this verse, he translated the Essence of Ambrosia Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches,[351] the greatest, the best, the supreme of all medical scriptures and instructions. He is also credited with composing Darkness-Dispelling Lamp of Explanation and Medical Dictionary in Five Parts.

d.div: [195] bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/ khyad par khri srong rje yi gangs can 'dir/ /a+yon sangs rgyas gnyis pa spyan drangs pa'i/ /drin las snying rje'i yul gyur 'gro ba'i srog /'tsho ba'i gso rig gtsug lag 'byams su klas/ / de 'dra'i rig byed rgyu skar 'phreng ba'i dbus/ /tshig nyung don rgyas rgyud bzhi'i chu shel dbang / /don gyi paN chen 'jig rten mig gcig pu/ /bai ro'i mkhyen dpyod rlung gi shing rtas drangs/ /de gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[350] Untraced.
[351] In other words, Four Tantras.

f.d:
gzhan yang thang yig le'u gya lnga pa las/
rgya nag sman pa ha shang de ba dang : bla sman nyang btsan shi la la sogs pas: yan lag brgyad pa bdud rtsi snying po dang : sman gyi bcud len byed thabs mang po bsgyur:[196] zhes rgyud bzhi 'di rgya nag nas bsgyur bar bshad pa'ang yod kyang / gzhung man ngag dang bcas pa'i bka' bai ro nyid la babs pas gong du 'phrin yig tshigs bcad mar gsal ba bzhin mnga' bdag rgyal po dang slob dpon sangs rgyas gnyis par phul/

The eighty-fifth chapter of Lotus Chronicles says:
The Chinese doctor Hvashang Deva, court physician Nyangtsen Shila,[352] and others translated the Essence of Ambrosia Eight Branches and many works on preparation of elixirs.[353] Here Four Tantras is said to be have also been translated from the Chinese. This exists, but the transmission of the actual words of the Buddha together with the transmitted instructions came to Vairocana, and therefore, as the verses in his letter to the king made clear, he offered it to the king and to the ācārya second Buddha.

d.div: [196] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 85_bod du gsung rab dam chos dag ther bton pa/ shog_501_phreng 5
[352] Biji or Tsenpashilaha.
[353] Orgyan Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 85.501.5.

f.d:
zab la rgya che ba'i tshig don phun sum tshogs par gzigs kyang / gsang rgyud man ngag 'tshol na mi rung bar mkhyen nas rgya cher spel bar mi mdzad cing / rang nyid kyi snying nor du bcangs rjes ma 'ongs pa na chos brgyud thag nye ba/ gdams pa lhad mi zhugs pa sogs dgos pa khyad par can la dgongs te gter du sba bar brtsams/ o rgyan sangs rgyas gnyis pa dang bka' bgros pas/ slob dpon chen pos/
'tsho ba'i srog skyob bla na med pa tshig nyung don rgyas kyi rgyud yid bzhin nor bu 'di da lta spel pa'i dus la ma bab/ 'dod lha'i zhag gsum gyi ring gter du sba bas legs par srungs shigces chos srung zhang blon rdo rje bdud 'dul la yang bskyar dang gter bdag yon tan gyi rgyal po shing bya can las byed shan pa hab se myur mgyogs ce spyang mdog dmar gsum la gtad/

Although the king saw that this work was vast as well as profound and that the meanings within were second to none, he understood that it would not be proper for the teachings of such a secret tantra to become corrupt. Therefore he did not disseminate it widely and kept it as the jewel of his own heart. Later, he decided to hide it as a treasure, because this would make the lineage shorter in the future, reducing the likelihood of the work becoming defiled, and so on. He approached the ācārya, who replied:
This supreme protector of life, this tantra of few words but vast meaning, this wish-fulfilling jewel: now is not the time for its dissemination. Protect it well by hiding it as a treasure for the duration of three days in the world of the desire gods.[354] Thus the tantra was again entrusted to Vajra Mārajit, to the treasure guardian Yönten Gyalpo Shingja Chen, to the butcher-like Hapsé,[355] and to the red jackal-faced protector.

d.div: [354] Untraced.
[355] Referred to in the homage as Apsé.

f.d: rje mnga' bdag gis ma 'ongs pa na las dang skal bar ldan pas gter nas phyungs te 'gro phan dpag med spyod par shog cig gi smon lam btab nas bsam yas dbu rtse bar khang gi ka ba'i nang du sbas ba gter ma'i lugs dang / bka' ma ltar na kha cig 'di yan dang rgyud lugs mi 'dra tsam yod kyang don la khyad par med par sems shing / de nas chos rgyal yab sras kyi bai ro la zhus par chig brgyud kyi slob dpon la phul grub tshul nas slob dpon la gsan par grags kyang gnya' rigs kyi yig rnying khungs mar rgyud gter du sbas pa'i rjes su sras mu ni btsan po'i dgongs pa la/ yab kyi gso dpyad thugs gtsigs che ba ni slob dpon gyis gnang nges par dgongs nas slob dpon la zhus pas/ slob dpon gyis khri srong lde btsan la ngas phul pa min/ 'on kyang rgyal bu khyod la sems can dang bstan pa la phan pa'i phyir bshad do gsungs nas rang 'gyur mdzad/ slar yab dang bai ro la yang bka' ma phar phul zhing gter ma tshur zhus par bzhed/ deng sang brgyud pa'i dus bai ro'i kyang sngon du slob dpon bzhugs pa'ang lo rgyus 'di'i bka' ma'i dbang du song ba'am yang na gter sogs dgos pa khyad par can gyi dgongs pa yin/

The king prayed that in the future it would be unearthed by someone of great merit and would be of benefit to countless beings. The tantra was then hidden high in a pillar in the middle floor of Samyé Monastery. This is according to the Treasure tradition. In the Transmission tradition, some assert different versions of events up to this point, and there are different traditions of the tantra, but I do not think they make any material difference. After this point it is generally accepted that the tantra was transmitted from the ācārya to whom it had been offered by the king and his son, who in turn had received it as a one-to-one transmission from Vairocana. However, in an old document from the Nya family line, it says that after the tantra was hidden as a treasure, the king’s son Muné Tsenpo was certain that his father’s beloved medical text had been offered to the king by the ācārya. He therefore approached the ācārya and requested it. “I did not offer the tantra to Trisong Detsen,” he replied. “However, for the sake of the doctrine and living beings, I will teach it to the prince.” Thus the ācārya made his own translation. The prince then offered this tantra to the father and Vairocana as transmission while receiving it from them as treasure. These days in the lineage of the tantra, the ācārya even precedes Vairocana. This is done either on the basis of it belonging to the Transmission tradition as recounted in this story or for special reasons, such as it being classified as a Treasure.
[rgyal po'i bla sman dgu ]

d.i: The nine royal physicians from surrounding countries

f.d: gzhan yang chos kyi rgyal po khri srong lde'u btsan gyi thugs dgongs la/ sngar yab mes rnams dang phyis bdag nyid kyis kyang gso ba rig pa'i bka' srol legs par btod pas dar rgyas su byung mod kyi/ da rang phyogs phyogs kyi sman pa mkhas pa du ma bsags/ sngon chad ma bsgyur ba'i rigs mtha' dag dar bar bya'o dgongs te

King Trisong Detsen thought to himself, “In the past my ancestors—and now I, too—have been instrumental in founding and establishing the science of medicine in Tibet. Now is the time to bring together scholar doctors from other lands and to propagate all those works that are yet to be translated.”

gser la sogs pa'i bya dga' mang du stsal/ pho nya ba yul so sor bka' yis mngags pa las/ 'phags yul nas shan+ti gar+b+ha/ kha che nas gu h+ya badz+ra/ rgya nag nas stong gsum gang ba dang ha shang ba la/ hang ta pi ta gsum/ stag gzigs nas ha la shan+ti/ gru gu nas seng mdo 'od chen/ dol po nas khyol ma ru tsi/ bal bo nas d+harma shi la ste mtha' bzhi nas byon pa'i rgyal po'i bla sman dgur grags pa gdan drangs/ zur mkhar pas mes ag tshogs kyi dus tsam pa shi la ha sogs la bshad kyang 'di skabs sman pa rnams nyams sad ched rgyal pos snyun rdzu btab/ pho brang 'phang thang ka med kyi nang du bzhugs/ sman pa rnams sgo phyir bzhag ste khyed cag gso ba rig pa la mkhas shing grags pa dang ldan pa yin pas rtsa lag pa dngos la blta ba ngo mtshar mi che yi/ tha gu 'di la rtogs las kha smar thogs shig gsungs/ byi bla'i lag par tha gu btags nas brtag tu bcug pas rgyal po 'grongs sam bdag cag nyams pa ji ltar na'ang phyi dal khong 'khyug pa gcan gzan tha ma byi bla'i rtsa 'dra ba zhig snang zhes dang / de pho'i lag par tha gu btags pa bstan pas kha 'dar la gting sbun pa 'dab chags tha ma khyim bya'i rtsa tsam las mi 'dug ces dang / de rjes rang 'thag la btags nas bstan pas kha bying la gting sra ba gor ma rdo dang 'dra ba sogs sman gyi lha mo'i mngon shes la brten nas so sor ma nor bar ngos zin pas rgyal po rab tu dgyes te/

With gifts of gold, and so on, he sent messengers to different countries and invited Śāntigarbha from India; Guhyavajra from Kashmir; Tongsum Gangwa, Hvashang Bala, and Hangti Pata from China; Halaśānti from Taksik; Sengdo Öchen from Drugu;[356] Khyölma Rutsi from Dölpo; and Dharmaśīla from Nepal. These became known as the nine royal physicians from surrounding countries. It was at this time that the king feigned illness in order to test these doctors, although Surkhar relates this as happening to Tsenpashilaha and others during the reign of King Mé Aktsom. The king remained inside Pangthang Kamé palace while the doctors stood outside the door. “You are wise and renowned in the science of healing,” said the king, “Therefore, coming to a diagnosis from examining my wrist pulse in person would be nothing special. Examine this cord and make a diagnosis from it.” So saying, the king tied a thin cord to the leg of a cat and passed it through a small hole in the door for the doctors to examine. On examination the doctors replied, “Either the king is dying or we have failed in our diagnosis. Outside the pulse is slow, but inside it beats fast. It seems that the king has the pulse of that lowest of animals, the cat.” Then the king tied the cord to the leg of a chicken and gave it to the doctors to examine. “On the surface the pulse is active, but deep inside it has no essence. It appears to be none other than the pulse of that lowest of birds, the chicken,” replied the doctors. Then the king tied the cord to himself. On examination the doctors remarked, “On the surface the pulse is sunken, but inside it is firm and solid like a rock,” and so on. Therefore, by relying on the clairvoyance of the medicine goddesses, the foreign doctors had correctly recognized each pulse. The king was pleased and

d.div: [356] Gru gu or Dru gu. Identified as present-day Yugu in northwest Tibet, “north of Ngari and south of Khoten” (Great Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, p. 1332).

f.d: 'tsho mdzad sman par gyur pa 'di rnams la/ / bod 'bangs mgo nag yongs kyis bkur bar gyis/ / ci phyir 'di ni tshe srog ster ba'i phyir/ / mgo nag yongs kyi lha ni btsan po ste/ / de yis bkur bas mtshan yang lha rjer thogs/ / 'gro ba'i mgon yin gral gyi gong la bzhog / 'bol grum stag gzig za 'og gdan du 'thing / / skyel bsu rtas gyis rkang gla gser du phul/ / ci gsungs dang long sman pa'i bka' ma bcag / rgyal srid yin yang mi phangs srog rin yin/ / bcos nor lag dgras shi yang stong ma len/ / sman du thal ba sbyar kyang sman rin gser du rdzongs/ / zhal du skyems zhus sha gzug rgyun du drongs/ / rgyun du bsten phyir ngo kha lkog smras spongs/ / nam ber dar zab lham dang rgyam thag phul/ / kun gyis 'khur las phyag dang zhe sa gyis/ / tshe 'dir drin che drin lan yun du soms/ / nga yis phul ba'i bla gtsigs bcu gsum po/ / gang gis 'gal yang chad pas bcad par bya/ / zhes sogs bka' gtsigs gnang /

bestowed the following honors on them:
People of Tibet! Revere these great doctors, bringers of health, Why? Because they grant the gift of life. The god of men, the ruler, he reveres them,[357] therefore, they are to be known as divine physicians. They are the guardians of living beings; place them on the highest seat with cushions of the highest-quality Taksik brocade. Welcome them with horses; if on foot, offer them gold. Follow willingly whatever they say or do; do not disregard the physician’s word. Though it may cost a royal kingdom, have no sense of loss—it is the price of life. Even though mistaken treatment or surgery may result in death, do not ask for blood money. If they prescribe dust as medicine, nevertheless send gold in payment. Offer them drinks, bring them meat. Because you must rely upon them always, leave behind any two-faced, deceitful words. Offer them cloaks, brocade, and boots, complete sets of clothing. Hold them in high regard, bow, and be courteous. They show us great kindness in this life; think long on how to repay them. These thirteen honors I bestow upon them. Those who disrespect them will be punished.

d.div: [357] In some versions “he” is replace by “I.”

f.d: pho brang du sne len dang zhabs tog gya nom pa bshams/ slob dpon pad+mas dpang po dang ska cog gnyis sogs rang rang gi skad la byang ba'i lo tsA ba dang bcas sman dpyad kyi gzhung lugs bsgyur cig par bka' gnang bas/

Inside the palace the best hospitality and service was arranged. With Ācārya Padma supervising and with translators, such as Ka Lotsāwa and Chok Lotsāwa, trained in their different languages, the king asked them to translate the medical texts.

rgya gar shan+ti gar+b+has sangs rgyas kyis gsungs par grags pa'i bal sgrom smug po'i rgyud dang / sh+loka sde bzhi/ bdud rtsi lhung bzed che chung / bdud rtsi bum snying spyan ras gzigs kyi gsung du 'bod pa spungs pa sde lnga/ klu sgrub kyi gsung du grags pa mdo lnga/ sgrol mas gsungs par grags pa sngo 'bum le'u brgya nyi shu pa/

The Indian doctor Śāntigarbha compiled and translated Tantra of the Brown Casket, Four Collections of Verses, great and lesser Begging Bowl of Ambrosia, and Essence of Vase of Ambrosia, all reputedly the word of the Buddha; Five Collections, reputedly the teachings of Avalokiteśvara; Five Treatises, reputedly composed by Nāgārjuna; and One Hundred Thousand Medicinal Plants in 120 Chapters, reputedly composed by Tārā.

rgya nag gi sman pa gsum pos 'jam dpal gyis gsungs par grags pa sbyor ba'i 'phreng ba/ byang khog don 'grems 'phrul gyi rgya long / yan lag phyag gi brda las byung ba rin po che'i mdzod lnga/ ja lag nor bu dri ma med pa/ me chu go bzlog / dug dpyad me lce 'khor lo/ thor bu'i nad kyi sgos bcos/ chu dpyad/ khyug dpyad/ me btsa'i lag len sgron me/

The three Chinese doctors translated Garland of Medicinal Compounds, Magic Mirror Exposition on Anatomy, Treatment of the Limbs: Five Jewel Treasuries from Arising from Gestures of the Hand, Untainted Jewel Remedial Treatment, Fire and Water Reversal, Wheel of Fire Treatment for Poisons, Specific Treatments for Miscellaneous Ailments, Urine Analysis, Magical Treatments,[358] and Beacon of Cauterization Practice, all attributed to Mañjuśrī.

d.div: [358] Text here and elsewhere has ’khug or khyug. Amended to mkhyud on the advice of Prof. Losang Tenzin.

f.d: kha che'i sman pas dpyad phreng sel bar byed pa mun pa'i sgron me/ dpyad mdo dgu pa/ man ngag gnad kyi pra yig /
The Kashmir doctor compiled and translated Beacon Dispelling the Darkness of the Difficulties of Medical Practice, Nine Works on Medicine, and Essential Prognostic Manuscript on Instruction.

stag gzig gi sman pas mgo bcos mu stegs kyi skor brgyad pa rtsa 'grel/ rtsa bcos man ngag ljon shing che chung / 'dus pa bcos thabs rin chen srog gi 'khor lo/ sog po sha stag can gyi rgyud/ dug gso ba gar log rgyal po'i shi gsos/

The Taksik doctor compiled and translated Eight Outsider Root and Commentary Collections on Treatments for the Head, Greater and Lesser Tree of Instructions on Channel Treatment, Precious Wheel of Life Treatment for Humor Combination Disorders, Sogdian Tantra, and Saving the Life of the King of Garlok: Treatment for Poisoning.
gru gu'i sman pas nag po rgyud gsum/ de'i mdo byang che chung / 'dra yig dung gi mig /nags su 'jag pa g.yu yi dra ba/ gu Na sha ta bam po lnga brgya pa/ rta'i dpyad me long skor gsum/

The Drugu doctor compiled and translated Three Black Tantras, Greater and Lesser Annotations on the Three Black Tantras, Eye of the Conch Illustrations, Turquoise Network: Entering the Forest of Medical Plants, Guṇaśata in Five Hundred Chapters, and Mirror of Equine Medicine in Three Collections.
dol po'i sman pas mi 'jigs pa brgyad kyi mtshon cha/ gab gsal byed/ 'tsho 'chi rtags kyi le'u/ rtsa'i la nye/ gtar kha'i dpyad/
The Dölpo doctor compiled and translated Weapons of the Eight Kinds of Fearlessness, Clarifying the Hidden, Chapter on Signs of Life and Death, Pulse Signs, and Bloodletting Therapy.
bal po'i sman pas 'gram pa ti/ sbyor ba brgya pa/ rin po che'i sman gyi 'khrungs dpe/ thur dpyad dang lhog pa'i gso thabs rnams brtsams shing bsgyur/
The Nepalese doctor translated Drampati, Yogaśataka, Illustrations of Precious Medicines, Minor Surgery, and Treatment of Lhokpa.

gzhan yang klu sgrub kyi mdzad par grags pa sman dpyad rin po che 'dus pa bam po bdun/ ke tu pradz+nyAs byas pa'i mgo dpyad bdud rtsi thigs pa skabs bdun pa/ be du ras byas pa'i gzhung bdud rtsi me long le'u brgyad/ klu sgrub kyis mdzad zer ba sgron ma lnga skor/ 'jam dpal gyi sprul pa ne tsos mdzad pa dug dpyad me lce 'khor lo/ drang srong nyi ma'i seng ges byas pa'i dug dpyad sha mo las dkyus/ rin po che ska rags 'ching 'grol/ zla gsang 'khor lo mtshon cha las kyi rgyud le'u bcu pa/ de 'grel sha mo las dkyus cha lag dang bcas pa rnams gnubs sangs rgyas ye shes kyi 'gyur/ gnubs rang gi mdzad byang smos pa/ bsrung ba rin po che 'od kyi gdams pa/ brtag pa rin po che 'od kyi gzugs brnyan/ gso ba dkar po lam gyi sgron ma dang gsum/

Furthermore, Nup Sangyé Yeshé translated Precious Compilation on Medicine and Treatment in Seven Fasicles, reputedly composed by Nāgārjuna; Ambrosia Drop Treatments of the Head in Seven Chapters, by Ketu Prajñā; Ambrosia Mirror in Eight Chapters by Vedura;[359] Five Beacon Collection, said to have been composed by Nāgārjuna; Fire Wheel Treatments for Poison, by Śuka, a manifestation of Mañjuśrī; Fungi Treatment for Poisons, by Rishi Sūryasiṃha; Precious Belt of Liberation; Candraguhya Weapon Wheel Activity Tantra; its commentary Greater Fungi Treatment; and various supplements. Works authored by Nup Sangyé Yeshé himself include Precious Protection: The Light of Instruction, Precious Examination: Light Reflection, and Traveling Lamp of Good Remedies.

d.div: [359] Be du ra; also found as Verura. Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo has Vaidūrya.

f.d: klu sgrub kyis mdzad zer ba'i dug bcos dpa' bo thub pa'i rgyud dang gzha' 'od 'khyug pa'i rgyud shrI badz+ra dang chos kyi dbang phyug gi 'gyur/
Śrīvajra and Chökyi Wangchuk translated Viramuni Tantra on Treatment for Poisons, said to have been composed by Nāgārjuna, as well as Rainbow Light Flash Tantra.
phyag na rdo rje dang klu sgrub zhus lan du mdzad pa'i gza' rgyud rin chen spungs pa le'u bzhi bcu rtsa drug paN+Di ta rin chen rdo rje dang bai ro'i 'gyur/
Pandit Ratnavajra and Vairocana translated Jewel Heap Planet Tantra, in forty-six chapters, composed as a dialogue between Vajrapāṇi and Nāgārjuna.

gza' bcos snying tig gsal sgron rgya nag ma/ klu sgrub dang klu rgyal 'jog po gnyis kyi zhus lan che ba le'u sum cu so bzhi/ 'bring po me long rab gsal/ chung ba mngon par rtogs pa/ don gsal sgron ma/ gsal byed sgron ma/ 'phrul gyi me long / thugs kyi sgron ma/ ro langs mkha' 'gro mas gsungs par grags pa mdze rtags mig yig / bcu drug pa drang srong me khyer gyi 'gyur/

The Chinese text Bright Beacon Quintessential Treatment for Planetary Disorder; Extensive Question and Answer in Thirty-Four Chapters between Nāgārjuna and the nāga king Takṣaka; the intermediate Clear Mirror; the lesser Clear Insight; Beacon Illuminating the Meaning; Illuminating Beacon; Magic Mirror; Beacon of the Heart; and the sixteen-part Signs of Leprosy Manuscript, reputedly spoken by Vetālaḍākinī, were all translated by Rishi Khadyota.

'jam dbyangs kyi gsung du 'dod pa rin po che sgron ma'i mdzod/ sgrol mas mdzad zer ba mkhris rims dug thabs zhi byed dang / sngo'i 'khrungs dpe rin chen sgrol ma le'u gsum pa shan+ti gar+b+ha'i 'gyur/

Precious Beacon Treasury, reputedly the speech of Mañjuśrī; Pacification of Infectious Bile and Poisoning, reputedly the words of Tārā, and Precious Beacon of Materia Medica in three chapters were all translated by Sāntigarbha.

'phags pa 'jam dpal dang drang srong bzhis zhus lan du mdzad pa sngo sbyor bdud rtsi 'chi med gsang ba sku gsung thugs kyi rgyud/ de'i 'grel pa dpal mgon klus mdzad par grags pa/ ha shang ma hA kyin das byas pa'i sngo sbyor le'u bcu gnyis pa be bum smug por 'bod pa/ de 'grel gsang ba'i yang tig /drang srong tsa ra kas mdzad pa tshe'i rig byed kyi rgyud rin po che khri mdzod 'od ldan/ de las bsdus pa le'u bdun cu pa/ bcud len sha sbyor rtsa ba'i rgyud bdud rtsi ljon shing le'u bdun pa spyan ras gzigs kyi sgrol mar gnang ba'i mkhris rims dug thabs gso ba la sogs ji snyed 'gyur/

Other works they translated include Secret Body, Speech, and Mind Tantra of Ambrosia Preparation of Medicinal Plants, written as a question-and-answer session between Ārya Mañjuśrī and four rishis; its commentary reputedly composed by the glorious Nāgārjuna; a twelve-chapter text on medical plant preparation known as Brown Compilation by Hvashang Mahākyinda; its commentary Secret Quintessence; Caraka’s Āyurveda Tantra: An Illuminated Treasury of Ten Thousand Jewels; a work compiled from that tantra known as Seventy Chapters; Ambrosia Tree: The Root Tantra on Meat Elixir Preparation in seven chapters; Treating Infectious Bile and Poisons, taught by Avalokiteśvara to Tārā.

rje'i thugs la bab cing 'bangs la phan thogs par byung bas/ btsad po'i zhal nas/
sman pa pha yin nad pa snying rjes skyong / / nad pa bu yin ngan mtshang phyir ma brjod/ / ces sogs bka' stsal zhing gtsigs che bar gnang /

The king was satisfied with these works and saw the benefits they were bringing to the people. He bestowed great honors upon the doctors and delivered a proclamation beginning:
The doctor is the father, caring for the patient with compassion. The patient is the child, never replying with a bad word.

de lta bu'i gso rig gi gzhung lugs chen po rnams phyogs gcig tu seng ldeng gi glegs shing du bzhugs pa la rgyal po'i bla dpyad po ti smug por grags/ bod 'bangs kyi byis pa blo rno ba dgu la gso ba rig pa bslab tu bcug pas stod na cher rje zhig po/ 'ug pa chos bzang / ba che legs mgon gsum/ bar na g.yu thog mgon po/ mi nyag rong rje/ brang ti rgyal bzang gsum/ smad na gnya' pa chos bzang / mtha' bzhi dar po/ stong pa grags rgyal te bod sman mkhas pa mi dgur grags pa byung / phyogs kyi sman pa rnams rnyed bkur gyi mchod pa bzang po dang bcas so so'i yul du bzhud/ de las ha cang mi ring ba na rgyal po snyun gyis btab par bod kyi sman pa mi dgu sogs yod kyang blon po rnams kyi 'dod pa ltar mtha' bzhi ga'i sman pa rnams spyan 'dren par btang bas/ gzhan rnams 'byon par ma bzhed cing / rgya nag gi sman pa stong gsum gang ba zhes bya ba spyir rig gnas mtha' dag dang / khyad par gso ba rig pa la mkhas shing / rje btsun 'jam dpal dbyangs kyi zhal gzigs pa zhig yod pa byon/ bshul lam gso ba dkar po lam gyi sgron mar grags dang / mtha' bzhi'i lugs zhu ba bzhi ldan sogs bstan bcos brtsams te skyes su phul/ gso ba'i dpyad byas pas mnga' bdag snyun las myur du dwangs/ mtha' bzhi ga'i sman pa'i go chod par 'dug pas ming yang mtha' bzhi stong gsum gang bar btags/ bya dga' la gzhung dang dol gnyis yul gzhis su stsal/ khab bzhes srid bskyangs pas mtha' bzhi'i rgyud pa rnams 'phel/ de ltar na chos kyi rgyal po khri srong lde'u btsan gyi bla sman gnang ba rigs kyi 'tsho byed dngos ni mtha' bzhi dang / bod sman gzhan brgyad po rjes 'brel tsam yin par mngon/ rgyal po glang dar mas bstan pa'i dngos gzhi so thar gyi 'dul khrims bshig pas snga dar phyi dar gyi tha snyad byung ba las/ gso dpyad ni srong btsan nas da lta'i bar rgyun nyams ma myong bas dar lugs kyi sgo nas snga dar dang / phyi dar zhes 'dogs mi dgos par sems/

These great medical texts from the various traditions were bound together between acacia-wood covers and became known as the King’s Brown Medical Volumes. Nine bright Tibetan children were chosen and encouraged to study medicine. They were: Chejé Shikpo, Ukpa Chösang, and Baché Lekgön[360] from the upper regions; Yuthok Gönpo, Minyak Rongjé, and Drangti Gyalsang from the middle regions; Nyawa Chösang, Thazhi Darpo, and Tongpa Drakgyal from the lower regions. They became known as the nine wise Tibetan physicians. The foreign physicians were laden with offerings given with great respect and returned to their countries. Not long after, the king became ill. Although the nine Tibetan doctors were available, in accord with the wishes of the ministers, invitations were sent out to the nine foreign doctors. Only the Chinese doctor Tongsum Gangwa accepted the invitation. He was learned in all sciences but was especially skilled in medicine and had received a vision of the venerable Mañjuśrī. On the way he composed a treatise known as Traveling Lamp of Good Medicine and one called Four Refined Ingredients Compound from the Tradition of the Surrounding Countries, among others, which he offered to the king as a visiting gift. With his treatment the king quickly recovered. Because he was said to encapsulate the doctors from all the borderlands, he was called Tongsum Gangwa of the Borderlands. As a reward he was granted land in Shung and Döl.[361] There he took a wife and became a local ruler, thereby establishing the borderlands tradition. Therefore, it seems that the doctors from the borderlands were the actual royal physicians appointed by King Trisong Detsen and the other eight Tibetan doctors[362] were merely followers. The destruction by King Langdarma of the pratimokṣa Vinaya code—the very foundation of the doctrine—divides the early and later disseminations of the Buddhist doctrine. However, there has been no such break in the lineage of the medical tradition from the time of Songtsen Gampo up to the present day. Therefore, in terms of its development, I do not think there is any need to talk of early and later disseminations.

d.div: [360] Ba che; variously spelled bir che, be che, and bi byi. The last is also the name of Tsenpashilaha mentioned earlier and also of a doctor who came to Tibet from India during the reign of Thothori Nyentsen. See introduction, p. 4.
[361] In Gongkar region west of Lhasa.
[362] Of the nine previously mentioned Tibetan doctors, it would seem that Yuthok Gönpo is not included here.

f.d: snga rabs pa kha cig ltar na/ brtan pa blo gros kyis mdzad pa dri med gzi brjid la sogs pa kha che'i lugs/ dzi na mi tras mdzad pa'i gso stong dgu bcu rtsa dgu la sogs pa a+yon gyi lugs/ shrI a nan+das mdzad pa'i gnas 'gyur gsum la sogs pa yul dbus kyi lugs/ su ma ti kirtis mdzad pa'i bsdus sbyor gsum la sogs pa bal pi lugs/ urba yas mdzad pa'i chos 'byung drug la sogs pa ta zig gi lugs/ rdo rje 'bar bas mdzad pa'i mi 'jigs mtshon cha la sogs pa dol po'i lugs/ legs pa rgyal mtshan gyis mdzad pa'i ga gon gyi brdol thabs sum cu rtsa lnga la sogs pa hor gyi lugs/ brtson 'grus snying pos mdzad pa'i su khugs la sogs pa mi nyag gi lugs/ rgyal ba rdo rjes mdzad pa'i yan lag bdun pa sogs li'i lugs/ tsan pa shi la has mdzad pa tshad pa 'bros 'ded la sogs pa khrom gyi lugs dang bcu'i yig cha dang phyag len man ngag rnams bod du rim gyis dar ba'i don thams cad phyi shes bya gzhung gi skor/ nang gdams pa don gyi skor/ gsang ba lag len smar khrid skor/ yang gsang nyams myong thabs kyi skor dang bzhir 'dus par bshad/

Earlier commentators talk of ten traditions: the Kashmir tradition with works such as Stainless Radiance by Sthiramati; the Oḍḍiyāna tradition with works such as One Thousand and Ninety-Nine Treatments[363] by Jinamitra; the central Indian tradition with works such as Three Translocations by Śrī Ānanda;[364] the Nepalese tradition with works such as Three Preparations Compilation by Sumatikīrti; the Taksik tradition with works such as Six Accounts by Urbaya;[365] the Dölpo tradition with works such as Weapons of Fearlessness by Vajrajvāla; the Hor tradition with works such as Thirty-Five Methods of Bursting from Gagön[366] by Lekpa Gyaltsen; the Minyak tradition with works such as Sukhuk by Tsöndrü Nyingpo; the Khotanese tradition with works such as Seven Branches by Gyalwa Dorjé; and the Trom tradition with works such as Chasing Fever by Tsenpashilaha. It is said that the texts, practices, and oral transmissions of these ten traditions gradually spread to Tibet, where their topics were compiled externally as texts of medical knowledge, internally as a collection of practical instructions, secretly as a direct-instruction collection for practice, and even more secretly as a collection of methods for direct experience.

d.div: [363] Previously listed as One Thousand and Ninety-One Treatments.
[364] Previously listed as being by the Nepalese master Anara.
[365] Also Urpaya. See Martin, p. 14.
[366] According to Martin (p. 12), could refer to an Uighur place name.

f.d: lha bla ma ye shes 'od kyi sku ring la paN+Di ta d+harma shrI warma dang / snye bo lo tsA ba dbyig gi rin chen/ mar lo rig pa gzhon nu/ dbyig gu dge slong shAkya blo gros rnams kyis yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa'i rang 'grel bsgyur/

During the time of Lha Lama Yeshé Ö,[367] the autocommentary to Essence of Eight Branches[368] was translated by Paṇḍita Dharmaśrī Varmā, Nyewo Lotsāwa Yikgi Rinchen, Mar Lotsāwa Rikpa Shönu, and Yikgu Gelong Shākya Lodrö.

d.div: [367] Ordained Ngari king of the tenth century responsible for inviting Atiśa to Tibet.
[368] Aṣṭaṅgahṛdayanāmavaidūryakabhāṣya; Vāgbhaṭa’s own commentary to Essence of Eight Branches.

f.d: [lo chen rin chen bzang po ]

d.i: The contribution of Lotsāwa Rinchen Sangpo

f.d: de rjes gu ge'i cha snyung waM rat+na ru sku 'khrungs pa/ sprul pa'i skyes mchog lo chen rin chen bzang po zhes bya ba/ dgung lo bcu bdun nas 'phags yul du lo bcu bzhugs/ jo bo nA ro ta ba sogs paN+Di ta bdun cu rtsa lnga bsten/ sangs rgyas skar rgyal btul ba sogs phyi dar la 'gran pa'i zla thams cad dang bral ba des/ kha che'i paN+Di ta dza na r+d+ha la gser srang brgya phul nas slob dpon dpa' bos mdzad pa'i yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa le'u brgya nyi shu'i bdag nyid can dang / de'i tshig don rgyas par 'grel ba zla ba'i 'od zer zhes bya ba kha che zla ba la mngon par dga' bas mdzad pa sogs legs par bsgyur cing gtan la phab pa'i bod yul du dar rgyas su gyur zhing /

Later the great emanation and great translator Rinchen Sangpo (958–1055) was born in a part of Gugé called Chanyung Vaṃ Ratna. From the age of seventeen he spent ten years in India, where he devoted himself to seventy-five pandits, including the great Nāropa.[369] In the later dissemination of the doctrine he was unmatched, as illustrated by his taming of Sangyé Kargyal.[370] He offered a hundred measures of gold to the Kashmir pandit Janarbha[371] and translated and established among others the Essence of Eight Branches in 120 chapters by Ācārya Śūra[372] and its extensive word commentary known as Moonlight written by the Kashmiri Candranandana. These became widespread in Tibet.

d.div: [369] Written as Nārotava.
[370] Also known as Lu Kargyal, a Tibetan shepherd possessed by a demon who, aided by various magical powers, preached a heretical doctrine in Tibet.
[371] As written.
[372] As mentioned before, nowhere does the author refer to the composer of this text with a name that translates as Vāgbhaṭa.

f.d: dpal phag mo gru ba'i dus tsi na'i rgyal khab tu'ang dar bas rgyal po hwang tha'i hu'i i tsi'i dus yar klungs mchig sman gyi bskul nas pho brang ta'i tung du ye shes dpal gyis zhus dag ste brkos pa'i rgya par yang yod/ lo chen de nyid la gso rig gi brgyud pa 'dzin pa'i slob ma mang du yod mod de/ grags che ba ni/ myang 'das seng ge sgra/ sha ka khri ye shes 'byung gnas/ ong sman a ne/ mang po sman btsun te spu rangs kyi sman pa mi bzhir 'bod pa yin la/ de'i nang nas kyang mang mo sman btsun mkhas shing 'phrin las che bas dbus gtsang gi sman pa phal cher gyis mjal/ lhag par che rje ti pang la gzhung zla zer dang bcas rdzogs par gnang / ti pang gis rang sras byang chub 'od/ u lang bkra shis mkhar/ dgra las rgyal po gsum la bshad/ u lang gi gzhung 'grel lag len kun la mkhas pas 'tsho byed gzhon nu'i sprul pa yin par yang bshad/ des gcen gyi sras dbon jo bkra/ g.yung drung / jo btsan/ rang sras zla ba dang / snying po/ gcung sras 'bro tsha dang drug la gsungs/ de dag gis rtag rtog rgyal/ jo 'phan/ jo nag gsum la bshad/ de'i snga ma grags pa che/ bar ba lung rgyus la 'dris/ tha ma gzhung gdams ngag lag len 'dzom/

During the time of the glorious Phakmo Drupa (1302–64), these works became widespread in China also, and during the reign of Huangti Huichi,[373] at the request of Yarlung Chikmen, these texts were edited and revised by Yeshé Pal (1350–1405) in the Taitung palace in China, and a Chinese woodblock edition was produced. The great Rinchen Sangpo had many disciples who held medical lineages, but the most famous were Nyangdé Sengé Dra, Shaka Tri Yeshé Jungné, Ongmen Ané, and Mangmo Mentsün. These were known as the four doctors from Purang. Among them Mangmo Mentsün was very learned and very prolific in his activities, and most doctors from the central region of Tibet came to see him. In particular, he taught in its entirety Essence of Eight Branches and Moonlight to Chejé Tipang, who in turn taught them to his sons Jangchup Ö, Ulang Tashi Khar, and Dralé Gyalpo. Ulang was learned in the scriptures, commentaries, and practices and was said to be a manifestation of Kumāra Jivaka. He taught the medical texts to his eldest brother’s sons Jotra, Yungdrung, and Jotsen, to his own sons Dawa and Nyingpo, and to his youngest brother’s son Drotsa. They passed it on to Taktok Gyal, Jophen, and Jonak. Of these three, the first became the most famous, the second was the most familiar with the teachings, and the third was renowned for combining the scripture[374] and instruction into practice.

d.div: [373] Possibly Huitsung (1333–70), last of the Yuan emperors.
[374] In this section “scripture” refers mainly to Eight Branches.

f.d: de gsum ga la snga rabs sman bla lta bu bcur grags pa'i nang tshan che rje zhang ston zhig po'am thugs rje khri 'od kyis zhus te sman dpyad mthar phyin par gyur/ shes bya spyi'i khog 'bugs rgyal mtshan rtser 'bar/ sa bcad don 'khrigs 'byed pa'i lde mig /dka' tshoms gegs sel gnam lcags 'khor lo/ tshig don zhib rgyas su 'grel ba mu tig gi 'phreng ba rgyas bsdus gnyis/ skyid smad khol ma'i zhang ston 'dul ba sogs kyi don du lag len smar khrid rgan mo mdzub tshugs kyi tshul du 'chad pa bdud rtsi thigs pa rnams brtsams/ gzhung la nag mchan legs par btab/

These three doctors were requested for teachings by Chejé Shangtön Shikpo, or Thukjé Triö, who was one of the ten doctors “likened to royal physicians of early times.” He mastered the science of medicine and composed Compendium of Knowledge Blazing from the Top of a Victory Banner, Outline: A Key to Open the Content, Meteor Destruction of the Hindrance of Difficulties and Doubts, The Pearl Garland: A Detailed and Extensive Word Commentary in its abridged and full versions. For Shangtön Dülwa from Kyimé Khölma and others, he composed the Drop of Ambrosia Direct Instruction on Practice in the Manner of an Old Woman Pointing Her Finger. He also supplied excellent annotations to texts.

slob ma bde ba dpal/ yon tan rgya mtsho/ gtsang ston dar ma mgon po la sogs pa du ma byung / dar ma mgon pos slob ma'i don du zin tig dang / bu'i don du yang tig ces pa'i man ngag gi yid 'jog kyang mdzad/ de dag gi brgyud 'dzin bo dong rog tsho'i skor na mang bar grags/ jo bo rje lha gcig dI paM ka ra dang nag tsho lo tsA ba gnyis kyis sha sbyor bdud rtsi dar ya kan bsgyur zhing / mgo dpyad dra ba sdom pa sogs man ngag kha 'thor mang du mdzad/

His many disciples included Dewa Pal, Yönten Gyatso, and the Tsang teacher Darma Gönpo. The last of these wrote down the oral transmissions: one for his disciples called Essentials and one for his son called Quintessentials. It is said that there many propagators of their lineages in the region of Bodong Roktso. The master and sole protector Atiśa Dīpaṃkara and Naktso Lotsāwa translated Daryakan Ambrosia Meat Preparations and compiled various medical instruction texts such as Net of Treatments for the Head.

yang 'jig rten gyi mig gcig lo chen rin chen bzang po'i slob ma zhang zhung pa shes rab 'od kyis rgya ston pa grags pa shes rab la gsungs/ shes rab 'od kyi mtshan gyi rnam grangs sam 'khor lo rgyal por grags pas mdzad pa bshad rgyud dang mthun pa'i gso dpyad yig rnying zhig dang sangs rgyas khog 'bugs gser gyi bang mdzod ces pa sogs mchis/ des g.yu thog rgya gar rdo rjer bshad de sa bcad yi ger bkod/ dka' 'phrang dpe'u chung du byas/ don mag stong thun du bsdebs/ 'khrugs 'byed dang lag len rnams yig chung du byas te rtogs sla bar bcos/ de nas g.yu thog brjid po/ khyud po/ mgon po sogs la rim par brgyud pa dang / yang zhang zhung pa shes rab 'od kyis rdog gyong sman/ g.yu thog grags se mgon po la sogs par brgyud pa'ang snang /

Shangshungpa Sherap Ö, a disciple of Rinchen Sangpo, the sole eye of the world, taught the Chinese teacher Drakpa Sherap. There is an old medical manuscript in accord with the Explanatory Tantra of Four Tantras, and a Golden Treasury History of the Buddha composed by someone known as Khorlo Gyalpo, who could be Sherap Ö under another name. He passed the teachings to Yuthok Gyagar Dorjé, who composed an outline, wrote out all difficult points as a small text, made a compilation of the main points, made clarifications, and wrote down the practices, thereby greatly facilitating their understanding. Then the lineages gradually passed to Yuthok Jipo, Yuthok Khyungpo, Yuthok Gönpo, and others. It seems that Shangshung Sherap Ö also passed the lineages on to Dokgyön Men, Yuthok Draksé, Gönpo, and others.
[zhang ston gzi brjid 'bar]

d.i: The contribution of Shangtön Siji Bar and others

f.d: yul yar klungs gad pa steng du yab dge bshes bsod nams dbang phyug dang yum mer bza' 'bum skyid gnyis kyi sras su 'khrungs pa zhang gzi brjid 'bar zhes bya ba des/ gnyags snying po rgyal mtshan la rab tu byung / byams chos lnga la sogs par mkhas par sbyangs/ ldum rar ri bong byung ba la rdo brgyab pas rkang pa chag / rgyogs bskur bas gsos pas ri bong sman par grags/ des brod kha rnyed pa lta bus sman dpyad slob pa'i blo skyes/ ming don mtshungs pa'i slob dpon ma rnyed pas/ mkhas pa mi dgu'i brgyud pa rnams la gtugs te the tshom chod par bya bar dam bcas nas/ thog mar smad kyi sman pa g.yo ru'i g.ya' gyong po/ stod lungs kyi lha rje sum smad/ dbu ru'i mtha' bzhi rnams bsten/ yig sna re re gnyis gnyis tsam zhus gnang las rnam rtog choms pa'i blo kha rdzogs pa ma byung / stod sman la gtugs kyang zhang shes rab che bas gong shor byung dogs gdams pa ma byin/ de'i slob ma 'phan yul rgyal ba dar sman bdud rtsi bya ba der gtugs/

Shang Siji Bar (b. eleventh century) was born on Yarlung Cliffs to father Geshé Sönam Wangchuk and mother Merza Bumkyi. He was ordained by Nyak Nyingpo Gyaltsen and became very learned, especially in the five treatises of Maitreya. Once while he was in a park, he threw a stone at a rabbit and broke its leg. Using the slingshot as a splint, he was able to heal it, and he became known as the rabbit doctor. Like a man discovering a new taste, he developed the desire to study medicine but was unable to find a teacher worthy of the name. Therefore, he studied with those who held the lineages of the nine learned doctors and vowed to find answers to his queries. In the beginning he studied with the lower-region doctor Ya Gyongpo of Yoru, Lhajé Sumen from the upper region of Tölung, and Thazhi from the central region. However, apart from receiving teachings on one or two small texts, he was not completely satisfied and had not resolved his doubts. He approached Tongmen, but because Shangtön was so much cleverer, Tongmen did not give him the teachings for fear of being superseded by him. He also studied with this master’s disciple Gyalwa Darmen Dütsi of Phenyül.

de nas g.yu thog rgya gar rdo rje la yan lag shing chen gyi 'khor lo/ mi nyag zla grags las sngo sbyor chen mo la sogs pa dang / brang ti rgyal po la mgo'i lhag chos la sogs pa gsan kyang sngon ma ltar gyur/ de nas stod kyi bi ji lhun ne+e/ 'ug pa chos seng / che rje stag la dga' gsum la rim bzhin gtugs pas cha lag mang la gdams ngag chung bar mthong nas gser mang du bsgrubs pa bsnams te rgya gar du byon/ lam du rngog blo ldan shes rab dang mjal/ sgra la mkhas par sbyangs/

He studied Limbs: Wheels of the Great Chariot with Gyagar Dorjé, Great Exposition on Medicinal Plant Preparation and so forth with Dawa Drakpa of Minyak, and Special Treatments for the Head with Drangti Gyalpo but still remained unsatisfied. He studied with Biji Lhuné of Tö, Ukpa Chösang, and Chejé Taklaga and realized that they possessed much supplementary material but little real practical instruction. Therefore, he saved up much gold and set off for India. On the way he met Loden Sherap of Ngok,[375] with whom he studied and became proficient in Sanskrit.

d.div: [375] See note 349 above.

f.d: rim gyis bgrod de dpal na len+d+rar phebs/ thams cad la sman pa su mkhas dris par/ drang srong tsan+d+ra bi bya ba mkhas zer bar kha mthun/ der drang srong 'jag ma'i spyil bu na bzhugs pa'i drung du phyin/ sgor zhag bdun gyi bar du bsdad pas khyod de tsam don du ci gnyer gsungs/ sman dpyad shes par 'dod pa'i rgyu mtshan zhus pas/ thugs thogs nas yan lag brgyad pa tshar gcig gnang / log par brtsams pas des mi 'khrol lam gsungs/ slar gser gyi man+Da_la dang bcas zhus pas dpe thog nas gzhung tshar gcig /khog dbugs/ man ngag lag len dang bcas rdzogs par stsal/ yig sna rtsoms la 'gro phan rgya che bar gyis shig gsungs pa ltar/ bod du byon/ slob ma bskyangs/

Finally he arrived at glorious Nālandā.[376] “Who is the most learned doctor?” he asked. All were agreed that the rishi Candravi[377] was the wisest. He approached the rishi, who was living in a grass hut, and sat outside his door for seven days. “What are you doing this for?” asked the rishi. “Because I want to learn medicine,” Shang Siji Bar replied. Thereupon, the rishi gave a single explanation of the eight branches from memory without using a text. As Shang Siji Bar was about to leave, the rishi asked, “Have you understood it all?” Again he beseeched the rishi with a gold mandala, and Candravi gave him a single explanation using a text. He also gave him the history, the instructions, and the practices. The rishi told him to write books on medicine and to be of great help to living beings. With that he returned to Tibet, where he nurtured disciples.

d.div: [376] Written na lendra.
[377] As written. Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo has Candrali.

f.d: gzhung dri med gzi brjid le'u bzhi pa/ de 'grel nyi ma'i 'od zer/ dpe don grangs kyi phreng ba gsum sbug ston rgya dkar rA dza dang bal ston shes rab khri 'bum gyi don du legs par brtsams/ de nas gdams pa sum cu pa dang stod smad kyi 'grel pa gsum rtsom 'phror bzhag pa sbug ston rgya gar gyis mu 'thud par grags/ zhang gi slob ma lha sa'i bal chung la phyi skor nang skor/ 'ol kha'i spang chung la khog snying dang 'dra ba'i dkyus bkod rnam gsum/ gnyal gyi rog chung la gdams pa sum cu pa/ nyer gnas skyogs shes rab khri la dri med gzi brjid ma bu rnams so sor gnang / de bzhi dang stong sman gyi slob ma dar sman lnga la dol pa ring mos zhus/ gdams pa sum cu pa'i zhal shes/ tshad 'phrang bcu gsum/ gdams phran gzhan dag dang / dri med gzi brjid las ma 'grel/ 'bru 'grel stong thun/ tshad pa gal 'gag gi gzer chen sogs brtsams/

For Buktön Gyagar Rāja and the Nepalese teacher Sherap Tribum, he composed Stainless Radiance in four chapters, its commentary Sun Rays, and Rosary of Illustration and Meaning. Thirty Instructions and the two commentaries to its first and later sections were left unfinished and reputedly taken up by Buktön Gyagar Rāja. For his disciple Balchung of Lhasa, Shang composed Outer and Inner Collections. For Trangchung from Ölkha he wrote Three Heart-Like Continuous Writings. For Rokchung from Nyal he wrote Thirty Instructions. For his disciple Sherap Tribum from Kyok he composed Mother and Son Stainless Radiance. Dölpa Ringmo requested teachings from the above four disciples and from Darmen, the disciple of Tongmen, and subsequently composed Essential Transmission of the Thirty Instructions; Thirteen Paths of Fever; other miscellaneous instructions; a handwritten commentary, word commentary, and overview of the main points on Stainless Radiance; Important Rivets for Fever; and many others.

mi nyag mi bskyod rdo rjes khog 'bugs/ mu tig 'phreng ba/ gzhung bshad thabs kyi yan lag /chos 'byung lo rgyus/ stong thun/ dpyad dgu / 'phrang bco lnga/ 'bru 'grel par bkab gser 'phreng zhes bya ba'i bstan bcos rnams mdzad/ tsha lung pa stong ston dkon cog skyabs kyis rgya gar du byon/ snyigs dus kyi thams cad mkhyen pa shan+ti pa phyi ma dang mjal/ gso dpyad yan lag brgyad pa rdzogs par gsan nas bod du phebs/ gzhung gi sa bcad bsdus don rin po che'i dra ba zhes bya ba brtsams shing / gzhung la mchan bu btab nas g.yu thog yon tan mgon po la gnang /

Minyak Mikyö Dorjé composed a medical history, Pearl Necklace; Supplement to Scriptural Explanation; Accounts from History; Main Point Overviews; Nine Treatments; Fifteen Difficult Paths of Illness; and Golden Garland Word Commentary. Tötön Könchok Kyap from Tsalung traveled to India, where he met the later Śāntipa, known as the omniscient one of these degenerate times. From him he learned the eight branches of medicine in their entirety and returned to Tibet. There he composed Jeweled Net Outline. He annotated the scripture and gave it to Yuthok Yönten Gönpo.
dpal mgon klus mdzad pa'i sbyor ba brgya pa dang / kha che zla dga'i sgra sbyor nges pa gnyis thar lo nyi ma rgyal mtshan gyis bsgyur/ lo tsA ba rang gis cong zhi'i gdams pa mdzad/

The Hundred Medical Preparations by Nāgārjuna and Lexicon of Medical Terms from the Commentary on the Essence of Eight Branches by the Kashmiri Candranandana were translated by Thar Lotsāwa Nyima Gyaltsen. The translator himself wrote Instructions on Calcite.
9. The Treasure Tradition and Drapa Ngönshé
gter ma

ye shes mkha' 'gro'i nad sel gdams pa 'ja' li pa dang khro phu lo tsA'i 'gyur/ bal po de ba tsan+d+ra'i snyan brgyud bdud rtsi'i thigs pa/ gter mar grags pa ni/ slob dpon pad+ma'i gsungs las/
ma 'ongs don du rin chen chos gter sbas: ji srid sangs rgyas bstan pa ma rdzogs par: de srid gter gyi bstan pa rdzogs mi srid: des na gter gyi 'gro ba dpag med 'dren:[197] zhes gsungs pa ltar a+yon gyi slob dpon pad+ma sam+b+ha was gtsos pa'i zab gter chos/ sman/ rtsis/ bon la sogs pa dpag tu med pa yod pa las/ bon po drag rtsal gyis bum thang rtsis lung gi lha khang nas rdzogs chen gu ru bzhi ba la sogs pa'i chos dang / sman dpyad bdud rtsi bum pa'i skor rgyas pa spyan drangs/

Yeshé Khadro’s Instructions on Curing Illness, translated by Jalipa and Tropu Lotsāwa, and the Nepali Devacandra’s Ambrosia Drop Oral Transmission are said to be unearthed treasures. On the subject of treasures Ācārya Padmasambhava said:
For the sake of those in the future the precious Dharma is hidden as treasure. For as long as the teachings of the Buddha exist, for so long will the treasure teachings exist. The treasures, therefore, will guide countless beings.[378] As this prophecy states, there are countless profound treasures in existence, as is well illustrated by those of Oḍḍiyāna Ācārya Padmasambhava. They comprise Dharma treasures, medicine treasures, astrology treasures, Bön treasures, and many more. Bönpo Draktsal recovered the Dharma text Four Great Perfection Gurus and the extensive medical collection Ambrosia Vase of Healing from Tsilung temple in Bumthang.

d.div: [197] ma 'ongs don du rin chen chos gter sbas:_ji srid sangs rgyas bstan pa ma rdzogs par:_de srid gter gyi bstan pa rdzogs mi srid:_des na gter gyi 'gro ba dpag med 'dren:_zhes 'di rnyed son ma byung /
[378] Citation untraced.

f.d:
thang yig las/
la stod btsan yul bon la gso nam byed: 'dzam gling rgyal po'i dpon brgyud 'bangs mi non: lho gter gter phran 'ga' zhig sbas pa 'di: mi bzhag 'don pa'i rtags der bstan nas byung : gter ston ku sa sman pa zhes bya 'byung :[198] zhes ku sa sman par grags pas spa gro bcal sogs nas chos/ sman/ bon gsum gyi zab gter du ma bton cing / gter chos gzhan las kyang sman dpyad kyis 'gro don rgya che ba 'byung ba dang /

Lotus Chronicles says:
When the people of the stronghold of Tsenyül use their weapons for farming[379] and descendents of the king of the world are suppressed by their subjects, signs will appear for unearthing the southern treasures and others, and the treasure finder Kusa Menpa will manifest.[380] The treasure finder known as the Kusa doctor discovered many profound treasures on Dharma, medicine, and Bön at Padrochal and other places. Of these treasures, the medical texts were of greatest benefit to living beings.

d.div: [198] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 92_sa rtags gter gyi 'byung dus bstan pa/ shog_561_phreng 2

[379] La stod btsan yul mtshon la so nam byed. This is the reading according to Orgyen Lingpa in the Lotus Chronicles, p. 561. The present text, however, has bon instead of mtshon and gso instead of so. Prof. Losang Tenzin suggests that mtshon refers to mtshon cha, weapons.
[380] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 42.561.2.

f.d: byang gi phyi gong ru ba 'tshub mas khyer:[199] zhes pa'i dus rtags thog byon pa yul stod lung du 'khrungs shing rus bon yin pas a ya bon po lha 'bum du grags pas sman rtsis chos bon bzhi ga ru mtshams nas phyungs/

A verse in the Lotus Chronicles begins: “In the northern region of Chigong, households will be carried away by a fierce storm,”[381] This is a prediction of signs foretelling the coming of Aya Bönpo Lhabum, so called because he was born in the region of Tölung and was of Bönpo stock. He discovered treasures of medicine, astrology, Dharma, and Bön from Rutsam in the central region.

d.div: [199] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 92_sa rtags gter gyi 'byung dus bstan pa/ shog_561_yig phreng 7

f.d:
thang yig las/
rgya gar ma phyin kun kyang lo tsAr bzhed: bod kyi mkhas btsun thams cad sa mthar 'khyer: hor dang yon mchod khrims gsar 'brel ba yong : nang nag phyi dkar dud kha'i snye ma bzhin: bod kyi bsod nams mar mar 'grib pa'i dus: pad+ma shel phug sbas pa'i gter kha 'di: mi bzhag 'don pa'i rtags der bstan nas byung : gter ston ra mo shel sman zhes bya 'byung :[200]

d.div: [200] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 92_sa rtags gter gyi 'byung dus bstan pa/ shog_564_yig phreng 4_tshig sna mi mthun/
[382] Dud kha’i snye ma.
[383] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 42.564.4.

f.d: zhes dpal ldan sa skya pa dang hor rgyal yon mchod thog mar 'brel ba'i dus yar stod ra mo sman chur 'khrungs pa 'dis/ sman chu'i rdzong brag ri'i phug pa nas bla rdzogs thugs gsum/ gso dpyad dang rtsis kyi skor mtha' yas pa thon kyang / thog mar gso rig dang phan bya gnod bya'i skor mang po nyams su blangs pas/ chos kyi 'gro don cher ma byung zhing / gsang sman sogs chu bcos kyi skor dang / 'bam nad la sman dkar sman nag / rdel nad sogs thor bu ma gtogs gter chos phal cher shog ser las 'bebs ma thub par lus/ chu dang 'bam gyi phyag len ni da lta'i bar ma nyams par yod/

This treasure finder was born in Ramo Menchu in Yartö when the teacher-patron relationship between the glorious Sakya and the Mongolian king was first established. From a cave near the Menchu mountain hermitage, he recovered the Guru, Great Perfection, and Enlightened Mind collections and many collections on medicine and astrology. However, in the beginning, because he practiced medicine together with other practices of help and hindrance, he was not greatly beneficial to people in terms of the Dharma. Moreover, regarding his secret medicines, apart from a collection on dropsy treatment, white radish, and black pepper preparations for elephantiasis-like disorders, and treatments for urinary stones, most of the treasure could not be transcribed from the yellow scroll and remained unread. The treatments for dropsy and elephantiasis-like disorders have remained in unbroken transmission to this day.

gu ge 'dam grog mkhar bya ba na/ bu tsha mang po la chung nad kyi gnod pas 'jigs par gyur pa'i tshe/ byis pa gcig la nad la sogs pa gang yang ma byung bar pha ma gnyis kyis de'i rgyu mtshan dris pas/ bu tsha na re/ nged rang gi grong gi dbus na la rdzas chen po yod pa de g.yengs pa'i gseb nas rdo'i bum pa zhig don pa kha phye ba'i nang nas shog dril la chas btums pa zhig rnyed pa nyin mtshan med par bdag gi lus la bcangs pas chung nad kyi rigs ma byung zer/ der pha mas sngags rnying ma la mkhas pa'i bla ma zhig spyan drangs/ shog ser spyan lam du phab pa bla mas gzigs pas/
ma 'ongs pa na gu ge 'dam grog mkhar 'dir chung nad chen pos nyen pa'i dus/ skal ldan byis pa gcig gis gter 'di rnyed nas 'gro ba la phan thogs par shog / ces sogs gtso bor chung nad dang / bsrung ba'i skor cha tshang 'dug pas shog ser las phab ste 'gro don che bar byung /

Once in Damtrok Khar in Gugé, many children were falling sick, and this was causing great anxiety. One child, however, was never ill and his parents asked him why. “In the middle of the village is a stone cairn. I moved it and took a stone pot out from inside. I opened the pot and inside was a folded scroll. I wear it day and night and never get sick.” His parents invited a lama learned in the ways of the old tantra schools. They gave the yellow scroll to him to study. It read:
In the future, in this Damtrok district of Gugé, when the children are threatened by disease, may this treasure be discovered by a blessed child, and may it be of benefit to living beings. The scroll continued with complete instructions for treating children’s diseases and for taking preventative measures. These were copied from the yellow scroll and were of great benefit to the population.

rgya gar gter ston badz+ra ma tis bal yul li shan+ti'i gnas nas mkha' 'gro'i zab gter ngo mtshar can rnams gdan drangs/ tshal gung thang pa gzhon nu bsam gtan gyi bal yul du byon pa gter ston dang mjal nas gnang ba'i chos skor du gu ru pad ma phag rgod la chibs pa'i rim srungs bcos thabs kyi rgyun dang / rig 'dzin rgod ldem gyis byang gter thugs sgrub kyi cha lag sman dpyad skor shog dril dkar ser sngon po/ snang gsal sgron me/ bdud rtsi'i bum chung / rdo rje khrab ring skor gnad kyi man ngag gnyan tshad bcos thabs/ khyung nag skor la lhog pa'i bcos thabs sogs spyan drangs pas mtshon gter ma mtha' yas shing /

The Indian treasure finder Vajramati unearthed the Extraordinary and Profound Ḍākinī Treasures in Liśānti in Nepal. Among the works of Shönu Samten from Tsalgung plains is Treatment and Prevention of Epidemics from Guru Padma’s Journey to Wild Boar Mountain, which he received from a treasure finder while in Nepal. There are many medical works in Rikzin Gödem’s (1337–1408) Northern Treasure collection as supplements to the practices known as the accomplishment of the enlightened mind (thugs sgrub). These include medical collections on white, yellow, and blue scrolls, Brilliant Lamp, and Small Vase of Ambrosia. The Vajra Armor collection includes Essential Instruction for the Treatment of Infectious Fevers, and the Khyungnak collection includes treatments for lhok. There are countless other treasures.
[gter ston rdor 'bum chos kyi grags pa]

bdag gi bla ma nges pa don gyi thams cad mkhyen pa ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsan yig gang+gA'i chu rgyun du bzhugs gras/ sprul pa'i gter ston rdor 'bum chos kyi grags pas khong ba'i nang gi snying ngam yid bzhin gyi nor bu lta bu'i dpe dang sbyar pas bdud rtsi bum chen gyi shog ser phal cher byang spra dun rtse'i rta mgrin dregs pa zil gnon gyi thugs ka nas spyan drangs shing / kha skong zur bkol du sbas pa 'ga' zhig byams sprin rdo sku'i 'og nas bton pa/ phyi ltar dkar chag tu bstan pa rtsa ba ma yig gi skor/ nang par thems ltar bstan pa dgongs 'grel mde thung sogs bu yig gi skor/ dkar chag dang bar thems las dngos su ma gsal ba thems med kyi skor/ de dag nyams su len pa la nye bar mkho ba dgongs gter gyi skor dang bzhi/

d.div: [384] Thems or them; precise meaning here is unclear. The term usually refers to the threshold of a door.

f.d:
dang po ni/ gter gzhung dkar chag las/
gdams pa bdud rtsi'i bum pa la/ / rgyud gsum gyad lnga srog gter gyad/ / gsang mdzod 'byed pa'i lde mig lnga/ / mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i snying khrag gcig[201] / ces pa ltar/ rgyud gyad lnga/ srog gter / gsang mdzod lde mig / mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i snying khrag / yan lag dang drug /

In the first collection, the treasure text’s catalog of contents, it says:
In this Ambrosia Vase teaching, three tantras, five forces, the life-treasure force, five keys to open the secret treasure house, secret ḍākinī heart blood.[385] These are classified into six main headings: (1) the tantras, (2) the five forces, (3) life treasure, (4) treasure-house keys, (5) heart blood of the secret ḍākinī, and (6) supplementary material.

d.div: [201] rgyal ba lnga pa blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsung / gter gzhung dkar chag las/ gdams pa bdud rtsa'i bu+im pa la/ /rgyud gsum gyad lnga srog gtar gyed/ /gsang mdzod 'byed pa'i lde mig lnga/ /mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i snying khrag gcig
[385] Cited in Jamgön Kongtrül Lodrö Thayé, Store of Precious Treasure, vol. ha, dkar chag, 1a2.

f.d: [rgyud ]
Tantras

dang po la 'chi med bdud rtsi'i bum pa rtsa rgyud gzhung yan lag brgyad pa le'u bcu'i bdag nyid can/ don skor gsum pa zhes bya ba 'jam dbyangs kyi thugs bcud brtag pa spyi dang khyad par don rtags gsum du mdor bsdus pa'i rtsa rgyud dang de'i bshad rgyud sngon 'gro'i dngos gzhi rjes gsum spyi dang bye brag so sor bstan pa snang gsal nyi ma'i dkyil 'khor te rtsa bshad 'di gnyis rgyud gcig tu byas pa/ gsang bdag gi thugs bcud phyi nang gsang ba bzlas sngags bsrung thabs sbyin sreg gtad rgyar bcas pa bshad rgyud gnam lcags rdo rje'i khrab ring zhes bya ba rnams/

The first of the three tantras in the first group is the Ambrosia Vase of Immortality Root Tantra on the eight branches, which is in ten chapters. It is also known as the Three Collections. The second root tantra is the Essence of the Mind of Mañjuśrī, which consists of a general examination and a specific teaching on the three signs. Its explanatory tantra is Illuminating Mandala of the Sun, in which the points are explained generally and specifically under the headings of preliminary, actual, and subsequent practices. These two tantras are counted as one. The third of the three tantras is the Vajra Armor of Thunderbolt Iron Explanatory Tantra on the essence of the mind of Vajrapāṇi, dealing with outer, inner, and secret mantra protection and with fire offerings and seals of entrustment.
gnyis pa gya lnga zhes pa
Five forces
dang po snod rung dbang gi gyad ni/ gtor ma'i bshoms dang bdag mdun dbang tshogs gtor bsngo phan yon rnams rtsa ba mdor bsdus pa bum pa 'degs pa'i gyad/

The first force[386] of the five forces is the initiation of suitable vessels, which is a root compilation on torma arrangement, deity visualization of self and assembly in front, initiations, the offering of the assembly torma, and dedications and their benefits. This is a force that supports the ambrosia vase.

d.div: [386] Gyad; literally, “strong man.”

f.d: gnyis pa ma las lhag pa bu'i gyad la/ nang gses kyi dang po bsrung ba dang / gso ba'i thabs rnam pa lngas byin log las rnam par rgyal ba ma las lhag pa'i bu/ gnyis pa bsrung ba'i zhal 'phang dang brtag thabs gnyis bcos thabs bzhis gzer thung las rnam par rgyal ba zhi sbyong sbrags ma ma las lhag pa'i bu/ gsum pa khyad par dmigs pas bsrung brtags gsum bcos thabs sman dpyad zas spyod rnams kyis lhog pa las rnam par rgyal ba bur 'joms/ zhi sbyong sbrags ma ma las lhag pa'i bu/ bzhi pa thun mong rdzas bsrung ba brtag pa spyi bye brag gnas rigs dbye ba bcos thabs sman dpyad zas spyod sngags rnams kyis gag pa las rnam par rgyal ba zhi sbyong sbrags ma ma las lhag pa'i bu/ lnga pa rigs gsum bsrung thabs phyi nang gsang ba 'khru mdog bcu dang brtag pa bzhi gso thabs rnam gsum lus zungs gsos te rgyu gzer las rnam par rgyal ba zhi sbyong sbrags ma ma las lhag pa bu'i rtsa ba/ drug pa rgyu rkyen rtags rigs bcos thabs log gnon bsrung ba skem pa rjes su rjes gcod phyir mi ldog pa gtar khas bcos pa rnams kyis 'brum bu las rnam par rgyal ba ma las lhag pa'i bu/ bdun pa ngos 'dzin bcos thabs snying por dril ba beg ge'i nad las rnam par rgyal ba ma las lhag pa'i bu/ 'di rnams la bu'i ming thogs kyang don ma yig gi khongs su bsdu ba yin/

The second force comprises the sections known as “the son exceeding the mother.” It has seven sections:[387] 1. Victory over jinlok with sections on protection and five treatments. 2. Pacification and cleansing combination victory over sertung with sections on protection (in which you are referred to the Vajra Armor Explanatory Tantra), two types of examinations, and four kinds of treatment. 3. Pacification and cleansing combination victory over lhok by eliminating the swellings with sections on the specifics of three protective measures, three examinations, treatment, medicine, therapies, diet, and behavior. 4. Pacification and cleansing victory over gakpa, with sections on protection by ordinary substances, general examination, specific examinations, divisions according to location in the body and type, treatment, diet, behavior, and mantras. 5. Pacification and cleansing victory over gyuser, with sections on the three kinds of the illness; outer, inner, and secret methods of protection; the ten colors of the diarrhea; four examinations; three treatments; and nourishing bodily tissue. 6. Curing and cleansing victory over smallpox, with sections on conditions, symptoms, types, treatment, reversal suppressants, protection, drying up of the pustules, convalescent treatment, complete cure to ensure the disease does not return, and bloodletting treatments. 7. Victory over beké, with sections on recognition and treatment. These seven sections have the name of “son texts,” but actually their subject matter is included in the more fundamental mother literature.

d.div: [387] The following seven sections deal with seven serious conditions or diseases (gnyan nad). A serious condition is described as being caused by the coming together of harmful external organisms and innate internal blood organisms. There are eighteen serious conditions (Dungkar, p. 974). The seven here are described in the glossary.

f.d: gsum pa yang gsang sbas pa mdzod kyi gyad ni/ spyan ras gzigs kyi thugs bcud cog 'gyel nag po gsum 'dril bcos thabs mdor bsdus pa 'chor ba med pa'i sman dpyad lag len bdud rtsi bum pa'i snying po sman gyi gtong thabs dang bcas pa gsal ba'i sgron ma/

The third force is the utterly secret hidden treasure. This is the elixir essence of the mind of Avalokiteśvara, “the essence of the vase of ambrosia, a bright lamp illuminating the practices.” It is a compilation of treatments for the three types of the black infectious chokgyal treated as one, an effective medical therapy, as well as instructions on administering the medicine.

bzhi pa 'chi med grub pa srog gi gyad ni/ ha la lcog 'gyel zhing bya ba'i nad gdon bcos thabs rgyal dbang pad ma'i mgur las srog gter chen po'i sbyor ba nye ba'i rgyu rkyen rtsa chu mthong ba sgra gsang rtags drug ngos 'dzin 'phrul gyi me long bcos thabs bsdu bsad sbyang ba sdong zla bsad pa/

The fourth is the force of life, the ambrosia attainment. This concerns the demonic illness hala chokgyal. Its treatment is “the great treasure of life medical compound spoken of in the songs of the lotus lord and master Padmasambhava.” It deals with the immediate causes and conditions of the illness, examination of pulse and urine, observation, questioning, the magic mirror for recognizing the six secret signs. Treatment consists of “gathering, killing, and cleansing” and “killing the companions.”
lnga ba gsang ba snying khrag gdams pa'i gyad ni/ rab gnas bdud rtsi sman sgrub rgyun mchod bshoms sogs sngon 'gro dang khrol bu phye ma ril bu sogs dngos gzhi dang rjes gso bsrung phan yon rnams/

The fifth force is the secret heart-blood instruction. This is the consecration of medicine as ambrosia, consisting of the preparatory rites of offerings, and so forth; the actual practice of meditation on the crushed herbs, powders, pills, and so on; and the subsequent practices of treatment, protection, and benefits of the practices.
[srog gter]
Life treasure

rtsa ba'i gsum pa srog gter gyi gyad ni/ ji skad du/
log gnon srog gi ka chen 'di/ / gud du bkol ba'i rgyud cig yin/ / zhes pa log gnon chings kyi shog dril mkha' 'gro'i lung bstan yang gsang srog gi ka chen sum sgril rta zhon 'jug sgo 'grims gsang gnas yul rdzong bsrung brtags gso ba 'chi 'tsho'i brtag rjes rnams tshang ba brgyud 'dzin re rer mthar thon par shog cig pa'i smon lam dang bcas pa/

The third main section is that of the life-treasure force. The text here says:
This great life pillar of reversal suppressants is written as a separate work. This is a scroll on reversal suppressants, containing a ḍākinī prophecy, the very secret great pillar of life, the three black forces as one, “riding the horses,”[388] entrances, pathways, regions and households, protection, examinations, treatments, signs of life and death, along with a final prayer that the scroll will be revealed to each lineage holder.

d.div: [388] Treasure texts often use enigmatic language. The actual text of Great Vase of Ambrosia as found in Store of Precious Treasures talks of illnesses and disease riding the horses of the four elements; hence the following imagery of roads, regions, and households to describe bodily entrances and locations for diseases. The “three black forces” refers to a pandemic when harmful external and internal organisms combine, and infectious disease, fever, and wind disorder arise simultaneously (Great Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, p. 1499).

f.d: [lde mig ]
Treasure-house keys

rtsa ba'i bzhi pa gsang mdzod 'byed pa'i lde mig lnga'i dang po gsang mdzod sgo 'byed gter srung la gdams gtad/ gnyis pa gces pa bco brgyad dang bsngags pa dgu'i bsdu don khog 'bugs/ gsum pa las kyi mtha' bsgyur zug gzer gcag pa'i lde mig / bzhi pa lud pa 'gyur du ma 'dod na 'phrul 'khor chen mo'i sbyor ba gdams pa gnad kyi yig chung gsang sgo 'byed pa'i lde mig /lnga pa 'khor lo'i lde mig gnad kyi nying khu bcas bstan pa/

The fourth section listed in the list of contents is the five keys to open the secret treasure house. The first is the entrustment instruction to the guardian of this secret treasure. The second is a compendium of the eighteen fundamentals and nine mantras. The third is “efficient transformation[389] to break the intestinal pain of gyuser.” The fourth is a “short text of essential instructions; the key to open the secret door,” describing “a great charm circle if one does not wish the mucus to change.” The fifth is the mandala key, taught by ten essential instructions.

d.div: [389] Las mtha’ bsgyur; described in the Ambrosia Vase itself as “designating specific powers to the particular medicine.”

f.d: [mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i snying khrag ]
Secret ḍākinī heart blood

rtsa ba'i lnga pa mkha' 'gro gsang ba'i snying khrag ni/ gleng gzhi rgyu rkyen dbye ba brtag pa bcos pa sman dpyad rtsa rgyugs tsha ba grang ba lus zungs mkhris gsum sha g.ya' ste le'u bcu gnyis sdoms dang bcas pa g.ya'i bdud rtsi ma lha mo'i khrag dar ya kan zhes bya ba bum pa 'degs pa'i gyad/ de'i zhar byung mkha' 'gro'i snying khrag drug shin tu gces pa'i yang snying lha mo'i snying khrag 'byed pa'i lde mig rnams/

This concerns “accretion” daryakan, the blood of the ambrosia goddess.[390] It is in twelve chapters, namely, introduction, causes, conditions, types, examination, treatments, racing through the channels,[391] hot bile, cold bile, bodily tissue bile, remedies for the three types of bile, and kṣaya,[392] ending with a summary. It is a “force that holds up the ambrosia vase.” Also taught in this section are “the six heart bloods of the ḍākinī, a precious and quintessential teaching,” comprising “the key to unlock the heart blood of the goddess.”

d.div: [390] G.ya’i bdud rtsi ma lha mo’i khrag. Identified as a synonym for daryakan (Dungkar, p. 2616). G.ya’i ma is also identified as Chrysoplenium carnosum Hook (Pas, p. 234) and as Pyrola incarnate (Clarke, p. 157) Although there are twenty-five types of daryakan, this is not among them. G.ya’ usually means dust, rust, or any type of accretion that gradually appears on a surface, In some accounts of the origin of this panacea, it refers to the mossy growth on rocks.

[391] Described in the actual Ambrosia Vase text (p. 548) as “the rider of a fierce infectious disease on the fire stallion of bile driven by the spurs of the wind humor, surrounded by the army of phlegm.”
[392] Kśaya; “end” or “destruction.” Refers to the incurable stage of a bile disease.

f.d: rtsa ba'i drug pa yan lag ni/
Supplementary material

yang gsang sbas ba'i mdzod chen la/ / dpa' bo gyad kyi ral skor yod/ / ces gong du bstan pa'i gyad lnga'i nang tshan gyad gsum pa'i yan lag sgo bsrung gi tshul du log gnon gyad kyi sbyor ba rlung mkhris bad kan khrag grang ba srin bu 'dus pa sogs gnyen po sbyor ba khrag 'thung pad ma rgyal pos yum la chig chod du gtad rgyar sbas bcol bka' zab rgyas btab smon lam dang bcas pa gnam lcags gyad kyi ral skor zhes bya ba gter srungs rgyal po sde bzhi dang yang le ber la gtad pa'i smon lam dang bcas pa/ lag len bdud rtsi'i 'phreng ba yang snying bcas pa gyad lnga'i nang tshan bzhi pa'i cha lag tu ha la cog 'gyel bcos thabs tshig rgyud thabs shes gsum dpa' bo bzhi khyung lnga dkar po drug g+hi haM bdun dri ldan brgyad ser po dgu sbyor spyi don brgyad kyi mthar thug pa bdud rtsi ril bu'i 'phreng ba mkhar chen bza' la gdams pa 'di yan gyis ma yig dkar chag gi tshig gis zin pa rnams rdzogs nas/

Here the contents list reads:
In the utterly secret hidden treasure is the heroic-force sword collection. This is a supplement to the third of the five forces mentioned above. These are reversal suppressants in the form of protections of the bodily entrances. They act as counteracting forces to wind, bile, phlegm, hot and cold disorders, organisms, complex disorders, and so on. A panacea entrusted as a treasure by the “blood-drinking lotus king” to his consort, sealed as a profound work together with a prayer, this “thunderbolt-force sword collection” was to be guarded, with the appropriate prayers, by the four kings and by Yangleber.[393] The list of contents says, “There is the ambrosia garland practice.” This is a supplement to the fourth of the five forces mentioned above. It teaches treatments for hala chokgyal, comprising single-ingredient treatment, three-method and wisdom combined treatments, the four-hero preparation, the five-garuda preparation, the six whites preparation, the seven types of animal bile, the eight aromatic medicines, the nine-yellow-ingredients preparation, the eight general principles, and finally “the garland of ambrosia pills as taught to the lady of Kharchen.”[394] This completes the mother text as documented in the list of contents.

d.div: [393] The Ambrosia Vase itself states that the text was hidden in the heart of “Eclipsing the Arrogant,” identified previously as Hayagrīva, from whom the treasure was recovered. There is an annotation to the Ambrosia Vase noting that “Eclipsing the Arrogant” refers to the upāsaka general Yangleber (yang le ber). He is a convert to the Buddhist pantheon, previously existing as a Tibetan mountain deity. He is foremost in the retinue of Vaiśravaṇa, one of the four guardian kings. Red in color, he rides a wild horse.
[394] Mkhar chen bza’, also known as Yeshé Tsokgyal, the consort of Padmasambhava.

f.d: [bu yig gi skor]
The inner, son documents presented as an intermediate step
rtsa ba'i gnyis pa nang par thems ltar bstan pa dgongs 'grel mde thung sogs bu yig gi skor la/ spyi dang khyad par gnyis/
The second collection includes the arrowhead teachings[395] and other teachings. This has a general section and a specific section.

d.div: [395] Mde’u; can also mean “pebble” or “slingshot.” These days the term means “bullet,” so presumably the medicine acted like a bullet to penetrate to the cause of the illness.

f.d: dang po spyir bstan pa la/ bshad rgyud kyi sbyin sreg rtsa tshig rkang pa bcu'i 'grel pa dol pos mdzad pa/ rgyu gzer bsrung ba phyi lha sngags gsang ba bsrung ba rgyas bsdus nang sman sngags bcos thabs rtsa tshig gi mjug rgyu gzer las rnam par rgyal ba zhi sbyong sbrags ma'i 'grel pa/

The general teaching consists of a commentary written by the Lady Yeshé Tsokgyal on ten lines of the explanatory tantra dealing with the fire offering; a section in extensive and abridged forms on protection against gyuser, consisting of an outer protection using urine and a charm circle, an inner protection using medicine and mantra, and a secret protection using deity and mantra; and treatment interspersed with root text, followed by “victory over gyuser: a pacification and cleansing commentary.”
bu yig
Son text on five forces

['di ]la nang gses kyi gyad lngar phye ba'i dang po gter ston la zhal gdams bdag 'jug gi don dang bcas pa/ gyad gnyis pa byin chung gso ba 'phrul gyi yang zhun gyi mde thung zhes bya ba/ gyad gsum pa bdud rtsi srog gter chen po dpa' rgod log gnon 'chi ba blu byed/ gyad bzhi pa chu la brtag pa de'i sad mda' gdon ngos 'dzin pa'i gdams pa dang bcas pa/ gyad lnga pa lha dgu'i sbyor ba ri lu byug pa phur ma gsum gyi gces pa'i shog dril/

The precious-scroll son literature is divided into five forces: 1. Advice to the treasure finder, together with a teaching on self-initiation 2. A treatment of jinchung called the arrowhead of refining 3. The reversal suppressant zedoary, the great life-treasure ambrosia, deceiver of death 4. Examination of urine, preparatory tests, together with teachings on the identification of demons 5.
