The essential scroll on the nine-deity medicinal preparation, pills, massage, and medicinal incense

rdzas la nus pa bskyed pa dpa' bo'i go cha rab gnas mnga' gsol gyi mde thung srog gi ka chen la nang gses kyi mde thung dgu yod pa'i dang po'i nang du zug gu gzud pa'i mde thung / gnyis pa phur mas bsrung ba'i mde thung / gsum pa byug pas gso ba'i mde thung / bzhi pa klad gzer rtags 'chos 'tsho 'chi brtag thabs dang bcas pa gsal byed nyi ma'i snying po thun mong ma yin pa'i mde thung / lnga pa stod babs kyi gzer thung bcos thabs bsil byed zla ba'i bdud rtsi zhes bya ba'i mde thung / drug pa smad babs kyi rgyu gzer rgya nad bcos pa'i mde thung / bdun pa gag pa'i bcos thabs gag khrag skyugs kyi mde thung / brgyad pa lhog pa'i bcos thabs tshig don bcu bzhi pa dngos su bsad pa'i mde thung / dgu pa bsrung ba me klong thod pa'i mde thung /

The armor of the hero consecration is the great pillar-of-life arrowhead that gives power to substances. It has nine sections: 1. The penetrating arrowhead of internal medicine 2. Arrowhead protection of medicinal incense 3. Arrowhead protection by healing with ointments 4. The special arrowhead known as essence of the illuminating sun, for symptoms, prognosis, and treatment of leser 5. The arrowhead treatment of töser, known as the cooling moon ambrosia 6. The arrowhead treatment of the foreign illness[396] gyuser 7. The arrowhead treatment of blood-vomiting gakpa 8. The arrowhead treatment and “killing” of lhokpa, under fourteen headings 9. The valley fire and skull arrowhead protection

d.div: [396] Rgya nad; the term rgya can be an abbreviation of rgya gar (India) or rgya nag (China).

f.d: ma dang 'dra ba'i bu brgyad kyi shog dril la
Eight son texts similar to the mother literature

nang gses kyi dang po tshad rims cham pa'i nad bdag mo'i srog sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / gnyis pa rgyu nad rgyu gzer nad bdag mo'i sro+og sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / gsum pa 'gros bzhi byin chung nad bdag mo'i srog sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / bzhi pa rgya nad mig ser bdag mo'i srog sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / lnga pa sa nad gag lhog nad bdag mo'i srog sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / drug pa 'brum nag go shol nad bdag mo'i srog sngags bsrung ba'i mde thung / bdun pa thabs shes nyi zla 'khor lor 'dri ba'i mde thung / brgyad pa 'tsho rgyal la gdams pa'i mde thung /

1. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress[397] of infectious fever and colds 2. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress of foreign gyuser 3. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress of four-way jinchung 4. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress of the foreign illness mikser 5. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress of sané gaklok 6. The protection arrowhead of the life mantra of the mistress of black goshöl smallpox 7. The protection arrowhead of writing on the method-and-wisdom sun and moon circle 8. The arrowhead instructions to Yeshé Tsokgyal

d.div: [397] Bdag mo; presumably the female personification of the illness or “owner” of the illness.

f.d: snying khrag gi dgongs pa la gab pa gter gyi yang zhun
Refinement of a hidden treasure with reference to heart-blood daryakan

rus dar ya kan zhes bya ba gleng gzhi spyi sdom mtshan nyid bcos thabs le'u bzhir phye ba/ gling gzhi chung gsum bskyed pa rang bsrung sgo 'byed de drug tu 'dus pa sha dar ya kan zhes bya ba/ zla zil dar ya kan zhes gling gzhi rtsa sbyong bsrung ba nad sel tshe sgrub ste le'u drug tu yon tan brjod pa/

This is the bone daryakan section divided into four chapters: introduction, general summary, characteristics, and treatments. The flesh daryakan section is in six chapters: introduction, the three nourishments when little,[398] protecting one’s body, opening the doors of the senses, curing the illness, and purging.[399] The bright-moon daryakan section comprises six chapters, in which its qualities are taught by way of introduction, presentation of the body,[400] channel cleansing, protection, elimination of illness, and longevity.

d.div: [398] Chung gsum bskyed; the Ambrosia Vase describes these as three medicinal substances and mantras given to newborn infants before their first food.
[399] The last two of the six are missing in the text, and have been added from the Ambrosia Vase itself.
[400] This chapter is omitted in the text and has been added from Ambrosia Vase itself.

f.d: gyad kyi ral skor gyi cha lag tu gtogs pa nang gses kyi dang po don snod kha 'dzin du bsdebs pa yang gsang sbas mdzod/ gnyis pa 'dzum kha rtseg 'chos pa brtag thabs gso ba spyod lam bstan pa snying po bdud rtsi 'chi med/ gsum pa khog 'bugs rtsa chings/

The next section is a supplement to the sword collection: 1. The very secret hidden treasure, gathering of restorative medicine for the solid and hollow organs 2. Tetanus: treatment, examination, cure, and behavior; the ambrosia essence of the teachings 3. Basic outline

bdud rtsi 'phreng ba bzhi la ngar 'dogs kyi gdams pa bdud rtsi rba klong la nang gses kyi dang po gso ba drag po kun 'dul/ gnyis pa srog 'dzin 'chi med kyi sbyor ba dpa' bo bdun sbyor gnyan nad 'joms pa'i bdud rtsi/ gsum pa bad kan grang rims brtag 'chos bdud rtsi 'chi gsos/ bzhi pa mi rta cha gcig kha 'dzin dngul chu'i sdeb sbyor/ lnga pa mkhris pa rlung gyur gso thabs thun mong ma yin pa'i nor bu/ drug pa khong lhog nag po cog 'gyel log gnon rgyu rkyen brtag gso phrad shog gi mtha' can khaN+Da ga'u ma ste/ sde brgyad la gter du gtad pa/

The next section consists of the ambrosia waves instructions giving intensity to the four ambrosia garlands: 1. Compound that tames all fierce disorders 2. The seven-hero preparation, a life-sustaining deathless compound, “ambrosia conquering all serious disease” 3. Examination and treatment for cold-related infectious phlegm disorder, “a life-restoring ambrosia” 4. “Horse and rider together” restorative mercury preparation 5. A special jewel for treatment of “bile becoming wind” infectious disorder 6. Examination, treatment, reversal suppressants, causes, and conditions of black lhok and chokgyel; ending with the prayer for the treasure to be recovered and the entrustment to the Kaṇḍagauma, or “the eight classes of protector”

gnyis pa khyad par sbas don gyi skor ni/ a+yon chen pos mnga' bdag la gdams pa bsam yas bzhengs nas zhes sogs gleng gzhi nas bzung ste sde tshan gcig tu spyi bye brag khyad par gsum du phye nas gsum brtag pa phyi nang gsang ba'i bsrung thabs gso thabs la rtsa ba yan lag kha 'dzin log gnon dang mthar smon lam phrad shog dang bcas pa/

The special, or hidden, collection consists of root and branch teachings. The root teaching is that of the great being of Oḍḍiyāna teaching the king and begins with an introduction commencing, “Having built Samyé….” The following branch section is divided into general, specific, and special sections on examination. This is followed by the branches of outer, inner, and secret methods of protection, treatments, restorative medicine for the organs, reversal suppressants, and a prayer for recovery of the treasure.
rtsa ba'i gsum pa dkar chag bar thems las dngos su ma gsal ba thems med skor la/
No-threshold collection, dealing with topics not clearly dealt with in the contents chapter and intermediate step collection

gyad bzhi'i dpon po lus srog bsrung ba'i go cha chig rkya thub pa 'khor lo'i gyad/ shin tu gces pa'i sad mda' lnga po phyi so so len pa gsum dang / mgyogs pa'i rta bzhi la tshod chen mi gsum bskyon pa'i gdams pa nang yan phugs tshol gyi lde mig / rgyal po drug / dmangs drug / blon po gnyis/ dar bskyed dang bcas pas rims bsrung ba nyi ma'i 'od zer bum pa 'degs pa'i gyad/

• The force known as the self-sustaining charm circle, the minister of four forces acting as armor for protecting the body • The instruction known as the key penetrating the inner secrets, comprised of the essential diagnoses of the early, later, and intermediate spies and the three wise men riding the four fast horses • “The rays of the sun guarding against infectious disease, a force that supports the vase,” comprised of the six kings, the six citizens, the two ministers, and spreading and development[401]

d.div: [401] The meaning of these is difficult to decipher as Desi is either picking out lines from the text or copying someone else who has done just that. This and so much of this section is really a list of verbatim notes. The source text, being an enigmatic treasure, is often not revealing either.

f.d: don tig shog dril bcu gsum bdud rtsi bum pa'i snying po la/
Thirteen[402] core scrolls, the essence of the ambrosia vase:

d.div: [402] Only eleven are listed. The author is copying because the Ambrosia Vase also speaks of thirteen scrolls but lists them at the end, and it might be that the dedication and summary make up the last two scrolls.

f.d: dang po lhog pa khog gsod kyi shog dril/ gnyis pa gnyan tshad 'joms pa'i shog dril/ gsum pa gag pa skyugs 'dren gyi shog dril/ bzhi pa mid 'chus sel ba'i shog dril/ lnga pa dmar gal gso ba'i shog dril/ drug pa byin log gso ba'i shog dril/ bdun pa dngul chus lhog pa gso ba'i shog dril/ brgyad pa stod gzer glo tsha 'joms pa'i shog dril/ dgu pa dpa' bo rkyang 'ded kyis gag lhog 'joms pa'i shog dril/ bcu pa gzhan gyis bcos nyes pa la sbyong gi shog dril/ bcu gcig pa lhag pa dngos su bsad pa'i log gnon phag nag lcags 'jib kyi shog dril/

1. Scroll on the killing of lhokpa 2. Scroll on the destruction of infectious fevers 3. Scroll on emetics for gakpa 4. Scroll on eliminating throat constriction 5. Scroll on curing red diarrhea 6. Scroll on curing jinlok 7. Scroll on curing lhokpa with mercury 8. Scroll on curing töser and bronchial fever 9. Scroll on curing gaklhok by being “chased by a warrior” 10. Scroll on purifying wrong treatments given by others 11. Scroll on the reversal suppressants that directly eliminate lhokpa, known as “sucked by Black Vārāhī”

gnyan nad ma lus sel ba 'khrud pa bdud rtsi chu rgyun 'chi ba las slong ba khyad par 'phags pa'i gdams pa/ rang bsrung dang sbyong gi zhal shes dpa' bo bzhi sbyor gyi gdams pa'i cha lag dang dri chu bar pa la brten pa'i bsrung ba/ sman gyi phyag tshad bstan pa'i mde thung / pho mo bcos thabs rigs gsum gyi ngos 'dzin so so'i gso byed rjes kyi spyod lam dang bcas bstan pa'i mde thung / byis rims bcos thabs 'khru lugs lnga gso thabs lnga rjes gcong rgyu ma'i rtsig / bsrung ba sogs bstan pa'i mde thung snying lta bu/ byis rims 'chos pa'i lag len gsal ba dngul gyi me long / bsil sbyor chen mo tsha ba me ltar 'bar ba'i gnyen po snying lta bu'i shog dril thun mong ma yin pa'i mde thung / smin mtshams su g.yung drung ris sgom pa sogs dmigs pas bsrung ba rdo rje'i khrab/ ha la cog 'gyel rgyu rkyen brtag thabs gso thabs gnyen po bzhis bstan pa 'chi ba dus btab nges par gsos pa bdud rtsi 'chi gsos/ zas spyad sman gyi spyang ki'i ngos 'dzin sogs gdams pa lag tu blang pa'i shog dril mthar dar pa'i smon lam gyi sgo nas rgyas btab pa rnams so/ / de yang chos rgyal bkra shis stobs rgyal gyis/ shin tu dkon pa'i tshil bu dar ya kan [202]zhes gsungs pa'i tshil bu dar ya kan dang gzhan yang sna 'ga' zhig yod tshod du 'dug

These are followed by: • The cleansing ambrosia stream that washes away all serious illness, exclusive instructions lifting one away from death • Self-protection, essential oral instruction on purification, supplementary instructions on the four-warrior preparation, protection in dependence on the intermediate-stage urine • The arrowhead of instruction on medicine measurements • Arrowhead treatment of yumo: recognizing its three types, their cures, and post-illness behavior • Heart-like arrowhead instructions on the treatment of children’s infectious diseases: diagnosis from the five kinds of diarrhea, five types of treatment, total elimination of the disease, and protection of intestinal juices • The clear silver mirror: practices for the treatment of children’s infectious diseases • The great cooling medicinal compound, antidote to the fever that rages like a fire: an exclusive arrowhead precious heart-like scroll • Vajra armor protection practice of meditating on a swastika between the eyebrows, and so on: a hala chokgyal taught by way of causes, conditions, examinations, treatments, and antidotes; a death-destroying ambrosia definitely reviving even from the brink of death • Instructions on recognizing the jackals[403] of eating, behavior, and medicine. This list continues and the text concludes with sealing prayers for the dissemination of these works. There is also a manuscript on resinous daryakan, compiled by Chögyal Tashi Topgyal, describing “the extremely rare resinous daryakan”[404] and various other documents.

d.div: [202] 'dir chos rgyal bkris stobs rgyas kyi gsung de gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[403] Spyang ki; can mean wolf also, but presumably refers to medicines, behavior, and food that “cleans up.” The text itself seems to bear this out.

[404] The Ambrosia Vase recounts the origin of this substance. The beautiful sons of Brahmā and Prajpāti were playing by a lake in the Himalayas when they were spotted by some maidens from the eight castes of nāgas. Overcome by desire they joined with each other on a rock. The red and white seeds were spilt; the white seed fell on the rock, the red fell between the rock. A resinous substance formed on the rock. It was known as chongshi ambrosia (calcite) or resinous daryakan. It is a panacea that has the power to cure all 404 diseases.

f.d: rtsa ba'i bzhi pa de dag nyams su len pa la nye bar mkho ba dgongs gter

d.i: The essential mind-treasure collection for the practice of the above

f.d: chos rgyal bkra shis stobs rgyal gyis le bsgrigs la lha sgom kha brgyan dpag bsam ljon shing / 'dzab dgongs mgul rgyan pany+dza li ka / sbyin sreg kha rgyan rma bya'i mdongs/ rdzas 'khor gyi gang zag re re dang yul khams bsrungs pa'i sdoms dang gter ston 'byung tshul sogs yig sna rnams nas khol bur phyungs pa dang gces pa bco brgyad nas khol bton mang yul byams sprin ma'i shog dril gyi don zur gyi bstan pa/

This collection was compiled from various manuscripts by Chögyal Tashi Topgyal. It includes: Dorbum Chökyi Drakpa’s Deity Meditation: A Wish-Fulfilling Tree Ornament, Pāñcalika-Necklace Mind Recitation, Peacock-Feather Fire-Offering Ornament, verses on the protection of individuals and the country through substances and charm circles, and texts on how the treasures were unearthed. Other works compiled from the eighteen fundamentals acting as supplementary teachings to the scrolls unearthed separately from Mangyül Jamtrin temple include:

khrab ring bshad rgyud dang / 'khor lo gyad dang khyung dang 'khor lo phyag rgya'i yang ti nyi shu mde thung gnad kyi nying khu sogs kyi zhal shes gsal sgron/ chig rkya thub pa'i 'khor lo khyung gsum ma'i gyad kyi phyag len skor/ bdud rtsi bum pa'i 'phrul gsang sngags byang mthong chog ma/ rnam dag dbang gi chu rgyun bum bcud ma'i dbang chog bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i dbang chog gsal byed bdud rtsi'i zla snang rnams/

• Bright Lamp of Oral Instruction Teachings on the Vajra Armor Explanatory Tantra, Charm-Circle Force, Garuḍa, Twenty Essences of Charm-Circle Mudra, The Arrowhead Essence, and so on • Three-Garuḍa Self-Sustaining Wheel Collection on the Practices of the Root Forces • Ambrosia Vase Secret Magic: Mantra Fulfilling to Behold • Stream of the Pure Initiations: The Vase-Elixir Initiation Rituals, which is my lama the Great Fifth’s Illuminating Ambrosia Moonlight Initiation Rituals
sprul sku dam pa dmar pos sba gro bcal gyi brag seng ge'i khog pa 'dra pa'i pha bong sdig ru can gyi rtsa ba nas spyan drangs pa'i dngos grub kun gyi rtsa ba bdud rtsi chen po'i bcud len gyi skor la/
Trülku Dampa Marpo revealed the Great Ambrosia Elixir Collection: Root of All Siddhis from the foot of Scorpion Rock[405] at Lion Cliff in Padrochal. It included:

d.div: [405] Sdig ru can. In Lives of the Treasure Finders from Jamgön Kongtrül’s Great Store of Treasures (vol. ka, p. 42), this famous place for the recovering of treasures is said to resemble an entanglement of scorpions (sdig ru ’dzings).

f.d: bdud rtsi'i byin rlabs dang / lung bdud rtsi 'byung pa'i rgyud le'u nyer gcig pa/ 'gor slob dpon chen po'i mtshan gyi rnam grangs bstan pa'i bdud rtsi'i lag len rin chen 'phreng sbyor/ bdud rtsi dri chen gyi sgrub thabs tshe'i gdams pa khyad par 'phags pa'i man ngag mi shes 'phrang sgrol gces pa'i lag len mdor bsdus rdzogs so'i mtha' can bdud rtsi lung 'bogs pa zhar byung mchod rdzas dka' thub kyi dbye ba sbyang bya rdzas kyi sgom thabs bcas ston pa don rtogs shog gi mtha' can/ bcud len lag tu blangs pa'i zhal gdams dka' thub dang bsrung ba'i skyobs kyi dbye ba bsrung bar bgegs skrod bya tshul bla ma dam pa'i gdams ngag rdzogs so'i mtha' can/ bdud rtsi mar du drangs pa'i gdams pa zhes pa 'jam dpal zla gsang las rdzas kyi bsrung ba dang bcud len bya thabs zhar byung phan yon nag po dgu thub la brten nas bdug pa/ byug pa/ ril bu/ phur ma sogs kyi kha bsgyur bstan pa bdud rtsi mar khu'i gdams pa rnam par snang mdzad mar khu bcud 'byung ba'i thabs zhes pa lag len/ rdzas sngags kyi kha bsgyur/ sbyang bya/ za ba'i tshad/ phan yon mdog legs par bya ba dang bcas ston pa/ bdud rtsi mar khu'i gdams pa don bdun gyis bstan pa mkhas khyad man ngag gi yig chung rdzogs so'i mtha' can/ gdon dang nad sogs brtags te gegs sel ba'i thabs sman gyi 'phrang bsal rdzogs byang gi mtha' can/ zhar byung gnas skabs mthar thug gi phan yon sku gsum gyi grol tshul dang bcas pa gu rus mdzad pa'o'i mtha' can rnams/

1. Blessings of Ambrosia 2. Tantra on Ambrosia-Producing Teachings in twenty-one chapters 3. Ambrosia Practice of Precious Garland Preparations, beginning with the different names of the great Ācārya 4. Excrement Ambrosia Accomplishment, ending with the words “This concludes these teachings on longevity, an exclusive transmission, an abridged but essential practice for liberation from the ravine of ignorance.” 5. Ambrosia Teachings, with an incidental section on offering substances, sections on types of ascetic practices and meditation on substances to be purified, and ending with a prayer that the finder is able to comprehend the meaning 6. Instructions on the Use of Elixirs, covering ascetic practices, types of protections, and ways to dispel hindrances to protection, and ending with the words, “This concludes the instructions of the sacred lama.” 7. Instructions on Ambrosia in the Form of Butter, which includes teachings on protective substances and the making of elixirs from the Mañjuśrī Secret Moon; incidental teachings on their benefits; instructions on using fumigation, ointments, pills, and medicinal incense in dependence on the nine-powerful-black-ingredients compound in order to change the direction of an illness; a text on liquid-butter ambrosia known as the Vairocana Method of Producing Elixir from Liquid Butter; instructions on changing the direction of a disorder by using substances blessed by mantra; sections on substances to be purified, diet, and the benefits of improved complexion; and a conclusion that ends with the words “This concludes a short manuscript on instructions concerning ambrosia liquid butter, taught under seven headings, a force for the wise.” 8. Clearing the Difficult Paths of Medicine, a text on eliminating hindrances by examining demonic influences, illnesses, and so on, that ends with a colophon 9. Incidental teachings on immediate and ultimate benefits and on modes of liberation into the three bodies; ending with the words, “composed by the guru”

mnga' bdag nyang ral pa can gyi zab gter dpa' bo lha gsum skor gyi las tshogs rnam brgyad kyi gras la/
smyo 'bog 'dul dang sre'u gso: mdze nad gso dang ser ba bzlog: ces pa tsam zhig dang /

In the Three Warrior Deities profound treasure collection of the king-like Nyang Ralpachen, in the section on the eight groups of activities, it only talks about:
Controlling insanity, averting infant mortality, curing leprosy, and averting hail.

drag sgrub las tshogs su/ yams nad bzlog pa/ sri'u gso thabs/ gza'/ mdze/ lhog / gzer sogs gnyan nad/ dug nad rnams 'chos pa/ smyo 'bog 'dul ba/ byis nad 'chos pa/ klad gzer/ bal nad/ khyi smyon/ pho mchin na ba/ skran nad rnams 'chos pa/ chu 'gags sel ba/ 'dre gnod pa'i nad pa gso ba/ ling tog dang mig nad sel ba/ lhog ro bsha' ba la sogs pa dang / bdud rtsi 'od ldan gyi rgyud le'u drug cu pa/

The section on wrathful activities has practices for averting epidemics, infant mortality, planetary demonic illness, leprosy, lhok, and other serious conditions; treatments for counteracting poison, controlling insanity, and curing infant diseases; treatments for leser, the Nepali illness, rabies, liver illness, and tumors; cures for urine-retention disorders, illnesses caused by spirits, and lingtok and other eye diseases; and ways to destroy lhog. He also revealed Tantra on Shining Ambrosia in Sixty Chapters.

gu ru chos kyi dbang phyug gis gter kha bco brgyad kyi dang po gnam skas can nas sman dpyad gzhung gcig /man ngag gsum/ drang srong nyer gcig gi dgongs 'dus gzhung snying tig rin po che'i khri mdzod bdud rtsi'i bum pa le'u nyi shu tham pa rnams gter nas bzhes pa las gsan yig gang+gA'i chu rgyun du bzhugs pa/

Guru Chökyi Wangchuk discovered eighteen treasures. The first was found at Namkechen[406] and contains one work on medical examination; three instructional teachings; and Ambrosia-Vase Heartdrop Treatise in Twenty Chapters: A Storehouse of Jewels and Compilation of the Thoughts of the Twenty-One Rishis. These can be found in Stream of the Ganges: An Account of Teachings Received.[407]

d.div: [406] In Lhodrak.
[407] By Ngawang Losang Gyatso, the Fifth Dalai Lama.

f.d: bdud rtsi sman sgrub bum pa'i rgya can la nang gses kyi man ngag tshan don bkol ba/ sman gyi sngags byang / sman sgrub/ sngags 'grel rnams chos sde gcig /de'i kha skong zhi ba'i las byang / sman gyi las tshogs la nang gses dgur gshad pa'i dang po gang la dgongs nas bshad pa/

His Sealed Vase Producing Ambrosia Medicine includes setting out the meaning of names[408] of the instructions, a list of medical mantras, instructions on creating medicine, and explanations of the mantras, all under one section. A supplement to the above work contains a list of peaceful ritual activities. Practices and activities concerning medicines are grouped in nine sections: 1. What the teachings are based upon

d.div: [408] Text has tshan (division) but should be read as mtshan (name) according to Prof. Losang Tenzin.

f.d: gnyis pa bdud rtsi lnga spyi sgrub kyi sbyor ba la bdud rtsi'i kha bsgyur la brten nas rims dug /khrag 'khrugs/ mchin pa/ glo ba/ snying / mkhal ma/ mkhris pa/ mcher ba/ rgyu long / mdze rnams kyi nad sel ba/ skra dang smin ma skye ba/ 'brum bu gsos pa/ gos mi dgos pa/ rkang mgyogs/ rkang pa mi gas pa/ thog ser 'bebs pa rnams/

2. Compounds from the general production of the five ambrosias, whose controlling powers will eliminate the poison of infectious illnesses, disturbed blood, diseases of the liver, lungs, heart, kidneys, gall-bladder, spleen, and intestines, and leprosy; encourage the growth of hair and eyebrows; cure smallpox; develop the ability to go without clothes; develop the power of fleetness of foot; prevent cracked feet; and cause thunder and hail

gsum pa bye brag so so'i sbyor ba la lus smin cing rdzogs pa/ rus pa mkhregs pa/ so tshags dam pa/ sri'u skye ba/ phyi ma rdo rje'i rigs 'grub pa/ mchog gi bcud len/ mdze rlung sel ba/ sha skye ba/ phyi ma rin chen rigs 'grub pa/ sems gsal ba/ grang ba mi skye ba/ 'brum nad/ rgyu rims thub pa/ phyi ma pad ma'i rigs 'grub pa/ bkrag bzang ba/ dug rigs thub pa/ phyi ma las kyi rigs 'grub pa/

3. Individual preparations for ripening and completing bodily development; strengthening the bones; ensuring the teeth grow close together; promoting healthy growth of infants; future development into the vajra family; producing the best elixirs; dispelling leprosy wind; developing muscle tissue; bringing later development into the jewel family; enhancing clarity of mind; preventing bodily cold power; combatting smallpox; overcoming infectious diseases of the intestines; future development into the lotus family; creating a good complexion; overcoming poisons; and future development into the activity family

bzhi pa dri chen rgyal blon dmangs sbyor la/ rtsa ba rgyal po lta bu/ kha bsgyur blon po lta bu/ zhag nyer gcig bsten pas klu nad/ gag lhog / glo gsar rnying / 'brum nad/ mig nad/ za rkong / dug nad/ sbyar dug rnams sel ba/ dmangs bdud rtsi sbrul pa/ 'dul ba/ spel ba/ dbyung ba/ grang rlung sel ba/ mig gsal ba/ bcud mi 'chor ba/ rtsa mig tu 'gro ba/ drod skye ba/ ril bu/ lde gu/ zan tshod/ thug pa/ chang / sman mar/ zan dron/ 'o thug /rgyun sgrub rnams/

4. The king, minister, and people excrement preparation:[409] the root preparation is like a king, while the disorder-changing preparation is like the minister. Taking them for twenty-one days will cure nāga-created illnesses, gaklhok, chronic and acute bronchial illnesses, smallpox, eye diseases, sakong, and natural and synthetic poisons. The people preparation is known as the ambrosia emanation. It is for taming, increasing, and dispelling; eliminating cold disorders caused by wind; improving sight; preserving essential nutriments; acting on the channel openings; generating heat; and for making pills, pastes, gruels, noodle soups, alcohol, medicinal butter, hot barley cake, milk noodle soups, and other everyday foods.

d.div: [409] Although dri chen can mean excrement as well as referring to the medicinal plant asafoetida (shing kun), Prof. Losang Tenzin says that here it means excrement.

f.d: lnga pa phyi nang gsang gsum la/ phyi dri chen la gzhi brten pa/ nang skye bdun la gzhi brten pa/ gsang ba phyag rgya ma la brten pa rnams/
5. Outer, inner, and secret preparations: the outer is prepared using the excrement preparation, the inner in dependence on the seven-births compound, the secret in dependence on a consort

drug pa las tshogs tha dad par sbyar ba la/ mig nad/ sbyar dug / mgul 'gags/ gag pa/ mdze nad/ 'du ba rnam bzhi rnams sel ba/ lus zungs rgyas pa/ mkhris pa/ snying rlung / mgo 'khor/ sha dug /lo dug /dug nad kun/ sha mdzer/ 'bras nad/ pho log / sha ro/ sha 'khrig / phol mig / rus nad/ grang nad/ tsha ba/ lhog pa/ rgyal gdon/ bsen mo/ rgyal phran/ klu gdon thams cad zhi ba/ tshe/ bsod nams/ nor/ gzhon sha rnams rgyas pa/ pho rigs/ mo rigs/ yul khams rnams dbang du bsdu ba/ mnan sreg 'phang gsum gyi kha bsgyur/ dug nad bsrung ba/ bu chung ltar gyur pa/ gzhon par gyur pa/ mchin nad sel ba/ rkang 'gyogs/ mkha' la 'phur ba/ bud med brgya la bu 'byin pa/ grang rlung stod nad/ sha g.ya'/ khrag nad rnams sel ba/ mig mthong / mdze rtsa bas 'byin pa/

6. Individual rituals: for pacifying eye diseases, synthetic poisons, throat constriction, gakpa, leprosy, and disorders of the four constituents; for increasing bodily tissues; for pacifying bile, heart winds, mental confusion, meat poisoning, poisoning of unknown origin, all disorders arising from poisoning, shazer, growths, polok, sharo, spasms, abscesses, bone disease, cold disorders, fevers, lhokpa, male and female spirits and demons, local rulers, and nāgas; for increasing one’s lifespan, merit, wealth, and youthful appearance; for bringing men, women, and land under one’s control; for enabling the three controlling activities of subduing, burning, and torma throwing; for protecting against poisons; for becoming like a little child; for becoming young; for curing liver disease; for attaining the fleet-foot superpower and the ability to fly through the sky; for granting the ability to give sons to a hundred women; for curing the upper cold and wind disorder, scabies, and blood disorders; for restoring sight; and for completely curing leprosy
bdun pa dam tshig / brgyad pa lag gnon/ dgu pa yon tan bstan pa rnams dang /
7. Pledges 8. Remedial treatment 9. Qualities

gzhan yang rgya ban rdo rje 'od kyis mkhar chu dpal gyi phug ring mda' sgro can nas gdan drangs pa sman rtag tu ngu'i bcud len skor/ thang sman drang srong don grub kyis gnyal smad brag nag mda' sgro nas spyan drangs pa bdud rtsi 'chi gsos rta ri ma/ rat+na gling pas kong po gsang ba yang mdzod nas spyan drangs pa sman sgrub gsang ba yongs rdzogs/ mchims phu'i dpal lha mo'i brla nas rkus sman gyis bton pa rin chen spungs pa/ lho brag nas dbon gsas khyung rgod kyis phyungs pa bdud rtsi bum pa 'bring po/ la stod dmar po'i gter ma bdud rtsi mar khu'i skor/ gu ru jo tse'i mar khu'i skor/ sangs rgyas gling pa'i mig sman/ rin chen gling pa'i bdud rtsi dngul chu'i bcud len dang mig sman/

Furthermore, Gyaben Dorjé Ö discovered the Elixir of Sadāprarudita Collection from the Dadrochen cave in Karchu Pal. Thangmen Drangsong Döndrup discovered the Tarima Death-Defying Ambrosia from Dadro Black Rocks in Lower Nyal. Ratna Lingpa (1403–79) discovered Creation of Medicine: The Complete Secrets from Kongpo Sangwa Yangzö. Kusa Menpa discovered Pile of Jewels from the thigh of Palden Lhamo in Chimpu. Pönsé Khyungö discovered the Intermediate Ambrosia Vase from Lhodrak. Latö Marpo discovered Liquid Butter Ambrosia Treasure Collection. Guru Jotsé discovered the Liquid Butter Collection. Sangyé Lingpa discovered Eye Medicine. Rinchen Lingpa discovered Ambrosia Mercury Elixir and Eye Medicine.

a+yon gyi slob dpon pad+ma sam+b+ha was kha che bon po'i don du bka' stsal nas tsha ba rong gi brag glang po'i sna dang mi reng 'dra ba'i mtshams gter du sbas pa tsa mi'i rgyal po si hi ha ras rnyed/ lha sras mu ni btsan por phul ba re zhig 'gro don dus la ma bab pas bum thang rin chen dben gnas su gter du sbas/ de nas gtsang ston chos 'bar gyis bton pa chung dpyad pad ma gces phreng cha lag dang bcas pa/

The work Lotus Precious Garland: A Short Work on Medical Treatments and supplementary texts were first taught by Oḍḍiyāna ācārya Padmasambhava for the benefit of Kashmiri Bönpo[410] and hidden as treasure between Elephant Nose Rock and Mireng Drawa in Tsarong. There it was discovered by Sihara, king of Tsami. He offered it to Muné Tsenpo, son of Trisong Detsen, who decided the time was not right for it to be of benefit to others and so hid it at Rinchen Ené in Bumthang. There it was discovered by Tsangtön Chöbar.

d.div: [410] This appears to be the name of a single person from Kashmir who practiced the Bön religion but could possibly refer to a whole community.

f.d: li'i rgyal pos khri srong la phul ba'i ske bcos sog po sman pa byang chub kyis gter nas bton pa/ dug bcos sha mo las dkyus slob dpon nyi ma seng ges mdzad pa bai ros bsgyur zhing mnga' bdag yab sras la phul ba lha sras kyis gter du sbas pa sna nam pas gter nas bton pa/ yan lag gter sgrom smug po lha sras kyis spa gro skyer chur gter du sbas pa lce g.yu bzher gyis bton pa/ bya 'dre'i bcos thabs snubs ston gyi gter ma sogs zab gter nas gdan drangs pa'i sman dpyad mtha' yas shing /

King of Khotan Treatment for the Neck, which was offered to Trisong Detsen, was discovered by the Mongolian Menpa Jangchup. Fungi Therapy for Poisons by the ācārya Sūryasiṃha, translated by Vairocana, and offered to the king and his son, was hidden by Muné Tsenpo and discovered by Nanam Thupa Gyalpo. The Brown Casket Branch Treasure was hidden by Muné Tsenpo at Padro Kyerchu and discovered by Cheyu Sher. Treatment for Bird Demons[411] was discovered by Nuptön. In this way countless medical texts were drawn from the great wealth of treasures.

d.div: [411] Demons who take the form of birds and threaten the lives of children.

f.d: gra pa mngon shes kyis sman spel tshul/

khyad par pad+ma bka'i thang yig las/
skabs su gcig las gcig nyid sdug pa yod: jing dang rgya rnams grog ma'i tshang zhing 'dra: dbu rtse gso rig rgyud gyi gter kha dang : jo mo gling gsum sbas pa'i gter kha 'di: mi bzhag 'don pa'i rtags der bstan nas byung : gter ston gra pa mngon shes zhes bya byung :[203] zhes lung bstan pa ltar bai ro'i yang srid gra pa mngon shes sam mtshan dngos dbang phyug 'bar ni/ gdung rus nas bzung rnam thar cung zad smos na/

In the Lotus Chronicle it says:
When the wall built by Tai Tu[412] is complete, and Jing[413] and the Chinese are like an ants’ nest disturbed, signs will appear for the unearthing of medical treasures from the central pillar and from the three Jomo places; the revealer will be Drapa Ngönshé.[414] This is the prophesy of Drapa Ngönshé (1012–90), an incarnation of Vairocana whose actual name was Wangchuk Bar. I will say a little of his life, beginning with his lineage.

d.div: [203] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 92_sa rtags gter gyi 'byung dus bstan pa/ shog_562_yig phreng 15

[412] Possibly Tai Tsu (927–76), Chinese emperor, military leader, and founder of the Sung dynasty. However, this rendering of the line is taken from the Lotus Chronicles, where it reads, ta’i tus brtsigs pa’i rtsigs pa stugs pa o’ng. This is vastly different from the rendering produced in this text: skabs su gcig las gcig nyid sdug pa yod. Prof. Losang Tenzin suggested the former reading was more probable.
[413] Probably short for Jing Gir Han (Genghis Khan), although he is usually credited as being born in the twelfth century while Drapa Ngönshé is said to be born in the eleventh.
[414] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 92.562.15.

f.d: chos rgyal khri srong lde'u btsan gyi blon po mchims rdo rje spre chung zhes bya ba nor ha cang mi che yang shes rab dang ldan zhing smra mkhas pas rje'i thugs zin pa zhig byung ste/ bsam yas kyi mchod rten sngon po sogs bzhengs pa'i lag dpon mdzad/ de la sras gsum las/ 'bring po lha rjes gra dgas po grong ngam skyi ru bzung / de'i sras gnya' ne nas rim par gnya' chung / dpal legs/ btsan 'od/ zhang se rtsa legs brtan sogs kyi mthar/ legs brtan la sras jo dga'/ de la sras zhang ston chos 'bar/ zhang stag dkar/ zhang bstan dang gsum las/ bgres pa shAkya'i bstan pa la rab tu byung zhing sngags mtshan nyid kyi dge bshes chen por gyur/ zhang stag dkar ba la sras stag tshab/ stag chung / zhan pa/ g.yang bzhi rnams dang / bu mo gnyis te drug byung pa'i che shos stag tshab ni/ lho brag mar pa lo tsA dang dgung mnyam du chu pho byi ba la 'khrungs/ mar pa'i rnam thar du bltams yul gra'i dgas po grong e dgas kyi dgas po dang nor ba sogs 'ga' zhig mchis/

Dharma king Trisong Detsen had a minister from Chimpu known as Dorjé Drechung. He was not wealthy, but he was very intelligent and a good speaker. Consequently, he became a favorite of the king, and he was made supervisor of the construction of the blue reliquary[415] and other projects at Samyé. He had three sons. The middle son, Lhajé, governed Dra Dakpo Drong, or Kyilru. He in turn had a son called Nyané, whose descendents were Nyachung, Palek, Tsenö, Shang Setsa, Lekten, and so on. The last of these, Lekten, had a son called Joga. He in turn had three sons called Shangtön Chöbar, Shangtak Karwa, and Shangten. The eldest entered the doctrine of the Buddha as a monk and became a great geshé in tantra and sutra. Shangtak Karwa had four sons—Taktsap, Takchung, Shenpa, and Yang—and two daughters. The eldest, Taktsap, was born in the male water rat year (1012), the same year as the translator Lhodrak Marpa. In the biography of Marpa there are a few mistakes, such as confusing Taktsap’s birthplace, Dra Dakpo Drong, with the Dakpo in Edak.

d.div: [415] This is the seven-story clay reliquary on the northeast side of the monastery.

f.d: gang ltar dgung lo gzhon nu'i dus snga yul ba'i ra rdzi lo lnga tsam mdzad/ de nas klu mes kyi mkhan bu dge bshes yab shud rgyal ba 'di la rab tu byung / mtshan shes rab rgyal bar btags/ lo lnga'i bar 'dul ba gsan/ rang gi khu bo zhang ston chos 'bar la mdo sngags kyi chos mang ba dang zus la gso dpyad gsan par yang grags/ zhang blon rdo rje bdud 'dul gyi sgrub pa mdzad pas zhal dngos su bstan cing 'phrin las sgrub par khas blangs/ zhang ston chos 'bar 'das pa'i 'ded la de'i slob ma zhig gis spyan drangs/ mdo sngags kyi gzhung la mi 'jigs pa'i spobs pa thob pa'i gsung bshad kyis mkhas pa rnams yid mgu bas dge bshes gra pa dang chos mngon pa la mkhas pas gra pa mngon shes su grags/

In his early years Taktsap was a goatherd for about five years in the region of Ba. Then he became ordained by Geshé Yapshü Gyalwa Ö, disciple of the preceptor Lumé, and received the name Sherap Gyalwa. For five years he studied Vinaya. It is also said that from his uncle, Shangtön Chöbar, he learned sutra and tantra, and from Sü[416] he learned medicine. By meditating on minister Vajra Mārajit, he gained an actual vision of this protector, who vowed to work on his behalf. After Shangtön Chöbar had passed away, one of his disciples invited Drapa Ngönshé to teach. Because of his attainment of a fearless confidence in the sutras and tantras, his teachings gave great pleasure to the scholars attending, and he was given the name Geshé Drapa. Moreover, because he was learned in the Abhidharma, he became known as Drapa Ngönshé—the “one from Dra who knows the Abhidharma.”

d.div: [416] The author comments on the identity of this figure below.

f.d: pha dam pa sangs rgyas la zhi byed sgron ma skor dgu'i gdams pa dang / kha che'i paN+Di ta zla ba mgon po la sbyor drug gi gdams pa rnams dpyis phyin par bzhes/ pho brang bug pa can par bu med pa la gsol ba btab pas/ dpal 'khor lo bde mchog gi sgo nas rigs bskrun pa'i cho ga gnang ste lo dus su bu byung ba'i mtshar kha la gser gri chu dar can/ dngul skyogs sha ba can/ ral gri phung skyu can/ khra sdig pa can rnams phul/

He mastered completely the instructions on the nine Lantern of Pacification collections from Phadampa Sangyé and the instructions on the six yogas of Kālacakra from the Kashmiri pandit Somanātha. A family from Phodrang Bukpachen who had no son came to him for help. He performed a fertility rite using Glorious Cakrasaṃvara, and a son was born within a year. For this he was presented with a tasseled gold-handled knife, a silver ladle embossed with a deer, a sword with an ornamented hilt, and armor embossed with a scorpion.

thang po cher khu ston brtson 'grus g.yung drung sngar rang ga slo+ib ma yin kyang phyis gzhan 'byor la phrag dog pas dgrar langs te mngon shes yod med nyams sad ched nad rdzu btab ste gdan drangs/ grum tse zhig gi khar na bzas gtums te mgo mjug mi shes par byas bzhugs pa'i tshe/ gra pas sku rgyab nas dge ba'i bshes gnyen chen po sku khams ji ltar bdog /phyag rtsa bstan par zhu zhus pas/

In Thangpoché, there was a person called Khutön Tsöndrü Yungdrung[417] who had been a disciple of Drapa Ngönshé but had become envious of his wealth and now regarded him as an enemy. In order to discover if Drapa Ngönshé had clairvoyance or not, he faked an illness and invited him to his house. There he wrapped himself in clothes in such a way that it was not possible to know the back of the person from the front and lay down on a carpet. Drapa addressed him from the rear, “Great geshé, how are you feeling? Please give your hand so that I can read your pulse.”

d.div: [417] Khutön Tsöndrü Yungdrung (1011–75) was one of Atiśa’s three main disciples from central Tibet along with Ngok Lepai Sherap and Dromtön Rinpoché Gyalwai Jungné. He had a reputation for vanity.

f.d: khu ston har gyis bzhengs nas gra pa mngon shes bya ba'i skad po che khyod nad pa'i rgyab mdun mi shes pa'i mngon par shes pa ya mtshar zhes smad pas/ nye gnas la me mched kyi sbyor ba bskur nas thang po che mer bsregs pa sogs mthu stobs lhag par che/ yab shud rgyal ba 'od kyi slob ma las gzus la thug min the tshom gyi gzhi tsam snang yang lo rgyus 'ga' zhig tu rang gi bla ma gzus snying chus bsnyun par chu sman gyis ma 'drongs par zhal rgyun du chu gtor bas dngangs pa dang lhan cig thur mas snying chu 'don rtsis la las kyi rnam par smin pas thur log tu song ste grongs pa'i sdig sbyongs su sna bshud kyi mtshams su gzan g.yang mi 'gyur lhun grub la dpe byas pa'i gra thang / spyan g.yas/ skyil ru/ kun dga' ra/ gzer khang / khong po/ dgra brgya sogs gnas gzhi brgya dang rtsa brgyad bzhengs pa dang / de'i nang nas gtso che ba bdun gyi phud la bzhengs pas bdun phud dga' ldan chos 'khor du grags/

Khutön jumped up and mocked him, “You are renowned as Drapa Ngönshé—the one from Dra with clairvoyance.[418] What a strange kind of clairvoyance it is that does not know the back of a patient from his front!” In response, Drapa Ngönshé initiated the yoga of increasing fire on the outskirts of town, and Thangpoché was burned down. This illustrates the great powers he possessed. Apart from being a disciple of Yapshü Gyalwa Ö, the identity of Sü remains in doubt. However in some accounts he is referred to as Drapa Ngönshé’s lama, who became ill with fluid accumulated in the heart. Medicine did not affect the fluid. Therefore, Drapa, according to tradition, splashed water on him, causing the patient to gasp, and at the same time began to remove the water from his heart with a surgical spoon. However, due to the ripening of karma, the surgical treatment had an adverse effect and the lama died. To atone for his misdeed he constructed 108 monasteries and temples, including Drathang Monastery on the border of Nashu, which was modeled upon Mingyur Lhündrup of Senyang, as well as Chenyé, Kyilru, Küngara, Serkhang, Khangpo, and Dragya. Of these the most important was built at Dünphü and so was called Dünphü Ganden Chökhor.

d.div: [418] Although ngönshé was explained earlier as meaning “knowing the Abhidharma,” it can also mean “clairvoyance,” with ngön meaning “clear” (abhi) and shé meaning “to know.”

f.d:
slob ma gra ston 'bum lhas 'bar gyis gnas skor/ gdon chung ston pas 'brog sga 'dra/ dge bshes lhabs kyis so thang / b+han+d+ha byang chub sems dpas ri phug rnams btab/ zhang blon rdo rje bdud 'dul gyis lung bstan pa ltar bsam yas dbu rtse snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud bzhi po gter nas bton pa bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/
sman gyi bla ma'i gsung rab 'o ma'i bcud/ / rang bzo'i chu yis bslad pa mi 'jug ched/ / gsang ba'i phyag rgyar rgyas btab sgo 'byed pa'i/ / sprul pa'i gter ston gra pa mngon shes zhabs/[204] / zhes gsungs pa ltar dang /

His disciples included Dratön Bumlhé Bar, who founded Nekor, Dönchung Tönpa, who founded Droga Dra, Geshé Lhap, who founded Sothang, and Bhandha Jangchup Sempa who founded Riphuk. In accordance with the prophecy of Rājānaka Vajra Mārajit he revealed the treasure of the Four Medical Tantras: Essence of Ambrosia Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches from the upper reaches of the middle story at Samyé. My lama, the Great Fifth, says:
The pure-milk words of the medicine guru were sealed as a secret mudra to prevent adulteration by the water of self-creation and revealed by Drapa Ngönshé, the incarnate treasure finder.[419]

d.div: [204] bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/ sman gyi bla ma'i gsung rab 'o ma'i bcud/ / rang bzo'i chu yis bslad pa mi 'jug ched/ /gsang ba'i phyag rgyar rgyas btab sgo 'byed pa'i/ /sprul pa'i gter ston gra pa mngon shes zhabs/ /ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[419] Citation untraced.

f.d: rgyud kyi bsdus don sogs bstan bcos brtsams shing 'gro phan mthar rgyas/ dgung lo bdun cu rtsa dgu la slob dpon la snying thur thur log tu song ba'i rnam smin sku tshe 'di gar byang bar slob ma zhig gis snying thur rgyab pa thal skyon gyis zhing gzhan du gshegs/ des gso rig gi gzhung man ngag dang bcas pa dbus pa dar grags la gnang / des ston chen dkon cog skyabs zhes 'khrungs yul mang mkhar tsha lung pa/ rus rog yin pa des dbus su mtshan nyid kyi slob gnyer la byon pa rkang 'bam gyis snyun g.yu thog yon tan mgon pos gsos/ rjes su dmu chus ltem pa dbus pa dar grags kyis bcos/ g.yu chen drug dmar nam mkha' gsal bzhes nas khal stong phrag ri ba de dar grags la phul nas rgyud bzhi rdzogs par zhus/

He composed many treatises, including Essence of the Tantra, and spent his life in extensive service to others. The karma for the failed operation on his master ripened and was purified in his lifetime when at the age of seventy-nine, while being operated on by a disciple, the heart surgery was excessive and he passed away. He passed on his medical works and their oral teachings to his disciple Üpa Dardrak. He in turn gave them to Tönchen Könchok Kyap, who was born in Mangkhar Tsalung and was of the Rok family. Roktön came to the central region to study the sutra vehicle and while there was cured of kangbam by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo. Later he became ill with abdominal dropsy and was cured by Üpa Dardrak. He offered red-cornered turquoise[420] as clear as the sky and worth thousands of khal of barley[421] to Üpa Dardrak and received the complete teachings on Four Tantras.

d.div: [420] Written drug dmar but according to Dungkar (p. 1875) should be gru dmar, “red corners.”
[421] Khal. A measure of about thirty pounds (14 kg).

f.d: g.yu thog yon tan mgon pos sman spel tshul/
10. The Earlier and Later Yuthok Yönten Gönpo

d.i: The contribution of the early Yuthok Yönten Gönpo

f.d:
des sngar rkang 'bam gyi nad gsos pa'i drin lan la g.yu thog par gtad pas/ bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/
dri med ring lugs 'chad byed gang+gA'i rgyun/ / thos bsam tshangs pa'i ral klungs nas 'bebs pa'i/ / g.yu thog mgon po'i ngo mtshar sgyu ma'i 'phrul/ / rigs 'dus dkyil 'khor spro bsdu'i byed por nges/[205] / zhes gsungs pa ltar khyab bdag sman gyi bla ma'i ngo mtshar ye shes sgyu ma'i rnam rol g.yu thog yon tan mgon por bshad srol mi 'dra ba thams cad kyi bka' babs/ de nyid kyi thog ma'i gdung rabs nas cung zad smos na/

In gratitude for curing him of kangbam, Roktön Könchok Kyap entrusted the teachings to Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, of whom my lama the Great Fifth said:
Through his extraordinary illusory works, Yuthok Gönpo brought the Ganges stream of teachings of this flawless tradition down from the study and contemplation valleys of the hair of Brahmā; he is truly one who emanated and withdrew the mandalas of the gathered enlightened families.[422] As this verse says, Yuthok Yönten Gönpo was a manifestation of the extraordinary illusion-like play of the gnosis of the all-pervading medicine guru and the receiver of all the different commentarial traditions. I will say a little of his life beginning from his early ancestry.

d.div: [205] bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos/ dri med ring lugs 'chad byed gang+gA'i rgyun/ /thos bsam tshangs pa'i ral klungs nas 'bebs pa'i/ /g.yu thog mgon po'i ngo mtshar sgyu ma'i 'phrul/ /de gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/

[422] Untraced citation. To emanate and withdraw mandalas is the practice of emanating and withdrawing the deities and mandala assemblies from oneself, as found in the generation-stage practices of highest yoga tantra.

f.d: gso dpyad ring lugs su dang po rgya gar gyi yul pad+ma'i gling gi grong khyer dgu'i dbus ma pad+ma'i snying por lha'i bu dam pa tog dkar po zhes bya ba mi yul du babs nas/ 'dod 'jo'i bas 'o ma phul ba bzhes pas ba nur grags/ de dang bram ze ma chos kyi blo gros bstang dbyal mdzad pas sras bram ze thog 'bebs dang shes rab kyi ral gri gnyis bltams/ de gnyis la yab kyis nor skal gser bum pa re gnang ste rmu thag brgyud lha yul du phyir byon/ shes rab kyi ral gri chang tshong gi bu mo yid 'phrog ma zhes pa sman gyi lha mo'i sprul pa de dang khyim thab tu gyur/ sras dga' ba'i blo gros 'khrungs/ yid 'phrog ma'i thabs 'phrul la brten/ dge 'dun 'dus pa las zhag re la gser khal re 'dzag pa'i glang bu/ drang srong sba mi sbas rgyal po bcing ba/ blon po bskrad pa/ dmag dpon rengs pa/ skye bo thams cad dbang du 'du ba la sogs pa'i 'khor lo dang / gang la btab pa mi 'tshor bar bzung chog pa ral ba'i zhags pa/ 'jam dbyangs sprul pa'i drang srong gis g.yul thams cad las rnam par rgyal ba/ 'byung lnga dbang du 'gyur ba/ klu'i dug bsrung / klu'i bla ma skar rgyal las gang bsam ci 'dod 'grub pa'i 'khor lo/ /

According to medical tradition, in Padmagarbha, the central city of the nine cities in the land of Padmadvīpa in India, the celestial youth Śvetaketu fell to earth. There a wish-granting cow offered him milk, and by accepting it he became known as Banu, “he who drinks cows’ milk.” He met with a brahman woman called Dharmamati, and they produced two sons called Brahman Paṭala and Prajñā Khaḍga. Their father gave them a pot of gold each as their inheritance and returned to the god realms by way of the celestial rope ladder. Prajñā Khaḍga met a beer seller’s daughter named Manohara, who was a manifestation of a medicine goddess, and they slept together on the hearth of the inn. A son was born to them called Nandamati. With her supernormal powers, Manohara was able to procure from the monastic community a calf that produced a measure of gold each day. She was also granted various siddhis, including the following. The rishi Gupta Agupta gave her the charm circle that, among other things, binds kings, expels ministers, stupefies generals, and brings all beings under one’s dominion. He also gave her a noose, made from his own hair, that binds whoever it touches. A rishi who was a manifestation of Mañjuśrī gave her the charm circles for victory in all battles, for control of the five elements, and for protection against the poison of nāgas. From the nāga teacher Tiṣya she gained a wheel that granted all her wishes.

a tsA ra las sman thams cad kyi sa bon thebs pa dang 'bras bu smin pa'i 'khor lo rnams kyi dngos grub gnang / de la brten nas phyug po gser mangs dang / rgyal bu ut+pa la'i gdong la sogs pa dbang du 'dus/ dga' ba'i blo gros rgyal po dang shes rab kyi ral gri blon por gyur/ tsan dan gor sha'i sdong bo lha yul nas drangs/ srin po'i rgyal po ma hA ta btul/ mu stegs kyi bstan pa bsnubs/ 'chi gsos kyi bdud rtsis mi ro mang po gson por bsgyur ba sogs kha thag ring po'i lo rgyus mang ba dang / gser 'dzag gi glang bu tshe dus byas pa'i kha chems bzhin/ drang srong sba mi sba/ bram ze yan lag mda' ring / AtsAR+ya mkha' lding nag po/ paN+Di ta khrus kyi sdong po'am pad+ma 'byung gnas/ rgyal po ut+pa la'i gdong / btsun mo bde byed ma/ blon po blo gros chen po/ rgyal bu dga' ba'i blo gros rnams rgya gar rdo rje gdan du 'dzom thog /

From Acara she received the charm circle for planting all seeds of medicinal plants and bringing them to fruition. With these powers she was able to bring others under her control, including a wealthy man known as Bahu Hiraṇya—“he with much gold”—and the king, Utpalamukha. Nandamati became king and Prajñā Khaḍga became minister. The celestial gośīrṣa sandalwood tree was brought from the god realms. Mahāta, the king of the rākṣas was subdued. The doctrine of the outsiders was destroyed. Many corpses were brought back to life with death-defying ambrosia. These and many other stories are recounted in great detail.[423] In accordance with the dying testament of the calf that produced gold, the rishi Gupta Agupta, the brahman Aṅga Vāṇādirghya, Ācārya Kṛṣna Garuḍa, Pandit Snānamukha or Padmasambhava, King Utpalamukha, Queen Śaṃkara, Minister Mahāmati, and King Nandamati all gathered at Vajrāsana.

d.div: [423] This refers to the life story of Yuthok, in which these stories are told in full: Darmo Menrampa, Brilliant Jewel Treasury: The Sealed Manuscript Biography of the Earlier Noble Yuthok Yönten Gönpo. Rje btsun g.yu thog yon tan mgon po rnying ma’i rnam par thar pa bka’ rgya ma gzi brjid rin po che’i gter mdzod (Beijing: Mi rigs dpe skrun khang, 1982). Translated as part of Tibetan Medicine by Rechung Rinpoché (Delhi: Sri Satguru Publications, 2001).

f.d:
yid 'phrog mas gser srang stong gi me tog gtor te/
rgya gar shar nub rgya nag yul khams dang / / li yul bal yul bod yul la sogs pa'i/ / yul khams rnams su phyi rabs sems can don/ / dug gsum nad sel sman gyi sa bon 'di/ / ji bzhin btab pa de bzhin thebs byas nas/ / lo 'dab rgyas shing 'bras bu smin par shog / ces sman gyi sa bon dang smon lam btab nas rang yul du log /

There Manohara cast a thousand pieces of gold into the air like flowers and prayed:
In India east and west, in the lands of China, in Khotan, Nepal, Tibet, and in other lands, for the sake of future generations, may the seeds of these medicinal plants that cure the diseases of the three poisons take root as they are planted, blossom with full leaves and petals, and ripen with fruit.[424] With the planting of the seeds and the prayer, they returned home.

d.div: [424] Darmo Menrampa, Brilliant Jewel Treasury, p. 45.

f.d:
mi ring bar yid 'phrog mas paN+Di ta pad+ma 'byung gnas spyan drangs sa bon dang smon lam thebs ma thebs dri ba zhus pa'i lan la/
yid 'phrog lha mo'i ngang tshul bdud rtsi ma/ / khyod kyis phyi rabs sems can don phyir du/ / sa bon smon lam gcig tu btab pa'i don/ / sangs rgyas byang sems rnams kyi byin brlabs smin/ / sems can spyi mthun las rnams 'grub pa'i mthus/ / khyod kyis smon lam thebs tshul 'di ltar 'dug /

A short time later Manohara invited Pandit Padmasambhava and asked him if the seeds and prayer had taken root or not. In reply he said:
Ambrosia goddess in the form of Manohara, your simultaneous planting of seeds and prayer, for the benefit of future generations, ripened by blessings of buddhas and bodhisattvas, empowered by the common karma of living beings— this planting of prayer and seeds I will describe.

d.div: rgya gar rdo rje gdan nas nub phyogs su/ / dpag tshad gcig dang rgyang grags phyed kyi sa/ / sman gyi ri bo spos ngad ldan zhes 'dug / de na tsan dan sbrul snying 'ba' zhig dang / / dpag tshad bcu tshun spos kyi ngad dang ldan/ / a ru'i nags tshal la sogs sman gyi rigs/ / ma 'khrungs ma tshang ba ni gcig kyang med/ / nad kyi rigs su gyur pa kun la phan/ / rin chen las grub g.ya' ri brag ri dang / / spang ri la sogs sprul pa'i ri bo yin/ / tsan dan las grub thugs sprul sman gyi bla/ / sku mdog dkar po mtshan dpe'i gzi brjid ldan/ / 'khor rnams thams cad rgyal sras byang sems yin/ / theg dman so skyes bgrod pa'i gnas min cing / / theg chen 'phags pa kho na'i spyod yul yin/

One league and half a krośa west of Vajrāsana in India are the medicinal mountains of Gandhamārdana, on which only the rare snake-heart sandalwood grows and whose aroma can be smelt ten leagues away. There are varieties of medicines, such as myrobalan forests, none not growing, none incomplete, curing every variety of illness and disease; there are smooth slate mountains, rocky mountains, grassy mountains, all magically manifest and made from precious stones. There is found the medicine guru mind manifestation, formed from sandalwood, of the color white, brilliant with the marks and features of enlightenment, an entourage solely of bodhisattva sons of buddhas, not a place reached by ordinary beings or by Hinayana adepts, but a place only enjoyed by noble ones of the Mahayana.

de nas nub phyogs dpag tshad gcig 'das nas/ / rin chen rat+na nor bu las grub pa'i/ / sman gyi grong khyer lta na sdug ces bya/ / mdzes shing bkod legs yid 'ong gzhal med khang / / rin chen las grub ka ba khri drug stong / / rat+na la sogs gdung gi mig mang ris/ / sgo bzhi rta babs bang rim brgyad dang ldan/ / rtsig pa lnga ldan 'dod yon pha gus spras/ / dra ba dra phyed rin chen shar bu 'phyang / / mda' yab pu shu gzhal med khang gi dbus/ / nor bu baiDUR+ya yi gdan steng na/ / sprul sku'i sangs rgyas sman pa'i rgyal po bzhugs/ / mtshan dang dpe byad gzi brjid 'od zer 'bar/ / lha dang drang srong phyi nang 'khor gyis bskor/ / drang srong lha mo rig 'dzin brgyud par bcas/ / ston pa nyi zla gnyis dang rigs gsum mgon/ / kun dga' bo dang 'tsho byed gzhon nu dang / / drang srong rig 'dzin cha byad mang pos bskor/ / 'khor rnams thams cad rgyal sras zhing bkod pa'i/ / bya dang ri dwags la sogs sprul pa'i rigs/ / gseg ma gyo mo ma dag rdzas med cing / / dag pa rab 'byams mchog gi sprul pa'i gnas/ / theg dman nyan rang rnams kyi spyod yul min/ / theg chen rigs sad 'phags pa'i bzhugs gnas yin/ /

West from there at a distance of one league, formed entirely of precious stones and jewels, is the medical city of Sudarśana, its beautiful and well-structured celestial mansion, sixteen thousand pillars, built of precious stones, crisscross jeweled beams, four doors, eight-story portals, five-layered walls embossed with friezes of sensory objects, garlands, half garlands, jeweled guttering, and parapets, and in the midst of this celestial mansion, on a throne of beryl, the king of medicine, the Buddha, manifest enlightened form, radiant with the marks and features of enlightenment, an entourage of Buddhist and outsider gods, with vidyādhara-lineage rishis and goddesses, teachers, the sun and moon, the three family guardians, Ānanda, Kumāra Jivaka, and many others in rishi vidyādhara form. The entire entourage is bodhisattva, the place filled with emanated birds and animals, no trace of gravel, dirt, or mud, a supreme and magic place of total purity, not to be enjoyed by the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, a place for noble ones of awakened Mahayana lineage.

sku sprul sangs rgyas sman bla'i zhal snga nas/ / yid 'phrog lha mos sa bon btab pa gang / / khrus kyi sdong pos ji ltar ltas pa bzhin/ / thebs par 'gyur la smin par gdon mi za/ / 'di nas shar phyogs dpag tshad gcig 'das na/ / sman gyi ri bo spos ngad ldan pa yod/ / sman gyi skyes 'khrungs ri bo'i yon tan rnams/ / khyod rang spyan gyis gzigs pa ltar yin pas/ / yon tan dran par gyis la gsol ba thob/ /

There the body manifestation of Medicine Buddha spoke: “The seeds planted by goddess Manohara, as you have seen Snānamukha, have taken root and without doubt will bear their fruits. One league east from this place are the medicine mountains of Gandhamārdana; the qualities of these mountains of medicinal plants are as you have seen with your own eyes; remember these qualities and make prayers.

'di nas lho phyogs dpag tshad gnyis 'das na/ / sman gyi ri bo 'bigs byed bya ba yod/ / de na tsan dan dmar po'i nag tshal yod/ / se 'bru pi pi ling sogs grang sel sman/ / ma 'khrungs ma tshang ba ni gcig kyang med/ / yon tan ldan pa'i ri bo de nyid na/ / me shel las grub yon sprul sman bla bzhugs/ / sku mdog phyag mtshan rgyan la nges pa med/ / mtshan dpe'i gzi 'bar yon tan sman gyi bla/ / 'khor rnams thams cad sprul pa'i rang bzhin te/ / yon tan dran par gyis la gsol ba thob/ /

“Two leagues south of this place are the medicine mountains of Vindhya. There forests of red sandalwood grow, with pomegranate, long pepper, and so on; there is no kind of medicinal plant for cold disorders that does not grow there. On those mountains blessed with these qualities is the medicine guru, formed from fire crystal, a manifestation of enlightened qualities, of no fixed color, ornaments, or implements, radiant with the marks and features of enlightenment, his entourage are all emanations. Remember such qualities and make prayers.

'di nas nub phyogs dpag tshad drug stong mtshams/ / sman gyi ri bo ma la ya zhes yod/ / de na tsan dan gor sha'i nags tshal dang / / bzang drug sdong po sman sdong bde ba skyed/ / gur gum spang ri tsha sna sna tshogs dang / / sa rdo la sogs 'byung ba'i sman gyi rigs/ / nor bu rin chen sman dang rtsi sman dang / / shing sman thang sman sngo sman srog chags sman/ / mdor na sman gyi rigs su gyur ba kun/ / ma 'khrungs ma tshang ba ni gcig kyang med/ / de na rin chen las grub gsung sprul ni/ / dug gsum nad sel sman pa'i rgyal po bzhugs/ / mtshan dpe'i gzi 'bar 'od zer rab tu 'phro/ / 'khor rnams thams cad dpa' bo mkha' 'gros bskor/ / yon tan dran par gyis la gsol ba thob/ /

“West of here, six thousand leagues away, are the medicinal mountains of Malaya. There forests of gośīrṣa sandalwood grow, the six excellent plants, the medicinal plant sukha, grassy meadows of saffron, various salts, medicine from stones and from the earth, medicinal jewels, extracts, medicinal trees, decoctions, medicinal plants, and animal medicines; in short, no medicine not growing and none incomplete. There, formed from precious stones and jewels, is the manifestation of enlightened speech, the king of medicine, dispeller of the ills of the three poisons, radiant with the marks and features of enlightenment, his entourage all ḍākas and ḍākinīs. Remember such qualities and make prayers.

f.d: 'di nas byang phyogs dpag tshad lnga brgya na/ / sman gyi ri bo gangs can zhes bya yod/ / de na tsan dan sa mchog nags tshal dang / / tig ta nim pa a ka ru la sogs/ / tsha ba'i nad rnams sel ba'i sman gyi nags/ / ma 'khrungs ma tshang ba ni gcig kyang med/ / de na chu shel las grub sman bla de'i/ / 'phrin las sprul pa sman pa'i rgyal po bzhugs/ / mtshan dpe ldan zhing 'gro ba'i don la mkhas/ / 'khor rnams thams cad lha dang lha mo'i tshogs/ / yon tan dran par gyis la gsol ba thob/ / ces sogs dang /

“Five hundred leagues north of here are the medicinal mountains of Himavat. There one finds forests of white sandalwood, forests of chiretta, neem, and aloe wood, every medicine for relieving heat disorders, none not growing or incomplete. There, formed from water crystal, is found the manifestation of my enlightened deeds, the medicine guru, king of medicine, radiant with marks and features of enlightenment, skilled in working for living beings, with an entourage solely of gods and goddesses. Remember such qualities and make prayers.”[425] And further on:

da rung khrus sdong can nga yid la bzung / / sman gyi ri bo rnam bzhi'i gnas su song / / yid 'phrog 'dod don 'grub par gyis shig gsungs/ / bdag gis ri bo bzhi yi gnas su phyin/ / sman pa'i rgyal po'i gsung la 'khrul pa med/ / yon tan dran pas dad pa gting nas g.yos/ / phyi rabs sems can nad las grol bar nges/ / yid 'phrog 'dod don 'grub bo dga' bar gyis/ / zhes gsungs pas dga' zhing mgu la yi rangs par gyur/

“Now, Snānamukha, hold me in your mind, go to the four medicinal mountains, see that the wishes of Manohara are realized.” I, Pandit Snānamukha, went to the four medicinal mountains, the words of the Buddha were not false; remembering these qualities I was moved by profound faith; without doubt future generations will be free of disease; the wishes of Manohara will be realized. Rejoice![426] Manohara was filled with joy.

rgyal po dga' ba'i blo gros la btsun mo dpal gyi khrims mdzes bsus par sras pad+ma'i dpal/ de'i btsun mo dpal sgron la sras dpal ldan phun tshogs/ de'i btsun mo dbyangs kyi lha mo la sras sdong dum skyes/ de'i btsun mo rol rnyed ma la sras rnga chen po dang legs pa'i blo gros gnyis/ rnga chen pos rnga bzo ba'i bu mo gang+gA'i lha mo dang 'grogs pa las sras bi byi dga' byed/ dril bzo ba'i bu mo dang bsdebs pa las sras mo bi lha dga' mdzes ma gnyis 'khrungs/ de gnyis chung grogs su gyur pa gso dpyad kyi bstan pa la zhugs/ rgyun shes kyi bu dang 'tsho byed gzhon nu la gso ba'i gdams pa mang du zhus/ bdud rtsi sman gyi sgrub pa mdzad pas 'chi med tshe'i dngos grub brnyes/

King Nandamati took Śrī Suśīla as queen and they produced a son, Padmaśrī. He took Śrī Pradīpa as his queen, and they produced a son called Śrī Saṃpanna. He took Svaradevi as his queen, and they produced a son, Gaṇiḍa. He took Sītā as his queen, and they produced sons called Dundubhi and Sādhumati. Dundubhi befriended the daughter of a drum maker called Gaṇgadevi, and together they had a son, Biji Rāma. A liaison with the daughter of a bell maker produced a daughter, Amaranandi. These two became childhood friends and studied medicine together. They received many teachings from Ātreya and Kumāra Jivaka. Having mastered the ability to produce ambrosia medicine, they achieved the ambrosia siddhi of longevity.

rje btsun ma sgrol mas/
tshe sngon smon lam btab pa'i mthus/ / khyed rang brgyud par bcas rnams kyis/ gso dpyad bstan pa 'dzin par nus/ / dga' bar gyis la bod du bzhud/ / ces bskul ba ltar mched gnyis bod du byon/

Noble Tārā told them:
By the power of prayers in former lives, you and your descendents will preserve the teachings of the science of medicine. Rejoice, and set off for Tibet. Urged by this prophecy, brother and sister traveled to Tibet.

lha tho tho ri snyan shal gyis pho brang yum bu bla sgang du spyan drangs/ gser srang du ma dang / bi byi dga' byed kyi chung mar lha lcam yid kyi rol cha zhes pa phul/ de la sras sman pa dung gi thor cog can bltams/ cher tshar [206]ba dang yab kyis sman dpyad 'tsho ba'i mdo lnga/ 'grel bshad khog 'bugs/ sa bcad lag len dang bcas pa gnang ste lcam sring gnyis rgya gar du phyir byon/

King Lha Thothori Nyenshal invited them to his palace, Yumbu Lagang. There he presented them with much gold, and to Biji Rāma he gave his daughter, Yikyi Rölcha, as a wife. They produced a son named Dungi Torchok Chen. When he grew up, his father gave him the five Jīva sutras, the commentaries, histories, outlines, and practices. Brother and sister then returned to India.

d.div: [206] 'tshar ba/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

f.d: dung gi thor cog can gyi sras blo gros chen po/ de sras blo gros mtshungs med/ de sras blo gros rgyal mdzod/ de sras blo gros bshes gnyen rnams rim par mnga' bdag khri gnyan gzungs btsan/ 'brong gnyan lde ru/ stag re gnyan gzigs/ gnam ri srong btsan/ srong btsan sgam po rnams kyi bla sman mdzad par grags pa sogs kyi lo rgyus 'di dag la dam pa tog dkar mi yul du phebs pa dang sangs rgyas gser thub kyi dus nas bod yul chags zin pa dang / srin po'i rgyal por mgo nyi shu rtsa gcig yod pa sogs gsung rab spyi dang mi mthun cing / rdo rje gdan nas dpag tshad gcig dang rgyang grags gcig gi sar grong khyar lte na sdug ri bo spos ngad ldan dang thug pa dang / phyogs bzhi'i ri rnams dpag tshad lnga brgya tsam gyi pha rol na yod pa'ang gso dpyad rtsa rgyud dang 'gal la/ lha mi'i rgyud lam la lha'i rmu thag yod pa g.yung drung bon gyi zer sgros dang / ci 'dod 'grub pa'i 'khor lo sogs rig byed kyi gtam rgyud lta bu las yid brtan du rung ba dka' na'ang / dung gi thor cog man chad don la gnas pa nas gong du smos pa blo gros bshes gnyen gyi sras 'dre rje rgya gar rdo rje de yul stod lung skyid snar sman dpyad kyi 'gro don skyong bzhin bzhugs pa las/ nyin gcig zam mo che'i 'gram du bud med mtshar mo zhig dang mjal te bdag gi yul du phebs par zhu zhes nan gyis gsol ba btab/

Dungi Torchok Chen’s son was Lodrö Chenpo. His son was Lodrö Tsungmé. His son was Lodrö Gyalzö. His son was Lodrö Shenyen. It is said that they became the physicians of kings Trinyen Sungtsen, Drongnyen Deru, Takri Nyensik, Namri Songtsen, and Songtsen Gampo, respectively. The list continues with further descendents of physicians and kings. In these various histories, the account of Śvetaketu coming to the human realm, the statement that Tibet was in existence during the era of Buddha Kanaka, that the rākṣa king has twenty-one heads, and so on, do not accord with the teachings in general. Also, to say that one league and one krośa from Vajrāsana the city of Sudarśana meets the mountains of Gandhamārdana, and that the mountains of the four directions are about five hundred leagues away, contradicts the Root Tantra. The concept of a celestial rope connecting the human and god realms is a notion of the Yungdrung Bön, while charm circles such as those that grant all wishes seem Vedic in origin and are difficult to accept. However, the history from Dungi Torchok Chen onward is factual. The son of Lodrö Shenyen, mentioned above, was Drejé Gyagar Dorjé. One day, while he was staying at Tölung Kyina working and caring for the sick, he met a strange woman near a bridge. “Please come to my country,” she insisted.

dar dkar yug gcig brkyang byung ba'i khar zhabs bzhag ma thag / rgyun gtan brag nag po smug 'thibs se ba yod pa de'i sar sngar gzigs ma myong pa'i grong yul mi mang pos gang ba'i dbus/ mkhar chen po bkod pas khyad par 'phags pa 'dod pa'i yon tan du ma dang ldan pa zhig gi nang du phebs/ de na gtso bo sngags nag gi cha byad can mi'i bongs tshod gsum tsam pa ral pa'i thor cog bcings pa zhig nad kyis btab ste 'khor mang po'i dbus na 'khun pa 'don cing 'dug /de'i sngas mgor dar zab kyi stan mthon po'i khar spyan drangs/ khyod kyi nad 'di rgyu rkyen ci las byung gsungs pas/ kho na re/ bdag gis yul che ge mo zhig tu ser ba phab pas sngags pa nus pa dang ldan pa zhig gi thun phog pa lags zhes lus kyi gso bsal nas bstan byung bas/ sha rus pags pa rtsa la sogs par yungs kar mang po thim nas 'dug /der khyung lnga dang dngul chus nang nas 'phul/ byug pa rgyan 'khor phyi nas byugs pas skad cig la klu bdud sngags pa'i gzugs can de nad las thar/ bya dga'i gtang rag la rdzas longs spyod du ma dang rang rtags srog gi snying po phul/

He stepped onto a white cloth she had unfurled and immediately found himself on a large black cliff shrouded continuously in dark mists. Before him lay a city he had never seen before filled with people. In the middle of the city sat a large castle decorated with exalted sensory objects. On going inside, he found the lord of the castle, dressed as a black tantric practitioner with his hair tied up on his head; he was the size of three ordinary men. Surrounded by his servants, he lay there struck down by illness, groaning with pain. At the head of his bed was a high seat draped with the best cloth to which the doctor was invited. “What brought about your illness?” The doctor asked. “I brought about hail in a particular country, and so I was hit with mustard seeds empowered by a powerful tantric practitioner.” “Show me,” said Drejé Gyagar Dorjé. The lord of the castle took off his clothes and revealed the places where the mustard seeds had penetrated flesh, bones, and veins. The doctor treated him internally with the five-garuḍa compound and mercury, and externally with an ornamented wheel massage. Immediately the demonic nāga in the form of a tantric practitioner was cured. As reward the nāga presented him with many gifts and enjoyments and, as a sign of his gratitude, offered his life to the doctor.

de nas snga ma'i bud med des dar yug brkyang byung pa'i steng zhabs bzhag ma thag zam sner phebs/ mo na re/ ngas kyang khyed la bya dga' 'bul bas sang nyin da tsam 'dir byon cig zer rlung 'tshub gcig tu yal/ phyi nyin zam khar byon pas 'brug glog char mun chen po'i gseb nas bud med rked pa yan gser g.yus brgyan pa'i ro gcig chus khyer ba zam pa'i 'khor la chags byung bas pho nya mos khas blangs ba'i bya dgar mkhyen/ ro chur sbyangs gser g.yu bsnams te khang thog tu bkram nas skams pas lug rdzi sogs kyi mthong nas g.yu'i thog 'dug go byas pas de nas bzung g.yu thog par grags/

The woman again unfurled the cloth for him to step onto, and immediately he was back at the bridge. “I too wish to offer you a gift,” she said. “Come here tomorrow at this time.” With that she disappeared into a whirlwind. The next day he returned to the bridge, and amid rain, thunder, lightning, and darkness, he saw under the bridge, being carried along in the river, the corpse of a woman ornamented from the waist upward with gold and turquoise. He understood this to be the gift promised by the messenger. He took the gold and turquoise, casting the body back into the river. These he spread on the roof of his house to dry. Local shepherds and others, on seeing this, exclaimed that he had a turquoise roof. From then on he was known as Yuthok—“roof of turquoise.”

de nas 'dre rje chen pos bdud rtsi sman sgrub sogs kyi don du 'phags yul du bteg /lho phyogs dpal gyi ri bor dpal mgon 'phags pa klu sgrub la gser srang stong phul nas mgo thig rin chen gnad 'grel cha lag kha skong dang bcas pa zhus/ pad+mo'i yul gling du byon pas tshong 'dus zhig na bram ze gzi brjid shin tu che ba dang mjal/ dri ba dri lan byas pas bi byi dga' byed yin par ngo 'phrod/

Then the great Drejé went to India to master the practice of ambrosia medicine. In the south, on Śrīparvata, he offered the glorious protector, Ārya Nāgārjuna, a thousand pieces of gold and requested Precious Essential Points Commentary on the Anatomy of the Head, together with all auxiliary and supplementary material. He then traveled to Padmavīpa and in a marketplace met a radiant brahman. After some questions the brahman introduced himself as Biji Rāma.

des khyod rang lho phyogs tsan dan gyi nags gseb tu nga dang sman pa'i rgyal po dbyer med du gsol ba thob gsungs pa ltar byas pas sman gyi bla ma/ lha mo brgyad drang srong mched gsum/ 'tsho byed gzhon nu rnams kyis rim par bdud rtsi sman sgrub cha lag dang bcas pa gnang ste bod du phebs/

“Go down south to the sandalwood forest and pray to me and the king of medicine as inseparable,” said Biji. Drejé followed this command, and there the medicine guru, the eight goddesses, the three rishi brothers, and Kumāra Jivaka all appeared and bestowed upon him the practice of achieving ambrosia medicine, together with all auxiliary material. He then returned to Tibet.

btsad po'i sras mo dga' skyong ma bya ba khab tu bsus par sras g.yu thog khyung po rdo rje bltams/ dad brtson shes rab ldan pas sku na phra mo nas mkhas pa'i go 'phang thob/ bdud rtsi sman sgrub mdzad pas lha mo dang drang srong rnams zhal gzigs/ de'i mthus nad pa'i lus la nad gang yod lag mthil du skyu ru ra bzhag pa bzhin gzigs/

There he married Gakyongma, the daughter of a local governor, and they produced a son called Yuthok Khyungpo Dorjé. Blessed with faith, perseverance, and intelligence, he became wise at an early age. With the attainment of ambrosia medicine, he received visions of the goddesses and the rishis. With these powers he could see any illness in a patient’s body as clearly as a berry in the palm of one’s hand.

yab shin tu mnyes te/
bu khyod skyes pa pha yi dpal/ / pha las bu dga'i skyes bu ni/ / yon tan mgon po zhes pa 'byung / / gso dpyad bstan pa'i nyi ma 'char/ / zhes sogs lung bstan pa ltar/ khyung po rdo rje'i khab tu rgya ba chos sgron bzhes pa las sras g.yu thog yon tan mgon po bltams/

His father was delighted:
Son, you being born is a father’s glory, and from the son of the father the joyous gift of a son, one whose name will be Yönten Gönpo, shining like the sun of the medical teachings.[427] Just as he had prophesized, Khyungpo Dorjé married Gyasa Chödrön, who gave birth to the son, Yuthok Yönten Gönpo.[428]

d.div: [428] The present account is of the eighth-century Yuthok Yönten Gönpo. The later Yuthok, or Yuthok the younger, was born in the twelfth century, and a short biography of him follows in the next section.

f.d: lhums su zhugs pa dang 'khrungs pa'i tshe dge mtshan gyi snang ba brjod las 'das pa byung / dgung lo gsum pa'i thog sman pa'i rgyal po drang srong rig 'dzin pho mo mang po'i zhal gzigs/ klog yig dang gso dpyad phal che ba bslab sbyangs la ma bltos par rang shugs kyis mkhyen/ slob ma dge ba rdo rje bya ba g.yog la bskos nas 'gro ba nad pa'i don byed du bcug / stod lung 'dre lung nag po'i pha bong reg pa dug can gyi steng tshogs 'khor bskor/ sman bla'i dkyil 'khor zhal gzigs pas thugs 'ur nas pha bong 'dam ltar brdzis/ dgung lo lnga par yab la bdud rtsi sman sgrub/ sman bla lha mo rig 'dzin brgyud pa dang bcas pa'i sgrub thabs rjes gnang zhus te gsol ba btab pas/ sman rgyal dngos su byon nas byin gyis brlabs/ dgung lo bcu bzhes pa na rgyal po mes ag tshom gyis spyan drangs bsam yas su phebs/ nyams sad phyir brang ti rgyal mnyes mkhar phug la sogs pa bod kyi sman pa rnams dang rtsod bcug pas kun las rnam par rgyal te bod sman mkhas pa mi dgu'i gtso bor gyur/

At his conception and birth, indescribable and wonderful omens were observed. From the age of three onward, he had visions of the king of medicine, rishis, and male and female vidyādharas. For the most part he did not need to study medicine or learn how to read and write, as it came to him naturally. His father gave him the student Gewa Dorjé as a servant, and he was encouraged to work for living beings. Once in Tölung, on Poisonous to Touch Rock in Drelung Nakpo, while performing a gaṇacakra offering feast, he had a vision of the Medicine Buddha mandala. His heart leapt, and as a result he left footprints on the rock as if it were made of mud. When he was five he requested from his father the ambrosia medicine practice and the practice permission and sādhanas for the practice of Medicine Buddha, goddesses, and the vidyādhara lineage. During his prayer requests Medicine Buddha came in person and gave him blessings. At the age of ten he was invited to Samyé Monastery by King Mé Aktsom. As a test, the king asked him to debate with the other doctors, such as Drangti Nyekhar. He defeated them all and became foremost among the nine wise Tibetan physicians.

bsam yas na sman pa sus kyang gso bar ma nus pa'i nad pa zhig yod pa rtsib ma glo bar 'byar bar mkhyen te rta rgyugs kyi sgo nas gsos pa dang / sman pa kun rgyug bya ba g.yu thog par 'gran sems phrag dog shin tu che ba de'i bu mo zhig bong bu dang phag pho mo 'dod pa spyod pa mthong bas yid rnam par myos te la phug smyon par pho dbang gi gzugs bcos mo rang gi mtshan mar bcug nas bshud pas la phug gi rtsa ba chad de lus pa las b+ha ga'i srin bu khros nas 'chi bar thug /thabs ci byas kyang ma phan pa'i tshe du tshwa sbyar ba snar blug ma thag sbrid pa bstud mar byung ste thon pa/ rgyal po'i spyan dang tshems snyun pa sman dang dpyad cher mi dgos par dngas pa sogs 'tsho byed gzhon nus gsos la 'gran nus pa'i thabs tshul dang ldan/

In Samyé was a patient no doctor could cure. Yuthok saw that his rib had attached itself to his lung and cured him by tying him behind a trotting horse. A doctor called Küngyuk was very jealous of and competitive with Yuthok. He had a daughter who had watched a pair of donkeys and a pair of pigs mating. This had made her mad with desire, and so she had fashioned a radish into the shape of a penis and inserted it into her vagina. However, the back-and-forth movement broke the radish, and it was lodged inside. This disturbed her genital organisms, bringing her close to death. After all else had failed, Yuthok prepared fumigating salt and burned it under her nose, causing her to sneeze repeatedly until the radish emerged. He cured the king, who had problems with his eyes and teeth, using hardly any medicine or surgery, and in this way his methods were comparable with those of Kumāra Jivaka Bhṛtya.

mchims phur rdo rje phag mo'i sprul pa rtog pa'i rang grol ma dang mjal/ nyams rtogs kyi mgur dang bstod dbyangs mdzad pa'i mthar/ sman pa'i rgyal po'i zhal gzigs/ bdud rtsi sman sgrub phrid sman khrid ral skor lnga'i phyag lan dang bcas pa gnang / dgung lo nyer lnga pa la mkha' 'gro'i lung bstan ltar slob dpon pad+ma sam+b+ha war bar chad mi 'jug pa'i sngags dang rdzas srung zhus nas rgya gar la byon/ bal po'i sman pa d+ha na shI la har man ngag tshad pa sgos bcos dang rngam ru sti ba'i man ngag zhus/ rgya bal gyi mtshams ri kun tu rgyur bod kyi lo tsA ba bai ro tsa na dang mjal/ gsung gleng zhib par byung / rgyud bzhi nged bod du ma sleb bar gter du mi sba bar gsol ba btab/

In Chimpu he met a manifestation of Vajravārāhī called Tokpai Rang Drölma. He sang a song of his meditation experience, and she sang a song of praise. At the end he had a vision of Medicine Buddha, who bestowed upon him the Garland of Ambrosia Medicine, Ambrosia Medicine Practice, and the Medical Teachings on Practices of the Five Sword Collections. As predicted by a ḍākinī, he set out for India at twenty-five years old, having first requested Ācārya Padmasambhava for protective substances and mantras to dispel hindrances. He met the Nepalese doctor Dhanaśīlaha,[429] from whom he received teachings on treatments for specific heat disorders and the practice of cupping. On the Nepal-India border at Parivrājaka Mountain, he met the translator Vairocana. They discussed many topics in great detail, and Yuthok asked him not to hide Four Tantras as treasure until he, Yuthok, had returned to Tibet.

d.div: [429] This person’s name is very close to that of Dharmaśīla, mentioned earlier as one of the nine royal physicians and also from Nepal.
