The lord of wealth (Pūrṇa) has thirty thousand verses, the father of Pūrṇa,[491] one hundred thousand. Limitless tantras have been explained by those gods and demigods who have faith in the Conqueror. These passages give some idea of the number of tantras.

d.div: [247] sde dge_805_bka'/ rgyud/ wa_'phags pa dpung bzang gis zhus pa/ le'u/ 10_shog_136_na4
[491] Notes Explaining the Text of the Questions of Subāhu Tantra identifies Pūrṇa as Vaiśravaṇa.

f.d: theg dman gyi lugs/

theg dman gyi lugs/ mngon mdzod gnas dang po las/
chos kyi phung po brgyad khri dag / gang rnams thub pas gsungs de dag / tshig gam ming yin de dag ni/ / gzugs dang 'du byed dag tu 'dus/ /
kha cig bstan bcos tshad ces zer/ / phung po la sogs gtam re yin/ / spyod pa rnams kyi gnyen por ni/ / chos kyi phung po mthun par gsungs/[248] /

In the first chapter of the Treasury of Abhidharma it says:
Eighty thousand collections of Dharma taught by the mighty Buddha are either word forms or names included in form and compositional factors.
Some say it has the measure of a treatise,[492] that it refers to each teaching of the aggregates, and so on. It is taught that the Dharma collections correspond to practices to counteract particular behaviors.[493]

d.div: [248] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod kyi tshig le'ur byas pa/ gnas/ 1_sh+loka25_nas 26_shog_3_na1
[492] Bstan bcos, śāstra.
[493] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa, 1:25–26, Toh 4089 Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 3a1.

f.d:
zhes pa la rang 'grel la sogs pa thams cad las rgyas pa mdzod 'grel rgyal sras mar/
sangs rgyas kyi gsung zhes bya ba 'di chos gang zhig ce na/ gang ming gi tshogs dang / tshig gi tshogs dang / ye ge'i tshogs rnams go rims su bkod pa dang / go rims su bzhag pa dang / go rims su yang dag par sbyar ba'o zhes 'byung ste/ chos mngon pa ltar na chos kyi phung po brgyad khri po de dag gzugs kyi phung po dang / 'du byed kyi phung pos bsdus pa yin no/ / mdo las ni/ bdag gis bcom ldan 'das las mngon sum du chos kyi phung bo brgyad khri lhan cig gzung ngo zhes kyang 'byung ngo / /sde pa gzhan gyi mdo las kyang chos kyi phung po brgyad khri bzhi stong 'byung ngo / /

In the Bodhisattva Abhidharma Commentary, a work more extensive than the auto-commentary and other commentaries, it says:
Just after that it says,[494] “What is this Dharma known as the speech of the Buddha? It is a collection of names, word forms, and syllables that were set down in order, formed in order, joined in order.” According to followers of the Abhidharma, the eighty thousand collections of Dharma belong to the category of form and compositional factors. A sutra says: “I have held all at once[495] the eighty thousand categories of Dharma heard directly from the Bhagavān.” Other types of sutra talk of 84,000 categories.

d.div: [494] Although this phrase is not reproduced in the text, I have included it here as it is found in the commentary to show that the commentary is quoting from another work entitled Entering Gnosis.

[495] Lhan cig, “together.” The quote as cited in Gendün Drup’s commentary to the Abhidharmakośa (Dam pa’i chos mngon pa’i mdzod kyi rnam par bshad pa thar lam gsal byed) has lhag cig, meaning “more than,” and is a source for asserting the existence of more than eighty thousand collections.

kha cig bstan bcos tshad ces zer/ /zhes bya ba ni kha cig na re/ chos kyi phung po'i mdo 'di ni bstan bcos kyi chad tsam mo zhes zer ro/ / de ni sh+loka drug stong ngo zhes bya ba ni bstan bcos chos kyi phung po zhes bya ba de'i gzhung gi tshad ni sh+loka drug stong yod de/ chos kyi phung po brgyad khri po de dag ni nub ste/ 'di gcig pu lus so zer ro/ /

“Some say it has the measure of a treatise.” On this some say “This Sutra of Collection of Dharma (Dharmaskandhasūtra)[496] is about the length of a treatise.” “That has six thousand verses” means that a treatise has a textual length of six thousand verses. The eighty-thousand collection has diminished, and this is all that is left.”

[496] Degé has “this collection of Dharma” (chos kyi phung po ’di), but I have gone with the reading from the text (chos kyi phung po’i mdo ’di). According to Abhidharma tradition, this sutra was compiled by Śāriputra.

phung po la sogs gtam re yin zhes bya ba ni gzhan dag ni zer ro zhes bya bar tshig kho nas drang ste/ phung po la sogs pa'i gtam re re ni chos kyi phung po yin la/ de dag kyang chos kyi phung po brgyad khri'i grangs yin par 'chad par byed do/ /

“Others say that the eighty thousand refers to each teaching on the aggregates and so on,” meaning that each teaching on the aggregates and so on is one Dharma collection (dharmaskandha). These are explained as making up the eighty thousand collections.

f.d:
spyod pa rnams kyi gnyen por ni/ /chos kyi phung po mthun par gsungs/ /zhes bya ba ni sngar bshad pa'i phyogs gsal ba'i phyir ram nges par gzung ba'i don yin no/ / 'dod chags dang / zhe sdang dang / gti mug dang / nga rgyal la sogs pa spyod pa tha dad pas zhes bya ba la sogs pa zhes bya ba'i sgras ni lta ba dang the tshom la sogs pa bsdus te/ sems can kha cig ni 'dod chags spyod pa yin la/ zhes nas/
zhe sdang ba ltar 'chos pa yin te/ de dag gi gnyen por bcom ldan 'das kyis de dag gsungs pa yin no/[249] / zhes bshad pa dang /

“It is taught that the Dharma collections correspond to practices to counteract particular behaviors.” This is said either to refute the previous point or as a definitive statement. “Differentiated by behaviors such as desire, anger, ignorance, pride, and so forth.” The phrase “and so forth” includes doubt and wrong views. The behavior of some beings is desire…. And so on, up to:
Some abandon anger but pursue desire. As practices to counteract these behaviors, the Bhagavān taught these Dharmas.[497]

d.div: [249] sde dge_4092_bstan/ mngon pa/ gu_slob dpon rgyal ba'i sras grags pa'i bshes gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod kyi 'grel bshad don gsal ba/ gnas/ 1_shog_47_ba5
[497] Yaśomitra, Abhidharmakośaṭīkā, chap. 1, Toh 4092 Tengyur, mngon pa, gu, 47b5.

f.d: theg chen gyi lugs la/

dbu ma chos kyi bshes gnyen gyis mdzad pa mngon rtogs rgyan gyi 'grel pa tshig gsal las/
spyod pa'i gnyen por zhes pa ni 'dod chags la sogs pa rtsa ba'i spyod pa bzhi dang / re re'i yang phye bas brgyad khri bzhi stong rnams so/ / de dag gi gnyen por gyur pa ni thub pa chen po'i chos kyi 'khor lo ma lus pa ste/ chos ni bstan pa'i chos gtso bor byas pa'o/ / 'khor lo ni gdul bya'i rgyud la 'pho bar snang bas sam tshogs kyi don gyi 'khor lo ste sgra'i don ni de dag dang nye ba'i phyir ro/ / ma lus pa ni chos kyi phung po brgyad khri bzhi stong ste/ de la chos kyi phung po gcig gi tshad ji tsam zhe na/ de gcig la ni tshig le'ur byas pa stong nyid de tshigs su bcad pa re re la yang yi ge'i 'bru sum cu rtsa gnyis nyid do/ / de ltar na chos kyi phung po thams cad la ni tshigs su bcad pa bye ba phrag brgyad dang 'bum phrag bzhi bcur 'gyur ro/ /

In the Clear Words Commentary to Ornament of Realization by Mādhyamika Dharmamitra it says:
“As practices to counteract particular behaviors” refers to the four main kinds of behaviors—desire and so forth—which when subdivided become the 84,000 types of behaviors. Every wheel of Dharma of the mighty Buddha exists as practices to counteract these behaviors. “Dharma” here mainly refers to the Dharma that is taught. “Wheel” is used to portray the image of something moving toward the mind of the disciple. It also means “collection” or “gathering.”[498] These two meanings of the word closely reflect its use here. “Every” means all 84,000 heaps of Dharma. So, what is the measure of one heap of Dharma? It is one thousand verses of thirty-two syllables each. Therefore, the collections of Dharma in their entirety consist of 84 million verses.

d.div: [498] The Sanskrit cakra (“wheel”) has many meanings, one of which is “gathering,” or “assembly.”

'di ni re zhig thun mong gi grangs su bgrang ba'o/ / theg pa bla na med pa'i dbang du byas te/ dbang po'i glang po che rab brtan gyis 'khur bar 'os pa'i snag tshas ni chos kyi phung po gcig 'dri bar nus so/[250] / zhes gsungs te/ de ltar byas na mdo gang dag las 'phags pa lhas byin gyis glang po che lnga stong gis 'khur bar 'os pa'i glegs bam rnams kha ton du brjod par byed do/ / zhes gsungs pa 'di yang rigs par 'gyur ro/[251] /

This is the shared position. The position of the peerless vehicle is, “One Dharma collection is the amount that can be written with a load of ink that can be suitably carried by Indra’s powerful elephant.” If that is so, the statement from a sutra that talks of Lord Devadatta reciting the number of volumes able to be carried by five thousand elephants also makes sense.

[250] sde dge_3796_bstan/ sher phyin/ nya_slob dpon chos kyi bshes gnyen/ shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i man ngag gi bstan bcos mngon par rtogs pa'i rgyan gyi tshig le'ur byas pa'i 'grel bshad tshig rab tu gsal ba/ shog_19_na7
[251] sde dge_353_bka'/ mdo sde/ aH_thabs mkhas pa chen po sangs rgyas drin lan bsab pa'i mdo/ shog_167_na6

f.d:
zhes dang /
chos kyi phung po de dag kyang sde snod gsum nyid du rnam par gzhag ste/ zhes bshad pa'i mdo gang dag ces drin lan bsab pa dang /[252] sde snod gsum ni 'dul ba mdo sde mngon pa gsum yin la/

Further on the text says:
These collections of Dharma are presented as the three baskets of scripture.[499] “Statement from a sutra” in the above passage refers to the Sutra of Repaying the Kindness of the Skillful Buddha,[500] and the three baskets are those of Vinaya, Abhidharma, and Sutra.

d.div: [252] sde dge_353_bka'/ mdo sde/ aH_thabs mkhas pa chen po sangs rgyas drin lan bsab pa'i mdo/ shog_167_na6
[499] Abhisamayālaṃkāraṭīkāprasphuṭapadā, Toh 3796 Tengyur, sher phyin, nya, 19a7.
[500] Toh 353 Kangyur, mdo sde, ah, 167a6.

f.d: theg chen thun mong min pa'i lugs la/

sprin chen po'i mdo'i dam pa'i chos kyi dkyil 'khor gyi phung po zhes bya ba le'u sum cu rtsa bdun pa las/
mdo sde rnams ni re re la/ / gang+gA'i klung gi bye snyed kyis/ / bsgyur pa'i don ni mang yod ces/ / chos gsungs pas ni nges par bstan/[253] / zhes sogs gzhan du bshad zin pa dang / dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting 'dzin gyi mdo las/
lha'i bu de bzhin gshegs pas chos ji snyed mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas pa'i chos de las bye bas cha'am/ bye ba stong gi cha'am bye ba brgya stong gi cha'i cha shas kyang ngas ma bshad do/ / gang ngas bshad pa de las bye ba brgya stong gi cha shas kyang dge slong kun dga' bos ma gzung ngo /[254] / zhes dang /

The thirty-seventh chapter of the Great Cloud Sutra, entitled “Collection of Sacred Dharma Mandalas,” says:
As much Dharma has been spoken, and therefore definitely taught, as the number of sutras multiplied by the number of grains of sands in the Ganges.[501] The meaning of this verse has already been explained elsewhere. The Samādhi of Śūraṅgama Sutra states:
Celestial son, of the Dharma of the Tathāgatha, I have not taught a ten millionth part, a ten thousand millionth part, a million millionth part of the Dharma of the fully enlightened Buddha. Of what I have taught, the monk Ānanda does not hold even a million millionth part.[502]

d.div: [253] sde dge_232_bka'/ mdo sde/ wa sprin chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 37_shog_172_na3
[254] sde dge_132_bka'/ mdo sde/ da dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting nge 'dzin gyi mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_300_na3
[501] Mahāmeghasūtra, Toh 232 Kangyur, mdo sde, wa, 172a3.
[502] Śūraṅgamasamādhisūtra, Toh 132 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 300a3.

f.d:
phal po che'i sangs rgyas kyi chos bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i le'u bam po drug cu re drug pa las/
sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rnams ni sku gcig la dbus sangs rgyas kyi zhing brjod du med pa'i yang brjod du med pa'i rdul shin tu phra ba snyed byin gyis brlabs te/ dbu re rer yang ljags sangs rgyas kyi zhing brjod du med pa'i yang brjod du med pa'i rdul snyed byin gyis brlabs nas/ de dag re res yang dbyangs kyi yan lag dang / sgra skad kyi gsung sangs rgyas kyi zhing brjod du med pa'i yang brjod du med pa'i rdul shin tu phra ba snyed re re brjod de/ chos kyi dbyings ma lus pa'i sems can gyi khams thams cad go bar mdzad cing dbyangs kyi yan lag dang sgra skad kyi gsung re res kyang mdo sde sangs rgyas kyi zhing brjod du med pa'i yang brjod du med pa'i rdul shin tu phra ba snyed bshad la/[255] zhes bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i spyod yul du bzhag cing /

In the sixty-sixth fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sutra, it says in the chapter called the “Inconceivability of the Dharmas of the Buddha”:
With a single body the bhagavān buddhas can grant blessings with as many heads as the number of very subtle particles in an indescribable-beyond-indescribable number of buddha realms.[503] In each head they can grant blessings with as many tongues as the number of particles in an indescribable-beyond-indescribable number of buddha realms. With each tongue they can speak with as many voices and languages as the number of very subtle particles in an indescribable-beyond-indescribable number of buddha realms, and be understood by every living being of every realm possessed of every conceivable disposition. Each voice and each language teaches as many sutras as the number of very subtle particles in an indescribable-beyond-indescribable number of buddha realms.[504] This passage expresses the inconceivable range of activity of the buddhas.

d.div: [255] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ gsangs rgyas kyi chos bsam gyi mi khyab pa'i le'u/ 39_bam po/ 4_shog_32_ba3

[503] The Avataṃsaka has its own system of numbering, and “an indescribable-beyond-indescribable number” is an actual number somewhere near ten to the power of 136. However, see Cleary, vol. 2, p. 201.
[504] Avataṃsakasūtra, chap. 4, Toh 44 Kangyur, phel chen, ga, 32b3.

f.d:
bcom ldan ral gris mngon pa kun las btus kyi 'grel par/
nges tshig ni 'pho ba dang gcod pa dang sngon du 'gro bar 'khor lo rin po che dang 'dra bas chos kyi 'khor lo'am/ rjod byed kyi chos du ma spungs pa la chos kyi phung po'am gsung rab kyi tshogs zhes bya'o/[256] / zhes pa'i bka' de dag gro ga shing shun shog bu la sogs pa mdog bsgyur ba dang ma bsgyur ba gang rung du glegs bam mam

Chomden Raldri (1227–1305), in his Commentary to the Compendium of Knowledge, says:
The etymological explanation is that because it moves, severs, and paves the way like a precious wheel, we talk of the wheel of Dharma. Alternatively, because it is a collection of spoken Dharma, we talk of collections of Dharma or the collection of teachings.[505] These teachings of the Buddha inscribed on paper made from birchbark,[506] dyed or not dyed, are known as “volumes.”

d.div: [256] bcom ldan rig ral gyi mngon pa kun btus kyi 'grel pa'i dpe lag son ma gyur mod/ gzhung 'di mtshan 'bras spungs dpe rnying dkar chag tu thon pas deng bzhugs par snang /
[505] Untraced.
[506] Grog ga, kṛtti.

f.d: legs par sbyar ba lha'i skad kyi dbang du btang na/ pU la dang pusta pi Da tshogs pa la'o/ /zhes pa'i byings pusta la/ kr-i tra gnyis par/ tri bu Na dag gos/ rkyen bu byin/

Concerning the etymology of this word in the celestial language of Sanskrit,[507] “Pūla and pustaviḍi mean ‘collection.’” Therefore the root is pusta. The affix vu is added because the second kṛta rule says, “tṛ, vu, and ṇ” (the affixes tṛ, vu and ṇ can be added to roots).

d.div: [507] The citations giving the meanings of the verbal roots are from the Sutra of Roots (Dhātusūtra) by Pūrṇacandra. The grammatical rules, or sūtras, are from the Sarasvati Grammar Sutra by Anubhūti. I have added explanations of the rules in parentheses. They are from the commentary on this sutra by Troru Tsenam.

f.d: kr-i tra drug par/ yu bu dz+ha rnams kyi an a ka an+ta rnams so/ /zhes pas bu byin a kar bsgyur
The vu becomes aka because the sixth kṛta rule says “yu and vu become ana and aka” (when affixes yuṭ and vuṇ shed their anubandha, yu becomes ana and vu becomes aka).
gong gi byings mtha' ta'i a brjod don yin pas phyis/
The final a of the letter ta on the root is for pronunciation purposes and is elided.
tra srog med a la drangs/ /
The letter t without its life-giving vowel is brought to the a of aka.
mthar don tsam gyi rnam dbye dang po si byin pas/ sra ra dag gi rnam bcad byas pas pu sta kaH_zhes

The first case ending si, which merely expresses the nominative, is added. This ending becomes a visarga because “s and r, visarga” (affixes s and r on nouns and word forms become visarga. The i of the first case si is elided because it is for pronunciation purposes). This results in the formulation pustakaḥ.
deng sang zur chag pa'i po ti'am glegs bam du grags pa sogs 'byung bar
These days we use the corruption po ti, which means “volume.”

sgra don ni/ 'phags pa thogs med kyis gtan la dbab pa bam po nyer gcig par/
rig pa'i gnas lnga bstan pa gang yin pa de la nang rig pa ni rig pa'i gnas thams cad dang / bstan bcos thams cad dang / gzhung lugs thams cad kyi nang na mchog dang gtso bo yin no/[257] / zhes dang /
sangs rgyas kyi bka' de yang mdor bsdu na tshul drug gis khong du chud par bya ste/ de kho na'i don gyi tshul dang / thob pa'i tshul dang / bshad pa'i tshul dang / mtha' gnyis rnam par spangs pa'i tshul dang / bsam gyis mi khyab pa'i tshul dang / dgongs pa'i tshul gyis so/[258] / zhes tshul drug gam/

Concerning the meaning of the term,[508] in the twenty-first fasicle of Ascertainment from Stages of the Yogacaryā by Ārya Asaṇga it says:
Of the five sciences, the inner science is the supreme and most important of all the sciences, all treatises, and all scripture.[509] Also:
In brief, the words of the Buddha should be understood in six ways: in terms of the truth of reality, in terms of attainment, in terms of explanation, in terms of abandoning the two extremes, in terms of inconceivability, and in terms of the Buddha’s intention.[510]

d.div: [257] sde dge_4038_bstan/ sems tsam/ zhi_thogs med/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba/ bam po/ 21_shog_187_na2
[258] sde dge_4038_bstan/ sems tsam/ zhi_thogs med/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba/ bam po/ 21_shog_187_na4
[508] This refers to bka’ (words) or to chos (Dharma), both in their sense of being the words of the Buddha.
[509] Yogacaryābhūmiviniścayasaṃgraha, Toh 4038 Tengyur, sems tsam, 187a2.

f.d:
grags che ba mkhas mchog dbyig gnyen gyi rnam bshad rigs [259] pa'i le'u dang por/
chos ni shes bya lam dang ni/ / mya ngan 'das pa yid kyi yul/ / bsod nams tshe dang gsung rab dag / 'byung 'gyur nges dang chos lugs la'o/[260] /zhes chos gang la 'dus byas sam 'dus ma byas zhes pa lta bu shes bya dang / yang dag pa'i lta ba ni chos zhes pa lam/ skyabs su song ba myang 'das/ skye mched yid/ 'khor dang lhan cig spyod pa bsod nams/ mthong chos gces par 'dzin par tshe/ mdo sde dang zhes sogs gsung rab/ lus 'di ni rga pa'i chos can sogs 'byung 'gyur/ chos bzhi zhes nges pa/ yul chos rigs chos zhes pa chos lugs te bcu la sogs pa sgra don dang /

Better known is the description given by the great scholar Vasubandhu in the first chapter of his Science of Explanation:
Dharma means objects of knowledge, path, nirvana, object of mind, merit, life, teachings, arising, certainty, and traditions.[511] To paraphrase and quote briefly from the same text: the term dharma refers to objects of knowledge because “a dharma can be a composite or noncomposite phenomena.” It is the path because “the right view is Dharma.” In terms of going for refuge to the Dharma, it is nirvana. As a mental phenomenon, dharma refers to an object of the mind. It is merit in the sense of your lifestyle and social circle.[512] It is life in terms of cherishing the experiences of this life. Dharma as the category of sutras, and so on, refers to the teachings. Dharma refers to arising phenomena as in, for example, “this body has the dharma of aging.” “Certainty” refers to the four dharmas.[513] Dharma as “traditions” refers to the dharmas of different countries and the dharmas of different races. These are ten etymologies of the word dharma.

d.div: [259] sde srid kyi ma dper rnam bshad rigs pa la skabs thams cad du sa yang 'jug med pa bris 'dug kyang sde dge bstan 'gyur ltar bcos/
[260] sde dge_4061_bstan/ sems tsam/ shi_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ rnam bshad rigs pa/ le'u/ 1_shog_36_na4
[511] Vyākhyāyukti, Toh 4062 Tengyur, sems tsam, shi, 36a4.
[512] Vasubandhu mentions entourages of queens and young friends.

[513] It is not clear what four dharmas Vasubandhu is referring to here. There is no further glossing of this term within Vasubandhu’s text, although he does refer to them as “the four dharmas of the monks.” He also quotes another explanation of certainty: “Monks, killing is not Dharma; restraining from killing is Dharma.” (36b)

f.d:
mtshan nyid ni/ ji skad du/
sdug bsngal dag ni thams cad dang / / sgrib kun sel byed dam pa'i chos/[261] / zhes pa lta bu/

Concerning the defining characteristics of the Dharma, or word of the Buddha, it has been said:
The sacred Dharma: dispelling all suffering, dispelling all obscuration.[514]

d.div: [261] sdug bsngal dag ni thams cad dang / /sgrib kun sel byed dam pa'i chos/ /tshigs rkang 'di gnyis gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[514] Untraced.

f.d:
dbye ba ni ngo bos dbye na/ mdzod gnas brgyad pa las/
ston pa'i dam chos rnam gnyis te/ / lung dang rtogs pa'i bdag nyid do/[262] / zhes pa ltar lung rtogs gnyis/

In terms of its nature, it can be divided into scripture and knowledge. The eighth chapter of the Treasury of Abhidharma says:
The sacred Dharma of our Teacher has two divisions: that of scripture and that of knowledge.[515]

d.div: [262] sde dge_4089_bstan/ mngon pa/ ku dbyig gnyen/ chos mngon pa mdzod/ gnas/ 8_sh+loka39_shog_25_na3
[515] Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa, 8:39, Toh 4089, Tengyur, mngon pa, ku, 25a3.

f.d:
gdul bya'i sgo nas dbye na/ mdo sde rgyan las/
sde snod dag ni gsum mam gnyis kyang rung /[263] / zhes 'dul ba mdo sde mngon pa gsum mam mdor bsdu na dman pa la mos par nyan thos kyi sde snod theg dman dang / rgya che ba la mos par theg chen gnyis su thams cad 'dus pa dang /

Division in terms of the type of disciple is spoken of in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
The baskets of scripture can be three or two.[516] The words of Buddha can be categorized into the three baskets of Vinaya, Sutra, and Abhidharma, or into the two baskets of the Small Vehicle of the śrāvakas, whose predilection is for the lesser, and of the Great Vehicle, whose predilection is for the vast.

d.div: [263] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 12_sh+loka1_shog_13_na5
[516] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra, 12:1, Toh 4020, Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 13a5.

f.d:
rgyu 'bras kyi sgo nas dbye na/ lo chen rin bzang dang bu ston sogs gdams ngag 'bogs pa'i rgyal por bzhed pa dang / tshig dngos gnas slob dpon dz+nyAn shrI'i mtha' gnyis sel bar drangs pa'i gsang ba lung bstan las 'byung ba/
'dren pa'i theg pa gsum po dag / bcom ldan nges par gsung lags na/ / rgyu 'bras lhun grub tu spyod cing / / sangs rgyas gzhan nas mi tshol ba'i/ / nges pa'i theg pa cis ma gsungs/ / zhes zhus pa'i lan du/

Division in terms of cause and effect is described by a passage asserted by Butön, Lotsāwa Rinchen Sangpo, and others to be from the King of Teachings and which is actually quoted by Jñānaśrī in his Eliminating the Two Extremes in the Vajrayana as being from the Sutra of Secret Prophecies:
If the three guiding vehicles are definitely taught by the Bhagavān, why has he not spoken of the definitive vehicle, in which cause and effect are spontaneous and which will not be taught by other buddhas? The answer:

rgyu la mos pa rgyu'i chos kyi/ / 'khor lo rab tu bskor byas nas/ / 'bras bu theg pa nye lam zhig / ma 'ongs dus na 'byung bar 'gyur/[264] / zhes pa ltar dbang brtul rgyu la mos pas rgyu lam du byed pa mtshan nyid kyi theg pa dang / dbang rnon rgyu 'bras lhun grub la mos pas 'bras bu lam du byed pa sngags kyi theg pa gnyis/

Having turned the wheel of causal phenomena for those predisposed to the causal path, the result vehicle—a swifter path— will appear at a future time.[517] Those of lesser faculties are attracted to the process of causality, and so that is taken as the path and known as the causal vehicle. Those of higher faculties are attracted to the spontaneous accomplishment of cause and effect, and so they take the result as their path, which is known as the path of mantra.

d.div: [264] sde dge_3714_bstan/ rgyud 'grel/ tsu slob dpon dz+nyA na shrI_rdo rje theg pa'i mtha' gnyis sel ba/ shog_115_ba2
[517] Vajrayānāntadvayāpoha, Toh 3714 Tengyur, rgyud ’grel, tsu, 115b2. The question part of this citation does not appear in the Degé edition.

f.d:
brjod bya'i sgo nas dbye ba ni/
sangs rgyas rnams kyi chos bstan pa/ / bden pa gnyis la yang dag bstan/[265] / zhes pa ltar kun rdzob rig pas mi gnas par ston pa dang / don dam rig pas 'thad par ston pa gnyis/

Divisions in terms of subject matter are two: that which is taught as nonabiding through conventional perception and that taught as valid through ultimate perception:[518]
The doctrine taught by the buddhas is well founded on two truths.[519]

d.div: [265] sde dge_3824_bstan/ dbu ma/ tsa_mgon po klu sgrub/ dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab/ rab byed/ 24_sh+loka8_shog_14_ba7
[518] Normally one would expect the reverse—nonabiding ascertained by ultimate perception and that taught as valid ascertained by conventional perception—but a case can also be made for this pairing.

[519] Nāgārjuna, Fundamental Stanzas on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), 24:8, Toh 3824 Tengyur, dbu ma, tsa, 14b7. This citation was so well known in monastic Tibet that the title and author did not need to be mentioned.

f.d: gnyen po'i sgo nas dbye ba la/ sde snod gsum du 'jog pa'i rgyu mtshan/ de'i nges tshig /yan lag bcu gnyis bsdu tshul/ so so'i nges tshig dang bzhis 'chad pa sogs mtha' klas shing /

Divisions of the words of Buddha in terms of their antidotal practices is dealt under many headings: reasons for the three-scriptural-basket categorization, the etymological explanation of the term basket, how the teachings fit into the twelve branches of scripture, their individual etymologies, and so on.

dus kyi sgo nas dbye na/ dus dang por gsungs pa la bden bzhi'i chos 'khor/ bar du gsungs pa la mtshan nyid med pa'i chos 'khor/ tha mar gsungs pa la don dam rnam par nges pa'i chos 'khor dang gsum/ spyir btang mdo sde dgongs pa nges 'grel las bshad/

Dividing the words of the Buddha in terms of the time of teaching results in the initial teachings known as the Dharma wheel of the four truths, the intermediate teachings known as Dharma wheel of no sign, and the final teachings known as the Dharma wheel of ascertaining the ultimate. In general terms this is explained in the Sutra of the Definitive Explanation of the Buddha’s Thought.

rjod byed kyi sgo nas dbye ba ni/ slob dpon shan+ti pas brgyad stong 'grel pa snying po mchog las/
mdo sde dbyangs bsnyad lung bstan dang / / tshigs bcad ched brjod gleng gzhi dang / / rtogs brjod de lta bu byung dang / / skyes rabs shin tu rgyas pa dang / / rmad byung gtan la dbab pa dang / / gsung rab yan lag bcu gnyis yin/[266] / zhes pa ltar yan lag bcu gnyis sam dus 'khor 'grel chen sogs las grangs mi gcig pa gzhan gsungs pa rnams dang /

Divisions on a textual basis are recorded in Ācārya Śāntipa’s Supreme Essence Commentary to the Eight Thousand Perfection of Wisdom Sutra:
Sutra prose, occasional verse, and prophecies, versed teachings, specific expressions of joy, introductions, parables, teaching through past events, past-life stories, vast teachings, wondrous deeds, teachings on ascertainment: these are the twelve branches of scripture.[520] Alternatively, Puṇḍarīka’s Kālacakra Great Commentary has another list with different numbering.

d.div: [266] sde dge_3803_bstan/ sher phyin/ tha rin chen 'byung gnas zhi ba/ brgyad stong dka' 'grel snying po mchog_shog_2_na2
[520] Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāpañjikāsārottamā, Toh 3803 Tengyur, sher phyin, tha, 2a2. These have been translated according to Śāntipa’s own explanation in the same work.

f.d: bdag rkyen gyi sgo nas dbye ba la zhal nas gsungs pa/ byin gyis brlabs pa/ rjes su gnang ba ste gsum las/ zhal nas gsungs pa mdo sdud pa lta bu/ byin gyis brlabs pa de la yang skus byin gyis brlabs pa sa bcu pa'i mdo lta bu/ gsung gis byin gyis brlabs pa ma skyes dgra'i 'gyod pa bsal ba lta bu/ thugs kyis byin gyis brlabs pa kun tu bzang po rang rtags kyi spyod pa ston pa phal po che'i mdo lta bu/

In terms of their determining causes[521] there are three divisions: teachings actually spoken by the Buddha, blessed teachings, and the words of the Buddha by permission. An example of a sutra actually spoken by the Buddha would be the Dharma Compendium. Blessed teachings are of three types. The Sutra of the Ten Levels is a teaching blessed by the enlightened body. The Sutra Dispelling the Remorse of Ajātaśatru is a sutra blessed by enlightened speech. The “Meditative Activities of Samantrabhadra” chapter from the Avataṃsaka Sutra is an example of a teaching blessed by enlightened mind.

d.div: [521] Bdag rkyen. Refers to a cause that determines the nature of the effect even though it may not actually be its substantial cause. The eye is said to be the determining cause of visual consciousness even though it is form and not in the nature of consciousness. Likewise there are instances of Buddha’s speech, such as blessed speech, in which the teachings are not delivered directly from the person of the Buddha but are determined by him.

f.d: de la yang thugs ting nge 'dzin byin gyis brlabs pa shes rab snying po lta bu/ thugs thugs rjes byin gyis brlabs pa ni lha klu gnod sbyin la sogs pas sngags smras pa rnams 'bras bu khyad par can 'byung bar byin gyis brlabs pa lta bu/ thugs bden pa'i stobs kyis byin gyis brlabs pa ni bcom ldan 'das kyis bden stobs thugs kyis brjod pas ri dang rtsi shing sogs las sgra byung ba lta bu ste gsum du bshad/

This third category can be divided into three further categories. The Heart Sutra is an example of a teaching blessed by the samādhi of the enlightened mind. Mantras uttered by the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and so on, to produce particular results are examples of teachings blessed by the compassion of the enlightened mind. Teachings blessed by the power of truth of the enlightened mind are, for example, those issuing from mountains, trees, and so forth, with the invocation, “By the power of truth of the Bhagavān’s enlightened mind.”
rjes su gnang ba gleng gzhi dang mtshams sbyor gyi tshig rnams chug la bka' thams cad bsdus shig dang 'di ltar rtsoms shig gsungs pa lta bu/
Words of the Buddha by permission are introductions to the teachings and sentences to link the narrative, inserted under the instructions “Compile the teachings” and “Do it in this way.”
bstan bcos kyi rnam gzhag las bstan bcos kyi mtshan nyid/
12. The Meaning of “Treatise”
de dag bstan 'dzin rnams kyis bkral ba'i bstan bcos la/ mtshan nyid/ nges tshig dbye ba ste gsum/
Those who have sought to preserve the teaching have commented on these teachings by composing treatises. This section has three headings: definition, etymological explanation, and types.
dang po [mtshan nyid ]ni/
The definition of “treatise” (śāstra)

rgyal ba ma pham pas rgyud bla ma'i skabs lnga pa las/
gang zhig rgyal ba bstan pa 'ba' zhig gi/ / dbang byas rnam g.yeng med yid can gyis bshad/ / thar pa thob pa'i lam dang rjes mthun pa/ / de yang drang srong bka' bzhin spyi bos blang /[267] / zhes bka' bstan gyi dbye bar shin tu khyab che zhing / snga rabs kun mkhyen rong po dang / 'gos lo gzhon nu dpal sogs kyang bzhed pa sna mang la/ phyis kyang ni lung 'dren mtha' dag gis mdzad par/ lung tshig la zhib nan gyi dpyad pa cher med pa'i rgyal ba'i bstan pa dang / rgyal ba ston pa sogs sna tshogs pa 'di'i thad kyi rgya dpe dbang po rdo rje'i sdeb sbyor yin la/ de'i rtsa ba'i skad dod/ byings las kr-ita rkyen gyis ming du sgrub pa dang / ti dang si sogs kyi tshig tu sgrub ba'i tshul las/ sho lo ka gcig po 'di rgyas par 'phral [268]te bshad na/

The conqueror Maitreya says in the fifth chapter of Uttaratantra:
Whatever is based upon the Conqueror, the sole Teacher, explained by those with undistracted mind in accord with the path attaining liberation, should be raised to the head as one would the words of the Sage.[522] This indicates the vast difference between a teaching of the Buddha and a treatise. There are various interpretations of this verse among early scholars such as Künkhyen Rongpo and Gö Lotsāwa. Later scholars, too, who have cited this verse have not examined the words closely, leading to variations such as “teachings of the Conqueror” and “Teacher, the Conqueror,” and so on. The Indian text is in indravajra meter,[523] and I will explain this verse in detail using the method of forming nominal stems from the roots by adding kṛt suffixes and word forms constructed through the addition of ti, si, and so forth.[524]

d.div: [267] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 5_sh+loka_shog_19_ba5
[268] grol te/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/
[522] Uttaratantra, Toh 4024 Tengyur, sems rtsam, phi, 19b5.
[523] A meter of four lines and eleven syllables per line.

[524] Kṛt suffixes are primary suffixes added to roots to form nouns or nominal stems (ming, nāman). “Ti, si, and so forth” refers to conjugational and case endings added to roots and nouns to create “word forms” (tshig, pada). As the Sarasvatī Sutra says, “With no case ending, a noun; with case ending, a word form.”

f.d: ya tI/ mchod pa'am rab tu 'bad pa la'o zhes pa'i byings la kwipa'o zhes pas kwipa byin/ byings mtha'i I brjod don te/ gang zhig itra kyi ming can de ni dbyi'o zhes pas phyis/ kwipa'o zhes pas kwipa kyang yongs rdzogs phyis/ yatra gang /

“Yatī means ‘offering’ or ‘great effort.’”[525] This is the root. “To the root kvip” (the kvip affix can be added to all roots to create nominal stems). Therefore kvip is added to the root. Ī at the end of the root is for pronunciation purposes. Moreover, “That which has the name of it is elided.” (Kṛt affixes and case endings that have no particular meaning and anubandha particles are known collectively as it. When they meet other affixes, their work is finished and they are elided.) Therefore ī is elided. The sutra says that the affix kvip is also to be elided. This leaves yat.

d.div: [525] Quotes that describe the meaning of the root or stem are from the Root Sutra. All other citations of rules are from the Sarasvatī Sutra.

f.d: as yod pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /chog 'byung ling gi par smai pa da'i skyes bu dang po'i gcig tshig yAta byin/ byed pa po la apa 'os/ bar du apa byin/ ad sogs las 'jig go zhes pas apa 'jig na ma as kyi a'o zhes pa'am/ namra as la'o zhes pas byings kyi a phyis/ dbyangs kyis dman pa pha rol tu yang dag par sbyor ro zhes pas sa srog med drangs pa s+yAtra/ ces gnas pa/ ca pa rnams a ba la dza pa rnams sos ta da ru bsgyur ba s+yAd zhig /

“As means ‘to be.’” This is the root. The parasmaipad first-person singular of the potential tense, yāt, is added. In-between ap is added, because, “For the agent, ap” (for expressing the agent from roots such as bhū, the in-between affix ap is added when followed by any of the eighteen affixes from tip to mahe). The ap is then elided because “with ad, and so on, it is destroyed.” (Karaṇa affixes such as ap are omitted from roots such as ad.) “Nam and a of as” or “for nam and as” (when meeting affixes without guṇa, the in-between affix nam is elided, and the root as loses its initial vowel a). Therefore the a of the root is elided. “That without a vowel carries over to the next,” and so the s without the vowel is brought forward to make syāt. “The ca to pa group becomes the ja to ba group with ava” (when word forms ending in consonant forms from the ca to the pa group meets ava, meaning a vowel or voiced consonant, they become by euphony equivalent forms from the ja to ba group). Therefore the t is changed to d to become syād. [With the previous syllable yat, this means “whatever.” ]
dgag pa'i sgra nakra bzhag /na a'o zhes pas na kra ar bsgyur bas da a med kyi steng drangs/

Nak is a negating particle. “Na, a” (in the process of compressing word forms, the negating particle na becomes a). Therefore nak becomes a and is brought to the preceding d without its vowel a. [This leaves syāda.]

bI rab tu skye ba dang / mdzes pa dang / 'dug pa dang / za ba rnams la yang ngo zhes pa'i byings bzhag /u Na la sogs pa ni rtag tu'o zhes pas Di rkyen du byin/ Ditra la Ti'o zhes pas byings kyi i phyis/ Da yang de'i don yin pas phyis/ i bzhag drangs pas bi rnam par/

“Vī means ‘to be created, beautiful,’ ‘to be in a place,’ ‘to eat.’” This is the root. “Uṇ ḍi, and so forth, always.” (The special category of affixes like uṇ can always be added to roots regardless of tense and case considerations), therefore the affix ḍi is added. “For ḍit, ṭi” (ḍi, or vowel endings, meeting affixes with anubandha are elided). Therefore the vowel of the root is elided. Ḍ follows the same rule and is also elided. The i is brought to the remaining v to create vi, meaning “having the aspect of.”

k+Shi pa ded pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /k+ta k+ta ba tu 'os/ kyen k+ta byin/ ka ni/ us ma yin pa'i kitra di tra la'o zhes pa ltar byings la yon tan 'gog pa'i don te phyis/ byings mtha'i a brjod don gyis phyis drangs pas k+Ship+ta g.yeng /

The next root: “kṣipa means ‘to take away.’” “Kta, ktavatu” (to indicate the bhāva of the past tense, add kta; to indicate the agent in the past, add ktavu), and so the affix kta is added. “Except for us, kit, and dit” (the guṇa is blocked when k and d follow a root except when following an us affix). Therefore the letter ka has the meaning of blocking the guṇa of the root and is elided. The final a of the root is for pronunciation and is elided. This makes kṣipta, meaning “distraction.”

man shes pa la'o zhes pas byings bzhag /bats+ra sogs la as 'o zhes pas as rkyen du byin/ byings mtha'i a brjod don phyis drangs pas mnasra/ de nas sa srog med ni/ sa ra dag gi rnam bcad do zhes pas rnam bcad/ ha ba la 'os rnam bcad u/ a u la o 'o zhes pas gong gi a dang u gnyis bsdoms te o byas pa/ mno yid can/ de la gsum pa'i mang tshig b+his byin/ sa rnam bcad/ nA mi las ra'o zhes pas rnam bcad ra byas pa b+hir gyis/

“Mana means ‘to know.’” This is the root. “On vac, and so forth, as” (vac, which means “speech,” and other roots such as mana take the affix as). Therefore the affix as is added. The final a of the root is for pronunciation and is elided, and the affix is joined on to form manas. “S and r become visarga.” Therefore, the s without its life-giving vowel becomes visarga. “To hava, u” (when a visarga is on a short vowel and meets hava, meaning a voiced consonant, that visarga becomes u). Also, “a and u become o.” Therefore, the a and the u join to become o, resulting in mano, meaning “with mind.” To that is added the plural of the third-person bhis. The s becomes a visarga. “From nāmi, ra” (when a nāmin vowel takes a visarga and meets a following a, the visarga becomes r). Therefore, the visarga becomes r to make bhir, which indicates the instrumental case.

btsa 'chad pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /k+ta k+ta ba tu 'os k+ta byin/ ka 'gro ba la yadza rnams kyi ya bra ra rnams i u r-i tra rnams su slar yang dag par bsgyur ba'o zhes pas ba u/ rkyen gyi ka de'i don gyis phyis tsa tsu'i ku 'os ka de drangs pas uk+ta_de la dang po'i si byin/ atra las am 'o zhes pas am du bsgyur/ am shas dag gi a 'os/ a dbyi/ ma rjes su nga ro byas pas uk+taM bshad pa 'dir gong rnam bcad kyi ra drangs/

“Vac means talk.” This is the root. “Kta ktavatu” (to indicate the bhāva of the past tense, add kta; to indicate the agent in the past, add ktavu), and so the affix kta is added. “The ya, va, ra of yaj, and so on, to ka anubandha take samprasāraṇa into i, u, ṛt” (when roots such as yaj meet anubandha affixes such as ka, the ya, va, and ra of those roots perform a vowel interchange, or samprasāraṇa, with i, u, and ṛ). Therefore the va becomes u. The affix ka follows the same rule and is elided. “Cu becomes ku” (the consonants of the ca group can become those of the ka group). Therefore the c becomes k, which is moved to the following consonant to form ukta. To that is added the first case si. “From at, am” (on neuter genders ending with short vowel a, both si and am become am). Therefore the si becomes am. “The a of am and śas” (with an a ending, the following a of am and as is elided). Therefore the a is elided, and the m takes an anusvāra to become uktaṃ, which means “explain.” The visarga that became r above is brought to this word form.

shA su rjes su ston pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /ngang tshul l-i tra nra 'o zhes pas tri nre rkyen du byin/ na khyad don nam dbyangs don te phyis/ byings mtha'i u brjod don yin pas phyis drangs pas shAs+t+r-i/ de la si sogs ni rtag tu'os rnam dbye gnyis pa'i am byin s+t+r-i'i Ara'o zhes pas rtags mtha'i r-i Ar du song / drangs pas shAstAramra/ de nas ma rang sar 'jog gam/ yang na ma ni rjes su nga ro 'os klad kor byas pa shAstAramaM ston pa/

“Śāsu means ‘to teach.’” This is the root. The affix tṛn is added because “for being of that nature, tṛn” (the affix tṛn is added to a root to give the meaning of “having the nature of” or being in the state of that particular root). The letter n is a marker or is there for the vowel, and is elided. The final u of the root is for pronunciation purposes and is elided. This forms śāstṛ. “Si and so forth always” (the endings of the seven cases and the three persons beginning with si are added as terminations). Therefore the am of the second case is added. “The ār of stṛ” (when a preceding vowel ṛ is followed by a different vowel it becomes ar). Therefore the final ṛ becomes ār, which is brought to the am to make śāstāram. The m is left as it is, or “ma can become an anusvāra,” and therefore a zero is added to form śāstāraṃ, meaning “teacher.”

ika dran pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /aT dag gos a rkyen du byin/ u pa d+hA thung ngu'i 'o zhes pas byings kyi u pad+hA'i i er bsgyur ba drangs/ der de la rnam dbye drug pa'i ngas atra las aM e kaM gcig pu ma 'ba' zhig /

“Ik means ‘remember.’” This is the root. “A and ṭa” (when a root has a previous noun and an action is applied to this noun via the root, the affix a or ṭa is added). To this a is added as an affix. “The upadhā letter is short” (when the penultimate or upadhā vowel is a short nāmin vowel, it becomes its guṇa). Therefore the upadhā i of the root becomes e. With the sixth case, ṅas is added and “from at, am” (a neuter gender with a short vowel a termination becomes am when preceding a subsequent si or am of the first and second case, although here this rule is taken to apply to the sixth case also), resulting in ekaṃ, meaning “sole.”

dzi rgyal ba la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /naT ki dag po zhes pas naT rkyen du byin/ Ta rjes 'brel yin pas phyis pa dzi na/ de la gsum pa'i byed sgra'i TA byin/ atra las A tra ma yin pa'i ama'o zhes pas TA am du bsgyur/ am shas dag gi a'os a phyis ma ni rjes su nga ro'o zhes pas ma klad skor byas pa dzi naM rgyal bas/

“Ji means ‘Conqueror.’” This is the root. “Naṭ and ki” (to express the bhāva from the root, naṭ or ki is added), therefore the affix naṭ is added. The ṭ is an anubandha and so is elided. To that is added the third-case instrumental ending ṭā. “From at the ātmanepada ending am,” therefore tā becomes am. “The a of am and śas” (when the previous gender ending of a non-root is the same letter as the following am and śas, the a of those two is elided), and so the a is elided. “M becomes anusvāra,” therefore a small zero is added to the m, and the result is jinaṃ, meaning “Conqueror.”

bad gsal bar byed pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /kwipra 'os kwi pra byin ka 'gro ba la ya dza rnams kyi ya ba ra rnams i u ra tra rnams su slar yang dag par bsgyur pa'o/ /zhes pas ba ur bsgyur/ kwipra 'os kwipra phyis pa ud gnas med pa la yang na 'os/ yang na da tar bsgyur ba utrA shin tu/

“Vad means ‘clarify.’” This is the root. “The affix kvip” is added. “The ya, va, ra, of yaj, and so on, to ka anubandha take samprasāraṇa into i, u, ṛt” (when roots such as yaj meet affixes devoid of meaning such as ka, the ya, va, and ra of those roots perform a vowel interchange, or samprasāraṇa, with i, u, and ṛ). Therefore the va becomes u. The kvip is elided to leave ud, for which “this also applies to completion” (when the consonants from jha group to the sa group engage word forms complete with case endings they can become consonants from the ja group). Therefore, alternatively, the d becomes a t to leave ut, and then the term means “well.”

di sha shin tu 'dor ba la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /atra las sha tu ste Ipra la yang na'o zhes pas rkyen du sha tu byin/ sha ni/ sha 'gro ba la bzhi po bzhin no zhes pa'i don te phyis/ ta'i u brjod don gyis phyis/ byings mtha'i a yang phyis drangs pas di shatra tsa pa rnams a ba la dza ba rnams so zhes pas ta dar song di shad bstan pa/ b+hisra bzhag /sa rnam bcad byas pa b+hiH_yis gong rgyal ba'i dzi naM gyi nga ro nas bzung dbyangs la ma/ tsa pa dza ba sogs mtshams sbyar bas mud+di shad+b+hiH

“Diśa means ‘to expel utterly.’” This is the root. “From at, śatu; īp also” (roots having the short vowel a ending take the affix śatu and the feminine affix ip also). Therefore the affix śatu is added. The śa behaves according to “the śa anubandha is like the four” (the affix śa as an anubandha marker and when in the position of a following particle behaves like the four affixes—tip, and so on—from the all-encompassing affix section). Therefore the śa of the affix is elided. The u of the tu is for pronunciation purposes and is also elided. The final a of the root is elided (although this seems to eliminate all vowels), and the two syllables are brought together to form diśat. “The ca to pa group become the ja to ba group.” Therefore the ta changes into da to become diśad, meaning “taught.” The s of the case ending bhis becomes a visarga to become bhiḥ, giving the instrumental case. Beginning from jinaṃ, the anusvāra becomes m, and by the euphonic rules of the ca to pa group and the ja to va group, the result is muddiśadbhiḥ.

muts-il thar pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /de la uN la sogs pa ni rtag tu 'os/ rkyen sapa byin byings kyi rjes 'brel l-i ni/ l-i 'gro ba dang sa Sha sogs la nga'o zhes pa'i don te phyis/ u pa d+hA thung ngu'i 'o zhes pa'i byings kyi u la yon tan byas/ rkyen sapa kyi pa de'i don yin pas phyis/ tsu'i ku'o zhes pas ca kar bsgyur/ ku i la la Sha ru byed de sa'o zhes pas sa Shar bsgyur/ ka Sha yang dag par sbyor ba k+Sha'am drangs pas mok+Sha thar pa/

“Mucḷ means ‘liberation.’” This is the root. “Uṇ and so forth always” (the special category of affixes like uṇ can always be added to roots regardless of tense and case considerations). Therefore the affix sap is added. The anubandha ḷ in the root is elided because, “The anubandha ḷ from puṣ and so forth, ṅ” (the anubandha ḷ on roots such as puṣ changes to ṅ, which is then elided because it is a marker indicating the blocking of the guṇa). The u of the root takes its guṇa to o because “The upadhā is short” (when the penultimate or upadhā vowel is a short nāmin vowel, it becomes its guṇa). The p of the affix sap has a similar meaning and is therefore elided. “Cu becomes ku” (the consonants of the ca group can become those of the ka group), therefore the c of the root becomes k. “From ku, i, and la, sa becomes ṣa” (when gender endings of the consonants in the ka group, the eight vowels beginning with i, and the five consonants ha, ya, wa, ra, and la take a subsequent sa, it becomes ṣa). Therefore the sa of the affix becomes ṣa. Ka and ṣa are joined to form kṣa, which when put together becomes mokṣa (“liberation”).
A p+l-i khyab pa dang dmigs pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /l-i rjes 'brel gong ltar phyis/ k+ti 'os k+ta byini/ ka ni yon tan 'gog pa'i don te phyis drangs pa A p+ti thob byed/

“Āpḷ means ‘pervading’ and ‘focus.’” This is the root. The anubandha ḷ is elided, as was done previously. “Kti” (the kṛt affix kti can be added to roots to give the bhāva form), therefore kti is added. K blocks the guṇa and so is elided. This results in āpti, meaning “causes to attain.”

Sham rnam par 'khrug pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag / kwipra 'os kwipra byin byings mtha'i a brjod don te phyis/ dang po'i Sha Na ni sa na'o zhes pas Sha sar bsgyur/ kwipra 'os kwipra phyis/ sam/ yang dag pa'am kun rdzogs pa sogs la 'jug

“Ṣama means ‘disturb.’” This is the root. “Kvip” (the kṛt affix kvip can be added to all roots to create nominal stems), therefore the affix kvip is added. The final a of the root is for pronunciation purposes and is elided. “Initial ṣa and ṇa become sa and na” (to create the agent, the initial ṣa and ṇa of a root become sa and na), therefore ṣa becomes sa. The affix kvip is elided. This results in sam, which means “perfect” or “complete.”

b+h-inya 'dzin pa la'o byings bzhag / dngos po la g+hanya 'os g+hanya rkyen du byin/ byings kyi nya ni nya ta dang swa ra ti'i gnyis ka 'o'i don te phyis/ byings kyi nA ma 'os byings mtha'i r-i 'phel ba Ar du song / rkyen gyi nya de'i go byed tsam yin pas phyis/ g+ha ni tsa dza dag gi g+ha 'gro ba la ka ga dag go zhes pas don de phyis srog gi a bzhag drangs pas b+hA ra/ gong dang sbyar bas sam b+hA ra tshogs pa'am yang dag par 'dzin pa ste/

“Bhṛñ means ‘to hold.’” This is the root. The affix ghañ is added because “for the bhāva, ghañ” (the affix ghañ is added to create the bhāva of the root). “Both from the anubandha ñ and the svarita” (from a root with an anubandha ñ and a middle tone svarita vowel, both parasmaipāda and ātmanepada word forms are made). Therefore the ñ of the root is elided. “The nāmin vowels of the root” means that the ṛ in the root is strengthened to ār by the vṛddhi process. The ñ of the affix follows the same rule and is elided. The gha of the affix is also elided because “ca and ja with anubandha gha become ka and ga” (the gha is an anubandha and is elided). A life-giving vowel a is brought to the bhār to form bhāra. Putting this together with the previous word-form results in sambhāra, which means “gathering” or “to hold perfectly.”

thar pa thob par byed pa'i thabs gang yin pa ni lam yin la de ni thar pa'i go 'phang la snyeg cing don gnyis phun tshogs kyi 'byor ba 'tshol ba rnams thabs shes kyi bzhon pas bgrod pa'i rten yin pas lam sa'i yon tan gyi gzhi 'dzin pas na yang dag par 'dzin pa dus gsum gyi rgyal ba sras bcas gshegs shing 'byon pa'i srol dod pas bstod pa gcig pa'i gang zag rnams kyi thun mong du bgrod byar gyur pas tshogs pa'am gzhan du bsags pa'ang 'dren no/ /

Anything that is a method to bring about the attainment of liberation is a path. Such a path elevates one to the level of freedom, and for those seeking the glories of fulfilling the wishes of oneself and others, it becomes the ground on which the vehicle of method and wisdom travels. Therefore, because it is the foundation of all the wonderful qualities of the paths and levels, it “holds perfectly.” Because it is universally praised by all traditions as the path of the conquerors of the past, present, and future and their bodhisattva princes, it is the journey to be commonly undertaken by living beings, and therefore it also means “gathering” or “accumulated.”[526]

d.div: [526] This paragraph has been inserted by author as a gloss on the previous paragraph.

f.d: yatra gnod pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /kwipra 'os kwipra byin de nas ming du grub/ kwipra 'os kwipra phyis/ de rjes ya tra la ka lA par/ rnam pa brjod pa la ni thA'o zhes pas thA byin/ rkyen dang rnam dbye'i gzhi mthun yin pas/ de nas t+yad sogs kyi si sogs la Ti a'o zhes pas ta phyis te Ti ar bsgyur/ ya thA ji lta ba bzhin nam ji bzhin/

“Yat means ‘harm.’” This is the root. “Kvip” (the kṛt affix kvip can be added to all roots to create nominal stems) can be added as an affix, and with the construction of a nominal stem it can be elided. On yat the Kalāpa Treatise says, “For vocal expression, thā.” Therefore thā is added. The affix and case share a common basis, and so, “The si, ṭi, and so forth of tyad and so on becomes a” (when tyad and other pronouns take endings si, ṭi, and so forth, they become a before a following form). Therefore, the t is elided, and the subsequent ṭi becomes a. This results in yathā, meaning “exactly as it is” or “like that.”
shwas srog la'o an yang ngo zhes pas an srog gi byings bzhag /ShAka u u kaN 'o zhes pas u rkyen du byin/ byings mtha'i a brjod don te phyis drangs pas anu rjes su/

“Śvas means ‘life,’ as does ana.” Therefore, ana is a root meaning “life.” “Ṣaka, u, ukaṇ” (the affixes ṣaka, u, and ukaṇ are added to show that the root possesses that nature), therefore the affix u is added. The final a of the root is for pronunciation purposes and is elided. The two parts are brought together to form anu.

kU la sgrib pa la'o zhes pas byings bzhag /nAmi u pad+hA las ka'o zhes pa'i ka rkyen du byin/ byings mtha'i a brjod don te phyis rkyen gyi ka ni upa ma yin pa'i kita ditra la'o/ /zhes pa ltar byings la yon tan 'gog pa'i don te phyis drangs pas kU la/ si byin/ a tra las am 'os si am du bsgyur/ am shas dag gi a 'os a phyis/ ma ni rjes su nga ro 'os ma rjes su nga ror byas kU laM/ gong du sbyar bas a nu kU laM mthun pa/

Added to this, the root “kūla means ‘obstruction.’” “From nāmi upadhā, ka” (when the upadhā, or penultimate, is a nāmin vowel, the affix ka can be added), therefore the affix ka is added. The final a of the root is for pronunciation purposes and is elided. “Except for us, kit and dit” (the guṇa is blocked when k and d follow a root, except when following an uṣ affix). Therefore the k of the affix has the function of blocking the guṇa of the root and is elided. This gives kūla. Si is added. “From at, am” (on neuter genders ending with short vowel a, both si and am become am), therefore si becomes am. “The a of am and śas” (with an a termination, the following a of am and as is elided), therefore the a is elided. “M can become anusvāra,” which produces kūlaṃ. This is joined to anu to form anukūlaṃ, meaning “in accord with.”

mr-i d+hu phun sum tshogs pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /naT ki dag go zhes pas ki rkyen du byin/ byings mtha'i u ni/ u tra 'gro ba las k+t+wA ste i Ta yang na'o/ /zhes pa'i don yin pas phyis/ su'i r-i ar 'o zhes pas r-i ur du bsgyur/ rkyen gyi ka de'i khyad don yin pas phyis/ srog gi i bzhag /ra ba la i u dag gi he sa la'o zhes pas ra'i u pa d+ha'i u ring por bsgyur drangs pas mU r+d+hi de la rnam dbye gsum pa'i gcig tshig TA byin/ nA mi las dbyangs la num 'os numra byin/ u brjod don ma rjes 'brel gyis phyis/ shas la sogs pa la a s+thi sogs kyi a tra yang ngo / /zhes pas rtags mtha'i i a tra du bsgyur/ shas la sogs pa dbyangs la ma ba yang dag par sbyor ba ma yin pa'i a tra dbyi 'os a tra phyis/ rnam dbye'i TA ni/ khyad don yin pas phyis/ srog gi A bzhag drangs pas mU r+d+hanA/ spyi bor/

The root “mṛdhu means ‘perfection.’” “Naṭ and ki” means that the affix ki is added (to express the bhāva from the root, naṭ or ki is added). The u of the root is elided because, “from ut anubandha, ktvā; iṭ also.” (From roots with short u ending the affix ktvā or the āgama it can be added. This sutra is found in some editions only.) The ṛ becomes ur because “the ṛ of su becomes ur” (untraced). The k of the affix follows the same rule and so is elided. This leaves the vowel i. “I and u to r and v to ha and sa” (the vowels i and u as upadhā or penultimate letters added to the letters r and v become long vowels when succeeded by any consonant). Therefore the upadhā of the r in the root becomes a long ū. Brought together this forms mūrdhi. To this is added the singular of the third case, ṭā. “From nāmin a vowel, num” (neuter genders with nāmin vowel endings, when meeting case endings beginning with a vowel, include the affix num), therefore num is added. The u is for pronunciation purposes, and the m is an anubandha particle, therefore they are both elided. “For śas and so forth, the at of asṭhi, and so on.” (Alternatively, “for the ṭā and so on with asthi and so on, at.” For case endings like śas, the āgama num is included in words like asṭhi, and the letter i becomes a, from ṭā onward.) Therefore the i of the gender ending becomes at. “For śas and so on, when ma and va are not connected to a vowel, the at can be elided” (when case endings such as those from second case śas onward, which do not include ma and va, begin with a vowel, the upadhā a is elided). Therefore the at is elided. The case ending ṭā is a distinguishing marker and can be elided. The life-giving ā is added and brought up, resulting in the construction mūrdhnā meaning “crown of the head.”

ta mu 'dod pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /u Na la sogs pa ni rtag tu'o zhes pas dka rkyen du byin/ ka ni us ma yin pa'i ki tra kitra la'o zhes pas phyis/ a brjod don yin pas phyis/ byings kyi u ni/ u tra 'gro ba las k+t+wA ste i Ta yang na'o zhes sam/ gang zhig i ta kyi ming can de ni dbyi'o zhes pas phyis/ a nu dA t+ta rnams dbyi ba nyid ngos byings mtha'i ma yang phyis gnas med pa la yang na 'os da yang tar bsgyur ba tata de/

The root “tamu means ‘desire.’” “Uṇ and so forth always” (the special category of affixes like uṇ can always be added to roots regardless of tense and case considerations), therefore the affix daka is added. “Except for uṣ, kit and dit” (the guṇa is blocked when k and d follow a root, except when following an uṣ affix), therefore the ka is elided. The a is for pronunciation purposes and is elided. The u of the root is elided because “from ut anubandha, ktvā; iṭ also” (from roots with short u ending, the affix ktvā or the āgama it can be added). Or, “Whatever has the name of it is to be elided” (kṛt affixes and case endings that have no meaning and anubandha particles are known collectively as it. When they meet other affixes, their work is finished and they are elided). The final m of the root is also elided because “the anudātta are elided” (the ñ and ma low-tone letters are elided). “This also applies to completion” (when the consonants from the jha group to the sa group engage word forms complete with case endings, they can become consonants from the ja group), therefore da becomes ta. This leaves tat, which means “that.”

a bi sgra la'o zhes pa'i byings la/ na Ta ki dag go zhes pas ki rkyen du byin/ byings mtha'i i ni/ i tra 'gro ba las mum 'o zhes pa'i don te phyis/ phul du byung ba'i yi ge rnam par 'gyur te zhes pas ba yig par bsgyur/ rkyen gyi ka yon tan 'gog pa'i don de phyis drangs pas a pi yang /

The root “avi means ‘sound.’” “Naṭ and ki” means that the affix ki is added (to express the bhāva from the root, naṭ or ki is added). The final i of the root is elided because “from anubandha i, mum” (when roots with an anubandha particle i meet tip and ap, the final vowel takes the āgama mum). The v becomes p because “the atiśaya letters change” (untraced). The k of the affix blocks the guṇa and so is elided. This leaves api, meaning “also.”

r-i Shi 'gog pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag / a ta dag go zhes pas rkyen a byin/ byings mtha'i i ni gang zhig i ta kyi ming can de ni dbyi 'os phyis/ u pa d+hA thung ngu'i 'o zhes pas byings r-i rang gi yon tan ar du song drangs pas a raSha/ de la si byin/ a tra las am 'os si amra/ amra shasra dag gi a 'os a mra gyi a phyis/ ma ni rjes su nga ro 'os ma rjes su nga ror byas pa a raShaM gtsug lag ste drang srong bka'/

The root “ṛṣi means ‘go.’” “A and ṭ” (when a root has a previous nominal stem and an action is applied to it via the root, the affix a or ṭ is added), therefore the affix a is added. The i of the root is elided because “whatever has the name of it is to be elided.” (Kṛt affixes and case endings that have no meaning and anubandha particles are known collectively as it. When they meet other affixes, their work is finished and they are elided.) “The upadhā is short” (when the penultimate or upadhā vowel is a short nāmin vowel, it becomes its guṇa), therefore the ṛ of the root becomes its guṇa—ar—to form arṣa. To this si is added. “From at, am” (on neuter genders ending with short vowel a, both si and am become am), therefore si becomes am. “The a of am and śas” (with an a ending the following a of am and as is elided). Therefore the a is elided, and the m takes an anusvāra to become arṣaṃ, which means “scripture,” “the words of the Sage.”

i Na 'gro ba la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /u Na la sogs pa ni rtag tu 'os/ byings gong gsal la k+ta k+ta ba tu 'os k+ta byin/ ka ni us ma yin pa'i ki Ta bi ta la'o zhes pa'i don te phyis/ byings kyi rjes 'brel Na ni/ a nu bA t+ta di tra dag gi Ata'o zhes pa ltar bdag don gyi byings kyi mtshan ma yin pas phyis/ pa tsa las ba 'os k+ta'i ta bar bsgyur/ ba nika nga 'gro ba yin pas byings la yon tan ma thob pas i ba bzhin/

The root “iṇ means ‘to go.’” “Uṇ and so forth always” (the special category of affixes like uṇ can always be added to roots regardless of tense and case considerations) and like the previous roots “kta, ktavatu are suitable” (to indicate the bhāva of the past tense, add kta; to indicate the agent in the past, add ktavu), and so the affix kta is added. The k is elided because “Except for uṣ, kit and dit” (the guṇa is blocked when k and d follow a root, except when following an uṣ affix). “From the anudātta and ṅit, the āt” (the anudātta or low tone acting as an anubandha at the end of roots and the anubandha ṅ take the ātmanepada form). Therefore the connecting consonant ṇ on the root is elided because it is a particle indicating the ātmanpada. The ta of the affix kta becomes va because “from paca, va” (from the root paca, a ta letter conjoined with the anubandha particle k becomes va). Because va is anubandha ka and ṅ, the root is not strengthened by guṇa. This results in iva, meaning “like.”

prA rab tu rdzogs par byed pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag / k+ti 'os k+ti byin/ ka ni i tra yin te/ gang zhig itra kyi ming can don dbyi 'os phyis/ nges pa'i tshig las yi ge nyams pa yod do zhes pas byings mtha'i A ring cha nyams par byas pa pra ti/ yongs grags so so/

The root “prā means ‘to perfect’ or ‘to complete.’” The affix kti is added because “kti” (the kṛt affix kti can be added to roots to give the bhāva form). K is it and “whatever has the name of it can be elided.” (Kṛt affixes, case endings that have no meaning, and anubandha particles are known collectively as it. When they meet other affixes, their work is finished and they are elided.) Therefore the k is elided. The long ā of the root weakens because “from ascertained word forms, the letters weaken.” This leaves prati, meaning “renowned.”

iShu 'dod pa la'o zhes pa'i byings bzhag /chog 'byung ling gi yA tra byin/ byed pa po la apa 'os par du apa/ apa kyi pa ni/ nu dang u'i pa la'o zhes dang gnyis las byings pa 'gro ba la u pa d+h+wa'i yon tan no zhes pa'i don yin pas phyis/ 'dir yon tan mi dgos te ha sa'i mtha' can yin pas so/ / byings mtha'i u ni/ gang zhig itra kyi ming can de ni dbyi'o zhes pas phyis/ gam rnams kyi tsha'o zhes pas Sha tshar bsgyur/ tsha yi'o zhes pas tsha gnyis su song / kha sa la dz+ha tha rnams kyi tsa pa 'os tsha gong ma tsar bsgyur/ a la ya'i 'o zhes pas yAtra kyi yA I ru song / a i la e'o zhes pas a dang I gnyis dril te er bsgyur drangs pa its+tshetra/ gong gi pra ti dang sbyar bas pra tI ts+tshetra blang bar gyis sam its+tsha 'dod yAtra rigs lta bu/

The root “iṣu means ‘desire.’” The potential-tense particle yāt is added. “For the agent, ap” (for expressing the agent from roots such as bhū, the in-between affix ap is added when followed by any of the eighteen affixes from tip to mahe), and so ap is placed in between. The p of ap is elided because of the meaning of “pa of nu and u”; alternatively, “nu and up” (when the vikāraṇa affixes nu and up meet certain case endings, they strengthen into guṇa) and also “from roots with two syllables with anubandha pa, the upadhā” (when certain roots of two syllables meet endings and affixes beginning with consonants and forms of anubandha pa beginning with a vowel, the root upadhā is strengthened). Here a guṇa is not necessary because of the endings from ha to sa (an ending in any consonant). “Whatever has the name of it can be elided.” (Kṛt affixes, case endings that have no meaning, and anubandha particles are known collectively as it. When they meet other affixes, their work is finished and they are elided.) Therefore the final u of the root is elided. The ṣ becomes cha because “the cha of gam, and so on” (individual parts of roots such as gam, iṣu, and yamu transform into cha before certain affixes). The cha is doubled because “of cha” (when a short vowel upadhā or ending meets cha, the cha is doubled). The first cha becomes c because “the jha and sa to kha and sa groups become ca and pa” (when consonant endings from groups beginning with the fourth or jha group up to sa meet consonants beginning from the second or kha group up to sa, the former consonant becomes a consonant from the first or ca group). The yā of the yāt becomes ī because “to a, ya” (untraced). The a and ī merge to become e because “a and i become e” (euphonic rule that short- or long-vowel a meeting vowel merges to become e). This forms icchet. This is put together with the former prati to form pratīcchet, meaning “lift up” in the imperative tense. Alternatively, iccha means “desire” and yāt means “type.”

de la thad 'gyur dbang btang na/
gang zhig rnam par g.yeng med yid can gyis bshad pa/ / ston pa gcig pu rgyal bas shin tu bstan pa yi/ / thar pa thob byed tshogs dang ji lta bzhin mthun pa/ / de yang gtsug lag bzhin du spyi bor blang bar gyis lta bu'ang 'byung ste lo tsA bas don 'gyur lugs su bkral ba dang bcas pa/
yat+sayadabik+Ship+tamanob+hiruk+taMshAstAramekaMdzinamud+dishad+b+hiH_dbang po rdo rje/ mok+ShAp+tisaMb+hArayathAnyanukUlaMmUr+d+hAtadapyaraShamibapratIts+tshetra
gang zhig rgyal ba ston pa 'ba' zhig gi/ / dbang byas rnam g.yeng med yid can gyis bshad/ / thar pa thob pa'i lam dang rjes mthun par/ / de yang drang srong bka' bzhin spyi bos blangs/[269] /

Therefore a direct literal translation would be:
That explained by those without a distracted mind, in line with the great gathering for the attainment of liberation, exactly as it is, well taught by the Conqueror, the sole Teacher, should be lifted like a scripture to one’s head. This is a rendering of:
yatsyadavikṣiptamanobhiruktaṃ śāstāraṃekaṃ jinamuddiśadbhiḥ mokṣāptisambhārayathānukūlaṃ mūrdhān tatapyarṣaṃiva pratīcchet. The translation of the meaning becomes:
Whatever is based on the Conqueror, the sole Teacher, explained by those with undistracted minds in accord with the path attaining liberation, should be raised to the head as one would with the words of the Sage. The usual explanation of this verse is as follows.

d.div: [269] sde dge_4024_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ rgyud bla ma/ skabs/ 5_sh+loka_shog_72_ba5 gang zhig rgyal ba'i bstan pa 'ba' zhig gi/ zhes gsal/

f.d: bstan bcos gang zhig rgyal bas ston pa'am gsungs pa'i lung 'ba' zhig gis dbang du byas nas don de brjod kyi/ rang gi rigs [270]pa dang ldan pas spobs pa'i brjod pa ma yin la/ 'on kyang ston pa'i lugs ltar yin nam/ phyi rol dbang phyug la sogs pas byas pa'i lugs ltar yin nam snyam pa'i phyi rol pa'i lugs la sems sam rtsom pa po'i gzhan la kun slong gi khyad par dang rang nyid la rnyed pa bkur bsti dang grags pa la blta ba sogs 'du 'dzi'i rnam g.yeng med pa'i yid can gyis bshad pa/ gang gi tshe de'i don tsam dang mtho ris kyi don tsam ston pa ma yin par thar pa mya 'das kyis thob pa'i lam dang rjes su mthun par bstan pa gang yin pa de yang drang srong gi bka' ste ston pa rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi bka' bzhin spyi bos blang zhing bzung bar bya'o//

A treatise presents its subject matter based solely on the transmissions of the teachings or words of the Conqueror and not based on the composer’s own self-belief derived from his own reasoning. It is to be explained with a mind undistracted by thoughts of the outsider traditions, wondering, “Does this accord with our Teacher’s tradition or does it accord with an outsider tradition, such as the Īśvara school?” Alternatively, the composer presents his work with a mind undistracted by aspects of motivation with regard to others, and by worldly thoughts of honor, personal gain, and reputation with regard to himself. Moreover, it is not taught merely for the things of this life, nor for the glories of a higher rebirth, but in accord with the path of attaining nirvana. Such a work should be raised and held above your head as you would revere a work containing the words of the Sage, our fully enlightened Teacher.

d.div: [270] rig pa/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

f.d: gnyis pa [bstan bcos kyi ]nges tshig ni
Etymological explanation of “treatise”
byings sgrub kyi dbang song na/ shAsu rjes su ston pa la'o'i byings la iman ta a su ka'o zhes pa'i tra byin byings mtha'i u brjod don gyis drangs pas shAs+t+ra bstan bcos su bshad pa yod de/

In terms of its formation from the root: “Śāsu means ‘to teach.’” Tra is added to the root because “iman, tra, asuka” (the affixes iman, tra, and asuka may be added to any root). The u of the root is for articulation only and is elided. This leaves śāstra, which has been rendered as “treatise” (bstan bcos).

skabs de na shAsu rjes su ston pa'i byings la/ yuT dag gso yu byin/ yu bu dag gi a na a ka dag gos yu a nar bsgyur/ su'i u rjes 'brel phyis drangs pas shA_sa na ste bstan pa'am 'chos ste nyon mongs pa dug gsum las bslab pa gsum ldan du 'chos pa dang /

In terms of how the term is used in this context, “śāsu means ‘to teach.’” Yu is added to the root because “yuṭ” ( yuṭ can be added to all roots to express the bhāva). “Yu, vu become ana, aka” (when affixes yuṭ and vuṇ shed their anubandha, yu becomes ana and vu becomes aka). Therefore, yu becomes ana. The u of the su is an anubandha particle and is elided. The s is brought to the following letters, and the result is śāsana, meaning “teaching.” It also means “transforms” because the mind is transformed from the three poisonous afflictions to become endowed with the three trainings.

tra ya skyob par bshad pa'ang yod de tra rgyal ba dang sgrol ba la'o'i byings la'ang bshad ma khad pa'i yu byin pa da a nar bsgyur/ yon tan nos-i ra yon tan gyi tar an dang mtshams sbyar/ Sha r-ir las mtha' ma yin pa'i na'i Na 'os/ na Nar bsgyur bas tar Na ste 'bras bu srid pa'i sdug bsngal las sgrol ba'am skyobs pas de dag rnams/ lhag ma 'jig rten las grub pa 'dir bshad par bya dang / gzhan yang gnyis te yi ge rnam 'gyur nyams sogs kyi byings mtha' sogs dbyangs rnams dang Na phyis srog a bzhag /shas tar a zhes gnas der byings kyis dman pa'i pha rol tu yang dag par sbyar ro zhes rim par drangs pas shAs+t+ra zhes 'grub/

Concerning the explanation that traya also means “protect”: The root “tṛ means ‘conquer’ and ‘save.’” As explained above yu is added to the root and is changed to ana. By guṇa strengthening, the ṛ becomes ar because “guṇa” (as long as it does not have the function of blocking the guṇa, affixes and endings that prompt the guṇa will strengthen the nāmin vowel of the root with its guṇa). Tar is joined to the ana. “From ṣa, ṛ, and ra, no-ending na becomes ṇa” (when ṣa, ṛ, and ra meet na not ending with a non-vowel—in other words, ending with a vowel—the na becomes ṇa). Therefore the na becomes ṇa. This results in taraṇa, meaning “to protect or save from the resultant sufferings of samsara.” The vowels and the ṇa are elided, and the life-vowel a is added because, concerning the endings of roots, “it is explained here that the remainder are from the world and other works” (all noun and word forms not taught in this text but which can be known from worldly usage and from other easy-to-understand treatises can be used as supplements to this treatise); “furthermore, there are two: letters change and become corrupted.” This leaves śās and tr with the life-vowel a. “That without a vowel is carried over to the next,” which leaves the formation śāstra.

rnam bshad rigs pa'i le'u lnga par/
sangs rgyas kyi gsung bstan bcos nyid du 'thad de/ nges pa'i tshig tu ni 'chos pa dang skyob par byed pas de'i phyir bstan bcos te/
nyon mongs dgra rnams ma lus 'chos pa dang / / ngan 'gro srid las skyob byed gang yin pa/ / 'chos skyob yon tan phyir na bstan bcos te/ / gnyis po 'di dag gzhan gyi lugs la med/ / de lta bas na sangs rgyas kyi gsung kho na don dam par bstan bcos yin pas 'chos pa dang skyob pa'i yon tan gyi phyir yang don bzung ba la 'bad pa dang ldan par bya'o/[271] / zhes byung zhing /

In the fifth chapter of the Science of Explanation it says:
It is correct to call the teachings of the Buddha treatises because the etymology of the term is “transform” and “protect”:
Transforming all the foe-like afflictions, protecting from existences in the lower realms, a treatise has the qualities of transforming and protecting, two qualities not found in other traditions. Therefore, only the words of the Buddha are true scriptural treatise and so possess these qualities of transforming and protecting. Therefore, you should strive to retain their meanings.[527]

d.div: [271] sde dge_4061_bstan/ sems tsam/ shi_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ rnam bshad rigs pa/ le'u/ 5_shog_123_na2
[527] Vasubandhu, Science of Explanation (Vyākhyāyukti), Toh 4061 Tengyur, sems tsam, shi, 123a2.

f.d:
phung po lnga'i rnam par 'grel ba dbyig gnyen gyi slob ma 'dul ba rang las mkhas pa yon tan 'od kyis mdzad pa ye shes sde'i 'gyur las/
'dir bstan bcos su 'dod pa gang zhe na/ de'i don gyi yi ge'i rnam pa dang / sgra'i spyi ste mi ldan pa'i 'du byed dang sbyar ro/ / nges pa'i tshig gi tshul du ni nyon mongs pa'i dgra 'chos pa dang / ngan 'gro dang srid pa'i 'jigs pa las skyob pa'i phyir bstan bcos te/ de lta yin pas mngon par mtho ba dang nges par legs pa rab tu bstan par 'gyur ro zhes brjod par 'gyur ro/ / ngan 'gro las skyob pas ni mngon par mtho ba rab tu bstan par 'gyur ro/ / nyon mongs pa'i dgra 'chos pa dang srid pa las skyob pas ni nges par legs pa rab tu bstan par 'gyur te/[272] slob dpon 'phags pa lhas kyang /
nyon mongs dgra rnams ma lus 'chos pa dang / / ngan 'gro srid las skyob pa gang yin pa/ / 'chos skyob yon tan phyir yang bstan bcos te/ / gnyis po 'di dag gzhan gyi lugs la med/[273] / ces brjod pa lta bu'o/ zhes rnam bshad rigs pa'i lung dang mthun pa 'dug pa dbyig gnyen gyis 'phags pa lha'i gsung 'dren pa mdzad dam/ phyi ma 'di 'gyur dang yi ge'i skyon gang rung yin nam snyam pa ltar bka' dang bstan bcos mi 'gal bar bstan pa dang /

Also, it says in Commentary on the Five Aggregates, translated by Yeshé Dé and composed by a disciple of Vasubandhu, Guṇaprabha, who in Vinaya was wiser than his own teacher:
What is it that is asserted as being a scriptural treatise? It is the forms of letters that represent its meaning, and the generality of their sounds classified as non-associated phenomena.[528] In terms of its etymology it is a treatise because it transforms the affliction enemies and protects from the fears of the lower realms and samsara. Therefore, “it teaches higher birth and definite happiness.” Because it protects you from the lower realms, it teaches higher birth. Because it transforms the affliction enemies and protects you from the fears of samsara, it teaches definite happiness. Ācārya Āryadeva also says:
Transforming all the foe-like afflictions, protecting from existences in the lower realms, a treatise has the qualities of transforming and protecting, two qualities not found in other traditions.[529] The citation in this passage is a duplication of the Science of Explanation citation above, which means that either Vasubandhu was quoting Āryadeva or that there is some error in the translation or scripting of the latter citation. Nevertheless, these passages indicate that the words of Buddha and a treatise are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

d.div: [272] sde dge_4067_bstan/ sems tsam/ si_yon tan 'od/ phung po lnga'i rnam par 'grel ba/ bam po+o/ 1_shog_2_ba1

[273] sde dge_4061_bstan/ sems tsam/ shi_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ rnam bshad rigs pa/ le'u/ 5_shog_123_na3_ma dper lung 'di'i khungs 'phags pa lha gsungs kyang de'i gzhung rnyed son ma byung bas rnam bshad rigs pa nas bkod pa yin/
[528] Mi ldan pa’i ’du byed.
[529] Pañcaskandhavivaraṇa, Toh 4067 Tengyur, sems tsam, si, 2b1.

f.d: gsum pa dbye ba
[bstan bcos kyi dbye ba ]la/ mchog dman/ byed las/ brjod bya/ bshad bya bka' rnams kyi sgo nas dang / bstan bcos kyi rigs bsdu ba ste lnga las/
Treatises are divided into types according to their status, function, subject matter, the teaching of Buddha that is being explained, and classification.
dang po [mchog dman ]ni/
Status

slob dpon thogs med kyis sa sde'i nang tshan sa gtan la dbab pa bam po nyer gnyis pa las/
bstan bcos ni gsum ste/ thos pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos dang / rtsod pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos dang / sgrub pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos so/ / de la thos pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos ni 'di lta ste/ / bram ze'i gsang tshig rnams so/ / rtsod pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos ni 'di lta ste/ 'di las phyi rol pa rnams kyi gtan tshigs kyi bstan bcos so/ / de la sgrub pa lhur len pa'i bstan bcos ni 'di lta ste/ sangs rgyas kyi bka'o/ / gzhan yang bstan bcos gsum ste/ don med pa'i bstan bcos dang / don log pa'i bstan bcos dang / don dam pa'i bstan bcos so/ / de dag kyang snga ma rnams dang ci rigs par sbyar bar rig par bya'o/ / gzhan yang bstan bcos gsum ste/ ngan g.yo'i bstan bcos dang / snying po med pa'i bstan bcos dang / sdug bsngal las nges par 'byung ba'i bstan bcos so/ / de dag kyang snga ma rnams dang ci rigs par sbyar bar rig par bya'o/[274] /

Ācārya Asaṅga says in the twenty-second chapter of his Ascertainment from Stages of the Yogacarya:
There are three kinds of scriptural treatise: those that concentrate on learning, those that concentrate on debate, and those that concentrate on practice. Examples of those that concentrate on learning would be the secret texts of the brahmans. Those that concentrate on debate are the logic treatises of the outsiders. Those that concentrate on practice are the words of the Buddha. Again, treatises can be divided into three: meaningless treatises, perverse treatises, and ultimate treatises. These three can be included, where appropriate, in the previous three types. Treatises can also be treatises of harmful distractions, treatises devoid of essence, and treatises that lift one out of suffering. These three too can be included, where appropriate, in the first three.[530]

d.div: [274] sde dge_4038_bstan/ sems tsam/ zhi_thogs med/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba/ bam po/ 22_shog_197_na4
[530] Yogacaryābhūmiviniścayasaṃgraha, Toh 4038 Tengyur, sems tsam, zhi, 196b4.

f.d:
zhes gsungs pa'i don sngon gyi mkhas pas bsdebs shing bkral pa bod rtsoms rnams su 'dren rgyun ltar na/
don med don log don dang ldan/ / ngan g.yo snying med sdug bsngal spong / / thos rtsod sgrub pa lhur len pa/ / bstan bcos drug bral gsum du 'dod/ / ces bya rog gi so brtag pa lta bu don med pa'i bstan bcos/ mtho ris kyi thabs su srog gcod pa'i mchod sbyin lta bu don log pa/ phung khams skye mched rdzogs par ston pa mngon pa mdzod lta bu don dang ldan pa/

These divisions have been compiled and written on by great scholars of the past and in Tibetan compositions are usually presented as follows:
Meaningless, perverse, and meaningful, distracting, of no essence, eliminating suffering, concentrating on learning, on debate, and on practice, six that lack and three that do not. The treatise that investigates whether a crow has teeth is an example of a meaningless treatise. A treatise on the performing of sacrifice in order to gain a high rebirth would be a perverse treatise. [Vasubandhu’s] Abhidharmakośa, which comprehensively teaches on the aggregates, spheres, and sources is a meaningful treatise.
