sgyu ma dang mig 'phrul gyi thabs ston pa lta bu ngan g.yo/ ngal zhing dub pa lus la me lnga bsten pa'i bstan bcos lta bu snying po med pa/ byams pa'i chos lnga lta bu sdug bsngal spong ba/ nyan thos sen+de pa'i bstan bcos lta bu thos pa lhur len pa/ rtog ge'i tshig don brgyad lta bu rtsod pa lhur len pa/ spyod 'jug lta bu sgrub pa lhur len gyi bstan bcos te/

Those treatises that teach how to create magic and illusions are examples of distracting treatises. Treatises that promote the hardships of putting the body through the ritual of the five fires are those that lack essence. The five treatises of Maitreya are treatises that eliminate suffering. The treatise of the Saindhava śrāvakas is a treatise that concentrates on learning. Treatises that teach the eight topics of logic are treatises that concentrate on debate. [Śāntideva’s] Engaging in the Practices of the Bodhisattva is an example of a treatise that concentrates on practice.
don ldan sdug bsngal spong ba sgrub pa lhur len gsum mchog dang gzhan drug po dman pa bstan bcos ltar snang du bzhed/
Treatises classified as meaningful, eliminating suffering, and concentrating on practice are said to be superior treatises, while the remaining six are inferior and only seemingly treatises.
gnyis pa byed las kyis dbye na/
Division according to function

bka' rgya chen po sdud pa slob dpon yon tan 'od kyi 'dul ba mdo rtsa lta bu/ zab mo rnam par 'byed pa rgyal ba byams pa'i mngon rtogs rgyan lta bu/ 'khrugs pa sdeb pa'i bstan bcos mdo sde rgyan nam bslab btus lta bu/

There are those that bring together large areas of Buddha’s teachings, such as Vinaya Sutra by Guṇaprabha; those that lay out the profound meanings, such as Ornament of Realization by the conqueror Maitreya, and those that are essentially compilations, such as [Maitreya’s] Ornament of Mahayana Sutras or [Śāntideva’s] Compendium of Practice.
gsum pa brjod bya'i sgo nas dbye ba la/
Division according to subject matter

shes bya ji snyed pa ston pa dang / ji lta ba ston pa/ thar pa dang thams cad mkhyen pa ston pa gsum las/ dang po la'ang phal pa dang khyad par can gnyis kyi dang po ni/ brtag pa brgyad dam bco brgyad la sogs pa 'jig rten lugs kyi bstan bcos rnams dang / rig gnas lnga ston byed kyi bstan bcos te gnyis su bshad/ gnyis pa shes bya ji lta ba ston byed ni/ bden bzhi rnam pa bcu drug tu ston pa'am/ gzung 'dzin gnyis med kyi don ston pa'am/ rang bzhin med pa'i bden pa ston pa ste rnam nges dang sum cu pa dang dbu ma rgyan lta bu'o/ / gsum pa thar pa dang thams cad mkhyen pa ston byed ni spyod 'jug lta bu'o/ /

These are of three types: those that teach varieties of conventional phenomena, those that teach the nature of phenomena, and those that teach liberation and omniscience. The first of these is again divided into ordinary and exclusive. Ordinary treatises of this type are worldly treatises, such as works on the eight or eighteen areas of investigations.[531] Exclusive treatises are those that teach the five sciences. Treatises that teach the nature of phenomena are those that teach the four truths in sixteen aspects, such as [Dharmakīrti’s] Ascertaining Valid Cognition, or those that teach the nonduality of subject consciousness and object of consciousness, such as [Vasubandhu’s] Thirty Verses, or those that teach the truth of no-nature, such as [Śāntirakṣita’s] Ornament of the Middle Way. An example of those that teach liberation and omniscience would be Engaging in the Practices of the Bodhisattva.

d.div: [531] The eight investigations are those on: oceans, water, and land; jewels and precious stones; clothing; mountains and trees; men; women; horses; and elephants (Dungkar, p. 1018).

f.d: bzhi pa bshad bya bka'i sgo nas dbye na/
Division according to the teaching of Buddha being explained

bka' spyi'i dgongs 'grel dang / bye brag gi dgongs 'grel gnyis las/ dang po ni/ bka' spyi'i tshig gi cha gsal bar byed pa la sgra dang / don gyi cha gsal bar byed pa tshad ma la grags kyang / phyi rol pa'i sgra tshad sogs kyis ma nges pa'i phyir ro//

There are two divisions: commentaries on the teachings in general and commentaries on specific teachings. The first of these is said to be of two kinds: grammatical commentaries that clarify the words of the teachings in general, and logic-based commentaries that clarify the meanings of the commentaries. However, such a division is rendered uncertain by the grammar and logic texts of the outsiders.

gnyis pa bka' bye brag gi dgongs 'grel la gsum las/ 'khor lo dang po'i lta ba'i cha gsal bar byed pa kha che bye smra ba bka' dang mdo sde pa bstan bcos su bzhed pa mngon pa sde bdun/ de dag gi don bsdus bye brag bshad mdzod chen mo/ de las kyang bsdus pa dbyig gnyen gyi mdzod lta bu/

Commentaries on specific teachings of the Buddha are of three types corresponding to the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma. Treatises of the first turning are divided according to view and practice. An example of a treatise that clarifies the view of the first turning would be the seven Abhidharma texts, which the Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas assert to be the words of Buddha while the Sautrāntikas maintain they are treatises. These texts were compiled into the Great Treasury of Detailed Explanation, which in turn was compiled by Vasubandhu into the Abhidharmakośa.

gnyis pa spyod pa'i cha gsal bar byed pa/ gzhi bcu bdun gyi rab byung gi gzhi dang por bstan nas rnam 'byed dang gzhi bcu drug ston pa gzhir byas pa la/ gzhung dam pa'i zhu ba 'dul byed sogs dang phran tshegs kyi skabs nas 'byung ba rnams ji ltar rigs par sbyar ba mdo rtsa dang / rnam 'byed gzhir bzhag nas gzhan ji ltar rigs par sbyar ba me tog 'phreng rgyud dang sum brgya pa lta bu'o//

A treatise that clarifies the practices or conduct of the first turning would be [Guṇaprabha’s] Vinaya Sutra, which first deals with the topic of ordination from the seventeen Vinaya bases[532] found in the Basic Vinaya and then deals with the Detailed Vinaya and the remaining sixteen bases, thereby forming the basis of the text. Explanations of the discipline of requesting and so on from the Later Vinaya and the discipline for specific occasions from the Short Vinaya are inserted where appropriate. Other such treatises would be [Viśākhadeva’s] Vinaya Flower Garland and [Vinītadeva’s] Three Hundred Verses, which take the Detailed Vinaya as their basis and comment on the others where appropriate.

d.div: [532] The discipline or Vinaya teachings of the Buddha are in four categories: Basic Vinaya (Vinayavastu, ’Dul ba gzhi), Detailed Vinaya (Vinayavibhaṅga, ’Dul ba rnam par ’byed pa), Later Works (Vinayauttaragrantha, ’Dul ba gzhung bla ma), and Short Vinaya (Vinayakṣudrakavastu, ’Dul ba phran tshegs). Together they comprise the first seven volumes of the Kangyur.

f.d: gnyis pa bka' bar ba'i lta ba'i cha gsal bar byed pa la/ shing rta'i srol 'byed bzhir grags pa las/ mdo las dngos su brjod pa'i don nam snying po'i don ston pa dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab de'i rab byed dang po las 'phros pa rtsod bzlog / bdun pa las 'phros pa stong nyid bdun cu/ rang sde bye brag tu 'gog pa rigs pa drug cu pa/ sgrub byed rtog ge'i tshig don bcu drug 'gog pa zhib mo rnam 'thag ste rigs tshogs lnga rtsod med kyi steng /

Treatises that clarify the middle turning are also divided into those of view and those of practice. Those of the view include the following works from among the four great founders of traditions: Fundamental Stanzas on the Middle Way, which explains the meaning, or the essential meaning, of the actual content of the sutras; Refutation of Arguments, which is an expansion of the first chapter of the previous work; Seventy Verses on Emptiness, which expands on the seventh chapter of the previous work; Sixty Verses of Reasoning, which specifically refutes those of our own insider tradition; and Finely Woven, which refutes sixteen logical positions. These are accepted by all as [Nāgārjuna’s] Five Collections of Reasoning. On top of these five texts,

snga rabs rnams tha snyad grub pa dang rin chen 'phreng ba ga las 'jigs med gsum gang rung du sbyar ba'i so so'i bzhed pa'i rigs tshogs drug 'dren pa dang / mtha' dag bgrangs na rigs tshogs brgyad du'ang bzhed dgos pa lta bu dang / 'jam mgon chos kyi rgyal po btsong kha pas snga rtsom gser phreng du snga rabs kyi bzhed pa bzhin mdzad na'ang / phyis rtsoms rigs pa'i rgya mtshor rin chen 'phreng ba bsnan pa'i yongs grags drug tu bzhed pa dang / shugs bstan gyi don nam mngon par rtogs pa'i don gtso bor dngos po brgyad kyi sgo nas ston pa mngon rtogs rgyan lta bu'o/ /

earlier scholars also included one of the following: Establishing the Conventional, Precious Garland, or No Fear from Anywhere: Commentary on Fundamental Stanzas on the Middle Way. This made varying sets of six collections of reasoning. By including all three works, they must have asserted eight collections also. Dharma king and Mañjuśrī incarnate, Tsongkhapa, in his earlier work, Golden Rosary of Eloquence, agrees with these earlier scholars, but in his later work, Ocean of Reasoning, he adds Precious Garland to make the now established Six Collections of Reasoning. Another example of this type of treatise would be [Maitreya’s] Ornament of Realization, which teaches the view of the middle turning only indirectly or through its realization primarily by way of the eight phenomena.[533]

d.div: [533] The eight topics and chapters of Ornament of Realization.

f.d: spyod pa'i cha gsal bar byed pa/ mdo kun las btus dang sgom rim la sogs pa lta bu'o// gsum pa bka' tha ma'i cha gsal bar byed pa/ mdo sde dgongs pa nges 'grel gyi 'grel pa thogs med kyis mdzad pa/ blo gros mi zad pa'i mdo 'grel dbyig gnyen gyis mdzad pa/ sangs rgyas kyis sa'i rnam gzhag ngang tshul bzang pos mdzad pa/ dkon brtsegs 'od srungs le'u'i rnam bshad blo brtan gyis mdzad pa/ 'jam dpal grags pa'i ting 'dzin rgyal po'i 'grel ba sogs dang / spyod pa'i cha gsal bar byed pa mdo sde rgyan/ sa sde lnga/ sdom rnam gnyis la sogs pa lta bu 'di la 'byed rnam gnyis kyis bka' gsum pa'i lta ba'i cha tsam ston pa dang / rags pa'i dus byams pa dang 'brel pa'i chos sde rnams theg chen thams cad kyi dgongs pa 'grel zhing 'khor lo gsum pa'i don gtso bor ston pa tsam la brten nas 'khyog bshad kyi rigs snang yang / mngon rtogs rgyan ni zhib cha'i dus nam yang 'khor lo bar pa las ma 'das so//

Treatises that clarify the practices of the middle turning would be [Nāgārjuna’s] Compendium of Sutra and [Kamalaśīla’s] Stages of Meditation. Treatises that clarify the view of the last turning include the following: Commentary to the Sutra Unraveling the Intent of the Buddha by Asaṅga; Commentary to the Sutra Requested by Akṣayamati by Vasubandhu; Presentation of the Levels to Enlightenment by Sīlabhadra; Explanation of the Kāśyapa Chapter from the Heap of Jewels Sutra by Sthiramati; and Commentary to the King of Meditative Concentrations Sutra by Mañjuśrīkīrti. Treatises that specifically clarify the practices of the last turning include Ornament of Mahayana Sutras, the five treatises on the levels, Compendium of Abhidharma, and Compendium of the Mahayana. Of the works of Maitreya, the two works, Differentiation of the Middle Way and Extremes and Examination of Phenomena and the Nature of Phenomena, only teach the view of the third-turning teachings. The superficial view that the works connected with Maitreya comment on all Mahayana thought while primarily teaching the message of the third turning has produced some confusing explanations. However, from a more precise view, the Ornament of Realization never moves beyond the middle turning.
lnga pa bstan bcos kyi rigs bsdu ba
Classification of treatises
['di ]la gsum ste bka' la brten pa dang / mi brten pa/ bka' bstan kyi khyad par bshad pa'o/ /
This has three headings: 1. Those reliant upon the words of the Buddha 2. Those not reliant upon the words of the Buddha 3. Differences between the words of the Buddha and a treatise
dang po [bka' la brten pa ]
Those reliant upon the words of the Buddha
['di ]la/ bka' nyid la 'grel pa btab pa dang / bka'i don rgyud du brtsams pa gnyis/ /
This is under two headings: commentaries based around the actual words of the Buddha and autonomous compositions on the meaning of the words of the Buddha.

dang po la/ tshig gi cha don go dka' ba'i don rnam par 'byed pa sdud 'grel gnyis lta bu dka' 'grel/ tshig gi cha spros pa dang bcas nas 'chad pa ched du brjod pa'i tshoms kyi 'grel ba lta bu tshig 'brel/ don gyi gtso bo bsdus nas ston pa sdud pa'i don bsdus lta bu bsdus don gyi 'grel pa/ ngag don dril nas ston pa ngag don gyi 'grel pa/ tshig don gnyis ga rgya cher 'grel ba so so thar pa'i 'grel ba bam po lnga bcu pa lta bu rgya cher 'grel ba dang lngar 'dus/

The first is of five kinds. A commentary on the words of the Buddha focuses on the words of the text and explains those parts difficult to understand. Examples would be the two Collected Verse commentaries.[534] A word commentary focuses on the words of the text and explains by expanding upon them. An example would be [Prajñāvarman’s] Commentary to Collection of Aphorisms. A concise commentary takes the essential meaning of the teaching and explains it. An example would be Synthesis of the Sañcayagāthā.[535] A commentary on the speech summarizes what has been said. An extensive commentary expounds on both text and meaning—the fifty-fasicle Extensive Commentary on the Sutra of Liberation, for example.

d.div: [534] Commentary to the Collected Verses on Precious Qualities of the Bhagavān by Haribhadra and Commentary on the Collected Verses by Buddhaśrījñāna.
[535] Probably a synthesis of the Abridged Perfection of Wisdom in Verse (Prajñāpāramitāsañcayagāthā).

f.d: gnyis pa bka'i don rang rgyud du brtsams pa la/ bka' gcig gi don rdzogs par ston pa mngon rtogs rgyan nam mdo rtsa lta bu/ thor bu ston pa dge tshul gyi ka ri ka lta bu/ bka' mang po'i don ston pa bslab btus dang bshes spring lta bu/ spyir gyi 'grel ba tsam dang / bshad pa dang / rnam bshad dang / bshad sbyar dang / don bsdus dang / dka' 'grel dang / rgya cher 'grel dang / legs par sbyar ba dang / rnam par phye ba la sogs te ming gis dbye ba mang du 'byung la/ de'i khongs nas bstan bcos yang dag dang ltar snang gi khyad par shes par bya zhing /

Autonomous compositions on the meaning of the words of the Buddha include those that explain fully one particular genre of teaching, such as [Maitreya’s] Ornament of Realization and [Guṇaprabha’s] Vinaya Sutra; those that teach parts of a teaching, such as [Kamalaśīla’s] Fifty Verses for the Monk; those that explain the meanings of many teachings, such as [Śāntideva’s] Compendium of Practice and [Nāgārjuna’s] Friendly Letter. Generally, treatises go under many names: commentary, explanation, presentation, root and commentary combined, compilation, word commentary, extensive commentary, composition,[536] analysis, and so on, but within these it is important to distinguish between genuine and false treatises.

d.div: [536] Susaṃskṛta (legs par sbyar ba): well joined, well connected; a sacred composition.

f.d: gnyis pa bka' la mi brten pa'i bstan bcos ni/
Those not reliant upon the words of the Buddha

thun mong ba'i dus sgra tshad du bzhed na'ang / thun mong min par tshad ma la 'jam mgon chos kyi rgyal po btsong kha ba'i dgongs pa sogs sgra tshad gnyis ga la don gyi bkar mi bzhed pa dka' gshis dper brjod tsam du snyan ngag me long dang zlos gar lta bu'o/ /

Ordinarily, treatises on logic and language are said to be examples of this particular kind of treatise. However, with respect to pramāṇa[537] in an exclusive sense, it is difficult to say that the thinking of the Dharma king and Mañjuśrī incarnate, Tsongkhapa, and others is that the words of Buddha are not actually found in treatises on both logic and language. Therefore, texts such as [Daṇḍin’s] Mirror of Poetics and [Candragomin’s] Drama are given merely to illustrate this classification of treatise.

d.div: [537] Tshad ma; often rendered as “valid cognition” but refers generally to a state of validity.

f.d: gsum pa khyad par ni/
Differences between the words of the Buddha and a treatise

sangs rgyas kyis dngos su gsungs pa lta ci smos/ bdag rkyen tsam mdzad nas 'khor gyi spobs pa bskyed de bshad pa dang / 'di ltar gyis zhes gdams pa rnams bka' yin zhing / de las gzhan pa rnams bstan bcos yin la/

It goes without saying that “word of the Buddha” refers to teachings actually spoken by the Buddha, but it also refers to teachings where the determining cause is set by the Buddha, a member of the entourage is inspired and proceeds to teach, and ends with the Buddha’s instruction to “do as has been explained.” All else is treatise.

de dag rtsom pa la theg chen gyi dbang du btang na/ 'phags pa thogs med kyis sa gtan la dbab pa bam po nyer gnyis par/
bstan bcos nye bar sbyor bas 'dod pas rgyu rnam pa drug gis bstan bcos nye bar sbyar bar 'os pa yin te/ chos kyi don mang du byas par 'gyur ro snyam pa dang / sems can rnams la mos pa sna tshogs yod pa'i phyir de dag kha cig 'dis 'jug par 'gyur ro snyam pa dang / don nyams pa rnam par dbye bar bya ba'i phyir ro snyam pa dang / don 'thor ba rnams bsdu bar bya ba'i phyir ro snyam pa dang / don zab mo rnams gsal bar bya ba'i phyir ro snyam pa dang / tshig 'bru mdzes pas mdzes pa bskyed par bya'i snyam pas so/[275] / zhes rgyu bsam pa'i khyad par drug dang /

The way to compose a treatise according to the Mahayana is explained in the twenty-second fascicle of Ascertainment from Stages of the Yogacaryā by Ārya Asaṇga:
Those who wish to compose a treatise should do so with the following six causes: the thought that the treatise will deal with many points of Dharma; the thought that the dispositions of living beings are wide and varied and that some will respond to this work; the thought that it will lay out clearly those points that have become confused; the thought that it will bring together points that have become scattered; the thought that it will throw light on the profound points; and the thought that it will create beauty with beautiful words.[538] Here, “causes” refer to intentions.

d.div: [275] sde dge_4038_bstan/ sems tsam/ zhi thogs mde / rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba/ bam po/ 22_shog_197_ba2
[538] Yogacaryābhūmiviniścayasaṃgraha, Toh 4038 Tengyur, sems tsam, zhi, 197b2.

f.d:
de nyid las/
bstan bcos nye bar sbyor bar 'dod pas bdag nyid yon tan bzhi dang sbyar nas bstan bcos nye bar rtsom par bya ste/ sngon gyi slob dpon rnams la nga rgyal mi byed pa dang / sems can rnams la snying rje ba dang / chos mthun pa rnams la byams pa dang / bdag nyid mi sgrog pa'o/[276] / zhes bstan bcos rtsom pa por yon tan bzhi tshang dgos pa dang /

The text continues:
Those who wish to compose a treatise should do so possessed of four qualities: an absence of pride in the face of one’s former teachers; compassion for living beings; affection for those in the Dharma; a absence of self-proclamation.[539] A composer of a treatise should possess all four qualities.

d.div: [276] sde dge_4038_bstan/ sems tsam/ zhi thogs med/ rnam par gtan la dbab pa bsdu ba/ bam po/ 22_shog_197_ba4

f.d:
tha snyad mkhan po'i dbang du btang na/ slob dpon dbyug pa can gyis/
rang bzhin gyis grub spobs pa dang / / mang du thos dang dri med dang / / mngon par sbyor ba mi dman pa/ / snyan ngag phun sum tshogs pa'i rgyu/[277] / zhes pa 'di la mchog dman nam sgra yangs dog gnyis kyi yangs pa'i dbang btang na/ skye ba gong ma gzhan du rgyal ba'i gsung rab phyi nang rig pa'i gnas rnams la goms pa sngon du byas pa'i mthu yongs su sad pa'i bag chags kyis tshe 'dir rang bzhin gyis grub pa'i spobs pa ste skye bas thob pa'i shes rab zab mo dang / bye brag spyir gong ltar dang khyad par rig gzhung 'di ga'i gzhung dang bstan bcos kyi tshogs de dang 'brel ba'i sngon gyi gtam rgyud ming gi mngon brjod la sogs pa legs bshad kyi tshogs mang du thos pa des kyang mi chog par the tshom gyi dri ma med pa/ de sems pa dang goms pa la mngon par sbyor ba'i gus sbyor dang rtag sbyor gyi brtson 'grus mi dman pa ste gsum ni skabs don snyan ngag dang gzhung lugs gang gi'ang rig tshul phun sum tshogs pa rgyud la bskrun pa'i rgyur bshad pa dang /

For those who have pretensions of being an author, Daṇḍin says:
A natural self-belief, much learning, free of taints, not lacking in application, the cause of perfect poetics.[540] In terms of it being a superior work as opposed to an inferior one or of it using a wide range of language as opposed to a narrow and restricted range, “a natural self-belief” refers to an innate and deep wisdom produced from the complete awakening in this life of potential developed in previous lives by accomplishing great familiarity with the teachings of the Buddha and with Buddhist and non-Buddhist sciences. More specifically, “much learning” means that one has studied many well-composed works, both generally, as explained above, and in particular the scriptures and texts of that particular field of knowledge, as well as the history, tradition, terminology, and so on, connected with it. Moreover, by never being satisfied by this learning, one will be “free of the taints” of doubt. “Not lacking in application” refers to perseverance, in terms of dedicated application and constant application to the mental engagement and familiarization with the above. These three qualities are the causes for producing within oneself a perfect knowledge of, in this context, poetics, but of any literary field.

d.div: [277] sde dge_4301_bstan/ sgra mdo/ se_slob dpon dbyig pa can/ snyan ngag me long / le'u/ 1_shog_322_na1
[540] Mirror of Poetics, chap. 1, Toh 4301 Tengyur, sgra mdo, se, 322a1.

f.d:
gso ba rig pa 'di dang gsang sngags bla na med pa'i lugs la/ kha che'i pan+Di ta zla dgas zla zer du/
bla ma'i lung dang yang dag don/ / gsal bar rtogs nas rtsom par bya/[278] / zhes rab chos nyid kyi bden pa mthong ba dang /

In terms of the science of medicine and of highest yoga tantra, the Kashmiri pandit Candranandana says in his Moonlight:
I venture into this composition, having clearly understood the truth and the transmission from the guru.[541] Therefore, the best qualification for composing is having perceived the nature of reality.

d.div: [278] sde dge_4312_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ ko_slob dpon zla ba mngon dga'/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po'i rnam par 'grel ba'i tshig gi don gyi zla zer zhes bya ba/ shog_1_na4_bla ma'i lung ni yang dag nyid/ /gsal bar rtogs nas brtsam par bya//
[541] Padārtha-candrikā-prabhāsa-nāma-aṣṭāṅga-hṛdaya-vivṛti, Toh 4312 Tengyur, gso ba rig pa, ko, 1a4. Degé has some differences in the wording.

f.d: dpal ldan dri med lha yis ni/ / yid ni rnam par drangs pas na/[279] / zhes 'bring yi dam lha'i gnang ba thob pa sogs dang /

Then:
Because the deity, glorious and pure, has taken hold of my mind…[542] The next best qualification is to have gained permission from the meditation deity, and so on.

d.div: [279] sde dge_4312_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ ko_slob dpon zla ba mngon dga'/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po'i rnam par 'grel ba'i tshig gi don gyi zla zer zhes bya ba/ shog_1_na3_dpal ldan sgrib med lha yi ni/ /snying ni rnam par drangs pas na//
[542] Ibid., 1a3. Degé has some differences in the wording.

f.d: tha ma dbang lung lag 'khrid sogs brgyud pa'i chu bo ma chad cing rang bsgrub phyogs kyi shes bya dang dgag phyogs spong bar mkhas la/ lung la 'dris pa dang sgra tshad snyan ngag la byang chub pas bstan bcos rtsom rung bar gsungs/ [170-171]

The minimum qualification is to be in receipt of the unbroken stream of initiations, transmissions, and explanatory teachings, and so forth, to be learned in the knowledge of what is to be established and what is to be refuted, and being familiar with the teaching and accomplished in the sciences of logic, language, and poetics, one is said to be qualified to compose a treatise.
sman gyi rgyud bzhi bka' yin tshul/
13. Yuthok’s Legacy
How Four Tantras is the word of the Buddha

skabs don rgyud chen 'di nyid nang don dang sbyar na g.yu thog chen po la sman blas gsungs pa'i gsang ba'i gnas sogs don la gnas mod/ phyi nang sogs spros pa dngab zhed pa ji snyed du gyur pa rnams dang sbyor na/ phyi gong du brjod pa'i drang srong gi gnas rnams gang mos su byas kyang 'gal ba cher med rung / don tshad grub ltar snang du bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i bzhed pa nub phyogs a+yon gyi yul du gsungs/ nang gsang g.yu rnying ma'i rnam thar du sman rgyal gyis gsungs pa gong song ltar dang / ston pas sum cu rtsa gsum sogs gsungs pa'i sngags rgyud rnams su'ang gdul bya'i dbang gi mi'i 'gro ba 'dul ba'i thabs tshul sna tshogs gsungs pa bzhin/ rgyud 'di a+yon gyi yul du gsungs kyang gangs can yul dus dang mtshungs par gsungs pa'i chos du ma 'byung bar som nyi ma dgos rung rtogs dpyod mkhan po rnams la 'chad bde ba'i phyir der ma 'dus pa gangs can yul dus kyi g.yu thog chen pos rtsa rgyud kyi le'u'i grangs dang / bshad rgyud du ja dang sman zas le'u sogs su thor bu'i bsnan kha dang bcos/

If this great tantra, the work in question, is considered in terms of its inner meaning, then the secret places and so on taught by the medicine guru to the great Yuthok are factual. However, if you consider the various assertions on the outer, inner, and secret locations, then it can be said of the outer location that the various designations of “place of the sages” mentioned previously are not that contradictory, no matter which one you prefer. Nevertheless, to give an appearance of definitiveness, my lama the Great Fifth asserts that the tantra was taught outwardly in the western land of Oḍḍiyāna. The inner and secret locations are as described by the medicine guru in the biography of the earlier Yuthok. In tantras taught in the Heaven of Thirty-Three and elsewhere, our Teacher also explained various methods for taming human disciples. Likewise, although this tantra was taught in the land of Oḍḍiyāna, it undoubtedly contains many elements that accord with conditions of time and place prevalent in Tibet. However, in order to make it easier for discerning masters, these elements were not originally included. To accord with the time and place of Tibet, the great Yuthok added to the chapter count in the Root Tantra, and in the Explanatory Tantra he added sections on tea and made miscellaneous additions to the chapters on medicines and diet.

phyi rgyud du sman dpyad zla ba'i rgyal po'i dgongs pa rtsa chu'i brtag pa dang ma bu dgra grogs/ ja dkar yol la sogs pa dang / man rgyud du'ang don gong mtshungs kyi bsnan kha dang zhus legs par dag par mdzad pa rnams kyang g.yu thog chen po de nyid nges don du rigs 'dus sman pa'i rgyal po'i skur bzhengs par ma zad/ rnam pa'i sgo nas kyang gong du bshad pa'i rtsom pa'i rgyu kun tshang zhing /

In the Final Tantra he inserted sections on pulse and urine diagnosis, the mother-son and friend-enemy cycles that follow the thinking of the Somarāja, and passages on the use of white-china tea bowls, and so on.[543] In the Instruction Tantra, too, he makes similar additions. He also conducted an excellent revision of the text. For all this work, not only did the great Yuthok arise in his definitive form of the medicine king, the synthesis of all lineages, but in his outward aspect he possessed all the necessary causes for composition explained above.

d.div: [543] As noted in the introduction, one of the pieces of evidence put forward by those who maintain Four Tantras is not the word of Buddha is the mention of white china or porcelain tea bowls, which they say were not found in India during the time of the Buddha.

f.d:
mdzang ma khang snying tig gi lo rgyus 'dren byed dge ba'i lcags kyur/
de dag rnams kyang rje g.yu thog pa rnam pa gcig du sid+d+hi rnam pa gnyis lus thog 'dir thob/ yi dam lha rnams kyis lung bstan rjes su gnang ba byin pa la brten nas/ gsang sngags bla na med pa'i rgyud dang byin rlabs khyad par spu tsam med/[280] ces dang /
rigs gsum mgon po la phyogs bcu'i rgyal ba sras dang bcas pas bskor ba la lha dang lha mo dpag tu med pa'i mchod pa 'bul ba dang bcas mdun gyi nam mkhar byon nas/ a la la rgyud chen po 'di nyid ma 'ongs pa na lus can rnams kyi skyabs bla na med pa'i yul du 'gyur zhing / 'di nyid bzhugs pa'i yul phyogs thams cad bkra shis shing bde legs phun sum tshogs par 'gyur/ 'di 'dzin pa dang / 'chang ba dang / klog pa dang / nyan pa dang / kun tu byang chub par byed pa dang / gzhan dag la rgya cher ston pa de dag kyang ni rgyal ba rnams kyi sras kyi thu bor 'gyur/ tha na gzhung 'di'i tshigs bcad blor zin pa de dag kyang slar 'khor bar lhung bar mi 'gyur zhing / thog ma med pa nas bsags pa'i sdig sgrib ma lus pa byang bar 'gyur/[281] zhes gsungs shing /

In the Dzemakhang History of the Heartdrop: Hook of Virtue it says:
Because the master Yuthok in a single form achieved the two types of siddhi in this life, and because of the prophecies and permissions given by the meditation deities, there is not the slightest distinction in terms of their blessings between these tantras and the highest yoga tantras. Also:
Surrounded by the buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions, gods and goddesses with countless offerings came to the space in front and said to the protector, synthesis of the three buddha families, “Ah! In the future this great tantra will become the supreme refuge for living beings. The country in which it dwells will have good fortune, happiness, and all that is good in all its quarters. Those who preserve it, hold it, read it, hear it, master it, and teach it widely to others will become the main disciples of the conquerors. At the very least, those that commit the verses of this scripture to memory will not fall within samsara again, and all wrongs and obstructions accumulated since beginningless time will be washed away.”[544]

d.div: [280] 'dir mdzad ma khang snying tig gi lo rgyus 'dren byed dge ba'i lcags kyu zhes pa'i gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[281] gong mtshungs gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[544] Untraced.

f.d: de ltar bsnan kha mdzad pa rnams bka' dang bsres te dbye ba med par mdzad pa ni/ snyigs dus kyi skye bo don la mi dpyod cing tshig la lta ba rnams kyi ngor blo drang ba'i phyir yin la/ de la nyes pa mi 'jug pa ni/ bka' gdams thig le bcu drug jo bo yab sras kyi ye shes sgyu 'phrul gyi rol gar las shar na'ang / don gyi brgyud pa rdo rje 'chang nas snyeg dgos pa bzhin yin par bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i bzhed pa ltar ro//

Making these additions so that they become indistinguishable from the words of the Buddha was done to guide the minds of those beings of these degenerate times that do not think about meanings but simply read the words. It is not wrong to do this. As my lama the Great Fifth has said, it is similar to the Sixteen Drops of the Kadampa appearing from the illusory play that was the gnosis of Atiśa and his main disciple but whose lineage in reality has to come from Vajradhara.

rgyud bzhi'i 'chad thabs su cha lag yig rnying 'ga' zhig tu/
yid bzhin nor bu'i rgyud chen 'di nyid la/ / med thabs med pa gces pa'i bu/ / bcu dang gsum gyi grangs bstan pa/ / rgyud kyi khog pa 'bugs pa la/ / khog 'bugs nyi 'od rab gsal yod/[282] / ces sogs rgyu mtshan dang bcas pa'i sa bcad shes rab nyin byed/ kha skongs lus kyi bu yig /gang ba snying gtam gyi skor/ gab yig ming don brda sprod/ bzhi brgya rtsa bzhi'i bsdus tshul/ zad 'phel byed pa'i 'bru 'grel/ nyes pa gsum gyi 'bru 'grel/ mgo chag zlum bcos shog gcig /gnyan lhog bcos thabs rigs gsum/ drang srong gza'i bcos thabs/ dbang po ril bu'i brtag thabs/ phan byed sngags 'bum rnams/ dkar chag 'phyugs med dam pa zhes par bshad 'dug pa dang /

Concerning the auxiliary texts for aiding the understanding of Four Tantras, some old manuscripts say:
For this wish-fulfilling jewel of a tantra, essential and treasured son texts numbering thirteen have been taught; these are the sunlight expositions shining on the exposition of this tantra.[545] Therefore, with the reasons for their composition given in the above verse, the thirteen are then taught in verse as follows: 1. Sunlight of Wisdom Outline 2. Son Manuscript Supplement on the Body 3. Complete Heart-Teachings Collection 4. Hidden Document on Names 5. Way of Compiling the 404 Diseases 6. Word Commentary on Causes of Excess and Deficiency 7. Word Commentary of the Three Humors 8. Page on Compress Treatment for Head Injury 9. Three Treatments for Lhok 10. Rishi Treatment for Planetary Illness 11. Investigation of Bezoar 12. Collection of Beneficial Mantras 13. Inventory without Fault

d.div: [282] 'dir yig rnying 'ga' zhig gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[545] Untraced.

f.d: bco brgyad du 'dod pa'i phyogs la/ khog 'bugs khyung chen lding ba/ stong thun mdzes pa'i 'ja' ris/ sa bcad stag mo'i rngam thabs/ Dik+ka mun sel sgron me/ 'grel pa 'bum nag gsal sgron/ rtsod bzlog gegs sel 'khor lo/ skor tshoms stong thun bcu gcig /ming don brda sprod rnam lnga/ lag len rin chen gter spungs/ kha thor rin chen spungs pa/ lag len smar 'khrid yig chung / med thabs med pa rnam gsum/ gab pa bco brgyad/ zab pa rnam gsum/ mkhas khyad ngo mtshar bzhi sprugs/ rgyud chung bdud rtsi snying po/ gso dpyad mu tig 'phreng ba/ phan bya sngags 'bum dkar po dang bco brgyad du bshad pa'i phyi ma grags che ba ltar gyi

Eighteen auxiliary texts are also asserted: 1. Great Garuḍa History of Medicine 2. Beautiful Rainbow Overview 3. Outline: Wrathful Pose of the Tigress 4. Darkness-Dispelling Lamp of Explanation 5. Illuminating Beacon: Black Commentary Collection 6. Refutation of Arguments: Hindrance-Destroying Wheel 7. Eleven Sectional Overviews 8. Lexicon in Five Parts 9. Precious Jewel Heap of Medical Practice 10. Precious Heap of Miscellany 11. Short Works on Incisive Medical Practices 12. Three Indispensables 13. Eighteen Secrets 14. Three Profound Instructions 15. Four Wondrous Superior Features 16. Ambrosia Essence Short Tantra 17. Pearl Garland Medical Practice 18. White Collection of Beneficial Mantras Of these two sets, the eighteen auxiliary texts are better known.

da lta bar du 'khod pa rnams 'grel pa 'bum nag ma 'byor bar 'bum chung gi go bcad pa dang / ngo bo ji ltar rung ming mthun pa rnams kyang de'i skabs ma dpe dag min ci rigs las phyag tu ma 'byor pa nas zhabs bskul zhu mi rnams kyi bsdos drag gi skyon tsam dang / par du ma 'khod pa phyis dpe 'byor ba cha lag gi gras yin nges sngo'i man ngag 'khrul sel sgron me/ g.yu thog shog dril skor gsum gnyis dang / par 'khod gras nas skor tshoms stong thun bcu gcig /lag len smar 'khrid yig chung / gab pa bco brgyad/ med thabs med pa rnam gsum/ kha thor rin chen spungs pa/ khyad par zab pa rnam gsum/ mkhas khyad ngo mtshar bzhi sprugs/ bdud rtsi snying po/ mu tig 'phreng ba rnams g.yu thog pa rang gi gsung yin par phal cher bzhed rung / brgyud pa'i rnam thar med thabs med pa zhes pa 'di'i stod cha'i sh+loka 'ga' zhig gi g.yu thog pa'i gsung yin du chug kyang / byings/ drang srong g.yu thog mgon po des/[283] /zhes dang / kho bo ru mtshams sum pa'i bu/[284] /zhes sum ston ye shes gzungs kyi gsung du gdon mi za zhing / bar du sum ston gyi gsung min par dogs pa 'bum chung 'khod 'dug ste rtsa ba'i dkar chag dang bstun na 'grel ba 'bum nag sum ston gyis mdzad nges rnams cha lag gras yin la/

Concerning those that survive in print to the present day, the Illuminating Beacon: Black Commentary Collection was never received and has been substituted by the Illuminating Beacon Small Collection Commentary. Other works with similar titles regardless of content are simply the result of overzealous supplicants for the printing of texts at a time when only various corrupt mother texts were available. Two other texts not included in the original publication, but which have since appeared in print, are definitely included in the auxiliary texts. They are Yuthok’s Teachings on Medicinal Plants: Lamp Dispelling Error and Three Scroll Collections. Of those in the original publication, Eleven Sectional Overviews, Short Works on Incisive Medical Practices, Eighteen Secrets, Three Indispensables, Precious Heap of Miscellany, Three Profound Instructions, Four Wondrous Superior Features, Ambrosia Essence Short Tantra, and Pearl Garland Medical Practice are mostly accepted as being Yuthok’s own work. However, some verses of the first part of History of the Lineage, which is one of the Three Indispensables, could be seen as being the work of Yuthok, but on the whole, lines such as “that great sage Yuthok Gönpo” and “I, the son of Rutsam Sumpa” indicate without doubt that this is the work of Sumtön Yeshé Sung.[546] The printed work Small Commentary Collection, over which there was some doubt for a while as to whether it was composed by Sumtön, and which is listed in the original inventory as Illuminating Beacon: Black Commentary Collection, is now established as the work of Sumtön. These works are all are part of the auxiliary collection.

d.div: [283] cha lag bco brgyad smad cha/ brgyud pa'i rnam thar med thabs med pa/ shog_691_phreng 16
[284] cha lag bco brgyad smad cha/ brgyud pa'i rnam thar med thabs med pa/ shog_691_phreng 12
[546] One of Yuthok’s main disciples.

f.d: gzhan ma par rnams 'khod nas Tik+ka mun sel sgron me dang ming don brda sprod rnam lnga bai ros mdzad par grags pa dngos de yin min ji ltar na'ang gong song dang / gzhan ma rdza ye shes gzungs/ shag ram pa nyi ma dpal/ 'bal sman/ brang ti/ rong ston dkon cog skyabs sogs bod snga rabs pa shes bya che chung ci rigs pas byas sam snyam/

Of the other works in the publication, Darkness-Dispelling Lamp of Explanation and Lexicon in Five Parts may or may not be the similarly named texts reputedly composed by Vairocana. Nevertheless, as the above they are included in the auxiliary collection. I think that the remaining works were composed by earlier Tibetan scholars of varying degrees of knowledge, such as Dza Yeshé Sung, Shakrampa Nyima Pal, Balmen, Drangti, Rok Könchok Kyab, and others.

gzhan yang sman pa'i rgyal po g.yu thog pa des/ sngo 'bum chen mo/ man ngag gi snying po dril ba 'bum khu tshur/ thor bu re len/ deb chings rgyogs sogs kyi dpe'u ris/ byang khog gi rtsa pra/ smug po gso ba chu rgyun gyi gdams pa/ lag len pod chung / chu'i 'khor lo dang pra gsal ba'i me long / bu don ma/ 'byung ba lus 'khrugs kyi gegs sel/ dug nad zhi ba/ mo nad bcos thabs yig sna bcu bzhi pa/ gzer sman gnyen po lnga sbyor/ sman pa'i bya ba mdor bsdus pa sogs mdzad de bod gangs can mun pa'i gling du gso rig bstan pa'i sgron me spar/ bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i bka' las/

Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, the king of medicine, also composed the following works: Great Collection on Medicinal Plants; Fistful Collection on the Gathered Essence of Instruction; Heat Lancing of Boils and so Forth; Illustrations of Bandages, Ties, and Splints; Clear Depiction of the Channels of the Abdomen; Stream of Instructions on Treatment of Brown Phlegm Disorders; Small Volume on Practice; Urine Charm Circle; Mirror of Clear Image; Texts for My Sons; Eliminating Physical Disturbance Caused by the Elements; Pacifying Poisoning; Fourteen Works on Women’s Diseases; Five-Ingredient Pain Medicine; Brief Document on the Work of the Doctor. With these and other compositions he shone the bright beacon of medicine in this dark land of Tibet. My lama the Great Fifth said of him:

sku gsum rigs 'dus sman rgyal rdo rje 'chang / / gdul bya'i snang ngor 'tsham pa'i zlos gar la/ / g.yu thog mgon por grags de nges don du/ / dkyil 'khor rgya mtsho'i gtso bo lhun gyis grub/[285] / ces gsungs pa ltar snyigs ma lnga ches cher bdo ba'i 'gro ba rnams kyi mgon skyabs dpung gnyen du rigs 'dus sman gyi bla ma'i gzugs su byon pa rgyal ba'i sras po g.yu thog yon tan mgon po zhes ngo mtshar ba'i bkod pa bsam gyis mi khyab pa dngos su ston par mdzad pa 'di'i thugs kyi dgongs pa'i klong nas nyams chos kyi tshul du rdol ba/

Fusion of all buddha families of the three enlightened bodies, the lord of medicine, Vajradhara, in the dance performed according to the minds of disciples, appears the one renowned as Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, in reality the naturally arising lord of myriad mandalas.[547] As this verse indicates, Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, a prince of the Conqueror, a support and protector for the beings of these hugely degenerate times, came in the form of the medicine guru, synthesis of all buddha families, performing inconceivable and wondrous deeds that burst forth from the valley of the thoughts of his mind in the form of direct vision teachings.

d.div: [285] rgyal ba lnga pa blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsung 'bum/ nga g.yu thog snying thig gi las byang dpag bsam ljon shing / shog_1_na2
[547] Ngawang Losang Gyatso, Wish-Fulfilling Tree: List of Practices from the Yuthok Heartdrop, Collected Works, nga, 1a2.

f.d:
dkar chag gsal ba'i sgron ma las/
thugs rje nyi 'od chos tshan sum cu lnga/ / rtsa ba gsum gyi thugs srog gcig dril 'di/ / dus gsum rgyal ba'i srog sgrub mthar thug yin/[286] / zhes zab pa las kyang ches zab pa snying tig gi chos skor/

In the Clarifying Lamp Inventory it says:
Sunrays of compassion in thirty-five chapters, the very souls of the three sources rolled into one, ultimate life practices of the conquerors of all times.[548] This refers to the most profound Heartdrop Collection.

d.div: [286] g.yu thog snying thig gi chos skor/ g.yu thog snying thig byin rlabs bla sgrub las byang / shog_2_na5
[548] Traced to the two-page table of contents at the beginning of Sumtön Yeshé Sung’s Sunlight of Compassion Clearing the Darkness of Suffering, 2a4.

f.d: kun gyi thun mong thog mar lo rgyus ni/ gdul bya nges shes 'dren byed lcags kyu yin/[287] / zhes pa ltar lo rgyus/

The text continues:
Common to all, first the history, a hook to seize disciples’ conviction. This refers to the teachings on the Heartdrop history.

d.div: [287] g.yu thog snying thig gi chos skor/ g.yu thog snying thig byin rlabs bla sgrub las byang / shog_1_na4

f.d: bde chen klong yangs skal ldan smin par byed/[288] / ces pa bzhin smin byed ras bris kyi dkyil 'khor du 'jug pa sngon du 'gro ba'i cod pan/ bum pa/ dbu rgyan/ gos rgyan/ sman rag gtor tshogs rnga chen/ rgyud bzhi'i glegs bam/ ka pA la me long sman bcas/ gtsags bu/ me btsa'/ skam pa/ mtshon kyung bu/ thur ma ste cha dpyad kyi dbang / rigs lnga'i phyag mtshan/ lhung bzed/ gri gug /thod khrag rnams phyi'i dbang / rigs 'dus lha dbang / ye shes lnga'i dbang / drang srong bka' srung dang bcas pas nang gi dbang / byang sems kyi gsang dbang / phyag rgya'i dkyil 'khor du rig pa brtul bzhugs kyi dbang / rdor dril me long man shel sogs la brten nas rig pa ye shes kyi dbang / lta sgom spyod pa 'bras bu ngo sprod de de kho na nyid kyi dbang / 'chi med tshe dbang lha mo'i rjes gnang / drang srong ser skya'i rig gtad rnams/

Great sphere of bliss, ripening of the fortunate.[549] This refers to the prerequisite ripening process of entering a cloth drawn mandala, a process that includes the following: the ceremonies of the crown, vase, head, and clothing ornaments, the medicine and alcohol torma collection, the great drum, the volume of Four Tantras, the skull, the mirror, and the medicine; the surgical-instruments initiation comprising the instruments for draining blood and cauterizing and for using forceps, surgical hammer, and surgical spoon; the external initiations of the hand implements of the five buddha families—the begging bowl, curved knife, and blood-filled skull cup; the inner initiations of the buddha families deity initiation; the five gnosis initiations together with the initiation of the rishi protector; the bodhicitta secret initiation; the wisdom-conduct initiation into the mandala of the mudra; the knowledge-gnosis initiation taken by way of vajra, bell, mirror, water crystal, and so forth; the reality initiation by way of glance meditation, conduct, and introduction to the result; the ambrosia-longevity initiation; the permission of the goddess; and the knowledge entrustment of Rishi Kapila.

d.div: [288] g.yu thog snying thig gi chos skor/ g.yu thog snying thig byin rlabs bla sgrub las byang / shog_1_na5
[549] The following paragraphs, beginning with this line, describe the main sections of Yuthok’s renowned Heartdrop Collection.

f.d: bskyed rim phyi nang gsang ba dril sgrub dang / / zhes lam mchog zab mo bla sgrub skor/

The text continues:
Generation-stage practices combining outer, inner, and secret. This refers to the collection on the profound guru practices of the supreme path.
phyi gtor las gzhung sman gtor lhan thabs ni/ / zhes mgron tshim zhing dngos grub 'byung ba 'phrin las skor/
Outer torma and the activities, medicine torma, and supplements. This refers to satisfying the invited guests and the section on the urging of activities for the production of siddhis.
rdzogs rim yang zab mkha' 'gro'i srog snying 'di/ / zhes tshe gcig sangs rgyas sgrub pa rdzogs rim skor/
The very profound completion stage, life essence of the ḍākinī. This is the completion-stage collection on attaining enlightenment in one life.
gegs sel lam rtags gsal byed gsol 'debs ni/ / zhes ma tshang ba tshang bar byed pa kha skong gi skor/
Eliminating hindrances, clarifying the signs on the path, and making the requests. This is the supplementary collection that completes what is incomplete.
'chi bdag bdud 'joms lhan thabs sbyin sreg dang / / zhes bar chad sel ba tshe sgrub bsrung sreg gi skor/
Destroying the demon of death, the supplement fire offerings. This is the collection on the long-life practice of obstacle elimination, longevity, protection, and fire offering.
pra sgrub rjes gnang sgab 'dre mnan pa gsum/ / zhes gzhan dring mi 'jog par nad pa gso ba sman gyi pra sgrub skor/
Prognostication practice, permissions, and suppression of hidden demons. This is the medical-prognostication collection on curing illness without relying on others.

mngon rtogs mdangs bskang gsol kha sngags byang srog / spu gri dug ngar gnam lcags thog dang 'dra/ / bstan pa'i dgra bgegs sgrol ba'i mtshon cha yin/ / zhes dgra bo cham la 'bebs pa bka' srung skor dang sde tshan dgu'i bdag nyid can gyi zab chos/

Insight, radiance, satisfaction for the protector, the list of mantras, like a knife, like powerful poison, and like a thunderbolt, weapons to destroy the enemies hindering the doctrine. This refers to the tantra-protector collection on annihilating enemies and the profound ninefold Dharma collection.

ji skad du/
rigs 'dus bla ma sman rgyal g.yu thog rje/ / rje btsun sum ston rnam 'phrul dbang po'i sde/ / sde bcas gdams pa'i mdzod 'dzin kun dga'i dpal/ / dpal ldan rdo rje 'chang de'i gsung gi bcud/ / bcud ldan 'chi med rnams kyi bdud rtsi gang / / gang zhig sangs rgyas sar 'khrid nus ldan tshe/ / tshe gcig kun mkhyen sgrub pa zab mo'i theg / theg mchog 'di yi dpe zlar 'os sam snyam/[289] / zhes pa ltar bdag gi bla ma lnga pa nges pa don gyi thams cad mkhyen pa ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtshos dbang lung man ngag yongs su rdzogs pa bzhes shing / las byang dpag bsam ljon shing bka' rtsom gyis mtshon dar rgyas su mdzad/

The Great Fifth said:
The master Yuthok, the medicine king, guru with all buddha families combined, venerable Sumtön, in the class of mighty manifestations, with the glory of Ānanda, keeper of the treasury of instruction and scripture; the very essence of the speech of glorious Vajradhara, the ambrosia of those elixirs of immortality, endowed with the power to lead to enlightenment, profound vehicle bringing omniscience in a single life; is there an illustration worthy of this supreme vehicle? As this verse indicates, my lama the Fifth, in reality an omniscient one, Ngawang Losang Gyatso, received the initiations, transmissions, and teachings of the Heartdrop in their entirety and propagated them widely, as illustrated by his Wish-Fulfilling Tree: List of Practices from the Yuthok Heartdrop.

d.div: [289] rgyal ba lnga pa'i gsung 'bum/ pod/ nga g.yu thog snying thig gi las byang dpag bsam ljon shing / shog_9_ba5

f.d: dpon slob brgya phrag skor gtsang gi tshong 'dus mgur mor btsad po jo dar yab sras kyis spyan drangs/ dbu ma rtsa ba shes rab la 'grel pa brtsams/ rdzogs pa chen po a ti yo ga'i 'khrid zla ba lnga'i bar bskyangs/ grol ba'i dga' ston gyi dus btsad pos tshogs 'khor dang 'bul ba rgya cher bstabs/ sman bla gsang sgrub la sogs pa'i dbang / rjes gnang / byin 'bebs sogs mang bar mdzad pa'i mthar/ nyin gcig nyi ma rtod la mnan/ sku lus kyi bkod pa sna tshogs bstan/ nam mkha' g.ya' dag pa la 'ja' 'od kha dog lnga pa'i gur phub/ sngon ma tshor ba'i dri zhim po 'thul/ me tog 'dab ma bcu drug yod pa mkha' las babs/ khyad par btsad po'i khang khyim gyi nye kor du a ru ra gser mdog rlon pa'i char babs/ de'i nang nas che chung snyim pa kha sbyar tsam kha dog ser po 'dzam bu chu bo'i gser gyi mdangs 'phrog pa zhig g.yu thog pa nyid kyi phyag tu byung / der tshogs kun gyis a ru ra rnams phyogs gcig tu bsdus nas bgos pas mi rer bre bco lnga dang phul phyed re thob skad/

Once, the chieftain Jodar and his family invited Yuthok, attended by a great number of masters and disciples, to a gathering in the Tsang market town of Gurmo. There he composed a commentary to Fundamental Stanzas on the Middle Way. He gave teachings on atiyoga Great Perfection for five months. During the customary celebrations at the end of the teachings, the chieftain sponsored the great gathering feast and made many offerings to him. Yuthok conferred, among others, the initiation for the secret accomplishment of the medicine guru, bestowed initiation permissions, and conferred blessings to many participants. One day at the end of the ceremonies, he prevented the sun from moving and performed miraculous physical displays. In the clear sky a rainbow of five distinct colors formed a canopy. A delightful aroma never before experienced pervaded the air. Flowers of sixteen petals fell from the skies. Around the chieftain’s house fell a rain of fresh, golden myrobalan. A myrobalan fruit, the size of a fist and of a yellow color that eclipsed the golden color of the Jambu River, fell into the hands of Yuthok. The assembly gathered the myrobalan together and distributed them, and it is said that each person received fifteen dré and half a phül[550] of myrobalan.

d.div: [550] One dré (bre) is one twentieth of a khel (khal) or load; one phül (phul) is one sixth of a dré.

f.d: rgya gar du 'tsho byed gzhon nu/ gu ru pad+ma/ dpa' bo/ dam pa/ bir wa pa/ skyes bu me lha/ bod yul 'dir g.yu thog rnying ma yon tan mgon po/ dwags po lha rje rnams thugs brgyud gcig pa la dgongs pa'i nga rang yin par zhal gyis 'ches/

In the sense of being of the same mind lineage, Yuthok declared that in India he was Kumāra Jivaka, Guru Padma, Śūra, Śreṣṭha, Virūpa, and Puruṣa Agnideva, and here in Tibet he was the elder Yuthok Yönten Gönpo and Dakpo Lharjé.[551]

d.div: [551] Probably Gampopa Sönam Rinchen (1079–1153), the well-known early master of the Kagyü school.

f.d:
mdor bsdu na/
ka ye gson dang skal ldan kun/ / legs par gson dang 'jig rten mi/ / lhag par 'dir tshogs lha mi rnams/ / khyed sngon chad ma nyan dgu nyan yang / / 'khrul tshig cal col lung ma bstan/ / de ring nyan pa don chen yin/ / sngon chad ma bltas dgu ltas kyang / / rdzun snang 'khrul ba'i ri mo yin/ / de ring ltos dang sgrib gnyis 'dag /

To summarize:
Hey! Listen! All you fortunate ones, listen well! People of this world, and you gods and humans gathered here, whatever you have heard or not heard in the past is but meaningless and flawed talk, of no significance, but what you hear today is of great importance. Whatever you have witnessed or not witnessed in the past are but misleading appearances, false pictures; look today and you will be free of obstacles.

d.div: ming ngo khyod kyis ma shes na/ / nga bde gshegs kun gyi pho nya yin/ / lus can kun gyi skyabs mgon yin/ / brtan g.yo shes bya gar khyab tu/ / nga yi lus ngag yid kyis khyab/ /

If you do not know my name, I am the messenger of all tathāgatas, the guardian and protector of all beings. Wherever animate and inanimate existence may be, there my body, speech, and mind will be too.
sgyu lus gzugs kyi phung po 'di/ / yi dam lha tshogs ngo bor grub/ / snyigs ma brdos bcas rang sar dag / 'ja' tshon lta bur ngos bzung med/ / chu zla'i gar bzhin ci yang 'char/ /
ngag grags stong brag ca'i glu dbyangs la/ / brgyad khri bzhi stong chos sgra sgrog / gang la gang 'dul chos char 'bebs/ / sems can smin grol lam la 'god/ /

My speech, the melody of an echo in an empty cave, proclaims the sounds of the 84,000 Dharmas, causing the rain of Dharma to fall whenever and wherever beings are to be tamed, ripening them and bringing them to freedom.

f.d: sems gsal stong spros bral gnyug ma'i ngang / / bde chen khyab brdal rgyun chad med/ / stong nyid snying rje dbyer med pas/ / spros mtshan rang sar grol nas gda'/ / zhes sogs dang /

My mind of clarity and emptiness is free of fabrication, the primordial state, and pervaded by great bliss, a continuum unending, an indivisibility of emptiness and compassion, with all signs and fabrications vanishing within its own abode.[552] Also:

d.div: [552] Darmo Menrampa, Biography of the Younger Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, p. 329.

f.d:
bdag 'dra g.yu thog mgon po yis/ / mi lo bdun cu rtsa drug tu/ / rin chen gso dpyad srog bzhin bskyangs/[290] / zhes pa ltar dgung lo bdun cu don drug gi ring 'gro don legs par mdzad de sku lus ma spangs par mkha' spyod kyi gnas su gshegs pa'i tshul yang /
da ltar bzhags dang snyad kyis 'byon/ / bu dang slob mas de ltar dgongs/ / re zhig zhing 'di'i dul bya rdzogs/ / da ni mkha' spyod gnas su 'gro[291] / zhes pa ltar dang /

I, Yuthok Gönpo, have for seventy-six years cherished the precious science of healing as I would my life.[553] Thus, for seventy-six years he dedicated himself to the welfare of others and then traveled to the land of the ḍākinīs without abandoning of his own body:
Those present and those to come, sons and disciples, understand this: now my work in this realm is complete, and now I go to the land of the ḍākinīs.[554]

d.div: [290] g.yu thog snying thag gi+i chos skor/ g.yu thog snying thig las byin rlabs bla ma sgrub pa'i chos skor sdug bsngal mun sel thugs rje'i nyi 'od ces pa'i thog mar lo rgyus dge ba'i lcags kyu/ shog_14_ba4
[291] da ltar bzhags dang snyad kyis 'byon/ /gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[553] Ibid.

f.d: g.yu thog pa'i slob brgyud/

rje btsun de la slob ma kun bsdoms na gnam gyi skar ma dang sa'i dreg pa'i dpe bzhin byung ba las/ yongs grags ni ljang sman leb se/ 'bal sman nyi ma dpal/ rdza ye shes gzungs/ ston pa a tshes/ shag rams pa nyi ma dpal/ g.yu thog 'bum seng dang / bsod seng / sum ston ye shes gzungs/ dge bshes rog chung rnams yin par/ de nang nas phyag na pad+ma rgyal ba bdun gyi rnam par rol pas 'gro don zam mi chad par mdzad pa bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i skyes rabs kyi 'phreng bar yang bzhugs pa/ sum ston ye shes gzungs ni/ yul ru mtshams snye mo'i mdar sum pa'i sras su bltams/ rig gnas gzhan rnams la'ang sbyangs pa mthar phyin par mdzad/ de nas rje g.yu thog pa nyid kyi rnam par thar pa gsan pas thugs 'phrogs/ gso dpyad kyi gdams pa don du gnyer bar dgongs te lo bcu gnyis kyi bar rim gro ba mdzad/ rgyud rgyal bdud rtsi snying po gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud bzhi ni shin tu zab pa'i dbang gi ye shes gzungs ma rtogs re zhig su la yang ma spel bas thugs kyi sras mchog dam par gyur te/

Were every disciple of this great being counted, they would equal the number of stars in the sky or specks of dust on the earth. That said, his most well-known disciples were Jangmen Lepsé, Balmen Nyima Pal, Jé Yeshé Sung, Tönpa Atsé, Shakrampa Nyima Pal, Yuthok Bumseng, Yuthok Söseng, Sumtön Yeshé Sung, and Geshé Rokchung. Among these disciples was Sumtön Yeshé Sung, who is counted in the garland of births of my lama the Great Fifth, and who worked unceasingly for the welfare of others through the manifested play of the seven lotus-holding conquerors.[555] He was born the son of Rutsam from Darsumpa in Nyemo. He trained in the other sciences until he had perfected them, and then one day he heard the life story of the master Yuthok. His mind was captivated. He decided to seek out teachings in medicine, and for twelve years he lived in the service of the master. Four Tantras: The Essence of Ambrosia Secret Instruction Tantra, a king among tantras because of its profound nature, was at that time expounded only to Yeshé Sung, and so he was truly the main heart-disciple of master Yuthok.

d.div: [555] Probably referring to seven royal manifestations of Avalokiteśvara. The Fifth Dalai Lama was said to be an incarnation of King Trisong Detsen, who was held to be a manifestation of Avalokiteśvara.

f.d:
sdug bsngal mun sel thugs rje nyi 'od las/
phyogs dus rgyal ba thams cad kyi sku gsung thugs yon tan 'phrin las thams cad dang gnyis su med pa'i ye shes kyi ngo bo gyur pa mtshan brjod par dka' ba g.yu thog zhabs kyi spyan sngar/ rje de nyid kyi thugs rje'i bka' drin gyis 'tsho ba ru mtshams su skyes pa'i sum ston ye shes gzungs bdag gis sgo gsum gus pa'i sgo nas lo grangs du mar zhabs la gtugs shing mnyes pa rnam gsum gyis dgyes par byas pa la brten nas/ gzhung dang gdams pa'i zab bcud bka' lung phyag len lhag ma med par bum pa gang 'byo'i tshul du pha phogs su phogs/ 'phyugs gol med pa'i zab gnad mtha' dag ni bstan/ nyams 'khrid zab mo'i rkya bar nas bton/ thugs kyi sras dam par ni dbang bskur/ mtshungs pa med pa'i rje btsun bla ma dam pa 'di nyid drug pa rdo rje 'chang chen po dngos su kha tshig tsam ma yin par zhe thag pa nas thag chod cing / de'i byin rlabs kyis bdag kyang stong nyid snying rje zung du 'jug pa'i gnas lugs thun mong ma yin pa phyin ci ma log pa'i lta ba zab cing phra ba yang ji lta ba bzhin bde blag tu rtogs pas/ rang gzhan gyi don gnyis 'bad med lhun gyis 'grub pa'i rten 'brel yang dag par bsgrigs/ khyad par du yang gso ba rig pa'i gzhung lugs thams cad kyi rgyal po dpal ldan rgyud bzhi cha lag dang bcas ba'i bka' gtad ni kho bo gcig pu las gzhan du ma gnang zhing / kho bo la brgyud pa gang thug tshad ni 'khor ba ma stongs kyi bar du 'gro don btsan sa zin nas gzhan don gso ba rig pas sems can la phan pa bsam gyis mi khyab brjod kyis mi lang ba byed par 'gyur ro/ / zhes lung bstan yang dgyes par mdzad pa yin la/

In his Sunlight of Compassion Clearing the Darkness of Suffering he says:
In the presence of the great Yuthok, whose name is hard to say, whose nature is the very gnosis inseparable from every deed, quality, body, speech, and mind of every buddha of every direction and of every time, through the kindness of the compassion of this great being, I, the physician Sumtön Yeshé Sung born of Rutsam, served him and delighted him for many years with the three ways of pleasing: through devotion in action, speech, and thought. Because of this I received the profound essence of the scriptures and instructions, the transmissions and practices in their entirety, in the manner of one full vase poured into another, and like a son receiving his inheritance from his father. Every profound and essential point was taught without error, and all arose from the churning stick of guidance through experience. I was appointed as his main heart-disciple. I can state, not with mere words but from my heart, that this unparalleled and venerable guru is truly the great sixth Buddha Vajradhara. Through his blessings I have also developed without difficulty the unmistaken, profound, and subtle view—exactly as it is—of that special state of emptiness and compassion combined, and so all auspicious conditions for effortlessly fulfilling the needs of oneself and others are in place. In particular, the transmission of Four Tantras, the very king of all medical scriptures, and all the auxiliary texts has been entrusted to no one else but me. As for the extent of my future lineage, he delightedly prophesized, “Having taken the firm ground of working for living beings until samsara has been emptied, you will be of inconceivable and indescribable help to others through the science of healing.”[556]

d.div: [556] Found in History of the Heartdrop: Hook of Virtue, 4b2.

f.d:
sku lnga lhun grub mar/
kho bo ru mtshams sum pa'i bu/ / dz+nya na d+ha ra bdag 'dra yis/ / dpon khong gi snyan pa rgyang nas thos/ / mtshan thos pa tsam gyis mos pa skyes/ /

In his Effortless Accomplishment of the Five Bodies, he also says:
A person such as I, Jñānadhara,[557] son of Rutsam Sumpa, heard of the fame of my master from afar, and merely hearing his name filled me with joy.

d.div: [557] Jñānadhara is the Sanskrit rendering of Yeshé Sung.
lam dka' ba spyad nas spyan sngar phyin/ / zhal mthong ba tsam gyis byin rlabs phog / longs spyod 'bul nor mi che yang / / pha zhing rta ru btsongs nas phul/ /

Enduring the journey’s hardships, I came into his presence, and merely seeing his face bestowed on me his blessings. Although I had no wealth with which to offer, I exchanged land for horses and made offerings.
lus kyis zhabs tog ma grub kyang / / bla ma ci gsung bka' ma bcag / tshig don spyod kham mi che yang / / g.yel 'khrul med par lo gsum bslabs/ /
Although I did not serve him physically, whatever he commanded I never disobeyed. Although my practice of the texts was not great, I studied for three years without distraction.
rgya phyed snyan grong sdod dus su/ / gdams pa'i rtsa ba ma chad kyang / / lan cig smon lam thugs rje yis/ / gso ba rig pa'i rgyud 'di gnang / /

While staying in Gyaché Nyendrong, though I had not ascertained the fundamentals of his teachings, I made a single prayer, and by his great compassion he gave me this tantra on the science of healing.
chad lhag med pa'i dbu snyung bzhes/ / drang srong brgyud pa'i byin rlabs mdzad/ /

chig brgyud rgyun mi bcad pa'i phyir/ / da res khyed la gtad pa yin/ / da yang mi spel gter du sbed/ / mched grogs gzhan gyis ma mthong bar/ / phag tu yig chung zin bris thob/ / lo skor gcig tu gsang thub gyis/ / de yis dngos grub thob bo gsung / /
He made the pledge to grant without omission or excess, the blessings of the Rishi lineage, and said,

“So that the one-to-one transmission remains unbroken, I now entrust it to you. For the time being, do not expound it but keep it as secret hidden treasure, and unseen by your companions, write it down secretly as a manuscript. Keep it secret for one yearly cycle,[558] the power of which will bring you siddhi.”
[558] Twelve years, the time it takes to complete the cycle of twelve animals in the calendar.
gsung ba bzhin du lag len byas/ / res 'ga' ri bo'i rtse la bris/ / res 'ga' grog po'i phugs su bris/ / res 'ga' shing gseb rtsig phag bris/ /
As he commanded, so I followed. Sometimes I wrote in secret on mountaintops, sometimes in the deepest valleys, sometimes in the deepest forest.

de nas lo grangs bcu gsum na/ / gnam lo rgyal po rta lo la/ / g.yas ru dpal skor lha khang du/ / phyi mo zin bris dpe la bshus/ / sngon chad thos tshor mthong ba med/ / da ni mkha' la nyi shar bzhin/ / 'gro ba'i dpal du shar bar shog /

Thirteen years later, in the jina horse year[559] in the Palkhor temple of Yeru, I put the writing into print. A scripture never before seen, heard, or experienced now shines like the sun in the sky. May it shine in glory for all living beings.
[559] The twenty-eighth year of a sixty-year cycle; possibly 1174.

mkhas pa g.yu thog mgon po de/ / rig pa'i ye shes lags pa 'dra/ / dngos rang yid las skyes sam snyam/ / tshe rabs kyi bla ma yin par nges/ / bsams kyin sku drin che ba'i phyir/ / mi brjed dus gsum gtsug tu khur/ / rgyun chad med par byin gyis rlobs/ /

The master Yuthok Gönpo is like Vidyājñāna, and I feel as if I am truly Manasija;[560] I think that surely he was my lama in lives gone by. His kindness was immense, and I never forget to place him upon on my head. Grant me constantly your blessings.
[560] As mentioned in the introduction, the sages Vidyājñāna and Manasija were emanations of Medicine Buddha that acted as teacher and requestor of Four Tantras.

dpon khong la bu slob grangs mang yang / / sku tshe'i stod la grags pa de/ / rtsis mda'i byang sman dpe le yin/ / che 'gran dpon la byed byed nas/ / gdams pa 'di yi rtsad ma chod/ / deng sang grags pa ci la byed/ /

This master had so many disciples, but in the early part of his life Jangmen Pelé of Tsida was the most renowned. He was very competitive with the master and did not penetrate to the root of these teachings. These days what has his fame accomplished?
sku tshe'i bar du grags pa de/ / khams kyi ston pa a tshes yin/ / brgyad pa'i rtsa 'grel bsgrig bsgrig nas/ / gdams pa 'di yi rtsad ma chod/ / deng sang gzhung bshad gang la byed/ /

In the middle part of his life, Tönpa Atsé of Kham was the most renowned. Constantly collating and comparing root texts and commentaries of the eight branches, he did not penetrate to the root of these teachings. These days what has his explaining of texts accomplished?
sku tshe'i smad du grags pa de/ / nub kyi dge bshes rog chung yin/ / rigs brgyud che sa 'dzin 'dzin nas/ / gdams pa 'di yi rtsad ma chod/ / deng sang 'khor la ci yis skyong / /

In the latter part of his life, Geshé Rokchung of the west was the most renowned. Constantly attached to his family line, he did not penetrate to the root of these teachings. These days who looks after his family?
thog mar dus med bsgril ba yis/ / sras po gnyis dang mag pa gnyis/ / dpon slob gang 'dris 'khyer 'khyer nas/ / gdams pa 'di yi rtsad ma chod/ / deng sang bu slob ci yis skyong / /

At all times the two sons and two sons-in-law were over-familiar in the master-disciple relationship, and they did not penetrate to the root of these teachings. These days who looks after the son disciples?

phyogs nas byon pa'i bu slob rnams/ / la la sdig thog sna re slob/ / la la snang chung gces par 'dzin/ / la la rtsad gcod nan zhus byed/ / la la byung tshad yig sna sgrub/ / la la zong med stong log byed/ / la la lag len bltas nas 'gro/ / la la gzhas dang dgod 'phyo byed/ / la la don med ldong ldong byed/ / gdams pa 'di yi rtsad ma chod/ / khong deng sang nad pa ci yis gso/ /

Of the disciples that came from afar, some only learned one important thing, some valued everything they saw, some concentrated on investigation, some wrote on whatever arose, some went away empty handed, some watched the practices and then left, some spent their time singing and dancing, some were content with meaningless things. Not penetrating to the root of these teachings, these days how will they heal the sick?
mkhas pa g.yu thog mgon po yi/ / gdams pa thob pa a po tsam/ / g.yu thog bka' babs bdag la babs/ / 'tsho byed gzhon nu byon lags kyang / / sman dpyad zhu rgyu med dam snyam/ /

The one who truly gained the teachings of the master Yuthok Gönpo was me alone. The stream of his words flowed into me; and if even Kumāra Jivaka himself were here, I think I would have nothing to ask of him.

f.d: bdag snyan grags bsod nams mi dgos te/ / bla ma drang srong dngos dang mjal/ / gdams ngag mi che'i ka thabs med//[292] ces dkyil 'khor rgya mtsho spro ba dang bsdu ba'i byed po g.yu thog yon tan mgon po'i sras kyi thu bor gyur pa sum ston ye shes gzungs yin la/ des g.yu thog pa'i rnam thar bka' rgya ma'am sku lnga lhun grub ma/ gsang ba'i rnam thar/ bshad rgyud kyi 'grel pa 'bum chung gsal sgron/ rkang 'bam gso ba snyan brgyud zin bris la sogs pa bstan bcos kha yar dang / gtso bor dpal ldan rgyud bzhi nyid kyi 'phrin las rgya cher bskyangs/

I do not need fame and fortune— I have truly met the guru rishi; there is no way I can be deficient in the teachings.[561] Therefore, the heart-disciple of Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, master of manifesting and withdrawing an ocean of mandalas, was Sumtön Yeshé Sung. As an author he composed a variety of works, such as the life story of Yuthok entitled Effortless Accomplishment of the Five Bodies or Sealed Biography of Yuthok; Secret Biography; Illuminating Beacon Small Collection: Commentary on the Explanatory Tantra; and Treatment of Kangbam: Notes from the Whispered Tradition. He concentrated primarily on spreading the teachings of the glorious Four Tantras.

d.div: [292] cha lag bco brgyad smad cha/ brgyud pa'i rnam thar med thabs med pa/ shog_691_phreng 16
[561] Untraced.

f.d:
de'i slob ma'i gtso bo ni gzhon nu ye shes yin te/ sku lnga lhun grub ma las/
rig pa'i ye shes g.yu thog mgon po lags/ / yid las skyes ni slob dpon lha rje lags/ / dngos rang 'tsho byed gzhon nu ye shes lags/ / tshe rabs thog ma med pa'i slob dpon lags/ / bla ma'i thugs rjes kho bo zin pa lags/ / snod ldan bdag la bla ma bka' drin che/[293] / zhes byung ba ltar dang /

His main disciple was Shönu Yeshé. In the Effortless Accomplishment of the Five Bodies it says:
Vidyājñāna was Yuthok Gönpo, Manasija was the divine master, I am Tsojé Shönu Yeshé.[562] He was my master in births without beginning; I have been held by the compassion of the lama; How kind the lama to this worthy vessel![563]

d.div: [293] cha lag bco brgyad smad cha/ brgyud pa'i rnam thar med thabs med pa/ shog_696_phreng 2
[562] Here he is playing with names. Tsojé Shönu was Kumāra Jivaka, the celebrated physician at the time of the Buddha and next in the Four Tantras lineage after Manasija.
[563] Untraced.

f.d: gzhan yang mnga' bdag rtse lde'i skabs a+yon gyi sman pa mig bcos sogs mdzad pa po dzi na mi tra'i sras gso rig rgya mtsho'i pha mthar son pas rgyal po'i bla sman mdzad/ btsun mo'i nad bcos pa'i tshe mi tshangs spyod kyi nyes pa shor bas gsod par phangs te phyag bcad pas b+ha ro phyag rdum mam skyes bu me lhar grags pa bod du phebs/ snyan brgyud be bum nag po/ chung dpyad be bum sngon po/ 'bum khu chur/ rde skor phyi nang gsang gsum sogs man ngag gi yig sna mang du mdzad/ mtha' bzhi/ dgon/ stong / ze'u sman pa ste thugs sras bzhi/ nyang / g.ya'/ 'be la sogs pa zhal slob kyang du ma byung ba sogs kha 'thor ba'i skor yang du ma yod/

Moreover, during the reign of the ruler Tsedé,[564] a doctor from Oḍḍiyāna came to Tibet. A specialist in eye treatments and so forth, he was a son of Jinamitra. He had so perfected his knowledge of medicine that he was appointed royal physician. Once while treating the queen, he committed a sexual indiscretion. The king thought it too great a loss to have him put to death, however, and so he was punished by having one of his hands amputated. Because of this he became known as Bharo of Amputated Hand. His other name was Puruṣa Agnideva. He composed many instructional works, such as Whispered Tradition Black Compilation; Blue Compilation of Children’s Disorders; Fistful Collection; Outer, Inner, and Secret Stone-Removal Collection. His closest disciples were Thazhi, Gön, Tong, and Seu Menpa. He had several other disciples, such as Nyang, Ya, and Bé. There were many other miscellaneous works during those times.

d.div: [564] According to Trinlé (p. 116) the dates of this ruler in the line of the kings of the past are not known but he was said to have established a great Dharma celebration in Ngari in 1076. This would have put him prior to Yönten Gönpo.

f.d: bir wa pa nas brgyud pa'i gcong sde bzhi'i man ngag thar los zin bris su btab pa dang / mi tra dzo gi lugs kyi mig 'byed mun sel sgron me/ kam po tse'i gling du bla ma a ba d+hu d+hi pa las jo bo a ti shas bzhes pa'i khyi dug gso thabs/ rgyud bzhi la brten pa'i gso dpyad kyi yig cha g.yu thog phyi ma man chad du dar ba/ g.yu thog kha rag lha rjes rje yon tan mgon po'i rnam thar nor bu'i 'phreng ba dang / kong po bde rgyal gyis rnam thar gzi brjid rin po che'i gter mdzod/ phag ston shAkya mgon pos don gsal nyi ma'i 'od ldan/ nub phyogs 'gro lding pa'i paN chen byA li ba dang sprul bas 'gro don mdzad pa'i sman pa bcu'i nang tshan spyad lung spud tra'i a+yon pa rin chen dpal gyis bsgyur ba dngul chu'i gzhung skor gsum dang rin chen ril bu'i skor/ dbyug bcos pha dam pa sangs rgyas kyis khyug dpyad dkar nag khra gsum dang rten 'brel gyi skor mang ba/ karma pa rang byung rdo rjes sman mang rgya mtsho/ brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa/ dbang ril sogs dang / ba ri lo tsA bas rig pa thor bu'i 'bum/ lo tsA ba grags seng gi nyer mkho phyogs bsdus be bum/ chag sman rin chen rgyal mtshan dang shAkya ye shes kyi phyogs bsgrigs man ngag mu tig 'phreng ba'am 'bum khu tshur dkar chag dang bcas pa/ de las lcang sman sangs rgyas mgon pos btus pa 'bum khu tshur gdams pa sum cu pa/ lha btsun 'brong rtse bas sman nag chen mo la sogs pa 'brong rtse be bum du grags pa dang / gdong nag lce sman dar rgyas kyis rtsa rgyud la 'grel chen/ bar sman pa'i 'jug khur mar grags pa'i man ngag mang ba/ spyi pa dpal mgon rdo rjes bshad rgyud kyi 'grel pa 'thad ldan 'od zer rab tu 'phro ba rnams/

They include the following: Instructions on the Four Categories of Chong Diseases handed down from Virūpa and written down in note form by Tharpa Lotsāwa; Opening the Eyes: A Lamp Dispelling Darkness, in the tradition of Mitrayogi; a cure for rabies received by Jowo Atiśa from his guru Avadhūtipa in the land of Kampoché;[565] a medical work based on Four Tantras that was extant from the time of the later Yuthok; Jewel Garland Biography of Zé Yönten Gönpo by Yuthok Kharak Lhajé; Brilliant Jewel Treasury Biography by Kongpo Degyal; Sunlight Clarity of Meaning by Phaktön Śākya Gönpo; Three Collections on Mercury and Precious Pill Collection by Panchen Jaliwa from Droding[566] in the west, translated by Orgyenpa Rinchen Pal from Changlung Pütra, who was one of the “ten physicians manifested to work for others”; White, Black, and Multicolored Magic Treatments and Charm Collections, and so on, by Phadampa Sangyé, famed for his stick treatment;[567] Ocean of Medicine Names and Brief Essence of Eight Branches and Bezoars, and so on, by Karmapa Rangjung Dorjé; Miscellaneous Knowledge Collection by Bari Lotsāwa; Compilation of Essentials by Lotsāwa Drakpa Sengé; Pearl Garland Instructions or Fist Collection together with a list of contents, compiled by Chakmen Rinchen Gyaltsen and Shakya Yeshé; Thirty-Two Instructions of the Fist Collection compiled from the previous work and composed by Changmen Sangyé Gönpo; the work known as the Drongtsé Compilation, which includes Black Exposition on Medicine and so on, by Lhatsün Drong Tsewa; Great Commentary to the Root Medical Tantra by Dongnak Chemen Dargyé; many instructional works known as Bag of Instructions for Entering by Barmenpa; and Commentary to the Explanatory Medical Tantra: Light Rays of Validity Radiating Afar by Chipa Palgön Dorjé.

d.div: [565] Kampoché: possibly Kampuchea. According to Gö Lotsāwa’s Blue Annals (p. 390), Avadhūtipa lived in East Bengal, Atiśa’s native region, though Atiśa is well known for having traveled widely.
[566] ’Gro lding; said to be another name for Oḍḍiyāna.
[567] Dbyug bcos: medical investigation using a small stick to tap the site of illness, pioneered by Phadampa Sangyé and others.

f.d: [brang ti ]
14. The Drangti Lineage and a Summary

de yang brang ti ni/ chos kyi rgyal po khri lde gtsug brtan mes ag tshoms su grags pa'i blon po dang / bla sman zung du 'jug pa brang ti rgyal mnyes mkhar phug nas bzung brang ti dar ma snying po/ brang ti grags pa 'bum/ brang ti jo btsun/ brang ti dpal ldan 'bum sogs gnang rigs rjes spyangs kyi sman pa bar ma chad par byung zhing bdud rtsi yur 'dren la sogs pa man ngag chig brgyud zab mo rnams rim gyi yi ger btab pa la brang ti'i pod khra pod dmar du grags/

The Drangti lineage began with Drangti Gyalnyé Kharphuk, reputed to be royal physician and minister to Dharma king Tridé Tsukten Mé Aktsom. It continued in an unbroken lineage of appointed royal physicians and ordinary trained physicians through Drangti Darma Nyingpo, Drangti Drakphuk Sumpa, Drangti Dartsün,[568] Drangti Palden Bum, and so forth. The lineage was also responsible for maintaining one-to-one lineages of profound instructions, such as “channeling the ambrosia,” that were eventually written down and became known as the Drangti Multicolored Works and Drangti Red Works.

d.div: [568] Other editions have Drangti Drakpa Bum, Drangti Jotsün.

f.d: de nas brang ti bsod nams 'bum/ de sras 'jam dpal bzang po ni/ gzhon nu nas shes rab dang thugs stobs shin tu che ba/ karma pak+shis kyang byang chub sems dpa' 'gro ba la phan pa rgya cher mdzad pa zhig 'ong zhes lung bstan/ yab la bstan bcos brgyad pa rtsa 'grel/ smar byang ma bu/ AtsAR+ya'i gso dpyad skor gsum la sogs pa'i bshad skor man ngag phyag len gsan/ sgo bzhi re thang du g.yu thog 'jam dpal dang mjal/ rgyud bzhi cha lag dang bcas pa dang g.yu thog pa'i phyag len man ngag rnams zhus shing thugs su chud/ rtsis phu byang mo khud du ljangs sman pa ye shes bzang po yun ring du bsten nas yan lag brgyad pa la mkhas par sbyangs pa sogs bod du grags pa'i gso dpyad phal mo che la dbang 'byor/ bla ma bdag nyid chen po'i gdan sar spyan drangs/ brgyad pa'i 'chad nyan btsugs/ brgya tsho byed kyi go sa dang bla sman kyi mthil mdzad/ dus chos la rgyud dang brgyud pa lag len po ti rnams ma chag par gsung ba sogs gzhan don kho nas dus 'da'/

Among the lineage was Drangti Sönam Bum. His son was Jampal Sangpo who from an early age showed exceptional intelligence and compassion. Karma Pakshi[569] proclaimed that he was a bodhisattva and prophesized that he would be of great service to others. From his father he received teachings, collections, instructions, and practices, including the root text and commentaries to the Treatise of Eight Branches, the Red Ink Son and Mother Texts, and the Three Ācārya Medical Collections. In Goshi Rethang he met with Yuthok Jampal, from whom he learned and mastered Four Tantras and its auxiliary works, along with Yuthok’s oral teachings and practices. In Tsiphu Jangmo Khyü he studied for a long time under the Jang doctor Yeshé Sangpo and became so learned in the eight branches and so on that he became renowned in Tibet as the master of nearly all of medical science. A great lama invited him to his monastic seat, and there he initiated classes in the study of the eight branches. He was given the position of governor of half a hundred[570] and became the principal of the senior physicians. He was constantly teaching the tantra, the eight branches, the practices, and the canonical scriptures. In this way his time was spent solely in the service of others.

d.div: [569] Karma Pakshi (1204–83) was the Second Karmapa.
[570] Rgya tsho; smallest unit of administration in Tibet; a subdivision of a dzong.

f.d: sde tshan lnga 'grel lam phyi ma rgyud kyi sbyor tshad yod pa lag len pod chung du grags pa tshad ldan sbyor ba rnams kyi khungs su byed cing / phal che ba g.yu thog lag len pod chung dngos dang 'khrul gzhi yod pa/ bya 'dre'i bcos rnams mdzad/

Jampal Sangpo composed the Five-Section Commentary, also known as the Small Volume on Practice, containing measurements and amounts for the medicinal preparation from the Final Tantra. This serves as an authoritative source for measurements in medicinal preparations and is probably confused with Yuthok’s Small Volume on Practice. He also composed Treatment of Bird-Like Demons.

de sras bgres pa brang ti shing rkang ngam rgyal ba bzang pos rang gi yab dang bi ji dpal mgon sogs bsten nas/ gzhung man ngag phyag len rnams thugs su chud/ g.yu thog 'tsho byed kyi spyan sngar byon nas rgyud bzhi cha lag dang bcas pa dang / lag len pod chung la sogs pa'i gdams pa du ma gsan/ sgo bzhi re thang du bshad gsar la byon par gzhan rnams khri chung logs su yod pa'i steng nas bshad pa bya dgos kyang / dpon 'tsho bas khyed gnang rigs kyi sman pa gzhan dang mi 'dra bas g.yu thog pa rang gi chos khri nas gyis zhes gsungs/

His eldest son was Drangti Shingkang, or Gyalwa Sangpo. He studied with his father and Biji Palgön among others and learned the scriptures, the oral teachings, and the practices. He came to Yuthok Tsojé,[571] from whom he received many teachings, such as Four Tantras, its auxiliary texts, and Small Volume on Practice. He came to give new teachings at Goshi Rethang, and whereas others had to teach from small side thrones, the physician in charge said to him, “You are a lineage physician like no other. Please teach from the throne of Yuthok.”

d.div: [571] Son of Yuthok Jampal (Trinlé, p. 168).

f.d: yab kyi gdan sa dang gdung brgyud khu dbon rnams kyi bla sman sngar mu ltar bskyangs/ stod smad kyi slob ma du ma la gzhung man ngag phyag len rnams legs par gnang ba sogs 'gro phan rlabs che/
