15. The Jang Tradition

'gro phan yar zla'i 'phel ba la 'gran pa mdzad kyang / phyis su gso rig spyi dang bye brag dpal ldan rgyud bzhi'i dka' gnad kyi mdud pa bkrol te rig gnas rtse mo 'di'i bstan pa'i bdag po lta bu mkhas pa byang zur gnyis zhes grags pa byung ba'i/ byang pa ni/ phun sum tshogs pa'i bsod nams kyi dpal las grub pa'i rgya nag gong ma'i khri la

In the benefits they brought to others, the renowned physicians listed above can be compared to the waxing of the moon. However, in later times[582] there arose two great scholars—Jangpa Namgyal Draksang (b. 1395) and Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé (1439–75)—who loosened the knots of the difficult points of medicine in general and of the four glorious tantras in particular, and in doing so were like masters of doctrine of this highest of sciences.

d.div: [582] The physicians listed in the previous chapter span up to the thirteenth century. This section deals with the end of the fourteenth century onward.

f.d: gnam gyi lung gis dbang bsgyur ba mi nyag se'u rgyal po nas gdung rabs bdun pa/ gong ma se chen rgyal pos rin po che'i tham ka dang si tu'i las ka gnang bas mngon par mtho ba/ gu'i gung chos grags dpal bzang dang yum si tu chos rin pa'i sras mo 'bum skyong rgyal mo gnyis kyi sras su rab byung bdun pa'i shing phag la dpal ngam rings kyi rgyal sde chen po byang phyogs sham+b+ha la'i 'dun sa nye bar 'phos pa'i bsti gnas su 'khrungs/

His father was Guigung Chödrak Palsang, who was a seventh-generation descendent of the Seu king of Minyak[583] and who was ordained by the writ of heaven as emperor on the Chinese throne, a position produced by the glories of extraordinary merit. The Sechen emperor[584] had presented to him a jeweled seal and appointed him to the position of Situ, greatly elevating his status. His mother was Bumkyong Gyalmo, the daughter of Situ Chörin, and Jangpa was born as their son in the wood-pig year of the seventh sixty-year cycle[585] in the great kingdom of Ngamring, a place to which the great capital of the northern land of Shambhala had seemingly moved.

d.div: [583] Tibetan and Western sources agree that this dynasty was founded in 1038 by the Tangut (Tib. tang zhang chang) tribe and took the Chinese dynastic name Hsi Hsia. This was corrupted in Tibetan to shis zha, and then to si hu and se’u. (Great Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, p. 2069). Minyak is now in Kansu province, in the Yellow River northern loop, and was previously known as Ning-hsia (Tib. nying zha). According to Fairbank and Reischauer, the Tanguts were actually Tibetans (p. 124).

[584] The Sechen emperor was the Mongolian Kublai Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan (1215–94). Western and Tibetan sources are in general agreement on his dates: he came to the throne in 1260, moved his empire from Karakorum to Beijing in 1264, and became the first ruler of the Mongolian Yuan dynasty in 1271.

[585] The wood-pig year of the seventh cycle is 1395, and Dungkar explicitly states this year. However, if Jangpa were born in 1395, he would have been born a hundred years after his father’s benefactor, Kublai Khan, died in 1294. Trinlé says that Jangpa was born in 1295, which would fit but does not correspond to the wood-pig year of the seventh cycle.

f.d: chung ngu nas sngon gyi bag chags rab tu sad de skyes bu dam pa'i kun tu spyod pas dus 'da'/ mkhas shing grub ba'i dbang phyug lo chen byang chub rtse mo dang / rang rigs gdung gi thig le 'dzin pa bstan pa'i rgyal mtshan/ mkhan chen zla mgon shes rab pa rnams la dam pa'i chos kyi dga' ston bdud rtsi'i skyes lan gcig min par bzhes/ dgung lo bzhi lnga'i dus lho phyogs bskyed ma'i pho brang du bzhugs/ yi ge 'dri klog brda dag gis mtshon pa thams cad tshegs med du mkhyen/ slar yang dpal ngam ring du phebs nas stan chags/ dgung lo bcu pa'i dus mnal lam dag pa'i snang bar o rgyan pad+ma dang mjal ba nas snga phyir bcom ldan 'das thub pa'i dbang po/ rgyal po gzugs can snying po dang zla ba bzang po/ thogs med sku mched/ mi la ras pa la sogs pa lha dang bla ma du ma'i zhal gzigs shing gsung gi gnang ba thob/ bka' lnga pa dpal 'byor shes rab rin chen dpal bzang / seng ge rgyal mtshan pa/ rgya gar rdo rje gdan gyi mkhan po shA ri pu tra/ paN chen nags kyi rin chen/ bo dong phyogs las rnam rgyal la sogs pa mtshan nyid dang ldan pa'i yongs 'dzin mang du bsten nas mdo sngags shes bya rig pa'i gnas thams cad la dpyis phyin par sbyangs/ hor bka' bzhi pa seng ge rgyal mtshan la dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa zhus pas mtshan chos rgyal rnam rgyal grags bzang du gsol zhing / de gong gi mtshan rgya rug dar ma rig 'dzin yin par grags/ dpal ldan sa skya pa kun dga' bkra shis rgyal mtshan dpal bzang rgya nag gong ma chen po ta ming gis gdan drangs/ theg chen chos kyi rgyal po'i lung las phul ba sogs bkur bsti phun sum tshogs pa mdzad pa'i bdag rkyen las/ rigs ldan chos kyi rgyal po 'di nyid la'ang dngul gyi tham ka dang ta'i si tu'i las ka stsal/

From an early age instincts of the past awoke within him, and he spent his days displaying the behavior of a noble being. From the great master of study and practice, Lochen Jangchup Tsemo, from Tenpa Gyaltsen of his own blood line, and from the high-ranking Dagön Sherap he received, on more than one occasion, the ambrosia gift from the great feast of the sacred Dharma. When he was four or five he lived in Kyema palace in the south. There, without any difficulty, he mastered subjects such as reading, writing, and spelling. Later he settled back in Ngamring. At the age of ten he had a pure-vision dream in which he met Orgyen Padma. From then on he had visions and received the gift of teachings from the Bhagavān Munīndra, from kings Bimbisāra and Sucandra, from Asaṇga and Vasubandhu, from Milarepa, and from many other deities and lamas. Under many qualified guardians,[586] such as the master of the five disciplines Paljor Sherap, Rinchen Palsang, Sengé Gyaltsen, Bodhgāya abbot Śāriputra, pandit Vanaratna,[587] and Bodong Choklé Namgyal, he studied to perfection the sutras, tantras, and the sciences. From the Mongolian master of four disciplines, Sengé Gyaltsen, he took the vows of a layman and was given the name Chögyal Namgyal Draksang. Until then he had been known as Gyaruk Darma Rikzin. The glorious Sakya lama Künga Tashi Gyaltsen Palsang had visited by invitation the great Chinese Tai Ming emperor, who bestowed upon him the title of Mahayana Dharma king and other tokens of respect. Following this precedent, the emperor also presented this high-lineage Dharma king with a silver seal and the position of Tai Situ.[588]

d.div: [586] Yongs ’dzin, one who “protects completely” from the extremes of samsara and nirvana.
[587] Vanaratna is said to be the last of the great Indian pandits to visit Tibet—in 1426. See Tibet Chronology, compiled by Dan Martin at www.thdl.org.

[588] The “high-lineage Dharma king” is Jangpa, who chronologically could have received these awards from a Ming emperor because the Ming dynasty did not begin until 1368, and Jangpa was born in 1395. Kunga Tashi Gyaltsen Palsang was born in 1349 and visited the emperor in 1413. By calling him a high-lineage (kalkī) Dharma king, the author is indicating that Jangpa is an incarnation of King Sucandra.

f.d: dgung lo so gcig gi khar seng ge rtse ba'i sras mo nam mkha' dpal 'bum khab tu bzhes/ rim gyis sras lcam sring rnams bskrun/ mkhas pa'i snyan grags kyis sa'i steng khyab pas dran dbang rdo rje rgya mtshan/ mi nyag chos grags bzang po/ rtses dang pa sangs rgyas lhun grub sogs du mas khengs pa'i ri bo bsnyil te zhabs kyi pad+mor gtugs/ paN chen byams pa gling pas kyang bsngags brjod kyi me tog 'thor/ thams cad mkhyen pa dge 'dun grub dang dri ba dris lan mdzad cing chos rgyal zla ba bzang po'i yang srid du ngos bzung / dgung lo bzhi bcu pa nas rim par gsang chen rgyud sde rab 'byams rgya mtsho'i gtso bor gyur pa dus 'khor gyi sku gsung thugs yongs su rdzogs pa'i blos bslang bkod pas khyad par 'phags shing rgyu gser dngul shas che ba las grub pa rin po che'i rgyan gyis spras pa/ byams chen dang dus 'khor gyi sku/ bka' 'gyur byang brtsegs ma sogs sku gsung thugs rten mang du bzhengs/ mnga' zhabs su tho btsun btus te byams phrug gi dge 'dun 'dus pa'i sde btsugs/ rje btsun sa skya paN+Di ta dbu gtsug nas thim pas dpal ldan sa skya pa'i dgongs pa'i zab gnad thams cad thugs la shar ba sogs rtogs pa'i yon tan mtha' las 'das/ bka'i rtsom pa yang de bzhin gshegs pa'i gdung rabs/ bstod pa/ bka' bstan du ma'i don btus sogs bstan pa spyi'i gnas las bsgrags pa'i bstan bcos sum cu rtsa lnga/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i phyi nang gzhan gsum las rtsis kyi bstan bcos byis pa bde blag tu 'jug pa sogs rgyud thog ma'i le'u gnyis kyi don 'grel gyi dbang du mdzad pa'i bstan bcos bzhi bcu zhe gnyis/ dbang chog bde ba chen po'i chu rgyun sogs dbang le dang bsgrub le'i don 'grel du mdzad pa lnga bcu rtsa bzhi/ lus dkyil rdzogs rim lam dus sogs ye shes le'u'i don 'grel bcu gnyis/ shes bya rab gsal/ mdor bsdus dang po'i rnam bshad sogs spyir bsdoms kyi 'grel pa drug / sgra rig pa'i nying khu ka lA pa'i mdo rgyan/ bzo rig par de bzhin gshegs pa'i sku gzugs kyi cha tshad/ tshad ma la bstan bcos ma mdzad kyang rigs par smra ba du ma'i khrod du thal 'gyur 'phen pa sogs rgyal po paN+Di ta zhes 'chad rtsod rtsom pas dus 'da'/

When he was almost thirty-one he took as a bride Namkha Palbum, the daughter of Sengé Tsewa, and eventually they produced sons and daughters. His fame spread throughout the land, and soon Drenwang Dorjé Gyaltsen, Minyak Chödrak Sangpo, Sangyé Lhündrup from Tsedong, and many others crushed their mountains of pride and came to worship at his feet. Even Panchen Jampa Lingpa offered flowers of praise. He engaged in question-and-answer communication with the omniscient Gendün Drup and was recognized as an incarnation of the Dharma king Sucandra.[589] From the age of forty onward, he created many representations of the enlightened body, speech, and mind. These include the construction of very special and complete three-dimensional body, speech, and mind mandala of Kālacakra—the supreme tantra among the vast ocean of the highly secret tantras—made almost entirely from gold and silver and adorned with precious stones. He also erected statues of Maitreya and Kālacakra and produced the Jangtsek Kangyur and Tengyur. Using his high position he chose people from the local community to become monks and founded the Jamtruk monastic community. He developed qualities of insight beyond measure. For example, by visualizing Sakya Paṇḍita on his head and dissolving him into his body, all the profound and essential points of Sakya thought dawned in his mind. As an author he composed thirty-five works on general aspects of the doctrine, such as a work on the lineage of the Tathāgata, various praises, and many compilations drawn from the Kangyur and Tengyur. From the outer, inner, and “other” divisions of the glorious Kālacakra, he wrote, based on the first two chapters of the tantra, forty-two explanatory works, such as the Easy to Understand Astronomical Treatise; based on the Initiation and Methods of Accomplishment chapters, he wrote fifty-four explanatory works, such as Stream of Great Bliss Initiation Procedure; he wrote twelve explanatory works on the Gnosis chapter, such as Body Mandala Completion Stage of the Path; and he wrote six general summarizing commentaries, such as Clarification of Phenomena and Explanation of the First Summary. On the essence of grammar he wrote Ornament to the Kalāpa Sutra. On crafts he composed Measurements of the Form of the Tathāgata. He wrote no works on logic, but in the company of logicians he would pose consequences, and so forth, and became known as the pandit king, spending his time teaching, debating, and composing.

d.div: [589] King Sucandra was the king of Shambhala who first received the Kālacakra tantra from the Buddha in India.

f.d: khyad par du gso ba rig pa phul du phyin pas yan lag brgyad pa thams cad kyi snying po bsdus pa yid bzhin nor bu rin po che zhes bya ba'i bstan bcos le'u brgya nyi shu yod pa zhig dang / rtsa ba'i rgyud kyi bshad pa rgyud don gsal byed sgron ma/ bshad rgyud kyi rgya cher 'grel pa bdud rtsi'i chu rgyun dang / Tika chung don gsal/ phyi ma rgyud kyi dka' 'grel dgos 'dod 'byung ba/ yongs gtad kyi 'grel pa tshig don rnam par gsal ba/ sman gzhung rin chen sgrom bu/ rtsom pa chung ba rgyud bzhi'i dka' 'phrang mun sel/ gso thabs sum brgya drug cu'i ngos 'dzin/ rtsa bshad gsal ba'i sgron me/ srog gcod nad dgu'i dbye ba/ 'tsho byed rnams la snying brtse ba'i 'phrul gyi yig chung / seng ge rtse 'tsho byed kyis dris lan sogs 'chad rtsod rtsom gsum gyi sgo nas gso ba rig pa'i srog 'thud pa lta bur gyur/

He excelled in the science of medicine in particular, and his medical compositions include the following: • Essence of All Eight Branches: A Precious Wish-Fulfilling Jewel in 120 chapters • Beacon Illuminating the Meaning of the Tantra: Explanation of the Root Tantra • Stream of Ambrosia: Extensive Commentary on the Explanatory Tantra • Short Commentary Illuminating the Meaning of the Explanatory Tantra • Fulfilling All Needs and Wishes: Commentary on the Final Tantra • Word Commentary on the Text of the Entrustment Section • Precious Casket Medical Text • Short Text Dispelling the Darkness on the Difficult Path of Four Tantras • Identifying the 360 Healing Methods • Beacon Illuminating the Root and Explanatory Tantras • Categories of the Nine Fatal Illnesses • Heartfelt Magical Manuscript for Doctors • Response to the Physician Sengé Tsé With these and other works his teaching, debating, and compositions began a renaissance within medical science.

pho brang du gnam lcags babs pa nye skor gyi mi phal cher brgyal ba dang dngangs pa sogs zug rngu mi zad pa byung rung sku la cung zad kyang brdzi bar ma nus pa dang / jo skyabs pa'i gzhis 'dzin ma gdon drag pos zin par phur gdab kyi gzigs stangs mdzad pa tsam gyis grol ba sogs grub mtshan kyang mang / de ltar dgung lo brgyad cu gya gcig gi bar bstan pa dang 'gro ba'i don rgya cher mdzad nas/ slar yang sa la spyod pa'i 'og min lhun grub sdings su zla gcig tsam sku cung zad snyun pa'i tshul bstan pa'i skabs nyin re bzhin yar 'chi ba med pa'i lag pad kyis gtor ba mad+d+ha ra ba'i char rgyun ma chad par babs pa'i ngang nas/ shing lug snron zla'i gral tshes drug gi nyin sprul sku rags pa'i za ma tog las longs sku ye shes sgyu ma'i sku zung 'jug dus kyi 'khor lo'i thugs kar bsdus/ 'ja' 'od dang me tog gi char dri bzang po'i ngad 'thul ba sogs dpag gis mi lang ba byung /

He revealed many indications of siddhi. For example, a thunderbolt once struck the palace, rendering most people inside unconscious or terrified, but it had no effect on him whatsoever. Also, one time when the wife of a local governor was possessed by a demon, he was able to exorcise it merely by posing with a ritual dagger. In this way, until the age of eighty-one, he accomplished much for the doctrine and for living beings. Finally, having retired to Salachöpa Ögmin Lhündrup Ding he showed signs of being slightly ill for about a month, and during that time a continuous shower of coral tree flowers fell each day, cast by the lotus hand of deathlessness. In the wood-sheep year,[590] during the sixth day of the Jyeṣṭha month, the union of the saṃbhogakāya and the illusory gnosis body arose from the container of his coarse nirmāṇakāya form and merged into the heart of Kālacakra.[591] Rainbow light, a rain of flowers exuding a beautiful aroma, and countless other wondrous signs were seen.

d.div: [591] Thus emulating the passing of King Sucandra of Shambhala, of whom he was an emanation.

f.d:
rje grol mchog gis/
theg pa'i mthar thug dus kyi 'khor lo nas/ / sman dpyad mo rtsis bar gyi rig gnas la/ / gdul bya rang rang bsam pa bzhin drangs te/ / kun kyang mkhas dang grub pa'i sa la bzhag[296] / ces pa ltar zhal slob bgrang bar mi nus pa yod kyang gtso bo bdag nyid chen po dpal ldan chos skyong gis dbu mdzad mkhan slob/ jo nang gdan sa ba 'jam dbyangs nam mkha' chos skyong / byams pa gser mchog 'od dpal/ tsha sna ba bsam gtan rgya mtsho/ shangs ston

Jé Drölchok says:
In the sciences, from ultimate-vehicle Kālacakra to medicine and astronomy, he led each disciple according to disposition, bringing them all to levels of scholarship and attainment.[592] The list of his disciples is beyond number. However, his main disciples were headed by the great being Palden Chökyong. Others include Jamyang Namkha Chökyong of Jonang Monastery, Tsanawa Samten Gyatso, and Shangtön Künga Palden. These were among his main disciples maintaining the tantra tradition.

d.div: [296] 'di jo nang kun dga' grol mchog gi rigs ldan chos kyi rgyal po rnam rgyal bzang po'i rnam thar mdor bsdus shig yod pa de'i nang 'tshol dgos/
[592] Untraced.

f.d: kun dga' dpal ldan sogs rgyud sde'i srol 'dzin du ma yod la/ de'i nang nas gso rig gi slob ma dang bla sman zung du 'brel ba mi'i nyi ma mthong ba don ldan nam byams pa dkon mchog rin chen ni/ rgyal ba phyag na pad+mo mi rje'i tshul bzung ba gnam lha babs kyis rgyal po/ 'greng mgo nag mi'i rje/ 'phrul gyi lha btsan po mes dbon rnam pa gsum la sogs pa bod chos rgyal gyi gdung dri ma med pa bsod nams rdo rje zhes bya ba'i sras su bltams/

Among the above was the medical disciple, and also court physician, Minyima Thongwa Dönden or Jampa Könchok Rinchen. He was born the son of Sönam Dorjé, who was of the pure lineage of the great Tibetan kings, which included the lotus-holding conqueror in noble human form, the lord of the black-haired people, and the emanated celestial emperor, known collectively as the three noble ancestors.[593]

d.div: [593] These are kings Songtsen Gampo, Trisong Detsen, and Tritsuk Detsen, or Ralpachen.

f.d: chung ngu nas dkon cog gsum bla mar 'dzin cing / dad pa dang brtson 'grus che ba/ ma rabs dbul phongs rnams snying rjes skyong ba sogs phal pa'i spyod tshul las 'das/ yi ge 'bri klog la sogs pa tshegs med du mkhyen/ sku nar son nas 'phags yul gyi paN+Di ta chen po nags kyi rin chen/ lo chen bsod nams rgya mtsho/ byang bdag po rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang / brang ti dpal ldan 'tsho byed kyis mtshon mkhas shing grub brnyes kyi slob dpon du ma bsten te/ sde snod gsum dang rgyud sde bzhi dgongs 'grel gyi bstan bcos dang bcas pas gzhi bzung / rig pa'i gnas spyi dang khyad par gso ba rig pa la phul phyin pas dpal ldan rgyud bzhi/ brgyad pa rtsa 'grel/ snyan rgyud 'grel chen/ phyi nang gsang gsum gyi 'grel pa/ rgyas btab nyer lnga rnams mtha' drug tshul bzhi'i sgo nas ston cing / gter rgyud la cha lag bco brgyad sogs bshad srol ma nyams pa dang / khyad par rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang la so ma rA dza/ zla zer/ bdud rtsi bum pa/ sbyor ba brgya pa/ mdo lnga sogs sman dpyad phal che ba dang / yab bsod nams rdo rje la bka' gtad rgya'i dbang / chu'i lha mo'i sgrub skor/ snyan brgyud kyi byin rlabs tshang ba/ brang ti la chu'i lha mo dang drang srong gi sgrub skor sogs gsan/

From an early age he held the Three Jewels as his lama and was blessed with great faith and perseverance. His behavior, such as his tendency to look after the poor and the wretched with compassion, was beyond the ordinary. He mastered reading, writing, and so on without any difficulty. In his youth he served under many masters of great scholarship and attainment, such as the Indian pandit Vanaratna, Lotsāwa Sönam Gyatso, the Jang master Rikden Namgyal Draksang, and Drangti Palden Tsojé, and built a solid foundation of the three scriptural baskets, the four classes of tantra, and the commentarial treatises. He mastered the sciences and, being particularly proficient in the science of medicine, he taught Four Tantras, the root text and commentaries to Eight Branches, the great commentaries of the Oral Tradition, commentaries on the inner, outer, and secret, and the twenty-five sealed works, all explained using the six limits and the four methods.[594] He maintained the teaching traditions of the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts to the Treasure tradition form of the tantra, and so forth. Specifically, from Rikden Namgyal Draksang he learned most medical works, including Somarāja, Moonlight Commentary on Eight Branches, Vase of Ambrosia, Hundred Medical Preparations, and the five sutras. From his father Sönam Dorjé he received the initiation for the entrustment of the tantra, the collection of goddess practices for urine divination, and the complete blessings of the oral transmission. From Drangti he received the urine divination goddess practices and the rishi practices.

d.div: [594] Mtha’ drug tshul bzhi. These are modes of interpretation of enigmatic tantras. One interpretation of these concepts is found in Dudjom Rinpoche’s Nyingma School of Tibetan Buddhism, pp. 290–92.

f.d: mdor na bod gangs can na dar so cog gi gso dpyad mtha' dag la mkhyen pa'i spyan ras mkha' ltar yangs pa'i snyan grags kyi ba dan phyogs bcur g.yo bas rje zur mkhar ba mnyam nyid rdo rje'ang thugs 'phrogs te/ rigs rus cho 'brang ming sogs la bsnyad nas don dbus phyogs su phebs thub min dang / bu slob 'dra legs bshad zhu bar gtong bzhed kyi dri ba zhus pa'i lan la/

In short, with his eyes of wisdom as open as the sky, alighting upon the whole range of medical science that had spread throughout this snow-mountain land, the banner of his fame flew in all ten directions. Even Jé Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé was captivated by him, and under the pretext of wanting to know about his family, lineage, name, and so on, Surkhar composed a letter to Minyima Thongwa Dönden. In reality Surkhar himself was unable to go to central Tibet to meet him and was in fact requesting teachings like a good disciple. The master replied as follows:

swa sti sid+haM/ dpal rdo rje sems dpa' la phyag 'tshal lo/ /
nyi ma'i gnyen mchog bu ram shing ba'i sras/ / gau tam thub dbang lha yi lha la sogs/ / bgrang yas mtshan mnga' shAkya'i rgyal po la/ / gus pas btud nas bdag gi ming bshad do/ /

Svasti siddhaṃ I prostrate to the glorious Vajrasattva.
To the great friend of the sun, Gautama, son of the Ikṣu[595] lineage, Munīndra, god of gods, to him with countless names, king of the Śākya race, I prostrate; and I will now explain my name.

d.div: [595] Bu ram shing, “sugar cane.” Ikṣvāku, one belonging to the sugar-cane lineage—the ancestral race of the Buddha.
lha rigs jo bo'i brgyud du bltams pa yin/ / legs sbyangs gso rig drang srong brgyud mar byon/ / gzhan yang rig gnas mkhas pa'i brgyud par skyes/ / ming la lha btsun jo sras bya ba yin/ /

I was born into a noble (jowo) family of celestial (lha) lineage and came into the well-trained Rishi lineage of medicine. Moreover, I was born into a lineage wise in the sciences; I am known as Lhatsün José.
legs byas dpal gyis mi dman dal 'byor thob/ / dad brtson brtse bar ldan pas bstan la dga'/ / ston par mi phyed dad pa'i rdo rje 'dzin/ / kho bo'i ming la dpal ldan rdo rje zer/ /

Not lacking in the glory (pal) of wholesome deeds, I have attained this form of leisure and opportunity. Endowed (den) with faith, perseverance, and compassion, I have great joy in the teachings. Holding the vajra (dorjé) of unshakeable faith in the Teacher, I am known as Palden Dorjé.
'gro kun skyong ba'i yid smon ci yang skyes/ / dkon mchog gsum las gzhan pa'i skyabs mi tshol/ / dge ba'i bshes gnyen rin chen cod pan 'dzin/ / ming la byams pa dkon cog rin chen zer/ /

Because I have developed to the fullest the joyful love (jampa) that cares for all living beings, not seeking a refuge other than the Three Jewels (könchok), holding spiritual friends as my crown jewel (rinchen), I am known as Jampa Könchok Rinchen.
rgya cher thos pa'i dkyil 'khor yongs gang zhing / / ris med brtse ba'i bdud rtsis kun nas gang / / rtsod dus mtshan mo'i kun+da bskyed byed pa/ / ming la drang srong zla ba'i 'od zer zer/ /

With the full-moon mandala of learning complete, satiated with ambrosia of nondiscriminating compassion, producing the kairava flower[596] in the dark night of the kaliyuga, I am known as Rishi Dawa Özer (Moonlight).
[596] Tib., kun da. Here probably refers to the white lotus flower that blossoms at night; sometimes refers to the kumuda flower.
gso rig gzhung lugs pad tshal legs par 'byed/ / shes 'dod rnams kyi blo mig don ldan byed/ / nad med tshe ring lo tog rgyas byed pa'i/ / ming la drang srong mi'i nyi ma zer/ /

Opening the petals of the medical tradition lotus grove, giving light to the inner eyes of those who wish to learn, ripening a bountiful harvest of health and long life, I am known as Minyima (Sun of Humanity).
sna tshogs rig pa'i kha dog ci yang gsal/ / shes bya'i chu klung 'bum phrag ngoms med 'thung / / dran dang shes bzhin gser gyi sa gzhis rten/ / ming la drang srong 'tsho byed rgya mtsho zer/ /

Reflecting the colors of the various sciences, drinking without satiation thousands of rivers of knowledge, supported by the golden foundation of mindfulness and awareness, I am known as Rishi Tsojé Gyatso (Ocean).
las nad che la tshogs gsog sgrib sbyong bstan/ / gdon du che la sgrib shing yas su che/ / 'chi nges rnams la'ang chos bshad 'phral zug gcog / ming la drang srong mthong ba don ldan zer/ /

For those struck by karma-caused illness, I teach the gathering of merit, the purifying of obstruction. For those greatly disturbed by spirits, I am equally the great hindrance destroyer.[597] Even to those who will die from their illness, I teach the Dharma, providing relief from the pain. I am known, therefore, as Rishi Thongwa Dönden (Beneficial to See).
[597] Sgrib shing. Literally, “hindrance stick,” the wearer of which cannot be harmed by spirits.
rang skyon rtogs nas ci nus spong bas drangs/ / gzhan skyon rtogs nas ci nus 'chos pas srong / / drang srong chen po'i ring lugs 'dzin pa'i rigs/ / ming la drang srong rgyud 'dzin bya ba yin/ /

Seeing my own faults and doing what I can to eliminate them, seeing the faults of others and doing what I can to remedy them, I am without pretension (drang) and honest (song). I am of the lineage that holds (zin) the great Rishi tradition (gyü). I am known, therefore, as Rishi[598] Gyüzin.
[598] Drang srong in Tibetan; has the etymology of being upright—without pretension (drang) and honest (srong).
bstan 'dzin rnams la srog las gces par 'dzin/ / sdig ldan drin gyis bskyangs nas bde la 'god/ / rang la gnod byed la yang ci phan byed/ / ming la drang srong kun gyi bshes gnyen zer/ /

Holding those who work for the doctrine dearer than my life, nurturing with kindness those of evil disposition and bringing them to happiness, helping as best I can even those who would harm me, I am known as Rishi Küngyi Shenyen (Spiritual Friend to All).
gzhan gyis btang ba'i yi chad nad pa gso/ / dbul phongs skyabs med rnams la lhag par byams/ / ma 'dris glo bur mgron la phebs par skyong / / ming la 'tsho byed skye dgu'i dpal zhes zer/ /

Healing the exhaustion in those sent by others, showing particular love to the destitute and friendless, taking care of visitors in unfamiliar surroundings, I am known as Tsojé Kyegü Pal (Supreme among Living Beings).
chen pos bkur yang khengs pa rnam par spangs/ / gzhan gyi don du sdug kyang skyo ba med/ / bsnyen bkur bsngags pa'i lan la re ba dor/ / ming la drang srong mi'i dpag bsam zer/ /
da lta mi rnams 'bras bu'i nad las skyob/ / slad nas 'gro kun dug gsum 'don par smon/ / rtag tu kun la phan 'dogs bsam sbyor can/ / ming la drang srong gzhan phan mtha' yas zer/ /

Now I protect human beings from the ripened fruits of disease. For the future I yearn to dispel the three poisons in all beings. At all times my thoughts and deeds are for helping all. I am known, therefore, as Rishi Shenphen Thayé (Of Boundless Help to Others).
gso rig mdo dang rgyud sde 'gyur ba dang / / lugs sde bzhi yi bstan bcos du ma dang / / gangs ri'i khrod kyi gso dpyad phal cher go / ming la drang srong gso rig rab 'byams zer/ /

The translated sutras and tantras on medicine, the many treatises of the four traditions, the medical practices in this snowy land, I understand most of them; I am known, therefore, as Rishi Sorik Rabjam (Of Vast Medical Knowledge).
rnyed dka'i sman rnams 'bad rtsol tshegs kyis sgrub/ / sgrub sla'i sman rnams le lo spangs nas bsags/ / gso bya kun gyi re ba yid bzhin skong / / ming la drang srong sman byin bya ba yin/ /
phyogs ris mnga' thang bdag tu bzung ba med/ / byams sdang mtho dma' 'byor rgud mnyam par bzung / / 'or che tsam yang don du gnyer ba med/ / ming la dge bsnyen 'tsho byed bya ba yin/ /
[599] Dge gnyen; literally, “moving closer to virtue.” Lay practitioner who has the basis of the five basic vows of liberation.
'tsho byed mkhas rnams bkur stis bstod cing bsngags/ / gzhon pa rnams la ma brnyas spro ba bskyed/ / rang dang mnyam pa rnams la phrag dog spangs/ / ming la drang srong sems dpa' legs sems zer/ /
'chi bdag zhags pa'i dra ba dum bur gcod/ / zug gzer dug mda' drag po gcur gyis 'don/ / zungs zad glo bur rgas pa dar mar bsgyur/ / ming la drang srong mi 'jigs srog sbyin zer/ /
nad pa'i tshogs rnams gsos par byas pa yi/ / de yi gnyen dang mdza' bshes 'khor rnams kun/ / 'bral bar mi phod de la dga' ston byed/ / ming la drang srong mya ngan med ces zer/ /
I cure the sick and produce a great festival of joy for their friends and loved ones unable to bear the thought of separation; I am known, therefore, as Rishi Nya Ngenmé (No Sorrow).
gso sla ba rnams zas spyod sman gyi gso/ / de las log rnams bya log khyug dpyad bsngags/ / gnyi ga min la 'phrul 'khor sngags dmigs bstan/ / ming la drang srong thabs tshul dpag med zer/ /
sman bla'i dgongs pa gsal byed rtsom pa dang / / rjes 'jug blo mig 'byed pa'i legs bshad dang / / log rtog rtsod pa gcod pa'i ral gri 'dzin/ / ming la drang srong gso rig bstan 'dzin zer/ /
nad med bsrung dang thabs kyi bcud len 'tsho/ / nad ldan 'du ba 'khrugs pa bde bar 'tsho/ / dge sdig blang dor bstan nas phyi ma 'tsho/ / ming la drang srong rtag tu 'tsho byed zer/ /
lha rigs mi'i rgyal pos bsngags shing bkur/ / bstan la rab dga'i 'chi med du mas bstod/ / mkhas pa du mas yi rangs legs so byin/ / ming la drang srong lha yi rje bo zer/ /
Honored and feted by kings of celestial lineage, praised by those gods devoted to the doctrine, and acclaimed with great joy by many a scholar, I am known as Rishi Lhayi Jewo (Lord of the Gods).
gang na'ang su zhig nyam thag de yi skyabs/ / ma 'dris kun la yid gcugs pha ma bzhin/ / sgo gsum spyod pa gzhan phan nyag gcig sgrubs/ / ming la drang srong 'gro ba'i pha ma zer/ /
nyin mtshan mun pa'i gling du 'thoms pa rnams/ / gser gyi thur mas chu sbur mig phye nas/ / sna tshogs gzugs kun 'phral du mthong byed pa/ / ming la drang srong gsal byed sgron me zer/ /

For those lost day and night in the land of darkness, I open the bubble of their eyes with the golden surgical spoon, causing them to see at once this world of forms; I am known therefore as Rishi Saljé Drönma (Illuminating Beacon).
mthong thos dran dang reg pa'i sems can kun/ / 'gal rkyen kun bral mthun rkyen ma lus 'dzom/ / drang srong chen po'i go 'phang 'thob par smon/ / ming la drang srong smon lam mtha' yas zer/ /

I pray that all who see, hear, remember, or touch me be free of all adversity and misfortune be endowed with wholesome conditions, and attain the state of the great rishi. I am known, therefore, as Rishi Mönlam Thayé (Limitless Prayers).
rnag khrag rtsa chu la sogs khyi phag bzhin/ / nad pa'i bya ba kun la bran g.yog bzhin/ / gso bya'i gnyen po kun la 'dod 'jo bzhin/ / ming la drang srong 'gro ba'i khol po zer/ /
don dam gnas lugs spros dang bral bar rig / kun rdzob rten 'brel rmi lam lta bur shes/ / thabs shes zung 'jug bgrod gcig lam du mthong / / ming la drang srong rgyal sras gzhon nu zer/ /

Perceiving ultimate reality as being free from mental fabrication, knowing conventional dependent arising to be like dreams, seeing method and wisdom combined as the sole path, I am known as Rishi Gyalsé Shönu (Young Prince of the Buddha).
nyes brgya'i rtsa ba chang gi btung ba dor/ / snying rje'i 'gal zla sha khrag bza' btung spangs/ / dge legs rtsa ba kun da byang sems bzung / / ming la drang srong dri med brtul zhugs zer/ /

Eschewing alcohol, the cause of a hundred faults, refraining from eating meat, the enemy of compassion, holding the kumuda flower of bodhicitta, root of virtue and goodness, I am known as Rishi Drimé Tülshuk (Of Pure Spiritual Conduct).
snod bcud dag pa'i 'khor la yid ches rnyed/ / dbang dang dam tshig thob dang bsrung bya rig / rim gnyis rdo rje theg pa'i srog rtsa mthong / / ming la drang srong 'chi med snying po zer/ /
skyabs gnas 'dus pa bla ma gcig por mthong / / mchod 'os 'dus pa jo bo sems can snyed/ / chos lugs thams cad 'khor 'das mnyam par go/ / ming la drang srong gsang ba'i mdzod 'dzin zer/ /

Seeing the lama as the sole incorporation of the refuge objects, seeing that my master sentient beings are the incorporation of those worthy of offerings, realizing that all Dharma traditions are as one as samsara and nirvana, I am known as Rishi Sangwai Dzözin (Keeper of Treasury of Secrets).
tshe rabs du mar gso dpyad gzhung lugs bslabs/ / 'phags yul gangs ri'i khrod du 'gro phan byas/ / tshul 'dis 'gro ba 'dren par yi dam bcas/ / ming la drang srong de dang de skad zer/ /
gso rig shes 'dod kun la spro bas slob/ / gangs can nad pa'i tshogs kun 'bad pas gso/ / gzhan phan gang du che sar kho bo gnas/ / ming la rgyal khams lha rje zer ba yin/ /

Joyfully teaching all those who wish to learn medicine, laboring to heal all the sick in this land of snow, staying wherever I will be of greatest help to others, I am known as Gyalkham Lhajé (Lord of the Land).
a kyang bdag la de 'dra'i yon tan ni/ / nye ring skye bo dbang gyur ga la zhig / phyin chad rang yang de 'drar smon phyir dang / / rjes 'jug rnams la'ang bskul ba'i slad du yin/ /

But I jest! Among living beings close and distant, where is the witness to say that I possess such qualities? This is a prayer that from now on, I may have such qualities, and also an encouragement to motivate my followers.
thag ring yul nas shin tu nye ba'i thugs/ / phyung ba bdag la chen por re ba khyod/ / ming med bdag la ming gi dri ba mdzad/ / som nyi med par the tshom grol bar mdzod/ /
In a faraway land, yet with yearning heart so close, you who have such great hopes in me, asking this nameless one about his name; be free of doubts, free of hesitation.

f.d: yid la smon pa rjes mthun rang gi ming / / mkhas pa mgu phyir yi ger bris 'di yis/ / ma 'ongs dus su mi ring 'gro ba kun/ / drang srong chen pos lung bstan ming 'thob shog[297] / ces gang gsungs pa'i rigs rus dang yon tan mnga' zhing /

These longed-for supposed names of mine I have written as a letter to please the wise. By its power may all beings in the not-too-distant future receive their prophesized names from the great rishi. In this way he writes of his lineage and his qualities.

d.div: [297] byang bdag pa'i slob ma'i gtso bo byams pa dkon mchog rin chen gyis rang tshul brjod pa'i tshigs su bcad pa 'di rnams sde srid kyis gzhung gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/

f.d: thugs las 'khrungs pa'i legs par bshad pa'ang gso dpyad kyi rgyal po zhes bya ba'i bstan bcos dang dpal ldan rgyud bzhir 'grel pa bkod pa rnam bzhi/ rgyun rnam bzhi zhes pa dang / mngon par rtogs pa'i gsol 'debs/ rgyud bzhi'i rnam nges sam bka' sgrub/ ma la ya'i dka' 'grel 'dod 'jo che chung / khyad 'phags spyi sman dang / ngo mtshar spyi sman/ rim bcos mi la srog sbyin/ bshad rgyud le'u bzhi pa'i 'grel pa gnas lugs rab gsal/ rtsa mdo'i 'grel pa snyan brgyud rdo rje'i tshig rkang gces bsdus rin chen 'phreng ba la sogs pa mdzad de gso ba rig pa'i gzhung lugs man ngag thams cad dang / khyad par rigs ldan zla ba bzang po'i rnam sprul phyag na pad+mo dge 'dun grub sogs dam pa du mas ngos bzung ba rgyal po paN+Di ta'i rtul shugs 'chang ba rnam rgyal grags bzang gi bzhed srol dar rgyas su mdzad pa yin no//

The perfect teachings born from his mind include the treatise known as King of Medical Practice; commentaries on Four Tantras called Four Presentations and Four Streams; Realization Requests; Ascertainment of Four Tantras also known as Established as Enlightened Speech; Large and Small Wish-Granting Cow Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Mālaya; Exalted General Medicine; Extraordinary General Medicine; Treatments of Infectious Diseases: Giving Life to Mankind; Illumination of the Truth: A Commentary on the Fourth Chapter of the Explanatory Tantra; Vajra Verse Oral Transmission Commentary on the Pulse Section; and Precious Garland Quintessence. He was responsible for spreading the works and oral teachings of medical science generally and, in particular, the doctrine of Jangpa Namgyal Draksang, holder of the spiritual discipline of a pandit king and recognized by the lotus holder Gendün Drup and many other holy beings as an incarnation of Kalkī [600] Sucandra.

d.div: [600] Rigs ldan, “holder of the lineage.” Some say that, strictly speaking, the first seven rulers of Shambhala, of which Sucandra was the first, are not referred to as kalkī but as Dharma kings. The kalkī lineage actually begins with Mañjuśrī Yaśas, who began the vajra lineage by initiating the non-Buddhist rishis.

f.d: de'i sras lha btsun bkra shis dpal bzang ni/ sku chung ngu'i dus mes po bsod nams rdo rjes gces par bskyangs shing / yi ge 'bri klog gis mtshon pa'i thos bsam rgya cher mdzad/ phyis mes dang yab gnyis ka gso ba rig pa'i gzhung lugs rab 'byams rgya mtsho mtha' dag dang / lhag par rgyud bka' gtad rgya'i dbang / chu'i lha mo/ snyan brgyud 'grel chen phyi nang gsang gsum/ rgyas btab nyer lnga'i bshad srol dang bcas pa gsan cing / skal ba dang ldan pa'i rjes 'jug rnams la gso dpyad kyi 'chad nyan legs par bskyangs/ paN+Di ta nags kyi rin chen/ lo chen bsod nams rgya mtsho/ sems dpa' chen po gzhon nu rgyal mchog /mus chen dkon cog rgyal mtshan/ grub dbang thang stong pa/ mkhas grub don yod dpal ba dang / legs bshad bzang po dang / chag lo thams

His son was Lhatsün Tashi Palsang. From an early age he was lovingly cared for by his grandfather Sönam Dorjé, and he pursued his studies extensively in disciplines such as writing and reading. Later on, with his grandfather and father, he studied the vast ocean of medical literature in its entirety. In particular, he received the initiation for the entrustment of the tantra, the urine divination goddess practices, the great commentaries on the inner, outer, and secret from the oral tradition, teachings on the twenty-five seals, and so on. He developed the teaching tradition of medical practice for future fortunate disciples. He sat at the lotus feet of many a great master and drank without satiation the nectar of sutra, tantra, and the sciences. These masters included Pandit Vanaratna, Lochen Sönam Gyatso, the great being Shönu Gyalchok, Müchen Könchok Gyaltsen, Drupwang Thangtongpa, Khedrup Dönyö Palwa, Lekshé Sangpo, and the omniscient Chak Lotsāwa.

cad mkhyen pa sogs 'khrul zad kyi yongs 'dzin dam pa du ma'i zhabs pad bsten te mdo sngags rig gnas kyi bdud rtsi ngom med du bzhes/ 'khor ba la nges par yid byung ste paN chen shAkya mchog ldan la bsnyen par rdzogs pa dge slong gi dngos por bsgrubs nas 'gro ba lha dang bcas pa'i yon gnas su gyur/ gnas skabs sems can thams cad la sngags mig / khyug dpyad/ ja log la sogs pa rten 'brel zab mo'i sgo nas phan pa rlabs che/ bka' rtsom kyang bshad rgyud kyi 'grel pa legs bshad nor bu/ phyi rgyud 'grel pa dgos 'dod 'byung ba rin po che'i bang mdzod dam bklags pa kun shes/ khog 'bugs 'dzum dkar bzhad pa'i nyi ma dang / rgyud bzhi'i rnam nges dpag bsam ljon shing la sogs pa mdzad/

Developing a renunciation of samsara, he took the full ordination of a monk from Panchen Śākya Chokden and became a worthy recipient of offerings for the gods and mankind. He brought great relief to sentient beings with his use of profound methods such as mantras, swift magical remedies, and reversal treatments. His compositions include Jewel of Excellent Explanation: A Commentary on the Explanatory Tantra; Treasury of Jewels Fulfilling All Needs: A Commentary on the Final Tantra, also known as All-Knowing When Studied; White Smile of the Sun: A History of Medicine; and Wish-Granting Tree: Verses on the Ascertainment of Four Tantras.

rim gnyis zab mo'i rnal 'byor la thugs gzhol ba'i ngang nas/ nga ni bde ba can du 'gro/ / zhes sogs zhal gdams du ma dang bcas dran dang shes bzhin du mya ngan las 'das/ me tog gi char babs/ 'ja'i gur phub/ bar snang nas rol mo'i sgra grags pa sogs ngo mtshar ba'i ltas du ma byung / rje btsun ma sgrol mas ma 'ongs pa na 'jig rten gyi khams spyan yongs su dag pa zhes bya bar sangs rgya'o zhes lung bstan pa sogs rnam thar 'gangs che ba mang /

Finally, from within the state of total absorption in the yoga of the two profound stages, he recited verses beginning, “I am going to Sukhāvatī,” and having issued many last instructions, he passed beyond sorrow with full mindfulness and awareness. A rain of flowers fell and the area was covered by a rainbow arc. Sounds of music came from the sky, and many other wonderful signs were seen. There are many important biographical details about him such as the prophesy by venerable Tārā that he would become a buddha in a world known as Śuddhilocana.

des sku tshe'i stod du bskrun pa'i sras drang srong bsod rnams ye shes rgyal mtshan pas yab kyi zhabs pad yun du bsten nas gso ba rig par sbyangs/ gzhung man ngag spyi dang khyad par dpal ldan rgyud bzhi'i bka' gter chu bo gnyis 'dres kyi gdams ngag zhal shes/ bka' gtad rgya'i dbang / chu lha dang drang srong gi sgrub skor/ snyan brgyud kyi phyag len/ 'grel bshad sogs bum pa gang 'jo'i tshul du bzhes/ byang rong dus 'khrug gi stabs phyis rin spungs pa'i bla sman du gyur/ gtsang rong ral lngar gso rig khog 'bugs pad dkar rgyas pa'i nyin byed mdzad/ 'jag thang du sku'i bkod pa bsdus/

Early in his life he had a son, who became known as Rishi Sönam Yeshé Gyaltsen and sat at his father’s lotus feet for many years to learn medicine. There he learned the texts, the oral instructions, and in particular the oral teachings on Four Tantras from the two rivers of Treasure and Transmission merged into one. Like a vase overflowing, he received the entrustment initiation, the collections of urine divination goddess practices and rishi accomplishment practices, the practices of the oral tradition, the commentaries, and so on. Through the circumstances of the troubles between Jang and Rong[601] he later became the chief Rinpung physician. In Tsangrong Ralnga he composed the medical history called Sun that Nourishes the White Lotus. In Jakthang he withdrew from this life.

d.div: [601] Byang rong. Either two districts or two families. May refer to the clashes between the Latö Jang rulers in southern Tsang and the Rinpungpas in central Tibet.

d.i: Lekdrup Pal and the Nya lineage

f.d: rigs ldan chos kyi rgyal po rnam rgyal grags pa dpal bzang po'i gso rig gtso bor gyur pa'i bu chen gcig ni gnang rigs rjes sbyangs kyi sman pa lhun sdings pa legs grub dpal ba yin te/ de'i thog ma'i rigs rus la sogs pa nas cung zad smos na/ sngon mdo khams byang phyogs ge sar gyi yul grur mnga' bsgyur ba'i chos rgyal dge ba 'dzin zhes bya ba lugs gnyis kyi mkhyen pa yangs shing / sems can thams cad la bu gcig pa ltar mnyen cing byams pas kun gyi mig gi bdud rtsir gyur nas/ thams cad kyis ngag mthun par 'di ni kun gyi gnya' bar khur rigs so zhes zer ba las gnya' bar grags/

One of the main medical disciples of the Dharma king and lineage holder Namgyal Draksang was the trained doctor Lekdrup Pal of Lhünding, who was also of royal physician lineage. I will begin with a brief account of the origins of his lineage. Once (ca. eighth century), the province of Gesar in the northern part of Dokham was ruled by a Dharma king called Gewazin, who had a vast knowledge of the two traditions and who looked upon each living being with love and gentleness as if he or she were his only child. Because of this he became to everyone like ambrosia for their eyes, and all agreed that he deserved to be carried on their shoulders. In this way he became known as Nya (“back of the neck”).

de'i sras lnga'i che ba gnya' ba chos kyi bzang po skye mched dwangs shing dad pa dang shes rab che ba'i snyan grags dang ldan pa/ lha btsan po mnga' bdag khri srong lde'u btsan gyis gsan te mdo khams nas dbus su 'gugs pa mdzad/ de nas gser gyi pa tra mang po dang grogs du mar bcas te rgya gar du rig pa slob pa dang lo paN spyan 'dren la sogs par brdzangs/ des kyang 'phags yul du lo mang bzhugs/ rig pa'i gnas phal cher sbyangs/ mkhas par gyur nas bod du byon/ rgyal po shin tu mnyes te bla mchod dang lha rje zung du dbang bskur/ a+yon sangs rgyas gnyis pa pad+ma 'byung gnas la rdo rje theg pa'i smin grol gyi gdams pa du ma gsan/ bod sman mkhas pa mi dgu'i gtsug rgyan du gyur pa nas mi rabs 'ga' zhig gi mthar/ gnya' ba nam mkha' gzhon nu g.yas ru byang gi phyogs su byon/ byang bdag ta dben nam brtan pas ya rong dang gtsang 'o lung gi mi sde dang / ri phug gi dgon pa sogs sbyor 'jags gnang / de sras gnya' ba rdo rje 'bum gyis byang bdag po'i bla sman dang phyag g.yog nang ma byas de sras lha'i rgyal mtshan mdo sngags kyi mkhyen pa rgyas pas dpal ngam ring gi mkhan sar 'khod cing / grags gzhon pas sman dang srid bskyongs/

The eldest of his five children was Nyawa Chökyi Sangpo. He was good-looking, his senses were bright, and he was renowned as one of great faith and intelligence. The noble emperor Trisong Detsen heard of him and summoned him from Dokham to central Tibet. He was given a great amount of gold leaf, provided with many companions, and sent to India to study and to invite translators and pandits back to Tibet. He stayed for many years in India, where he mastered most of the sciences and became a great scholar, and then he returned to Tibet. The king was delighted with him and conferred upon him the status of a lama worthy of offering and as a master physician. Under the Oḍḍiyāna second Buddha, Padmasambhava, he studied many Vajrayana practices of ripening and liberating the mind and became the foremost of the nine wise Tibetans. Several generations later Nyawa Namkha Shönu came to northern Yeru. There the Jangdak Tawen[602] or Jangdak Tenpa presented him with the communities of Yarong and Tsang Olung, local hermitages, and so on. Nyawa Dorjé Bum, the son of Nyawa Namkha Shönu, became the chief physician and personal attendant to Jangdak. His son, Lhai Gyaltsen, had a vast understanding of sutra and tantra and became an abbot at Pal Ngamring Monastery. There, with his fame and youth, he furthered the science of medicine and administered the affairs of the district.

d.div: [602] Ta (ta’i) dben (Ch. da yuan), general name given to the Mongol or Yuan dynasty that began in the thirteenth century. Tibetan masters who served as spiritual preceptors to Mongolian rulers were known as ta’i dben ti shri.

f.d: de'i sras dkon cog gzhon nu gso ba rig pa dang sngags rnying ma la mkhas/ sems can thams cad la thugs brtse bas/ byang chub sems dpar grags/ theg chen chos rje rgya'i bla mar byon pa'i bla sman bgyis te rgya'i lung dang 'ja' sa lon/ de'i sras legs grub dpal rig gnas phal cher dang khyad par gso rig la mkhas/ rje btsun ma sgrol ma'i bsnyen pa song zhing / gter ston dngos grub rgyal mtshan gyi zhabs la thug /zab pa dang rgya che ba'i chos du ma nos pa las gu ru mthing gar rtsal du thon pas gtor ma dngos su phyin te dgra bo tshar gcod pa sogs byung / rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang la gso rig gi gzhung bshad gdams pa mang du gsan cing bu chen du mnga' gsol/

His son Könchok Shönu was a master of medicine and Nyingma tantra. He had great compassion for all beings and was renowned as a bodhisattva. He went to the Thekchen Chöjé, lama to the Chinese,[603] and became his chief physician, whereupon he received a royal proclamation and was conferred great honor. His son was Lekdrup Pal. He mastered most of the sciences, particularly the science of medicine. He sat meditation retreats on venerable Tārā and studied at the feet of Tertön Ngödrup Gyaltsen. From having received so many teachings on the vast and profound, many wonderful events occurred. Once while he was concentrating on offering a torma to Dark Blue Guru,[604] the torma actually traveled toward the deity, and the enemies were destroyed. From Rikden Namgyal Draksang he received many teachings and instructions on the medical texts and was conferred as his chief disciple.

d.div: [603] Künga Tashi Gyaltsen Palsang, who was born in 1349 and visited the Chinese emperor in 1413.
[604] Probably a form of Padmasambhava.

f.d: de'i sras shes rab dpal ldan 'khrungs rtags ya mtshan pa sogs byung bas rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang la ming zhus par 'tsho byed pad ma sri thar du btags/ paN+Di ta nags kyi rin chen bod yul du lan gsum byon pa'i phyi ma'i skabs yar lam mjal/ shes snying rgya skad ma'i lung dang dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i dbang yongs su rdzogs pa gnang / dgung lo nyer drug pa la grub pa'i dbang phyug thang stong rgyal po'i drung du byon/ mjal ba'i mod la byin rlabs khyad par can zhugs/ lo bcu drug gi bar sku dngos kyi nyer gnas mdzad/ gdams pa mtha' yas pa gsan cing nyams su bzhes pas thugs sras dam par gyur/ grub dbang nyid zhing khams 'phos nas lo sum cu so gnyis kyi ring gsang khog nas sku tshab mdzad de dngos dang dbyer med pa'i 'gro don dpag med byung / mkhas grub shes rab dpal ldan grub chen thang stong pa'i drung du ma byon gong gi sras lhun sdings dge mas gso rig gi bshad srol bskyangs/ g.yas ru byang ba'i bla sman du gyur/

His son was Sherap Palden. Many wonderful omens were observed at his birth, and so Rikden Namgyal Draksang was asked to name the child. The master gave the name Tsojé Pema Sithar. When Pandit Vanaratna came to Tibet on his third and last visit, Sherap Palden met him on the way,[605] and the pandit gave him the transmission of the Heart Sutra in Sanskrit and the complete initiation of the glorious Kālacakra. When he was twenty-six he came into the presence of the powerful siddha Thangtong Gyalpo[606] and immediately received a very special blessing. For sixteen years he lived close to this yogi. By receiving and practicing countless teachings he became Thangtong Gyalpo’s chief disciple. After this great siddha passed away, Sherap Palden secretly acted as his replacement for thirty-two years, during which time he brought immeasurable benefit to living beings, comparable to that of his master himself. His son Lhünding Gema, who was born before the master Sherap Palden met Siddha Tongthang Gyalpo, preserved and developed the medical tradition and became chief physician to the Yeru Jangpa.[607]

d.div: [605] According to Trinlé (p. 267) this was in 1453.

[606] Thang stong rgyal po. This famous yogi lived for 125 years. According to Dungkar his dates are 1361–1485. According to the Great Tibetan-Chinese Dictionary, 1385–1509. Others give the dates 1385–1464. For more on this figure, see Cyrus Stearns’ King of the Empty Plain: The Tibetan Iron-Bridge Builder Tangtong Gyalpo (Ithaca, NY: Snow Lion Publications, 2006).
[607] G.yas ru byang pa/bdag. Literally, the “northern lord of Yeru.”

f.d: de'i sras bstan pa dar rgyas chung ngu nas bzang po'i las sad pa'i dad brtson shes rab snying rje dang ldan/ 'dzin shes yangs pas gos tshags byed ring la mda' tshad ma'i shog logs re blor zin/ byang bdag por rgyud bzhi 'grel bcas dang snying po bsdus pa'i rgyugs phul/ de yang byang sman lha'i btsun pa bkra shis dpal bzang gi sras drang srong bsod rnams rgyal mtshan 'jag thang du rin spungs pa'i sgar la sku tshe'i 'phen pa btang bas/ byang pa'i dpon zhen dang gdams pa'i chu bo nub na 'phangs par dgongs bod par mi ched bstad kyis brdzangs te/ bdag gi rigs chos gnyi ga'i bu de ni lnga lam du song bas chig brgyud kyi gdams pa 'di byang pa rang gi bla sman thugs blos 'khel zhing shes rab che ba zhig la 'bul bas rdzong ster mdzod zhus pa bzhin/ bstan pa dar rgyas bla sman gyi rgyud dang shes rab che ba bcas gtong ba mdzad pas zhabs pad yun du bsten te mdo sngags rig gnas dang / khyad par gso ba rig pa'i gzhung man ngag drang srong yid las skyes nas bzung yi ger 'drir ma btub pa'i snyan brgyud zhal shes dang bcas pa bum pa gang 'jor stsal/ gnya' rigs gong ma rnams rigs ldan sogs kyi zhabs la thug pa'i mkhas pa sha stag yin kyang / byang lugs bka' gter chig brgyud kyi gdams pa zab mo 'di yan la ma byung bar grags/

His son in turn was Tenpa Dargyé, whose virtuous imprints were awoken at an early age, and who soon became endowed with faith, enthusiasm, wisdom, and compassion. He had such a great capacity for memorizing that in the time it took to put on the monastic robes, he was able to memorize one page the length of an arrow. To the Jangdak he offered a memorization test of Four Tantras, its commentaries, and its synthesis. Rishi Sönam Yeshé Gyaltsen, the son of Jang physician Lhatsün Tashi Palsang, withdrew from his life in the Rinpung settlement in Jakthang. Because of his fondness for the Jang hierarchy and concern that his own transmission of teachings would dry up and vanish, Lhatsün Tashi Palsang sent a messenger to the Jangdak. It read, “My son, successor to my family and my Dharma lineage, has died, and I offer the one-to-one lineage to your trustworthy and intelligent chief physician. Therefore, I request you to send him to me.” Accordingly, Tenpa Dargyé, with his chief-physician lineage and his great intelligence, was sent to Lhatsün Tashi Palsang, at whose lotus feet he studied for a long time. He received like a vase full to overflowing the sutras, tantras, the sciences, and in particular the literature and instructions on medicine, including the transmission and teachings of the Oral tradition, which since the time of Rishi Manasija had never been written down. Although the previous masters of this Nya family line were all great scholars who had served at the feet of many noble dynasties, it is said that up to this time the profound teachings of the Jang one-to-one lineage of Treasure and Transmission had not appeared in their tradition.

bstan dar ba'i sras bsod nams chos 'phel snyan brgyud zhal shes man ngag gi bdag por gyur cing / ngo mtshar rtsa bdun la nang byan chud pas kha smar thams cad mngon shes yod pa lta bu byung / de sras bdud rtsi 'gyur med gso ba rig par mchog tu mkhas pas jo nang sprul ba'i sku kun dga' snying po'i bla sman dang / rgyud bzhi par du rko ba'i do dam dang zhus chen mdzad/ gso dpyad kyi lag len dgos 'dod kun 'byung brtsams/

Tenpa Dargyé’s son was Sönam Chöphel, who became a master of the Oral tradition, the oral teachings, and instructions. He had mastered fully the seven extraordinary pulses,[608] and so in diagnosis he was as if clairvoyant. His son was Dütsi Gyurmé. He became supreme in his knowledge of the science of healing and consequently became chief physician to the Jonang incarnation Künga Nyingpo.[609] He also oversaw and was editor of a new publication of Four Tantras. He composed a work called Practices of the Science of Medicine: Fulfilling All Needs and Wishes.

d.div: [608] A technique of reading the pulse as a means of divination. See Drungtso, p. 264.
[609] Better known as Tāranātha (1575–1634).

f.d: de sras rnam rgyal rdo rje zhes shes bya spyi dang / khyad par 'chi gsos kyi gzhung chen po 'di nyid la rgyud bzhi blor byang / 'grel pa man ngag dang bcas par gzhig pa chug /rang rigs bdud rtsi 'gyur med sogs mkhas nas mkhas su brgyud pa'i chig brgyud kyi rim pa nyams su longs/ na tshod drug cur nye ba'i bar nyin star sh+loka re blo 'dzin dang / 'bru bsnan rgyud rgyugs sogs la thogs pa med pa zhig yin 'dug kyang /

His son was Namgyal Dorjé. He mastered knowledge in general and specifically Four Tantras, supreme among the works of healing.[610] He examined minutely the commentaries and oral instructions, and practiced the one-to-one lineages passed from the wise to the wise, such as those of his father, Dütsi Gyurmé. Up to the age of almost sixty, he could still memorize one verse a day. He was unhindered in his ability to thoroughly undertake word-for-word memorization tests on the tantra, and so forth. However,

d.div: [610] This line has been translated according to Trinlé (p. 271).

f.d:
legs bshad rin po che las/
mkhas pa rtsad cing ma dris pa/ / de yi bar du gting mi dpogs/ / rnga la dbyug gus ma bsnun par/ / de srid gzhan dang khyad ci yod/[298] / ces pa ltar lus pa rdo ring la yi ge sbyar ba sogs nas rje bla ma lnga pa chen po'i sku tshe'i smad du spyan sngar thogs te 'bru 'dzin sogs stsal/ yul thig sdong 'grems gnyug mar gnas pa rnams la'ang 'khrid du 'jug pa'i dgongs pa tsam bstad mtshams su lus shing rjes su kho bos khengs gcog 'jur bkag gi dri mal mang ba dang / rnam gling paN chen dang khyams steng du dri mal kha yar bgyid bcug pa ha cang gi khengs pa dang nga rgyal che zhing bzang rtsi chung ba las rjes 'dzin gyi rig pa 'dir gzhung bshad sman ngo rtsa yul sdong 'grems sogs dus skabs 'dir 'gran zla dang bral bar mngon te kho bos kyang yul thig sdong 'grems la sogs pa chig brgyud kyi zhal shes mang du nos pa yin la/

as the Treasury of Wise Sayings states:
As long as the wise are not thoroughly questioned, their depths have not been measured. As long as a drum is not struck, its difference from others remains unknown.[611] Because of his writings affixed to the Lhasa stone pillar and other reasons, he came to the notice of the Great Fifth in the latter part of his life, who presented him with grain coupons, and so forth. He then ignored a request by the Great Fifth to give teachings to the local residents on measurements of the body and the allegorical tree of medicine. After that I set out with many questions designed to stump him and break his pride. Namling Panchen, too, was encouraged to ask him various questions in the upper courtyard. As a result it became clear that—his arrogance, great pride, and disrespect aside—there is none these days in this science of caring for others who can match his abilities to explain texts, identify medicinal plants, or reveal knowledge of the channels, the body, the medicine tree, and so on. Therefore I, too, received from him many oral teachings in one-to-one transmission on the measurements of the body, the allegorical tree of medicine, and so on.

d.div: [298] sa skya paN+Di ta'i gsung 'bum/ thas skya legs bshad/ shog_1_ba6_sa skya'i bka' 'bum pod lnga pa/
[611] Sakya Paṇḍita, Collected Works, tha, 1b6.

f.d: de'i brgyud 'dzin dga' ldan sman bla rgyud nges shing sman ngo 'jags pa tsam snang yang / snyoms las dang le lo che zhing brtson pa chung ba'i sa paN gyi khu byug rgya khra'i dper gsungs pa thog tu babs kyi dgos/ de ltar byang lugs la bka' ma dang / gter ma'i brgyud pa gnyis su snang ba'i/ gter brgyud ni/

His lineage, the Ganden Medicine Guru lineage, survives merely in the form of its study of the tantra and in identification of medicine. However, because of indolence, laziness, lack of effort, one has to wonder if Sakya Paṇḍita’s example of the cuckoo and the hawk is not applicable here.[612] Therefore the two lineages of Transmission and Treasure appeared within the Jang medical tradition. Their transmission of each is as follows. Treasure lineage:

d.div: [612] A cuckoo does not naturally kill, but one reared in a hawk’s nest will copy the behavior of the hawk.

The Yuthok son lineage:
Yuthok Bumseng Yuthok Jampal Drangti Jampal Sangpo[614] His son Drangti Gyalsang His youngest son Drangti Palden Tsojé Jangmen Sangyé Rinchen The royal physician Sönam Dorjé Jampa Könchok Rinchen, also known as Minyima Thongwa Dönden Tashi Palsang

d.div: [614] In the section on the Drangti lineage it states that the father of Drangti Jampal Sangpo was Drangti Sönam Büm and that the latter only met Yuthok Jampal later as a teacher. Therefore, the term “son lineage” means only that it began with the sons of Yuthok and not that each successive transmission has to be passed down from father to son.

From here on it is asserted that the two streams of the Treasure and Transmission lineages combine as one. The lineages continue: Nya Tenpa Dargyé, Sönam Chöphel, Dütsi Gyurmé, up to the master orator Namgyal Dorjé. In the twenty-fourth chapter of the Crystal Rock Lotus Chronicles it says:

Then Padmasambhava went to the land of Padmavati, where he met with the son of Kumāra Jivaka. “What do you know?” he asked. “Medicine,” he replied. “Teach me medicine,” he asked. “I am old, my body shakes;[615] I am no longer a scholar. The ācārya did not come. If you had, I would have taught.”[616] Orgyen Padma actually studied with Kumāra Jivaka himself, and although the verse is written this way, I think there must have been some corruption with the sixth grammatical case, resulting in “son of Kumāra Jivaka.”[617]

d.div: [299] pad+ma bka' thang / le'u/ 24_shog_167_yig phreng 1
[615] Lus ’dar, “body shakes.” Some editions have lus ’dir, “in this body,” which also makes sense.
[616] Orgyen Lingpa, Lotus Chronicles, 24.167.1.

[617] The Crystal Rock Lotus Chronicles, another name for the Lotus Chronicles, is an account of the life of Padmasambhava, and this particular verse tells of Padmasambhava’s acquisition of medical knowledge. Desi’s comment here is a reference to the Treasure lineage listed above, which explicitly states that Padmasambhava received the transmission from Kumāra Jivaka himself and not his son. The sixth grammatical case corresponds approximately to the genitive.

The master lama, the Great Fifth said:
In those times, in the dance of the magic net of beryl light, many intelligent beings, masters of the science of healing— Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé and the nephew-based succession, and so on— smiled from within the joy of help and happiness for living beings.[618] The glorious Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé was renowned with names such as Tsojé Drupa, Könchok Rinchen, Yuthok Bang, Pawö Kyang, Künla Jampai Lodrö, Lhündrup Gyaltsen, and Dharmaswami—Dharma in Tibetan is Chö, and Swami is Jé, making Awo Chöjé. He was born in Latok Surkhar in Dakpo in the east, in the earth-sheep siddhārtha year of the seventh sixty-year cycle.[619] His father was Rikzin Phüntsok of the Gyerkar medical lineage, which included Bangrimpa and Gyama Rinchen Gangwa and is said to be of celestial descent. His mother was the daughter of the omniscient Tashi Namgyal.

[619] The dates of Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé are commonly agreed to be 1439–75.

At the age of ten he stayed for three days on Dharmadhātu Peak, where he made single-pointed requests to Yuthok Yönten Gönpo. As a result Yuthok actually appeared and gave him the transmission on the oral instructions, as well as the interpretations and textual meanings of the Heartdrop Collection, Four Tantras, and the scroll collections. Yuthok also pointed out where previous generations had unknowingly corrupted the supplements to the Heartdrop and Four Tantras and told him to correct the mistakes. As it is written:
On the waves of your faith-filled requests, Mañjuśrī Guṇa[620]—in reality or in dreams— gave you continuous teachings in great delight; to you, physician dispeller of errors, crown jewel of all…[621] Therefore, in reality or in dreams, the venerable Yuthok gave him teachings, and a flawless understanding of the meaning of profound emptiness was born within him, enabling him to dispel all errors.

When he was fourteen he composed a letter with questions for the Jang physician Minyima Thongwa Dönden:
Śrī Vajrasattva nāmamī We sent a scholar physician and Dharma teacher from Erong[622] to learn more about you. Hearing his report filled my mind with joy. However, the distance makes it difficult for me to come to meet you myself. In which particular sciences are you learned and to whose kindness do you owe that to? What is your family, your lineage? Which of the great texts do you rely upon? Whose oral instructions are you familiar with—those of the nine scholars or those of others? Which special medical practices do you perform? For your experience which collections do you have confidence in? In Buddhism, for your deity practice, which Oral traditions and Treasure traditions do you hold as the essence of your meditations? Do you have a fixed residence? If some who are connected with me were made known to you by way of messengers or letters, would it be acceptable for them to gain an audience with you? If you were entreated to travel here for the sake of others, would you consider coming? How many works have you composed? By what name should I address you? I have on many occasions been convinced that you and I are linked by virtuous past karma. Please send me a genuine reply that is neither distant nor disapproving and bring my hopes to fulfillment. The reply he received did not respond directly to the questions asked but instead consisted of verses on the meanings of his names, lineage, and so forth, as is clear from the life story of Jang Thongwa Dönden above.

d.div: [622] E rong, a Nyingma hermitage seventy-five miles southeast of Lhasa.

From around the age of sixteen he thought of composing a supplement, based on oral instructions, to Meditation on the Guru: Sunlight of Compassion Clearing the Darkness of Ignorance,[623] as well as four works on dispelling obstacles to its practice. These four were an external work on elemental disturbances to the body, an inner work on disturbances to meditative concentration, a secret work on types of hindering demons, and a work on all four in common. He first composed, as a single book with many sections, the work on the disturbances to the body, using both prose and verse. From this one small volume, the size of a holy relic, comes millions of oral teachings. It is therefore known as Relic of Millions. It consists of the following sections.[624]

d.div: [623] Found in Yuthok Heartdrop, but a work of a similar name was composed by Yeshé Sung.

dkar chag 'chad tshul dang bcas ba'i gleng mo rnams te khyon dpe tshan bzhi brgya dang bcu drug yod pa dang / dpal ldan rgyud bzhi'i 'grel chen pod shal khra mo/ spyi don nam rgyud kyi dka' gnad rnams la dri tshig dngul dkar me long dang / legs bshad nyi zer/ phyogs kyi sman pa rnams la springs yig / rang gzhan la phan pa'i bslab cha/ nyams gyi rdo rje'i glu dang bstod tshogs skor/ dpal dus kyi 'khor lo'i 'grel bshad/ phyag chen dang gcod yul gyi 'khrid yig / rdzogs pa chen po'i chos skor la pod chung bcu drug pa zhig legs bshad gser thur sogs bka' rtsom kyang mang /

Together with a table of contents and an account of how the work is set out, there are 416 sections to this work. Other works of Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé include: • A Work of Fine Crystal: Extensive Commentary on the Four Glorious Tantras • Mirror of White Mercury: Questions on the Difficult Points of the Tantra. Also known as Overview • Sunrays: A Well-Composed Work • A Letter to Far-Flung Physicians • Advice Beneficial for Others and Myself • Vajra Songs of Experience and Collection of Praises • Commentary on the Kālacakra Tantra • Guidance on Mahamudra and on Places for Cutting-Off Practice • Sixteen small works on Great Perfection called Golden Spoon of Excellent Explanation

shar phyogs mngon dga' zhes bya bar gnyal lor byar gsum e nyang kong dang bcas pa'i sman pa thams cad bsdus te/ rin chen 'khrungs dpe'am sman ngo gsal byed/ ro skor lcags kyi 'phreng ba/ bdud rtsi rdzing bu/ bdud rtsi gter mdzod/ sman gyi byings la sogs pa ro nus zhu rjes ngo bo nges tshig byed las kyi sgo nas gtan la 'bebs pa'i bstan bcos rnams 'chad cing sman ngo sprod pa sogs 'chad rtsod rtsom gsum gyi sgo nas gso rig gi bstan pa spel/

In Ngönga in the east he gathered all the physicians of Nyal, Lor, and Jar, together with those of E, Nyang, and Kong[629] where he taught definitive reference works on the tastes, powers, post-digestive tastes, natures, etymologies, and functions of medicines, works such as Precious Illustrations or Identification and Clarification of Medicines; Iron Garland Collection on Tastes; Ambrosia Pool; Ambrosia Treasury; Fundamentals of Medicines. He also taught the identification of medicinal plants and so forth. Therefore, in composition, discussion, and teaching, he added to the development of the science of medicine.

d.div: [629] Trinlé (p. 210) identifies these six places as being in present-day Lhokha, in southern Tibet.

f.d: rab tu byung ba'i sdom pa dngos su ma bzhes kyang phyi ltar tshul chos btsun pa'i jo mo dang sras sogs med cing dgung lo nyi shu tshun nas sha ra rab 'byams pa dang mjal bas stod rjen sgom thag mdzad par grags/ lam gyi gegs sel bogs 'don du mtshan ldan rig ma gsang ba'i tshul gyi+is bstan/ grub pa dang brtul zhugs kyi spyod pa mngon par shes pa la mnga' brnyes/ 'di nyid kyi rnam thar blo gros rgyal pos bsgrigs pa 'gags pa med pa yi ge'i gtam du/ rdzogs chen skor la bka' rtsom mdzad pa dpe khyab ches gshis 'gog ma thub pa las/ nyams len gyi mthil phyag chen dang gter brdzus 'don pa'i tshul mdzad pa sogs ni bsgrigs pa po rang nyid gter dang rnying ma sun 'byin pa'i ched du bkod pa las/ rjes 'di nyid zab mo snying tig sogs rdzogs pa chen po'i chos skor nyams su bstar bzhin du de lta bu mi mdzad par bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po bzhed pa don la gnas/

Although he did not actually take monastic vows, he outwardly maintained the aspect of a monk, with no wife or children. Moreover, from the age of twenty onward, after he had met with Shara Rapjampa, it is said he went naked from the waist up and made use of meditation straps. As a way to remove obstacles on the path, he secretly used a consort endowed with the proper signs. He also gained mastery over tantric powers and tantric behavior and clairvoyance. The biography Irrefutable and Extensive Written Account compiled by Lodrö Gyalpo says though Nyamnyi Dorjé’s compositions on the Great Perfection cycles are undeniably prolific, his main practice was in fact Mahāmudrā, noting also that he rooted out false treasure scriptures, and so on. Such assertions were made by the compiler in order to discredit the Nyingma and the Treasure traditions. In reality, this great master did no such thing, and he simultaneously practiced the profound heartdrop and other practices of the Great Perfection. This is the assertion of my lama the Great Fifth.

dgung lo so bdun pa shing lug gro bzhin zla ba'i tshes bco lnga la sku'i bkod pa bsdus/ rang gi gcung dpon rje btsun dang / tsha bo mi 'gyur/ slob ma phrag dpon dang tshe 'bum la sogs pas pur bzhu bar nye ba na gdung shin tu chung bar gyur pas kun yid ma ches pa'i tshe/ nam mkha' la 'od sna tshogs 'dzin pa'i khongs nas A li kA li'i sgra grags pa kun gyis thos pas yi rangs shing mos pa gting tshug /phung po lhag med du 'gro rgyur bu slob rnams kyis rings stabs su zhugs la phul bas 'ja' 'od sogs rtags phun sum tshogs pa byung /

At the age of thirty-seven, in the wood-sheep year, on the fifteenth of the srāvana month (in 1475), he withdrew his physical formation. His younger brother Pön Jetsün, his nephew Migyur Tseten, and his disciples Trakpön Sönam Tashi, Tsebum Dorjé, and others took the body to the cremation ground. As they approached the site, the body shrunk and became very small, causing consternation all round. Suddenly, from an array of lights in the corners of the sky came the sounds of the Sanskrit vowels and consonants. This was heard by everyone present, bringing great joy and a deep faith. In order to ensure that the body burned without remain, the disciples offered the body swiftly to the fire. In the course of the cremation, rainbow lights and many other perfect signs appeared.

de lta bu'i bdag nyid chen po de la gso ba rig pa'i phyogs mthar phyin gyis slob ma bzhi zhes grags pa las/ man ngag mthar phyin mi 'gyur tshe brtan/ 'phrin las mthar phyin phrag dpon bsod nams bkra shis/ lag len mthar phyin tshe 'bum rdo rje/ bshad pa mthar phyin li chung pad+ma skyabs dang bzhi/ gzhan yang byin rlabs zhugs pa'i slob ma brgyad/ shes rab can gyi slob ma bcu drug / grags pa thob pa'i slob ma nyi shu/ bla dwags can gyi slob ma bcu drug sogs du ma zhig byung ba

It is said that this great master had four disciples who were accomplished in medicine: Migyur Tseten was accomplished in the transmitted instructions, Trakbön Sönam Tashi was accomplished in his medical activities, Tsebum Dorjé was accomplished in the practices, and Lichung Pema Kyap was accomplished in teaching. He had many other disciples: eight in whose minds blessings had entered, sixteen disciples of great wisdom, twenty disciples who found great fame, and sixteen disciples known by their titles.

de dag las/ skyem pa tshe 'bum rdo rje'i slob ma tshe dbang gis rtsa rgyud la 'grel pa snying po snang ba/ bshad rgyud la tshig don nyi ma/ man rgyud la bde ba'i 'dod 'jo/ phyi rgyud la lag len gsal byed bcas pa'i 'grel pa dang / sman dpyad lag len tshe dbang brgya rtsar grags pa rnams brtsams/

Of his many disciples, Kyempa Tsewang,[630] who was a direct disciple of Tsebum Dorjé, composed a commentary on the Root Tantra called Arising of the Essence, a commentary on the Explanatory Tantra called Sun Word Commentary, a commentary on the Instruction Tantra called Granting Wishes of Happiness, a commentary on the Final Tantra called Clarification of Practice, and a work known as Medical Practices: Hundreds of Life-Granting Empowerments.

d.div: [630] Kyempa Tsewang is elsewhere in the text called Lata Tsewang. According to Trinlé (p. 212), he was born in 1479.

d.i: Kawa Śākya Wangchuk or Tsomé Khenchen

f.d: skyes mchog ska ba dpal brtsegs sogs mkhas shing grub pa'i dbang phyug dang / bod rgyal po'i mdun na 'don sogs dpa' mdzangs brtul phod rim par byon pa ska ba'i brgyud stod lung glang grong du bltams shing / lha rje dge ba 'bum gyi skye ba gsal bar dran par rang nyid nas zhal gyis bzhes la/ mtsho smad lha khang gi mkhan po dang bsti gnas ngo bo yab phu dpal gyi ri khrod du bzhugs pa/ phrag dpon bsod nams bkra shis sogs bsten nas rig gnas spyi dang gso rig pa mkhas pa jo bo'i dus kyi ska ba shAkya dbang phyug dang rus gcig pa la brten rang nyid kyis btags pa'i mtshan ska ba shAkya dbang phyug gam mtsho smad mkhan chen du grags pa des khog 'bugs legs bshad dngul dkar me long / phyi rgyud 'grel pa bka' gnad gsal sgron rigs lnga'i gsal byed me tog 'phreng ba/ lag len smar 'khrid du sdebs pa snying po bsdus pa sogs mdzad cing / glang bu chos rje sogs bu slob kyang mang /

Kawa Śākya Wangchuk was born of the Kawa lineage in Langdrong in Tölung, a line that included those rich in scholasticism and practice, such as the great being Kawa Paltsek, and many brave, wise, and noble beings such as the attendants[631] of early Tibetan kings. He himself said that he clearly remembered his birth as Lhajé Gewa Bum. He became abbot of Tsomé temple and lived in the hermitage of Tiné Ngowo Yaphu Pal. Relying upon Trakbön Sönam Tashi and other masters, he became learned in the sciences and especially in medicine. Because he was a descendant of the Kawa Śākya Wangchuk who lived at the time of Atiśa, he too named himself Kawa Śākya Wangchuk. He was also known as Tsomé Khenchen. His compositions include: Mirror of White Silver: A Well-Composed History of Medicine; Commentary on the Final Tantra: An Illuminating Lamp on Its Difficult Points; Flower Garland: Clarification of the Five Families; and Explicit and Essential Compilation of Practices. He had many disciples, such as Langbu Chöjé.

d.div: [631] Mdun na ’don. A phrase that in earlier translations referred to brahman priests (purohita) who recited scriptures to the king (Dungkar, p. 1136).

f.d: bka' brgyud pa'i grub mtha'i ring lugs pa dwags sman sgom rdo rje rgyal mtshan gyi slob ma drang srong don grub dar zhes snga 'gyur gyi gter yang bton pa de'i mi rabs gsum pa/ karma pa chos grags rgya mtsho'i bla sman dang sman gyi slob dpon gyi bsko 'ja' gnang ste 'chad nyan tshugs pa'i 'tsho byed pad+ma dkar po/ de'i sras karma pas bsko 'ja' sogs gzengs bstod cing / rang mes kyi srol dang skyem pa tshe 'bum la gtugs pa'i zur mkhar ba'i lugs la sbyangs pas byar po paN chen zhes mtshan thogs shing lho brgyud du gso dpyad kyi bstan pa dar bar mdzad pa po des rgyud bzhi ga'i 'grel pa dang / khog 'bugs legs bshad gser gyi snye ma/ bye ba ring bsrel gyi dkar chag sogs mdzad/

Jarpo Panchen[632] was an adherent of the Kagyü tradition, a disciple of Dakpo Mengom[633] Dorjé Gyaltsen, and a third-generation descendant of Döndrup Dar, revealer of early-translation treasure scriptures. He was born the son of Pema Karpo, Karmapa Chödrak Gyatso’s[634] chief physician, who had been appointed minister of medicine and had founded a center of learning.[635] Jarpo Panchen was also honored by the Karmapa by being appointed ācārya of medicine. He trained in his own family medical tradition and in the Surkhar tradition under Kyempa Tsebum Dorjé. He was known, therefore, as Jarpo Panchen.[636] He contributed to the spread of the science of medicine in the south and composed commentaries on all four tantras, as well as Golden Sheaves: A Well-Composed History of Medicine; Table of Contents for “Relic of Millions”; and other works.

d.div: [632] According to Dungkar (p. 1485) Jarpo Panchen’s dates are 1447–1506.
[633] Sman sgom, “physician and meditator,” indicating that he, like so many doctors of those times, was also a great practitioner.
[634] The Seventh Karmapa (1454–1506).
[635] This center is said by Trinlé (p. 216) to be the Lekshé Ling Dharma center in Tsurphu Monastery.
[636] “Jarpo” because he was from the region of Ja, and “Panchen” (paṇḍita) because of his great learning (Trinlé, p. 217).

f.d: glang bu chos rje'i slob ma zur mkhar ba'i zhal ngor byon pa/ thog ma tshe brtan rgyal dang / karma 'phrin las pas gtsug phud bzhes pa'i ming dpal ldan don grub rnam rgyal/ karma pa brgyad pa mi bskyod rdo rjes legs bshad 'tshol dang / zhwa dmar bas blo gros rgyal po/ rang gi mes po'i 'bangs rnams su mtshan btags pa ni/ brjod ma khad pa ltar zur mkhar ba'i rigs su rab byung dgu pa'i dkar po sa sbrul la 'khrungs/

Lodrö Gyalpo of the Surkhar family was a disciple of Langbu Chöjé. At first he was named Tseten Gyalwa. Karma Trinlepa (1456–1539) then gave him the name Palden Döndrup Namgyal at the hair-cutting ceremony. The Eighth Karmapa Mikyö Dorjé (1507–54) named him Lekshé Tsöl and Shamarpa[637] named him Lodrö Gyalpo. He took his ancestral name because, as mentioned above, he was born into the Surkhar family in the śukla earth-snake year of the ninth sixty-year cycle (1509).

d.div: [637] Zhwa dmar ba; presumably the Fourth Shamarpa, Chödrak Yeshé (1453–1524).

f.d: chung ngu nas gong ma'i rgyun gyis gsod dpyad mdzad kyang bar skabs su phyag chen sogs la thugs gzhol/ karma 'phrin las par rab tu byung nas chos gra legs bshad gling du rgyu mtshan nyid kyi theg par sbyangs/ skyogs lo'am smon grub lo tswa bar snyan ngag gsan/ rje karma pa'i gsung bzhin slar mtsho smad mkhan chen pa'i slob ma glang bu chos rje'i drung du gtugs nas g.yu thog snying tig gi dbang lung / rgyud bzhi/ bye ba ring bsrel sogs mang du zhus/ byang ba rigs ldan dang mi'i nyi ma yab sras dang thog mi mtshungs shing / de tshun byang lugs kyi yig cha rnams su mi gsal yang rgan po'i kha 'chems su byung bas bkra shis dpal bzang nas rim par brgyud pa'i phyi ma yin nam snyam pa'i drung gnas byang ba sku mched/ dpon tshang phan dar ba/ mnga' ris phyag sman rin rgyal gyi dpon po/ gu ge ba 'a ba tshe ring / bi byi'i dpon po/ 'ug pa'i tsha bo/ byang stag rtse 'tsho byed rnams dang / khyad par sa skya sman grong du brang ti'i zhal ngo yab sras la yan lag brgyad pa/ de'i rang 'grel/ zla zer/ cha lag bco brgyad/ gser bre dngul bre rnams kyi lung gsan/ snying tig gi tshig don la yang dag par btags pas g.yu thog pas yig cha kho na rtsad gcod dgos par go nas/ nyang smad phyogs su legs par btsal bas g.yu thog pa'i phyag dreg ma'i rgyud bzhi gser mtshan rnyed par grags/ der sa spyod dbang rgyal grags pas mthun rkyen sbyar te lo bzhi'i bar rtsa bshad 'grel pa mes po'i zhal lung brtsams/

From an early age he followed the medical tradition of his predecessors, although at times he immersed himself in Mahāmudrā and other practices. He was ordained by Karma Trinlepa and trained himself in the causal Sutra Vehicle at the Lekshé Ling Dharma center. Under Kyok Lotsāwa [Rinchen Tashi], also known as Möndrup Lotsāwa, he studied poetry.
