On the advice of the Karmapa he went back to Langbu Chöjé, the student of Tsomé Khenchen, and received the initiations and transmissions of Yuthok’s Heartdrop, Four Tantras, Relic of Millions, and others. He received the transmissions of [Candranandana’s] Eight Branches and its autocommentary, Moonlight; the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts; [Drangti Palden Gyaltsen’s] Golden Measuring Dish of Instructions; and Silver Measuring Dish of Instructions from Drungné Jangpa Kuché; Pöntsang Phendarwa; the nephew of Chakmen Ringyal of Ngari; Apa Tsering from Gugé; the nephew of Biji; the grandson of Ukpa; Jang Taktse Tsojé; and particularly from the Drangti family lineage within the Sakya medical tradition. I think that he received these Jang transmissions from a later lineage stemming from Jangpa Tashi Palsang[638] because the Jang lineage founder Namgyal Draksang and his disciple Minyima were of a different time, and there is nothing about this transmission in the Jang literature from those times, but this list does occur in Lodrö Gyalpo’s Testament of an Old Man. Examining carefully the words of Heartdrop, he came to understand that he should concentrate solely on the teachings of Yuthok. To this end he came to the area of Lower Nyang, and it is said that after much searching he discovered the work on Four Tantras by Yuthok called Golden Annotations, which became known as the “well-worn copy.” There the local king Wangyal Drakpa provided for all his requirements, and over four years he composed a commentary on the root and explanatory tantras called Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors.

d.div: [638] Son of Minyima of the Jang lineage.

f.d: dbus su byon te gzhi lam 'bras gsum las brtsams pa'i dri tshig gi yi ge lha sa'i rdo ring la lan gsum sbyar bas phyogs mthar khyab cing lan ma byung bas nang so don yod pa sogs slob ma 'dras 'grel pa dgos tshul ltar rang 'grel gser gyi phra tshoms mdzad kyang phal cher gyis ma go bar mngon zhing / dus thog der gso rig 'dzin pa dol mda' nyang khang pa/ 'phyong rgyas rol khong pa/ sde ba lha sa rdzong pa/ yar klung gces grong nang so don yod/ skyem nas bla rta tshe dbang / skyid shod na bo blo gros brtan pa/ ko rab gad la ba rnams dang / rgan po'i kha chems su la stod byang nas bdag po chos rgyal chen po zhes byung ba/ rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang sogs dang dus mi mtshungs shing / snga phyi'i babs chos rgyal bkra shis stobs rgyas kyi yab tsam dang de skabs gso dpyad dar ba rang ma byung 'dug na'ang / gang ltar de dag gi lan kha shas byung ba thugs la ma rangs pas rang lan rgan po'i kha chems mtshan mo mun nag gi glog 'od lta bu zhes pa mdzad/

He came to central Tibet, and on a Lhasa stone pillar he attached a manuscript of questions concerning practices of the basis, path, and result.[639] Though he did this three times and the document consequently became widely known, still no one came up with answers. Therefore, Nangso Dönyö and other disciples requested an explanation of the questions. Accordingly Lodrö Gyalpo wrote his own commentary known as Golden Ornament, but apparently most did not understand it. Medical scholars of the time included Dölda Nyang Khangpa, Chongyé Röl Khongpa, Depa Lhasa Dzongwa, Nangso Dönyö from Yarlung Chedrong, Lata Tsewang from Kyem, Lodrö Tenpa from Kyishö Nawo, and Korap Gelawa. The Testament of an Old Man also mentions someone called “the great Jangdak Dharma king from Latö.” Since these events did not occur during the era of the lineage founder Jangdak Namgyal Draksang and so on, only the father of Dharma king Tashi Topgyal fits the description at that time. Moreover, a good knowledge of medicine was not so prevalent during that time. Whatever the reason, these scholars advanced some responses to the manuscript that did not please Lodrö Gyalpo, and consequently he composed My Own Response: The Testament of an Old Man, a Flash of Lightning on a Dark Night.

d.div: [639] This must refer to the basis of medical science, the practices, and the beneficial results of treatment.

f.d:
rang nyid kyis dpyad pas dag pa'i rgyud par du brko ba'i sbyin bdag rin spungs su zhus par thog ma zhal gyis bzhes kyang phyag tu ma khel bas/ da lta gra thang rgyud kyi par byang du yar rgyab pa'i bsngags pa rnams brjod rjes/
sngon chad 'di ltar bgyid do zhes/ / du mas ngal brgya lhur blangs kyang / / bya rog lnga par gyur pa bzhin/ / kun gyi dpal du ma gyur ro/ / zhes zur za'am bsting tshig gsungs/ slar yar rgyab pas sbyin bdag mdzad de brkos pa deng sang gra thang du bzhugs/

He asked the Rinpung ruler[640] to sponsor the printing of the edition of Four Tantras that he himself had revised and edited, and although the ruler initially agreed, the sponsorship was not forthcoming. Therefore, in the present Drathang[641] edition of Four Tantras, in the colophon after the praises to the Yargyap,[642] he says in a mocking or biting tone:
In the beginning promising, “I will do this,” they willingly take on a host of difficulties, but like the crow that died, they never achieve their crowning glory.[643] Finally the Yargyap sponsored the publication himself, and these days it can found in Drathang.

d.div: [640] As the author makes clear below, this refers to Rinpung Jikten Drakpa (’Jig rten grags pa), which must be a variant spelling of Rinpung Ngawang Jikmé Drakpa (Rin spungs Ngag dbang ’jigs med grags pa) born 1482 or 1542, the son of Rinpung ruler Ngawang Namgyal.
[641] Dra thang. Also known as Dranang (dra nang), Drathang Monastery is in Lhoka (Trinlé, p. 220).
[642] Yar rgyab. An official, but I am unable to say more.
[643] I cannot place the crow reference.

f.d: drang srong mnyam nyid rdo rje'i rnam thar 'gog pa med pa yi ge'i gtam chen po/ rnam thar gsol 'debs dad pa'i rol mtsho gsar pa/ drang srong rnam gnyis la thugs rje bskul ba mya ngan gdung sel/ bye ba ring bsrel bzhugs tshul gegs sel chen mo'i nang ltar dkar chag mkhas pa'i yid 'phrog /de'i lhan thabs dad ldan snyim pa'i me tog /byang ba'i bka' sgrub kyi lan dkar po chig thub bam dbang po'i lag nyal/

Lodrö Gyalpo’s other works include: • Irrefutable and Extensive Written Account of the Life and Liberation of Rishi Nyamnyi Dorjé • Requests Based on Biography: A New Enjoyment Ocean of Faith • Dispelling the Torment of Sorrow: Entreating the Compassion of the Two Rishis • An Outline to Captivate the Minds of the Wise: Contents of Relic of Millions—Great Dispeller of Hindrances • A supplement to Relic of Millions called Flower in the Cupped Palms of the Faithful • White Singly Powerful Medicine, or the Vajra of Indra: Reply to Jang Position on Establishing the Tantra as the Word of the Buddha

rgyud bzhi bka' bstan gyi 'gal spongs la phyi ltar sangs rgyas kyi bka'/ nang ltar paN+Di ta'i bstan bcos/ gsang ba ltar na bod kyi bstan bcos su bzhed pa mkhas pa'i dbang po gong ma na rim dang / khyad par rang rigs kyi rje d+harma swa mi'i spyi don dngul dkar me long gi dum bu tsam las byings dang rgyud bzhi'i 'grel pa pod shal khra mo sogs yod 'dug pa sngar phan mig lam du ma gyur rung dngul dkar me long gi dum bur rgyud bzhi'i bka' sor gnas rgyud nang ltar mdzad 'dug pa dang / bla rta tshe dbang gi yig char gros tshogs gnyis rgya mtsho'i baiDUR+ya'i chu rgyun du kha 'phangs 'dug pas rje d+harma swa mi yang zhib cha lugs de dang mthun par go zhing /

In order to resolve the debate over whether Four Tantras is the word of the Buddha or a later treatise, he asserts that it is outwardly the word of the Buddha, inwardly a treatise composed by Indian pandits, and secretly a Tibetan treatise. The position of a succession of great scholars of the past is that it is the word of the Buddha. In particular, it is possible to understand that Jé Dharmaswami, Lodrö Gyalpo’s own ancestor, was also of this view because of the following. I have only seen one small section of his Mirror of White Mercury Overview up to now and have not seen his Work of Fine Crystal: Extensive Commentary on the Four Glorious Tantras and other works. However, in that small section of Mirror of White Mercury, the words of Buddha in Four Tantras have been left as they are. Also, there is a reference to this in a manuscript by Lata Tsewang[644] cited in Stream of Beryl by Drö Tsoknyi Gyatso.

d.div: [644] A disciple of Dharmaswami Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé.

f.d:
rang gi bla ma'i slob dpon mtsho smad mkhan chen pa'i khog 'bugs shin tu gsal ba rnams la khyad gsod kyi nga ro cher sgrog pa ni/ sa paN gyis/
gting nas nyams pa'i khrel 'das rnams/ / rang gi gtam ngan ngo sor khyer/ / kan tsa'i yul gyi rgyal rigs 'ga'/ / pha bsad pa la rgyal rnga brdung /[302] / zhes pa ltar ram 'phral skad gso dpyad rang lugs kyi mgo rmog nang nas bcag pa de dang /

Moreover, his shout of blatant disregard for the very clear assertions in Well-Composed History of Medicine by Tsomé Khenchen, the master of his own teacher, could be explained by Sakya Paṇḍita’s verse:
Having lost all sense of shame, holding their own wicked words in high esteem, those of royal caste in Kāñci beat the drum of victory at the murder of their father.[645] Alternatively, it may be a case of vulgar language breaking the helmet of his own medical tradition from the inside.[646] Other compositions besides that one include:

d.div: [302] sa skya paN+Di ta'i gsung 'bum/ thas skya legs bshad/ shog_9_na2_sa skya'i bka' 'bum pod lnga pa/ shog_108_na2
[645] Treasury of Wise Sayings, Collected Works, tha, 9a2, Collected Works of the Sakya, vol. 5, 108a2.

[646] A helmet that should protect the wearer from outside dangers has itself been broken from the inside, because Lodrö Gyalpo has himself gone against his own tradition. This criticism is of the previously listed text and probably a work by Lodrö Gyalpo called Lamp Dispelling Darkness: Presentation of Four Tantras Being the Word of the Buddha and Treatise, in which Lodrö Gyalpo presents these three views of Four Tantras. His own position is somewhat ambiguous. In his work on the history of medicine, General Compendium (p. 312), after listing the many positions of others, he says he cannot say whether Four Tantras is the word of Buddha or a later treatise, and that declaring the word of Buddha as not being so is just as bad as declaring something not the word of the Buddha to be so. He also says that spending so much time arguing over this matter is pointless, and that we should be able to infer its origins in the same way we infer fire from smoke and the presence of water from ducks. Kachuwa Chölotar (p. 26) states that although Lodrö Gyalpo presents all three positions, we can clearly infer that he believes Four Tantras to be the work of Yuthok Yönten Gönpo. This whole section is actually a continuation of listing the works of Lodrö Gyalpo begun previously. However, Sangyé Gyatso does not even mention Lamp Dispelling Darkness by name but is possibly referring to it as “that one” in the next paragraph.

f.d: g.yu thog mnyam nyid rdo rje sogs bla ma lhag pa'i lha rnams la bstod tshogs kyi 'phreng ba/ sman gyi ro nus zhus rjes kyi re'u mig d+harma swa mis rdo rje pha lam la mig phug pa ltar mdzad par slar srad bu brgyus pa dang mtshungs pa/ gong sman dkon cog phan dar la dri ba tsu ta'i 'khri shing / pa snam 'tsha bye+od kun legs par dri ba blo gsal 'jug ngogs dang / dris lan legs bshad skyugs pa/ zla thigs nyin byed 'od mtsho/ dbyar skyes rnga sangs/ ga bur gur kum a kar tsan dan sogs kyi skyon sel 'ga' zhig / rgyud bzhi par bkod mjug rtsom gyi skyon sel/ chu skol gyi rnam bshad/ 'phan yul gyi sman pa rlung khams langs pa'i dris lan dbyar nyi'i zhun thigs/ ma nu'i dri lan sogs gso dpyad skor la mang ba dang / snyan ngag tu me long ma'i me long ma sogs rig gnas gzhan la yang bstan bcos kha yar snang /

• A collection of praises to Yuthok, Nyamnyi Dorjé, and other holy masters • Table of the Powers, Tastes, and Post-Digestive Tastes of Medicines. The previous work on this topic by Dharmaswami can be compared to holing a diamond, while this work is like threading that diamond. • The Cuta Vine: Questions Put to Gongmen Könchok Phendar (1511–77) • Ford for Those of Bright Minds: Questions to the Panam Physician Künga Lekpa • Questions and Answers: A Well-Composed Emetic • Moondrops: An Ocean of Light • Thunder: The Rousing Drum of Summer • Eliminating the Impurities of Camphor, Saffron, Eaglewood, Sandalwood, and the Like • Eliminating Mistakes: Comments after the Printing of Four Tantras • Boiling Water • Refined Drop of Summer Sun: Answers to Questions from a Phenyül Doctor on the Rising of the Wind Element • Questions and Answers on Manu With these and other works he contributed much to the medical collection. It seems that he also composed various works on the other sciences, such as a treatise on Mirror of the Mirror of Poetics.

'on kyang de dag thams cad du rje g.yu thog pa dngam nyam nyid rdo rje karma pa mi bskyod rdo rje gsum las/ gso dpyad dngos kyi slob dpon glang bu chos rje yin 'dug pa dang snyan ngag smon grub lo tswa ba'am skyogs lo rin chen bkra shis su grags par gsan 'dug ste bla ma'i rigs gang du'ang bsngags phyogs mi mdzad pa ni/ phyi ma rgyud du/ slob dpon gsang zhing rang che 'byin pa dang /[303] / zhes gsungs pa'i thog tu babs pa 'dra la/ phyi rgyud mes po'i zhal lung dang sman gyi chos 'byung gang dag byang chub sems dpa'i spyad spyod par 'dod pa'i sman pa rnams kyis mi shes su mi rung ba'i phyi nang gzhan gsum gyi rnam gzhag shes bya spyi'i khog 'bugs drang srong kun tu dga' ba'i zlos gar gtan pa med pa'i mchod sbyin gyi sgo 'phar yangs por phye ba gnyis gsham ma tshang ba steng grib kyis btab pa'i mdzad 'phror lus/

However, in all the above works, apart from Jé Yuthok, Nyamnyi Dorjé, and Karmapa Mikyö Dorjé, nowhere does he praise or pay homage to those with the status of lama, such as his actual medical teacher Langbu Chöje, or to his poetry teacher Möndrup Lotsāwa, also known as Kyok Lotsāwa Rinchen Tashi. This seems to be a perfect illustration of the line from the Final Tantra: “Keeping the master secret while promoting oneself.”[647] In this connection, the Final Tantra section of his Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors commentary on Four Tantras, and his General Knowledge History: A Presentation on the External, Internal, and Other, Indispensable for Physicians Wishing to Engage in the Practices of the Bodhisattvas, the Wide-Open Door to the Unending Ceremonial Offering, a Dance Delighting the Rishis[648] were both left unfinished as he was afflicted by a stroke.

d.div: [303] g.yu thog yon tan mgon po'i rtsom sgrig mdzad pa/ bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud las phyi ma rgyud/ le'u/ 27_shog_665_yig phreng 17
[647] Four Tantras, Final Tantra, 27.665.17.
[648] This is the text cited as General Compendium in earlier notes.

f.d: skye ba'i rigs bka' gter sogs tshad ldan gyi lung nas zin pa dang rang nyid nas sngon gyi bag chags ched du sad pa'i spyod pa ma bstan na rang gar khas blangs par nges pa ma mchis kyang / khong rang gis d+ha_rma swa mi'i skye bar zhal gyis bzhes la zhwa dmar bas ngos 'dzin mdzad par grags shing / snyan ngag dang mtshan nyid phyag chen gyi lta ba rig gnas gzhan la hol tsam sbyangs pa'i skad g.yu 'brug sngon mo las gso dpyad la zur mkhar gong ma'i shul zin lta zhog skyem pa tshe dbang tsam yang ma byung bar mngon/

If the status of one’s birth is not authenticated by valid prophecy, such as that found in the Treasure and Transmission traditions, and if from one’s own side one does not display evidence of conduct that is a direct awakening of imprints from previous lives, then there can be no reliability from merely making claims. However, he himself stated that he was the rebirth of Dharmaswami, and it is said that this was recognized by the Shamarpa. Moreover, the sounds emanating from his rather superficial training in other disciplines such as poetry and sutra-mahāmudrā philosophy are merely those of the blue dragon,[649] while in medicine far from being the successor to Surkhar, it is clear he does not even measure up to Kyempa Tsewang.

d.div: [649] Very loud and impressive but essentially empty because no one has ever seen a dragon (Prof. Losang Tenzin).

f.d: gzhi nas rang gi slob rgyun mtsho smad mkhan chen gyi gsung la khyad gsod/ byang pa sogs snga rabs tshad ldan gyi gzhung lugs rnams la rtog ge'i rig pa dang snyan ngag shes pa sor bzhag gi dgag pa sogs gso rig la rma 'byin pa/ rang gi bzhed pa'i rgyud bzhi par rko rin spungs pas thog mar zhal gyis bzhes kyang rjes su phyag thog mi 'gel ba yang sa spyod ngag dbang 'jig rten grags pa de gser dang ra gan mi nor ba zhig yin pas gzhung don 'khyogs bshad sogs kyi mtshang rig par mngon zhing / de'i 'grel pa mes po'i zhal lung dang bcas pa'i gso rig skor rnams rang nyid kyi gsung las/ bya rog lnga par gyur pa bzhin/ / kun gyi dpal du ma gyur ro/[304] / zhes pa'i thog tu babs/ rgan po'i kha chems su/ kho bo ri gsum gyi khar sleb dus dang / drang srong chen po'i gnod pas nyam thag pa'i dus su bris tshul 'dug pa/ de min khungs ma'i lo rgyus ma rnyed kyang ma 'gyangs par dus kyi chos nyid du gyur ram snyam/

His fundamental disregard of the words of Tsomé Khenchen, who is within his own teaching lineage, his over-intellectual attacks on authoritative medical works of the past such as those from the Jang tradition, and his refutations of standard poetical wisdom are a wound inflicted upon medical science. He makes the claim that the Rinpung ruler at first promised to sponsor a publication of Four Tantras but then failed to deliver on his promise. However, this ruler, Ngawang Jikten Drakpa, was someone who did not mistake brass for gold, and he was clearly aware of the errors of the other’s twisted interpretations of the text. His corpus of medical literature, including his commentary on Four Tantras called Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, are illustrations of his own words, “like the crow that died, they never achieved their crowning glory.”[650] In Testament of an Old Man he writes, “When I was approaching the age of sixty-three” and “When I was weakened by the harms of the great rishi.” I can find no authoritative references to his life and activities beyond this age, and he probably died soon after.

d.div: [304] bya rog lnga par gyur pa bzhin/ /zhes sogs kyi tshigs rkang gnyis po'i gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[650] This is Lodrö Gyalpo’s own verse, which he used to mock the Rinpung ruler who refused to sponsor his publication of Four Tantras.

d.i: Other physicians of the Sur tradition

f.d: gzhan yang bya pa bkra shis dar rgyas kyis bshad rgyud rkyang sel la 'grel pa sman gyi 'khrungs dpe dang sbyar ba sogs dang / gru seng ge'i mtshan can nam drang srong mthu stobs rdo rje'i sman dpyad bdud rtsi'i gter/ dpa' bo gtsug lag gi sman dpyad zin bris snying po bsdus pa dang rdo zhun gsal sgron sogs bye ba ring bsrel bshus pa lta bu/ skyid shod na'o 'tsho byed blo gros brtan pa'am sems dpa' chen po blo bzang rgya mtshos phyi rgyud la dka' 'grel gsal ba'i me long dang / khog 'bugs drang srong dgongs rgyan/ dwags po 'tsho byed karma kun phan pas bye ba ring bsrel gyi 'grel zhal shes bcas pa dang / man ngag gi skor zab gnad mtha' dag bsdus pa'i snying po bdud rtsi gser 'phreng / 'bam bcos sogs mang ba rnams/

Of the many other physicians of the Sur tradition, Tashi Dargyé of Jayül composed a commentary on the powers of individual medicines taught in the Explanatory Tantra in connection with a materia medica and other works. Dru Sengé or Drangsong Thutop Dorjé wrote Ambrosia Treasury of Medical Practice. Pawo Tsuklak Trengwa composed Quintessential Notes on Medical Practice, Illuminating Beacon on Mineral Exudates, and so on, which seem to have been copied from Relic of Millions. The Kyishö Nao physician, Lodrö Tenpa, also known as Bodhisattva Losang Gyatso, composed Clear Mirror: A Word Commentary to the Final Tantra and Ornament to the Thoughts of the Rishis: A History of Medicine. The Dakpo physician Karma Künphen composed a commentary to Relic of Millions together with orally transmitted instructions, Golden Rosary of Ambrosia: Quintessence of All the Profound Points of the Instruction Collections, Treatment of Kangbam, and others.

de ltar zur lugs kyi brgyud pa
ston pa sman gyi bla/ gsung pa po drang srong rig pa'i ye shes/ sdud pa po drang srong yid las skyes/ 'tsho byed gzhon nu/ dpal mgon klu sgrub/ dpal ldan dpa' bo/ kha che'i paN chen zla ba mngon par dga' ba/ lo chen bai ro tsa na/ mnga' bdag khri srong lde'u btsan/ gter ston gra pa mngon shes/ dbus pa dar grags/ rog ston dkon cog skyabs/ rigs 'dus sman pa'i rgyal po g.yu thog yon tan mgon po/ sum ston ye shes gzungs/ 'tsho byed gzhon nu ye shes/ g.yu thog mkhas pa 'bum seng / gtsang ston sangs rgyas rin chen/ mkhas pa don grub rin chen/ bstan 'dzin don grub rgyal mtshan/ brang ti dkon cog rgyal mtshan/ brang ti dpal ldan 'tsho byed

The Sur lineage, therefore, runs as follows:
Our Teacher the buddha of medicine The speaker of the tantra, Rishi Vidyājñāna The compiler, Rishi Manasija Kumāra Jivaka The master Nāgārjuna Śrī Ācārya Śūra The Kashmiri Pandit Candranandana The great translator Vairocana King Trisong Detsen The treasure finder Drapa Ngönshé Üpa Dardrak Roktön Könchok Kyap The king of medicine, combiner of lineages, Yuthok Yönten Gönpo Sumtön Yeshé Sung Tsojé Shönu Yeshé The Yuthok scholar Bumseng The Tsang teacher Sangyé Rinchen The scholar Döndrup Rinchen Tenzin Döndrup Gyaltsen Drangti Könchok Gyaltsen Drangti Palden Tsojé

de 'di yan byang lugs gter ma dang / kun dga' bo dang slob dpon pad+ma sogs 'dren tshul rgyas bsdus las 'dra zhing / de nas
dge slong tshal pa dbang grags/ mkhas mchog phun tshogs bzang po/ zur mkhar mnyam nyid rdo rje/ skyem pa tshe 'bum/ byar po paN chen/ de'i dngos slob kyi thu bo zla ba'i dbang po/ chu shul na'o 'tsho byed blo gros brtan pa'am skyid shod pa'i bla sman mdzad cing byang chub lam rim thugs nyams su bstar/ rin sdings su bzhugs pas rin chen sdings pa sems dpar grags pa blo bzang rgya mtsho 'dis gong du brjod pa ltar gyi bstan bcos kyang du ma mdzad/

Up to this point, apart from the extension to their list to include Ānanda, Ācarya Padma, and others, this lineage is similar to the Jang Treasure lineage. It continues:
The monk Tsalpa Wangdrak The great scholar Phüntsok Sangpo Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé Kyempa Tsewang Jarpo Panchen His direct and chief disciple, Dawa Wangpo He is followed by the Chushöl Nao physician Lodrö Tenpa, who served as physician to the Kyishö governor and, because he practiced the graduated path to enlightenment and lived in Rinding, was also known as Rinchen Ding Bodhisattva Losang Gyatso. He also composed several works, as mentioned above.

de nas stod lung smon byang gad gsum zhes pa'i byang ngos pa'i mi ngo sgar pas bkag por phud pa la brten/ rin sdings sems dpa' chen po'i gan du yid dbyung gi gso dpyad lo bdun gyi ring bslabs/ dwags po 'tsho byed karma kun phan du yang gtugs par sang 'byon rgyu'i nub mo g.yu'i mchod rten ngo mtshar ba rmis pas/ 'tsho byed kyis da ring khyed dang mjal ba'i rten 'brel yin 'dug pas skyid shod lha sa'i phyogs su 'gro don rgya che ba dang sman dpyad bstan pa'i rgyun 'dzin 'byung bar lung bstan/ gros gnas brtan la snying thur mkhal thur mig thur sogs thur ma'i skor gyi phyag 'khrid nos/ paN chen blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan la dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa zhus pa'i mtshan drang srong bstan 'dzin rgyal por thogs/ thams cad mkhyen pa yon tan rgya mtsho sku ltem tshul gyi 'phrod bsten zhus dus sman blas rjes su bzung ba yin pa'i lung bstan ngo mtshar ba byung bar grags/

He is followed by Rishi Tenzin Gyalpo. He was driven out of the northern or Jang region of Tölung—which is divided into the regions of Mön, Jang, and Gé—by the local community. He came to Rinding Bodhisattva to seek relief and studied medicine there for seven years. On the night before he met Tsojé Karma Künphen, he dreamed of an extraordinary turquoise stupa. “This reflects the auspiciousness of our meeting today,” said Tsojé, who predicted that Tenzin Gyalpo would be of great benefit to those beings living on the Lhasa side of Kyishö and would contribute greatly to the preservation of the lineage of medical teachings. From Drosa Neten, Tenzin Gyalpo received teachings on the use of surgical spoons in the treatment of the heart, kidneys, eyes, and so on. From Panchen Losang Chökyi Gyaltsen (1567–1662) he took the vows of a novice monk and received the name Rishi Tenzin Gyalpo. When he was caring for the health of the omniscient Yönten Gyatso,[651] who had displayed some illness, it is said that Tenzin Gyalpo received the extraordinary prophecy that he would always be cared for by Medicine Buddha.

d.div: [651] The Fourth Dalai Lama (1589–1616).

f.d: byang pa chos rgyal bkra shis stobs rgyas la g.yu thog snying thig gi dbang lung chos skor dang bcas pa gsan pa sogs gso ba rig pa la mkhas shing grub pa'i bdag nyid chen por gyur zhing / tshangs pa dung thod can gyi'ang bsngags pa mdzad/ gshegs pa'i tshes grangs kyang g.yu thog dang dus mtshungs/ sum ston ye shes gzungs kyi sprul pa yin par kyang grags/ 'di nyid kyi rigs sras byang ngos nang so dar rgyas dang gcung gzhan phan dbang po/ slob ma'i thu bo gling stod chos rje blo bzang rgya mtsho sogs mang /

From the Dharma king Jangpa Tashi Topgyal he received, among other teachings, the initiations and transmissions of Yuthok’s Heartdrop and Dharma works. He became a great master much learned and practiced in the science of medicine. He was also praised by Tsangpa Dung Töchen. The date and month of his passing coincides with that of Yuthokpa. He was said to be an incarnation of Sumtön Yeshé Sung. His son disciples were Jang Ngö Nangso Dargyé and his younger son, Shenphen Wangpo. His main disciple was Lingtö Chöjé Losang Gyatso.

bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i gsan yig gang+gA'i chu rgyun ka bar rgyud chung gsum po'i bshad pa sa dpyad rdel 'grems lag len ngo sprod kyi dus drang srong bstan 'dzin rgyal po nas de sras drang srong dar rgyas/ des gcung mkhas mchog gzhan phan dbang po/ 'di mched gnyis kyis gcung sku tshe thung bas gzhan phan gyi 'gro don rgya chung / gcen gyis rje bla ma chen pos dbus mchod yon gong ma rnams kyi bla sman dang / lha dbang lcog tu slob grwa'i gso dpyad kyi 'gro don rgya che bas slob ma rgyud kyi rgyugs sprod pa brag mjug pa dang / gcung gi sger g.yog lta bu nas lha rjer gyur pa lhag bsam mam sum dga'/ thog ma gso dpyad slob grwa'i tho btsun gyi gras dang rjes su rje bla ma'i bka' dang bcas bskyar slob mdzad pa dar mo blo bzang chos grags sogs mang ba'i gcung gzhan phan dbang po las bzhes shing /

My teacher, the Great Fifth, in his Stream of the Ganges: An Account of Teachings Received, in the ka volume, in the section on the explanation, outline, stone layout, and introduction to the practices from the three shorter tantras,[652] talks of the lineage passing from Rishi Tenzin Gyalpo to his son Rishi Dargyé and in turn to his younger brother Khechok Shenphen Wangpo.[653] The younger son had a short life and so his contribution to the welfare of others was small. His brother, the elder son, was appointed physician to the great patronized lamas, as exemplified by my great lama, and was also hugely beneficial to many beings in his capacity of teacher in the medical school in Lhawang Chok.[654] He consequently had many disciples that he took over from his younger brother, Khechok Shenphen Wangpo. These include Drak Jukpa, who gave recitation examinations on Four Tantras, Lhaksam or Sumga, who rose from being like a personal servant to the younger brother to being a chief physician, and Darmo Losang Chödrak, who began as a monastic entrant of the medical school and later, under the direction of the Great fifth, took over the revision classes.

d.div: [652] Of the four tantras in Four Tantras, the Root, Explanatory, and Final Tantras are the three shorter tantras. The Instruction Tantra is the longest.
[653] Ngawang Losang Gyatso, Stream of the Ganges.
[654] According to Trinlé (p. 285) this medical school, also known as Sharchen Chok, was situated in the Potala.

f.d: man rgyud dang bcas pa'i lung gi brgyud pa ni drang srong bstan 'dzin rgyal po nas gling stod chos rje blo bzang rgya mtsho 'dis byang bdag bkra shis stobs rgyas la g.yu thog snying thig gsan cing khong rang la zur chos dbyings rang grol gyis gsan dus yer pa sman dris khengs pa dang / mtsho smad mkhan chen gyi skye ba yin pa'i lung bstan byung ba gsan yig tu gsal/[305] de'i sprul pa'i sku 'khrul med deng sang yang mkhas btsun bzang gsum 'dzom par bzhugs pa sogs zhib pa gzhan du gsal/

The tantra transmission lineage together with the Instruction Tantra passes from Rishi Tenzin Gyalpo to Lingtö Chöjé Losang Gyatso, who received Yuthok’s Heartdrop from Jangdak Tashi Topgyal. While Surchen Chöying Rangdröl was receiving teaching from Lingtö Chöjé, Yerpa became filled with the aroma of medicine. It is clear from the list of teachings received that there was a prophecy predicting him as an incarnation of Tsomé Khenchen. His own unmistaken incarnation lives on today as a being with a combination of the wise, noble, and good qualities. His details can be found elsewhere.

d.div: [305] rgyal ba lnga pa blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsung 'bum/ ka gsan yig

f.d: gling stod chos rje blo bzang rgya mtsho nas snga 'gyur snying tig dang bcas grub thob kyi rnam thar skyong ba sman sgom 'brang rgyas pa gar dbang / des rje mi la'i yang srid rtogs brjod rgyas pa rje bla ma'i bka' 'bum du bzhugs pa khyab bdag blo mchog rdo rje brgyud de lung bzhes/ lung dang bshad pa lag len mtha' dag gsan yig rin po che dang ji bzhin mthun pa zur lugs zhig thob nas lugs 'dir lhad 'khrul chad pa sogs byang lugs nas gso 'dod skom pa chu 'dod ltar gyur kyang / rje bla ma nyid la g.yu thog snying tig dang bdud rtsi bum pa'i skor la ni sku na smin pa dang spyan mi gsal ba sogs gnas dus du ma'i sgo nas rgyud bzhi'i ljags lung zhu ba'ang bsod nams kyi skal bar ma shom/

From Lingtö Chöjé Losang Gyatso, the transmission lineage, together with the early translation Heartdrop, passed to Mengom Drangyé Garwang, the maintainer of the biographies of the siddhas. He passed it to Khyapdak Lochok Dorjé, an incarnation of Vimalamitra,[655] whose extensive life and deeds are found in the collected works of my great lama. Like a thirsty man wishing for water, I yearned to acquire all the transmissions, teachings, and practices of this Sur tradition as listed in the precious Account of Teachings Received in order to correct any corruption, errors, and omissions it might have had by comparing it with the Jang tradition. However, although I requested from my great lama the oral transmission of Four Tantras, due to his advanced age and his illnesses such as eye ailments, I had not the merit to receive it, receiving only the Yuthok Heartdrop and Vase of Ambrosia.[656]

d.div: [655] Bi ma la, although other editions have rje mi la (Lord Milarepa).
[656] In this paragraph, there is no pronoun “I” at all and no unambiguous indication that the agent was Desi Sangyé Gyatso. Even Prof. Losang Tenzin had doubts about this.

f.d: 'on kyang gsan yig dang mthun gshis lung brgyud zur lugs 'di nyid zhus pa'i brgyud pa'i gsham gsan yig rin po che dang cung zad mi 'dra ba/ rje mnyam nyid rdo rje nas/ sgyer rigs bkra shis dbang phyug / bsod nams bzang po/ rdzogs chen pa bsod nams rin chen/ 'phrin las don yod/ snying phu ba rig 'dzin snying po/ gsung sprul tshul khrims rdo rje/ rig 'dzin 'phrin las lhun grub/ bai ro'i yang srid khyab bdag 'gyur med rdo rje bar ro//

However, the lineage I received of this Sur tradition, which accords with the accounts of teachings received, and therefore differs somewhat in the latter stages from that found in the precious Account of Teachings Received, runs from Jé Nyamnyi Dorjé to Tashi Wangchuk of the Gyer family, Sönam Sangpo, the Dzokchen practitioner Sönam Rinchen, Trinlé Dönyö, Rikzin Nyingpo of Nying Phu, Sungtrül Tsültrim Dorjé, Rikzin Trinlé Lhündrup, up to the Vairocana incarnation Khyapdak Gyurmé Dorjé
17. The Gongmen Tradition

gzhan yang stod lugs kyi ya gyal gong kha ba chos kyi rdo rje nas gso ba rig pa mdzad kyang / brang ti'i pod dmar du grags pa las/
brang ti chos rgyal bkra shis ngas/ / sa skya'i nyi thog sman grong du/ / snod ldan dkon cog bde legs la/ / zhes byung bas 'di nas brang ti'i rjes su zhugs nas mkhas pa'i go sar sleb ste gong sman par grags pa'i lugs la/ dkon cog bde legs kyis gangs ri'i ljongs na grags pa'i gso rig gi yig cha phal mo che la gzigs shing / rgya bod kyi mkhas pa du ma'i snyan brgyud gab pa rnams kyang khol du bton nas rang dang gzhan rnams la phan pa'i ched du/ rtsom pa khrigs su bsdeb par mdzad pa ni/

In the work known as Red Works of Drangti it states:
I, Drangti Chögyal Tashi, in the two-story Sakya medical school, to the suitable vessel Könchok Delek… Therefore, although Könchok Delek practiced medicine in a branch of the Upper tradition under Gongkhawa Chökyi Dorjé, he became a follower of the Drangti tradition and rose to a very prominent position as scholar, and he became the most prominent figure of the medical lineage known as Gongmen.[657] Könchok Delek studied most of the well-known medical books in this land of snow. Moreover, he brought out the hidden oral traditions of many Chinese and Tibetan scholars, and for the sake of self and others composed several compilations. These include the following seven volumes:

d.div: [657] Gong sman, literally, “doctor of high position.”

f.d: man ngag pu ti dmar po/ pod nag / pod khra/ phyi rgyud la dka' 'grel gnas thams cad gsal ba'i sgron me dang brgyud pa'i rnam thar sman ming brda sprod/ rgyud kyi bka' 'phang 'grol ba'i shog ser te pod bdun dang / rtsa chu'i gnad 'grol zhal gyi gdams pa dmar 'byin/ sngo'i 'khrungs dpe don bsdus/ ro nus kyi sdeb sbyor sogs phran bu bsdus pa/ khyad par rgyud la mchan shin tu rgyas pa dag 'debs par mdzad pa la rgyud chen khra mo be bum seng ldeng mar grags pa slob dpon bsten mi dgos par bltas pa tsam gyis grol bar bzhed pa rnams mdzad/

1. Red Volume of Instructions 2. Black Volume of Instructions 3. Multicolored Volume of Instructions 4. Beacon Illuminating All Places: Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Final Tantra 5. Biographies of the Lineage 6. Medical Lexicon 7. Yellow Scroll that Disentangles the Precipice Path of the Difficult Points of the Tantra Other shorter works include Direct Teachings on Disentangling the Main Points of Pulse and Urine Analysis, Brief Illustrative Descriptions of Medical Plants, and Compilation of Tastes and Powers. A particular noteworthy composition is his extensive annotations and corrections to the tantra known as Khadira Tree Multicolored Compilation on the Great Tantra, for which it is claimed that merely looking at this work will bring about a liberation, without the need to rely upon a master.

gong sman dkon cog phan dar gyis drang srong brgyud pa'i gsol 'debs rdzogs ldan ma/ sman gyi byin 'bebs rab gnas kyi cho ga / sman gyi lha mo'i sgrub skor/ dngul chu grub pa'i bstan bcos sman nag chen mo'i sbyor ba rgyas 'bring bsdus gsum gyi dkar chag /rtsa rgyud kyi 'grel pa me long mthong gsal/

Gongmen Könchok Phendar’s compositions include: • Caturyoga Requests to the Rishi Lineage • Consecration Ritual for Calling Down Blessings for Medicine • Collection on Medicine Goddess Practices • Table of Contents for the Extensive, Intermediate, and Abridged Preparation of the Great Black Medicine • Treatise on Preparing Mercury • Clear Mirror: Commentary on the Root Tantra

man ngag gi skor la gso rig dgos 'dod 'byung ba nor bu'i 'phreng ba zhes bya ba man ngag rten 'brel gyi skor ma tshang ba med pa'i shin tu rgyas pa pod gsum du longs pa zhig dang / de las bsdus pa dgongs pa don 'dus/ de las kyang bsdus pa dgos pa kun bsdus/ de dag gi dgongs don snying por dril ba la nyams yig brgya rtsar grags pa rnams mdzad/ gong sman dkon cog phan dar la slob ma ka bzhi gdung brgyad du grags pa las/ ka ba lta bu bzhi ni stod du mkhas pa mnga' ris 'a pa bde chen/ sman du mkhas pa gong dkar gser tog pa/ bar du mkhas pa zur tsho'i drang srong lha shug pa/ snyan pa dang ldan pa tshwa rong chos rje dang bzhi/ gdung brgyad ni mang mkhar bde gling ba nyi ma grags/ bsam gtan dpal bzang / thang rings pa nam mkha' bkra shis/ dbon po kun dga' bkra shis/ mnga' ris shag pa don grub rgyal/ dpal ldan legs pa/ blo gros 'phags pa/ bsam grub bzang po rnams/

His collection on transmitted instructions and charms is a very extensive and fully comprehensive collection in three volumes known as Jeweled Garland Fulfilling All Needs within the Science of Medicine. A more abridged composition is Summarizing the Thoughts. An even more abridged work is Compilation of the Essentials. There is also a summary of the main points of these works known as Hundred Works of Experience. Gongmen Könchok Phendar had disciples known as the four pillars and the eight beams. The four pillar-like disciples were Apa Dechen from Ngari, the scholar from the upper regions; Gongkar Sertokpa, the scholar from the lower regions; Surtsé Drangsong Lhashakpa, the scholar from the middle regions; and the renowned Tsarong Chöjé. The eight pillars were Nyima Drak from Mangkhar Deling, Samten Palsang, Namkha Tashi from Thangring, his nephew Künga Tashi, Döndrup Gyal from Ngari, Palden Lekpa, Lodrö Phakpa, and Samdrup Sangpo.

de'i nang nas tshwa rong chos rje dpal ldan rgyal mtshan gyis gso rig gi spyi don nam/ bshad pa'i srol 'byed mun sel sgron me la sogs pa tshwa rong pa'i snyan brgyud be bum du grags pa dang / de'i dbon po nam mkha' bde legs kyis rgyud bzhi'i spyi don legs bshad snang ba/ rtsa mdo'i sa dpyad bsdus don/ phyi rgyud kyi nad dang gnyen po gso thabs gsum gyi dbye bsdu/ man ngag thor bu sna tshogs pa'i skor bdud rtsi 'phreng ba/ gcong sde bzhi'i ngos 'dzin mdzub tshugs ma dang / de'i bcos thabs rdo rje pha lam la sogs pa mdzad/

Among these disciples Tsarong Chöjé Palden Gyaltsen composed Overview of Medicine or Lamp Dispelling the Darkness: A New Tradition of Teaching and more, all of which became known as the Tsarong Oral tradition compilation. His nephew Namkha Delek’s compositions include: • Light of Excellent Explanation: An Overview of Four Tantras • Abridged Outline of the Pulse Compendium from Four Tantras • Divisions and Abridgements of the Ailments, Remedies, and Healing Methods of the Final Tantra • Ambrosia Garland; a collection of miscellaneous instructions • Identification of the Four Classes of Chronic Degenerative Disorders • Diamonds; remedies for the above chronic disorders

de'i sras drang srong tshe dbang rig 'dzin gyi skabs sde pa lhun po rtse bas spor kha ba stod lugs kyi lag len slob pa dang / tshwa rong pa tshe dbang rig 'dzin byar po paN chen gyi sar smad lugs slob par brdzangs nas smad lugs su 'gyur/ 'dis gso dpyad la zur mkhar pa'i chos 'byung ji lta ba'i steng smad du bsnan kha dang bcas bskal bzang bgrod pa'i myur lam mdzad nas khong rang gi brgyud pa tshe dbang rnam rgyal gyi bar lhun rtse dang gtsang pa rnams kyi bla sman gyi rgyun bzung ste slob grwa'ang bskyangs/ bstan 'dzin chos kyi rgyal po'i mtshan don rgyug par nye nas slob grwa rnams chad na'ang / slar gong ma lnga pa'i chos srid gdugs dkar gyis khyab nas slob grwa mu 'thud kyi bdag rkyen dang / rjes su de'i bu tshe brtan rdo rjes rgyud gra thang ma'i tshig rgyugs phul zhing bca' yig bka' rtsom dang bcas pa'i bdag rkyen je mtho gnang ba dang /

His son was Rishi Tsewang Rikzin, and at that time local governor Lhünpo Tsewa sent Porkhawa to study the practices of the Upper tradition, while Tsarong Tsewang Rikzin was sent to the place of Jarpo Panchen to study the Lower tradition and thereby became a follower of that system. On his contribution to medicine, he extended Surkhar’s work on history and composed Swift Path Traveled by the Fortunate. The lineage up to Tsewang Namgyal maintained a succession of physicians to the Lhünpo Tsewa and the Tsang rulers and also founded medical schools. When the reputation of Tenzin Chökyi Gyalpo[658] began to spread, the schools were discontinued. However, later when they were covered by the religious and secular white umbrella of the Great Fifth, they were restarted. Later on his son Tseten Dorjé offered a word recitation of the Drathang Four Tantras, and the Great Fifth wrote a constitution for the school.[659] These factors were instrumental in raising the status of this tradition.

d.div: [658] Title given to the Mongolian chieftain Gusri Khan by the Fifth Dalai Lama.
[659] The school was Drangsong Düpai Ling (“Place of the Assembled Rishis”) in Shigatsé (Trinlé, p. 257).

f.d: kho bo cag gis kyang lcags sprel lo 'bras spungs su chibs bsgyur dus 'bel gtam lan gcig bgyid bcug pa khong rang tshang gi chos 'byung nas byas song zhing / gnang rigs kyi sman pa'i bzos tsam bgyis na'ang / rgyud tshig rgyugs dang khong rang gi chos 'byung tsam las gso dpyad la gzhig pa chug pa zhig mi 'dug rung lar babs pher yod 'dzom pa 'dug pa bcas mig rgyang gang che'i zhal che ba sogs byas shing slob grwa'i mu yang skyong bzhin du yod kyang dus las 'das/ slob grwa rnams la dpe 'dzin las ngo sprod bshad pa sogs byed mi med khar dpe 'dzin de ga yang byed du mi 'jug pa'i sger las sogs sna tshogs la brten rdzong sdod phug pa tshangs byin gyi dus nas slob grwa'i sa dpyad de yang dor bar snang /

During the visit[660] to Drepung in the iron-monkey year (1680), I had the opportunity to engage Tseten Dorjé in conversation. He had followed his family tradition, and he gave at least the impression of being a lineage physician. However, despite his ability to pass the examination of reciting the words of the tantra and his possession of the family tradition, he did not have an in-depth understanding of medical science. Nevertheless, he was basically a very capable person who had initiated some far-sighted rules, and the schools still continue. However, he has since died. While memorization of the scriptures happens at the school, there is no one there to give teachings and so on. Moreover, various private activities go on that undermine even the focus on memorization, so that from the time of the rule of district governor Phukpa Tsangjin, all auspicious conditions for the school have been destroyed.

d.div: [660] There is no explicit subject to this verb, and it is not clear if it refers to Tseten Dorjé because it is in high honorific (chibs bsgyur). It is tempting, therefore, to think that the subject is the Fifth Dalai Lama.

f.d: gzhan yang gong sman pa'i lugs la gsal ba sgang pa dpal mgon lhun grub kyis gso rig gi spyi don legs bshad 'phreng ba/ dus bzhi'i ngos 'dzin la 'khrul ba spong thabs/ drung 'tsho dbang ldan pas nyi zla gza' 'dzin/ nyi ma ldog mnyam sogs rtsa la things tshul smra ba la dri ba legs bshad 'tshol ba'i pho nya rig pa'i lcags kyu/ phyag rdor mgon pos mi'i nyi ma'i gces bsdus las ming yang ji bzhin du bris pa rin chen 'phreng ba dang phyi rgyud kyi sa bcad mdzad/ sde ba rong tsho bas lta na sdug gi ngos 'dzin brgyud pa'i lo rgyus sogs la dris pa'i lan rig pa'i 'khor lo/ man ngag zab bsdus bdud rtsi thigs 'phreng sogs mang du mdzad/ 'brug pa sprul ba'i sku pad+ma dkar pos rgyud bzhi'i rnam gzhag gzhan la phan pa'i gter dang / dus bcos le tshan/ zhwa dmar ba drug pas gso rig gi bstan bcos 'chi ba med pa'i bdud rtsi/ dpa' bo gtsug lag 'phreng bas sman gyi chos 'byung dang 'bam bcos/ sog bzlog pas rgyud bzhi'i bka' sgrub nges don snying po la sogs te

Other followers of the Gongmen tradition include the following: Gangpa Palgön Lhündrup who composed Garland of Excellent Explanation: An Overview of the Science of Medicine and Method to Avoid Errors in Identifying the Four Times. Drungtso Wangdenpa wrote Hook of Wisdom: Messenger in Search of Excellent Explanation, which answers questions on how eclipses of the sun and moon, the solstices and equinoxes, and so on affect the pulse. Chakdor Gönpo composed an outline of the Final Tantra and Precious Garland Quintessence, whose title he copied from Minyima’s Quintessence. Depa Rongtso composed many works including Mandala of Wisdom, which answers questions on the identification of Sudarśana, the history of the lineage, and so on, and Garland of Ambrosia Drops: Abridgement of Profound Instructions. The Drukpa incarnation Pema Karpo composed Treasure for the Benefit of Others: A Presentation of Four Tantras, and Chapter on Treatment of Poisoning. The Sixth Shamarpa Chökyi Wangchuk wrote Death-Defying Ambrosia: Treatise on Medical Science. Pawo Tsuklak Trengwa composed a history of medicine and a treatment for kangbam. Sokdokpa[661] composed Essence of the Definitive: Four Tantras as Enlightened Speech.

d.div: [661] Sodokpa Lodrö Gyaltsen (1552–1624).

f.d: mdor na spyir grags che ba stod lugs smad lugs zhes gnyis las stod pa la byang pa/ phyogs mtshungs gong sman pa dang / lho lugs sogs dang / smad pa la zur mkhar khu dbon/ de dang phyogs mtshungs byar po paN chen dang skyem pa sogs tha dad du gyur pa'i gangs can gyi ljongs 'dir gso dpyad kyi lugs 'dzin dang yig cha'ang ji snyed cig mchis pa mtha' dag brjod kyis mi lang ngo //

To summarize: the two most renowned medical traditions are the Upper and Lower traditions. The Upper tradition includes the Jang lineage, by similarity the Gongmen lineage, the southern lineages, and so on. The Lower tradition includes the Surkhar uncle-to-nephew tradition and by similarity the Jarpo Panchen and Kyempa family traditions. These various lineages have preserved the tradition of medicine in this land of snow, and their literary output is beyond description.
rgyal dbang lnga pa blo bzang rgya mtshos sman spel tshul/
18. The Great Fifth Dalai Lama and Desi Sangyé Gyatso

d.i: The contribution of the Great Fifth to the science of medicine

f.d:
'jam dpal rtsa ba'i rgyud kyi le'u rab 'byams so drug pa las/
ston pa'i gsung rab sa steng du/ / dus mthar 'jin rten nyams pa na/ / sdom brtson rgyal po'i tshul gyi ni/ / 'byung bar 'gyur ba the tshom med/[306] / ces dang /
yi ge ma zhes gzhon nu zhes/ / dang po tha mar chos la dga'/[307] / zhes mtshan sgra mdzad pa sogs dang /

The thirty-sixth chapter of the Mañjuśrī Root Tantra says:
When the doctrine of the Teacher on this earth has deteriorated in the extremity of time, he will without doubt appear in the form of a vow-holding king.[662] The same text talks of his name:
The letter ma and youth, loving the Dharma at the beginning and end.[663]

d.div: [306] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na 'phags pa 'jam dpal gyi rtsa ba'i rgyud/ le'u/ 36_shog_325_na7
[307] sde dge_543_bka'/ rgyud/ na 'phags pa 'jam dpal gyi rtsa ba'i rgyud/ le'u/ 36_shog_325_na7
[662] Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Toh 543 Kangyur, rgyud, na, 325a7.

[663] Ibid. There are many such cryptic predictions in the Mañjuśrī Root Tantra. According to Prof. Losang Tenzin, “the letter ma” refers to mati (blo) meaning “mind,” part of the Great Fifth’s name, Losang. He “loved the Dharma,” meaning he devoted himself to Buddhist practice at the beginning and end of his life, whereas in between he ruled the country.

f.d:
bka' gdams glegs bam pha chos las/
de'i dus kyi skye ba de me'i sa bon las rus byas pa'i lugs yin/ chos gang byas ngar che/ lhag par lha drag po'i bsnyen pa la dgyes shing bsngags/ bdud sde dang sdig can gyis mi bzod par tshar gcod pa'i rigs yin/ gsang sngags kyi drag las la dgyes pa'i rgyu des slar rtsod pa mang ba dang phan tshun gyi zer sgros mang / 'o na'ang rang pham par mi nus/[308] zhes sku rus dgung snying mdzad pa dang bcas pa bstan/ de mtshungs bu chos las kyang /
bod kha ba can pa'i sems can rnams/ / bu snying med pha la gshe ba bzhin/ / nga phan bde'i 'byung gnas rin chen la/ / sems rtog pa che zhes dmod par byed/[309] / ces mdzad pa sogs lung gsal bar bstan/

The Book of Kadam: Father Teachings predicts the sign of his birth year[664] and talks of his deeds:
His birth at that time will be a birth from the seed of fire. Whatever Dharma he practices will be of great power. In particular, he will take great delight in and praise the meditation practices of the wrathful deities. He will be someone that the māras and their cohorts will not be able to withstand and he will defeat them utterly. Because of his great liking for the wrathful activities of mantra, again there will be much argument and much discussion. But he will not be defeated.[665] Similarly the Book of Kadam: Son Teachings:
He will berate them, saying, “The people of Tibet, of this land of snow, like a heartless son despising his father, now doubt me, the precious source of happiness.”[666]

d.div: [308] bka' gdams pha chos kyi lung 'di 'tshol zhib byed kyang rnyed son ma byung /
[309] jo rje dpal ldan a ti sha bka' gdams bu chos/ rgyal bu dkon mchog 'bangs su skye ba bzhes pa'i le'u/ shog_167_yig phreng 19
[664] The Great Fifth was born on the twenty-third day of the ninth month of the fire-snake year, or 1617 (Trinlé, p. 290).

[665] From the Prophecy chapter of the Book of Kadam, one of three supplementary chapters to the Father Teachings that may be a later addition. Not included in the Institute of Tibetan Classics edition.
[666] Book of Kadam: Son Teachings, 167.19.

f.d:
blon po'i bka' thang las/
rgyal po khri srong lde btsan nyid: sku gsung thugs yon 'phrin las lnga: 'phrul lnga bsgyur ba'i stobs su 'gyur: 'dra min zhig dang ma nor na: gzugs sku gnyis kyis 'gro don mdzad: byang mi 'dul skyong gnam sa'i bdag: za hor chab las 'bebs par 'byung :[310]zhes mnga' bdag tshangs pa lha'i me tog gi sku gsung thugs yon tan 'phrin las kyi sprul pa mdo sngags kyi bstan pa skyong ba lnga re 'byon zhing de dag thams cad gcig tu bsdus pa'i mthu stobs dang ldan pa byang mi shas che ba'i gdul bya skyong ba/ za hor gyi gdung sogs dang /

The Chronicles of Ministers says:
The body, speech, mind, qualities, and activities of the great king Trisong Detsen, the power of these five manifest and unmistakably united as one; two form bodies working for living beings; a master of heaven and earth, taming and cultivating the people of the north, will come from the rains of Sahor.[667] This verse predicts that the five manifestations—of the body, speech, mind, qualities, and activities—of the great ruler Tsangpa Lhayi Metok[668] will appear in order to guard the doctrines of sutra and tantra and that the power of all five will be united in one endowed being, who will care for his disciples comprising most of the people of the north, and who will be of Sahor ancestry.

d.div: [310] rgyal po khri srong lde btsan nyid:_ces sogs kyi lung 'di blon po'i bka' thang nang rnyed son ma byung bas rgyal ba lnga pa'i rnam thar du kU la'i gos bzang du gsal bas de'i gsung 'bum/ ca rnam thar du kU la'i gos bzang / ka_shog_146_na5
[667] Orgyen Lingpa, Five Chronicles, untraced.
[668] Another name for King Trisong Detsen.

f.d:
rat+na'i lung chen mo las/
de nas sngon gyi thugs bskyed rgyal po ni: thugs rje chen po'i sprul pa dbus nas 'byung : blo gros stobs ldan bzang po'i mtshan sgra can: sna tshogs thabs kyis 'gro ba'i kha lo bsgyur: chos kyi rgyal po dpung dang bcas pa 'byung :[311]zhes dang /
dbus gtsang thams cad sku yi chab 'og 'dus: rdzu 'phrul mthu ldan bstan pa'i bdag po 'byung : zhes sprul gzhi/ mtshan zur/ dus rtags/ mdzad pa la sogs pa gsal ba'i shin tu rgyas pa dang /

Ratna Lingpa in his Extensive General Transmissions says:
A king with bodhi mind previously developed will then appear in central Tibet as a manifestation of compassion, his name meaning, “wise, powerful, and good.” With various means he guides living beings and becomes a Dharma king with his own army.[669] From the same work:
The center and Tsang[670] all gathered in his domain, of great power and magical feats, a master of the doctrine will appear. These passages and others refer extensively to the basis of his emanation, the components of his name, the time of his coming, his deeds, and so forth.

d.div: [311] rat+na'i lung chen mo zhes pa'i gzhung de'i dpe cha lag tu ma son pas 'di dang gsham gyi lung gnyis kyi khungs phul ma thub/
[669] Untraced.
[670] Tsang can be said to be southwestern Tibet, in the vicinity of Shigatsé, and the “center” in this line is the area around Lhasa.

f.d:
zhig po gling pa'i gter lung du/
khra 'brug mchod rten srin po'i kha gnon 'di: zhig gso med pa'i rang 'gyel byung ba'i dus: srong btsan phyogs kyi za hor brgyud pa yis: bstan pa dbus gtsang yongs la gcu bar 'gyur: zhes dang /

In Shikpo Lingpa’s Treasure Transmissions it says:
When the Tradruk stupa holding down the demoness[671] falls apart and becomes irreparable, the Sahor descendent from the Songtsen line brings the doctrine to the whole of Central Tibet and Tsang.[672]

d.div: [671] A famous temple in the Yarlung valley built by King Songtsen Gampo as one of four temples built at certain Tibetan locales that correspond to the shoulders and hips of a demoness.
[672] Untraced.

f.d: de bzhin du rdo rje gling pa/ rig 'dzin srog sgrub / yol mo sprul sku/ gter bdag gling pa/ zla ba rgyal mtshan sogs zab gter gyi lung bstan/ karma pa mi bskyod rdo rje sogs skyes bu dam pa'i nyams snang dang bcas pa'i lung gis gsal por zin pa/ bdag gi bla ma sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das kyi ring lugs pa chen po/ 'jig rten thams cad la rgyu med par yang gcig tu mnyes gshin pa'i ngang tshul can/ ring mo zhig nas byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa rlabs po che dag gi pha rol tu son pas stobs bcu mi 'jigs pa bzhi la sogs pa gzhal du med pa'i yon tan rnams dang mtshan dpes rab tu brgyan pa rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas 'od zer kun nas 'phags pa dpal brtsegs kyi rgyal po'i go 'phang mngon du mdzad de/ ma dag pa'i 'jig rten gyi khams rnams su 'khor lo bsgyur ba dang / khams kyi rgyal po dang / brgya byin/ tshangs pa/ khyim bdag /rab byung la sogs pa gdul bya dang 'tsham pa'i rnam par 'phrul pa/ ji ltar nam mkha'i lam las zla ba'i dkyil 'khor gcig gis sa'i steng du chu snod tha dad pa sna tshogs pa zhig gi nang du cig car rang gi gzugs brnyan 'bad rtsol med par ston pa bzhin/ bsil ldan kha ba'i ljongs kyi 'gro ba rnams kyi ngor sdom brtson rgyal po'i tshul du rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas dang bltams pa'i gza' skar sogs cha phra mos kyang dbye ba med par phebs pa/

Similarly, Dorjé Lingpa, Rikzin Sokdrup, Yölmo Trülku, Terdak Lingpa, Dawa Gyaltsen, and others produced predictions from the profound treasures. He was also clearly foretold by the predictions of Karmapa Mikyö Dorjé and others who were possessed of the visionary experiences of great beings. My lama, great adherent to the tradition of the Bhagavān Buddha, is one whose nature is of love and affection for all beings of all worlds, even for those he has no cause to love. Long ago he arrived at the perfection of the great powers of the bodhisattva deeds, with the immeasurable qualities of the ten powers, the four confidences, and so on, and became the perfect buddha Rasmi Samudgata Śrīku Rāja, beautifully adorned with the marks and signs of enlightenment. In the impure worldly realms, in accord with the minds of disciples, he manifested as universally sovereign emperors, world monarchs, Indra, Brahmā, householders, monks, and so on. Like the single sphere of the moon effortlessly showing from its path in the sky its reflections in various and separate waters on this earth simultaneously, he appeared to the minds of the beings in this cool snowy land in the form of a monk king, with not a fraction of his auspicious birth and so forth distinct from that of a perfect buddha.

don slad mtshan nas smos pa thams cad mkhyen pa ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho 'jigs med go cha thub bstan lang tsho'i sde chen po'i chos srid gdugs dkar gyis rgya bod hor gsum khebs te/ gnam sa'i bdag por gyur pa nas thub bstan spyi dang bye brag mdo sngags rig gnas thams cad yar ngo'i zla ba ltar 'phel zhing rgyas par mdzad cing / gso ba rig pa la spyir sangs rgyas 'phags par ma zad rnam pa'ang rgyud bzhi/ bdud rtsi bum pa/ bye ba ring bsrel/ gong sman pa'i nyams yig sogs gso dpyad kyi yig cha'i lung ma lus pa dang / zab mo g.yu thog snying tig gi gdams pa nyams su bzhes/ bdud rtsi bum pa'i rnam dag dbang gi chu rgyun gyi gsal byed bdud rtsi'i zla snang stsal ba sogs rigs 'dus sman pa'i rgyal por gyur na'ang / tshur mthong gi ngor rgyud chung gsum thugs 'dzin dang bshad pa sa dpyad rdel 'grems phyag len sman gyi ngo sprod rags pa gsan tshul las phra zhib mkhyen pa'i tshul dang bka' 'bum gyi rigs ma stsal zhing /

To illustrate his qualities by his name, he was the all-knowing mighty Ngawang Losang Gyatso Jikmé Gocha Thupten Langtso Dé. His great white-umbrella administration of religion and secular activities protected Tibet, China, and Mongolia, and having become a ruler of heaven and earth, he expanded and developed like the waxing moon the doctrine of the mighty Buddha, specifically sutra, tantra, and the other sciences. In the field of medicine, he gave, not only as an enlightened being but in this present incarnation, too, all the transmissions of medical texts such as Four Tantras, [Dorbum Chökyi Drakpa’s] Vase of Ambrosia, [Surkhar Nyamnyi Dorjé’s] Relic of Millions, and the Gongmen texts of personal experience. He practiced the instructions taught in the profound Yuthok Heartdrop and bestowed the Illuminating Ambrosia Moonlight Initiation Rituals comprising the Stream of the Pure Initiations from the Vase of Ambrosia treasure text, and so on. In doing so, he was the king of medicine, the combiner of lineages. However, to the minds of ordinary beings he memorized the three shorter tantras and studied their explanations, stone layout, practices, and recognition of medical plants only superficially, not displaying any in-depth knowledge or providing any such compositions of his own in his collected works.

de dag gi dbang gi byad ngos nas nang so dar rgyas kyis zhabs bskul zhus pa bzhin bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud bzhi grwa thang par ma'i bu ji bzhin la 'dra zhus slob dpon don grub dpal ba sogs byed 'jug gnang ba dang / dar mo sman rams pas gsol ba btab pa dang ma dpe 'bul mi gang byung ltar gyi cha lag bco brgyad/ dar mo nas dang rnam gling paN chen zung gis gsol ba btab cing rnam paN rang zhus dag byed 'jug pa gnang ba'i zur mkhar ba'i mes po'i zhal lung rtsa bshad gnyis dang phyi rgyud chu mdo yan sogs la rje nyid kyi ljags zhus tshad ldan ma stsal te phyogs tsam gyi med pa las drag par dgongs te yo byad mtha' dag 'bad med du sbyar bar gnang ste par du bskrun pa'i 'dzad med chos sbyin gyi sgo 'phar phye/ 'bras spungs dga' ldan pho brang nub mar thog ma nyi thang drung chen blo bzang rgya mtsho slob dpon dang / rjes su byang ngos nas kyis do dam byas te gso rig 'gro phan gling dang / gzhis ka bsam grub rtser tsha rong pas do dam byas drang srong 'dus pa'i gling ste slob grwa khag gnyis kyi rgyun 'dzugs pa gnang bas rgyud bzhi'i rgyugs 'bul ba yang snga thog mang ba byung bar snang zhing / lha dbang lcog gam shar chen lcog tu byang ngos nang so dar rgyas dang rjes su dar mo sman rams pa'i slob grwa/ gzhan yang lhag bsam dang na bza' gling pa sogs kyi slob ma la yang phogs mthun rkyen sogs stsal/

Therefore, in response to the entreaties by Jang Ngö Nangso Dargyé, he urged Ācārya Döndrup Palwa and others to replicate the mother text of Four Tantras: Essence of Ambrosia Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches located at Drathang Monastery. Publication of [the later Yuthok’s] Eighteen Auxiliary Texts was requested by Darmo Menrampa Losang Chödrak and by others who offered him the mother text. Publication of Surkhar [Lodrö Gyalpo’s] Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors commentary on the Root, Explanatory, and Final Tantra as far as the section on urine analysis was requested by Darmo Menrampa Losang Chödrak, and he [the Fifth] asked Namling Panchen to redact the text. In these undertakings my great lama did not make any in-depth revisions himself, providing only minimal input, thinking that at least it would be better than nothing. He gave without fuss all necessary prerequisites for the printing, and in so doing opened wide the door to an unending offering of Dharma in the form of published texts. He ensured the continuity of two different medical institutes. One was the medical college Sorik Drophen Ling[673] to the west of Drepung Ganden Phodrang, whose first master was Drungchen Losang Gyatso of Nyithang and which was subsequently run by Jang Ngö Nangso Dargyé. The other was Drangsong Düpai Ling medical school in Shika Samdrup Tsé,[674] which was run by the Tsarong family. Consequently, it seems that the number of recitation examinations on Four Tantras increased at that time. He also established the medical schools in Lhawang Chok or Sharchen Chok run by Jang Ngö Nangso and subsequently by Darmo Menrampa. He also gave money and provisions to the students of Lhaksam and Nasa Lingwa.

d.div: [673] Founded in 1643 (Trinlé, p. 296).
[674] More commonly known as Shigatsé.

f.d: rgyud las/ rin po che yis mi sel gang yang med/[312] / ces pa ltar dug rigs sogs ldan 'dus gtsor gyur gyi nad rigs bzhi brgya rtsa bzhi+i' gnyen po bla na med pa tshe bsring ba/ lang tsho dar la 'bab pa/ lus la bcangs pa tsam gyis thog ser mtshon dang sde brgyad la sogs kyi gnod pa bsrung ba/ longs su spyad pas ngan song gi skye sgo gcod pa sogs phan yon du ma dang ldan pa'i rin chen ril bu sngar rgyal rtse/ yar stod pa/ yar rgyab/ zhwa dmar nag /'bri gung / rtse chen pa sogs sde dpon bla chen mang dag gis rtsol ba mdzad kyang sman sna gya gsum tsam la mang mtha' dang / rin po che dkon pa'i rigs chur sbangs pa bsre ba/ bu mo stag lo ma glo bur du bsad de kha na ma tho bas sbags pa sogs tshad dang mthun pa zhig byung bar mi snang bas/ 'gro srog skyob pa'i mchod sbyin du dgongs te

In the tantra it says, “With gems there is nothing that cannot be dispelled.”[675] They are the best remedy for the 404 kinds of illness, especially dual and complex disorders such as poisoning. They lengthen life and restore youth. Merely by wearing them on the body, you are protected from violent storms, hail, and weapons, and from the eight types of spirits. When made use of, they close the door to birth in the lower realms. Therefore, gem pills have great benefits. Many past nobles and high lamas, such as Gyantsé, Yartöpa, Yargyap, Shamarnak, Drigung, and Tsechen, tried to make gem pills. However, they only used up to a maximum of eighty-three different medicines, they used the water in which rare gems had been soaked, and girls born in the tiger year were suddenly being killed, and so the process became tainted by crime.[676] Therefore, because gem pills were not being manufactured correctly, the Great Fifth decided to perform a great act of giving in order to guard and protect the lives of living beings.

d.div: [312] rin po che yi mi sel gang yang med/ /ces pa'i tshig 'di gang las drangs rgyud ngos bzung ma thub/
[675] Four Tantras, Final Tantra, 11.621.13.

[676] According to Prof. Losang Tenzin, rather than procure rare gems for use in medicine they instead used the water in which these gems had been soaked. In order to obtain some medicinal part of the body, such as bile, one or more young girls born in the tiger year were killed.

f.d: phyag mdzod khag nas ma thon pa las sgo yas mas tshang mar stsol sgrub kyi sman 'dzom che ba'i steng twang kun gyi rgyal khab chen por chibs bsgyur skabs khab len rdo dang lcags phye ltar 'bul mi byung ba dang / rgyal mo rdo rje rab brtan mas stod hor nas byung ba/ cung wang gis phul ba ste srid na dkon pa'i rin po che mang po/ 'o skol gyi ston pas gtsos byang sems nyan rang slob mar bcas pa'i ring bsrel/ a ru ra gser mdog snyim pa tsam pa/ dung dkar g.yas 'khyil/ seng ge dkar mo'i 'o ma/ stag gson ma'i sma ra/ pha lam/ baidUR+ya kha dog sna tshogs/ sbur len/ spug / mu tig sogs lha klu mi'i rdo rje rin po che bsam gyis mi khyab pa sa rdo lta bur 'phang med du gtong ba gnang ste/ sngon gyi rin chen ril bu du ma'i rta dang bcas grang sbyor/ tsha sbyor/ rta ri ma/ dbang phyug chen po'i sku gsung thugs kyi rgyud gsum las gsung rgyud me lce 'bar ma'i dgongs don gyi dug 'joms dbang ril sogs phon che bar lha'i bdud rtsi 'chi med/ lha min bdud rtsi 'chi gsos/ mi'i bdud rtsi bde byed du 'gyur bar byin gyis brlabs te dge ba'i rgyun bzang btsugs/

He put a great deal of effort into collecting medicines from many other sources in search of those ingredients not found in his own storerooms. Moreover, when he visited the country of Tangkün people came to him like iron filings to a magnet to make offerings. Queen Dorjé Rapten Ma came from upper Mongolia, and Emperor Chung Wang also brought offerings. These offerings included many rare gems, holy relics of our Teacher and also of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, a handful of golden myrobalan, clockwise-coiled white conches, milk from a white lioness, whiskers taken from a live tigress, diamonds, beryl of various colors, amber, quartz, pearls, and other inconceivable vajra jewels of men, gods, and nāgas. All these he gave up without any sense of loss, as if they were stones on the ground, thereby seeding a wonderful and virtuous tradition that resulted in the large-scale production of many varieties of gem pills, such as the cold-ingredient precious compound, the hot-ingredient precious compound, the precious pill tarima, the poison-destroying bezoars as taught in the Blazing Fire speech tantra from the three body, speech, and mind Maheśvara tantras, together with their accompanying drinks. These were all blessed to become the immortality ambrosia of the gods, the death-defying ambrosia of the asura, and the happiness-creating ambrosia of humans.

'phags yul nub phyogs ma ho ra'i bram ze se nya si go da ra rany+tso ra dang / ma hA lo tsA ba 'dar ba ngag dbang phun tshogs lhun grub gnyis kyi tshe'i rig byed mtha' dag gi snying po bsdus pa dang / rgya gar pha ha'i sman pa dA na da ba'i sman bcas phan byed kyi 'khor lo rigs mi gcig pa bdun cu rtsa gnyis/ ma ng+hu ra'i rgyal rigs tshe'i rig byed 'dzin pa ra gu nA thas tshangs pa rig byed rgya mtsho'i yan lag 'dzin pa g.yo ba can zhes bya ba dang / phan byed man ngag lag len thor bu/ shA dzang gi sman pa ma na hos mig 'byed mthong ba don ldan rnams lo tswa ba gong bzhin gyis byas te pho brang chen po po ta lar bsgyur ba'i bka' lung phebs shing mthun rkyen stsal/

He authorized and provided for the translations of texts in the great Potala palace by such translators as the great Lotsāwa Ngawang Phüntsok Lhündrup from Dar and the brahman Saṃnyāsin Godara Rañcara[677] from Mahora in western India. These texts were: • Essence of Āyurveda [by Brahmaputra Hāsavajra] • The Remedies of Dānadāsa, by the Indian Paha doctor Dānadāsa, with its seventy-two different remedial charm circles • Caraka Supplement to the Ocean-Like Brahmā Āyurveda by the royal Āyurvedic practitioner Ragunātha from Mathurā • Miscellany of Beneficial Advice and Practices • Meaningful to Behold: Opening the Eyes by the Shājang doctor Manaho.[678]

d.div: [677] “Godara Rañcara” is as transliterated.

[678] Of these five works, all but the fourth are in the Degé Tengyur as written. The third however is attributed to Sarvahitāmṛta Datta, and the fourth may well be Toh 4442, Advice from the Royal Āyurvedic Practitioner Ragunātha from Mathurā, which has become confused with the third.

f.d: gangs can gyi ljongs nas kyang gra phyi stod lugs pa gnas lugs ched kyis bos te mi tra dzo ki dang bod lugs kyi mig 'byed/ gtsang stod dar mgon gyi brgyud pa dge slong gzhan phan snying po bsdus pa/ zin tig gces bsdus/ gser bre/ byang pa rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang gi bshad rgyud 'grel chen sogs lung man ngag du ma/ gnya' nang nam mkha' lhar grub thob a+yon pa lugs kyi dngul chu gtso bkru rnams dar mo sman rams pa dang lhag bsam gnyis gtsor gyur gyi gnyug mar gnas pa rnams la 'gro phan gyi ched slob tu 'jug pa gnang /

With indigenous Tibetan material also, he arranged for many transmissions and oral instructions to be made available. These include the transmission of both the Mitrayogi and Tibetan traditions’ treatments for recovering sight from Neluk, a specially invited Upper-tradition practitioner from Drachi; works such as Quintessence, Essential Compilation of Treatments, Golden Measuring Dish, Stream of Ambrosia, and Jangpa Rikden Namgyal Draksang’s Extensive Commentary on the Explanatory Tantra from Gelong Shenphen, holder of the tradition of Darma Gönpo from upper Tsang; and teachings on purifying mercury from the Druptop Orgyen tradition passed down to Namkha Lha from Nyanang. For the sake of living beings he encouraged the study of these works by local medical scholars, especially Darmo Menrampa and Lhaksam.

rnam gling paN chen dang dar mo ba blo bzang chos grags zung du 'jug pas mes po'i zhal lung gi 'phro phyi rgyud mchu mdo man gyi 'grel pa rdo rje mdud 'grol/ dar mo sman rams pa blo bzang chos grags dang mer mo ba/ la ra ba rnams kyi 'dri mchan sor bzhag gi 'bru 'grel ma yin par 'bri mchan dang / sngar 'grel yod rnams de bstun dang / 'grel med rnams rang sar bzhag pa'i dka' 'grel gyi tshul gser rgyan/ g.yu thog gsar rnying gi rnam thar yang la ra bas yig rnying las bsdus pa rnams kyang gdul bya'i blo bstun gyi bgyid 'jug tu stsal/ de dag zhabs bskul dang bstun par du rko rgyu'i par byang sogs stsal/ gzhan yang sku 'di thog nyi thang zhabs drung ngag dbang gzhon nus rgyud chung gsum gyi 'grel pa dang / bod mkhas mi pham dge legs kya bying khog yul thig sman gyi ro nus/ lhun sdings rnam rgyal rdo rjes rdo ring rgyan mchog sogs bstan bcos rtsom mi'ang mang tsam byung bar snang /

In keeping with the wishes of disciples he also encouraged medical compositions. In a commentary called Loosening the Vajra Knots Darmo Losang Chödrak and Namling Panchen together completed the unfinished section of Oral Transmission of Our Ancestors, beginning from the urine analysis chapter of the Final Tantra. Darmo Menrampa Losang Chödrak, Mermopa, and Larawa[679] composed Golden Ornament of Excellent Explanation[680] in the manner of a difficult-point commentary. This work left existing annotations in the text as they were but added annotations where there was no word commentary. In its commentary on the text, it followed previous commentaries where they existed but left untouched those parts for which there was no previous commentary. Larawa compiled from old manuscripts the biographies of the earlier and later Yuthok.[681] Also, in response to requests, the Great Fifth also wrote the colophons for the above works. Quite a few authors of medical works appeared during the life of the Great Fifth. These include Nyithang Shapdrung Ngawang Shönu, who composed a commentary on the three shorter tantras; the learned Tibetan Mipham Gelek, who wrote Anatomy of the Torso and the Explanation of the Tastes and Powers of Medicines; and Lhünding Namgyal Dorjé, who wrote the Great Adornment of the Stone Pillar.

d.div: [679] Mermo Lodrö Chöpel and Larawa Losang Dönden were disciples of Darmo Menrampa.
[680] According to Trinlé this work is on the Instruction Tantra of Four Tantras.

[681] Darmo Menrampa, Biography of Yuthok the Elder and the Younger. According to Trinlé (p. 294), Mermopa was also involved in this work, and according to the colophon of the Yuthok biography, it was compiled by their teacher Darmo Menrampa, with these disciples as scribes.

f.d: sde srid rang nyid kyis sman spel tshul/

d.i: The contribution of Desi Sangyé Gyatso

f.d: ra gan gser brdzus mkhan kho bo cag ni na tshod chung ngu'i dus byis pa'i rtsed mor sngo sna tshogs btus te sman yin khul dang / sa gzhong la ri mo sna tshogs 'bri ba/ chos 'chad ser sbrengs gtor rgyag la sogs pa'i bag chags yod pa de dus gam na 'khod pa dag gis gleng ba tsam las/ rang blor byang 'phags sogs kyi sprul pa lta zhog / skye ba snga mar rig gnas sogs la sbyangs pa che ba'i yang srid tsam yang yin bsam pa med na'ang /

As for myself, this person of brass masquerading as gold, when I was a child, I played by collecting various plants and pretending they were medicines, drawing diagrams in astronomy trays, and showing an instinct for teaching Dharma, taking part in religious processions, making tormas, and so on. I write of these only because those around me at that time have mentioned them. In my own mind, not only do I have no thoughts of being the incarnation of an ārya bodhisattva and the like, I do not even have any thoughts of being the incarnation of someone greatly trained in the sciences. Despite this,

yab rje rgyal ba'i dbang po thams cad mkhyen pa lnga pa chen pos chung ngu nas sri'u gso ba lta bu dang / rang lo brgyad pa'i thog nas zhal mjal gsung thos kyi skal bzang myong zhing / skyabs gsum 'dzin pa'i dge bsnyen gyi sdom pa stsal/ de nas rim gyi na tshod dang sbyar te lugs zung gi yon tan gang 'jags kyi bslabs ston lhug par stsal zhing sku'i zhabs rim la yun ring du bcar/ bong ba'i rang bzhin gser du gzigs te tshig tsam ma yin par chos srid yongs kyi rgyal tshab tu dbang bskur nas/

I was treated from an early age like a son by my master and father figure, the all-powerful, all-knowing Great Fifth, and from the age of eight onward, I had the great fortune of seeing him and hearing his words. He gave me the lay-practitioner vows that take hold of the three refuges. Then, in keeping with my age, he instructed me progressively, in an easy-going manner and to a level that I could assimilate, on all matters of religion and state. I remained in his service for many years afterward. Seeing a lump of earth as gold, he appointed me, and not in name only, as his representative in all affairs of religion and politics.

rgyal po'i bka' thang las/
nam zhig snyigs ma'i dus la babs pa'i tshe: rgyal sras skye lus bcu gnyis kha 'thor mtha': bod yul gangs ri rtse dgu'i ljongs 'di ru: rje rigs rgyal po gdug pa'i tshogs rnams 'dul: rgyal po'i mtshan ltas legs pa lnga dang ldan: thugs sgam bka' btsan khong rgyud yangs pa dang : zung thub dpyad pas mthu stobs rab tu che: rgyal po'i dpung tshogs longs spyod du ma ldan: kha ba can du dus kyi mtha' la 'byung :[313] zhes mnga' bdag tshangs pa lha'i me tog gi sras su mu tig btsan po'i skyes lus bcu gsum pa yin tshul dang / bka' gdams glegs bam gyi rngog legs she'i skye srid rnams kyi bka' 'phros yang yang stsal ba/

Then, as it says in Chronicles of Kings:
At the end of time in the age of degeneration, after twelve different incarnations of the prince, there will appear in Tibet, this land of many snow peaks, a king of the noble class, a subduer of the poisonous hordes, possessed of the five auspicious signs of a king— deep thought, powerful speech, vast mind, ability to withstand, great power with discernment— and the military might and provisions of a king.[682] Therefore, it is as if I am the thirteenth incarnation of Mutik Tsenpo, the son of Tsangpa Lhayi Metok.[683] Moreover, the Great Fifth would often talk of the subsequent births of Ngok Lekpai Sherap[684] from the Book of Kadam.

d.div: [313] bka' thang sde lnga/ rgyal po'i bka' thang / mtha' ma'i dus su ji ltar byung tshul/ shog_213_yig phreng 13
[682] Orgyen Lingpa, Five Chronicles, chapter on “Predictions at the End of Time,” 213.13.
[683] Tsangpa Lhayi Metok was King Trisong Detsen, of whom the Great Fifth was an incarnation. His third or fourth son was Mutik Tsenpo.

[684] Ngok Lotsāwa Lekpai Sherap (1018–1115), the renowned disciple of Atiśa. His Ngok ancestry is traced to a minister of King Trisong Detsen, which provides the connection to the passage above. Desi Sangyé Gyatso describes Ngok Lotsāwa as an incarnation of Prince Mutik Tsenpo in his Yellow Beryl as well.

f.d:
mdo ting 'dzin rgyal po las/
nyi zla skar mar bcas pa gnas lhung zhing / / ri dang grong du bcas pa'i sa gzhi la/ / nam mkha'i khams ni rnam pa gzhan gyur kyang / / khyod ni mi bden pa yi tshig mi gsung /[314] / zhes pa ltar yin pa la min pa dang / ma yin pa la yin zhes mi gsung ba sangs rgyas 'phags pa'i chos nyid du snang bas 'gog par ma btub cing / gter kha gsar rnying nas kyang lung bstan gsal tsam 'dug pa dang / lha sras kyi skye ba yin na nyan thos chen po ma 'gags pa/ 'phags pa thogs med sogs skyes chen du mar ma zad/ rgyal po'i bka' thang las/
rgyal sras mjing yon legs pa'i blo gros ni: bdag gis mtshan gsol mu tig btsan po zhes: 'das dang ma byon da lta'i dus la ni: bskal pa brgyad khri bzhi stong sngon rol du: bde gshegs klu rigs sgrol ma'i spyan snga ru: nor bu dbang gi rgyal po phul ba'i dus:[315] zhes thugs bskyed pa dang /

The King of Meditative Concentrations Sutra states:
Sun, moon, and stars may fall from the sky, the mountains, the earth, and its cities may be destroyed, space itself may change, yet you will never speak a word untrue.[685] As we see here, it is the nature of a buddha never to claim that something is when it is not or that something is not when it is, thus it cannot be refuted. There are also quite clear predictions in the early and later treasures. If I am the incarnation of that prince, consider the following from Chronicles of Kings where, after saying that the births of Mutik Tsenpo included such great beings such as the ārya Asaṅga and the śrāvaka Aniruddha, it says:
Concering the past, present, and future of Prince Jingyön Lekpai Lodrö, who I have named Mutik Tsenpo: eighty-four thousand eons in the past, in the presence of Sugata Nāgakula Pradīpa, while offering the cittamaṇi jewel…[686] This refers to his developing the bodhi mind. The text continues:

d.div: [314] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da 'phags pa ting nge 'dzin gyi rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 14_bam po lnga pa/ shog_48_na2
[315] bka' thang sde lnga/ rgyal po'i bka' thang / mtha' ma'i dus su ji ltar byung tshul/ shog_209_phreng 23
[685] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 14, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 47a2.
[686] Orgyen Lingpa, Five Chronicles, 209.23.

f.d: 'dzam gling 'di yi stong gsum shar phyogs su: zhing khams rdul dang bral ba zhes bya ru: de bzhin gshegs pa skyes bu kha lo bsgyur: lha mi'i ston pa bye ba'i 'dus pa skyong : bde gshegs dri ma med pa'i rgyal mtshan zhes: yon tan mtha' yas rdzogs pa'i rgyal ba 'byung :[316] zhes don dam par skyon kun ma lus par spangs shing / yon tan thams cad rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas dngos yin 'dug pa de lta bu'i re ba ci/

In the east of this billionfold world realm, in a realm known as Viraja, he became a tathāgata, guide of living beings, teacher of gods and men, nourishing tens of millions with the name of Sugata Vimaladhvaja, a conqueror with all good qualities complete. This passage explains that Mutik Tsenpo is also ultimately a buddha, with all faults vanquished and all good qualities perfected. How could I ever have such a hope?

d.div: [316] bka' thang sde lnga/ rgyal po'i bka' thang / mtha' ma'i dus su ji ltar byung tshul/ shog_212_phreng 18

f.d: 'on kyang gong ma lnga pa chen pos daN+Di'i gzhung kun bzang 'khor los mtha' brten pa/ mdo sngags spyi bye brag gi bslab don mang ba/ mkhas dbang dpal ldan phun tshogs la ming tshig brjod gzhi yi ge/ / 'dar ba lo tsA la skar rtsis dang sgra rig pa sum rtags lam pa/ sgra'i gzhung rkyang gi ri mo'i 'phro 'thud mkhas dbang blo gsal phun tshogs la nos shing / skar rtsis ri mo phyed 'gugs yan las 'khrid mi med rung / de man gyi ri mo dngos dang sbas pa shugs bstan rnams dang / sgra'i dngos bstan min pa'i shugs kyi ri mo sogs gong ma drin can bla ma'i thugs rje'i 'jug pa las 'char bde ba tsam dang / spor thang / dpal dbyangs 'char ba'i rgyud kyi 'grel pa le tshan gsum po'i nang gsal rnams lu 'go bla mkhyen ngag gi dbang por nos pa tsam las/ rig pa'i gnas gang la yang thos pa rang blo khengs pa zhig ma thub rung /

Nevertheless, the Great Fifth taught me the Wheel of Samantrabhadra[687] section of Daṇḍin’s work and gave me many teachings, both generally and specifically, on sutra and tantra. From Khewang Palden Phüntsok I learned the alphabet, the basis of being able to express oneself verbally. With Dar Lotsāwa I studied astronomy and, in the science of language, the Tibetan grammatical treatises Thirty Verses and Use of Affixes [by Thönmi Sambhota]. I continued my grammatical studies with Khewang Losal Phüntsok by learning the syllable tables of the grammatical treatises. I was only taught up to the half-curve astronomy diagrams and had no one to teach me more.
