However, the remaining diagrams, both explicit and implicit, as well as grammatical tables implied but not actually taught in the texts, and so on, became easy to understand by being a recipient of the great compassion of my kind lama. Porthang divination[688] and the contents of the three-section commentary to the Arising Letters Tantra were taught to me by the Lugo astrologer Ngakgi Wangpo. Apart from these few studies I was not able to fill my mind to satisfaction with a full range of learning in the sciences.

d.div: [687] Kun bzang ’khor lo. According to TBRC (code T1418) this is “a poetic adornment described in the third chapter of the Kāvyādarśa of Daṇḍin comprising wheels of words in which the syllables read in any direction have a meaning.”
[688] Spor thang. A system of divination originating in China based on applying six elements to the sixty-year cycle to give 360 possibilities.

f.d:
gter ston dri med kun dga'i lung bstan du/
sangs rgyas blo gros rin chen mtshan mnga' ba: 'brug sbrul lo pa rta'am lug gi lo: bstan bcos rtsom zhing rang skad thon pa 'byung : bar gcod bdud kyi mtshan ma bzlog gyur na: sku tshe mthar phyin 'gro ba dpag med 'dren:[317] zhes ming dang lo snying 'grig cing / bstan bcos rtsom pa'i bag chags rang ni cung zad yod 'dra bas rang lo sum cu bzhi bcu skor gyi dus gzhung lugs gang yang 'char bde ba dang bcas sgra tshad/ bzo gso/ nang rig pa ste gnas chen lnga'i yig 'jog gi rang rtsom po ti tshad nyi shur bcar ba rgyal srid 'dzin skyong gi zhar las su grub pa dang / ngag 'di 'chos pa sogs skyon dang ldan pa ma gtogs mchod sdong chen po'i rab gnas kyi dus gdan sa chen po rnam gsum sogs rang phyogs zhwa ser cod pan 'chang ba'i ring lugs dang / sku'i gam du bcar ba rnam par rgyal ba phan bde legs bshad gling 'dus pa'i tshogs/ rdor brag e wam lcog sgar/ smin gling dang bcas pa'i snga 'gyur gyi 'dus gra/ yar klungs bkra shis rtse sa lugs kyi 'dus gra rnams su de lugs kyi mdo sngags gnyis ka dang / snga 'gyur gyi bka' brgyad khag gsum/ sa lugs kye rdor rnams la deng dus kyi mdo sngags kyi gra skor ba'i bshad pa'i tshod na gra skor mi 'dra ba drug gi bshad pa nyin 'khyongs dang /

However, in the predictions of treasure revealer Drimé Künga it says:
He with the name of Sangyé Lodrö Rinchen, born in the dragon or snake years, will compose texts in the horse or sheep year, and his own voice will emerge.[689] If he is able to overcome obstructions, he will complete his life and guide countless beings.[690] This matches my name and my birth year.[691] Also it seemed that I had a few imprints for composition. Therefore, between the ages of about thirty and forty, using the more accessible scriptural traditions, I undertook various written compositions on the five sciences of grammar, logic, crafts, medicine, and the inner science of Buddhism amounting to twenty volumes. This I did incidental to supervision of the country. Notwithstanding problems such as my speech defect,[692] I gave daylong explanations, which amounted to six monastic symposiums by today’s standards, to congregations consisting of those from our own “Holders of the Yellow Hat” tradition from the three great monastic seats and so on during the consecration of the great reliquary; from the monastic community of Namgyal Phendé Lekshé Ling,[693] who were in service to the Great Fifth; from those of Dorjé Drakpa Ewaṃ Chokgar and Mindröling monasteries[694] of the Nyingma school; to the Sakya monastic community from Yarlung Tashi Tsé Monastery on topics such as the sutra and tantra of their traditions, the three sets of the eight transmitted precepts of the early-translation school, and the Sakya Hevajra tradition.

d.div: [317] gter ston dri med kun dga'i lung bstan gyi dpe cha lag tu ma son/

[689] This idiom is explained by Desi Sangyé Gyatso himself in his Yellow Beryl as “having the capability of founding a new tradition,” and he says in the same text that his name “Sangyé” (buddha) will become an actuality.
[690] Untraced.
[691] Sangyé Gyatso was born in the water-snake year of 1653.
[692] According to Prof. Losang Tenzin, Desi Sangyé Gyatso apparently suffered from a serious stammer.

[693] Monastery generally said to be founded by the Great Fifth in 1651 primarily for rituals to protect the state. According to Dungkar (p. 1231), however, it dates back to the time of the Third Dalai Lama and was founded when he was invited to Mongolia in 1579.

[694] Dorjé Drakpa Ewaṃ Chokgar was founded in 1632, and Mindroling was founded by Terdak Lingpa, teacher of the Great Fifth, in 1676. Together, they were the two main Nyingma monasteries in Central Tibet.

f.d: tshogs mchod lo bdun gyi ring thog ma rmad byung bskal pa ma lung dang 'bru bshad/ de bzhin bdud bzhi rab bcom la lung dang 'bru bshad/ sangs rgyas 'phags par bsag sbyang dgos min gyis mtshon pa'i tshogs mchod rang gi khrigs dang dgos pa skabs don/ rang phyogs bstan pa'i bdag po btsong kha pa chen po'i thugs bskyed nas bzung nges don sangs rgyas tshul/ sangs 'phags 'pho 'jug gi mdzad pa'i tshul las brtsams pa/ ngo mtshar bskal pa mar 'bru bshad sogs mi 'gro ba re dang snying po tshogs mchod rang gi dgos pa'i thugs 'dun dgos lugs re/ drug pa chen po thog mar mnyes thang du phebs pa nas bzung dga' ston gal che rigs la so so'i dgos pa dmigs bsal dngab stun pa sogs ngag bshad kyi rigs mchog dman kun gyis nges pa dang / thog ma so thar la mos pa che ba zhig yod pa sum skas bca' yig tu gsal ba ltar rung / gong bshad dge bsnyen dang yan yag brgyad pa'i khrims long bstun las sngon chad lag tu ma lon zhing / gong ma lnga pa chen pos gsang sngags kyi dkyil 'khor phyi nang gnyis dang / gsang ba yongs su rdzogs pa smin par stsal zhing / yi dam kha shas kyi grangs kyi bsnyen pa thengs shing legs nyes mtshan ma mngon sum du'ang byung ba dang / rgyun sdod tshang ma zhes mi 'khrel bar srod tho rangs bskyed rdzogs kyi nyams len yun mi thung ba dang / byang chub kyi sems rang la bsngo ba dang shugs ma thub min 'gro ba mi'i srog mi gcod pa'i dam bca' dang / gzhan yang rgyal srid khrims kyi lar snying rje'i sems kyi gnod par nye ba tsam las gang du'ang rngo thogs dka' zhing /

For seven years at the Great Offering Ceremony,[695] I first gave the transmission and word commentary to the Wondrous Eon and, similarly, to the Destruction of the Four Māras. As illustrated by the teachings on an enlightened being not needing to purify wrong deeds and accumulate merit, I set about the immediate tasks of the organization and purpose of the offering ceremony itself. I gave teachings on how the master of our doctrine, the great Tsongkhapa, developed the bodhi mind but in reality was a buddha, on the deeds of the Buddha from the moment he first appeared in this world, a word commentary on the Marvelous Eon and so on. These became a important tradition for living beings and essential for fulfilling the aspirations that were the purpose of the Great Offering Ceremony itself. Since the time of the arrival of the Great Sixth in Nyethang, I have given speeches, accessible to those of all walks of life, at important festivities in keeping with the needs of the occasion. As is made clear in the Sumké constitutional document,[696] I had a great liking for the pratimokṣa vows, but apart from the lay-practitioner vows mentioned earlier and the eight daylong vows taken when opportune, they did not come my way. The Great Fifth granted me outer and inner mandalas of secret mantra and [Guru Chökyi Wangchuk’s] Consummation of Secrets to ripen my mind. I have completed meditation retreats to the required count on a number of deities and have even received direct signs concerning their progress. Without blame or condemnation from those around me, I spent a not inconsiderable amount of time in the practice of the generation and completion stages in the evenings and early mornings. I have maintained the bodhicitta dedication, keeping to my vow of not taking the life of a human except when powerless to do otherwise. Furthermore, in order to maintain the rule of law when governing the country, I have come close to harming the mind of compassion, but it is difficult to be of help in every case.

d.div: [695] Great Offering Ceremony was set up by Desi in 1694 (Dungkar, p. 1716), twelve years after the Fifth Dalai Lama passed away and when details of his death were no longer secret. The teachings mentioned all emphasize the point that a being may be an enlightened being but in the eyes of the world still has to undergo the trials and tribulations of ordinary life. This is a reference to the fact that although the Fifth Dalai Lama is already an enlightened being, he nevertheless passed away, and offerings, such as this great ceremony, are needed to ensure that he returns. Therefore, the “aspirations” refer to the wishes of the Fifth to return, but he can only do so if the merit of his people is ripe. The titles are untraced but according to Prof. Losang Tenzin may have been written by Desi himself.
[696] According to Prof. Losang Tenzin, these days this document is to be found in the Potala.

f.d: lhag par gso ba rig pa 'dir snga thog rgyud chung gsum blo 'dzin tsam dang / gling stod chos rje blo bzang rgya mtsho wa le tsam yid la nges pa dang / byang ngos nas nang so dar rgyas ma rgan snga phyir snyun pa dang / sa skyong 'phrin las rgya mtsho gshegs pa'i dus/ rang yang lan kha shas bro ba sogs kyi skabs zhib mjal gyi babs la bltas na rgyud thugs la 'jags che tsam las man ngag zur bkol gyi rigs la thugs 'jog chung zhing phyag len mi mdzad pa zhig tu mthong / sman sgom 'brang rgyas pa yang 'dris te grub thob bcos lta bu las gso dpyad skor ha cang gi gzigs pa mi che/

In the field of medicine, early on I memorized the three shorter tantras. I can remember Lingtö Chöjé Losang Gyatso distinctly. On the occasions when I saw Jang Ngö Nangso Dargyé up close—such as during the illnesses of my elderly mother, when Sakyong Trinlé Gyatso died, and a few times when I was ill—I observed that he had the tantra quite firmly established in his mind but that he had little knowledge of any other oral instructions and was not someone who practiced clinical medicine. I also knew Mengom Drangyé, who apart from the remedies of the siddhas, for example, did not have an extensive knowledge of medical literature.

lhag bsam mam sum dga'ang zhib par 'dris te rgyud chung ba gsum tshig rags nges tsam dang / lag len bdud rtsi bum pa dang mtsho smad mkhan chen shas che ba'i man ngag gtsor 'don las gso dpyad kyi skor rgya mi che na'ang / nad pa'i don la snying rje dang brtson pa che zhing phran bu'i khro 'dzin dus dbang gis yong ba gzhir bcas/ gzhan ma ming dang mtshungs par kun la bsam pa dge ba rgyud las/ byang sems che bas gzhan don gtso bor len/[318] / zhes pa'i rgyu drug nas gcig tshang ba yin nam snyam/ dar mo sman rams pa phan bde legs bshad gling 'dus gra dang sku gam du bcar ba sogs dkyil 'khor re gnyis kyi smin byed kyang stsal ba'i skyabs mgon nyid dang dngos cag bcas par dam tshig 'brel che zhing shin tu zhib/ rje bla ma'i gzigs pa dang rang gi'ang brgyag bskur gyi phan cha du ma bsgrubs shing / lag len gyi rim pa stod lugs shas che ba'i man ngag sna tshogs lag tu bstar ba thugs rje'i 'jug pas sman bsod kyang lhag par che bar snang /

Lhaksam, or Sumga, I knew very well. He had only a rough knowledge of the text of the three shorter tantras. His practices were those of the Vase of Ambrosia, and he mainly followed the transmitted instructions Tsomé Khenchen, but his knowledge of medical literature was not extensive. Nevertheless, he had great compassion for his patients and worked hard. At times he could be gruff. Otherwise, he lived up to his name[697] and had a good mind toward everyone. As the tantra says, “With the mind of enlightenment holding the welfare of others as most important”; therefore, I think he fulfilled at least one of the six requirements.[698] By way of the monastic community of Namgyal Phendé Lekshé Ling, by serving the Great Fifth and through the Great Fifth conferring upon him a few ripening practices of entering into mandalas, Darmo Menrampa had a strong and deep bond with the great protector and with me. He helped my great lama with his sight and provided me too with much support. His medical practice was mainly that of the transmitted instructions from the Upper tradition, and by undertaking it with great compassion, his merit in terms of medical practice was very great.

d.div: [318] kun la bsam pa dge ba rgyud las/ byang sems che bas gzhan don gtso bor len/ /zhes pa'i gzhung de ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[697] “Lhaksam” (lhag bsam) connotes an uncommonly caring attitude toward others.
[698] The requirements for becoming a doctor; these are explained below.

f.d:
sum dar gnyis ka dang rang lo sum cu phan bro nad kha yar thebs pa'i dus dang de'i gong mnyam gshibs bcas ha cang 'dris ches pas zhar byung gi thog nas zhib par byung ba sman ngo dang gzhung gi go ba len lugs rags tsam du mthong zhing / gzhan pa'i lha rje'i rigs rnams rje mi la'i gangs dkar te se'i dpe ltar snyan grags las/ don sman ngo sdong 'grems lag len dang gzhung don rgyas bshad kyi tshar lugs 'dir sbyangs pa'i rgan po'i khur 'dzin rnams kyang ljags shin tu thung ba/ rje bla ma srid zhi'i gtsug rgyan lnga pa mchog gi bka' las/
'on te snyigs mar spyod pa'i khung bu nas/ / 'khyog 'gro'i nyes par bshad pa'i lce brkyang ste/ / 'gro ba'i srog la rgol ba'i gdug pa'i sbrul/ / 'chi bdag sman pa'i gzugs gzhan bsgyur bas gang /[319] / zhes gang bka' stsal pa ltar nyag shin tu phra ba 'dug na'ang / gong du brjod pa'i gnya' rigs rnam rgyal rdo rje nas sman ngo / sdong 'grems/ yul thig sogs len dgos byung bas gzhung don re gnyis ma gtogs phal cher 'khrol/

From the age of thirty onward, during those times when I came down with various ailments, and during the times I spent with them prior to that, I became very acquainted with Sumga and Darmo Menrampa. Therefore, incidentally, I saw that their precise identification of medicinal plants and the way they had gained their understanding of the tetxs was quite superficial. There are other renowned physicians who are like Jetsün Mila’s example of the snow mountains: they may be famous, but in matters of identification of plants, the layout of the medical tree, medical practices, and the ability to give extensive teachings on the medical texts, those who carry the responsibility of being elders trained in this medical tradition have very short tongues. In the works of my great lama, the Supreme Fifth, crown jewel of samsara and nirvana, he says:
However, with its tongue of erroneous and wayward teachings poking out of the hole of the behavior of these degenerate times, the poisonous snake that threatens the lives of beings, the lord of death disguised as a doctor…[699] As his words indicate, these are very difficult times. However, from Namgyal Dorjé of the Nya line as described earlier, I necessarily studied the identification of medical plants, the layout of the medical tree, anatomy, and so forth, and except for a few points, I was able to comprehend most of it.

d.div: [319] rje bla ma srid zhi'i gtsug rgyan lnga pa mchog gi bka' las/ 'on te snyigs mar spyod pa'i khung bu nas/ /'khyag 'gro'i nye+os par bshad pa'i lce brkyang ste/ /'gro ba'i srog la rgol ba'i gdug pa'i sbrul/ /'chi bdag sman pa'i gzugs gzhan bsgyur bas gang / /rgyal ba lnga pa'i gsung 'di rnyed son ma byung /
[699] Untraced.

f.d: re gnyis lus pa rnams brgyad pa rtsa 'grel gyis dbus rgya 'gyur bstan 'gyur gras su bzhugs pa dang bod rtsom gyi 'grel pa sogs sgor mar zhib bcug pas sngon chad 'bru bsnan gyi bshad pa med pa rnams kyang yid du 'doms/ rnam rdor gyis dbus man rgyud kyi tshig la 'bru bsnan gyi dri rmed dang dpe blta dogs gcod ches gshis rgyud chung gsum snga sor blo 'dzin byas pa dang man rgyud ma bzung ba cha 'dra ba'i tshig 'bru gso ba re ma byas par mnan rgyugs mi 'gro ba las don cha mtha' dag dang khyad par dka' gnas rnams shin tu yid la 'jags pa byung ba dang /

For those points I did not understand, I applied myself to a complete and detailed study of the translations of Indian commentaries found in the Tengyur, exemplified by Śūra’s Eight Branches root text and commentary, as well as indigenous Tibetan commentaries. As a result, even those works I had not previously received word-by-word teachings on arose in my mind. Masters, especially Namgyal Dorjé, were able to clear up questions I had on the text of the Instruction Tantra and resolve doubts I had from other texts. Therefore, though I had initially memorized only the three shorter tantras and did not cultivate the actual words of the unmemorized Instruction Tantra—without which there can be no individual-word recitation examination—nevertheless, all the points of the tantra, especially the difficult points, were planted firmly in my mind.

rig pa 'di rnyed par dka' ba'i dal 'byor gyi lus khams drug ldan gyi nad thams cad zhi bar byas te lus ngag yid gsum la bde ba'i bcud len chen po ster bar byed pa'i spyi nor bla na med cing / khyad par bdud rtsi snying po yan lag brgyad pa gsang ba man ngag gi rgyud gso dpyad rang lugs su ston pa thub pa'i dbang po'i bka' dri ma med pa lo chen bai ro'i 'gyur la gangs can yul gyi dbang po dang 'tsham par rigs 'dus sman pa'i rgyal po g.yu thog yon tan mgon pos gong smos bzhin bsnan kha dang zhus dag gnang ba dpal ldan rgyud bzhir grags pa 'di gso rig kun gyi gtso bo rgyal mtshan gyi tog ltar mngon par mtho zhing gces pa zhig snang yang / byang pa rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags bzang dang mi'i nyi ma mthong ba don ldan zur mkhar d+harma swa mi rnams las snga rabs pa rnams kyis tshong 'dus 'o ma bzhin bslad cing ci rigs su gyur ba/ yar rgyab pas sbyin bdag mdzad de zur mkhar blo gros rgyal pos zhus dag pa'i gra thang rgyud bzhi zhes snyan pa'i ba dan srid rtser sgreng ba'i dar rgyas su mdzad pa/

In this hard-to-gain body of leisure and opportunities composed of six elements, this science pacifies all illness, and by providing the great elixir of physical, verbal, and mental happiness, it is the supreme wealth shared by all. In particular, the Essence of Ambrosia Secret Instruction Tantra on Eight Branches is, in the tradition of medical science, the undefiled word of our Teacher, the mighty Buddha, translated by the great lotsāwa Vairocana, and as explained previously, added to and redacted for the Tibetan context by Yuthok Yönten Gönpo, a king among physicians and a combiner of lineages; renowned as the glorious Four Tantras, it is the greatest of medical works, precious and prominent like the very peak of a banner of victory. However, with the exception of Jangpa Rikden Namgyal Draksang, Minyima Thongwa Dönden, and Surkhar Dharmaswami, those of the past spoiled this tantra like milk in the marketplace, and it lost its identity. Under the sponsorship of Yargyapa it was redacted by Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo, who propagated the Drathang Four Tantras, as it became known, until its banner hoisted aloft upon the peak of samsara.

bdag gi bla ma nges pa don gyi thams cad mkhyen pa lnga pa chen pos shes bya ji lta ba dang ji snyed pa don dam par lag mthil skyu ru'i rnam pa ltar gzigs kyang / dman ngor rnam thar rin po cher gsal ba ltar rig pa 'dir rtsa bshad phyi gsum thugs 'dzin dang sa dpyad dang rdel 'grems rags tsam gsan tshul las spros mi mkhyen pa'i tshul bstan cing / byang ngos nang so dar rgyas de nyid kho bo dang phrad dus na tshod je mthor gyur kyang rgyud nges shing brtan cha che ba sogs gong bshad ltar mchis na'ang / 'grel pa'i rigs la gzhig pa ma chug pa'am rang gi a pha'i gsol zhal gyi dper song ba ji ltar rung / slob 'khor sogs lha rje dkyus ma gzhan dang mthun par byang zur gnyis bzhed pa tha dad pa lta bu dang / gra thang rgyud bzhi 'di ga ches khyad par 'phags tshul zhus pa snang ngo dang bstun te rab byung bcu gcig pa'i chu stag lo gra thang sor bzhag par du brko ba gnang ba dang par byang sogs stsal kyang /

My lama the Great Fifth was in reality the omniscient one who ultimately saw all phenomena as many as there are, exactly as they are, as clearly as he would see a berry in the palm of his hand. However, in the eyes of the inferior and as his precious biography makes clear, in the discipline of medicine he memorized the Root, Explanatory, and Final Tantras, and apart from a seemingly superficial study of the outlines and the stone layout, he did not reveal any in-depth knowledge on the subject. As I’ve already mentioned, I had met Jang Ngö Nangso Dargyé, and he was already advanced in age yet his understanding and ascertainment of the tantra was strong. However, he either did not comprehend the commentaries in great detail or, as the saying goes, “he prefers his father’s cup,” and so like other ordinary physicians, such as his disciples and entourage, he maintained that the Jang and Sur traditions held different assertions, for example, and made representations to the Great Fifth on the greatness of the Drathang edition of Four Tantras. Therefore, in keeping with this view, in the water-tiger year of the eleventh cycle (1662), the Great Fifth organized the woodblock carving of the Drathang edition and composed the print colophons.

rab byung de ga'i lcags khyi la par phud kyi thog nas kho bos rgyud chung ba gsum blo 'dzin skabs rnam rtog ji snyed cig shar ba/ rje bla ma nyid la jo nang kun snying du bka' bkyon zhor byang zur gnyis bzhed pa mi gcig pa sogs phebs pa lha rje dkyus ma rnams sngo sman yul babs ngos 'dzin mi 'dra ba dang lag len gyi khyad par stod smad phran bu las/ gzhung don du rim par snga ma'i lam la phyi ma brten pas mi 'dra ba med pa dang / gra thang rgyud 'di la yang bcos bsgyur gyis sa dpyad 'khrugs pa tshig chad pa sogs mang ba'i ha cang khungs chod par ma sems pas/ da lam gyi par byang bka' rtsom bcad lhug 'di cung zad thal tshul sogs zhib pa snyan du phul bas dgyes pa'i tshul dang bcas te byang ngos nas sogs de bzhin gsung ba sor bzhag tu bgyis na'ang / khyod kyis ji ltar zer ba bden 'dug pas slar bcad brdar zhig thub na legs 'dug pas gyis shig ces bka'i gnang ba thob/

However, in the iron-dog year of the same cycle (1670), while I was memorizing the three shorter tantras from the first printings of this new edition, a few thoughts arose in my mind. These were that the belief that the Jang and Sur traditions held different positions, and so on, came to my great lama while he was busy reprimanding Künga Nyingpo [a.k.a. Tāranātha] of Jonang. Among the ranks of ordinary physicians, the differences in the identification of medical plants was attributable to geography; in terms of medical practices, the Upper and Lower traditions differed little. However, in terms of the primary topics of the literature, any later path depends upon an earlier path, and in that sense there were no differences. Also the present Drathang tantra had a confusing layout, with many omissions and so forth, and I thought it no longer served as a trustworthy reference. Therefore I felt that the present publication colophon composed in verse and prose was a little excessive.[700] I reported all this in detail to the Great Fifth, and with delight he replied, “I merely accepted what Jang Ngö and others said. However, what you say is true. It would be excellent if you can look at it again, so do it.” He therefore gave me permission.

d.div: [700] Each of the four tantras in the Drathang edition had a colophon composed by the Fifth Dalai Lama that praised the work fulsomely.

f.d:
g.yu thog snying tig gi dbang zhus dus rgyud bzhi cha lag bcas pa spyi bor byin gyis rlobs/ lag tu stsal nas/ 'gro lnga ma rig dug lnga'i rgyud las ni/ / zhes sogs/
rgyud chen sde bzhi mjug don bcas pa lnga/ / bco brgyad cha lag dang bcas gso dpyad kyi/ / gzhung dang gdams pa kun gyi dbang bskur bas/ / tshig don ji bzhin rtogs pa'i dbang thob shog / ces gzungs dang bcas gsungs shing / cang te yun ring bsgrag pa gnang ba'i dus sngar bzung ba'i tshig blor nges don bka' ba rnams kyi don rang blo rang lam gyi 'char ba'i snang ba dang bshad srol skyongs shig pa'i dus 'phral du bya snyam yid la dur dur shar ba'i byin rlabs thugs rje'i 'jug pa sgo gsum la zhugs pa dang rang gi gso ba rig pa las bgyis pa rnams kyang rje 'dis byin gyis brlabs pa'i bka' yin nam snyam pa tsam las de 'phral gang ci nas zhus dag par ma thub/

While receiving the Yuthok Heartdrop initiation, he placed Four Tantras and [Yuthok’s] Eighteen Auxiliary Texts upon my head as a blessing, and after he put them in my hands, the passage beginning, “From the minds of the five kinds of beings with their five poisons of ignorance” was recited up to:
The four sections of this great tantra, with the final section making five, together with the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts, this initiation of every medical text and instruction: may it grant the power to understand exactly their meanings.[701] This was followed by the granting of the mantra, and he beat a ḍamaru drum for a long time. At this time the meanings of those points of the text I had memorized earlier whose definitive comprehension had been so difficult, arose in my mind as my path. When the instruction to nourish the tradition of teaching was given, the thought to undertake this task immediately arose vividly in my mind. This was the blessing of great compassion entering my body, speech, and mind; all my deeds in the science of medicine I thought of as being solely the blessed speech of this great being. These were just thoughts, however, and I was unable to redact and reprint Four Tantras at that particular time.

d.div: [701] Untraced.

f.d: phyis 'grel pa bai sngon brtsam pa dang sbrags rtog gzhig bcug par/ man rgyud blo 'dzin dang nad pa skyong ba sogs ma thub cing / gong du song ba'i sman ngo rtsa yul gyi thig sogs las dus dbang gis slob dpon mkhas pa yang yun ring du bsten ma thub pas tshul bzhin dka' yang /

Later I concentrated my thoughts on this undertaking when beginning to write the Blue Beryl commentary. I had definitive reference works on tastes, powers, post-digestive tastes, natures, etymologies, and functions of medicines; I had been unable to memorize the Instruction Tantra, treat patients, and so on; and aside from the identification of plants, the channels, anatomy, and so on, restrictions on my time meant that I had not been able to devote much time to the great masters, and it was going to be difficult to undertaking this properly. Nevertheless, I diligently consulted the following important works:

dus kyi 'khor lo/ rdo rje mkha' 'gro/ mkha' 'gro rgya mtsho sogs rgyud sde/ gser 'od dam pa dang dkon brtsegs sogs mdo sde/ lung gzhi dang phran tshegs sogs 'dul ba/ gdags pa dang mdzod rtsa 'grel sogs mngon pa/

• Various tantras, including the Kālacakra, Vajraḍāka, and Ḍāka Ocean Tantra • Sutras, including Sutra of Golden Light and Heap of Jewels Sutra • Vinaya texts, such as Basic Vinaya and Short Vinaya • Works on Abhidharma, such as [Vasubandhu’s] Abhidharmakośa and [Maudgalyāyana’s] Cause Terminology and Karma Terminology
yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa/ de'i rang 'grel/ zla zer/ sbyor ba brgya pa/ gces grub/ 'tsho ba'i mdo/ dngul chu grub pa sogs rgya gar nas 'gyur rigs/

• Indian translations, such as [Pitṛceṭa’s] Treatise of Eight Branches, its autocommentary, [Candranandana’s] Moonlight, [Nāgārjuna’s] Hundred Medical Preparations, [Ravigupta’s] Essential Medical Siddha, [Nāgārjuna’s] Sutra of Life, and [Bhalipa’s] Treatise on Mercury Preparation
sman dpyad zla ba'i rgyal po sogs rgya nag nas 'gyur rigs/ 'khor lo rgyal po'i be bum gyis dbus zhang zhung nas 'gyur ba/
• Translations from Chinese, such as the Somarāja • Shangshung translations exemplified by Universal Emperor Compilation
bdud rtsi bam po bdun pa/ bdud rtsi mchog gi gzhung lugs/ bdud rtsi bum pa/ snang gsal shel bum sogs snga 'gyur rdo rje theg pa bka' gter gyi rigs/

• Works from the early-translation Vajrayana lineages of Treasure and Transmission, such as the Seven Ambrosia Fasicles, the Supreme Ambrosia Scriptures, [Dorbum Chökyi Drakpa’s] Vase of Ambrosia, and [Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo’s] Clear Crystal Vase

bi byi bu ti kha ser/ sgron gsal gdams pa sum cu/ bdud rtsi snying po che chung / rdzong 'phrang 'phrul gyi lde mig /yan lag bzhi pa/ cha lag bco brgyad dang bcas bod du snga rabs byung ba'i gzhung lugs/

• Early Tibetan works, such as Biji’s Yellow Collection,[702] Illuminating Lamp of Thirty Instructions, the great and lesser Essence of Ambrosia, the Magic Key on the Difficult Fortress Path, Four Branches, and the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts

d.div: [702] See under Tsenpashilaha.

f.d: rtsa bshad phyi gsum la 'grel pa'i rigs shin tu mang ba dang yang bstun/ man rgyud du sngar phan 'bru 'grel tshad ldan mdzad mi cher ma byung 'dug cing / g.yu thog pa'i gser mchan/ de la yang zong mchan smar mchan gnyis/ bu don ma/ phyag dreg ma/ zur mkhar rnying ma'i rgyud bzhi sgam nang ma/ byang lugs mkhas pas mdzad pa'i dgos 'dod kun 'byung sogs dang /

• Many commentaries on the Root, Explanatory, and Final Tantras and other related works (nobody qualified to write a word-by-word commentary on the Instruction Tantra text has seriously appeared); Later Yuthok’s Golden Annotations together with his Copper Annotations and Explicit Annotations; Compositions for My Sons; the “well-worn copy”[703] of the Four Tantras; the old Surkhar Gamnang edition of Four Tantras; Fulfilling All Needs and Wishes[704] by a great scholar of the Jang tradition; and others

d.div: [703] Phyag dreg ma, literally, “hand-stained.” In other words, the handwritten copy of Four Tantras was stained by so much thumbing of the pages.
[704] Probably Practices of the Science of Medicine: Fulfilling All Needs and Wishes (Gso dpyad kyi lag len dgos ’dod kun ’byung) by Dütsi Gyurmé.

f.d: mang yul gung thang khyung rdzong dkar por mu khri btsan po'i sprul pa khri bsod nams ldes sbyin pa'i bdag po mdzad de dge slong rin chen dpal bzang gis khur 'khur/ 'a ba dge slong bkra shis [320]dang rang nyid/ chos rje kun dga' rgyan/ rab 'byams pa/ chos bde bzhis zhus legs par dag pa rdzong dga'i par du grags pa dang / sgam po nor rgyan pas khur bzhes sman pa don grub pas bskul ba dang zhus dag byas pa sgam po'i par ma dang / rtag brtan du rje btsun kun dga' snying pos khur bzhes kyi 'phro 'thud dbon kun dga' rgyal mtshan gyis mdzad cing / zhus dag pa gong du rgyas par song ba'i gnya' pa'i rigs sman byang lhun grub sdings kyi 'tsho byed gzhon nus gsos sam bdud rtsi 'gyur med kyis byas pa rtag brtan par ma/ bo dong pa'i par ma sogs dang /

• Other editions of Four Tantras: these include the Dzong Ga edition, a publication sponsored by Tri Sönam Dé—an incarnation of Mutri Tsenpo in Khung Dzong Karpo in the Gungthang district of Mangyül—that was undertaken by the monk Rinchen Palsang and edited by himself along with the Awa monk Tashi, Chöjé Künga Gyen, and Rapjampa Chödé; the Gampo edition undertaken by Norbu Gyenpa (1589–1633) of [Daklha] Gampo, which was requested and edited by the physician Döndrup; the Takten edition undertaken by Jetsün Künga Nyingpo in Takten Monastery, completed by his nephew Künga Gyaltsen, and edited by the master physician Tsojé Shönu Sö of Lhündrup Ding, also known as Dütsi Gyurmé, of the previously flourishing Nya family; and finally the Bodong edition

d.div: [320] 'di'i ma dper shog grangs brgya dang go gnyis mjug rdzogs shing / shog grangs brgya dang go gsum pa shog stong du 'dug la shog bu brgya dang go bzhi pa/ dang rang nyid/ zhes pa nas dbu tshugs/ de ltar yang gzhung gi tshig 'gros la brtags na gzhung chad par mi snang la/ phal cher dpar bskos skabs shog bu ang grangs zhig mchongs sam snyam/

f.d: lcags smyug gis bris pa'i yig rnying le tshan 'dra dang yang bstun pa sogs gangs can gyi ljongs su grags so cog gi sman dpyad phra mo dang bcas pa phal cher la sla thabs ma yin par so sor zhib tu brtags/

• Old handwritten manuscripts, copies of the chapters, and miscellaneous other works In short, I studied assiduously, and with no shortcuts, almost every renowned medical text, both great and small, in this snow mountain land.

khyad par zur mkhar rnying ma'i rgyud sgam nang ma dang phyag dreg ma gnyis gzhir bzhag /gra thang gi rgyud bzhir tshig chad pa sogs rnying pa rnams mthun par 'dug rigs rang gi rigs pas kyang dpyad de/ dper na bsdoms tshig tu bshad pa nang gses dus ma tshang rigs/ nad rtags bshad par bcos chad pa/ sa dpyad 'khrugs pa sogs dang / la la dag 'bru nor gyi rnam pa sogs 'ol spyi rtog bzo min pa'i lung rigs khungs thub kyi sgo nas gtan la phab/ brda rnying go dka' nges rnams gsal du btang ba bcos zhus legs par dag ste par du brkos nas gtan pa med pa'i chos sbyin gyi sgo 'phar phye/

In particular, I used the old Surkhar Gamnang edition of the tantra and the Chakdrekma copy as two fundamental reference works. In the Drathang Four Tantras, wherever there were missing words and so forth and this was replicated in the old texts, I used my own reasoning. For example, sometimes the number of divisions in the summary sections was incomplete; the remedies were omitted from the teachings on symptoms of illness; there was confusion in the outlines, and so forth; and there were incorrect and misspelled words. These I determined not with superficial inventions from my own mind but with sound scripture and reasoning. I also clarified archaic and difficult-to-understand terms. In this way, correcting and revising the tantra and publishing it opened the gateway to an unending offering of Dharma.
bai sngon sogs sman gzhung mang po brtsams tshul/

d.i: Composition of Blue Beryl and other works

f.d: de bstun bar du nub pa dang log lam 'phyan pa rnams rnam dag gi lam du gcur nas rgyud bzhi ga'i 'grel pa sman bla'i dgongs rgyan rgyud bzhi'i gsal byed baiDUR+ya sngon po'i ma l+li ka zhes dpe shog tshad ma stong dang nyis brgya skor longs pa brtsams pa'i dbu btsugs pa dang / dge bshes chags pa chos 'phel 'dzin she gzhan las che ba 'dug pas 'dzin bcug pa srid kyi brel g.yeng dang bstun gshis bzung bar lag gtugs dogs pa'i bris gdan lta bu las brling ba zhig sngar phan zhus dag ma thub rung rtsa bshad phyi gsum man rgyud dang bcas yongs su rdzogs pa'i 'bru bsnan dang / de'i don ma lus pa lag mthil skyu ru'i rnam [321]pa bzhin mkhas nas byis pa'i bar gyi bde blag tu rtogs par gtan la phab pa sngon med kyi bris cha'i skor la/

Similarly, having turned onto the right path those who for a while had wandered off and those treading the wrong path, I began composing my commentary to Four Tantras called Ornament to the Mind of Medicine Buddha: Blue Beryl Lamp Illuminating Four Tantras, with about 1,200 pages. Geshé Chakpa Chöphel had a greater ability to memorize than others, and so he was encouraged to memorize the tantra. Being continually distracted by affairs of state, I feared that I would lose what had been memorized, and so up to then any work had been in draft form like chalk on a writing board, and I had been unable to make any reliable redaction of the tantras. However, now I was able to supplement the words of the Root, Explanatory, and Final Tantras as well as the Instruction Tantra. As a way for everyone from the scholar to the child to easily understand the entire meaning of the above as clearly as seeing a berry in the palm of one’s hand, I commissioned a collection of medical paintings, something never before accomplished:[705]

d.div: [321] bsnam pa/ mtsho sngon deb dpar/

[705] Seventy-seven of the seventy-nine paintings are in included as color plates in Tibetan Medical Paintings (London: Serindia Publications, 1992). That volume does not include paintings 6 and 7 below.

f.d: dang por rtsa rgyud le'u dang po'i gling gzhi'i don sprul pa'i gnas sman gyi nags tshal dang grong khyer kyi dbus tsha grang ldan 'dus kyi gnyen po'i sman skye zhing stobs dang ldan pa'i ri bo'i rtser phyi'i grong khyer lta na sdug ces bya ba gzhal yas khang gi nang du phun sum tshogs pa lnga'i sgo nas ston pa sman gyi bla baiDUR+ya 'od kyi rgyal po des gso rig rgyud 'di nyid gti mug rnam dag me long ye shes/ zhe sdang rnam dag stong nyid ye shes/ nga rgyal rnam dag mnyam nyid ye shes/ 'dod chags rnam dag sor rtog ye shes/ phrag dog rnam dag bya grub ye shes te lnga'i rang bzhin drang srong mched lngas zhu ba zhu lan gyi phyi nang gi 'khor tshogs du mar gsungs pa'i tshul kha byang dang bcas pa/

1. The first painting depicts the introduction to the first chapter of the Root Tantra. In the center of the manifested location of the medical forest and medical city, on the mountains endowed with the powers and the medicinal plants that act as effective remedies to hot, cold, simple, and complex disorders, is the celestial mansion of the external city of Sudarśana. Inside, endowed with the five perfections,[706] sits the teacher, Medicine Buddha, the king of beryl light. The five rishi brothers—whose natures are the mirror-like gnosis of purified ignorance, the emptiness gnosis of purified anger, the equality gnosis of purified pride, the analysis gnosis of purified desire, and the accomplishment gnosis of purified jealousy—teach the tantra to the assembled audience of Buddhists and non-Buddhists in the form of requestor and receiver. The painting is accompanied by a written description.

d.div: [706] The five perfections: perfect teacher, Dharma, entourage, time, and place.

f.d: gnyis par le'u gnyis pa'i rig pa'i ye shes dang yid las skyes sprul tshul/ le'u gsum pa gnas lugs nad gzhi'i rtsa ba las rnam par ma gyur ba'i sdong po dang gyur pa'i sdong po gnyis te/ dang po las nad dang lus zungs dri ma gsum gyi yal ga gsum/ lo 'dab nyi shu rtsa lnga/ gnyis par rgyu rkyen/ 'jug sgo/ gnas/ lam/ ldang dus/ 'bras bu/ ldog rgyu rnams kyi yal ga dgu / lo 'dab drug cu rtsa gsum/ dril bas lo 'dab brgyad cu rtsa brgyad/ me tog nad med pa dang tshe ring ba gnyis las/ 'bras bu chos nor phun sum tshogs pa dang bde ba ste phung po 'od skur grol ba'i tshul rnams/

2. The second painting shows the emanation of Vidyājñāna and Manasija described in the second chapter of the Root Tantra. It also shows the third chapter’s description of the two trunks of balanced and imbalanced humors arising from a single root—the condition of the body—as the basis of illness. From the first trunk arise the three branches of the humors, bodily constituents, and waste products. These branches together have twenty-five leaves. The second trunk has nine branches. These are: causes and circumstances, entrances, locations, pathways, times of arising, results, reaction imbalances,[707] and categories. These branches contain sixty-three leaves. In total the branches together have eighty-eight leaves. The flowers are those of good health and long life. They produce the fruits of Dharma, wealth and fortune, and happiness, represented by the depiction of the aggregates dissolving into the enlightened form.

d.div: [707] Ldog rgyu; I have gone with Clark in the translation of this term, although “side effects” is a possibility.

f.d: gsum pa ngos 'dzin rtags kyi rtsa ba las/ blta ba/ reg pa/ dril ba'i sdong po gsum/ dang po blta ba'i sdong po las lce mchu'i yal ga re la lo 'dab gsum re ste drug / gnyis pa reg pa'i sdong po las rlung mkhris bad gsum gyi yal ga gsum las lo 'dab re/ gsum pa dril ba'i sdong po la rlung mkhris bad gsum gyi yal ga gsum las/ rlung la lo 'dab bcu gcig dang / mkhris par bdun/ bad kan la bcu gcig ste nyer dgu / dril bas sdong po gsum/ yal ga brgyad/ lo 'dab sum cu rtsa gcig tu yod tshul/

3. The third painting shows the root of diagnosis producing the three trunks of observation, palpation, and questioning. The observation trunk has branches of the tongue and the urine, each branch having three leaves. The trunk of palpation has branches of wind, bile, and phlegm, each producing one leaf. The trunk of questioning also has branches of wind, bile, and phlegm. On this trunk the wind branch has eleven leaves, the bile branch seven, and the phlegm branch eleven, making twenty-nine leaves in total. Therefore, there are three trunks, eight branches, and thirty-eight leaves.

bzhi par gso dpyad thabs kyi rtsa ba la zas spyod sman dpyad kyi sdong po bzhi las/ dang por nyes gsum zas skom gyi yal ga drug / rlus zas kyi lo 'dab bcu/ skom lo bzhi/ mkhris zas kyi lo 'dab bdun/ skom lo lnga/ bad zas kyi lo 'dab drug / skom lo gsum ste khyon so lnga/ gnyis par nyes gsum gyi yal ga gsum las gnyis res lo 'dab drug / gsum par ro nus zhi sbyong sogs yal ga bco lnga/ nyes gsum ro nus kyi lo 'dab bco brgyad/ zhi byed kyi lo 'dab nyer gsum/ sbyong byed kyi dgu ste lnga bcu/ bzhi par nyes gsum gyi yal ga gsum/ lo 'dab bdun/ dril bas sdong po bzhi/ yal ga nyi shu rtsa bdun/ lo 'dab dgu bcu rtsa brgyad yod pa dang / rig pa'i ye shes thugs kar thim tshul te rtsa ba thugs kyi rgyud la bris cha bzhi/

4. The fourth shows the methods-of-treatment root with four trunks: diet, behavior, medication, and therapies. The diet trunk has six branches made up of food and drink corresponding to each of the three humors. The wind-food branch has ten leaves, the wind-drink branch four. The bile-food branch has seven leaves, the bile-drink branch five. The phlegm-food branch has six leaves, the phlegm-drink branch has three. This makes thirty-five leaves in total. The behavior trunk has three branches corresponding to the three humors, each branch having two leaves, six in total. The medication trunk has fifteen branches spread among those of taste, powers, pacification, and cleansing. There are eighteen leaves of tastes and powers divided among the three humors, twenty-three leaves on the pacification branch, and nine leaves on the cleansing branch, making fifty leaves in all. The fourth or therapies trunk has three branches corresponding to the three humors and seven leaves. In total this root has four trunks, twenty-seven branches, and ninety-eight leaves. This painting also shows Vidyājñāna dissolving back into the heart of Medicine Buddha. These are the four paintings depicting the Root or Mind Tantra.
lnga par bshad rgyud le'u dang po nas sprul pa'i drang srong spros pa dang gnyis pa'i grub pa lus gnas skor/ drug par lhun sdings lugs bshad rgyud kyi rtsa thig bdun dang / bdun par rgyab/

5. The fifth painting depicts the emanation of Rishi Vidyājñāna described in the first chapter of the Explanatory Tantra and the formation of the body described in the second. 6. The circulatory system from the front as taught in the Explanatory Tantra and according to the tradition of Lhündrup Ding. 7. The posterior view of the same circulatory system.

brgyad par le'u gsum pa 'dra dpe dang bzhi pa'i stod cha pho mo'i lus zungs zla mtshan ldang tshad yan/ dgu par gong 'phros kyi rus rigs nas bzung gzugs ngan rang khru phyed bzhi yan ston pa'i mdun dang / bcu par de dag gi rgyab/

8. Similes of the body as taught in the third chapter, and the quantities of bodily constituents in men and women up to the quantity of menstrual blood taught at the beginning of the fourth. 9. The ninth painting continues from the previous textual depiction and shows the description of the bone structure up to the three-and-a-half-cubit dimension of a poorly formed body. 10. The posterior view of the above.
bcu gcig par rang lugs/ chags srid 'brel ba'i rtsa thig mdun dang / bcu gnyis par de'i rgyab/ bcu gsum par rtsa phran sum brgya drug cur gyes tshul/
11. The circulatory system of formation, existence, and connecting channels according to our own tradition. 12. The posterior view of the above. 13. The channels dividing up into 360 minor channels.

bcu bzhi pa yang phran lus dang dra bar gyes tshul dang / tshe'i rtsa zur mkhar ba'i gtar rtsa don bdun rnams/ bco lnga pa klad pa nas thur du rtsa dkar zug pa'i chu rtsa dang phyi rol gyi rtsa 'brel tshul/ bcu drug pa sha gnad nas bu ga'i gnad kyi bar bcas pa'i mdun dang /

14. The anterior view of the network of a further division of minor channels throughout the body, the life channels,[708] and the bloodletting channels according to the Surkhar tradition. 15. The white water channels[709] running down from the brain and its connections to the outer channels. 16. An anterior view of the vulnerable points, from those of the flesh up to the textual description of the orifices.

d.div: [708] Described in the painting notes from Blue Beryl as being “like the life force” (bla).
[709] “Water” or “white” channels are usually nerves and tendons. Red channels are blood vessels.

f.d: bcu bdun par de'i rgyab/ bco brgyad par le'u lnga pa'i mtshar bsdus/ drug pa rten gyi dbye ba dang 'du ba'i rang bzhin bstan pa/ bdun pa la nye'i rtags zla zer nas kha skong bcas pa/ bcu dgu pa le'u bdun pa sman pa'i lam ltas dge ba 'bru'i snod gang nas zla zer kha skong rmi lam yid 'jug gi skor bcos pa/

17. Posterior view of the above. 18. A wonderful synopsis of the fifth chapter of the Explanatory Tantra, a classification by gender and by humor from the sixth chapter, and various signs from the seventh chapter, with supplementary material from Candranandana’s Moonlight. 19. The seventh chapter’s description of the omens seen by the doctor on his way to meet a patient, beginning from the auspicious sign of a full container of grain; supplemented by Candranandana’s Moonlight on signs in dreams and descriptions of how dreams enter the mind.

nyi shu par tshe ring nad med kyi rmi lam bzang ba lha tshangs pa nas nye ba'i 'chi ltas bzlog pa'i bar/ nyer gcig pa le'u brgyad pa dgu pa bcu pa bcu gcig pa bcu gnyis pa rnams kyi mtshar bsdus/ nyer gnyis par le'u bcu gsum pa dang bcu bzhi pa bco lnga pa bcas pa/

20. Dreams auspicious for good health and long life, beginning with dreams of Brahmā up to the reversal of the signs of imminent death. 21. A wonderful synopsis of the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth chapters. 22. The thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth chapters.

nyer gsum par le'u bcu drug pa'i 'tsho ba zas sde 'bras nas chu skyo'i bar/ nyer bzhi par g.yos sde zan chang nas/ bcu bdun pa zas bsdams gyur dug gyur tshul/ bco brgyad pa'i mtshar bsdus/ nyer lnga par le'u bcu dgu pa'i 'byung lngas sman skyed tshul dang nyi shu ba brkyang sel nas mo d+he yan/

23. The wholesome diet taught in the sixteenth chapter, from rice up to light soup. 24. Wholesome diets starting from barley-beer stew in the section on prepared foods, up to the way food becomes poisonous explained in the seventeenth chapter on dietary rules, and including a synopsis of the eighteenth chapter. 25. A depiction of how medicines are formed from the five elements as taught in the nineteenth chapter and a depiction of medicines for the elimination of single-type disorders up to female stones from the twentieth chapter.

d.div: [715] The analogy rests on the idea that the milk of a lioness would crack an ordinary clay pot and be lost and must therefore be kept in a precious container. Similarly, unsuitable disciples are not able to retain the elixir of this teaching.

f.d: bsil ldan 'dir sdus dkon pas sman pa phal cher gyis mi 'grub pa'i sman rnams kyang ma tshang ba med par rtsol ba chen pos bsgrubs/ cha dpyad rnams kyang dka' tshegs dang rgyu 'gror ma bltas par gzhung nas ji ltar bshad pa bzhin gsar du bzo ba'i bkod pa byas/ lag len gyi rim pa la shin tu mkho zhing man ngag chig brgyud nus pa nyams kyi dogs pa rnams ma gtogs gsal bar ston pa man rgyud kyi lhan thabs zug rngu'i tsha gdung sel ba'i kat+pU ra dus min 'chi zhags gcod pa'i ral gri rtsom par yid nem nur gyi skabs bgyis na legs pa'i mtshan ma gsal zhing / sngar bod du skye ma myong ba'i dan rog sogs 'phrul snang bar khang gi dkon gnyer nad sos btab pa legs par skyes pa'i sdong po nged rang gi gam du skyel bar yong ba dang 'di nyid rtsom pa'i dbu btsugs pa ma bsgrigs lhun grub tu 'grig / nyin snga ma kha shas sbyar ba'i yin nam gang ltar sman gyi dri ngad bzang pos nye skor khyab pa beg ge'i nad chad pa sogs dge ltas du ma byung /

I have gone to great lengths to acquire prime-quality medicines that are not produced by most doctors because of the rarity of good ingredients in this cold country. I have also newly created surgical instruments exactly as described in the texts without regard to the difficulties and shortage of necessary tools. Because the Instruction Tantra reads very clearly, I had doubts about composing the supplement to it called Camphor to Cool the Burning Torment of Pain: A Sword to Cut the Noose of Untimely Death. However the Instruction Tantra has vital importance for medical practice and there were concerns about the one-to-one transmission of its core instruction being weakened, and I received clear omens that it would be beneficial to do so. When I was beginning this work, all that needed to be organized fell effortlessly into place. Among the omens, well-formed medical plants that had never previously grown in Tibet, such as the castor oil plant—which cured the illness of the middle-floor temple keeper of the Trülnang Lhasa temple[716]—were delivered to me. A few days before beginning, whether some medicine was being prepared the day before I cannot say, but the aroma of medicine pervaded the area, and illnesses such as beké subsided. Many such auspicious signs appeared.

d.div: [716] Better known as the Jokhang.

f.d: nang rigs rjes sbyangs kyi sman pa lhun sdings rnam rgyal rdo rje rkyang sel skor 'tsho byed spyi la dri ba zhig ra sa'i rdo rings su sbyar bar/ byis pa'i tshig ngan lta bu'i cal sgrog las dngos lan thebs pa ma byung 'dug pas dri lan nam gsal byed drang thig srid sgrub kyi mda' zhes bya ba dang / smin grol gling nas tshe rig 'dzin pa ngag dpal gyis baiDUR+ya sngon por dogs gnas kyi rgyu mtshan byung ba'i lan/ bod mkhas pa mi pham dge legs snyan dngags kyi rtsom pa brling ba tsam las shes bya spyir ming don mtshungs pa zhig yod mdog ma kha yang / 'bri klog dang tshig rtsom shes pa rgyu mtshan du byas pa'i bstan bcos kha yar 'dug pa nas sman rtsis gnyis kyi nor 'khrul rnams la dgag pa tsam byas pa sogs sman dpyad skor gyi yig cha thor bu'ang mang /

The trained lineage physician Lhünding Namgyal Dorjé posted questions on the Rasa[717] stone pillar addressed to doctors in the area on the subject of the capacities of various medicines. He received no real answers to his questions, only those devoid of substance and resembling the ramblings of children. Therefore I composed Answers to the Questions: The Arrow of Arjuna that Illuminates the True Flight. I also composed many other short works on the science of medicine. These include one in response to queries on Blue Beryl expressed by Ngawang Palden, a maintainer of the medical tradition from Mindröling, and another to refute the errors in medicine and astronomy made by Tibetan Scholar Mipham Gelek,[718] who composed some reliable works on poetry, and who appeared to be someone who lived up to his title in the field of general knowledge, but who composed a few works only because he knew how to read, write, and string words together.

d.div: [717] Old name for Lhasa.
[718] Mipham Gelek Namgyal, 1618–85. The prefix Tibetan Scholar (bod mkhas pa) was affixed to his name like a title, a fact to which the author refers in the same sentence.

f.d: sman gyi rig pa ji ltar slob tshul/
Part 4. THE STUDY OF MEDICINE AND THE THREE SETS OF VOWS
19. The Reason to Practice Medicine

drin can rtsa ba'i bla ma rgyal dbang lnga pa'i sku'i bsag sbyangs la dmigs lha sa bar skor nas jo bo shAkya mu ner skor 'bum gcig bsags pa rdzogs te jo rags skor rdo'i tshul du gling skor la phyin/ phyi dro lcags kha ri'i gnas mjal byas pa'i rtser sleb skabs sngon gyi yig cha ltar na phyag rdor gyi bla ri seng ge gnam mchongs kyi dbyibs su bzhed kyang / rang gi yid ngor ri bo ngos gsum dang bzhi'i khyad par las sprul pa'i grong khyer lta na sdug de yang 'di lta bu zhig yin nam snyam pa sogs 'char sgo dang mthong snang ya mtshan pa 'ga' zhig byung ba dang / lhun sdings dga' ldan sman bla ri bo'i ngos rnams su blta rtog la btang bar tsha bsil gyi nus stobs gdags sribs dang ma 'dzol zhing de 'dra ba'i sman ri der skye gi yod bsams pa su la'ang med pa du ma rnyed pa sogs kyi rkyen byas/ [244-245] rje bla ma lnga pa chen pos nub mar gso rig 'gro phan gling 'dzugs pa gnang yang 'thor zhig gis lam du ma rgyugs pa'i dgongs pa skong slad dang / gong du brjod pa bzhin gso ba rig pa 'di tshes gsum zla ba'i spun zlar gyur ba dang / spyir mngon par 'byung ba'i mdo las/
mi rnams kyi tshe lo mar 'grib pa lnga brgya man chad du snyigs ma lnga po 'di lta ste/ tshe'i snyigs ma dang / nyon mongs pa'i snyigs ma dang / sems can gyi snyigs ma dang / lta ba'i snyigs ma dang / dus kyi snyigs ma shas che ba yin/[322] zhes pa dang mthun par 'dul ba la sogs pa du ma nas gsungs pa bzhin snyigs ma lnga ches cher bdo zhing /

As a practice of purification and merit accumulation focused on the form of my kind root lama, the Great Fifth, I made one hundred thousand circumambulations of Jowo Śākyamuni from the Lhasa Barkor, the inner circumambulation path. After I had completed this practice I went to the Lingkor outer path in the manner of laying a stone at the Jorak shrine.[719] In the afternoon I went on a pilgrimage to Chakha Mountain.[720] I arrived at its summit—and although the early texts describe it as the exalted mountain of Vajrapāṇi, shaped like a lion leaping into the sky, to my mind, from its three and four sides,[721] I thought it looked just like the manifested city of Sudarśana—and some astonishing sights occurred. The Lhünding Ganden chief physician was sent to inspect the sides of the mountain and discovered they possessed hot and cold powers, corresponding perfectly with the sunny and shady sides, as well as many medicinal plants of these powers that no one knew were growing there. This was one condition for the construction of the Chakri Medical College. Other reasons were to fulfill the hopes of my lama, the Great Fifth, who had instituted the Sorik Drophen Ling medical school to the west of Drepung but which fell into ruin and was no longer in operation. Also, as stated previously, the science of medicine has become the twin of the moon on the third day of the month.[722] Moreover, the five degenerations generally increase over time. The Sutra of Going Forth says:
The lifespan of humans will decline. When it falls below five hundred, the five degenerations will predominate. These are the degenerations of lifespan, of mental afflictions, of living beings, of views, and of the times.[723] Many other texts including the Vinaya speak similarly.

d.div: [322] sde dge_301_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa_mngon par byung ba'i mdo/ shog_4_ba3

[719] Jowo Rakkha: a mound of stones, originally erected as a dam, standing on an embankment of Lhasa’s Kyichu River. It was an annual tradition to bring stones to this mound. What exactly is being referred to here I cannot say.
[720] Also known as Chakpori or Chakri, this is the hill on which Desi Sangyé Gyatso founded the famous Chakri Medical College.
[721] The Chaka mountain is actually three sided, but Sudarśana, as it appeared in Desi’s vision, is four-sided (Prof. Losang Tenzin).
[722] This is an expression meaning “fragile,” as the moon on the third lunar day is barely visible.

[723] Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra, Toh 301 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 4b3. The degeneration of lifespan means that on average lifespan will shrink to about fifty years. The degeneration of mental afflictions means that anger, desire, ignorance, and so on will become more prevalent. The degeneration of living beings means that behavior, attitudes, and wealth will decline. The degeneration of views means that the number of nonbelievers in the Three Jewels, cause and effect, and past and future lives will increase. The degeneration of the times means that epidemics, famines, wars, and poor harvests will become widespread.

f.d:
gso ba rig pa rang du'ang /
lnga brgya dus kyi tha mar gyur tsa na/ / mi rnams 'dod pa'i dbang gis log par spyod/ / sngags pa rnams ni rdo rje'i nang dme dar/ / dge 'dun btsun pa rnams ni sde 'khrugs byed/ / mu stegs ban bon rnams ni zor kha 'phen/ / skye bo rnams ni mna' thab shan dmar byed/ / de dus ma mo mkha' 'gro kun 'khrugs te/ / nad kyi kha rlangs sprin du chags pa las/ / bal nad rgyu gzer gag lhog 'brum nag 'byung /[323] / zhes bshad pa ltar nad rigs mang bar 'gro ba rnams zug rngu'i 'jigs pa las skyob par gzhan las gso ba rig pa nyid ches khyad par du 'phags pa gong du bshad pa bzhin dang /

In the medical literature also:
When the five hundred years of the end of time arrives,[724] human behavior will degenerate under the control of desire, practitioners of tantra will destroy the internal vajra bonds, monastic communities bring about sectarian troubles, heretics, Buddhists, and Bönpos will cast curses, living beings will break their words, fight, and turn to butchery;[725] at that time the mātṛkā and ḍākinīs will be disturbed, and from the clouds of disease formed from their breath will come Nepali illness, gyuser, gaklhok, and poxes.[726] Therefore, sentient beings live in fear of the sufferings brought on by the many kinds of illness, and the science of medicine, as stated previously, is superior to other sciences in giving protection from these fears.

d.div: [323] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ man ngag rgyud/ le'u/ 23_shog_243_yig phreng 5
[724] The last five hundred years of the five thousand years that the Buddha’s doctrine will last.

[725] Mna’ thab shan dmar byed. Here thab means “fire” or “fireplace,” and Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo’s Transmission of Our Ancestors (p. 328) renders it accordingly, but I have gone with the Dharamsala edition of Four Tantras, which has ’thab, meaning “fight.”
[726] Four Tantras, Instruction Tantra, 23.243.5.

f.d:
bshad rgyud le'u so gcig pa las/
sman pa'i 'bras bu gnas skabs mthar thug gnyis/ / gnas skabs 'bras bu tshe 'dir skyid pa dang / / dbang dang longs spyod dga' bde ldan par 'gyur/[326] / zhes pa dang /
mthar thug 'bras bu g.yo sgyu 'dod pa rnams/ / spangs nas nad pa gso ba la 'jug pa/ / bla med sangs rgyas sa la bgrod 'gyur zhes/ / 'tsho mdzad sman pa'i rgyal pos bshad pa yin/[327] / zhes gsungs pa dang /

In the thirty-first chapter of the Explanatory Tantra:
The fruits for the doctor are temporary and permanent. The temporary is happiness in this life, power, wealth, and joy.[729] Also:
As for the permanent results: having abandoned pretense and desire, one engages in healing the sick and walks the path to buddhahood. This the king of physicians has said.[730]

d.div: [326] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ bshad rgyud/ le'u so gcig pa/ shog_101_yig phreng 5
[327] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ bshad rgyud/ le'u so gcig pa/ shog_101_yig phreng 11
[729] Four Tantras, Explanatory Tantra, 31.101.4.

f.d:
tsa ra ka las/
de ltar byas pa'i 'bras bu ni/ / gnas skabs dang ni mthar thug go[328] / zhes dang / slob dpon chen po dpal ldan dpa' bo'i brgyad pa'i phyi mar/
g.yo sgyu spangs shing 'dod pa med/ / gang zhig gso ba la 'jug pa/ / sman pa bla med 'bras thob 'gyur/[329] / zhes dang /

In the Caraka it says:
The fruits of such work are temporary and ultimate.[731] The great ācārya, the glorious Śūra, says in the later Eight Branches:
Abandoning pretense, devoid of desire, those who engage the science of healing will gain the fruit of becoming the supreme doctor.[732]

d.div: [328] tsa ra ka'i gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[329] slob dpon dpa' bos/ g.yo sgyu spangs shing 'dod pa med/ / ces sogs kyi lung 'di 'tshol zhib byed kyang rnyed son ma byung /
[731] Untraced.
[732] Pitṛceṭa, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitanāma. Untraced.

f.d:
g.yu thog mgon po'i yang snying bsdus par/
tshe 'di rnyed dang bkur sti dang / / bde ba'i snyan grags longs spyod rnams/ / 'bad rtsol med par 'grub pa ni/ / tshe yi rig byed 'bras bu yin/[330] / zhes rang don phun tshogs pa 'di phyi gnyis 'grub pa'i dgos pa dang / gzhan don 'gro mchog gtso bor gyur pa mi lus 'di nyid la/ skye rgas na 'chi'i duHkha 'byung ba dngos su sel ba'i don nus pa ni/ 'di nyid rang las/ gnod med bde bar myur du btsal ba yin/[331] / zhes sogs skye ba'i sdug bsngal sel ba'i cho ga dang /

Yuthok Gönpo says in his Quintessence:
In this life: fortune and respect, wealth and happiness in fame, all accomplished without effort— these are the results of practicing medicine.[733] Therefore, one reason for practicing medicine is that it will accomplish your wishes in this and future lives. For accomplishing the welfare of others, in which living beings are held as supreme, it is able to relieve this human body of the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death. For example, “Birth will come quickly and easily, without danger,”[734] and so on, thereby describing practices for relieving the sufferings of birth. Also:

d.div: [330] g.yu thog yon tan mgon po'i yang snying bsdus pa dpe lag tu ma son/
[331] 'di yang gong du smros pa'i g.yu thog gi gzhung de las drangs/
[733] Yuthok Yönten Gönpo (Later), Yang snying bsdus pa. Untraced.
[734] Untraced.

f.d: rgas pa'i rtags nub bcu drug lta bu'i lus/ / rma bya'i mdangs ldan mgyogs pa cang shes rta/ / tshe srog nyi zla gnyis dang mnyam par 'gyur/[332] / zhes pa rgas pa gso ba'i cho ga dang /

The body with its signs of aging, its sixteen kinds of decline, (will develop the agility of the lion, the strength of a bull,)[735] the sheen of a peacock, and become sprightly like the best of horses, with a lifespan to rival the sun and moon.[736] This is from a section on rejuvenation procedures. Also:

d.div: [332] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ man ngag gi rgyud/ le'u/ 90_shog_549_yig phreng 15
[735] These parenthetical lines are found in the Dharamsala Four Tantras.
[736] Four Tantras, Instruction Tantra, 90.549.15.

f.d:
de ltar gso thabs dgu bcu rtsa brgyad po/ / yengs med gus pas brtson par bsten byas na/ / nad kyi 'dam las yongs su grol bar 'gyur/[333] / zhes dang /
nad kyi dgra dpung 'joms pa'i dpa' bo yin/[334] / zhes bzhi brgya rtsa bzhi sogs nad yin no cog zhi bar nus pa dang /

In this way the ninety-eight techniques of healing, if relied upon single-mindedly, with effort and respect, will rescue you from the great swamp of disease.[737] Further:
A great warrior defeating the enemy of disease.[738] These indicate the power of the science of medicine to pacify all illnesses, which are illustrated by the 404 types. Also:

d.div: [333] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ rtsa rgyud/ le'u/ 5_shog_13_yig phreng 9
[334] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ phyi ma rgyud/ le'u nyer bdun pa/ shog_665_yig phreng 5
[737] Four Tantras, Root Tantra, 5.13.9.
[738] Four Tantras, Final Tantra, 27.665.5.

f.d: 'chi ba srog skyabs mi 'jigs sbyin pa dang / / 'chi ba slong byed bdud rtsi bum pa yin/[335] / zhes dus ma yin par 'chi ba'i 'jigs pa las skyob pa ste/
Protector of life, granter of fearlessness, vase of ambrosia, lifting one from death.[739] This illustrates its ability to protect from the fear of untimely death.

gzhan yang / dpa' bo'i yan lag brgyad par/
nad kyi 'dam du bying ba la/ / lag nas 'dren pa sman yin no/[336] / zhes pa dang /

Furthermore, Śūra in his Eight Branches says:
Medicine is the hand lifting one from the swamp of disease.[740]

d.div: [336] sde dge_4310_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ he_pha khol/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po bsdus pa/ le'u/ 14_shog_334_na5
[740] Pitṛceṭa, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitanāma, chap. 14, Toh 4310, Tengyur, gso rig, he, 334a5.

f.d:
tsa ra ka las/
de ltar gso dpyad rnam brgyad kyis/ / chu bo che la gru ldings bzhin/ / mi zad nad kyi rba klong las/ / myur du sgrol bar byed pa yin/[337] / zhes dang /

Caraka states:
The eight branches of medicine, like a boat in the great sea, quickly rescues those from the great waves of unceasing illness.[741]

d.div: [337] tsa ra ka'i gsung 'di gang las drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[741] Untraced.

f.d:
klu sgrub kyis/
dmigs zin dpyad kyis nad kyi rgya mtsho skem/[338] / zhes gsungs pa sogs de ltar gzhan don phun sum tshogs pa byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyis smon lam ltar dngos su grub pa'i dgos pa yod de/

Nāgārjuna says:
Targeted medical practices empty the ocean of disease.[742] Therefore, through the practice of medicine, the bodhisattva will accomplish the welfare of others in accordance with his prayers. This is also a reason for practicing medicine.

d.div: [338] mgon po klu sgrub kyi gsung 'di'i khungs 'tshol zhib zhus kyang ma brnyed/
[742] Untraced.

f.d:
zhi ba lha'i gsung las/
'gro ba nad pa ji snyed pa/ / nad gsos gyur gyi bar du ni/ / sman dang sman pa nyid dag la/ / de yi nad g.yog byed par shog[339] / cas deng /

In Engaging in the Practices of the Bodhisattva it says:
For all beings that are sick, may I, until they are all healed, be their medicine, doctor, and nurse.[743]

d.div: [339] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la slob dpon zhi ba lha/ spyod 'jug /le'u/ 3_sh+loka7_shog_6_ba7
[743] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 3:7, Toh 3871, Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 6b7.

f.d:
mkhas pa skye dgu'i dpal gyis/
phyogs bcu'i 'jig rten thams cad du/ / sman dang sman pa dag dang yang / / nad g.yog mthun pa'i bza' btung sogs/ / yo byad kun tu 'gyur bar shog[340] / ces pa ltar

The scholar Kyegui Pal[744] also says:
In every realm of the ten directions may there be medicine, doctors, and nurses, suitable food, drink, and every provision.[745]
