[767] Twenty Verses on the Bodhisattva Vow (Bodhisattvasaṃvaraviṃśaka), Toh 4081 Tengyur, sems tsam, hi, 166b2.

f.d:
spyod 'jug las/
rtag par dge ba'i bshes gnyen ni/ / theg chen don la mkhas pa dang / / byang chub sems dpa'i rtul zhugs mchog / srog ga phyi+ir yang mi btang ngo /[359] / zhes dang /

In Engaging in the Practices of the Bodhisattva it states:
Never will I, though it may cost my life, give up the spiritual friend wise in the Mahayana and possessed of the supreme bodhisattva conduct.[768]

d.div: [359] sde dge_3871_bstan/ dbu ma/ la_slob dpon zhi ba lha'i/ spyod 'jug /le'u/ 5_sh+loka_102_shog_14_na5
[768] Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, 5:102, Toh 3871 Tengyur, dbu ma, la, 14a5.

f.d:
dbu ma bzhi brgya ba'i 'grel par/
bla ma slob ma'i bsam shes shing / / rjes su 'dzin par nus pa gang / / de yis slob ma bsdu bya yis/ / rmongs pas slob ma bsdu 'os min/[360] / zhes dang /

The Commentary on Four Hundred Verses says:
The guru who knows the minds of disciples and is capable of caring for them should gather disciples; the ignorant should not collect disciples.[769]

d.div: [360] sde dge_3865_bstan/ dbu ma/ ya_slob dpon zla ba grags pa/ bzhi brgya pa'i rgya cher 'grel ba/ rab byed/ 6_shog_110_na6_bla ma gang zhig bsam shes na/ /slob ma rjes su 'chos nus pa/ /de yis slob ma gzung bya ste/ /blun pos bco bar 'os ma yin//
[769] Candrakīrti, Catuḥśatakavṛtti, chap. 6, Toh 3867 Tengyur, dbu ma, ya, 110a6. Wording here differs slightly from the Tengyur.

f.d:
'dul ba 'od ldan du/
tshul khrims ldan zhing 'dul ba'i cho ga shes/ / nad par snying brtse 'khor ni dag pa dang / / chos dang zang zing phan 'dogs brtson pa ste/ / dus su 'doms pa de dag bla mar bsngags/[361] / zhes dang /

Vinaya Light states:
Those who are possessed of ethics, who know the rituals of Vinaya, who have compassion for the sick, whose entourage is without blemish, who are enthusiastic in benefiting with Dharma and with worldly goods, who teach at the right time, they are commended as gurus.[770]

d.div: [361] sde dge_4125_bstan/ 'dul ba/ shu_slob dpon shAkya 'od/ 'grel pa 'od ldan/ shog_155_ba6
[770] Śākyaprabha, Śrāmaṇeraprabhāvati, Toh 4125 Tengyur, ’dul ba, shu, 155b6.

f.d:
mngon rtogs rgyan skabs dang por/
sems mi 'gong ba nyid la sogs/ / ngo bo nyid med sogs don byed/ / de yi mi mthun phyogs bor ba/ / rnam pa kun tu yongs 'dzin yin//[362] zhes sogs mang kyang 'doms che ba mdo sde rgyan du/
bshes gnyen dul ba zhi ba nyer zhi ba/ / yon tan lhag par brtson bcas lung gis phyug / de nyid rab tu rtogs pa smra mkhas ldan/ / brtse ba'i bdag nyid skyo ba spangs la brten/[363] / zhes tshul khrims dang ldan pas dul ba/ ting nge 'dzin dang ldan pas zhi ba/ shes rab dang ldan pas nyon mongs pa nye bar zhi ba/ yon tan gzhan las khyad par 'phags pas lhag pa dang / gzhan don la le lo med pas brtson 'grus dang bcas pa/ thos pa che bas lung gis phyug pa/ shes par bya ba'i de kho na nyid rab tu rtogs pa/ tshig smra mkhas pa dang ldan pa/ zang zing la mi blta bas brtse ba/ chos ston pa la skyo ba med pa ste chos bcu ldan nam/

The first chapter of Ornament of Realization says:
With mind not discouraged and so forth, who teaches no nature and so on and dispels its opposing forces, is in all respects a guide and protector.[771] There are many similar citations, but they can be summarized by the verse in the Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
Rely upon a spiritual friend who is disciplined, pacified, well pacified, of exceptional qualities, who has perseverance, is rich in scripture, has insight into reality, is wise in words, is of a compassionate nature, and who has put all discouragement behind him.[772] Because he has ethics he is disciplined. Because he has meditative concentration he is pacified. Because he possesses wisdom he has well pacified the mental afflictions. Because his qualities are higher than others they are exceptional. Because he shows no laziness in working for others he has perseverance. Because of his great learning he is rich in scripture. He has gained insight into the nature of reality. He has great skill in speaking. He has a compassion that does not look to worldly gain. In teaching Dharma he is never discouraged. These are the ten qualities of a guru. Alternatively,

d.div: [362] sde dge_3786_bstan/ sher phyin/ ka_byams pa mgon po/ mngon rtogs rgyan/ skabs/ 1_sh+loka_37_shog_3_na7
[363] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_rje btsun byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 18_sh+loka_10_shog_25_ba2
[771] Maitreya, Abhisamayālaṃkāra, 1:37, Toh 3786 Tengyur, sher phyin, ka, 3a7.
[772] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra, 18:10, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 25b2.

f.d: byang chub sems dpa' thos mang dang / bden mthong smra mkhas brtse ba can/ / skyo med skyes bu dam pa ni/ / chen po yin par shes par bya/[364] / zhes lung gi yon tan thos pa mang ba/ rtogs pa'i yon tan bden pa mthong ba/ tshig smra mkhas pa/ bsam pa zang zing la mi lta ba'i brtse ba can/ bsam sbyor snyoms las med pas skyo med de chos lnga ldan/

he has the following five qualities:
The bodhisattva has much learning, sees the truth, is wise in words, has compassion, is not discouraged; such a holy one is truly a great being.[773] By his quality of knowing scripture he has much learning. By his quality of insight he sees the truth. He is skilled in speaking. In his thoughts he has the compassion that does not turn to worldly gain. In thought and deed he is not lazy and so is never discouraged.

d.div: [364] gong mtshungs/ le'u/ 14_sh+loka8_shog_18_na1
[773] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra, 14:8, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 18a1.

f.d:
yang na/
rgya che the tshom spong ba dang / / gzung 'os de nyid gnyis ston pa/ / 'di ni byang chub sems dpa' yi/ / ston pa phun tshogs yin zhes bya/[365] / zhes mang du thos pas thos rgya che ba/ shes rab che bas gdul bya'i the tshom spong ba/ sgo gsum dge bas bla mar gzung 'os pa/ nyon mongs pa dang rnam byang gi de kho na nyid ston pa ste

Also:
Vast, dispels doubt, worthy of regard, teaches two realities: this the perfect teacher of bodhisattvas.[774] Being very learned he has vast learning. Because of his great wisdom he dispels the doubts of disciples. Because he is virtuous in word, deed, and thought, he is worthy of being regarded as a guru. He teaches the reality of the afflictions and the path of liberation.

d.div: [365] gong mtshungs/ le'u/ 13_sh+loka5_shog_16_ba6
[774] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra, 13:5, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 16b6.

f.d:
chos ldan rnams phal cher 'phags pa'i chos yin pas ldan par dka' na'ang / med thabs dang bral ba ni gsum ste/ mkhas pa'i shes rab/ brtse ba'i bsam pa/ sbyor ba bzod pa ldan pa'o/ / de yang gang 'chad pa de'i tshig don lung rigs man ngag dang ldan pas gdul bya'i the tshom gcod nus pa'i bshad bya la mkhas pa/ rjod byed kyi brda dag pa dang / gang nas bshad kyang 'brel ba/ ji tsam bshad kyang ran pa/ ji ltar bshad kyang 'thad pa gsum gyis ngag 'brel/ gzhan dga' bar nus pa'i dbyangs snyan pa ste 'chad byed la mkhas pa'am/ mdo sde rgyan las/
le lo dang ni mi go dang / / skabs mi 'byed dang ma nges dang / / the tshom dag ni mi gcod dang / / de dang bral bar bstan mi byed/ / skye ba dang ni ser sna nyid/ / 'di dag gtam gyis nyes par 'dod/[366] / ces gtam gyi nyes pa brgyad dam/

These qualities are mostly found in ārya beings and so are difficult to find. However, there are three qualities that are essential: the wisdom of a scholar, an attitude of compassion, and activities endowed with patience. The first of these means being wise in the topic one is teaching and wise in the art of teaching itself. Wise in the topic means that its explanation possesses the support of scripture, reasoning, and oral tradition, by which one has the ability to remove the doubts of disciples. Being wise in the art of teaching means using clear and correct grammar and language; staying relevant to the topic at hand; teaching at a suitable depth and duration; and ensuring your words have relevance by evaluating them with the three criteria.[775] Moreover, the delivery should be elegant and inspiring, bringing joy to others. Alternatively, the wisdom of a scholar here could mean being free from the eleven faults taught in the Science of Explanation,[776] or from the eight faults of teaching listed in Ornament of Mahayana Sutras:
Lazy, unintelligible, not beginning the teaching at the correct point, unsure, unable to dispel doubts, unable to instill certainty[777] though teaching without doubt, becomes bored with teaching, is miserly in teaching Dharma: these are the faults of speech.[778]

d.div: [366] gong mtshungs/ le'u/ 13_sh+loka_12_shog_17_na3
[775] Inference, experience, and convention.
[776] Vasubandhu, Vyākhyāyukti, Toh 4061 Tengyur, sems tsam, shi, 63b6.

[777] In this line the word for certainty (brtan pa) is taken from Gyaltsap Jé’s commentary (p. 144). The Degé Tengyur and the root text as reproduced in Gyaltsap Jé’s commentary has brten (reliance), while both citations as quoted in our text have bstan (teach).
[778] Maitreya, Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra, 13:12, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 17a3.

f.d: rnam bshad rigs par skyon bcu gcig tu gsungs pa rnams bral ba/[367] rang dang / gdul bya/ snod gsum gyi kun spyod rnams la mkhas pa/

This quality could also refer to being free from the eleven faults taught in the Science of Explanation, where it means being wise concerning the three types of behavior in yourself and the disciples, likened to the three types of containers.[779]

d.div: [367] sde dge_4061_bstan/ sems tsam/ shi_slob dpon dbyig gnyen/ rnam par bshad pa rigs pa/ shog_63_ba6_1_snod ma yin pa la brjod pa'i skyon dang / 2_brjod pa yongs su ma rdzogs pa'i skyon/ 3_brjod pa bar chad pa'i skyon/ 4_brjod pa go bar mi byed pa'i skyon/ 5_brjod pa mchod par mi 'gyur ba'i skyon/ 6_don 'thad pa med par brjod pa'i skyon/ 7_spyod yul ma yin pa brjod pa'i skyon/ 8_rnam par g.yengs nas brjod pa'i skyon/ 9_dom med pa dang ldan pa brjod pa'i skyon/ 10_mi 'tsham par brjod pa'i skyon/ 11_nyon mongs pa can gyi bsams pas brjod pa'i skyon no//
[779] A dirty container, a leaky container, and an inverted container. See also the discussion of the three “pots” below on p. 471.

f.d:
gnyis pa brtse ba'i bsam pa ni/ 'jam dpal rnam par 'phrul pa'i mdo las/
chos ston kyang nyan pa po rnams la snying rje chen po mi bskyed pa ni bdud kyi las so/[368] / zhes pa ltar snying rje bskyed pa/

The second essential quality of a teacher is compassionate mind. In the Mañjuśrī Manifestation Sutra:
To teach but with no compassion for the listeners is the work of Māra.[780]

d.div: [368] sde dge_97_bka'/ mdo sde/ kha 'jam dpal rnam par 'phrul ba'i le'u zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ shog_251_ba6
[780] Mañjuśrīvikurvāṇaparivarta, Toh 97 Kangyur, mdo sde, kha, 251b6.

f.d:
sbyor ba bzod ldan ni/ 'chad dus kyi ngal dub dang dka' las la skyo ba med pa dang / slob mas dri ba/ gzhan gyis rtsod pa gsum la bzod pa dang ldan pa ste chos gsum ldan ni nges par dgos pa dang / spyir nang don rig pa gtso bor gyur pa la dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi yon tan thams cad dang ldan pa/ tha snyad rig pa spyi'i dbang du btang yang / dbyug pa can gyis/ mang du thos dang dri med dang /[369] / zhes gong du bshad pa bzhin gyi rgyu dang ldan pa/ gso ba rig pa rang nyid du gong bshad rgyu drug dang ldan pa dang / thu mis sum cu par/
gzhung nyid bla ma rnams la nyan/ / slob dpon de nyid du 'dzin cing /[370] / zhes gang slob pa'i slob dpon de dge ba'i bshes gnyen du 'dzin dgos par bshad/

The third quality, being endowed with patience, means not being discouraged by the hardships and fatigue experienced while teaching, and being patient with disciples’ questions and the arguments of others. These three qualities are essential requirements. Generally, the concept of the spiritual friend possessed of all excellent qualities found primarily in the inner, principal science of Buddhism can also apply to the other sciences. Daṇḍin talks of “being learned and without blemish,”[781] echoing the criteria discussed above. Here in medicine we talk of the six qualities needed to be a physician, as mentioned previously. Thumi Sambhota in his Thirty Verses says:
Listen to the texts from the lamas; hold them as your masters.[782] Therefore, in whatever subject they are teaching, masters who teach should be regarded as spiritual friends.

d.div: [369] sde dge_4301_bstan/ sgra mdo/ se_slob dpon dbyig pa can/ snyan ngag me long / le'u/ 1_shog_322_na1
[370] sde dge_4348_bstan/ sna tshogs/ co_slob dpon a nu/ lung ston pa'i rtsa ba sum cu pa/ shog_161_ba2
[781] Daṇḍin, Mirror of Poetics (Kāvyādarśa), chap. 1, Toh 4301 Tengyur, sgra mdo, 322a1.
[782] Vyākaraṇaliṅgāvataraṇa, Toh 4348 Tengyur, sna tshogs, co, 161b2.

f.d: 21. The Pratimokṣa Vows

de lta bu'i yul de'ang dkon brtsegs 'dus pa nyer gcig pa sgyu ma mkhan bzang po lung bstan pa'i mdor/
bzang po bzhi po 'di dag ni byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi spyod pa yongs su dag pa yin te/ bzhi gang zhe na/ sdom pa gsum yang dag pa dang / gnas yongs su dag pa dang / shes rab yongs su dag pa dang / skye ba yongs su dag pa ste bzhi po de dag yin no/[371] / zhes gsungs par sa skya paN+Di ta kun dga' rgyal mtshan gyis/
dad ldan sangs rgyas gsung bzhin sgrub 'dod pa/ / de la sdom gsum dbye ba bdag gis bshad/[372] / ces gsungs pa ltar sangs rgyas thams cad kyis gdul bya'i mos blo dang mthun par chos bstan pa las gdul bya dman par mos pa rnams la chags bral gyi spyod pas theg pa dman pa'i chos kyi 'khor lo ji snyed cig bskor ba thams cad kyis ni yon tan ma lus pa'i rtsa ba so sor thar pa'i sdom pas bsdus pa'i lhag pa tshul khrims kyi bslab pa gzhir byas te zhi gnas kyis bsdus pa lhag pa sems kyi bslab pa dang lhag mthong gis bsdus pa lhag pa shes rab kyi bslab pa gnyis kyis sems rnam par grol ba'i thabs ston/

In connection with such a person, the Prophecy of Bhadra Māyākāra Sutra from the twenty-first volume of the Heap of Jewels collection says:
Bhadra, these four provide for the purity of bodhisattva practice. What are they? They are the purity of the three vows, the pure place, a pure wisdom, and a pure birth.[783] On this topic Sakya Paṇḍita Künga Gyaltsen wrote:
For the faithful who wish to practice in accord with the words of the Buddha, I will explain the three divisions of vows.[784] All buddhas teach the Dharma in accordance with disciples’ mental faculties and dispositions. For those disciples attracted to the lower paths, the lower-vehicle wheels of Dharma were turned by way of teachings on conduct free of desire. All these turnings teach the foundation practice of the exceptional training in ethics—encapsulated in the pratimokṣa vows of liberation, the very root of all good qualities—and the two practices that form the actual means to liberation. These are the exceptional training in concentration, encapsulated in the practices for developing śamatha quiescence, and the exceptional training in wisdom, encapsulated in the practices for developing vipaśyanā exceptional insight.

d.div: [371] sde dge_65_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_sgyu ma mkhan bzang po lung bstan pa'i mdo/ le'u/ 21_shog_28_na1
[372] sa skya paN+Di ta kun dga' rgyal mtshan/ gsung 'bum/ tha sdom pa gsum gyi rab tu dbye ba'i bstan bcos/ shog_1_ba3_sa skya'i bka' 'bum pod lnga pa/
[783] Bhadramāyākāravyākaraṇa, chap. 21, Toh 65 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 28a1.
[784] Treatise on the Classification of the Three Vows. Collected Works of the Sakya, vol. 5, 1b3.

f.d: gdul bya rgya chen por mos pa rnams la theg pa chen po pha rol tu phyin pa'i chos 'khor bskor bas ni/ theg chen yon tan kun gyi rtsa ba sems bskyed cing byang sems kyi sdom pa gzhir bzung ste phar phyin drug la slob pa'i sgo nas byang chub kyi spyod pa yongs su rdzogs pa ston/

For those disciples disposed to the vast practices, the Perfection wheel of the Mahayana was turned. This turning taught the foundation practice of developing bodhicitta and the bodhicitta vows—the very root of Mahayana qualities—as well as the complete bodhisattva practices of training in the six perfections.

gdul bya zab mor mos pa rnams la 'dod chags kyi spyod pa'i sgo nas rgyud sde bzhi'i chos 'khor bskor ba thams cad kyis ni/ sngags kyi dngos grub kyi rtsa ba thun mong dang thun mong ma yin pa'i dam tshig dang sdom pa gzhir byas te/ drang don dang nges don gyi lha'i rnal 'byor yan lag dang bcas pas dngos grub rnam pa gnyis myur du 'grub par byed pa ston te rgyu mtshan des na sdom pa gsum dang de'i bslab bya la rdzogs par slob pa'i nang du ma 'dus pa'i sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa ni yod pa ma yin pas/ bdag legs su 'dod pa spyi dang khyad par dge ba'i bshes gnyen dag gis mi bsten du mi rung ba'i yan lag tu snang bas de gsum gyi rnam bzhag cung zad 'chad na/

For those disciples inclined to the profound, the Dharma wheels of the four classes of tantra were turned by way of the application of desire. These teachings revealed the foundation practice of the vows and the common and exclusive pledges—the root of all tantric siddhis as well as provisional and definitive deity yogas and their supplementary practices as means to develop swiftly the two kinds of siddhis. For these reasons, there is no doctrine of the Buddha not included within the three vows and the complete training in their commitments. Therefore, because it is recognized as being for the common good in general and because they are in particular indispensable endowments for spiritual friends, I will give a short presentation on these three.

rnal 'byor rgyud kyi bshad rgyud rdo rje rtse mo las/
so so thar dang byang chub sems/ / rig 'dzin sngags kyi sdom pa'o/[373] / zhes so thar byang sems/ sngags sdom dang gsum las/

In the explanatory Vajraśekhara Tantra it talks of the pratimokṣa, bodhicitta, and tantric vows:
The vows of pratimokṣa, bodhicitta, and vidyādhara mantra.[785]

d.div: [373] sde dge_480_bka'/ rgyud/ nya gsang ba rnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud rdo rje rtse mo/ shog_199_ba5
[785] Toh 480 Kangyur, rgyud, nga, 199b5.

f.d: sdom gsum gyi rnam gzhag las so thar gyi sdom pa/

dang po ni/ prA rab tu rdzogs pa la 'o'i byings la/ k+ti 'os/ k+ti byin/ ka yon tan 'gog pa'i don de phyis tshig phrad las a thung ngur byas pas pra ti dang po sogs la'ang 'jug mod de gtso bo so so/ muts-il grol ba'am thar ba la'o'i byings la/ un las sa 'os/ sa rkyen dang apa bi ka ra Na byin/ l-i rjes 'brel gyi phyis/ a pa bi ka ra Na'i yon tan gyi u o/ tsu'i ku'os/ tsa kar bsgyur/ ku i la la Sha ru byed de 'os/ sa Shar bsgyur drangs pas pra ti mo k+Sha so sor thar pa ste

“Prā means complete” is the root,[786] to which can be added the affix kti, because “kti is suitable,” (the kṛt affix kti can be added to roots to give the bhāva form). The particle k blocks the guṇa and so is elided. Because of the nipāta conjunction, the vowel a becomes shortened to leave prati, which can mean “first” and so on, but primarily it means “individual.” “Mucḷ means rescue or freedom.” This is the root. “From un, sa” (untraced). Therefore, the affix sa and vikaraṇa affix ap are added. The vowel ḷ is an anubandha connecting particle and so is elided. The ap vikaraṇa causes the vowel u to become its guṇa letter o. The c becomes k because “ku for cu” (formations ending in the ca consonant group that are roots meeting consonants from jha to sa, or that are nominal stems meeting consonants from ra to sa, become their equivalents from the ku consonant group). “From ku, i, la, sa becomes ṣa” (when gender endings of the consonants in the ka group, the eight vowels beginning with i, and the five consonants ha, ya, wa, ra, and la take a following sa, it becomes ṣa). Therefore, the sa becomes ṣa. This leaves pratimokṣa, meaning “individual liberation.”

d.div: [786] As in previous glossing of Sanskrit terms, the rules quoted are from Anubhūti’s Sarasvatī Grammar Sutra and their explanations in parentheses from the commentary by Troru Tsenam.

f.d:
sgra bshad kyi dbang btang na/ pra ti ni so so'am tha dad pa ste sdom pa thob pa'i tshe sdig pa'i chos kyi gnyen po skyes pas spang bya las rgyud so sor gyur ba'am 'gags pa'o/ / mok+Sha ni thar pa'am grol bar gyur ba ste dngos su sdig pa las thar zhing brgyud nas ngan song dang 'khor ba las grol ba 'di ni/ chos kyi rgyal mo'i mdo las/ so so thar pa zhes bya ba'i tshul khrims 'di bzung na/
mun pa las snang ba phrad pa dang mtshungs so/ / mi dbul pos nor rnyed pa dngam tshungs so/ / nad pas sman rnyed pa dngam tshungs so/ / btson khri mun nas phyungs pa dang mtshungs so/ / 'di ni thams cad kyi mkhan po chen po yin pas sangs rgyas 'jig rten na bzhugs pa dang mi mtshungs pa med do/[374] / zhes dang /

To explain this term by its etymology, the word prati means “individual” or “separate,” and when you receive the vows, the antidote to wrong activity is born, and so the mindstream rejects or separates from those traits to be abandoned. The term mokṣa means “liberation” or “to be freed.” Directly you find liberation from wrong activity, and gradually you are freed from the lower realms and samsara. On this point Buddha Vairocana’s Teachings on Bodhisattva Practice says:
Keeping to the ethics of this pratimokṣa is like moving from the darkness into the light, like finding wealth when poor, like finding medicine when sick, like being plucked from a dark prison. This is the great preceptor of all and is not unlike the Buddha abiding in the world.[787]

d.div: [374] sde dge_256_bka'/ mdo sde/ za chos kyi rgyal mo/ bam po+o/ 1_shog_74_na6
[787] Toh 256 Kangyur, mdo sde, za, 74a6. This text entered the Kangyur from the Chinese.

f.d:
tshul khrims yang dag par ldan pa'i mdo las/
ji ltar mig med gzugs mthong mi 'gyur ltar/ / de bzhin tshul khrims med na chos mi mthong / / ji ltar rkang med lam 'jug ga la nus/ / de bzhin tshul khrims med na thar mi 'gyur/[375] / zhes dang /

The Sutra of Pure Morality says:
Just as one without sight cannot see forms, one without ethics cannot see the Dharma. Just as one without legs cannot walk, one without ethics will not find freedom.[788]

d.div: [375] sde dge_303_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa tshul khrims yang dag par ldan pa'i mdo/ shog_127_ba2
[788] Śīlasaṃyuktasūtra, Toh 303 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 127b2.

f.d:
dge slong la rab tu gces pa'i mdor/
so thar tshul khrims 'di ni bde ba'i mchog / so thar tshul khrims 'di ni thar ba'i lam/ / so thar tshul khrims 'di ni yon tan zhing / / so thar tshul khrims 'di ni sangs rgyas rgyu/[376] / zhes dang /

In the Sutra on What Is Precious to a Monk it says:
These pratimokṣa ethics are the greatest joy, these pratimokṣa ethics are the path to freedom, these pratimokṣa ethics are excellent qualities, these pratimokṣa ethics are the causes of buddhahood.[789]

d.div: [376] sde dge_302_bka'/ mdo sde/ sa dge slong la rab tu gces pa'i mdo/ shog_126_ba6
[789] Bhikṣupriyasūtra, Toh 302 Kangyur, mdo sde, sa, 126b6.

f.d:
so sor thar ba'i mdo las/
sangs rgyas 'dul ba gangs can mtsho/ / gting mtha' med pa thams cad kyi/ / gnas pa'i snying dang snying po ni/ / so so thar pa 'di yin no/[377] / zhes dang /

In the Pratimokṣa Sutra:
The center and the very heart of the fathomless mountain lakes of the Vinaya of the Buddha is this pratimokṣa.[790]

d.div: [377] sde dge_2_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ca so sor thar ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 1_shog_1_na4
[790] Pratimokṣasūtra, Toh 2 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ca, 1a4.

f.d:
slob dpon chos kyi tshong dpon gyis 'dul ba la bstod pa las/
ji ltar 'di ni shing rtsa gtso bo ste/ / rnam par 'phel dang kun 'dzin gnyis kyi gzhi/ / de bzhin dam chos tshogs rnams kun gyi yang / / rgyu dang rtsa ba 'dul ba yin par gsungs/[378] / zhes dang /
rgyal ba ston pa de yi dam chos dag / mdo dang chos mngon yin gsungs 'dul ba ni/ / ston dang bstan bcos dngos yin de yi phyir/ / gnyis gyur phyag byas sangs rgyas khyod gcag bzhi+in/[379] / zhes mngon pa dang mdo sde'i sde snod kyis bstan pa'i go chod kyang ston pa'i go mi chod/

Dharmaśreṣthin in his Praise of Vinaya says:
Just as the roots of a tree are the foundation for its growth and for all it bears, so the roots and causes of all within the sacred Dharma is taught to be the Vinaya.[791] In the same work:
The teaching of the conquering Teacher is taught to be Sutra and Abhidharma. Vinaya is both teacher and teachings, therefore worthy of double reverence, like Buddha and Dharma as one.[792] In this verse the scriptural baskets of Abhidharma and Sutra serve as the teachings but not as the teacher.

d.div: [378] sde dge_4136_bstan/ 'dul ba/ su slob dpon chos kyi tshong dpon/ 'dul ba la bstod pa/ shog_133_na4

[379] sde dge_4136_bstan/ 'dul ba/ su slob dpon chos kyi tshong dpon/ 'dul ba la bstod pa/ shog_133_ba2_rgyal ba ston pa de yi bstan bcos dag /zhes dang / gnyis gyur phyag byas sangs rgyas chos gcig bzhin/ /zhes byung /
[791] Vinayastotra, Toh 4136 Tengyur, ’dul ba, su, 133a4.
[792] Ibid., 133b2. Last line read chos (Dharma) instead of khyod (you) as in Degé.

f.d: 'dul ba'i sde snod kyis gnyi ga'i go chod pas gzhan las phul du byung ba'i chos 'di'i brjod don dbye ba/ bsdu ba/ mtshan nyid/ go rim/ grangs nges/ sgra don dang sa bcad drug gis gtan la 'bebs pa la/

The basket of Vinaya, however, functions as both teacher and teachings. It is therefore an exalted topic, and its subject matter can be ascertained under six major outlines: 1. Divisions 2. Abridgement 3. Definitions 4. Stages 5. Fixed number 6. Etymology
dang po dbye ba ni/
Divisions

lung las/
rab byung gso sbyong gzhi dang ni/ / dgag dbye dbyar dang ko pags dang / / sman dang gos dang sra brkyang dang / / ko sham+b+hi dang las kyi gzhi/ / dmar ser can dang gang zag dang / / spo dang gso sbyong bzhag pa dang / / gnas mal dang ni rtsod pa dang / / dge 'dun dbyen rnams bsdus pa yin/[380] / zhes pa ltar gzhi bcu bdun yin la/

The Basic Vinaya states:
Ordination, purification ceremony, removal of prohibitions, summer retreat, animal hides, medicines, clothing, laying out the robes, Kauśāmbhi, formal acts, Pāṇḍulohita, persons, moving, removal from purification ceremony, dwelling places, arguments, and schism.[793] These are the seventeen foundations of Vinaya.

d.div: [380] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka lung gzhi/ bam po+o/ 1_shog_1_na4
[793] Vinayavastu, vol. 1, Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 1a5.

f.d: gnyis pa de bsdu ba ni/
Abridgements

rab byung gi gzhi'i sum cha dang / las dang gnas mal gyi chos ma thob pa thob par byed pa dang phyir bcos kyi gzhi bdun dang las kyis nyams na phyir 'chos pa dang / lhag ma rnams kyis thob pa mi nyams par bsrung ba ste gsum mam/ bslab pa yongs sbyong ba'i dang / bde bar gnas pa'i rkyen rten pa dang / thams cad 'grub pa'i dang / phyir bcos pa'i dang / thams cad kyi rten byed pa'i gzhi ste lngar bsdu/

These seventeen divisions can be condensed into three: 1. Ordination 2. Attaining clothing for the road and for dwelling, the seven reparation foundations, and repairing degeneration through formal acts 3. Guarding against degeneration by any of the remaining foundations Alternatively, they can be condensed into five: 1. Purification of broken commitments 2. Supports for living 3. Supports for accomplishing all 4. Supports for reparation 5. Supports for all
gsum pa mtshan nyid ni/
Definitions
'jug ldog gnyis kyi nang nas dang po gtso bor gyur pa'i tshul khrims ni brjod bya'i dang / de ston byed ni rjod byed kyi mtshan nyid do/ /

The definition of the subject matter that is taught is that from among the two ethical practices—adopting and discarding—it is primarily a practice of the first type. The definition of the actual teaching is the revealing of this subject matter
bzhi pa go rim ni/
Stages

ma thob pa thob par byed pa dang / thob pa mi nyams par bsrung ba dang / nyams na phyir 'chos pa rnams rab byung gi gzhi dang / bar skabs na shas che ba'i gzhi brgyad dang / tha mar shas che ba'i bdun rnams kyis ston pas rgyu 'bras kyi go rim mo//

One attains what has not been attained, then protects what has been attained, and then repairs, if necessary, what has been weakened. This initial stage is taught by the ordination foundation [and purification ceremony];[794] the next eight foundations constitute primarily the intermediate stages, and the remaining seven foundations constitute primarily a final stage. In this way the stages have a causal sequence.

d.div: [794] As the Great Fifth, Ngawang Losang Gyatso, points out in his Golden Victorious Myrobalan Vinaya Ceremonies commentary (6b6), this stage also includes the purification ceremony. In this way the count of the stages comes to seventeen.

f.d: lnga pa grangs nges ni/
Fixed number

gang zag gcig gis mngon mtho nges legs thob par byed pa la dang por bstan par ma zhugs pa 'jug zhugs nas bslab pa bsrung nyams na phyir 'chos pa rnams dgos pas gzhi bcu bdun las nyung na mi 'dus shing de tsam gyis dgos pa de phun sum tshogs par 'gyur bas mang mi dgos pa yin la/

For persons to attain the level of a high rebirth and the definitive happiness of nirvana, they must first enter into the doctrine as yet unentered. Having entered the doctrine, they have to guard their practices and when weakened repair them. Therefore, if there were less than seventeen foundations these stages would not be complete. With these seventeen the above requirements are met perfectly, and so more than seventeen is unnecessary.
drug pa sgra don ni
Etymology

lhag pa tshul khrims kyi bslab pa phun sum tshogs pa nyid du sgrub pa'i rten nam gzhir gyur pas gzhi zhes bya ba dang drug gi nang du 'dus pa'i rgyas bshad bdag gi bla ma nges pa don gyi sangs rgyas ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho'i las chog rnam rgyal gser mdog dang / 'jam mgon btsong kha pa'i bslab bya che chung / 'dul 'dzin grags pa rgyal mtshan/ thams cad mkhyen pa dge 'dun grub/ paN chen bsod nams grags pa'i yig cha sogs su blta bar bya la/

They are called foundations because they provide the foundations or supports for the perfect practice of the exceptional training in ethics. For a more extensive explanation of this topic, which here has been condensed into these six points, see the Golden Victorious Myrobalan Vinaya Ceremonies by my lama Ngawang Losang Gyatso, in reality the Buddha; the extensive and concise monastic advice of Mañjuśrī Tsongkhapa; and the works of Dülzin Drakpa Gyaltsen, the omniscient Gendün Drup, Panchen Sönam Drakpa, and others.

don nye bar bsdu na/ 'jam mgon btsong kha pa'i 'dul ba rgya mtsho'i snying por/
bsnyen gnas dge bsnyen pha ma dang / / dge tshul pha ma dge slob ma/ / dge slong ma dang dge slong ste/ / so so thar pa rigs brgyad do/[381] / zhes bsnyen gnas/ dge bsnyen/ dge bsnyen ma/ dge tshul/ dge tshul ma/ dge slob ma/ dge slong / dge slong ma rnams dang brgyad dam/ jo bo rje la sogs pa bsnyen gnas yun thung ba ma bgrangs pa'i so thar rigs bdun du bzhed pa yod pa/

The essentials of this topic are summed up in Mañjuśrī Tsongkhapa’s Essence of the Ocean of Vinaya:
The eight daylong upavāsa vows, the male and female upāsaka lay vows, the male and female śrāmaṇera novice monastic vows, the vows of the trainee śikṣamāṇā nun, the vows of the fully ordained bhikṣuṇī nun and bhikṣu monk: these the eight types of pratimokṣa.[795] This passage lists the eight types of pratimokṣa, which are those of the daylong upavāsa, the lay male upāsaka, the lay female upāsikā, the male śrāmaṇera novice monastic, the female śrāmaṇerikā novice monastic, the trainee śikṣamāṇā nun, the fully ordained bhikṣuṇī nun and the fully ordained bhikṣu monk. Alternatively, the master Atiśa and others list only seven kinds of pratimokṣa, omitting the daylong upavāsa vows because of their short duration.

d.div: [381] rje tsong kha pa'i gsung 'bum/ kha gsung thor bu/ 'dul ba rgya mtsho'i snying po bsdus pa/ shog_61_na5
[795] Collected Works, kha, miscellaneous, 61a5.

f.d: thams cad 'khor ba las nges par 'byung ba'i blos myang 'das don du gnyer bas blangs na so thar mtshan nyid pa dang / tshe 'dir nad dang rgyal po'i chad pa sogs las thar ba'i slad du blangs pa 'jigs skyob kyi tshul khrims dang / phyi mar lha mi'i bde ba tsam zhig don du gnyer bas blangs pa legs smon te phyi ma gnyis sdom pa nyi tshe ba yin la/

If all of these vows are taken with a mind wholly renounced of samsara that works for the attainment of nirvana, then they become true pratimokṣa vows. Taken for the purposes of this life, such as for freeing from illnesses or from the punishments of authority, they are known as ethics for protection from fear. Taken solely in pursuit of the pleasure of the gods in future lives, they are known as ethics aspiring to future benefit. These last two are vows of lesser significance.

de yang dge slong ni lus ngag gi mi dge ba bdun sdom ba'i spong bdun 'khor bcas sam gzhan du bshad zin pa'i khrims nyis brgya lnga bcu rtsa gsum/ dge tshul ni lus kyi gsum dang rdzun spong ba 'khor bcas sam spang bya rags pa bzhi bcu/

The fully ordained monk pledges restraint from the seven nonvirtuous physical and verbal acts[796] and other related nonvirtuous acts. These are known as the seven types of abandonment and their associates. Elsewhere these are described as the two hundred and fifty-three rules. The novice restrains from the three nonvirtuous physical acts and from the verbal act of telling lies, together with all associated acts. Alternatively, these are known as the forty coarse acts of abandonment.

d.div: [796] There are the three physical acts—mentioned several times below—of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and the four verbal acts of lying, gossip, slander, and harsh language.

f.d: dge bsnyen ni srog gcod lta bu gcig spong ba dang / ma byin len dang gnyis spong ba phyogs gcig spong ba dang / lus kyi gsum dang brdzun spong ba phal cher spong ba dang / chang dang lnga spong ba yongs rdzogs dge bsnyen spong ba dang / mi tshangs spyod spong ba tshangs spyod kyi dge bsnyen/

Lay practitioners who vow to refrain from one nonvirtuous act, such as killing, are known as single-abandonment upāsaka practitioners. Those who vow to refrain from two acts, such as killing and stealing, are known as partial upāsaka practitioners. Those who take vows against the three physical acts and the verbal act of telling lies are known as almost upāsaka practitioners. Those who add the vow of abstinence from alcohol are complete upāsaka practitioners. Those who take the vow of celibacy are known as celibate upāsaka practitioners.

dge tshul ma'i steng du chos drug dang rjes su mthun pa'i chos drug spong ba dge slob ma/ rin po che len pa ma gtogs dge tshul dang cha mthun bsnyen gnas rnams la sdom pa skye ba'i rgyu ni mdo sde pa sogs dud 'gror kyang skye ba mang yang 'dul ba lung dang mdo sde du mar bcom ldan 'das dang de'i nyan thos dag gis 'phrog ma dang 'brog gnas la sogs pa'i gnod sbyin pho mo du ma dang klu la dge bsnyen dang bsnyen gnas sogs kyi bslab pa la bkod par gsungs pa ni bar ma dge ba'am legs par spyad pa tsam la dgongs pa yin gyi/ sdom pa mtshan nyid pa skye ba'i rten ni gling gsum gyi skyes pa bud med gang yang rung ba las 'gro ba gzhan du ma yin par 'dul 'dzin kun bzhed pa mi 'dra ba med/

The trainee nun adds six root restraints and six associated restraints to the vows of a female novice nun. Apart from the proscription against accepting anything precious, the upavāsa vows correspond closely to those of the novice monastic. Concerning the conditions necessary for the growth of these vows, the Sautrāntika school and others talk of instances of these vows even taking root in animals. However, regarding the accounts in the Vinaya and the sutras of the Bhagavān Buddha and his śrāvaka disciples bestowing lay upāsaka and one-day upavāsa commitments on male and female yakṣa demons, such as Hārini and Gopāla, and on nāga serpents, this was done merely to develop some minor virtue or to bind them to good behavior. The type of birth needed for a true production of these vows is that of a man or woman from the three continents and not of any other form. All the great monastic scholars of Vinaya are agreed on this.

nang gses bsnyen gnas ni/ bye brag smra ba rnams dge slong las len dgos par bshad kyang 'dul ba lung nas khyim bdag mgon med zas sbyin gyis sdom pa 'phog par [382]gsungs pas so thar kho na dgos pa min la/ blang ba'i cho ga skyabs 'gro 'dzin pa sngon du 'gro bas khas len lan gsum byas pa las skye zhing / de mthar bslab pa brjod/ zla ba byung ngo cog gam lo gcig la sogs pa nya stong brgyad gsum la ma chag par byed na dus gcig du blangs pas kyang rung la/ nyin zhag ril po'am nyin mtshan so sor kyang khas len pa yod/ sdom pa'i spang bya rtsa ba bzhi dang / chang / gar sogs 'phreng sogs/ mal stan che mtho/ dus min gyi kha zas te brgyad du bzhed/

According to the Buddhist Vaibhāṣika schools, the upavāsa vows must be taken from a fully ordained monk. However, a Vinaya passage talks of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada giving the vows,[797] and so the presence of an ordained monastic is not always necessary. The ceremony for taking the vows consists of going for refuge followed by taking the pledge three times. Then the commitments are recited. If you have decided to keep the commitments on every fifteenth, thirtieth, or eighth day of the month for a whole month or for a year, and so on, it is acceptable to undergo just one ceremony for that whole period. You can take the vows for a whole solar day or you can regard night and day as separate. The eight acts to be abandoned under the vows are the four root acts; drinking alcohol; singing, dancing, and wearing jewelry counted as one; sitting on high seats; and eating at the wrong time.

d.div: [382] sde dge_1_bka'/ 'dul ba/ ka sman gzhi/ shog_304_ba2
[797] Basic Vinaya (Vinayavastu), Toh 1 Kangyur, ’dul ba, ka, 304b2.

f.d:
dge bsnyen ni/ ming chen gyi mdo las/
ming chen 'di ltar khyim pa gso dkar po bgos pa skyes pa pho'i dbang po dang ldan pa zhig sangs rgyas la skyabs su 'gro/ chos dang dge 'dun la skyabs su 'gro zhing bdag dge bsnyen du bzung du gsol zhes tshig tu smra na 'di tsam gyis dge bsnyen du 'gyur ro/[383] / zhes gsungs pa ltar nyi 'og pa sogs skyabs 'gro tsam gyis dge bsnyen du 'gyur bar 'dod pa dang / bye smra ba bslab pa lnga ga ma tshang na dge bsnyen mtshan nyid par mi bzhed pa sogs snang zhing / len pa'i cho ga dang por skyabs 'gro lan gsum/ de nas bslab pa brjod pa lan gsum/ de rjes bdag sna 'di tsam spyod pa'i dge bsnyen du slob dpon gyis gzung du gsol zhes brjod pas sdom pa skye/ ltung ba phra rags ni bsnyen gnas dang chos mtshungs la/ gtong ba'i rnam gzhag phal cher rab byung dang 'dra'o/ /

On becoming a lay upāsaka, the Mahānāman Sutra says:
Mahānāman, it is like this: the householder who wears the white clothes, has the marks of a male, goes for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and utters the words, “Accept me as an upāsaka”—by this alone he becomes an upāsaka.[798] In keeping with this passage, the Aparāntaka[799] Buddhist school and others assert that just by going for refuge one can become an upāsaka practitioner. For the Vaibhāṣika school, those who have not taken all five vows are not true upāsakas. The ceremony consists of going for refuge three times, reciting the commitments three times, and saying, “Master, accept me as an upāsaka practitioner who will practice just this conduct.” By this procedure the vows are generated. The coarse and subtle levels of the downfalls are similar to those of the upavāsa. The giving-up procedure is very similar to that of an ordained monastic.

d.div: [383] ming chen gyi mdo zhes pa 'di ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[798] Sutra untraced.
[799] Avantaka, nyi ’og pa; usually asserted to be a western division of the Vaibhāṣika school.

f.d: rab tu byung ba'i sdom pa tshigs snga phyi gnyis kyis ma thob pa thob pa byed pa la/ len pa po bu lon chags pa dang / bran dang / pha mas ma gnang ba dang / rgyal pos ma gnang ba sogs la sdom pa skyes su zin kyang / de dag gi dbang gis myur du 'bab dgos pas gnas la bar du gcod pa dang / skyes tsam nas skra ser po dang ser skyar 'dug pa sogs sdom pa skyes su zin kyang lus byad mi sdug pa'i rkyen gyis khyim pa rnams bstan pa la mi dad pa'i rgyu byed pas mdzes pa la bar du gcod pa dang / sdom pa skyes su zin kyang nad kyi dbang gis bslab pa sogs la sbyor mi bzod pas yon tan gong 'phel la khyad par du 'gyur ba'i gegs byed pa'i bar du gcod pa dang / mtshams med pa byas pa dang / za ma dang / ma ning dang / sprul pa dang / byang gi sgra mi snyan sogs 'gro ba rigs mi mthun pa sogs sdom pa skye ba la bar du gcod pa ste 'gal rkyen bar chad bzhi spangs shing / yul dang / rgyud dang / rtags dang / bsam pa dang / cho ga ste mthun pa'i rkyen lnga tshang ba zhig dgos pa las

There are four hindrances to the “attaining what is not attained” by way of the two stages of receiving ordination vows.[800] In the hindrance to duration, the recipient is in debt, is enslaved as a servant, does not have parental permission, or does not have permission from the king. In such cases, although the vows can be taken, they are soon lost. In the hindrance to attractiveness, the recipient is one born with white hair or with pale skin.[801] Here, the vows can be generated but the recipient’s unattractive appearance could hinder the laity from developing faith in the teachings. In the hindrance that is a specific obstacle to the development of qualities, someone may take the vows but through ill health is unable to fulfill the commitments. Hindrances to actually generating the vows includes various types of unsuitable recipients, such as those who have committed heinous acts, hermaphrodites, eunuchs, spirits, and those living in the northern continent of Uttarakuru. As well as being free from the above hindrances, you need the presence of five conducive conditions. These are place, continuity, signs, thought, and ceremony.

d.div: [800] The first of these refers to taking the upāsaka vows and the intermediate ordination of leaving the life of a householder. The second stage is the taking of the main vows.
[801] Usually explained as referring to albinos.

f.d: yul ni/ sangs rgyas kyi sku gzugs bzhugs pa/ dam pa'i chos ma nub pa/ zhu ba'i yul dge 'dun du longs pa sogs dang / mkhan po brtan pa'i yan lag bsnyen par rdzogs nas lo bcu phrag lhag pa lon zhing / 'dul ba'i tshig don la mkhas pa bsnyen par rdzogs pa ma yin/ mi 'dug par 'greng ba ma yin/ gang la bya ba ma yin pa sogs kha skong gi chos bcu gsum dang / lnga phrugs nyi shu rtsa gcig las gang yang rung ba rnams dang ldan pa dang / dge tshul gyi slob dpon de'i sdom pa 'bogs pa dang bslab bya brjod pa la mkhas pa/ gsang ston mkhan po'i tshig gis gsol ba btab pa khas blangs pa la dge 'dun gyis las kyis bskos shing lkog tu bar chad 'dri ba'i cho ga la byang ba/ las slob dge 'dun gyi dbus su las chog tshig phyed kyang ma 'khrul bar blo la thon pa rnams dang / yul dbus su bcu dang mtha' 'khob tu lngas nyung mtha' byas pa'i dge 'dun grangs tshang ba/

Place refers to places where the Buddha has appeared, where the Dharma has not disappeared. Place in the sense of “object” refers to a quorum of Sangha present to act as objects of request during the ceremony. The preceptor should fulfill the criterion of an elder by having been a fully ordained monk for more than ten years. The thirteen Sangha supplementary factors should be present, which include the monks present being fully ordained and learned in the Vinaya, not standing but sitting, not subject to actions such as punishment, and so on. At least one of the twenty-one sets of five criteria[802] should be fulfilled. The preceptor of the novice monk should be learned in giving the novice monk vows and explaining the commitments. The revealer of secrets preceptor is skilled in performing the ceremony of revealing hindrances to the ordination in a secret manner, and is ceremonially appointed by the Sangha after being verbally petitioned and then accepting the petition. There should be the ritual preceptor in the midst of the Sangha who knows by heart the words of the ordination ceremony and recites them without making the smallest mistake of even half a word. In a central land there should be a minimum of ten members of the Sangha present and in remote areas a minimum of five.

d.div: [802] These refer to sets of criteria necessarily fulfilled by the preceptors.

f.d: rgyud ni tshogs su tshang ba gang len pa'i sdom pa de sngar thob la nyams pa ma yin pa/
Continuity means that the vows to be taken should not have degenerated in those present.
rtags ni/ dge tshul la rab byung gi rtags dang cha lugs/ dge slong la chos gos gsum lhung bzed dang bcas mkhan pos byin gyis brlabs te tshul bzhin bskon pa/ khrus byas pa rnams dang ldan pa/

Signs means that the would-be novice monk should have all the signs of one to be ordained and be appropriately attired. The would-be fully ordained monk should have the three robes and the begging bowl blessed by the preceptor, and should be holding them correctly. He should also be washed and clean.

bsam pa ni rang bzhin du gnas pa/ sdom pa de bsam pa thag pa nas len pa 'dod cing / sdom pa thob dus shes pa nges 'byung gi bsam pas zin pa rnams dang ldan pa'i sgo nas bstan pa'i rtsa ba tshigs snga phyi'i sdom pa nges par thob pa zhig dgos/

Thought means that the mind is at ease, with a heartfelt desire to take the vows; the recipient knows that the vows have been received; and the mind is taken with thoughts of definite renunciation. With these conditions in place, there is a definite conferral of the vows of the earlier and later stages, the very root of the doctrine.[803]

d.div: [803] It is not clear if this sentence refers to ceremony, the last of the five conducive conditions. Normally, ceremony refers to the whole procedure consisting of preparation, actual ceremony, and conclusion. The earlier stages refer to the presence of the upāsaka and probationary vows.

f.d: thob pa mi nyams par bsrung ba ni/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen khyad par can la brten te bsrung ba/ rang gi bsam pa rnam par dag pa'i sgo nas bsrung ba/ bslab pa yongs su sbyong ba'i sgo nas bsrung ba/ bde bar gnas pa'i rkyen brten pa'i sgo nas bsrung ba/ mi mthun phyogs ngo shes par byas te bsrung ba ste yan lag lnga'i sgo nas bsrung ba yin la/

Protecting the received vows from degenerating is done by five methods: • Relying on a special spiritual friend • Maintaining a pure mind • Purifying the commitments • Living in conducive circumstances • Recognizing their opposing forces

de yang dge tshul ni bstan pa la zhugs kyang ma rdzogs pa yin pas bslab pa dang 'gal ba'i ltung ba la sde tshan rigs mi gcig pa du ma med kyi/ ltung ba thams cad nyes byas bya ba'i ming rigs gcig tu zad la/ dngos su blangs pa las 'das pa'i ltung ba sum cu rtsa drug las/ rtsa ltung bzhi pham pa dang 'dra ba'i nyes byas/ de dag dang chang spang sogs ltung ba phyed dang bco brgyad dge tshul la ltung med yin pas de dag ma gtogs pa dge slong gi bslab pa'i gzhi ji snyed yod pa de dag las dge tshul gyis 'das pa la yang bsdam bya'i nyes byas yin cing / dge slong gi bslab pa dang 'gal ba'i ltung ba ni pham pa dang / lhag ma dang / ltung byed dang / so sor bshags par bya ba dang / nyes byas te sde tshan lngar mtha' dag 'dus shing / bslab pa nyis brgya lnga bcu rtsa gsum gzhis bsdus kyi nyes byas dang bcas pa thams cad kyi bsrung mtshams dang ltung ba'i rgyu tshogs zhib par shes pa dgos/

The novice monk has entered the doctrine but not completely. Therefore, novice monk downfalls that contradict the commitments are not grouped under different headings but all fall into the single category of faults (nyes byas, duṣkṛti).[804] Of the thirty-six novice monk downfalls that transgress the vows taken, the four root downfalls are known as faults similar to the defeats (pham pa, parājita) of a fully ordained monk. These and the vow of holding on to robes and others that make up the seventeen and a half downfalls are non-downfalls for a novice monk. Apart from those, all novice monk transgressions of the commitments of fully ordained monks are known as faults to be restrained. The downfalls that transgress the commitments of a fully ordained monk can all be put into five groups: defeats, punishable by excommunication, those that cause downfalls, those to be declared, and faults. The two hundred and fifty-three commitments and their associated faults, the boundaries for protection of the vows, and the causes for downfalls should be studied in greater detail.[805]

d.div: [804] The downfalls of fully ordained monks, in contrast, are grouped under five headings.

[805] Although it is deemed inappropriate to make details of the vows and downfalls accessible to the general public, they can be found in the Pali translation of the Pātimokkha Sutta in Sacred Books of the East, vol. 13 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1881).

f.d: nyams pa phyir bcos la/ pham pa 'chab bcas kyis nyams pa ni/ shing ta la'i mgo bcad pa ltar chos 'dul ba 'di la skyer mi rung ba'i chos can yin pas ldang ba'i thabs kyi phyir bcos pa'i cho ga med cing / pham pa 'chab sems ma bskyed pas nyams pa man chod kyi ltung ba rnams las chog nas bshad pa ltar phyir 'chos par byed pa rnams dang ldan na dus dbang gi bslab pa sna gcig bsrung ba'i phan yon kyang bsam gyis mi khyab ste/

Concerning the restoration of generated vows: degeneration brought about by a defeat and intentionally concealed is like cutting the head off a palm tree and is described in the Vinaya as something that will not grow again. Therefore there is no procedure for restoring the vow in this situation. Degeneration brought about by a defeat that is free of any intention to conceal it—and all manner of downfall below that—is capable of being restored, as explained in the ordination ceremony. The benefits of keeping just one commitment at particular times are immeasurable.

ting 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo le'u so drug pa las/
bskal pa bye ba gang+gA'i bye snyed du/ / dad pa'i sems kyis zas dang skom rnams dang / / gdugs dang ba dan mar me'i 'phreng ba yis/ / sangs rgyas bye ba khrag khrig rim gro byas/ / gang gis dam chos rab tu 'jig pa dang / / bde gshegs bstan pa 'gags par gyur ba'i tshe/ / nyin mtshan du ni bslab pa gcig sbyod pa/ / bsod nams 'di ni de bas khyad par 'phags/[384] / zhes dang /
sngon gyis sangs rgyas bdag gis bstod pa yi/ / tshul khrims dri ma med pa sus bsrung ba/ / de dag gis ni sems can mang po yang / / dmyal ba dang ni sdig pa'i chos las 'dren/ / gang gis tshul khrims dri ma med/ / sangs rgyas bsngags pa bsrungs pa ni/ / de yis ji snyed sngon byung ba/ / bde gshegs thams cad ri mor byas/[385] / zhes dang /

The thirty-sixth chapter of King of Meditative Concentrations Sutra says:
For as many millions of eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, with a pure and joyful mind, one may revere and honor billions of buddhas with food, drink, parasols, and banners, garlands of lights and lamps; but for one who at the disintegration of the Dharma, when the teachings of the Tathāgata are lost, holds to just one commitment for a day and night, the merit is by far the greater.[806] Also:
Praised and exalted by the buddhas of the past, those who hold to flawless ethics will draw many beings away from hell and sinful acts. Those holding to the flawless ethics praised by the buddhas are venerating every tathāgata past.[807]

d.div: [384] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da ting nge 'dzin rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 36_shog_128_na6
[385] sde dge_127_bka'/ mdo sde/ da ting nge 'dzin gyi rgyal po'i mdo/ le'u/ 36_bam po/ 12_shog_127_ba2
[806] Samādhirājasūtra, chap. 36, Toh 127 Kangyur, mdo sde, da, 128b6.
[807] Ibid., 128b2. Wording in Degé is a little different.

f.d:
dkon brtsegs 'dus pa nyer gnyis pa lha'i bu ded dpon gyis zhus pa las/
gang dag sngon chad byung ba'i sangs rgyas dang / / gang dag ma byon 'byung dang bzhugs pa rnams/ / de dag skyon mang khab ni ma spangs par/ / bla med byang chub zhi ba thob pa med/ / rab byung de bzhin gshegs pa thams cad kyis/ / rab tu bstod cing bsngags la bkur ba ste/ / gang zhig sangs rgyas kun la mchod 'dod pa/ / rgyal ba'i bstan la rab byung gzung bar gyis/[386] / zhes sogs du mar gsungs pa ltar dang /

The Sutra Requested by Susthitamati Devaputra from the twenty-second volume of the Heap of Jewels collection says:
Buddhas who appeared in the past, those who have not yet appeared, and those who are presently appearing, do not gain the peace of enlightenment without abandoning many faults. Ordination has been praised by every tathāgata, and those who wish to please the buddhas should seize ordination in the Conqueror’s teachings.[808] There are many such passages.

d.div: [386] sde dge_66_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca chos 'phrul chen po bstan pa zhes bya ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 22_shog_48_ba2
[808] Susthitamatidevaputraparipṛcchā, chap. 22, Toh 66 Kangyur, bkon rtsegs, ca, 48b2.

f.d: byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa/
22. The Bodhisattva Vows

gnyis pa byang sdom ni/ sa paN gyis/
sems bskyed la ni nyan thos dang / / theg pa chen po lugs gnyis yod/[387] / ces sems bskyed la theg pa che chung gnyis kyi dman pa la dgra bcom rang rgyal sangs rgyas gsum gyi sems bskyed yod kyang de dag gangs can du ma dar/

Sakya Paṇḍita said:
Generation of the mind is of two kinds: that of the śrāvaka and that of the Mahayana.[809] Generation of the mind is found in both Great and Lesser Vehicles. The lower vehicle has a generation of the mind for an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, and a buddha, but this tradition did not spread to Tibet.

d.div: [387] sa skya paN+Di ta'i gsung 'bum/ na sdom gsum rab dbye/ shog_14_na6_sa skya'i bka' 'bum pod lnga pa/ na_shog_14_na6
[809] Treatise on the Classification of the Three Vows, Collected Works, na, 14a6.

f.d: theg pa chen po'i 'jug pa sems bskyed cho gas bzung nas byang sems kyi sdom pa mnos te tshul bzhin slob pa la bod kyi mkhas pa mang po mi pham 'phags pa thogs med dang dpal mgon klu ste shing rta chen po gnyis lta ba la dbu sems gnyis su bzhed pa ltar 'dir yang / mgon po byams pas/ bshes gnyen dul ba zhi ba nyar zhi+e ba/[388] / sogs dang / klus/ chog shes snying rje tshul khrims ldan/[389] / zhes sogs gsungs pas blang bya'i yul mi 'dra/ sems tsam pa/ so so thar pa rigs bdun gyi/ / rtag tu sdom gzhan ldan pa la/ / byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa yi/ / skal pa yod kyi gzhan du min/[390] / zhes byang sdom len rten la so thar rigs bdun gang rung dang ldan dgos pa dang / dbu ma pa 'gro ba rigs drug mtha' dag dang rgyal po nas shan pa'i bar thams cad la skye bar bzhed pas len pa'i gang zag mi 'dra bas mtshon/ blang ba'i cho ga / blangs nas bsrung tshul/ nyams na phyir bcos la sogs pa mi 'dra ba yod par gsungs kyang /

On the procedure for the ceremonial generation of the engaged bodhi mind of the Mahayana with its subsequent taking of the bodhisattva vows and their proper commitments, many Tibetan scholars maintain that just as Maitreya and Ārya Asaṅga on the one hand and the glorious protector Nāgārjuna on the other, whose traditions are renowned as the two great chariots, professed the two different philosophies of Cittamātra and Madhyamaka, so on this topic also there are different assertions. Firstly, scholars maintain, there are differences in the type of person from whom you take the vows, because on this point the protector Maitreya begins, “Rely upon a spiritual friend who is disciplined, pacified, well pacified…”[810] and so on, whereas Nāgārjuna says, “Content, compassionate, moral…”[811] and so on. On the type of person who can take the vows, the Cittamātra position is summed up in the verse beginning, “The seven types of pratimokṣa” up to “these are fortunate, others are not,”[812] meaning that the one who takes the bodhisattva vows must hold one of the seven pratimokṣa disciplines. According to a Mādhyamika, the vows can take root in any of the six types of sentient being and in any person from a king to a butcher. They assert that this demonstrates a difference between these two traditions concerning the type of being who can take the vows. They also maintain there are differences in the way you guard the vows and restore them if they degenerate. However,

d.div: [388] sde dge_4020_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_byams pa mgon po/ mdo sde rgyan/ le'u/ 18_sh+loka10_shog_25_ba2
[389] sde dge_4158_bstan/ skyes rabs/ ge_klu sgrub/ rin chen phreng ba/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka92_nas 93_shog_125_ba4
[390] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_jo bo rje/ byang chub lam gyi sgron ma/ sh+loka20_shog_239_na4
[810] Ornament of Mahayana Sutras (Mahāyānasūtralaṃkāra), 18:10, Toh 4020 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 25b2.
[811] Precious Garland (Ratnāvalī), 5:92, Toh 4158 Tengyur, skyes rabs, ge, 125b4. These two citations were quoted in full above.
[812] Atiśa, Light on the Path (Bodhipathapradīpa), v. 20, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 239a4.

f.d:
mkhas grub dge legs dpal bzang po'i sdom gsum rnam bzhag thub bstan byi dor du/
dang po kho nar blang ba'i yul mi 'dra ba'i tshul smras pa de mi 'thad de/ lung de gnyis tshig tha dad pa tsam du zad kyi/ des bstan pa'i dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi mtshan nyid cung zad rgyas bsdus ma gtogs don gcig tu snang ba'i phyir ro/[391] / zhes mi 'dra ba'i khyad par thams cad bkag cing /
de'i phyir 'phags pa klu sgrub dang thogs med gnyis cho ga'i yan lag 'ga' zhig mi 'dra ba ma gtogs sdom pa thob pa'i cho ga la don khyad par med cing / gzhan dag dbu ma lugs kyi phyogs su 'dod pa'i slob dpon dze ta ris kyang smon sems dang sdom pa zung ba'i rim pa gnyis mdzad la/[392] zhes gsungs pa ltar

Khedrup Gelek Palsangpo, in his Broom of the Buddha’s Precious Doctrine: A Brief Presentation on the Three Sets of Vows, refutes any suggestion of differences between the two:
Firstly, positing different types of person from whom one takes the vows is incorrect because the difference in those two passages is only in the wording. The definitions of the true spiritual friend they teach differ a little in terms of detail, but the meaning of each is the same.[813] Also:
Therefore, apart from differences in some secondary elements of the ceremony, the actual ceremony of taking the vows is essentially the same for the traditions of Ārya Nāgārjuna and Ārya Asaṅga. Ācārya Jetāri, whose assertions veered toward the Madhyamaka, also talked of the two stages of aspiring bodhicitta and taking the vows.[814] Therefore,

d.div: [391] mkhas grub dge legs dpal bzang gsung 'bum/ nya sdom gsum rnam gzhag thub bstan byi dor/ shog_71_ba4
[392] gong mtshungs/ shog_82_na6
[813] Collected Works, nya, 71b4.

f.d:
mdor bsdus na/ mi pham 'phags pa thogs med kyis byang sa'i tshul khrims le'u las/
ngo bo nyid dang thams cad dang / / dka' ba dang ni sgo kun dang / / skyes bu dam pa ldan pa dang / / de bzhin rnam pa thams cad dang / / phongs shing 'dod dang ldan pa dang / / 'di dang gzhan du bde 'gyur dang / / rnam par dag dang rnam dgu ste/ / mdor na tshul khrims de yin no/[393] / zhes spyi'i mtshan nyid de ngo bo/ dngos po'i dbye bas thams cad/ sgrub dka' ba la 'jug pas thun mong ma yin pa'i khyad par/ ji ltar 'jug pa'i dbye ba'i sgo/ byed pa po rten gyi khyad par skyes bu dam pa/ rnam pa'i rab tu dbye ba thams cad/ yul dang byed pa'i khyad par gyi phongs shing 'dod pa/ 'bras bu'i khyad par gyi 'di dang gzhan du bde ba dang / rnam par dag pa ste/

this topic is summarized by Maitreya and Asaṅga in the chapter on ethics from Stages of the Bodhisattva under nine categories, or outlines:
Nature, the whole, difficulty, entrances, the special being, all aspects, loss and want, happiness here and elsewhere, and purification: with these nine points is ethics summarized.[815] “Nature” refers to the general definition. “The whole” refers to all the divisions of the topic. As one is entering something difficult to accomplish, “difficulty” refers to the exclusivity of these ethics. “Entrances” describes the methods of entering this undertaking. “Special being” refers to the type of person undertaking these ethics. “Aspects” refers to all the aspects of ethics. “Loss and want” refers to features of objects and actions. Future results of this practice of ethics is happiness both “here” and “elsewhere” in future lives, as well as “purification.”

d.div: [393] sde dge_4037_bstan/ sems tsam/ wi_'phags pa thogs med/ byang sa/ le'u/ 10_bam po/ 8_shog_73_ba6
[815] Asaṅga, Bodhisattvabhūmi, chap. 10, Toh 4037 Tengyur, sems tsam wi, 73b6.

f.d: byang sdom la sa bcad [394] dam rnam grangs dgur bzhed pa'i tshul khrims kyi ngo bo la sdom pa nod pa'i yul/ len par byed pa'i gang zag / gang srung bar byed pa'i tshul khrims/ de nyid ji ltar srung ba'i tshul/ sdom pa gtong ba'i rgyu/ nyams na phyir bcos pa'i sgo rnams kyis gtan la 'bebs pa las/

Of these nine categories in this topic of ethics, general definitions consists of the following: • The object in front of which one takes the vows • The form of the person who takes the vows • The ethics to be guarded • The way to protect bodhisattva ethics • Causes for losing the vows • Ways to restore degenerated vows

d.div: [394] ma dper sa dpyad ces byung yang sa bcad yin nges pas de ltar bcos/

f.d: dang po sdom pa nod pa'i yul

d.i: The object in front of which one takes the vows

f.d:
['di ]la slob dpon yod pa dang med pa gnyis las/ dang po sdom pa nod yul smon sems bskyed pa/ byang sdom la gnas pa/ theg pa chen po la mkhas pa/ bslab pa nod par gsol ba 'debs pa la sogs pa'i ngag gi rnam par rig byed kyi tshig 'bru 'dzin nus shing don go ba las blang bar bya ste slob dpon tsan+d+ra go mis sdom pa nyi shu par/
byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi khrims/ / bsod nams kun gyi gter gyur gang / / de ni bsam pa dam pa yis/ / bla ma sdom la gnas shing mkhas/ / nus dang ldan las blang bar bya/[395] / zhes gsungs pa ltar byang sdom 'bogs pa'i mtshan nyid dang ldan pa'i bla ma'am/ de ma rnyed na byang sa las/
de bzhin gshegs pa'i sku gzugs de nyid kyi spyan sngar phyogs bcu'i sangs rgyas dang / byang chub sems dpa' bzhugs shing 'tsho ba thams cad kyi zhabs la gtugs te/[396] zhes pa ltar de bzhin gshegs pa shAkya thub pa la sogs pa'i sku gzugs kyi spyan sngar yan lag bdun pa sogs sngon du btang / rang nyid kyis phyogs bcu'i rgyal ba sras dang bcas pa la mkhyen par gsol te/ dus gsum gyi byang chub sems dpa' thams cad kyi bslab pa'i gzhi mtha' dag la slob par khas len pa lan gsum gyis len par bya ba yin la/

This procedure can be undertaken in the presence of a master or without a master. In the first scenario, you take the vows from someone who themselves have generated the aspiring bodhicitta, who keeps the bodhicitta vows, who is wise in the Mahayana, who has memorized and can recite and enunciate the words of the ceremonial requests for the commitments and so on, and who is understandable. Ācārya Candragomin says in his Twenty Verses on the Bodhisattva Vow:
The vows of the bodhisattva, a veritable treasure of every merit, are taken with the highest of minds from a guru dwelling in the vows who is wise and capable.[816] Therefore, the vows are taken from a guru fully qualified to bestow them. If such a lama cannot be found, Stages of the Bodhisattva says:
In front of an image of the Tathāgata, touch your head to the feet of the buddhas and bodhisattvas living and dwelling in the ten directions.[817] Therefore, in front of an image such as that of Buddha Śākyamuni, you first perform the seven-branch practice and so on, and then ask the conquerors and their sons of the ten directions to hear your words; you pledge three times to train in the foundations of every practice of all bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future. In this way, you take the vows.

f.d: len pa'i rten nam gang zag kyang

d.i: The form of the person who takes the vows

f.d: rgya gar gyi grub chen dze ta ris/ rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo rten dang bsam pa phun sum tshogs pa dang ldan pas/[397] zhes gsungs pa ltar lha dang klu la sogs pa rten de la rdzogs pa'i byang chub don gnyer gyi sems bskyed rung ba thams cad smon sems len pa tsam gyi rten du rung yang / byang sems kyi sdom pa'i dngos rten mtshan nyid tshang bar song ba'i smon sems cho gas 'dzin pa'i rten la ni/ skyes bu chung 'bring dang thun mong gi bsam pa dang man ngag rgyu 'bras bdun la sogs pa la legs par blo sbyangs pas/ byang chub kyi sems la yid 'gyur ba'i myong ba sna zin rgyud la skyes pa yan chad gcig dgoszhes mkhas grub rje gsung la/[398]

The Indian siddha Jetāri states: “A son or daughter of the family, with the perfect form and the perfect mind….”[818] Therefore, the forms of gods, nāgas, and so on, in which the mind striving for full enlightenment can be generated, are suitable simply for the generation of the aspiring bodhicitta. However, those forms of living beings grasped by the ceremony of aspiring bodhicitta, and who are fully qualified for the taking of the bodhicitta vows, will have, at the very least, states of mind in common with the paths of the lower and intermediate scopes, a mind well trained in the seven cause-and-effect transmitted instructions, and so forth, by whose power some mind-affecting experience of bodhicitta has grown within their being.[819] This is the position of Khedrup Jé.

d.div: [397] sde dge_3968_bstan/ dbu ma/ gi_slob dpon dgra las rnam rgyal/ byang chub kyi sems blang ba dang yi dam blang ba'i cho ga_shog_242_ba5
[398] mkhas grub dge legs dpal bzang po'i gsung 'bum/ nya sdom gsum rnam gzhag thub bstan byi dor/ shog_64_ba1
[818] Rituals for Taking the Bodhisattva Vows and Meditation Deity (Bodhicittotpādasamādānavidhi), Toh 3968 Tengyur, dbu ma, gi, 242b5.

[819] Broom of the Buddha’s Precious Doctrine, Collected Works, nya, 64b1. The “seven cause-and-effect transmitted instructions” refers to the tradition of developing bodhicitta involving the six causes of recognizing living beings as your mothers, remembering their kindness, resolving to repay that kindness, developing affectionate love, developing compassion, and developing the special attitude, followed by the result of bodhicitta.

f.d:
jo bo a ti shas lam sgron du/
so so thar ba'i rigs bdun gyi/ / rtag tu sdom gzhan ldan pa dang / / byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa yi/ / skal ba yod kyi gzhan du min/[399] / zhes pa 'di la/ 'jam mgon btsong kha pa chen pos byang chub gzhung lam du/
zhes gsungs pa yang las dang po pa la so thar rigs bdun gang rung med na tshul khrims kyi sdom pa khyad par can skye ba'i skal ba med la so thar rigs bdun dang thun mong ba rang bzhin spong ba med na byang sems kyi sdom pa tsam skye ba med ces ston pa yin gyi/ so thar rigs bdun mtshan nyid pa gcig med na byang sems kyi sdom pa mi skye bar bzhed pa min te/[400] zhes lam sgron 'grel pa dang / thub dgongs 'dren par mdzad la/

In Light on the Path by the master Atiśa it says:
Those who possess without break vows of seven types of pratimokṣa have the good fortune for bodhisattva vows; others do not.[820] On this verse Mañjuśrī Tsongkhapa, in conjunction with citations from [Atiśa’s] Autocommentary on Light on the Path to Enlightenment and [Abhayākaragupta’s] Ornament to the Thought of the Buddha, says in his Highway to Enlightenment: An Exposition of Bodhisattva Ethics:
This has been stated. However, what it means is that if a beginner does not possess any of the seven pratimokṣa vows, he does not have the good fortune to develop any exceptional vow based upon ethics; and if he does not possess any natural abandonment[821] in common with the seven types of pratimokṣa vows, then he does not have the good fortune simply to develop the bodhisattva vows. It does not mean that if he is not a qualified holder of the seven pratimokṣa vows he cannot develop the bodhisattva vows.[822]

d.div: [399] sde dge_3947_bstan/ dbu ma/ khi_jo bo rje/ byang chub lam gyi sgron ma/ sh+loka20_shog_239_na4
[400] rje tsong kha pa chen po'i gsung 'bum/ ka tshul khrims kyi rnam bshad byang chub gzhung lam/ shog_10_na2
[820] Bodhipathapradīpa, v. 20, Toh 3947 Tengyur, dbu ma, khi, 239a4.
[821] If by his nature he does not kill, steal, and so on.
[822] Collected Works, ka, 10a2.

f.d:
gzhan yang de ltar na lha la byang sdom mi skye bar bzhed dgos kyang / der byang sdom skye ba shing rta chen po gnyi ga dgongs pa mthun cing 'khor lo bsgyur ba'i rgyal po la byang sdom skye ba bka' bstan du ma las bshad mod de/ de la dge bsnyen dang yan lag brgyad pa la sogs pa'i so thar yod du zin kyang de las dman pa/ mdo sde bskal pa bzang po las/
rgyal ba phan bzhed grong dpon gyur pa'i tshe/ / de bzhin gshegs pa rin chen dpal de la/ / nyin gcig srog gcod sdom pa blangs nas su/ / dang por byang chub tu ni sems bskyed de/[401] / zhes dang /

Also, if that were its meaning, you would have to accept that this statement means that bodhisattva vows could not develop in gods. However, on this point, both great chariot traditions are in agreement, and there are many accounts in the scriptures and canonical treatises of universal sovereigns generating the bodhisattva vows. Even though these beings may have already possessed various pratimokṣa disciplines, such as the lay upāsaka vows or the eight daylong restraints, these vows were seen as inferior to their receiving the bodhisattva vows. The Sutra of the Good Eon states:
When the conqueror Hitaiṣin became a local governor and vowed in the presence of Tathāgata Ratnaśrī to restrain from killing for a day, he first generated the mind of enlightenment.[823]

d.div: [401] sde dge_94_bka'/ mdo sde/ ka 'phags pa bskal ba bzang po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ bam po/ 23_shog_293_ba2_de bzhin gshegs pa phan bzhed grong dpon bur gyur tshe/ /de bzhin gshegs pa bsod nams 'od ces bya ba las/ /nyin gcig srog gcod spong ba'i bslab gzhi mnos nas kyang / /dang po byang chub tu ni sems bskyed do//
[823] Bhadrakalpika, fascicle 23, Toh 94 Kangyur, mdo sde ka, 293b2. Degé reading preferred.

f.d: de bzhin du bdag cag gi ston pas kyang drin lan bsab mdor/ dmyal ba'i shing rta 'dren pa'i gyad du gyur dus grogs kyi sdug bsngal la bsam te byang sems 'khrungs pa/[402] phung po gsum par tshong dpon gyi bu mngon dga'i dus dang /[403] bskal bzang du dman pa zhes mu to ba lta bu/ 'dul bar rgyal po 'od ldan dang / rdza mkhan yangs pa'i 'od/ myang 'das su dbul po/ snying rje pad dkar du rgyal po rtsibs kyi mu khyud kyi mdun na 'don bram ze rgya mtsho'i rdul rnams su gyur dus thugs bskyed pa dang /[404] spyan ras gzigs la mtshon na/ sgyu ma lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin mdor rgyal po dpal gyi gzi brjid kyi glo g.yas g.yon nas rdzus skyes kyi khye'u rin chen mchog dang /[405] chos dang don rnam par 'byed pa'i mdor 'khor lo bsgyur ba'i rgyal po rgyal ba thob kyi btsun mo rin chen dpal gyi pang pa nas brdzus te skyes pa khye'u rin chen 'byung gnas su gyur dus thugs bskyed par bshad pa sogs/[406]

Similarly, the Sutra of Repaying the Kindness recounts how when our Teacher was born as a brave being forced to drag a cart in the hell realms, he thought of the suffering of his companion and the mind of enlightenment was born within him.[824] Also when born as the merchant’s son Abhinanda, as retold in the Sutra of the Three Heaps;[825] or as Mutoba in Sutra of the Good Eon; as King Prabhāvati and as the potter Vipulaprabhā in the Vinaya; as the beggar in the Great Nirvana Sutra; and as the brahman Samudrarajas, minister of King Aranemi, in the White Lotus of Compassion Sutra:[826] in all these accounts he developed the bodhi mind. The same point can be illustrated using Avalokiteśvara. In the Illusion-Like Samādhi Sutra he was miraculously born as the son Ratnottama from the left and right lungs of king Śrītejas.[827] In the Differentiating the Dharma and the Meaning Sutra he was miraculously born from the lap of Ratnaśrī, queen of Cakravartin Jayin, to become the son Ratnasambhava.[828] At these times too he developed the bodhi mind.
