The pratimokṣa, with its aspect of relinquishing harming others, and the aspect of engaging in the welfare of others found in the bodhisattva vows are both complete and intact within the skillful means of effortlessly accomplishing the welfare of others that arises from the sphere of the great equalizing wisdom of the tantric vows. Moreover, it is explained that by becoming higher in terms of substance, these two vows have changed their status to become the substance of the tantric vows.
so thar dang byang sdom gang las len pa'i rten/

d.i: Who can give the pratimokṣa and bodhisattva vows?

f.d: so thar gyi sdom pa 'bogs pa'i mkhan pa'o_nga gcig rang du ma nges te/ 'dul ba lung du khyim bdag mgon med zas sbyin gyis bsnyen gnas kyi sdom pa 'bogs pa'i mkhan po byas par bshad pa dang / dkon brtsegs drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i le'u bam po gnyis pa las/[531]

It cannot be said with any certainty that there is only one kind of preceptor who necessarily bestows the pratimokṣa vows, because in the Vinaya there is reference to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bestowing full monastic vows. Also in the third fascicle[973] of the Sutra Requested by the Householder Ugra from the Heap of Jewels collection:

d.div: [531] ma dper bam po gsum par gsungs kyang / sde dge bka' 'gyur dkon brtsegs nang bam po gnyis par 'dug pas bcos/
[973] In Degé found in fascicle 2.

f.d: de nas bcom ldan 'das kyis byang chub sems dpa' byams pa dang / byang chub sems dpa' spyod pa thams cad rnam par dag pa la 'di skad ces bka' stsal to/ / skyes bu dam pa khyod gnyis kyis bdag 'di rnams rab tu byung la bsnyen par rdzogs par gyis shig ces bcom ldan 'das kyis gnang nas/ byang chub sems dpa' byams pas khyim bdag dgu stong rab tu byung ngo / / byang chub sems dpa' spyod pa thams cad rnam par dag pas ni khyim bdag bdun stong rab du byung ngo /[532] / zhes byang sems de gnyis khyim pa'i cha byad can yin kyang bsnyen rdzogs kyi mkhan po mdzad pa gsal bar byung la/ dge slong zhes pa'ang dbu zlum zhabs rjen chos gos rnam gsum 'chang ba kho na la 'dod mi nus pa yang /

Then the Bhagavān Buddha said to bodhisattva Maitreya and bodhisattva Viśuddha, “You great beings, ordain these householders with the full monastic vows.” With the permission of the Bhagavān Buddha, the bodhisattva Maitreya and the bodhisattva Viśuddha performed the ordination. The bodhisattva Maitreya ordained nine thousand householders, and the bodhisattva Viśuddha ordained seven thousand householders.[974] Therefore, although these bodhisattvas were in the form of householders, they clearly acted as preceptors for ordination. Also the term “monk” cannot be applied solely to those with shaven heads, bare feet, and wearing the three robes.

d.div: [532] sde dge_63_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga khyim bdag drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_275_ba5
[974] Ugraparipṛcchā, Toh 63 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 275b5.

f.d:
sa'i snying po 'khor lo bcu pa'i mdo las/
rigs kyi bu gzhan yang dge slong rnam pa bzhi yod de/ bzhi gang zhe na/ don dam pa'i dge slong dang / kun rdzob kyi dge slong dang / lug lkug pa lta bu'i dge slong dang / khrel ba dang ngo tsha ba med pa'i dge slong ngo / / de la ji ltar na don dam pa'i dge slong gang zhe na/ 'di lta ste/ sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das sam/ byang chub sems dpa' chen po'i dge slong yon tan chen po dang ldan pa chos thams cad la dbang du gyur ba'am/ rang sangs rgyas kyi byang chub bam/ dgra bcom pa'am/ phyir mi 'ong ba'am/ lan cig phyir 'ongs pa'am/ rgyun du zhugs pa ste/ gang zag rnam pa bdun po 'di dag ni don dam pa'i dge slong du bsdu ba dang / skye bo gang khyim na gnas shing skra dang kha spu yang ma bregs/ chos gos kyang mi gyon/ rab tu byung ba so sor thar pa'i tshul khrims thams cad kyang ma mnos/ gsol ba dang / zhu ba'i las dang / gso sbyin dang / tshul gyi las thams cad kyi nang du mi chud mod kyi/ 'phags pa'i chos dang ldan la 'phags pa'i 'bras bu thob pas na de yang don dam pa'i dge slong du bsdus te/ de dag ni don dam pa'i dge slong zhes bya'o/ /

In the Ten Cakra Kṣitigarbha Sutra it says:
Son of the family, furthermore, there are four kinds of monk. What are they? They are the ultimate monk, the conventional monk, the monk like a stupid sheep, and the shameless and immodest monk. Who is the ultimate monk? The Bhagavān Buddha, the great bodhisattva monk possessed of great achievements, with control over all phenomena, or those of pratyekabuddha enlightenment, the arhat, the nonreturner, the once-returner, and the stream enterer: these seven types of being make up the category of ultimate monk. Also, those beings who live in houses, do not shave their heads and their beards, do not wear the three robes, have not taken all the monastic pratimokṣa ethics, do not take part in requesting, ceremonies, purification rituals, and monastic activities: if they possess the dharmas of the āryas and they possess the fruits of those dharmas, they are also known as ultimate monks. This is the meaning of being an ultimate monk.

d.div: de la ji ltar na kun rdzob kyi dge slong gang zhe na/ skra dang kha spu bregs te gos ngur smrig gyon cing rab tu byung la so sor thar pa'i tshul khrims dang ldan na de ni kun rdzob kyi dge slong zhes bya'o/ / de la ji ltar na lug lkug pa lta bu'i dge slong gang zhe na/ rtsa ba'i sdig la sogs pa nyams sam ma nyams sam mi shes/ lci ba'am yang ba yang mi shes/ nyes pa phra mo rnam pa sna tshogs byas kyang 'gyod cing 'thol mi shes/ nyes pa byas pa la bla gyid [533] byed cing sdig pa phra mo la mi lta mi 'jigs mkhas pa'i skyes bu la ni mi bsten/ skabs skabs su mang du thos pa shes rab dang ldan pa la bsnyen bkur dang / g.yog kyang mi byed/ bsti stang dang bcas te zhu zhing 'dri yang mi shes/ dge ba ni gang / sdig pa ni gang / sdig pa med pa ni gang gang byas na legs/ gang byas na ma legs pa yang zhu ba dang 'dri ba mi byed pa'i gang zag de dag ni lug lkug pa lta bu'i dge slong du bsdus te/ lug lkug pa lta bu'i dge slong zhes bya'o/ /

What is a conventional monk? He who shaves his head and beard, dons the orange robes, and goes forth to become endowed with the pratimokṣa ethics is a conventional monk. Who is the monk like a stupid sheep? He is ignorant of whether he has weakened his root vows or not. He is ignorant of whether the fault is heavy or light. Although he incurs various small breaches, he shows no remorse and does not declare them. He does not think about the faults he commits and pays no heed and has no qualms over minor faults. He does not devote himself to wise beings. He does not, from time to time, honor or serve the learned and those of great wisdom. He does not approach them respectfully and ask them questions. He does not ask, “What is good? What is bad? What is not bad? Why is this good? Why is this wrong?” Such a person is a monk like a stupid sheep.
[533] bla col byed cing / mtsho sngon deb dpar/

de la ji ltar na khrel ba dang / ngo tsha ba med pa'i dge slong gang zhe na/ sems can gang 'tsho ba tsam gyi phyir nga'i bstan pa la phyogs te rab tu byung ngo / / rab tu byung ngo / / so sor thar pa'i tshul khrims bsrung ba thams cad nyams te khrel ba dang ngo tsha ba med la/ 'jig rten phyi ma'i sdug bsngal gyi 'bras bu la mi lta/ mi 'jigs/ khong rul cing btsog pas gang ba'i srin kA lA 'dra ba/ dung gi sgra la khyi'i spyod pa dang ldan pa/ rtag tu rdzun smra zhing bden pa'i tshig med pa ser sna dang / phrag dog dang / gti mug dang / nga rgyal gyis mngon par zin te las kyi mchog dam pa gsum las ring du gyur pa/ khe dang bkur sti dang / grags pa la chags te yul drug la mos pa/ 'dod chags kyis g.yengs pa gzugs dang / sgra dang / dri dang / ro dang / reg bya'i yul la chags pa'i gang zag de dag ni khrel ba dang / ngo tsha ba med pa dam pa'i chos la 'phya zhing skur ba'i nang du bsdus te/ de ni khrel ba dang ngo tsha ba med pa'i dge slong zhes bya'o/[534] /

Who is the shameless and immodest monk? He approaches and is ordained into my doctrine merely for a livelihood, is without shame, breaks all the ethics of the pratimokṣa, and pays no heed to and has no fear of the suffering coming in the next life. Full of filth and decay, he is like the kāla worm.[975] He behaves like a dog at the sound of the conch. He constantly lies and does not know words of truth. He is in the grip of miserliness, jealousy, and ignorance, and is far from the three supreme activities. Attracted to gain, honor, and reputation, he delights in the six objects of the senses. Distracted by desire he is drawn to objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Such a person is shameless and immodest and is included among those who ridicule and slander the holy Dharma. This is the shameless and immodest monk.[976]
[534] sde dge_239_bka'/ mdo sde/ zha_'dus pa chen po las sa'i snying po 'khor lo bcu pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ le'u/ 3_shog_138_ba7_'di yin nam snyam tshig ji bzhin ma brnyed/
[975] Srin kālā. Possibly sṛkāla (“jackal”).
[976] Daśacakrakṣitigarbha, chap. 3, Toh 239 Kangyur, mdo sde, zha, 138.

f.d:
zhes da lta dge slong rnam dag tu 'dod pa 'di dag kun rdzob dang don dam pa'i dge slong ni 'phags pa'i chos dang ldan zhing de'i 'bras bu thob pa zhig la gsungs pas na/ dpal mgon 'phags pa klu sgrub bsnyen par rdzogs pa'i mkhan po 'dul ba rgya mtsho'i pha rol tu son pa sa ra has/
mda' mkhan ma phyag rgyar zhes te/ kha sang phan chad dge slong min/ / de ring tshun chad dge slong yin/[535] / zhes pa 'di lta bu 'phags yul gyi paN grub du ma'i rnam thar du 'byung zhing /

Therefore, those we assert these days to be pure monks are conventional monks, while ultimate monks are taught to be those endowed with the Dharmas of the āryas and the fruits of those Dharmas. Because of this, Saraha, preceptor for the full ordination of the glorious guide Ārya Nāgārjuna and one who had already crossed the vast ocean of Vinaya, said:
Taking the arrow maker’s daughter as consort, until yesterday I was not a monk; from today onward I am a monk.[977] Similar statements can be found in many biographies of Indian pandit practitioners.

d.div: [535] sa ra has/ mda' mkhan ma phyag rgyar bzhes te/ kha sang phan chad dge slong min/ / zhes sogs kyi gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[977] Untraced. In this discussion on what constitutes being a monk, the term used is dge slong, bhikṣu.

f.d:
gangs can 'dir yang rwa lo tsA ba rdo rje grags pas/
sha chang bza' ba tshogs kyi 'khor lo yin/ / dam nyams gsod pa sngags kyi dam tshig yin/ / bud med bsten pa las kyi phyag rgya yin/ / nga yis de ltar shes pa'i gnas skabs na/ / 'dul 'dzin dge slong dag dang 'gal ba med/[536] / ces gsungs shing /

Here in Tibet, too, Ra Lotsāwa Dorjé Drakpa (1016–1198) said:
Partaking of meat and alcohol is the ceremonial feast, killing those who break their vows is a tantric pledge, relying upon women is karmamudrā: when I came to understand this, it did not conflict with being a Vinaya-holding monk.[978]

d.div: [536] rwa ye shes seng+ges ya ge+i bkod pa/ rwa lo tsA ba'i rnam thar/ shog_267_phreng 9
[978] Found in Biography of Ra Lotsāwa by Ra Yeshé Sengé, p. 267.

f.d: de mtshungs zhang 'gro ba'i mgon po g.yu brag pa dang bo dong paN chen 'jigs bral rtag brtan sprul pa'i sku kun dga' snying po sogs phyi ngur smrig bla gos kyis mdzes kyang nang phyag rgya chen po'i ye shes kyi rgyud gtams pa sha chang bud med la longs spyod bzhin du gdul bya rnams rjes su 'dzin pa'i phyir bsnyen rdzogs kyi mkhan po mdzad pa sogs mnyam rjes mi 'gal ba'i skyes chen du ma zhig byon pa'ang gong gi lung don rnams dang mtshungs sam snyam la/

Similarly, there were many other great beings, such as the Shangdro abbot Yudrakpa,[979] Bodong Paṇchen Jikdral,[980] and the Takten incarnation Künga Nyingpo,[981] who externally were adorned with the red robes, but internally their minds were integrated with the gnosis of the mahāmudrā, and they were able to make use of meat, alcohol, and women while at the same time acting as ordination preceptors in order to develop and take care of their disciples. These beings, for whom there was no contradiction between meditation and post-meditation, I think also demonstrate the point of the above citations.

d.div: [979] Shangdro Yudrakpa Tsöndrü Drakpa (1123–93), founder of the Tsalpa Kagyü sect.
[980] Jikdral Namtrül Jampa Chönyi (fifteenth century).
[981] Better known as Tāranātha.

f.d: 'on kyang de dag lta bu'i lung rtogs kyi yon tan bye ba phrag brgya'i cha shas tsam yang med bzhin du stag gis mchongs sar wa'i dpe bzhin/ zal mo brag pa dang 'jam mgon sku skye/ rgyal ba karma pa'i rim gro pa brgyad gra rab 'byams pa kun tu bzang po sogs nag chang la 'dzem med spyod bzhin du rab byung bsnyen rdzogs kyi mkhan po dang slob dpon sogs las gral la 'jug pa du ma zhig snang ba ni gong drangs kyi lung khongs su nya dang nyung ma mi bsre'o//

However, don’t confuse fish and turnips by including here people such as Salmo Drakpa, the Gyalwa Karmapa attendant Gyedra Rapjampa Küntu Sangpo, the Jamgön incarnation, and many others who shamelessly indulge themselves in drinking alcohol and sleeping with women while at the same time acting as ordination preceptors, ācāryas, and so on. They do not have even a billionth of the knowledge or realization of these great beings and are merely like the jackal who tries to follow where the tiger jumps.

byang sdom len yul gyis mtshon pha rol tu phyin pa'i theg pa'i dge ba'i bshes gnyen nam slob dpon kyang / phal po che sdong pos brgyan pa'i le'ur [537]tshong dpon gyi bu nor bzang gis rgya gar lho phyogs grong khyer skyid pa'i 'byung gnas su 'phags pa 'jam dpal gyis lung bstan te dge slong sprin gyi dpal nas bzung / mthar khang pa brtsegs pa chen po rnam par snang mdzad kyi rgyan gyis brgyan par byang chub sems dpa' byams pa sogs dge ba'i bshes gnyen brgya dang bcu bsten pa la/ yul chu ba gtsang ma'i 'jigs mchog dbyangs sogs drang srong / yul yongs su tshol ba'i drod kyi skye mched sogs bram ze/ grong khyer seng ge rnam bsgyings kyi rgyal po seng ge dpal gyi bu mo byams ma sogs bud med/ yul sgo bzang po'i dbang phyug sogs khye'u/ sgyu 'phrul chen mo sogs lha mo/ zla ba bzang po sogs khyim bdag / rgya mtsho'i ngogs kyi grong khyer khang pa brtsegs pa'i mnyan pa dpa' bor grags pa sogs rten la ma bltos pa du ma dang /

To illustrate this point in the context of the object from which you take the bodhisattva vows, the Perfection Vehicle spiritual friend or master is illustrated in the Avataṃsaka Sutra in the Flower Ornament chapter.[982] Sudhana, the son of a merchant in the southern Indian town of Sukhākara received a prophecy from Mañjuśrī and devoted himself to a hundred and ten spiritual friends, beginning with the monk Meghaśrī and ending with bodhisattva Maitreya, in a great building adorned with the ornaments of Vairocana. They include rishis such as Bhayāgrasvara from the region of Sucinala; brahmans such as Uṣmanāyatana from Parīṣṭi; girls such as Maitrī, daughter of Siṃhaśrī, the king of the city Siṃhavijṛmbhita; youths such as Īṣvara from Sumukha; goddesses such as Mahāmāyā; householders such as Sucandra; and Nāvikaśūra from the town of Kūṭāgāra on the coast. From these beings he took the vows without the need for any formal basis (rten).

d.div: [537] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ ga_sdong po brgyan pa'i le'u zhe lnga pa/ shog_317_ba7
[982] Avataṃsakasūtra, chap. 45, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, ga, 317b7.

f.d:
lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo bam po dang po las/
bcom ldan 'das bdag gis deng slan chad/ byang chub sems dpa'i theg pa pa'i gang zag khyim pa'am rab du byung yang rung ste/ 'dod pa'i yon tan lnga la rtse zhing longs spyod pa mthong na/ ma dad pas ma gus pa bskyed dam/ de la ston par 'du shes ma bskyed na bdag cag gis de bzhin gshegs pa bslus par 'gyur ro/[538] / zhes dang /

In the first fascicle of Encouraging the Exceptional Thought it says:
Bhagavān, from now on, when we see someone of the bodhisattva vehicle enjoying the five sense pleasures, be they a householder or a monk, if we show disrespect or dishonor to them, or refuse to recognize them as teachers, then we are failing the Tathāgata.[983]

d.div: [538] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_lhag bsam bskul ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 1_shog_133_ba5
[983] Adhyāśayasañcodana, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 133b5.

f.d:
mya ngan med kyi byin pa lung bstan pa'i mdo bam gcig ma las/
rab 'byor gyis smras pa/ bu mo khyod khyim na gnas bzhin du 'di lta bu'i chos la gnas shing 'di lta bu'i rnam pa dag ston pa ni ngo mtshar ro/ / bu mos smras pa/ btsun pa rab 'byor byang chub sems dpa' sems dpa' chen po la ni khyim pa'am/ rab tu byung ba zhes mi bya'o/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ de dag ni bsam pas phye ba yin/ shes rab kyis phye ba yin/ ye shes kyis phye ba yin pa'i phyir ro/[539] / zhes dang /

In the single-fascicle Prophecy of Aśokadatta Sutra it states:
Subhūti said, “Girl, it is extraordinary that while dwelling in a house you dwell in such Dharma and give such a pure teaching!” The girl replied, “Venerable Subhūti, do not think of the mahāsattva bodhisattvas in terms of laymen or monks. Why? They are to be distinguished by their minds, by their wisdom, by their gnosis.”[984]

d.div: [539] sde dge_76_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_mya ngan med kyis byin pa lung bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 1_shog 236_na6
[984] Aśokadattavyākaraṇa, Toh 76 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 236a6.

f.d:
pha rol tu phyin pa lnga bstan pa'i mdo bam po gsum par/
gal te byang chub sems dpa' khyim na gnas shing gsum la skyabs su song bar gyur la/ de yang thams cad mkhyen pa nyid du yongs su bsngo na/ de 'dod pa lnga'i yon tan rnams la longs spyod du zin kyang / de tsam gyis na de byang chub sems dpa'i tshul khrims la gnas/ tshul khrims dang ldan pa zhes bya'o/ / byang chub sems dpa' gang byang chub sems dpa'i tshul khrims la gnas pa de ni/ tshul khrims kyi pha rol tu phyin pa dang ma bral ba yin no/[540] /

In the third fascicle of Teaching the Five Perfections Sutra:
If a bodhisattva dwells in a house and goes for refuge to the Three Jewels, dedicating all for the attainment of the omniscient mind, even though he enjoys the five sense pleasures, by doing just this much he dwells in the ethics of the bodhisattva and is endowed with the ethics of the bodhisattva. The bodhisattva who dwells in the ethics of the bodhisattva is not divorced from the perfection of ethics.[985]

d.div: [540] sde dge_181_bka'/ mdo sde/ tsa_pha rol tu phyin pa lnga bstan pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_32_ba7
[985] Pañcapāramitānirdeśa, Toh 181 Kangyur, mdo sde, tsa, 32b7.

f.d:
zhes byang sems dang ma bral na cha lugs dang spyod pa gang la yang ma bltos pa dang / khyad par sangs rgyas phal po che bam bo dgu bcu rtsa lnga par/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen spos tshong kun tu lta bas lung bstan pa bzhin/
grong khyer ta la'i rgyal mtshan du rgyal po me tshol ba'i phyir phyin te/ yul de'i mi rnams la rgyal po me gang na bzhugs zhes dris pas/ rigs kyi bu 'dir/ rgyal po me ni seng ge'i gdan la bzhugs shing rgyal po'i 'phrin las mdzad do/ / khams rab tu skyong ngo / / chad pas bcad par 'os pa ni chad pas gcod do/ / bya dgas bsdu bar 'os pa ni bya dgas sdud do/ / g.yon yod pa rnams la ni gyod rmed do/ / rtsod pa rnams kyi zhal che ni yongs su gcod do/[541] / zhes sogs kyi bstan pa dang /

Therefore, as long as you are not without the bodhi mind, your attire and behavior is of no regard. In particular, the ninety-fifth fascicle of the Buddha Avataṃsaka Sutra, in accordance with the prophecy of his spiritual friend Gandhaka Samantadarśin:
Sudhana went to the land of Tāladhvaja to search for King Agni. On his arrival he asked the people for the whereabouts of King Agni. “Son of the family,” they replied, “King Agni is sitting on the lion throne performing the activities of a king. He is protecting the kingdom. Those who deserve to be punished, he is punishing. Those who deserve to be rewarded, he is rewarding. Those who are deceitful he is questioning. On those with disputes, he passes judgment.”[986] And so on.

d.div: [541] sde dge_44_bka'/ phal chen/ a_sdong po brgyan pa'i le'u/ bam po/ 2_shog_23_na3
[986] Avataṃsakasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, a, 23a3.

tshong dpon gyi bu nor bzang gis de gang na ba der phyin pas/ lang tsho dar la bab pa/ gzugs mdzes pa yid du 'ong ba/ mtshan rnams kyis brgyan pa/ rgyal po'i gzi dang dbang chen po la gnas pa/ srid la gzhan gyi 'khor gyis gtse ba med pa/ dgra'i 'jigs pa dang bral ba'i dbang phyug dang ldan par 'dug pa mthong ngo / / de'i 'khor kun nas kyang blon po stong phrag bcu tshogs shing rgyal po'i dgos pa sgrub pa la brtson pa mthong ngo / /

f.d:
The text continues:
Sudhana, the merchant’s son, went to where the king was sitting. There he saw him, in the prime of youth, of handsome and attractive form, adorned with special marks, dwelling in regal splendor and might, immune from the harm of the forces of others in this world, sitting there with the might and power that fears no enemy, with an entourage of ten thousand ministers all working to fulfill the king’s needs.

d.div: de'i mdun na chad pas gcod pa'i mi sems can dmyal ba'i srung ma lta bu/ gshin rje'i g.yog 'khor lta bu 'jigs 'jigs lta'i gos gyon pa gtum zhing mi bzad la 'jigs pa chen po bskyed pa/ mig dmar ba/ so gtsigs pa/ gdong gi gnyer ma gsum khro gnyer du bsdus pa/ ral gri dang / sta re dang lcags kyi chang mdung dang / mda' dang / ber ga dang / mdung la sogs pa'i mtshon cha dang lag cha thogs pa/ lus dang bzhin gyi dbyibs mi sdug cing / 'jigs su rung ba/ sprin nag po ltar 'dug pa/ mi snyan cing brlang la/ sdang ba'i sgra drag po 'byin pa/ gzi blta bar dka' ba 'jigs pa chen po bskyed pa/ srog chags brgya phrag stong gi snying 'gem par byed pa de lta bu dag chad pas bcad par 'os pa'i sems can chad pas gcod pa la brtson pa mthong ngo / /

In front of the king were those in charge of carrying out punishments. They were men resembling the guardians of hell or the attendants of the lord of death. They were covered in fearful armor, wrathful, unbearable and terrifying to look at, with red eyes, fangs, the three lines on their brows knit to form a dreadful grimace. They carried weapons and instruments such as swords, axes, daggers, arrows, clubs, and spears. Their bodies and faces were ugly and frightening. Standing there like black clouds, angrily emitting fearsome snarls, their presence was unbearably frightening. He gazed upon these figures who would tear the hearts out of a hundred thousand creatures, as they strove to punish those beings that had been deemed worthy of punishment.

de na srog chags rku ba/ gzhan gyi nor la 'phrog pa/ sems can gyi longs spyod chud son pa/ lam sgugs shing 'phrog pa/ grong dang grong khyer dang / grong rdal dang / lhas la mes gtong ba/ grong du chom po byed pa/ khyim phugs 'debs pa/ sdig sdig ltar byed pa/ dug ldud pa/ dkrugs ma byed pa/ thong mi byed pa/ byi ba byed pa/ log par zhugs pa/ gnod par sems pa/ 'dod chen che ba/ sdig pa sna tshogs kyi las mi bzad pa byed pa/ brgya stong mang po bcing ba dam pa lngas bcings shing / rgyal po me'i drung du khrid pa dag kyang mthong ngo / / de dag la'ang rgyal po mes ci rigs par chad pas bcad par gyur pa mthong ngo // des de na rgyal po mes bsgo zhing / la la ni rkang lag bcad/ la la ni rna ba dang sna bcad/ la la ni mig phyung / la la ni yan lag dang nying lag dang mgo bcad/ la la ni lus thams cad mes btang / la la ni ba tsa'i chu khol mas lus la gtor cing / pags pa bsnyil ba la sogs pa de lta bu'i chad pa sna tshogs du ma mi bzad pa/ drag pa brlang ba yid du mi 'ong ba/ srog 'phrog pa dag kyang byed par mthong ngo / /

Among the offenders were those who had committed all manner of crimes: thieves who had stolen the wealth of others, those who had misused the possessions of others, bandits who had ambushed and robbed on the roads, those who had burned down villages, cities, towns, and farmsteads, those who had burgled and attacked villages. There were committers of atrocities, poisoners, slanderers, killers, and adulterers—perverse, malicious, and lustful committers of countless evils. He watched as many thousands of them, each tightly bound by five chains, were brought in front of the king and were handed down the appropriate sentence. Then, commanded by the king, some had their hands and feet cut off, some their ears and nose, some had their eyes plucked out, some had parts of their body cut off, some were burned alive, some had boiling nitrous water poured over their bodies until their skin blistered. He watched as they endured these dreadful and unbearable barbaric punishments and killings.

bsad pa'i sa de na yang / bsad pa'i rkang lag dang / rna ba dang mig dang sna dang / mgo dang yan lag dang / nying lag gi phung po ri tsam du spungs pa mthong ngo / / khrag gi mtsho dpag tshad gsum tsam du zabs su zab la chu zheng du dpag tshad du ma yod pa yang mthong ngo / / de na shi ba'i keng rus yan lag dang / nying lag dang / mgo dag bral ba brgya stong du ma la/ spyang ki dang / wa dang / khyi dang / bya rgod dang / khra dang / bya ku ra ra mang bas gang ste/ 'drid cing 'thog pa mthong ngo / / de la yang la la ni kha dog gyur te/ sngon por gyur pa tsam/ la la ni rnags pa tsam/ la la ni bam pa tsam/ la la ni 'bu zhugs pa tsam du gyur te/ shin tu skyi g.ya' zhing 'jigs 'jigs ltar 'dug pa mthong ngo / /

On the killing ground he saw the hands, feet, ears, eyes, noses, heads, and other body parts of those who had been killed piled up like a mountain. He watched as the ocean of blood rose to a depth of three leagues and many leagues wide. He watched as the place became filled with jackals, foxes, dogs, vultures, eagles, and kurara hawks,[987] picking apart and devouring the thousands of bones, arms, legs, and headless torsos. Some of the corpses became discolored and turned blue. Some began to decay, some became putrid, and some were infested with maggots. He watched this terrifying and chilling scene unfold before him.
[987] Or osprey, according to Monier-Williams.

bsad pa de dag gsod pa'i tshe/ mi sdug cho dgur byas pa na 'jigs 'jigs skad dang / snying rje rje skad du sgra 'byin zhing / cho nges 'debs pa'i sgra chen po thos na skyi g.ya' zhing mi dga' ba chen po bskyed pa/ sems can dmyal ba chen po ris gzhom pa'i sgra lta bu yang thos so//

While being executed, so many dreadful atrocities were done to them that they cried out in terror, begging for mercy. When Sudhana heard these anguished cries, he trembled with fear and was filled with revulsion. They were sounds like the sounds of the great Mountain Crushing Hell.

des de ltar kha btags te btungs pa dang / shin tu 'jigs pa'i drag shul mthong nas 'di snyam du gyur to/ / bdag ni sems can thams cad la phan pa dang bde ba'i phyir/ bla na med pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i byang chub tu mngon par zhugs te/ byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa yongs su tshol zhing 'bad de/ dge ba'i bshes gnyen rnams la dge ba ni ci zhig bgyi/ mi dge ba ni gang zhig spang zhes 'dri 'dri na/ rgyal po me 'od la ni dge ba'i chos kyang med de/ kha na ma tho ba chen po'i las la spyod pa/ yid kyi yongs su rtog pa shin tu gtum pa dang ldan pa/ sems can pha rol gyi srog bcad pa la zhugs pa/ sems can pha rol shin tu mnar ba la brtson pa/ tshe phyi ma blta ba med pa/ ngan song gi g.yang sa'i gad kha na 'dug pa zhig na/ 'di las ci byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa yang thob par 'gyur ram snyam ste/ de de ltar sems shing yid la byed de nem nur dang the tshom la gnas pa'i tshe/ snying rje chen po'i sems dang ldan pa de la/ steng gi nam mkha'i dbyings las lha mang pos bos pa/ rigs kyi bu drang srong rgyal ba'i drod kyi dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi gdams ngag tu bya ba mi dran nam/ des gyen du nam mkha'i dbyings la bltas nas dran no zhes brjod do/ /

Having witnessed this furious and frightening slaughter, Sudhana thought to himself, “In order to help and bring happiness to all living creatures, I have entered the path of the unsurpassed and perfect enlightenment. I have sought out and made efforts in the practices of the bodhisattvas. I have asked spiritual friends what virtuous deeds are to be cultivated, what nonvirtuous deeds are to be left behind. But this King Agni has no virtue; he engages in great wrongs; his thoughts are those of violence; he engages in the killing of other living beings; he works to bring torment to other beings; he pays no heed to future lives; and he is standing on the edge of the great cliffs of hell. What bodhisattva practice is there to be gained from him?” With these thoughts he stood there in doubt and hesitancy. Suddenly, celestial beings from the realms above called out to this greatly compassionate being; “Son of the family, do you not remember the instructions given to you by your spiritual friend Rishi Jinoṣman?” He looked up to the sky and replied, “I remember.”

f.d: lha rnams kyis smras pa/ rigs kyi bu khyod dge ba'i bshes gnyen gyi gdams ngag la de ltar the tshom ma bskyed cig /rigs kyi bu dge ba'i bshes gnyen rnams ni/ yang dag pa ma nor bar ston gyi log pa ma yin no/ / rigs kyi bu byang chub sems dpa' rnams kyi thabs mkhas pas spyod pa'i ye shes ni bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can yongs su sdud pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab po/ / sems can la phan 'dogs pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can tshar gcod pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can gzengs bstod pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can yongs su sbyong ba'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can yongs su skyong ba'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can 'dzud pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can yongs su smin par byed pa'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / sems can 'dul ba'i ye shes bsam gyis mi khyab bo/ / song rigs kyi bu de la byang chub sems dpa'i spyod pa dris shig[542] ces sa chen po la zhugs pa'i byang sems 'gro ba'i don du sdig spyod kyi rgyal po'i tshul bstan pa yin pas log lta dang the tshom med par bshes gnyen du bsten par bshad cing /

The gods continued, “Son of the family, do not have such doubts about your teacher’s instructions. Son of the family, the spiritual friends teach truly and flawlessly and do not mislead. Son of the family, the bodhisattvas’ knowledge of skillful activities is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to gather sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to help sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of how to destroy sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to exalt sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to purify sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to protect sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to bring in sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to ripen sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Their knowledge of ways to tame sentient beings is beyond comprehension. Therefore, son of the family, go ask him about the practices of the bodhisattva.”[988] This passage teaches that because this was a bodhisattva of the high levels who had shown himself in the form of a king performing evil acts for the sake of living beings, Sudhana should regard him as a spiritual teacher and devote himself without entertaining wrong views and doubts.

d.div: [542] 'di lung shin tu ring po drangs pa de gong gi phal chen gyir pod de ga'i nang yod nges pas mchan 'dogs dgos/
[988] Avataṃsakasūtra, Toh 44 Kangyur, phal chen, a, 23a3ff.

f.d:
gzhan yang rgyal po dge ba'i dbang pos mdzad pa'i skyes rabs rtogs brjod dpag bsam khri shing yal 'dab lnga bcu rtsa gsum par/ bdag cag gi ston pa slob pa lam gyi gnas skabs su yul wa ra NA si'i rgyal po legs bshad tshol du gyur ba'i tshe/ rang gi blon po'i gtso bo blo bzang gis/
rngon pa gdug pa can zhes pa/ / nags rgyu mtha' 'khob dag la gnas/ / de las rtag tu legs bshad kyi/ / rin chen gsar pa gsar pa thob/[543] / ces lung bstan pa ltar rgyal po rang nyid gcig pur rin po che'i do shal rin thang med pas spras te nags nang du byon/
de yis 'bad pas btsal bas rngon pa ni/ / rngon la rab chags ri yi ngos su rnyed/ / glang po rnams kyi bde ba'i mi mthun phyogs/ / ri dwags rnams la yug pas 'debs byed mkhas/ / 'khyogs po'i rim pa shin tu ma rungs gzhu/ / rang sems lta bu lag pa g.yon pas 'dzin/ / rtag tu nags na gnas pa'i mi mthun phyogs/ / gsod pa gcig pu la mkhas lag g.yas kyis/ / lag ldan sde rnams mtha' dag byang grol la/ / rnam par 'god pa'i mda' ni rab tu 'dzin/[544] / zhes gsod pa la dga' ba mda' gzhu lag tu thogs pa'i rngon pa la rin po che'i do shal rin thang med pa phul te legs bshad stsol bar gsol ba btab pa na/

Also, the fifty-third branch of the Wish-Fulfilling Tree of the Bodhisattva’s Lives by King Kṣemendra tells of the time our Teacher, while still on the path, was Subhāṣitagaveṣa, king of Vārāṇasī, and of how he went in search of wise counsel:[989] His chief minister Sumati said,
“In the remote forest roams a hunter who is known as Lubdhakrūraka.[990] From him you will gain counsel, new and precious and consistently wise.”[991] With this prediction the king, adorned with a priceless string of jewels, set off and traveled alone through the forest:
Searching with great resolve, he found the hunter on a mountainside, busy in his fervent love of hunting, enemy to the contentment of elephants, skilled in spearing and clubbing animals. In his left hand and like his own mind was a crooked and fearsome bow, the adversary of all those in the forest; accomplished solely in the art of killing, his right hand held the arrows that bring the elephants to liberation.[992] To this hunter, this lover of killing, holding in his hands a bow and arrow, the king offered the priceless string of jewels and made a request for wise counsel.

d.div: [543] sde dge_4155_bstan/ skyes rabs/ khe_dpa' bo/ rtogs brjod dpag bsam 'khri shing / yal 'dab/ 53 shog_30_na2
[544] gong mtshungs/ shog_30_na2
[989] Legs bshad. The king’s name, Subhāṣitagaveṣa, means “in search of wise counsel.”
[990] The name of the hunter means “cruel hunter.”
[991] Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā, story 53, Toh 4155 Tengyur, skyes rabs, khe, 30a2.

f.d:
de na re/
dge ba dam tshig gis ni legs bshad sbyin/ / gal te ri 'di'i rtse las rang gi lus/ / legs bshad thob pa'i 'phral la mchong na'o/[545] / zhes legs bshad thob pa'i de ma thag g.yang sar mchong na ster zer ba bzhin dam bcas pas/ rang bde'am lam gyi rtag tu gdung byed sdig dang nyon mongs gdung mi bya/[546] / zhes sogs legs bshad tshigs bcad sh+loka gcig blangs rjes ri'i rtse mo las the tshom med par mchongs par mdzad pa/

The hunter replied:
By the pledge of virtue I will give you wise counsel. As soon as you receive the counsel, you must throw your body from this mountain.[993] The hunter said he would give the king wise counsel if he immediately jumped off the cliff upon hearing it. The king pledged that he would. The hunter recited one verse, which in essence said, “Do not touch wrong deeds and mental affliction that torment your path to happiness.”[994] Having received this verse he jumped off the mountainside without hesitation.

d.div: [545] gong mtshungs/ shog_31_ba2
[546] gong mtshungs/ shog_32_ba2_ma dper/ rang bde'i lam gyis drag tu gdung byed sdig dang nyon mongs gdung byed sdig dang nyon mongs gdung mi bya/ /zhes byung yang sde dge bstan 'gyur ltar bcos/

[994] Only the first line of the verse is reproduced here. The rendering in the text seems a little corrupt, and so I have given the sense of this verse that appears in the Degé edition and in the commentary by Somendra.

f.d: de bzhin rtogs brjod 'di ga'i le'u brgya dang bdun par khyim bdag zas gtsang gis rgyal po tshangs byin gyi sras mo las legs bshad cung zad tsam gyi phyir rin po che'i phung po byin te/ legs bshad nor bu legs ldan rnams kyi snying gar brtan pas yon tan gyis brtags shing /[547] / zhes sogs legs bshad ster mkhan gyi yul du ma ltos par gsungs pa dang /

Also in the hundred and seventh branch of this Wish-Fulfilling Tree of the Bodhisattva’s Lives, the householder Śuddhodana offered a huge pile of jewels for just the smallest of wise counsels from the daughter of King Brahmadatta. The text says, “With the jewel of wise counsel firm in their hearts, they are bound by excellent qualities,”[995] and so on. These accounts talk of teachings being received without recourse to an object[996] of wise counsel.

d.div: [547] sde dge_4155_bstan/ skyes rabs/ khe_dge ba'i dbang po/ dpag bsam 'khri shing / yal 'dab/ 53_shog_290_na6
[995] Kṣemendra, Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā, story 107, Toh 4155 Tengyur, skyes rabs, khe, 290a6.

[996] “Object” (yul) here means a recognized and formal object from whom one receives vows and teachings, such as a monk. The author’s main point here, which he has been making over many pages, is that that the presence of a pratimokṣa-holding monk is not necessary for the imparting of teachings and vows. This has now been extended to include the point that an intention to teach is not necessary for a teaching to be imparted. In the first account, the hunter only gave his counsel because, according to the commentary, he wanted the jewel, and he had the king jump off a cliff because he feared that if the king remained alive he would take the jewel back. In the second story Śuddhodana heard the wise counsel being sung by the king’s daughter as he walked past her room. In neither account was there an intention to give teachings. Mere reverence on the part of the listener was enough to receive them, a point emphasized below in the account of the queen’s servant girl.

f.d:
mdo sde za ma tog bkod pa'i bam po gsum pa las/
rigs kyi bu khor mor 'jig pa'i grong khyer chen po na/ gang yi ge drug pa'i rig sngags chen mo 'di 'dzin par byed/ klog par byed/ tshul bzhin du yid la byed pa'i chos smra ba yod do/ / rigs kyi bu chos smra bar byed pa mthong nas the tshom mi skye bar bya'o/ / rigs kyi bu khyod byang chub sems dpa'i sa nas 'phos shing ngan song du skyes sa re/ chos smra ba de ni tshul khrims nyams pa/ spyod pa nyams pa/ chung ma dang / bu dang bu mos yongs su bskor ba/ ngur smrig kyang bshang ba dang gci bas yongs su gang ba/ spyod lam ma bsdams pa yin no/ / de nas bcos ldan 'das la sgrib pa rnam par sel bas 'di skad ces gsol to/ / bcom ldan 'das kyi bka' bzhin du 'tshal zhes yul khor mo 'jig tu song nas chos smra ba de'i rkang pa la mgo bos phyag bgyis te yi ge drug pa'i rig sngags mnyan no/[548] / zhes sogs rgya cher byung ba dang /

In the third[997] fascicle of the Boxed Arrangement it says:
“Son of the family, in the great town of Vārāṇasī there is a Dharma teacher who holds in his mind the great six-syllable mantra, who recites it and contemplates it correctly. Son of the family, when you see this Dharma teacher, do not have doubts, for if you do, son of the family, you may fall from the bodhisattva levels and be reborn in the lower realms. That Dharma teacher will have degenerate ethics and degenerate behavior and will be surrounded by wives, sons, and daughters. He will even cover the orange robes with excrement and urine, and his behavior will be unrestrained.” Then Viṣkambhī said to the Bhagavān, “I will do as the Bhagavān has instructed.” He went to Vārāṇasī, bowed his head at the feet of that Dharma teacher, and listened to the six-syllable mantra.[998] This point is taught extensively in this sutra.

d.div: [548] sde dge_116_bka'/ mdo sde/ ja_'phags pa za ma tog bkod po'i mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_235_ba1_ma dper bam po gsum pa gsungs kyang bam po bzhi par gsal/
[997] Found in fascicle 4 in Degé.
[998] Karaṇḍavyūha, fascicle 4, Toh 116 Kangyur, mdo sde, ja, 235b1.

f.d: rgyal po ma skyes dgra'i bu mo mya ngan med byin mas nyan thos rnams la ldang ba tsam ma byas par ston pa mnyes par bgyis shing / des shA ri'i bu dang mong+gal gyi bu/ 'od srungs chen po dang / rab 'byor sgra gcan 'dzin sogs chos kyi gtam gyis zil gyis mnan te ston pas bskal pa grangs med bdun gyi mthar 'jig rten dri ma med pa'i 'od du sangs rgyas par lung bstan pa dang /

Also Aśokadatta, the daughter of King Ajātaśatru, pleased the Teacher by not rising from her seat in the presence of the śrāvakas.[999] She surpassed Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, and others with her Dharma oratory, and the Teacher prophesized that at the end of seven countless eons she would become enlightened in the world known as Vimalaprabhā.

d.div: [999] This is told in the Prophecy of Aśokadatta (Aśokadattavyākaraṇa), Kangyur Toh 76, dkon brtsegs, ca.

f.d: chang tshong bi na sas kyang chos bstan te 'gro rnams smin grol gyi lam du bkod pa dang / 'ga' zhig tu rgyal po shar pa zhes kyang phal cher rgyal po ma skyes dgra'i btsun mo sngo sangs can gyi bran mo sgur 'jog gis sgo rgyab nas chos bstan pas btsun mo rnams bden pa ma mthong de'i rgyu ci lags bcom ldan 'das la zhus pas bsti stang gis len par gsungs pas slar sgur 'jog seng ge'i khrir bton te chos bstan pas btsun mo rnams bden pa mthong ba sogs rten la ma ltos bsti stang gi yul gtso bar gsungs pa dang /

Even the beer seller Vinasa taught the Dharma and brought others to the path of ripening and liberation. Natasthāpana was a servant of Queen Śyāmāvatī, who in some accounts is the queen of King Paurastya but most say was the queen of King Ajātaśatru. Natasthāpana taught the Dharma from behind closed doors. Because of this the queens did not realize the truth. They asked the Bhagavān why this was, and he replied that through reverence it could be realized. So Natasthāpana was placed on a high seat where she taught Dharma, and soon the queens realized the truth. This is an account where no formal object is relied upon but where an object of reverence is of importance.

gzhan yang khyim bdag des pa drag shul can/ lag bzang / blo gros bzang mo/ bu mo dri ma med byin ma/ bu mo rnam dag / tshong dpon bzang skyong / li tsa byi dri ma med/ lha mo dpal 'phreng sogs rten so thar ma yin pas dge slong la sogs par chos du ma ston pa dang / gsang sngags rdo rje theg pa la ni/ ston pa shAkya thub pa nyid gnyis med dus 'khor/ pha rgyud 'dus pa/ ma rgyud bde mchog sogs bla med kyi ston 'khor thams cad chags can gyi tshul sha stag tu bstan nas a+yon gyi yul du rgyal po in+d+ra b+ho ng+hi rgyal po'i cha lugs kyi pha rgyud 'dus pa dang snga 'gyur gyi chos du ma ston pa'i bstan pa'i rtsa ba lta bu dang /

Furthermore, the householder Surata, the householder Ugra, Sūbahu, Sumati, the girl Vimaladatta, the girl Vimalaśraddhā, the merchant Bhadrapāla, Licchavi Vimala, the goddess Śrīmālā, and others have all taught fully ordained monks and others without possessing the pratimokṣa as a basis. In the Vajrayana Buddha Śākyamuni himself taught the highest yoga yantras such as the nondual Kālacakra, the father tantra Guhyasamāja, the mother tantra Cakrasaṃvara, and so on, with teacher and audience all manifested solely in the form of desire. Later in the land of Oḍḍiyāna as King Indrabodhi, he taught the father tantra Guhyasamāja and also many tantras of the early translation school. These works are the fundamental texts of tantra. Similarly,

tsan+d+ra go mi sogs gzhan yang rgya paN mang la/ gangs can gyi ljongs 'dir chos kyi rgyal po srong btsan sgam pos thugs rje chen po'i chos skor pha bong khar gsungs nas ral pa can brgya phrag du ma smin grol gyi lam la bkod pa dang / bka' gdams kyi bstan pa'i rtsa ba jo bo chen po a ti shar slob ma dge slong sogs rgya mtsho lta bu'i nang nas sras kyi thu bo dge bsnyen gyi tshul can 'brom ston rgyal ba'i 'byung gnas la bstan pa yongs su gtad pa/
bdag gi bstan pa 'di ni khyod la gtad/ / de na khyod kyi yon tan ji tsam pa/ / gang zag gcig gi bslang bar mi nus pas/ / las can brgyad cur bgos la mtha' rgya bskyed/[549] / ces sogs gsungs pa'i gtso bo dge bsnyen gyi cha byad du mdzad pa/

there were many lay Indian pandits such as Candragomin, and here in Tibet the Dharma king Songtsen Gampo gave the Mahākaruṇa teachings at Pabongkha, and many hundreds of “long-haired” (ral pa can) practitioners were brought to the path of ripening and liberation. The great master Atiśa, founder of the Kadam tradition, had a body of disciples, including monks, as vast as the ocean, but he entrusted the complete tradition to his main disciple Dromtön Gyalwai Jungné in his form of an upāsaka lay practitioner:
My teachings I entrust to you; yet no matter how many qualities you may possess, no one person could take them all on. They will be divided, therefore, among eighty others of fortunate merit, and by this they will prosper.[1000]

d.div: [549] jo bo rje'i gsung 'di sde srid kyis khungs gang nas drangs ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[1000] Untraced.

f.d:
sa skya pa'i bstan pa'i rtsa ba dkar po rnam gsum dang 'brog mi/ dkar rgyud pa'i rtsa ba mar pa/ mtshur/ mi la/ shangs pa'i ni gu sogs dang / gzhan yang rong pa sga lo rta nag 'gos kha che zla mgon sogs rten la ma ltos par khyim pa'i cha byad kyis 'gro ba rnams smin grol gyi lam du bkod pa'i bshes gnyen mang bas rten rang du mtha' ma bkag pa bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen pos rnam thar du kU la ka pa par ma'i grangs brgya nyer dgu pa'i rgyab tu/
lha pa sku skye dang lha bris pa btsun chung sogs kyis mi skya la bla ma bcol zhes kha zer ba khyim pa la ngos 'dzin na/ rnying mar ma zad/ 'brog / mal/ mar pa/ mar do/ 'gos/ sa chen/ rwa 'bum seng / khu dbon/ rgwa lo rnam rgyal rdo rje lta bu gsar ma pa la yang shin tu mang / de dag sngags pa yin pas mi 'dra zer na/ rgya gar du chos rgyal dge dbang / bod du srong btsan sgam po/ rigs ldan rnam rgyal grags pas mtshon pa ji snyed/[550] ces phebs pa ltar yin kyang

Those who built the foundations of the Sakya tradition, such as the three white-robed practitioners[1001] and Drokmi Lotsāwa; those at the root of the Kagyü tradition such as Marpa, Tsurpa, Mila, and Shangpa Nigu; also Rongpa Galo, Tanak Gö Lotsāwa, the Kashmiri Somanātha, and many other spiritual friends, without relying on any ordained basis, brought beings to ripening and liberation in the form of lay practitioners. Therefore, there is nothing decisive about the need for an ordained basis. My guru, the Great Fifth, says in his Silken Robe Biography, in the ka volume, page 129b:
It is said dismissively, “Oracles who reveal deities, painters of deities, young monks, and so on mistake the non-ordained for gurus.” If this refers to lay people, then you should know that not only in the Nyingma but also in the new translation schools there are many lay gurus, including Drokmi, Mal Lotsāwa, Marpa, Mardo Lotsāwa, Gö Lotsāwa, Sachen Künga Nyingpo, Ra Bumseng, Khubön, and Ga Lotsāwa Namgyal Dorjé. If you say, “They are different because they are practitioners of tantra,” then you should know that in India there were those such as King Kṣemendra and in Tibet, King Songtsen Gampo and Rikden Namgyal Drakpa.[1002] However,

d.div: [550] rgyal ba blo bzang rgya mtsho'i gsung 'bum/ ca rnam thar du kU la'i gos bzang / ka_shog_129_ba4
[1001] The three white-robed practitioners are Sachen Künga Nyingpo (1092–1158) and his sons Sönam Tsemo and Drakpa Gyaltsen.
[1002] Ngawang Losang Gyatso, Collected Works, ca, 129b4.

f.d: ngo bo'i sgo nas gong bshad kyi yon tan mtha' dag tshang ba dgos la/ khyad par bran mo sgur 'jog gi lo rgyus dang bcas bsti stang gi yul du gyur pa zhig gal lhag par che zhing /

in terms of their nature, they should possess all the necessary qualities mentioned previously, and it is especially important, as emphasized by the story of the servant Natasthāpana, that they are objects of reverence.
25. Benefits

de ltar chos ston par 'os pa de nyid kyis 'chad pa 'i phan yon ni/ dkon brtsegs 'dus pa nyer gsum pa byams pa'i seng ge'i sgra las/
stong chen 'jig rten khams ni gser dag gis/ / bkang ste gang la sbyin par byed pa ni/ / tshig bzhi'i tshigs su bcad pa gcig brjod pas/ / ji ltar phan 'dogs de ltar 'gyur ma yin/ /
phan 'dogs byed par 'dod pa gang zhig gis/ / 'jig rten gsum na sems can thams cad kyi/ / bde ba gang dag yod pa de dag kun/ / sems can gcig la sbyin pa byas pa bas/ / gang gis de la sangs rgyas lugs kyi ni/ / tshig bzhi'i tshigs su bcad pa gcig bsgrags na/ / de ni shin tu phan 'dogs mchog yin te/ / des ni sdug bsngal dag las grol bar 'gyur/[551] / zhes dang /
mi gang zhig gis gang+gA'i bye snyed kyi/ / 'jig rten khams mchog rin chen gang byas te/ / dga' rab sems kyi rgyal la phul ba dang / / gang gis sems can gcig la tshigs bcad byin/ / rin chen byin pa shin tu rgya chen des/ / tshigs bcad sbyin pa snying rjes bsgrubs de la/ / char yang mi phod grangs su'ang ma yin na/ / gnyis sam gsum la bsam du ga la yod/[552] / ces dang /

As for the benefits of the teachings given by those worthy of teaching Dharma, the Lion’s Roar of Maitreya, from twenty-third volume of the Heap of Jewels collection, says:
Giving away as much gold as would fill the great thousand-world realm would not match the benefit gained from teaching just one four-line verse.
For those wishing to benefit others, of far greater benefit than bestowing on a single being every happiness of every living being in the three realms is to teach that person one verse of the Buddha’s doctrine, for it will deliver that being from suffering.[1003] Also:
Were one person to fill with precious jewels world realms as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges and with a joyful mind offer them to the king, while another gave just a single verse to a single sentient being, that great gift of jewels would not amount to a fraction of— would not even compare to—the gift of the verse offered in compassion. If that is so, how could we possibly conceive the merit of giving the same to two or three beings?[1004]

d.div: [551] sde dge_67_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_byams pa seng+ge'i sgra chen po zhes bya ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_82_na1
[552] sde dge_67_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca_byams pa seng+ge'i sgra chen po zhes bya ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_82_na4
[1003] Maitreyamahāsiṃhanāda, Toh 67 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 82a1.

f.d:
sbyin pa'i phan yon bstan pa'i mdo las/
chos kyi sbyin pa byin na rnam par smin pa skye ba dran pa thob par 'gyur ro/[553] / zhes dang /
shes rab khri pa las/ rab 'byor de de bzhin no/ / ji skad smras pa de bzhin te/ rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo de tshes brgyad dang / tshes bcu bzhi dang / tshes bco lnga la shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa 'di kha ton du byed pa dang 'chad par byed pa na bsod nams kyi phung po dpag tu med/ grangs med/ tshad med/ bsam gyis mi khyab/ gzhal du med pa mang po dag bskyed par 'gyur zhing de shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa 'di kha ton du byed pa dang 'chad par byed pa na lha'i 'khor mdun du gnas par 'gyur ro/[554] / zhes dang /

The Sutra Teaching the Benefits of Giving states:
Giving the gift of Dharma results in the ripening of remembering past lives.[1005] In the Ten Thousand Perfection of Wisdom Sutra:
Subhūti, it is like that. Just as you have said, it is like that. Should a son of the family or a daughter of the family, on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the fifteenth day of the month recite or teach this Perfection of Wisdom, the accumulation of merit created is immeasurable, uncountable, limitless, inconceivable, and inestimable. Should such a person recite or teach this Perfection of Wisdom, they will come to dwell among the retinue of gods.[1006]

d.div: [553] sde dge_183_bka'/ mdo sde/ ca_'phags pa sbyin pa'i phan yon bstan pa/ shog_96_na3
[554] sde dge_11_bka'/ sher phyin/ nga shes rab khri pa/ le'u/ 19_shog_207_ba4
[1005] Dānānuśaṃsānirdeśa, Toh 183 Kangyur, mdo sde, ca, 96a3.
[1006] Daśasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā, chap. 19, Toh 11 Kangyur, sher phyin, nga, 207b4.

f.d:
lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba las/
byams pa gal te byang chub sems dpal zhal ta byed pa la brtson pas rin po che sna bdun dag gi mchod rten gyis stong gsum gyi stong chen po 'di bkang na/ des ni nga mnyes par byed pa ma yin/ ri mor byas pa ma yin/ bkur stir byas pa ma yin gyi/ byams pa gal te byang chub sems dpa' tha na pha rol tu phyin pa dang ldan pa'i tshig bzhi pa'i tshigs su bcad pa gcig tsam 'dzin nam/ 'chang ngam/ klog gam/ kun chub par byed dam/ 'chad na des ni nga la bkur stir byas/ bla mar byas/ ri mor byas/ mchod par byas pa 'gyur ro/ / de ci'i phyir zhe na/ byams pa de bzhin gshegs pa rnams kyi byang chub ni mang du thos pa las byung ba yin gyi/ dngos po yongs su 'dzin pa las byung ba ma yin pa'i phyir ro/[555] / zhes dang /

In Encouraging the Exceptional Thought:
Maitreya, should a bodhisattva, working hard as my attendant, fill this great billionfold world realm with shrines made from the seven precious gems, that would not please me, it would pay me no reverence, it would not venerate me. But Maitreya, should a bodhisattva take at the very least a four-line verse of the Perfection of Wisdom and commit it to memory, keep it in his mind, read it, understand it, or teach it, that is paying me reverence, seeing me as guru, venerating me, pleasing me. Why is that? Maitreya, the enlightenment of the tathāgatas arises from learning. It does not arise from the possession of material things.[1007]

d.div: [555] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_150_na4
[1007] Adhyāśayasañcodana, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 150a4.

f.d:
spyan ras gzigs kyis zhus pa chos bdun pa las/
gang gis gang+gA'i bye snyed 'jig rten khams/ / de dag rin chen phyur bur bkang byas te/ / dga' rab sems kyis rgyal la phul ba bas/ / gang gis tshigs bcad gcig gcig sems can byin/ / rin chen sbyin pa shin tu rgya che des/ / snying rje bskyed nas tshigs bcad byin pa la/ / gang gi cha dang grangs su mi phod na/ / lan gnyis lan gsum sems pa ga la zhig[556] / ces nyung mtha' tshigs bcad gcig tsam byin pa'i phan yon de lta bu gsungs pa dang /

In the Seven Dharmas Requested by Avalokiteśvara:
Were one person to fill to overflowing with precious jewels world realms as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges and with a joyful mind offer them to the king, while another gave a single verse to a single person, that vast gift of precious jewels would not be fraction of—would come nowhere near— the gift of a verse offered with compassion. If this is so, how could we possibly conceive the merit of doing it two or three times?[1008] These passages speak of the merit of giving the minimum of just a single verse.

d.div: [556] ma dper spyan ras gzigs kyi chos bdun par gsungs kyang / sde dge_67_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca byams pa seng+ge'i sgra chen po/ shog_82_na4_nang bzhugs pas de'i khungs bkod/
[1008] Although there is some slight variation in the wording, this verse is a repetition of the verse above in the Maitreyamahāsiṃhanāda, Toh 67 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 82a4.

f.d:
byams chos dbus mtha' rnam 'byed las/
yi ge 'bri+i mchod sbyin pa dang / / nyan dang klog dang len pa dang / / 'chad dang kha ton byed pa dang / / de sems pa dang sgom pa ste/ / spyod pa 'di bcu'i bdag nyid kyi/ / bsod nams phung po gzhal du med/[557] / ces bsod nams kyi phung po gzhal du med pa'i rgyu bcu gsungs pa'i lung 'chad pa'am klog pa ni ngag gi chos spyod bzhi'i nang tshan gsungs te/

Differentiating the Middle Way and the Extremes from the works of Maitreya states:
Writing, making offerings, giving, listening, reading, memorizing, preaching, recitating, contemplating, and meditating: the merit of these ten activities is incalculable.[1009]Preaching a text, or reading a text, has been described as one of the four verbal Dharma activities,[1010] and is one of the ten causes producing an incalculable amount of merit.

d.div: [557] sde dge_4021_bstan/ sems tsam/ phi_dbus mtha' rnam 'byed/ le'u/ 5_sh+loka9_nas 10_shog_5_na4
[1009] Madhyantavibhaṅga, 5:9, Toh 4021 Tengyur, sems tsam, phi, 5a4.
[1010] Chos spyod. These ten causes are known as the ten Dharma activities. The term is often used these days to refer to liturgical books of prayers and praises.

f.d:
'grel par/
tshig dang don 'chad pa ni 'bad pa chen pos 'os pa rnams la chos ston par byed pa'o/[558] / zhes sogs phan yon bsam gyis mi khyab pa dang /

The commentary to Differentiating the Middle Way and the Extremes states:
Preaching the meanings or the words means to teach Dharma with great enthusiasm to those who are suitable.[1011] Therefore, the benefits of teaching are inconceivable.

d.div: [558] sde dge_4032_bstan/ sems tsam/ bi_blo gros brtan pa/ dbus mtha' rnam 'byed 'grel bshad/ le'u/ 5 shog_294_na5
[1011] Sthiramati, Madhyāntavibhaṅgaṭīkā, chap. 5, Toh 4032 Tengyur, sems tsam, bi, 295a5.

f.d: nyan pa'i phan yon ni/

gang pos zhus pa'i mdo'i bam po bzhi pa las/
kun dga' bo khyod kyis 'di snyam du me tog dang / spos dang / spos kyi phye ma dang / byug spos dang / gdugs dang / rgyal mtshan dang / ba dan dang / na bza' dang / rol mo sil snyan mchog dam pa dang / de bzhin gshegs pa la bsngags pa brjod pa ni mchod pa mchog dam pa yin no snyam du bsam par mi bya ste/ kun dga' bo de lta bu dag ni mchod pa mchog dam pa zhes mi bya'i gang gis mdo sde zab mo 'di lta bu thos nas/ len pa dang / 'dzin pa dang / klog pa dang / kha ton du 'dan po dang / lung nod pa dang / ji skad bstan pa bzhin du mngon par bsgrubs pa gang yin pa de ni mchod pa'i yo byad mchog dam pas de bzhin gshegs pa la mchod cing rim gro byas pa dang / bkur bstir byas pa dang / bla mar byas pa dang / bsngags pa brjod par byas pa zhes bya'o/[559] / zhes chos thos pa dang lung nod pa ni zang zing gis mchod pa gang las kyang phul du phyin par bshad pa dang /

In the fourth chapter of the Sutra Requested by Pūrṇa:
Ānanda, do not think that scents, aromatic powders, perfumed lotions, incense, victory standards, banners, beautiful clothes, the sweet sounds of cymbals, and songs of praise to the tathāgatas are the best offerings. Ānanda, do not hold these to be the best type of offerings. Listening to these profound sutras, taking them to your mind, remembering them, reading, reciting, receiving transmissions, and practicing them exactly as they are taught are the best offerings. Such activities, therefore, are offerings to the tathāgatas, are acts of service, of veneration, of respecting them as gurus, and are words of praise to them.[1012] Therefore, listening to Dharma and receiving transmissions are far superior to making material offerings.

d.div: [559] sde dge_61_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga 'phags pa gang pos zhus pa'i mdo/ bam po bzhi pa/ le'u/ 5_shog_206_na2
[1012] Pūrṇaparipṛcchā, chap. 5, Toh 61 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 206a2.

f.d:
yab sras mjal ba'i mdo'i le'u nyer bdun pa las/
shA ri'i bu byang chub sems dpa' theg pa la yang dag par zhugs pa'i rigs kyi bu'am/ rigs kyi bu mo gang gis bskal pa bcu'i bar du pha rol tu phyin pa lnga shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa dang bral bar spyad pa bas/ shA ri'i bu gang gis byang chub sems dpa'i ting 'dzin de kho na nges par bstan pa 'di tha na thos par gyur kyang / de nyid de bas bsod nams ches mang du 'phel lo/[560] / zhes sbyin pa dag byin tshul khrims bsrungs/ bzod pa sgoms/ bsam gtan la mnyam par bzhag ste pha rol tu phyin pa lnga spyad pa las chos zab mo thos pa tsam phan yon che ba dang /

The twenty-seventh chapter of the Meeting of Father and Son Sutra says:
Śāriputra, say a son of the family or a daughter of the family who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle practices for ten eons the first five perfections divorced from the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra, one dwelling solely in the single-minded concentration of the bodhisattva who hears just this teaching accumulates far greater merit.[1013] Merely listening to the profound Dharma is of greater benefit than the five perfections—giving, guarding one’s ethics, developing patience, increasing effort, and abiding in meditative absorption.

d.div: [560] sde dge_60_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga 'phags pa yab sras mjal ba'i mdo/ le'u/ 27_shog_167_ba6
[1013] Pītaputrasamāgamasūtra, chap. 27, Toh 60 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 167b6.

f.d:
dkon cog brtsegs pa 'dus pa bco lnga pa mjam dpal gyi zhing bkod las/
rigs kyi bu gang la las phyogs bcur de bzhin gshegs pa'i spyan sgrib pa med pas sangs rgyas kyi zhing ji snyed cig gzigs pa de dag thams cad rin po che sna bdun gyis yongs su bkang ste de bzhin gshegs pa re re la phul ba bas/ gzhan zhig gis chos kyi rnam grangs 'di thos nas 'dzin nam/ 'chang ngam/ klog gam/ kun chub par byed pa dang / 'dzin par byed na bsod nams kyi phung po de la bsod nams kyi phung po snga mas brgya'i char yang nye bar mi 'gro/ / stong gi char yang nye bar mi 'gro'o/[561] / zhes dang /

In the Qualities of the Buddha Realm of Mañjuśrī from the fifteenth volume of the Heap of Jewels collection:
Son of the family, someone may fill with the seven types of precious gems as many buddha realms as can be seen by the unobstructed sight of the tathāgatas in the ten directions and offer them to each tathāgata. Another will listen to this particular Dharma, take it to their mind, hold it, read it, understand it, or practice it. The merit of the former does not approach a hundredth of the latter, a thousandth of the latter.[1014]

d.div: [561] sde dge_59_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ga_'jam dpal gyi sangs rgyas kyi zhing gi yon tan bkod pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 4_shog_295_ba6
[1014] Mañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūha, Toh 59 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ga, 295b6.

f.d:
drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i mdo'i bam po gsum pa las/
kun dga' bo gang chos kyi rnam grangs 'di nyan cing kun chub par byed la/ dam pa'i chos yun ring du gnas par bya ba dang / sangs rgyas kyi rigs rgyun mi chad par bya ba'i phyir/ gzhan dag la yang rgya cher yang dag par rab tu ston cing slab pa gnas na/ des 'das pa dang / ma 'ongs pa dang / da ltar byung ba'i sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das rnams la mchod pa byas par 'gyur ro/ / gus pa dang bcas pas bsnyen bkur byas par yang 'gyur ro/[562] / zhes dang /

In the third chapter of Sutra Requested by the Householder Ugra:
Ānanda, someone who listens to and comprehends this particular Dharma, who teaches it extensively and perfectly to others in order to preserve the sacred Dharma and to ensure that the family of the Buddha does not die out, and who dwells in the practices is one who is making offerings and performing devoted service to the bhagavān buddhas of the past, present, and future.[1015]

d.div: [562] sde dge_63_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ nga khyim bdag drag shul can gyis zhus pa'i mdo/ bam po/ 3_shog_287_ba6
[1015] Ugraparipṛcchā, Toh 63 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, nga, 287b6.

f.d:
rim gyis byang chub yang dag par 'byung ba'i mdo las/
kun dga' bo gang de bzhin gshegs pa blta bar 'dod pa dang / sems can rnams la sangs rgyas kyi mdzad pa bya bar 'dod pa des/ chos kyi+i rnam grangs 'di nyan par bya/ gzung bar bya/ bcang bar bya/ gzhan dag la yang bstan par bya'o/[563] / zhes dang /

In the Sutra of the Gradual Arising of Enlightenment:
Ānanda, those who wish to see the Tathāgata, and who wish to perform the deeds of the Buddha for sentient beings, should listen to this particular Dharma, take it into their minds, keep it there, read it, and teach it to others.[1016]

d.div: [563] rim gyis byang chub yang dag par 'byung ba'i mdo zhes pa'i gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/
[1016] Untraced.

f.d:
byams pa seng ge sgra'i mdo bam po gnyis pa las/
'od srungs gang gis stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di chu'i phung po nas bzung ste tshangs pa'i 'jig rten gyi mthar thug pa'i bar du 'bru mar gyis yongs su bkang ste/ mar me'i snying po ri rab tsam btsugs nas/ de bzhin gshegs pa la mchod pa'i las kyi phyir mar me bus pa bas ni/ lhag pa'i bsam pa phun sum tshogs pas mkhan po'am slob dpon gyi drung nas tshig bzhi pa'i tshigs su bcad pa gcig lung mnos te/ kha ton du byed cing gom pa bdun 'dor bar byed pa gang yin pa de de bas bsod nams ches mang du byed pa 'gyur ro/[564] / zhes dang /

From the second chapter of the Lion’s Roar of Maitreya:
Kāśyapa, someone may fill this billionfold world realm with oil whose height reaches from the oceans to the world of Brahmā, plant a lamp wick the size of Meru, and light it as an act of offering to the Tathāgata. Yet another who sits in front of their preceptor or master with a perfect mind and intention and receives one four-line verse, recites it, and then takes seven steps earns by far the greater merit.[1017]

d.div: [564] sde dge_67_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca byams pa seng+ge'i sgra chen po zhes bya ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_91_na3
[1017] Maitreyamahāsiṃhanāda, Toh 67 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 91a3.

f.d:
lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo'i bam po gnyis pa las/
byang chub mngon par 'dod phyir nga yis ni/ / rang gi yan lag lan stong snyed du btang / / chos nyan pas ni nga la ngoms med na/ / de dag chos nyan pa la skyo bar 'gyur/ /
tshig bzhi pa yi tshigs su bcad pa'i phyir/ / nga ni chung ma bu la dga' ma gyur/ / rgyal srid dag dang longs spyod ngas spangs na/ / mkhas pa ja ltir chos ni nyan mi byed/[565] / ces dang /

In the second chapter of Encouraging the Exceptional Thought:
Because I yearned for enlightenment, I gave away my limbs thousands of times. If I am never sated by listening to Dharma, why do they become bored with listening?
For the sake of a single four-line verse, I turned from my wife and child. If I renounced my kingdom and possessions, how can the scholars not listen to Dharma?[1018]

d.div: [565] sde dge_69_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca lhag pa'i bsam pa bskul ba'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_144_na2
[1018] Adhyāśayasañcodana, Toh 69 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 144a2.

f.d:
bu mo blo gros bzang mos zhus pa'i mdo bam gcig ma las/
'jam dpal de bas na mdo sde rin po che 'di lta bu 'di yi ger bri ba dang / lung 'bogs pa dang / bcang ba dang / bklags pa dang / gzhan dag la rab tu bstan pa'i phyir/ byang chub sems dpa' sems dpa' chen po rnams kyis brtson 'grus brtsams par bya'o/ / 'di ni nga'i rjes su bstan pa yin no/[566] / zhes dang /

In the one-fasicle text called Sutra Requested by the Girl Sumati:
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas should with all effort strive to write these precious sutras, to transmit them, to hold them in their minds, to read them, and to teach them to others, for this will be the legacy of my doctrine.[1019]

d.div: [566] sde dge_74_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca bu mo blo gros bzang mos zhus pa'i mdo/ shog_221_ba6
[1019] Sumatidārikāparipṛcchā, Toh 74 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 221b6.

f.d:
mya ngan med kyis byin pa lung bstan pa'i mdo las/
kun dga' bo gang gis stong gsum gyi stong chen po'i 'jig rten gyi khams 'di rin po che sna tshogs kyis yongs su bkang ste sbyin pa byin pa bas/ gang gi chos kyi rnam grangs 'di tha na rna lam du thos na/ 'di ni de bas ches bsod nams mang du bskyed na/ gang 'dzin pa dang / kun chub par byed pa dang / 'chang ba dang / klog pa dang / brjod pa dang / lung ci skad phog pa bzhin du nan tan du sgrub pa lta ci smos/[567] zhes dang /

In the Prophecy of Aśokadatta Sutra:
Ānanda, someone may fill this billionfold world realm with various jewels and give them away. Another may simply listen to this particular Dharma. If this latter action creates so much more merit than the former, what need to speak of the merit of working hard to take this Dharma to mind, to comprehend it, to not forget it, to read it, and to transmit it in the appropriate language?[1020]

d.div: [567] sde dge_76_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca mya ngan med kyis byin pa lung bstan pa'i mdo/ shog_240_ba4
[1020] Aśokadattavyākaraṇa, Toh 76 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 240b4.

f.d:
bu mo dri ma med kyis zhus pa'i bam po gnyis pa las/
lung mnos kha ton brjod la dran par byed/ / gzhan la yid du 'ong ba'i sgra yang sgrogs/ / skyo ba med par chos kyang rjod par byed/ / ting 'dzin sgom pa mtshan ma legs par 'dzin/ /
chos bzhi 'di dag nges par bstan byas na/ / mthu chen ldan zhing tshe rabs dran par 'gyur/ / bskal ba stong phrag bsam yas rjes su dran/ / rnam par 'dren pa'i mchog nyid rab tu thob/[568] / ces dang /

In the second chapter of Sutra Requested by Vimaladatta:
Receiving, reciting, and remembering the teachings, addressing others with words pleasing and attractive, tirelessly teaching the Dharma, and cultivating the signs of meditative concentration:
devoting yourself to these four practices develops power and the memory of previous lives, the memory of thousands of eons gone by, and the attainments of the supreme guide.[1021]

d.div: [568] sde dge_77_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ ca dri ma med kyis byin pas zhus pa theg pa chen po'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_256_na1
[1021] Vimaladattāparipṛcchā, Toh 77 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, ca, 256a1.

f.d:
dkon brtsegs 'od srung gis zhus pa'i 'dus pa las/
'od srung rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo gang la las 'jig rten kyi khams gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed rin po che sna bdun gyis yongs su gang bar byas te de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas rnams la sbyin pa byin pa dang / sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed rnams la de bzhin gshegs pa re re'i gtsug lag khang rin po che sna bdun las byas pa gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed brtsigs pa dang / sangs rgyas bcom ldan 'das gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed rnams las de bzhin gshegs pa re re'i nyan thos kyi dge 'dun dpag tu med pa dag la bskal pa gang+gA'i klung gi bye ma snyed du bde ba'i yo byad thams cad kyi rim gro byas pa dang / de bzhin gshegs pa yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa de dag gi mchod rten rin po che sna bdun la byas pa bas/ rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo dad pa dang ldan pa gzhan gang gi dkon cog brtsegs pa theg pa chen po'i chos kyi rnam grangs de las tshigs su bcad pa gcig tsam lung mnos te/ lung mnos nas kyang mi spong na/ de ni de bas kyang bsod nams ches mang du bskyed do/[569] / zhes dang /

In the Sutra Requested by Kāśyapa from the Heap of Jewels collection:
Kāśyapa, a son of the family or a daughter of the family may fill as many world realms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with the seven kinds of gems and give them as offerings to the tathāgata arhat fully enlightened and perfect buddhas. For as many bhagavān buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they may build temples of each tathāgata constructed from the seven types of precious gems and numbering as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges. For as many bhagavān buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they may serve and honor with every form of pleasure and comfort for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges the immeasurable number of communities of śrāvaka monks of each tathāgata. They may build shrines to all those tathāgatas who have passed into nirvana. But a son of the family or a daughter of the family filled with faith who takes a transmission of one verse from the Mahayana Heap of Jewels collection, and having taken it does not forsake it, generates merit far, far greater.[1022]

d.div: [569] sde dge_87_bka'/ dkon brtsegs/ cha'od srung gi le'u zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo/ bam po/ 2_shog_150_ba1
[1022] Kāśyapaparivarta, Toh 87 Kangyur, dkon brtsegs, cha, 150b1.

f.d:
sher phyin brgyad stong ba'i bsod nams rnam grangs kyi le'u las/
kau shi ka de bas de ltar rigs kyi bu'am/ rigs kyi bu mo gang la la zhig gis de bzhin gshegs pa dgra bcom pa yang dag par rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas yongs su mya ngan las 'das pa mchod pa'i phyir rin po che sna bdun gyi mchod rten de bzhin gshegs pa'i ring bsrel gyi snying po can bye ba du ma byed du bcug ste byas nas kyang des de la nam 'tsho'i bar du lha'i me tog dang / lha'i bdug pa dang / lha'i dri dang / lha'i phreng ba dang / lha'i byug pa dang / lha'i na bza' dang / lha'i gdugs dang / lha'i rgyal mtshan dang / lha'i dril bu dang / lha'i ba dan dag dang / kho ra khor yug tu mar me'i phreng ba dang / lha'i mchod pa rnam pa mang po dag gis mchod par byed de bkur stir byed/ bla mar byed/ rjod par byed/ mchod par byed/ ri mor byed/ bsnyen bkur byed na kau shi ka de ji snyam du sems ci rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo de de'i gzhi las bsod nams mang du bskyed dam/ brgya byin gyis gsol ba/ bcom ldan 'das mang ngo / / bde bar gshegs pa mang ngo / / bcom ldan 'das kyis bka' stsal pa/ kau shi ka de bas kyang rigs kyi bu dang rigs kyi bu mo 'dis bsod nams mang du bskyed de/ gang shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa 'di la mngon par dad de rtog cing mos la sems dang bas byang chub tu sems bskyed nas lhag pa'i bsam pas nyan pa dang 'dzin pa dang / 'chang ba dang / klog pa dang / kun chub par byed pa dang / rab tu 'don pa dang / ston pa dang / nye bar ston pa dang / lung 'bogs pa dang / kha ton du byed pa dang / gzhan dag la yang rgya cher yang dag par ston pa dang / 'di'i don rnam par 'grel ba dang / yid kyi rjes su rtog pa dang / ji lta bur grub pa'i shes rab kyis 'dir yongs su dpyod par byed pa dang sangs rgyas kyi tshul rgyun chad par ma gyur cig /dam pa'i chos nub par ma gyur cig / dam pa'i chos yun ring du gnas par bya ba dang / tshul dang ma bral bas byang chub sems dpa' sems dpa' chen po rnams la phan gdags pa sgrub par byas par 'gyur bar chung ngu na glegs bam du chud par byas te 'chang ngam/ bzhag la shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa de la me tog dang / bdug pa dang / dri dang / phreng ba dang / byug pa dang / phye ma dang / na bza' dang / gdugs dang / rgyal mtshan dang / dril bu dang / ba dan dang / kho ra khor yug tu mar me'i phreng ba dag dang / mchod pa rnam pa mang po dag gis mchod par byed/ de bkur stir byed/ bla mar byed/ brjod par byed/ mchod par byed/ ri mor byed/ bsnyen bkur byed na kau shi ka rigs kyi bu'am rigs kyi bu mo de nyid de bas ches bsod nams kyi phung po dpag tu med do/[570] / zhes dang /

In the Eight Thousand Perfection of Wisdom, in the Types of Merit chapter:
“Kauśika, more than that, a son of the family or a daughter of the family, in order to venerate the tathāgata arhat fully enlightened and perfect buddha who has passed into nirvana, may undertake the building of many millions of shrines built of the seven gems and containing tathāgata holy relics at its core. And once the shrines are constructed, that son or daughter of the family for the rest of his or her life may make many celestial offerings to those shrines consisting of celestial flowers, celestial incense, celestial perfumes, celestial garlands, celestial lotions, celestial silks, celestial parasols, celestial victory standards, celestial bells, and celestial banners, and ring the whole shrine with garlands of lamps. With such a host of celestial offerings, he or she may revere it, venerate it as a teacher, prostrate to it, make offerings to it, honor it, and worship it. Kauśika, what do you think? From this practice would that son of the family or a daughter of the family create much merit?” Indra replied, “Much merit, Bhagavān. Much merit, Sugata.” The Bhagavān continued, “Kauśika, this son of the family or daughter of the family will create merit much more than the previous. Yet he or she with great faith in this perfection of wisdom who thinks on it, who has great liking for it, who with joyful mind generates the bodhicitta and with an exceptional state of mind listens to it, takes it into their mind, keeps it in their mind, studies it, comprehends it, reads it, teaches it, teaches it well, transmits it, recites it, teaches it extensively to others, explains its meanings, contemplates it, and examines it with his or her development of wisdom; who works for the sacred Dharma to be preserved for a long time, praying, ‘May the way of the Buddha never cease; may the sacred Dharma not disappear’; who turns it, if small, into a bound volume of text and keeps it and preserves it so that it may prove beneficial for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, because it possesses the way of the Buddha; who offers all kinds of offerings to this perfection of wisdom such as flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, lotions, powders, silks, parasols, victory standards, bells, and banners, and encircles it with garlands of lamps; who reveres it, venerates it as a teacher, prostrates to it, makes offerings to it, honors it, and worships it; Kauśika, that son of the family or daughter of the family will create merit immeasurably greater.”[1023]

d.div: [570] sde dge_12_bka'/ sher phyin/ ka 'phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa brgyad stong pa/ gzhal du med pa'i yon tan 'dzin pa'i le'u gsum pa/ shog_35_na3_ma dper bsod nams rnam grangs kyi le'ur gsungs kyang le'u gsum par gsal/
[1023] Found in the Gaining Immeasurable Qualities chapter; Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā, chap. 3, Toh 12 Kangyur, sher phyin, ka, 35a3.

f.d:
paN chen zla ba mngon da_gas/
lung brgyud pa las bstan bcos kyi don rtogs pa thob pa'o/[571] / zhes dang / slob dpon blo brtan gyis dbus mtha'i 'grel par/
gzhan klog pa la nyan pa ni bsti stang du nyan pa'o/[572] / zhes dam pa'i chos thos pa'am nyan pa'am lung nod pa la phan yon mtha' yas par mdo sde rin po che du ma las 'byung ba ltar yin/

Pandit Candranandana says:
Through transmission of the teaching, understanding of the text is gained.[1024] Ācārya Sthiramati in his Commentary to Differentiating the Middle Way and the Extremes says:
When listening to others reading, listening with respect.[1025] Therefore, many precious sutras talk of the limitless benefits gained from studying, listening, or receiving transmissions of the sacred Dharma.

d.div: [571] sde dge_4312_bstan/ gso ba rig pa/ ko_zla ba mngon dga'/ yan lag brgyad pa'i snying po'i rnam par 'grel ba'i tshig gi don gyi zla zer/ shog_16_ba1
[572] sde dge_4032_bstan/ sems tsam/ bi_blo gros brtan pa/ dbus mtha' rnam 'byed 'grel bshad/ shog_294_na5
[1024] Moonlight: A Commentary on the Essence of Eight Branches, Toh 4312 Tengyur, gso rig, ko, 16b1.

f.d: gso ba rig pa'i slob dpon gyi mtshan nyid/
26. Qualities of a Master of Medicine

sgos bstan gso ba rig pa'i slob dpon nam sman pa'i mtshan nyid ni/ bshad rgyud le'u nyer gcig par/
de ltar gso bar byed pa'i gso ba po/ / bya ba byed pa sman pa'i gnas bstan pa/ / rgyu dang ngo bo nges tshig dbye ba dang / / las dang 'bras bu rnam pa drug gis bstan/[573] / zhes sman pa'i rgyu/ ngo bo/ nges tshig dbye ba/ las/ 'bras bu dang drug las/

On the characteristics of a master of medicine, or physician, the thirty-first[1026] chapter of the Explanatory Tantra from Four Tantras says:
The healer who heals, the doctor who practices: this section has the headings of causes, nature, etymology, types, function, and results.[1027] Therefore, there are six sections: the causes of a doctor, the nature, etymology, types, function, and results.

d.div: [573] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ bshad rgyud/ le'u/ 31_shog_95_yig phreng 16
[1026] Both editions of the text have “twenty-first chapter” but the passage is clearly from the thirty-first chapter.
[1027] Four Tantras, Explanatory Tantra, 31.95.16.

f.d: dang po rgyu la/

rgyu ni blo ldan bsam pa dkar ba dang / / dam tshig ldan zhing rnam pa bzo ba dang / / bya ba la brtson mi chos mkhas dang drug[574] / ces sman pa mkhas pa'i rgyu'i gtso bo ni chos rab tu rnam par 'byed pa'i blo gros dang ldan pa dang / sems can thams cad la phan par 'dod pa'i lhag pa'i bsam pa mchog tu dkar ba dang / 'chad par 'gyur ba'i dam tshig rnams dang ldan zhing / lus ngag yid gsum gyi rnam pa bzo ba dang / bya bar 'os pa'i bgyi ba dus las mi yol ba'i brtson 'grus dang / 'jig rten mi'i chos lugs la mkhas pa dang rnam pa drug gis mdor bstan nas/

The causes are intellect, a virtuous mind, keeping the pledges, well skilled, endeavor, wise in traditions of the world.[1028] The main causes for becoming a wise doctor are possessing an intelligent mind capable of discriminative analysis; possessing a supremely virtuous and exceptional state of mind that wishes to be of benefit to all living creatures; holding the pledges, which will be listed later; being manually, verbally, and mentally well skilled; endeavoring in the proper activities at the proper time; and being wise in the ways and customs of the world.

d.div: [574] sman gyi rgyud bzhi las/ bshad rgyud/ le'u/ 31_shog_95_yig phreng 17

f.d:
rgyas bshad/
