May the creator of this, endowed with the power of a specially virtuous mind, by the instincts planted, by teaching and composing, even by the flow of speech, be victorious in the battle over the hindering enemy hordes of those humans and nonhumans of poison minds.

d.div: [*] rdzas brjod bar gsal/

f.d: 'chi bdag ri bo bcom pa'i rdo rje'i tshe/ / mi shigs srog gi dngos po mthar phyin nas/ / bsams pa'i snod du yangs pa'i za ma tog / 'dod don nor gyis rtag tu gang bar shog /[*]

Having perfected the indestructible life force, whose vajra of longevity sunders the mountain of the lord of death, may the vast amulet within the container of my thoughts be forever full with the jewels of my wishes fulfilled.

d.div: [*] dbang po'i rdo rjes ri bo bcom pa'i gtam dang sbyar ba' ldin gzugs/

f.d: tshe 'di'i nyi ma nub pa'i phyi mar yang / / rnam 'dren gong ma lnga pas rdo rje'i gsung / / mi 'gyur tshems dkar 'dzum pas zhal 'chem bzhin/ / skye srid kun tu 'bral med rjes 'dzin cing / /[*]

In the future, too, after the sun of this life has set, may I be cared for without separation in every birth by the mighty guide, the fifth great emperor, as promised with his vajra words spoken with an unchanging white-toothed smile.

d.div: [*] yan lag gcig gzugs/

f.d: mthar thug byang chen spyod pa'i chu bo cher/ / lan brgyar bkrus pa'i sku bzhi'i rin chen mchog / rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas thob nas 'gro ba kun/ / 'dren pa'i ded dpon chen por bdag gyur cig /[*]

Finally, having become a fully enlightened buddha with the supreme gem of the four bodies, a result of being cleansed a hundred times in the mighty river of a bodhisattva’s deeds, may I become a great guide for all beings.

d.div: [*] ldan pa'i gnyis gzugs/

f.d: 'di nyid nyams bstar thos 'dzin 'dus pa'i grwa/ / 'chi med grub pa'i brda thabs lcags kyi rir/ / baiDUR+yar snang sman pa'i rgyal po yi/ / 'gro la phan pa'i tshe rig bdud rtsi'i rgyun/ /[*]

The monastic community practicing, studying, and memorizing this science, on Chakri hill symbolizing the creation of the nectar of immortality, from which flows the Āyurveda ambrosia stream of the king of medicine shining with beryl light,

d.div: [*] mchog nges bstan/

f.d: spro bas lta na sdug gi grong khyer dang / / ngos dang ngos bzhi gsum 'khor gyi 'dus pa'i khyad par las/ / gzhan du dbyer med ngo mtshar gso dpyad kyis/ / chos kun bdag med don kyang rig byed gling / /[*]
of sustenance to all living beings, the mountainsides and the environment inseparable from the beautiful-to-behold town of Sudarśana; by its practice of the wondrous science of medicine,

d.div: [*] phul byung gi rgyan gyi dbye ba'am nang gses/

f.d: thos bsam mu khyud rab yangs pa'i/ / 'khor lo bshad sgrub lte ba can/ / dug gsum gtum pa'i nad kyi dpung / / ma lus phye mar 'thag byed cing / /[*]
even though all dharmas have no self, may the wheels of this place of knowledge— with a hub of teaching and practice and vast rim of study and contemplation—

d.div: [*] bsdus gzugs la 'jigs rung nyams kyis spa ba/

f.d: rang gzhan don gnyis lhun grub pa'i/ / 'phrin las dbyar gyi chu klung bzhin/ / 'phel ba'i mthu des lus can kun/ / dus min 'chi las rgyal gyur cig /[*]

grind to dust the armies of the ferocious three poisons’ diseases; and with its spontaneous enlightened activities for self and others swelling like the cascade of summer rivers, may all beings gain victory over untimely death.

d.div: [*] chos dpe/

f.d: sbyar byang nang du khog 'bugs mang po'i rtsom tshul gsal bar bshad pa/
30. Previous Histories of Medicine

ces gso ba rig pa'i khog 'bugs kyi rim pa la cha lag gras su khog 'bugs khyung chen lding ba bod snga rabs kyis byas pa rgyud bzhi'i che ba/ ston pa rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas kyi chos 'khor sogs mdzad pa/ rig gnas kyi bshad pa/ gso rig bkar sgrub pa dang /

Earlier histories of medicine include: • Great Garuḍa History of Medicine[1180] found in the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts composed by earlier Tibetans, with sections on: the greatness of Four Tantras; deeds of our Teacher the fully enlightened Buddha, such as the turning of the wheels of Dharma; explanations of the major sciences; and the establishment of the science of medicine as the word of the Buddha.

d.div: [1180] Usually attributed to the later Yuthok Yönten Gönpo; first of the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts.

f.d: stong thun mdzes pa'i 'ja' ris 'go'i brjod bya gong dang mthun zhing dngos gzhi bshad rgyud kyi le'u'i sa bcad/
• Beautiful Rainbow Overview,[1181] also found in the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts, has an opening section similar to the above and a main body of text on the outlines of the Explanatory Tantra chapter.

d.div: [1181] Attributed to the later Yuthok.

f.d: brang ti dpal ldan 'tsho byed kyi shes bya rab gsal spyir dam pa rnams kyi 'gro ba rjes su bzung ba dang / bye brag bskal bzang gi sangs rgyas/ khyad par bdag cag gi ston pa byon tshul/ phan bde sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa dang bslab pa gsum gyi rnam gzhag /rig gnas spyi dngag so dpyad rgya bod du dar lugs/ rgyud bzhi sangs rgyas sman blas gsungs/ drang srong rnams kyis bsdus/ bai ros bod du bsgyur/ chos rgyal khri srong gi phyag tu phul/ des gter du sbas pa gra pa mngon shes kyis bton/ g.yu thog pas dar rgyas mdzad pa sogs bdag gi bla ma lnga pa chen po'i dgongs pa dang shas cher mthun pa/

• History of Medicine: Illumination of Knowledge by Drangti Palden Tsojé deals generally with the way great beings cared for living beings, and specifically on the coming of the buddhas of the good eon, with special reference to the appearance of our Teacher the Buddha; presentations of the doctrines of Buddha, bringer of happiness, and the three trainings; and the way the sciences and especially the science of medicine developed in India and Tibet. In his assertions that Four Tantras was taught by Medicine Buddha, compiled by the rishis, translated into Tibetan by Vairocana, presented to the Dharma king Trisong, who then concealed it as a treasure that was discovered by Drapa Ngönshé and disseminated by Yuthok, he is more or less in agreement with my guru the Great Fifth.

'phan yul gra sa ba tshogs gnyis rgya mtshos mdzad pa rgyud bzhi'i khog 'bugs baiDUR+ya'i chu rgyun gsang sngags snga 'gyur shas che ba'i gso dpyad skor spyi mthun dang / rgyud bzhi bka' 'khor lo bar pa'i dus a+yon gyi yul du gsungs pa/ sde snod gsum las 'dul bar gtogs tshul las gter mar mi bzhed pa/

• Stream of Beryl: A History of Four Tantras by Tsoknyi Gyatso of Phenyül Drosawa. Generally, this work is in keeping with most of the early-translation medical canon. It asserts Four Tantras to be the word of the Buddha taught in the land of Oḍḍiyāna during the middle turning of the wheel of Dharma, that it belongs to the Vinaya basket of the three scriptural divisions, but that it is not a revealed treasure.
byang pa lha'i btsun pa bkra shis dpal bzang gi bka' sgrub rnam nges dpag bsam ljon shing tshigs bcad ma rgyud gsungs sa rdo rje gdan du 'dod pa/
• Wish-Granting Tree: Verses on the Ascertainment of Four Tantras as Word of the Buddha, by Jangpa Lhatsün Tashi Palsang. He asserts that Four Tantras was taught in Bodhgāya.

de sras byang sman bsod nams ye shes rgyal mtshan gyis mdzad pa gso rig pad tshal 'byed pa'i nyi 'od sangs rgyas mtshan gyis mdzad pa gso rig pad tshal 'byed pa'i nyi 'od sangs rgyas kyi bstan pa spyi'i rnam gzhag /thun mong gso rig gi khog 'bugs/ thun mong min pa ston pa rdo rje 'chang gis a+yon du gsungs pa'i dpal ldan rgyud bzhi/ der yang bka' gter gnyis las byang lugs la gnyi ga'i chu bo 'dus tshul/

• Sunlight that Opens the Lotus Grove of the Science of Medicine[1182] by the Jang physician Sönam Yeshé Gyaltsen, son of the above. This work has a general presentation on the doctrines of the Buddha and a commonly accepted history of medicine, but with the unique assertions that Four Tantras was taught by our Teacher Vajradhara in the land of Oḍḍiyāna, that it is found in both Treasure and Transmission traditions, and that the two streams combined within the Jang tradition.

d.div: [1182] Also known as History of Medicine: Sun that Blossoms the White Lotus.

f.d: mi'i nyi ma yab sras dang bsod nams ye shes rgyal mtshan yan gyi rnam thar sogs byang lugs kyi rtsa ba lta bu/
• The biographies of the main physicians of the Jang tradition up to and including Minyima Thongwa Dönden, his son, and Sönam Yeshé Gyaltsen.

mi'i nyi ma yab sras kyi rjes su byung ba'i byang lugs pa zhig gis mdzad pa khog 'bugs rin chen sgron ma 'chad lugs kyi gzhi brang ti'i shes bya rab gsal dang cha 'dra zhing / rgyud bzhi a+yon gyi yul du rdo rje 'chang gis gsungs par bzhed pa

• Jeweled Lamp History of Medicine, composed by a Jang physician who came after Minyima Thongwa Dönden and his son, whose style of composition is similar to Drangti’s Illumination of Knowledge. He asserts that Four Tantras was taught in Oḍḍiyāna by Vajradhara.

mtsho smad mkhan chen ska ba shAkya dbang phyug gis mdzad pa legs bshad dngul dkar me long tshigs bcad ma don byings brang ti'i shes bya rab gsal dang byang pa bkra shis dpal bzang gi rnam nges dang mthun zhing / rgyud bzhi ston pas a+yon du gsungs/ drang srong yid las skyes la gtad/ de rjes ri bo gangs can du rdzu 'phrul gyis gshegs par ston pa'i zhal nas 'od zer 'phros pas yid las skyes byon/ 'tsho byed gzhon nur rgyud bzhi gsungs/ rnam sras kyi bu rgyal ba khyu mchog gam zhang blon rdo rje bdud 'dul rgyud bzhi'i srung mar bskos pa sogs zur khyad can/

• Mirror of White Silver: A Well-Composed History of Medicine in verse by Tsomé Khenchen Kawa Śākya Wangchuk. Its general message is in keeping with Drangti’s Illumination of Knowledge and Jangpa Tashi Palsang’s Ascertainment of Four Tantras. This work contains the particular assertions that Four Tantras was taught by our Teacher in Oḍḍiyāna and entrusted to Rishi Manasija, and that later our Teacher manifested miraculously in the Himalaya Mountains and emitted light from his mouth from which Manasija appeared. Four Tantras was then again taught to Kumāra Jivaka. Jinarṣabha or Rājānaka Vajra Mārajit, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, was appointed guardian of Four Tantras, and so on.

byar po paN chen rdo rje pha lam gyis mdzad pa khog 'bugs legs bshad gser gyi snye ma rig gnas lnga'i spyi bshad dang gso rig gsar rnying gnyis/ 'gyur byed/ dar lugs/ mdzad pa ste sa bcad lngar phye ba/ rgyud bzhi ston pas sman blar sprul nas a+yon du gsungs pa/ nag rtsis dang dkar yol sogs rgya gar du med pa'i dogs gcod 'khrul spong / g.yu thog pas ma tshang kha skong dang gab dkrugs gsal bar bzhed pa dang cha lag bco brgyad kyang mdzad tshul/

• Golden Sheaves: A Well-Composed History of Medicine, by Jarpo Panchen Dorjé Palam. This work has five major sections: a general description of the five sciences; early and later medical traditions; translations; dissemination; and the deeds of the great physicians. Asserting that Four Tantras was taught in Oḍḍiyāna by our Teacher manifested as Medicine Buddha, he refutes mistaken notions by resolving doubts concerning such things as porcelain bowls and elemental divination not existing in India. He also explains how Yuthok supplemented the tantra and clarified obscure and confusing sections, and how the Eighteen Auxiliary Texts were composed.

'brug pa pad+ma dkar pos mdzad pa rgyud bzhi'i bshad pa gzhan phan gyi gter dpal ldan rgyud bzhi 'o skol gyi ston pas 'tsho byed gzhon nu ri bo spos kyi ngad ldan du 'khrid nas de'i khengs pa bcag rjes slar zlos bur gsungs par 'dod pa dang /

• A Treasure for the Benefit of Others is an explanation of Four Tantras by Drukpa Pema Karpo, who asserts that our Teacher took Kumāra Jivaka to Gandhamārdana Mountain to break his pride, after which he taught him the glorious Four Tantras by having him repeat it back.

byang bdag chos rgyal dbang po'i sde dang dus mnyam du byung ba'i lha rje mi pham bzang pos byas pa khog 'bugs 'chi med phun tshogs lnga ldan rgyud bzhi ston pas rgya gar rdo rje gdan du gsungs shing snga 'gyur bdud rtsi yon tan gyi rgyud du gtogs par 'dod pa/

• History of Medicine: Endowed with the Five Ambrosia Perfections, by Lhajé Mipham Sangpo, a contemporary of the Jangdak Dharma king Wangpo Dé.[1183] He asserts that our Teacher taught Four Tantras in Bodhgāya in India, and that it is to be included in the Enlightened Qualities Ambrosia Tantras from the early-translation tradition.

d.div: [1183] To be identified with Jangdak Tashi Topgyal (1550–1603)

f.d: de dang don gcig pa la tshig sbyor rgyas pa bde chen chos 'khor gyi sman pa rat+na'i ming can gyis sbyar ba/
• A very similar but more extensive work was written by the Dechen Chökhor physician Ratna Mingchen.[1184]

d.div: [1184] This refers to his Well-Compiled History of Medicine.

f.d: skyid shod pa'i bla sman rin chen sdings sems dpa' chen po blo bzang rgya mtshos mdzad pa chos 'byung drang srong dgongs rgyan chos spyi dang rig gnas lnga khyad par gso rig byung tshul gyi khog 'bugs/ chos la nyan bshad bya ba/ rgyud bzhi bdag cag gi ston pas sman blar sprul nas a+yon du gsungs shing / bya ba'i rgyud du gtogs pa bai ros bod bsgyur ba dang gra pas gter nas bton pa sogs rje bla ma lnga pa'i dgongs bzhed dang shin tu mthun pa/

• Ornament to the Thoughts of the Rishis: A History of Medicine by the foremost Kyishö physician Rinchen Ding Bodhisattva Losang Gyatso. This is a history covering the Dharma in general and the five sciences, with particular reference to the origins of medical science. On the Dharma he covers listening and teaching. He asserts that Four Tantras was taught by our Teacher manifest as Medicine Buddha in the land of Oḍḍiyāna, that it is to be classified as action tantra, that it was translated into Tibetan by Vairocana and revealed by Drapa Ngönshé, and so on. In this he is very much in accord with the assertions of my master, the Great Fifth.

dgas po 'tsho byed karma kun phan pa'i slob ma zhig gis byas pa gso rig spyi'i rnam bshad rin chen bang mdzod rgyud bzhi bkar sgrubs shing / gter ma'i skabs spyi mthun dang / zur khyad ston pas rgyud gsungs pa drang srong rnams kyis bsdus/ mkha' 'gro'i gtso mo dpal ldan 'phreng bar bka' gtad gnyer du bskos par phyis g.yu thog pas zhus nas gtan la phab pa dang / sman bla dang shAkya thub gcig min chos rgyal srong btsan sgam po'i skyes rabs drangs nas dpyad pa sogs snga ma rnams dang cung mi 'dra ba /

• Treasury of Jewels: A General Explanation of the Science of Medicine by a disciple of the Dakpo physician Karma Künphen.[1185] His establishment of Four Tantras being the word of Buddha and a revealed treasure follow generally accepted assertions. His particular assertions are that Four Tantras was taught by our Teacher, compiled by the rishis, entrusted to Śrīmālā, chief of the ḍākinīs, from whom it was requested by Yuthok, who checked and settled various points of the text. He investigates the possibility that Śākyamuni Buddha and Medicine Buddha are not the same being, citing passages from Songtsen Gampo’s work on the lives of the Buddha. In this he differs a little from previous commentators.

d.div: [1185] Author’s name is not mentioned.

f.d: bla rta'am skyem pa tshe dbang gi spyi don legs bshad 'dod 'jor rgyud phyi nang gsang gsum du bzhed pa/
• Granting Wishes: Well-Explained Overview of Medicine by Lata or Kyempa Tsewang. In it he divides the tantra into outer, inner, and secret tantras.

byar po paN chen dang dus mtshungs tsam du byung ba zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'am legs bshad tshol gyis mdzad pa khog 'bugs gtan pa med pa'i mchod sbyin gyi sgo 'phar yangs po'am drang srong kun du dga' ba'i zlos gar du grags pa skabs dang po phyi gnod byed kyi rkyen yan lag dang bcas pa zhes 'jig rten gyi khams/ gnyis pa bcud/ gsum pa ston pa'i thugs bskyed nas bzung ste bstan pa spyi'i rnam gzhag nas nub pa'i bar/ bzhi pa gso dpyad lha yul dang mi yul du dar tshul/ lnga pa 'phags yul du ji ltar byung ba'i skor/ drug pa bod du dar tshul/ bdun pa gzhan lugs bkod nas de dgag pa/ brgyad pa gso dpyad kyi brjod don dngos bshad pa'i g.yu thog rnam thar dang de'i slob ma sum ston ye shes gzungs yan dang / de nas rang nyid bar 'chad rigs par rkyen ci 'dra zhig yin kyang sum ston gyi rtogs brjod kyang 'phror lus/ de nas tha ma nyams su len par sa dpyad gsum bkod de mdzad rtsis kyi rig gnas lnga bshad khyug tsam dang yi ge'i bshad pa zhig mdzad pa snod bcud sangs rgyas kyi mdzad pa sogs rang nyid kyis gang mthong gso dpyad chos 'byung du ngom pa lta bu'i tshig tshogs shin tu che/ de yang 'phror lus pa 'brug pa sangs rdor bas dbu ma'i skor la rje btsun btsong kha par dgag pa dang bcas 'phro rdzogs par 'thud pa/

• General Knowledge History: The Wide-Open Door to the Unending Ceremonial Offering, also known as Dance Delighting the Rishis by Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo or Lekshé Tsöl, who lived around the time of Jarpo Paṇchen. Its first chapter called “External Causes of Harm” together with related material deals with the external world. The second is on the internal world. The third is a general presentation of the doctrine, beginning with our Teacher’s development of bodhicitta up to the disappearance of his teachings. The fourth details how the science of medicine developed in the celestial and human worlds. The fifth explains how medicine appeared in the noble land of India. The sixth describes how it spread to Tibet. The seventh is a presentation and refutation of other traditions. The eighth is on the science of medicine itself and includes a biography of Yuthok and the beginnings of a biography of his disciple Sumtön Yeshé Sung. From then he should have continued with biographies up to his own time, but for some reason he did not, and the biography of Sumtön was left unfinished. The last chapter is on practice and was planned under three outlines, but contains only a very brief explanation of the five sciences plus a presentation on the alphabet. This whole work on the world, its inhabitants, the deeds of the Buddha, and so on is a very extensive collection of words presented in an affected and ostentatious manner by someone writing about medicine and history as he sees it. The unfinished sections were completed by Drukpa Sangyé Dorjé (1569–1645), who in a work on Madhyamaka refutes Jetsün Tsongkhapa.

tsha rong a yu'i ming can gyis 'go'i che brjod sogs shog bu bzhi lnga'i bar zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po'i drang srong kun tu dga' ba'i zlos gar ji bzhin bshus pa la/ de nas lhu mchongs dang / ma mchongs pa'i rigs tshig bshus kho na'i sum ston man khong rang gis byas 'dra pa'i chos 'byung bskal bzang bgrod pa'i myur lam du grags pa sogs dang /

• A work known as Quick Path for the Fortunate: A Religious History by someone called Tsarong Ayu.[1186] The first four or five pages on the praises and so forth are copied from Surkhar Lodrö Gyalpo’s Dance Delighting the Rishis. This is followed by connected and disconnected passages that have simply been copied from the above. From the biography of Sumtön onward, it seems like his own work.

d.div: [1186] According to Trinlé (p. 256) this work was composed by Namkha Delek, the uncle of Tsarong Chöjé Palden.

f.d: zur mkhar pa'i slob ma rud+d+ha a nan+das mdzad pa spyi don legs bshad rgya mtsho drang srong kun tu dga' ba'i zlos gar/ spyi don gyi tshul du khog phub pa/ tshig don gyi tshul du gzhung bshad pa ste sa bcad gnyis kyi dang po/ snod kyi 'jig rten/ bcud kyi sems can/ bskal bzang gi sangs rgyas/ bye brag bdag cag gi ston pa'i mdzad pa bcu gnyis/ bka' bsdu/ mdo sngags kyi chos bka' dang bstan bcos/ byams pa 'jig rten du 'byon tshul/ gso dpyad byung tshul/ bka' bstan gyi rnam gzhag /bod du sman dpyad dar ba dang sman pa'i ming / 'tsho byed nas g.yu thog yan gyi rnam thar sogs tshig tshogs shin tu che ba don gyi snying po blo gros rgyal po'i rjes su zhugs pa/

• Well-Explained Ocean-Like Overview: A Dance to Delight the Rishis by Ruddha Ānanda, a Sukhar disciple. It is arranged under two main headings: a history in the form of an overview and a commentary in the form of textual explanation. The first section deals with the external world, the inner world of sentient beings, the buddhas of the fortunate eon, in particular the twelve deeds of our Teacher, the councils, sutra and tantra from the Kangyur and Tengyur, how Maitreya will appear in the world, the origins of the science of medicine, a presentation on what is Kangyur and what is Tengyur, how medicine spread in Tibet, a materia medica, biographies of physicians from Jivaka to Yuthok, and so on. It is an extensive text that essentially follows Lodrö Gyalpo.

de mtshungs 'di tshun gyi zur lugs rnams rtsa rgyud kyi 'grel pa man ngag 'phreng ba zhes sogs rgyud g.yu thog pas gsungs par bzhed pa las gsungs sa shar phyogs baiDUR+ya snang gi zhing khams su 'dod pa sogs seng ge'i ya 'gal dang rnga mo'i ma 'gal mi 'grig bzhin du sbyar ba'i yig cha shin tu mang /

Similarly, there are many compositions in the Sur tradition following on from the above—such as the Root Tantra commentary, Garland of Core Instructions—that assert the tantra was the work of Yuthok, but like the misfit of an upper jaw of a lion and a lower jaw of a camel, assert that the place where the tantra was taught was the eastern land of Beryl Light, and so on.

tshig dang don gzhan 'khrul pa yod med cha ma things te rgyud ston pas gsungs pa sogs khog 'bugs la snga ba rin chen spungs pa/ cher rje zhig pos mdzad pa'i gsal byed sgron me/ 'phags ston shAkya mgon pos mdzad pa'i don gsal nyi ma'i 'od ldan/ sman ston gzhon nu rin chen gyis mdzad pa'i stong thun chen mo/ chos kyi dbang phyug gis mdzad pa'i don bzhi gsal sgron/ snye mo kun dga' don grub kyis mdzad pa'i lo rgyus 'byung tshul/ dpal mkha' spyod dbang pos mdzad pa'i khungs kyi yig chung sogs snga rabs kyi yig cha 'ga' yod par snang ste mig lam du ma chub/

Other histories that assert our Teacher to be the author of Four Tantras and so on—though whether they have other scribal or substantive errors is not determined—include the early work, Heap of Jewels; Illuminating Beacon by Chejé Shangtön Shikpo; Sunlight Clarity of Meaning by Phaktön Śākya Gönpo; Great Overview by Mentön Shönu Rinchen; Lamp Illuminating the Four Points by Nyemo Chökyi Wangchuk; Histories by Nyemo Künga Döndrup; and Short Work on Sources by Pal Khachö Wangpo. These and other early works I have not seen.

yan lag brgyad pa phyogs la zhang ston zhig pos mdzad pa'i rgyal mtshan rtser 'bar ston pa'i thugs bskyed tshogs bsags/ mdzad pa bcu gnyis/ chos 'khor bar pa'i skabs gcer mthong rig pa'i rgyud gsungs pa dang drang srong rnams kyi che brjod/ dpa' bo'i 'khrungs yul ga le mi 'grig pa rnams bsal ba sogs rnam thar/ snying po bsdus pa sogs brtsams pa/ de dag bod du 'gyur tshul/ bka' bstan gyi rnam gzhag /lugs bdun skor bzhi/ 'gyur dus gnyis rnams bshad pa/ de'i don bsdu byang pa lha btsun bkra shis dpal bzang gis mdzad pa rgyal mtshan rtser 'bar chung ba/ g.yu thog rgya mtshos mdzad pa'i khog 'bugs rig gnas spyi dang ston pa'i thugs bskyed mdzad pa'i skor rags tsam brjod nas/ dpa' bo'i rnam thar mi 'dra ba dang 'phags lha sogs spyi bzhin/ brgyad pa rtsoms tshul dang bcas pa/

Histories on the theme of Eight Branches include: • Compendium of Knowledge Blazing from Atop a Victory Banner, by Chejé Shangtön Shikpo, presents the development of the bodhi mind by our Teacher, his accumulation of merit, the twelve deeds, the teaching of the Clearly Seeing Knowledge Tantra during the second turning, the greatness of the rishis, a biography of Śūra identifying and refuting all wrong assertions about his birthplace, the composition of Essence of Eight Branches, its translation into Tibetan, a classification of word of Buddha and treatise, the seven medical traditions, the four medical literature collections, and the two translation periods. • A synthesis of the above, called Shorter Blazing from Atop a Victory Banner, by Lhatsün Tashi Palsang. • A medical history by Yuthok Gyatso beginning with a general presentation of the five sciences, an outline of our Teacher’s development of the bodhi mind and deeds, followed by an alternative biography of Śūra and the generally accepted biographies of Āryadeva and others, together with an account of how Essence of Eight Branches was composed.

gzhan yang mtha' bzhi shi la saM g+has mdzad pa'i bdud rtsi chu rgyun/ mi nyag mi bskyod rdo rjes mdzad pa'i khog 'bugs/ sgrung 'phreng / stong thun/ gdams pa sum cu pa'i khog 'bugs/ bdud rtsi snying po'i khog 'bugs rnams yod par snang ste mig lam du ma gyur/ phyis stag lo'i rig kun sogs chu bum yar 'jo mar 'jo'i tshul ji snyed dang bcas mchis kyang /

Stream of Ambrosia by Thazhi Śīlasaṃgha, a medical history by Minyak Mikyö Dorjé,[1187] Garland of Narrative, Overview, Thirty Instructions History,[1188] and Essence of Ambrosia History are also examples of histories, but I have not seen these. There are later works, such as Knowledge of All Sciences by Taktsang Lotsāwa Sherap Rinchen, that are all like filling a water pot from here, there, and everywhere.[1189] Despite the existence of all these histories,

d.div: [1187] Possibly his Accounts from History.
[1188] Possibly by Shangtön Siji Bar. See bibliography.
[1189] In other words, all the same (Prof. Losang Tenzin).

f.d: gso ba rig pa rang gi lus yongs su rdzogs pa zhig ma mthong bas/ khog 'bugs bgyid 'dun gyi 'go rang lo sum cu skor nas btsugs rung g.yeng ba dang bstan bcos gzhan je 'phel gyis sa bon tsam las lag tu ma lon pa/ rab byung bcu gnyis pa'i chu pho rta'i lo chu stod zla ba'i rgyal ba lhums su zhugs pa'i dus chen tshes bco lnga'i zla ba gro bzhin gyi 'grub sbyor nas dbu bzung /

I had not seen one that covered the whole body of the science of medicine, and thus the aspiration to write a medical history began when I was about thirty. However, distractions and an increase in the number of other compositions meant that it was not taken up and remained as an idea. The work was actually begun in the male water-horse year of the twelfth sixty-year cycle, in the aṣaḍha month on the fifteenth day, which is the day commemorating the Conqueror’s entry into the womb, and was also a Monday coinciding with an auspicious stellar combination of the śrāvana constellation.[1190]

d.div: [1190] The male water horse year of the twelfth sixty-year cycle is 1702, three years before he died. The aṣaḍha month is usually the sixth Tibetan month and corresponds to the months of July and August. The auspicious combination (’grub sbyor) of the śrāvana constellation is one seven auspicious stellar combinations matched to the days of the week. Therefore, śrāvana, which is also the name of a month, is always linked to a Monday.

f.d: khog 'bugs snga ma phal cher gyis snod bcud chags tshul/ ston pa'i thugs bskyed nas bzung ba'i mdzad pa/ rig gnas lnga'i bshad pa sogs rang gis gang mthong gso dpyad khog 'bugs su bkod pa shas che na'ang da lam de dag rnams gzhan du rgyas par bshad zin pas/

Most of the previous medical histories mainly include topics such as the formation of the world, the deeds of our Teacher beginning from his development of the bodhi mind, and explanations of the five sciences, all presented according to the authors’ experience. However, these days such topics have been fully explained elsewhere.
31. Colophon

gso ba rig pa rang nyid kyi skor rdzogs pa dang / de dag 'chad nyan nas brtsams pa'i slob dpon dang slob ma'i rnam gzhag / de'i slob dpon gyi 'phros don las gsum ldan rdo rje 'dzin pa'i skor dang / chos ston pa po'i rten gyi khyad par dang bcas dpal ldan gso ba rig pa'i khog 'bugs legs bshad baiDUR+ya'i me long drang srong dgyes pa'i dga' ston zhes bya ba 'di ni/

ji skad du/
'bri phag rgya ma g.ya' bzang pa/ / tshal pa bya yul lha 'brug gsum/ / bsdebs pas dbus kyi khri skor drug / mnga' ris la stod lho byang gnyis/ / chu mig zha lu byang 'brog bcas/ / bsdebs pas gtsang gi khri skor drug / gtsang min dbus min yar 'brog gi/ / khri skor dang bcas bcu gsum mo/ /[687] zhes pa'i nang tshan tshal pa khri skor gyi khongs su 'du ba dbu ru shod chen btsan po mnga' bdag gi yul stod smad gnyis su phye ba'i smad kyi char gtogs pa/ gnam 'khor lo rtsibs brgyad/ sa pad+ma 'dab brgyad/ logs bkra shis rtags brgyad kyis bskor ba'i dge bcu ma lus pa tshang ba'i nang nas/

Therefore, with a discussion of the complete literary corpus of the science of medicine, as well as a presentation on masters and students in terms of the study of this science, a section on the vajra-holding master possessing all three vows as an offshoot of the previous topic, and a section on the characteristics a teacher of the Dharma, this has been Mirror of Beryl: A Well-Explained History of the Glorious Science of Medicine, A Feast to Delight the Rishis. A manuscript says:
Driphak, Gyama, Yasang, Tsalpa, Jayül, and Lhadruk: these the six regions of Ü; Ngari, Latö, Lhojang, Chumik, Shalu, and Jangdrok: these the six regions of Tsang; and Yardrok, in neither Ü nor Tsang. These are the thirteen regions.[1191] In the Tsalpa region of these thirteen, containing the feudal district of Uru Shöchen[1192] divided into upper and lower regions, and of these two, in the lower region, where the sky hosts the Dharma wheel of eight spokes, the earth is laid with the eight petals of the lotus, and on all sides are paraded the eight auspicious symbols; it is a place where all ten virtues are complete.

d.div: [687] ji skad du/ 'bri phag rgya ma g.ya' bzang pa/ /zhes sogs kyi gzhung ngos 'dzin ma thub/

[1191] Untraced. These regions (khri skor, literally “myriarchy,” an area of around ten thousand households) were first drawn up by Drogön Chögyal Phakpa when he was appointed ruler of Tibet by Kublai Khan in the thirteenth century.
[1192] According to Dungkar (p. 1533), this is to be identified with upper and lower Kyi (skyid stod skyid smad).

f.d: nang dpal 'khor lo sdom pa'i pho brang dngos dang phyi khams gsum ma lus khyab pa'i gdugs/ bkra shis g.yas su 'khyil ba'i dung dkar/ phyogs las rnam par rgyal ba'i rgyal mtshan gsum gyi rang byon chu zla ltar gsal ba dang shin tu nye ba'i rgyab ri bzang pos skyabs shing / nyang ting 'dzin bzang po'i bran du gyur pa'i yul grong sde'i stod smad gnyis kyi phyi ma'i char mtshur ston dbang gi rgyal po'i rus las chad pa yin zhes dpya khral gyis 'tsho ba'i rigs su skyes pa/

There under the protection of the nearby backdrop of wonderful mountains, whose interior contains the actual palace of Śrī Cakrasaṃvara and whose exterior hosts a parasol covering the three realms, an auspicious clockwise white conch, and a banner of victory in all directions—all three self-arising phenomena as clear as the moon’s reflection in water—in Nyang Dren Drongmé—meaning the area of those who were serfs (dren) to Nyang Tingsin, in the lower (drongmé) of the two upper and lower communities—I was born into a family that made its living by collecting taxes and was descended, it is said, from Tsurtön Wangi Gyalpo.[1193] From the moment of my birth,

d.div: [1193] An eleventh-century disciple of Marpa Lotsāwa.

f.d: yab rje kun mkhyen rgyal ba'i dbang po lnga pa chen pos btsas ma thag nas sri'u gso ba'i tshul du brtse bas bskyangs shing / phyi ltar chos srid yongs su rdzogs pa stsal ba'am dbang bskur/ nang ltar bka' gter gsang rgya dang bcas pa las lha sras rgyal po'i skye ba zhig 'byung bar ngos 'dzin dang / gsang ba yang gsang de kho nyid kyi dkyil 'khor du mar dbang bzhi rdzogs par stsal te rdo rje slob dpon chen po la mnga' gsol ba sogs tshig tsam ma yin pa'i bka' drin gyis 'tsho ba/

I was lovingly cared for as a parent would a child by my father-like lord and master, the all-knowing, mighty king of kings, the Great Fifth. Externally, he conferred or granted me religious and secular rule in its entirety; internally, he recognized me from the Oral and Treasure traditions and secret documents as an incarnation of an earlier, celestially descended king; secretly, he conferred on me completely numerous four-empowerment initiations into highly secret mandalas of suchness and enthroned me as a vajra master, thereby caring for me in these and other ways with a kindness that went beyond mere words.

legs par sbyar ba saM skr-i ta'i skad du bu d+d+ha.a p+ti ste ri kha ba can gyi ljongs su sangs rgyas rgya mtsho/ byA ka ra Na'i gtsug lag tu thos pa'i kun bshad kyi ming dbyangs can dgyes pa'i blo ldan gdong drug bsnyems pa'i lang tsho gsar pas

I, who am known as Buddha Apti[1194] in the well-constructed language of Sanskrit and as Sangyé Gyatso in the language of this land of snow, was awarded the Explainer of All title for competence in the Vyākaraṇa[1195] texts with the names One with the Intelligence Pleasing Sarasvatī and One with the Newfound Youth of Proud Ṣaṇmukha.

d.div: [1194] Although the root ap is usually translated as “water,” rather than “ocean.”
[1195] Vyākaraṇa is the study of Sanskrit grammar. Explainer of All (kun bshad) is a title given to those competent in their studies of grammar.

f.d: rang lo bcu phrag lnga dang nyag ma gcig dang / rgyal ba don kun grub pa ser skya'i grong khyer du bltams pa'i tshul bstan nas bgrang bya gnyis stong drug brgya re gsum/ rtsA can du gzugs sku'i bkod pa bsdus nas nyis stong lnga brgya gya gsum rnams 'das pa/ sgrub pa'i tshul khrims kyi bslab pa'i dus/ dus kyi 'khor lo'i rtsod ldan 'char nas lo brgya dang lnga song ba/ drag po'i 'khor los kla klo bcom nas rdzogs ldan 'char ba la bdun brgya nyer gcig yod pa/ legs par sbyar ba lha'i skad du b+hAnu/ stod 'grel ba nyi ma/ ma hA tsi na'i skad gu'i wu'i/ ljongs 'dir dbang thang dang bstun pa'i chu mo lug / 'byung ba bzhi ldan/ zla ba'i klungs kyi lo'i nyin mor byed pa 'khrig pa'i khyim du spyod cing / dus 'khor ba'i dbyar 'bring rags pa snon gyis nya ba/ spor thang ba'i ston ra lcags sprel che ba'i dkar phyogs kyi rgyal ba gsum pa/ dus 'khor ba'i dbyangs ra/ gsal byed ga / 'byung ba me/ 'dod yon ro/ dbyangs 'char ba'i dbyangs u/ gsal byed kha/ 'byung ba me/ 'dod yon gzugs/ gnyi ga mthun pa'i dar gud lang tsho/ res gza' zla ba'i bu stobs dang ldan pa/ las skar mdza' lha'i lha mo dang dga' mgur spyod pa'i 'chi med 'grub pa'i sbyor ba/ 'phrod gzhon nu/ khams sbyor lang tsho/ 'phrod chung 'phel nyi/ sbyor ba grub bya/ byed pa til brdungs/ rten 'brel dus 'khor ba'i sred pa/ dbyangs 'char ba'i 'du byed/ nyi ma me stag /tshes spar li dang / sme ba bzhi ljang rnams kyi gza' tshes skar sbyor dge zhing rta bdun gyi dbang po go la'i khyim nas lho bgrod du phyogs pa'i nyin gyi dus nam langs phyi cha sa yos/ dus spar khon/ dus sme lnga ser/ ta t+kAl la ka rka Ta/ phyed lha rags pa brtan pa/ gza' phur bu ste bdud rtsi'i thun/ zla snyigs rnam dag legs so 'char ba'i dus dge ba'i thog /

In my fiftieth year plus one, 2,663 years after the Conqueror Siddhārtha, accomplisher of all, manifested his birth in the town of Kapilavastu, 2,583 years after he withdrew his physical form in Kuśinagarī, in the era of the practice of ethics, 105 years after the Kālacakra kaliyuga era of troubles began, 721 years before the caturyuga era of completion that dawns after Rudracakrin has destroyed the barbarians; in the year known as bhānu in the celestial language of Sanskrit or “sun” (sūrya) according to the Cakrasaṃvara Commentary,[1196] as gei wei in the language of Greater China, in this land as the female sheep year[1197] of the water element in harmony with the wangthang power element—a year possessed of four elements, a moon-element year with the sun occupying the mansion of Gemini—in the Jyeṣṭha month and the middle summer month according to Kālacakra coarse astrology, in the early autumn month and greater iron-monkey month according to Chinese Porthang divination, on the third Victory lunar day[1198] of the bright side or waxing phase whose Kālacakra Tantra vowel is ṛ, consonant ga, element fire, and sensory pleasure taste; whose Arising Letters Tantra vowel is u, consonant kha, element fire, and sensory pleasure is form; whose development, in common with both traditions, is that of the youth; whose day of the seven-planet week is the powerful Son of the Moon (Wednesday) joined in nuptial joy with the activity lunar-mansion goddess Anurādhā[1199] to form the yoga of ambrosia joy; whose correspondence is kumara, whose element combination is that of the youth, whose lesser correspondence is Increase of the Day, whose astrological yoga is sādhya, whose karaṇa sector is taitila, whose link from the twelve links of dependent origination is “craving” according to the Kālacakra Tantra and “compositional factors” according to Arising Letters Tantra, whose sun is the fire tiger,[1200] whose date parkha trigram is li, and whose date mewa is four and green: on this day when planets, date, and constellations are in auspicious combination, and when the lord of the seven horses is moving through the houses of the gola firmament on his southern passage, at the earth-rabbit hour of the second half of dawn, when the time parkha is kun, the time mewa is five and yellow, when the tatkāla ascendant is Cancer, the semigod star of coarse calculation is sthāvara, at the Jupiter ambrosia period, when the true moon remainder is “excellence,” at this virtuous hour, I have completed this work.[1201]

d.div: [1196] Vajrapāṇi, Cakrasaṃvara Commentary, Toh 1402, rgyud ’grel, ba. Commentary on the first fifty chapters of the Shorter Cakrasaṃvara; one of the Three Bodhisattva Commentaries.
[1197] This is 1703. Therefore, he completed this work in a year. With this date as a fixed reference, the other dates mentioned can be calculated; e.g., Rudracakrin’s coming in 2424.

[1198] This is the thirteenth lunar day. The thirty days of the month share five names between them, each repeated six times. Victory (rgyal ba) is third in the list, and so its third occurrence is on the thirteenth.
[1199] Anurādhā is the fifteenth lunar mansion.
[1200] Nyi ma me stag. I am not sure what this refers to.
[1201] I have sought to understand these astrological terms through research and questioning scholars, but it may be that some are translated literally without depth of understanding.

f.d: rang lo lnga bcu phan du ngag dpod kyi rigs dag sgra 'chol bas 'dri mis ji bzhin ma go ba'i skyon dang bcas rtsom pa mtha' dag yi ge zhes kyang sug bris kho na yin rung / lnga bcu nas 'dri ba'i lcogs pa'ang zhan/ snga dgongs la sogs rab rib kyis phra ba rnams mthong ba yang dka' ba sogs kyis sug bris ma thub pas/ yi ge pa cha dkar ba pad+ma bsod nams kyis bgyis pa phyogs dus kun tu bkra shis par gyur cig/ //

Up until the age of fifty, all my compositions, even the most modest of letters, were written in my own hand partially because dictation meant that my speech defect caused scribes to hear incorrectly, leading to mistakes. However, since the age of fifty my ability to write by hand has declined, and in the mornings and evenings poor sight has made it difficult to see clearly. Therefore, the task of writing has been undertaken by the scribe Pema Sönam of Chakar. May there be fortune and prosperity at all times and in all places.
